I should say this first, I only recommend this if you can get it on sale.
Evoland 2 like its predecessor goes for a nostalgia-vibe with its old-school RPG mechanics and references, but instead of 'upgrading' the game like the first one did this time around you travel to different eras in time which are themed along the lines of classic games.
Since they couldn't just repeat the first game this time around they also mixed up the gameplay formula, so instead of just RPG segments there are also shoot 'em up, endless runner and such segments.
These segments are unskippable, so if like me you dislike these other genres and bought the game because you like RPGs you're SOL.
There are also a couple of unskippable minigames based on retro concepts and a couple of (RPG) segments that use unfortunate and annoying mechanics that go on too long.
If you can get it on sale and you accept these flaws (or if you don't consider them flaws) it's still a fun and charming adventure.

I really like Screeps. A game you play almost entirely through programming?! Awesome :D Test your programming skills, learn a ton, make a mistake that destroys your colony, rebuild even stronger... it's really cool. And it's easy to use your own IDE, sync through GitHub, or program via the Screeps interface that is complete with memory watching as well! And the API documentation is plenty sufficient.
With that said, the downsides: I don't like JavaScript... I've always used C#- it's object oriented, typed, and compiled... and so I've had a *lot* of hangups with JavaScript since it's not object oriented, not explicitly typed, and since it's run-time scripting. Even though JavaScript is a huge turn-off for me (as are a lot of languages that run the web- PHP, PERL, etc), I have to say the game is a fantastic sandbox.
10/10 would accidentally destroy my colony with a bug in the code just to re-do it all over again!

That feeling when your little autonomous minions are dancing along to a carefully ochestrated sontata you've composed. That feeling when you go to bed knowing your farm is in good automated hands, and wake up to realize you were right. That feeling when you've been at work all day and come home to a wall of script errors because you're you, and that's the kinds of things you're likely to do as a human (and you're inability to catch an improperly cased variable name will be the death of you).
I write code all day for a living. The last thing I thought I wanted to was to come home and write more code as a way to "unwind". But honestly, that's exactly what this gives. Yes, it's writing code. Yes, it requires you to think about and architect CLEAN, reusable, and solid code, which is stressful and difficult. But some how, for some reason, once you've completed that harvester behavior refactor you've been working on, it all becomes worth it when you look at the little moving dot and say "Yes, little one. THAT is what I wanted you to do."
I can assert that I've only barely scratched the surface of what the full long-term game is going to feel like, but I've already found myself, multiple times, saying "I can't believe a game like this exists." I'm truly shocked and elated that there is actually a way to unwind AND code at the same time. It has been an absolute delight to bring my little minions to life and automate their existence.
I've been writing JavaScript for a couple years now. It's never been my main toolkit, but as a Web Engineer it certainly does pop up a lot. So an excercise that forces you to think in clean, modular, and maintainable JS that accounts for things that may or may not happen is a godsend. Bonus points for being super fun and relaxing, too!
Cannot recommend this enough. If you're a hardcore JavaScript guy/gal, come in here and rule the world. If you're a mid-level like myself, you'll find ample fun and enjoyment out of this game. If you're completely new, come get wreckt! Because you will... at first. But if you can read the docs, find all the online help available for this game, and piece it all together in a way that works, you'll have a blast and learn more than you ever thought you could from a game.
10/10 would automate existence again

First of all, if you think this game will teach you to program think again.  You need to know how to program before playing this game because if you're struggling with that alone you'll never get anywhere.  You need to understand pathfinding, dependency graphs, etc, beyond just programming.
It's also way too much work for somebody who has a life.  I'm a full time software developer and even with my experience there's just too much work to do.  Things break easily unattended so it takes a lot of time tweaking your software to handle various situations.  You can clone somebody else's repo (or copy paste somebody else's code) but that's not very fun and still needs close monitoring.
It may be feasible if a few developers worked together optimizing the software for a single account.  But even then, I do this all day at my job.  This isn't a very fun "game".  It's work.
This is an early access game and is missing the following as of right now:
* No debugger capabilities (even in simulator)
* Poor API documentation
* API objects aren't unit testable (no dependency injection)
* software syncing UX is poor
* simulator state can't be saved

Blackguards is a turn based RPG game. A very difficult, very unforgiving one. The backbone of the game is made up by the Dark Eye system, a system similar to DnD and (from what I understand) very popular in Germany. I've played  alot of DnD, and read a lot about the game's system and guides before playing Blackguards, but didn't really feel like it made much of a difference. The RNG is very unforgiving, in that if your characters' builds are not razor optimized, you will have an incredibly difficult time with the game, more than it already is. I STRONGLY suggest looking at character guides and just following one to the T in terms of what are good skills, what are must haves, where to put your points, and the like, as it is very easy to render a character effectively useless in a battle as you continue to invest points in skills.
Damage and  status efects stay with characters after fights, and consumables are in relatively short supply, meaning strings of fights become very dicey. Magic casting runs off of the same RNG as the melee attacks do, so it's possible to cast spells, have them fizzle entirely, but still lose mana - very frustrating since you then need to use one of your limited resources in money or mana potions to get them back to the point to where they can even begin to be useful again - or so you hope.
These difficulties in learning the games system will unfortunately turn people away from what is a very enjoyable and very think-y turn based combat game. Almost every single individual map is handcrafted and presents new challenges to the party, and the game often forces you to use various party members in different compositions: Aggravating if you chose to focus on one in particular, but from a game design standpoint, if executed well lets you offer all sorts of new challenges. The problem lies in the game's very punishing permanent levellnig system. With no way to undo bad choices and mistakes (and don't be fooled: there ARE mistakes and just bad choices you can make in character builds), you might be stuck at a fight you now have no way of winning, fifteen hours into the campaign.
The story is not particularly interesting, in my opinion, but I have played  alot of very intensely narrative focused games so I admit my bar may be set a little bit high. The characters are interesting, and it's fun to see a story told from the perspective of sly ne'er-do-wells rather than heroic caricatures. Unfortunately, I never really felt like anything groundbreaking or innovative was really done with the characters or situations they could have used, and instead it just sort of became background set up fora relatively generic story that could have been done with the more "Usual Suspects" of heroic characters.
Ironically, I garnered the most fun from the game when my frustration was at its peak and I simply used Cheat Engine to level my characters to the max immediately, giving myself essentially unlimited skill points and ability points to make the characters I actually wanted to make. Due to the punishing RNG and the thoughtful, puzzle-y situations the game likes to put you in, in every single combat, this takes less of the challenge out of the game than you might immediately think (it DOES make it much easier, of course.). Your mileage may vary, but for someone that wants to experience the combat system and the story, i would actually recommend just cheat engining your characters to max level and giving them all the skills you want them to have, and then enjoy using them in the varied combat situations the games put you in.
In the end, I give the game a thumbs down - but only because I think the game's opaqueness and difficulty in learning the system is such a a negative that many people will feel immediately turned off by a combinatioin of that and the game's innate difficulty that they'll be unable to enjoy the game for its positive sides.

It may seem like a generic FPS, having the most generic title ever. The single player is your typical Warhammer 40k scenario, Orkz attack a planet, SM have to stop them.
The multiplayer (team death match/capture the point) was some of the most fun I had on release, but due to the lack of dedicated servers and fast progression the player base dwindled quickly. If you weren't there went it first released, then you missed out on the games glory days.
The wave-based mode is enjoyable for a short time. If you consider picking this up, do it for the single player campaign, and for some 4 player horde type multiplayer.

Another example of a great (in places) game putting off players do to poor presentation of core game mechanics to player base / very poor ingame feedback.
I don't know what the developers were aiming for with the way the final product turned out (it is NOT due to technical ineptitude or lack of creative ability - the game mechanics are consistent with its defined rule set, full of intelligent puzzles and reasonably bug free).
The lack of transparency (markedly unsound - it badly hurts their sales numbers by quickly alienating the "shallower" player base. ) seems to be caused largely due to intended design. Maybe TDE (dark eye) game rules are were so second nature to the developers they coudn't see how difficult it will be for "foreigners" to make sense of their otherwise "working within parameters" product.
It almost like the game is made by aliens strangers to earth based game interface progression in the last 20 years. Maybe this what a game made by programmers/designers that don't play computer games should be expected to turn out (speculation).
cons
-very limited ruleset/mecanics exposition and ingame feedback (steam guides mostly fixes this)
-alien game interface: bits of relevant information are scattered all over the place (need to navigate 5-6 "screens" to gather basic info about a character - a feat the good modern games can achieve in 1-2 "screens" with overwelmingly superior amount of detail - wastes player time, hurts immersion)
-stoneage like combat log functionality (mising a lot game critical events and the ones presented lack detail)
-rough spell/ weapon class balance
-nearly impossible to read opponent's percentage based resists ( some even have vulnerabilities to certain damage types but it is extremely hard to tell due to the hidden resist stats , RNG damage component and poor combat log features)
-liniar story, set drops(limited itemisation issues) and poor spell/abilities balance (few powerbuilds builds) leads to poor replayability value. (maybe the obfuscation was intended to mask/hide the poor balance to the players - or the poor balance is the result of the obfuscation making it hard for the devs to see the problems ?)
pros
-the community with a bit of help from developers managed to unwind most of the critical game mechanics (check out the game's player guides section)
-the game is well oiled (very few bugs), the creative people did great - very high intelligent puzzle combat variation(enjoyable once you start grasping the game mechanics).

I still recommend this game despite its numerous flaws because it has the capability to enthral players for hours, but wait for significant special offer discounts .

An imperial forge-world, where machines of war are made, has been invaded by the Ork scum, and it falls on the shoulders of you, a heroic space marine captain, to slaughter them all and save the day.  But wait!  Chaos!
First person linear story shooter, with a multiplayer extension.
The campaign is both fun and involving, no matter if you're familiar to the setting or not.  The story carries a couple of predictable twists, but also a couple of unpredictable ones also,
.  A worthwhile multiplayer experience lets you continue the enjoyment after the game has been completed.
The weapons are simple to master for most part, and enemies are both varied and run with a decent AI.  The graphics are very high-standard, from environmental detail to droplets and giblets as you stomp on an orc's head, to smoke coming off the weapon.  Sound quality is quite well-rounded, giving in-game speech without being too overwhelming, and without drowning the player in explosion noises.
A very polished piece of work.

This much-anticipated sequel to To the Moon didn’t get me quite as emotional as the first game, but the story it tells is complex and engaging. The game deals in themes about the relationships between imagination, memory, and reality, and how we are shaped by our memories, and the banter between protagonists Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts remains as fun as ever. I saw the game’s twist coming well in advance, but was still caught off guard by the implications and consequences of that twist, culminating beautifully in the game’s ending, which is accompanied by another fantastic and tear-inducing song from Laura Shigihara. Even just writing and thinking about Finding Paradise right now is making me a little misty-eyed again. I played the entire thing through in one sitting last night as of this writing, and I already can’t wait for To the Moon 3.

Finding Paradise had the immense challenge of living up to its critically acclaimed predecessor To the Moon... AND IT MET IT FULL ON! It managed to stay true to the former game's humor and style while telling an entierly different story that most certainly PUNCHED ME IN THE EMOTIONAL GUT.
All poor attempts at being funny aside, if you enjoyed To the Moon (which while not entirely necessary to play for this, is still VERY highly recommended and enhances this game's experience) then you will defintely enjoy Finding Paradise.

I really don't like this game. At first, it's a little interesting, it talks about how you were betrayed by your friends,going back to get revenge, then it starts you on some tutorial levels, that basically show you that you can change the background by pressing z/x/c, and if the background matches the color of an object, the object disappears. For me, it just got worse from there. The double jump is much similar to if you had rocket boots - unlike most game where its the same height as the normal jump or less, this one is about 5 times bigger, and can kill you because you can reach off-screen areas with it (like spikes that you didn't know were there). The worst part for me was how if you get hurt in any way, there's about a 15 second long animation just for you getting back up, and its really bad, too, because you're flashing the entire time so it looks really chopped up. And when every other object can hurt you, it makes this game really boring. Another thing I found annoying was how bad the controls are. The controls in this game are insanely clunky, the color buttons can't be spammed the way they SHOULD BE, and the movement buttons just don't give you the feeling of truely being able to sontrol your character, which, imo, should be top priority in any platformer, because in platformers, death is very frustrating, but whats much, much more frustrating is when the player dies because the controls were poorly done. On top of that, this game fails to keep me interested. It gives you the same 5 problems over and over, just in a different order. Honestly, I'm really disappointed, this is the kind of game I would've expected from a Game Boy Color, not Steam.

This is my, perhaps, final review of this game - I followed it from the very start, until this unification to one, complete and even better game.
It's an aRPG, in the full meaning of what aRPG is, and what it should be like. It resembles, reasonably closely, to Diablo 2. It offers a classic hack'n'slash experience, levelling, item hunt and character progression. In addition to this, rather uncommon to the genre, story is excellent, and game could even be played as an adventure. Ridiculously funny and witty, game follows a number of cliches - protagonist is a Monster Hunter, which (ever accompanied by his sharp-witted and even sharper-tongued ghost companion Katarina), comes to a fictional land of Borgovia, to rid it of a great evil - a group of scientist who took over the land after his father defeated ruling Vampire Princes. But the story just starts to unroll...
The game was, and still is, sold in three different installment (and combination thereof) - The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing 1, 2 and 3. If you have *all* three games, in any combination (bought on Steam, than you own the game already - similar being true for GoG - or combination of both, this was said by developers, but I cannot confirm it). If you have a part(s) missing, you can buy them for normal price, the game will work - no need to buy what you have already...
A long time ago, a group of (somewhat) young, but lavishly talented, programmers (we didn't have 'devs' then) made Diablo 1, which basically redefined the aRPG genre. Few years later, Diablo 2 was made, and it remained the best aRPG ever made (with its expansion LoD).
Many years later, a group of /skips the comments/ young and /skips the comments/ tried to redefine the genre, with much waited, but largerly disappointing /skips the game name/, which lacked way too much of the content, charm, and shall we say 'magic' of the genre foundation (D2).
About the same time, another group of (mostly) young programmers and artists from the Hungarian-based independent studio NeoCore made Van Helsing 1, the game which resembled much most closely, but wasn't a carbon-copy of already named 'father of the genre'. The game grew. New classes were added. The sequels followed each year. Some were slightly disappoining (VH3) - but it shouldn't influence buyers decision. Now, some 5 month after VH3 - we get Van Helsing - Final Cut, which is a fusion of all three games.
But it's not all - the initial game is improved in many, many ways, graphics are better (they were already on the par with that unnamed AAA+ title), interface - which was in true 'father D2' style and good enough already is improved further, and initial flaws of previous titles are corrected.
There is an online component (though the game can be played in offline mode, a feature that doesn't mean so much nowadays, but still) - namely Multiplayer and Scenarios, which represent endgame. The team announced that each day there will be a special, daily, scenario (one can accumulate 5 of those, so no need to wait fanatically each day) and special weekend events until the end of the year, and if there is interest - throughout whole 2016. Since release day was delayed for more than a month, I suspect that guaranteed daily events time will be prolonged...
- There are six classes, losely divided in melee, ranged and magic users (and combinations)
- There are eight starting skills, each of which can be levelled to level 10, with possiblity to add powerups and special 'upgrades'
- At character level 20, each of starting skills unlocks Tier 2 skill (which isn't necessarily, just upgraded version of previous, often it is a completely different skill, and mostly is just loosely grouped with the rest). Level 40 unlock last tier of skills, and final skill in 'tree' can be modified to a substantial degree to suit players preferences
- Replayability is VERY high - each character can be played in several ways and playstyles, and there are 6 of with 24 skills each...
- Not to forget, a passive skills (Auras) are pressent too, and are not the same for each character (though some do overlap)
- Each character has an unique addition - for instance, one of them has a 'weapon platform', a flying contraption that follows player around and can be modified and improved in several ways, another is a master of stealth...
- Story is funny and witty and writting surpasses by far what player normally expects from a computer game. I've heard that head writter is a publisher author, and it shows well
- Gameplay is linear and quests are rather typical for the genre (bring *that*, kill *it*, free *her*), but clever writing parodies and ridicules these cliches, which I find appealing
- UI is excellent - casual player can play with a hand on the mouse and a hamburger in the other, while a micro-fanatic can use keyboard shortcuts in a way which surpassed D2 (there - I said it. Configurability of the UI is better). Controller is also supported, but I hate those things and can't say anything about how well it works, only that I've *heard* it's fine
- Voice acting is nothing short of SPECTACULAR (especially compared to some other games, who relies not on striking voices of actors, but rather on effects, which is not remotely closely) - this is a *very* important feature to me
[This is one of the few games where I listen to the dialogues I've heard tens of times already - listen to the Prisoner7 striking voice and excellent... wording, and compare it to a certain overweight demon found with heavily processed voice and a childish master-plan... I'll put a youtube link with Prisoner7 - this link caused problem in posting the review. I put it in a comment below. - Rest of the character are also voiced in similar quality, but this one is my favourite]
- Graphics are worthy of an AAA title, and team showed unique creativity in making unique mixture of Slavic-mythology and Steampunk
- Enemies and terrain are designed masterfully, fully comparable to, for instance, Bethsheda games (and surpassing currently available aRPGs by a large margin - yet one additional feature player doesn't expect when buying hack'n'slash'). See some beautiful footage, the link I posted previously shows in in general, though the game itself isn't normally so much interrupted by a cut-scenes - which are good, but don't get the wrong impression that the game will be interrupted every 20 seconds)
- Companion, Lady Katarina is an immortal ghost, which adds much to the gameplay diversity - she has her own skills and attributes, can do tiresome tasks like selling items, or helping out player as melee, ranged and special 'ghost form' (where she cannot attack or be attacked, but boosts player attributes)
- Kataring has a rather sharp tongue and is cynical both to Van Helsing and the events in the game. She also has deep background story, which is unfolded during the game
I was a beta tester for all three games, this one included. I have invested many hours in this game(s) and regret none of it. I also helped game financially, by buying it as the gift for friends who like and play aRPG. I am happy that I did, because small independant studios couldn't otherwise afford to develop a game for years, as the major studios do. The result is here, and it's questionable if it would be anything, if there wasn't players who supported it. ALWAYS support what you like, or you won't get it...

Do you like games like Path of Exile or Diablo 3?
Then you'll like this game. It's similar in many aspects and if you really enjoy these type of games, you'll enjoy this one. It's got a pretty interesting story. Has some good parts, some funny, etc. The classes are pretty interesting. If you've played Diablo 2 or PoE, you'll see some similar themes. Such as when I was playing the engineer (you build these robotic spider things as pets), it reminded me a bit of the Druid summoner in D2. I like most of the classes and their design.
The game offers a follower system, just like D3/D2. You upgrade it, choose what skills it can get, which combat roles it fills, etc. Pretty standard, but a good aspect of the game.
Now I wont say this is a PoE clone/Diablo clone. There a lot of ways it sets itself apart from it. But I also can't ignore that the games are similar.
The setting/theme is a steampunkish in teh Van Helsing universe (duh). I enjoyed it. It was a nice change of pace.
The developers are also pretty cool. They sent all the beta testers a copy of one of their other games for testing. In a world where pratically every company is selling access to testing with the "Early Access" none sense, it was really refreshing to see.
Finally, one of the most important parts. You can play offline!
Overall if you like Diablo or PoE, you should really give this game a try.

I feel the best way to describe this game is, "More than the sum of its parts." This is because it might seem, as it does to me, that there isn't a vast number of assets, and there are a lot of seeming placeholders, or what seems like unity store assets. The combat is... really bad. NPCs are either motionless props, passive mobs that walk around aimlessly ignoring you, or they are hostile (rush you to melee or stand still and shoot you, with no variance). The combat itself feels hollow and clunky, with bad hitboxes.
All that being said, I still really like this game. Why?
This game is really solidly delivering on the concept of being stranded on an alien planet, working your way up with decent enough character progression, colonisation of the planet's challenges and eventually other planets, all while using creativity to design your bases and ships.
There's something that is just so satisfying about making a makeshift base out of the engine room of a crashed capital vessel, surviving, building a fighter to take on bases, looting said bases and/or taking them over for yourself... The overall process is really satisfying. I'm also looking forward to cooperating with a friend who is about to get this game. This game is quite multiplayer-friendly. To a degree it almost suffers from multiplayer focus if you play solo, but not too much. Mainly because you lose the functionality of trading or keeping things interesting with factions, tribes, and the depth attainable through multiplayer. I suppose I hope the devs do not place too much reliance on that.
So the game itself is fun. How about those devs?
Honestly, I can't think of anything negative to say about these developers. They are a small team, and are known for being friendly, helpful, and responsive to the players. Progress in development might not be super fast, and maybe it could use some more features, but when the devs say they are adding a feature, they add it. I'm on my second playthrough now, and I can see they have expanded and improved the game since I played last year. I have an uncanny amount of trust in these devs, and I feel a good game is in good hands (so rare these days).
I definitely recommend this game. I also recommend turning resource and experience gained to low, as making progress gradually is more rewarding for me. Both exploration/discovery, and keeping ideas for what you want to do long-term while slowly realising them is better than instant gratification, in my opinion. However, on the flip side, there is a creative mode.
Have fun, Captain!

TL:DR a massive improvement over its predecessor, Evoland 2 is a more fleshed out and enjoyable game that is a lot of fun
Having played the first Evoland and finding that it relied too much on the novelty factor to be a good game, I wondered why they would make a sequel to such a mediocre game. But Evoland 2 is surprisingly a very good game. It seems the devs learned from the first game and this time around we have a more structured and fun game that manages to build the "history of gaming" element around the story rather than the other way around, which is where its predecessor fell down.
Anyone who was a gamer in the 90's will appreciate a lot of the not so subtle nods to famous games from that period. The gameplay in Evoland 2 frequently changes to mimic the gameplay of some famous games like Street Fighter, Bomberman and Double Dragon for example. They arent just some shoddily thrown together sequences either and are mostly enjoyable to play. This is all tied together by a story that isnt great but works well enough to incorporate the time travel element which justifies the change in 2d to 3d graphics.
Overall I found Evoland 2 to be a fun enjoyable game that acts like a love letter to some of the gaming classics from my childhood.
Good Points:
- has a broad variety of gameplay styles inspired by classic games like Street Fighter and Zelda. It even has a hearthstone inspired card game that is quite addictive.
- the pixel graphics look nice and the 3d sections lookvery nicely animated as well
- I like how the game incorparated time travel and it makes for a great plot device
Bad points:
-it could very well just have been my machine but I found the music would glitch every now and again.
-depending on your gaming preferences some secions might be a bit boring or unenjoyable.

For most of the part, this is a fun game. It has many challenges (though most puzzles are too obvious) and some variety. But as you get closer to the end, you start noticing this game doesn't have much original content: it is an amalgam of games and anime/cartoons put together in the form of cameos and references. For example, there's a fighting scene where
. I mean, it's kind of fun (some are
funny), but it gets old. The most infurating part however is where you have to play
. Yes, Candy Crush in an RPG!! And, oh man, it's bad. It's difficult, boring, pointless, and has the worst music of the entire game.
The story is generic. Somehow, for some reason, a disaster happened in the past (or in the future while you were trying to fix the past---I don't know, I don't care; it's confusing). So now "Chrono and Lucca"... I mean, Kuro and Velvet must travel through time to fix it. The NPCs are lazy. They always say the same thing and your characters always react the same way. If an NPC tells you something unexpected, your characters will act surprised everytime you speak to them. Some NPCs are quite obnoxious and many are only there to drop a reference or a meme.
But the biggest issue is that some parts are very boring. Not difficult, neither easy... they just take time. Unlike Chrono Trigger, you can only fly between eras by going to special stones. And of course, being an RPG, you get a flying ship, but so late in the game you'll have already explored almost the whole world map.
The final boss is disappointing. It's just too easy. Maybe you'll die once, but as soon as you get its pattern, you can probably do it without even trying. Not to mention that this is the most obvious villain since Final Fantasy X. You know this dude is the final boss the first time you meet them.
Again, that's not to say the game doesn't provide its share of fun. Most of the time it's a decent Zelda/Chrono Trigger mix. Some parts are quite enjoyable and they actually make you wonder why they didn't make a full game out of them. The card game is much better than in the first Evoland. Most of all, I really enjoyed the 2D platforming in the game.
Bottomline, this is not a bad game. You can see that the developers put real effort into producing it. Despite having a few glitches, it's mostly a decent game. But it got me to a point where I eventually just wanted to beat it and go play something else.
I really wish I could not give it neither "thumbs up", neither "thumbs down". But since Steam doesn't have a "meh" option yet, this is what I'm going with. If you really would like to try this game, I suggest you wait for the next discount. It's a game worth playing, but not for the price it's currently asking.

The real selling point of this game is that if you can imagine a game genre (other than FPS), there's almost certainly a segment of the main campaign that plays that way.
It does sometimes feel forced when gameplay style changes, but it's all done so well that it doesn't matter.
Off the top of my head, there are segments in these genres (and probably a few more I've forgotten):
SNES-era Zelda-like (most of the game)
Platformer
Final Fantasy turn based combat
Wargame / Turn-based tactics / campaign map
Street Fighter
Shoot-em-up
Beat-em-up
Rhythm game
Puzzle Quest
Stealth

I love it. I love every second I spent on it.
The characters are full of life, the story is easy and fun to follow up on (although you'd need to play To The Moon and A Bird's Story to get all the shoutouts), though for me the climax was sadly not as impactful as the first game. Some of the gameplay segments caught me off-guard, but I enjoyed them and they weren't unwelcomed at all.
The game's pacing, well, being a story-heavy game, is very relaxed. It's not something you should speedrun. It should be experienced, felt, and read properly. Everything should be interacted and discovered so you don't miss any bit of detail. And the music? Good Lord in heavens, Kan Gao really nailed it as always. I highly recommend buying it bundled with the soundtrack.

It's difficult to say, and I'm a bit surprised, but I honestly didn't really enjoy this game. To The Moon is obviously an incredibly difficult act to follow and I wasn't expecting this game to surpass it, but I feel as though it really dropped the ball.
To The Moon had a bunch of problems: slow movement speed, out-of-place humor that interupts the story at bad times, unnecessary puzzles that really only serve as padding, etc. yet I could easily look past all that for the phenomenal story it told. I don't think I can say the same for this one.
I don't want to spoil the story too much, but it wasn't nearly as good, in my opinion. The individual memories didn't feel that significant; rather, they felt somewhat bland and generic. There's a ton of plot threads introduced in the miniseries and the first game that are left unresolved, and aren't even really expanded upon. My main problem is with the central plotline though;

Honestly, without padding, I feel as though this game would have only taken 2 hours, and while a good story can be told in that amount of time, I don't think that this game did that. I really wanted to like this game, and statistically you  probably would if you played TTM, as shown by the other steam reviews. However, I really can't recommend it.

The story is also quite amazing and original in my eyes, I can't say much about the story without spoiling it. Every bit of the plot keeps you glued to the screen, much like a good book. After the great game 'To The Moon' was, 'Findind Paradise' manages to achieve a level as high as that of its predecessor. I just finished the story, so here is my review:
Pros:
- Flawless and outstanding presentation in graphics, sound and gameplay.
- Interesting foreign world with mystical creatures.
- Story is there, but not throwing itself in my face, but not boring either.
- Without focus on completing it 100% you get around 6 hours of fun, which is perfectly fine for the price, considering the overall quality of the game. They could have easily charged more for this.
Cons:
- Finishing the story locks the savegame from loading, so you can't 100% this game after the final story scene.
Ori and the Blind Forest is an outstanding side scrolling jump'n run by Microsoft Studios. You can very clearly see that there has been put a lot of work into this game. The controls are tight and super precise, it's a lot of fun maneuvering Ori around. The soundtrack is just wonderful, always underlining the current scene and adding to the overall experience. From a graphical standpoint it is stunning, the devs really know how to make engaging scenes. You will not be bothered with graphical glitches or sickening color schemes, everything is beautifully rendered, the colors are harmonizing perfectly well. And the story is as mystical as the world itself. Most people have seen the death scene of the big guy. Let me tell you that the ninjas cutting onions retreat after that, maybe one returns at the end of the game, but altogether this game isn't an emotional rollercoaster. After said scene the game focuses on the main plot and game goals.
Ori and the Blind Forest feels like a love letter to Metroid fans. You unlock passive abilities during the journey, where the upgrades are often sort of hidden and have to be picked up. As an addition you can level up Ori, gaining new powers and active abilites, while maintaining a nice balance to not make it too easy or too hard. Some of the platforming scenes are a bit more difficult than the rest (you'll recognize them while playing) and require very, very precise movement of the player. It may be a bit frustrating from time to time, but at the end it's all very doable.
Here's my one big complaint: after completing the story, you can not go back into the savegame to get 100% (all abilites, max level). The save game just gets locked. I hope they're patching this, I'm not okay with playing an additional 6 hours just to get to the same point and completing it.

Honestly, this is the first game of 2015 that I can say is pretty much a must-have.
If you enjoy the 'metroidvania' style of games, where you explore a world unlocked by new skills and abilities, then this is right up your alley.  If you enjoy platformers at all, this is also an extremely responsive and thrilling jaunt. But even if these games are not in your wheelhouse, I would still recommend this game for its beauty and polish.
This game is not 'pretty' in the same sense that graphically-intensive first person shooters with lots of texture detail are pretty.  It is beautiful in an artistic sense, bringing back memories of Dust: an Elysian Tail and Okami, where every creature and environment is presented to you with a flourish.  The music is perfect, supporting the story in moments of sorrow, excitement, and awe, and would be wonderful to listen to even if it weren't making each scene better.
Speaking of the story, it manages to be simple and unintrusive while still providing depth and emotion.  You don't spend much time in cutscenes where you can't control your character; instead you learn about the world around you through exploration and brief comments from the narrator or your spirit allies.  Much like Wall-E, you will find yourself empathizing with characters who have tugged at your heartstrings without uttering a single word.
That comparison is actually rather apt, as this game has about the same accessability as a pixar movie: everyone can enjoy it, yet no one will ever tell you it's just for kids.
If I had any criticism of this game, it's that you may get a framerate hitch or two depending on your machine, but those are infrequent enough that they don't mess up the gameplay. And some people might get frustrated if they're not used to getting through platformer challenges through death, trial, and error. But even the hardest parts of this game are at the same time thrilling, as you race through tunnels while avoiding tidal waves or falling rocks while the amazing music urges you on.
So in short, get the game.  The only way I can see someone not enjoying this game is if they don't like video games at all.  And for some people like that, I think it might even change their minds.

I'll keep it simple.
The controls are tight and responsive. It feels good to move Ori around the screen.

The metroidvania mechanics are paced well.
The story is good. Though the most moving part is the introductory level.
The difficulty is good. It's not so hard that it's impossible to finish, but it's also hard enough that you feel good to beat it.
The escape sequences are difficult since you can't save during them. Basically you have to complete them about 70/80/90% perfect (the later the escape sequence the more perfect you need to do it), especially the final escape sequence. They almost feel like they are too long without giving you the ability to make a checkpoint, but then you beat it and you think, "well, actually that was just about right."
I finished it in about 12 hours, but about 4 of those hours were either sitting in the pause menue while I talked to my wife or washed dishes, or they were spent backtracking to collect powerups. So when people say that the game can be beaten in about 8 hours, they're not wrong.
But you know? That's just about perfect. I'm an adult, I don't have 60, 80, or 120 hours to spend on a game. I want to finish the game and collect all the powerups in a weekend or two. 8 to 16 hours is just about perfect for my schedule, and at $20 I feel that I got my money's worth. Personally I would have paid $30 and still felt that I got my money's worth.

Imagine Origin Systems circa 1992 just after the release of Ultima 7. It's a magical game and every day after school, you rush through your homework before sitting down in front of the computer screen and losing yourself in the world of Brittania. Continue to let your mind dream, and picture a world where Origin didn't fritter it away - all that tremendous creative energy, soul, and beauty. That imaginary company would have eventually created a game like Divinity Original Sin.
It is a very long game that manages the rare accomplishment of being fun the entire way through, even for veterens who often get that been-there-seen-that feeling.
If you like fantasy RPGs, or tactical combat, or co-op, or any combination of those three genres in the slightest, you should get this.

If you like tactical turn-based combat, a rich fantasy story in an open-ended world, deep character customization, and a bit of a challenge... play this game right now.
The enhanced edition puts a nice glossy coat of paint over an already brilliant game. Veterans of the original game will want to skim through the enormous change list here:
. In short, they made small changes to every aspect of the game, but the highlights include: controller support, full 360 degree camera rotation, dual-wielding (yuss!), improved graphics and spell effects, nearly every npc is voiced, reworked quests, fully reworked end-game and ending, and plenty more. It's also FREE for anyone who has already purchased the base game. The only downside is that you can't transfer your save game, so you'll need to start over.
This is a top-down, story driven, turn-based RPG that demands you to use your brain to solve puzzles and get the most out of its brilliant combat system. Success is determined by how well your party's skills work together, and how you adapt to enemies (who have access to the same skills you do). If you want comparisons, the best I can think of is a Baldur's Gate type world with fantasy XCOM-style strategic combat. But if you have any better comparisons I'd love to hear them in the comments!
Oh did I mention it's co-op? Ya, grab a friend and give it a shot. You won't regret it.
(Hours are low because the enhanced edition was just released. I've played many dozens of hours of the standard edition.)

TLDR: Controls for this game are very bad, makes it frustrating to play and leads to unintended deaths and constant replays of missions.
I was excited when I bought this game on the winter sale. The idea of a stealthy, goblion assassin makes for a great game concept, but the terrible controls and gameplay didn't let me get much farther in the story than finding out he also suffers from substance abuse. The environments are beautiful with a lot of cover and hiding places, as well as dynamic lighting. The AI seems to have a decent amount of perception and timing out the guards routes is consistent and intriguing enough. There are even little planned guard exchanges where they talk about the area or another guard, which was nice and immersive.
The issue is with the movement.
First the climbing. Most of the areas are rather dark which makes it hard to find handhold without using amber vission (illuminates enemies, handholds, interactive objects). Whatever, manageable. However, the climable features on the buildings are poorly depicted. Ledges often have breaks at smooth edges, you can't climb around an inside corner, grabbing a railing immediately pulls you up onto it, drawing attention of anyone in view. There doesn't seem to be a good way to hang of a ledge other than walking off and praying the game realizes you want to grab on. With the climbing systems in games like Assassin's Creed (even the oldest ones) and Shadow of Mordor (just to name two of the top of my head), this game is sorely lacking in what should essentially be the most crucual feature in a stealth game set in a vertical environment.
The cover. The cover system is terribly clunky. Would often find myself fighting against it so i could try to navigate around corners and small outcrops before the timing window on a patrol would be gone.
The combat. I understand that you are not supposed to fight the guards when you get caught, sometimes you need to kill one before you can hide again. The parry system and timing just feels bad in this game. Some strike it is too slow, some too fast, it just doesn't feel good to play. Can't really describe it any better.
Overall, I can't recommend the game, and am not sure I will even finish it. The combat could almost be overlooked for being subpar if the main gameplay (stealth) was enjoyable, but in my very brief time playing the game I found myself frustrated and wanting to play something else. It should be noted that my few hours was spread out over 3-4 different attempts at liking the game. The controls are really that bad.

Final Score: 5.9
Long Review:
Gameplay: 5 Stars.
I'll consider as gameplay all the stealth aspects. As a goblin, you take all the advantages of your size, hiding in the furniture, running through holes and climbing buildings. You have lots of tools to solve your problems and there are many solutions to be found. The game is hard, but is forgiving and fair most of the times. But you have to go sneaky. The game ends up feeling like a puzzle and a platformer when playing, since you'll avoid getting caught. The spells are fair, and the clone gives you many possibilities, which makes everything very exciting to solve. Very fun to play overall.
Combat: 1 Star.
It sucks. I get it, it's a stealth game and you shouldn't fight your way through. But it's not an excuse for a bad fighting system. When you're caught, you lock yourself in duel mode with an opponent, where they will strike at you and you'll have to parry their attacks until you get them off balance, where you kill them. The problems are two: others can attack you while in duel mode and the camera is locked in your opponent's face. You're there trying to traverse a corridor and boom, spotted. You have to run. As you run, you get close to a guard and bwam, the camera is at his face and you can't see where you're going, you can't hide or run straight. You have to get far enough to get ouf duel or kill the sucker. In my honest opinion, no combat system is better then a bad one. They could simply outright kill you when you're caught at melee range with instead of having this half♥♥♥♥♥fighting system. I know it's supposed to discourage fighting, but you discourage fighting by making fighting hard, not bad. Bad and hard are too very different things, some things are easy and bad and others are good and hard. And nothing in a game should be bad.
Controllers: 2 Stars.
Everything but jumping and hanging off ledges is easy to execute. Since you'll be avoinding confrontations, you'll find yourself running and jumping through rooves, pipes and other structures. The game feels like a platformer in this aspect, and the precision of jumps should be sacred. There are many gaps that you're insecure if you can or cannot jump through. Jumping from an obstacle to another is kinda weird and imprecise, and I found myself falling to death a lot of times when it was not my fault, really. Also, sometimes you want to jump and hang instead of climbing through and stand on top of it. But you have no control over it, and most of the times he automatically stands. It's infuriating, since it means you show yourself to the open sometimes.
AI: 3 Stars.
The old nemesis of every game. It's actually decent to be honest. They're not absurdly stupid, and most of their actions make sense. They will search the whole place if they suspect anything, and if you're spotted once, they will alert everyone and they will be more alert of you. They might do weird stuff like walk into one another like they're not seeing each other when their routes collide, or sometimes run into some obstacles in the same fashion.
Level Design: 4 Stars.
The learning curve is good. It gets more challenging as you progress and some maps are reused with different missions, so you know your way around them better the second time you're in them. The maps are so well designed with so many different paths to them that they barely need any work to make a level other than give you an objective and fill every room with enemies. Only critique is that somethings feel unrealistic, such as some very convenient holes on walls and those things on walls for you to hang and climb. The rooms themselves are a bit odd when you stop to think about them, but nothing that really breaks immersion.
Storyline: 4 Stars.
Beautiful story. It's linear, so you have no choice whatsoever and can't change anything to it, and that's why it's not 5 stars. Every character is plausible and have their reasons. The protagonist is very charismatic and full of personality. The world makes sense and the little you know about it is well made.
Graphics: 4 Stars.
They're beautiful to look at. Dark and immersive. It is very clear and there is nothing that really hampers your game experience. Even though it's all very dark, the enemies do stand out and it's easy to see your path. The issues are that in some levels, when the rooms are too bright, the amber visions feels a bit odd to find useful stuff. But then, if it's bright, you probably don't need it to find it. And then, sometimes it's difficult to find holes in walls, since amber vision don't brightens them out.
Sound: 4 Stars.
The sound effects are good, the voice acting is awesome but the music is not memorable. Only a few songs are good, the rest is just background stuff I don't even remember. Overwall, the audio is clean and you can even use it to your advantage most of the time. It's very immersive.

It's pretty good but could use improvement. My biggest complaint would be that it's not always obvious what is going to alert a guard. Depending on the animation, a "silent" kill might make enough noise to catch the attention of an enemy. The game also uses physic objects as obstacles, if you bump into one you make noise, but this isn't always obvious what objects you can bump into, such as a chair, which I expected to just be part of the environment. Absence of light doesn't always seem to make a difference in whether or not I get spotted sometimes, but the game's title is "Master of Shadows" so you think that Shadows might help you a bit.
The game has some good concepts but I think it could have executed them better. I also wish things were a little less random, because it seems like after I make a mistake, I get information, form a plan, suddenly the guards change their patrol pattern while I'm crossing the room. The problem is last time the guard didn't turn around so I should be able to safely assume he won't this time. I don't like having to try the same thing over and over and this game seems to make that happen more because it changes situations ever so slightly whenever you die.
The game is fun but can be frustrating. I want to try Shards of Darkness and see if it's better.

KINDA SPOILERY REVIEW:
Welp, after a 5 years wait, here we are: the second installment to the "To the moon" franchise (I don't have any better names for it). I'm just gonna cut it short: the game's good. Is it "To the moon" levels of good tho? Eeeehhh, it depends.
I felt like it wasn't anywhere close as a tearjerker as "To the moon", mainly because this acts more like a set-up kinda chapter. Don't get me wrong, the plot was good and all, but when you reach the end of the game (which I'm not gonna spoil), it's becomes obvious that the folks at FreeBird used the whole "changing-memories-of-dying-patients-shenanigans" as a plot-device for the "Greater Sub-Plot" (Poetic license).
That's not bad per-se, they're just playing the long game which, if done correctly, can deliver a huge payoff in the end. It's just that with having two installments of the same series 5 years apart from each other, doesn't look like this payoff will be delivered anytime soon.
And don't get this as a "this dude is just complaining and calling them slow and yada yada ♥♥♥♥ off", cuz I really don't mean that. I'm sincerely telling this for their (FreeBird) good, cuz I really wanna see them getting the praise they deserve, without their name fading out of existence because of how much time it takes for another chapter to come out.

This time their patient, Colin, wants his life to be changed as little as possible but wants it to feel more meaningful. It's hard to go further without spoiling anything, but it's a journey about life, regrets, love, and friendship told in a very captivating way. And the music is as good as the first game.

Of course no game is perfect, but I truly can't find any flaw with this game.
- Presentation -
The audiovisual presentation is phenomenal. This is by far the most beautiful game I've ever played yet. The attention to detail is captivating, especially in motion. The environment surrounding you reacts to your every move, and the background parallax effect is breathtaking. Even just moving and jumping around is pure joy, thanks to the smooth and responsive character animations. The music is absolutely wonderful and fits the mood of the game at all times. The sound design is impeccable; I got chills every time I learned a new ability. The story is somewhat simple, yet very touching and memorable, and the execution is remarkable. It really pulls you in and motivates you to save the forest.
- Gameplay -
Ori and the Blind Forest is a metroidvania game, which means you progressively unlock new abilities that allow you to go to places you couldn't reach or access before. Backtracking never felt tedious to me in this game, because it's mostly up to you as a player. You don't
to go back and collect all the secrets and uncover the whole map, but doing so is extremely satisfying.
What I especially adore about the game's flow is the absence of hand-holding. This is a game that respects your intelligence as a player and your ability to figure things out on your own. The game may guide you subtly, but it never explicitly tells you what you need to do. Instead, it uses clever level design to introduce new gameplay mechanics to you. It all feels very instinctive and natural.
There's a simple but very welcome level-up system, with 3 perk trees that gradually improve your character's current abilities in a different way or add convenient info to your map. You get XP orbs every time you kill an enemy, and some bigger XP orbs are hidden in secret locations, so this gives you another incentive to kill enemies and explore the map. Plus, it improves the sense of progression and gives you that nice RPG feel of choosing what perk tree you level up first.
Heck, even the saving system is cool and exciting. The game doesn't save automatically for you; you have to do it manually by lighting a kindle. This can cause some really intense moments, and it punishes players for being too reckless.
The difficulty curve is also perfect; the whole game offers a solid challenge, but if you remember to save often, it's quite forgiving. Though, If this game is giving you a rough time, you should try collecting as many life, energy and ability orbs as possible before going to your next objective. These orbs aren't just fun to collect, they help you more than you might think!
By the way, this game has no loadings, so the fun never stops and the sense of immersion is never interrupted.
I believe this is gaming at its finest. A masterpiece in game design.
★★★★★
- Personal stats -
First playthrough: 8 hours, 25 minutes.
Second playthrough: 5 hours, 45 minutes. Map 100% discovered. All life & energy orbs found. All skills unlocked.

This is a fun game. It's fast paced, graphically interesting even though it's all 8-bit retro style, and quite challenging. After watching the Game Grumps play this, I decided I wanted it, but the $15 price tag was far too high, especially since I wanted 2 copies. When it went on Holiday sale, I grabbed the 2 pack and was mostly pleased. The local single player is well done, especially because the enemies get increasingly more difficult. It also appeared that they started to learn my tactics and how to defend against them, much like another human player would do. Another aspect that I enjoyed was the maps. Right now there are 4 maps, each with their own features/hazzards. I enjoy the complexity of having to not only play against another player, but also how to tie the map's features into my approach. The multiplayer, however, needs much more polishing, and as such is my cheif complaint with this game. Playing with my brother in the same room over LAN proved to be remarkably laggy. A few times, we actually de-synchronized, leading him to see one thing while I was seeing something completely different. Since the single player is limited, multiplayer is an essential feature. For it to be broken like this is quite a drawback on this game. Don't get me wrong, though. I do recommend getting this game. However, in its current state with the multiplayer issues, avoid paying the full price for it. Maybe, when/if the multiplayer gets refined, the normal price would be accptable.

(Reviewed playing Alpha 7.3 final)
+Single player or co-op in PvP or PvE.
+Creative mode.
+No Microtransactions.
+Workshop blueprints and scenarios.
+Switch between FPS or third-person view.
+Great community for learning and modding.
+Hard working devs (constant updates and bug fixes).
+Numerous planets; moons; asteroids to explore with enemies unique to each environment.
+Alternate ways to gather resources keeps it from feeling monotonous.
+Building feels good, and rarely am I unable to accomplish what I imagine.
+True to life signal logic and gates.
+Hosting a dedicated local server for friends couldn't be easier (i7 & 16GB RAM recommended).
-General aesthetics.
-Discouraging tutorial.
-Enemies and AI could use a polish.
-Planets currently have red and green walls due to the maps not being a full sphere yet.
-Driving the hovercraft is a nightmare on Akua (easy starter planet). Just save for an SV.
In-depth:
If one can see past any current aesthetic problems, there is substantial depth to Empyrion.
I weighed it against Space Engineers; Astroneers; and Osiris, based on price; hardware demands; and personal interest:
-SE seemed to focus on crafting, and less of the exploration and gameplay I was looking for.
-Astroneers was a close second, but the crafting seemed limited, and the price (even on sale) never dipped as low as Empyrion.
-I held out on Osiris, as it was the most expensive, and I was worried about hardware limitations.
Empyrion lived up to my expectations for an early access game; and exceeded them the more I played.
Early in the game you will face a daunting tutorial, but don't let it discourage you. If you have any wits, it'll teach you what you need to get started. Just take your time, and save often. The game may break, and it sucks to start over.
Next, practice in creative mode before jumping right in to survival. Learn the feel for crafting while flying your drone; build creatively without grinding (or being eaten); or test, design, and save blueprints for use in your future survival game(s).
Check out the workshop for amazing ideas, and useful blueprints, that you can utilize in both creative and survival modes.
One can also read the guides provided on how to build your own scenario; or find a server where you can join and contribute to a faction, while also learning from experienced players.
My favorite part is solving the puzzles to destroy the unique enemy POI's with minimal damage, so I can steal the parts for my own bases and ships.
Despite any frustrations with the game, I keep finding myself thinking of creative fixes, rather than feeling totally discouraged from playing again.
Within weeks of owning the game, Alpha 7.5.3 was released, now with solar energy; selling goods to merchants; sparkling wine; and a Christmas tree deco. Best of all, it feels good to be a part of a game where the dev team is striving to create a product it's users want to play.
I don't regret supporting Eleon to create and continue work on this game.

If only Steam would allowed that, I'd post it under the neutral banner. The game is neither all good or all bad, it's somewhat of any of those extremes.
I really liked the story part, especially the main villain figure, and all that dark cult agenda, it was really fitting. With that said, I'm quite not happy with the pace and rhythm the game plot proceed, the characters making their moves and all such things. It's all... static and boring. Yeah, again, the story is good, the way it was written and told is really subpar.
I liked the subquests, some of them are really creative and interesting... But buggy and not really rewarding.
I... liked the battles, at least, good bunch of them. The maps are challenging, the variety of abilities and ways to get going is really good. With that... Have you noticed the time counter Steam thinks I was playing? Something around 100 hours? Well, in truth it's maybe around 20. I've played the Blackguards on holidays, I never really needed to shut the game. So I was just playing over the moment I get bored and frustrated, and then just leaving the game without closing it. Mostly, it was around some combats, where you abide, and abide... And tarry the tide, if you know that verse.
You see, some of the combats are really long, with big maps, lots of enemies, unobvious goals or some freaky bugs not letting you to finish the fight. Like, for example, a crystal you have to break to proceed. You're standing next to it, with a hammer and 100% hit chance. And then you miss. 5 times in the row. The hit percentage is maybe the one of the worst abominations that Blackguards shows to the world of turn-based RP games. They are so unfair, as loaded dices.
Finally, with all that pro and contra stuff going hand in hand, there are broken achievements and over-the-top strange pattern to make a good ending. In the end, all the game is unrewarding. Unworthy. My mark is 5.8/10. Think twice over this buy, even on the lowest price possible.

How is that associated to strength at all?
Most irritating part is some fights are just not properly balanced. There is one fight I spent over an hour on, had the moves mapped to a science, and just needed the RNG to connect. If you let the guy hit you on the second turn and poison you, you simply cannot win. So one companion has to move the perfect amount of tiles away from the enemy so it will chase him, while the other moves away and shoots at the non poisoning opponent. Kiting of this level doesn't have a place in a game like this. When I have to take my tank and run him in circles to not die, I feel like the developers missed something...  And to put it in perspective, I have the best armor and stats possible at the current place for a tank, and he cannot tank nor do I even consider him "tanky". Your shield will add a lot to your parry, but you can only parry once per turn turn so what is the point? My mage honestly has just as good of a chance to survive as he does wearing cloth without a shield.
I love games like this, and this one just doesn't shine enough for me to recommend it over what is out there. As I said I don't feel it is bad, but I am not finishing the game.

So you think you can program? You love to compete with code. You like strategy games? I have good news: this game is for you! Don't let the simple graphics fool you, this game has huge depth. Essentially you are programming the AI of the game – or rather _your_ AI, competing against the AIs of your opponents.
Find you starting place, decide on your strategy, pour it into code, and see your colony die, because you forgot to think about a special case leading to a deadlock when collecting ressources. Fix the bug, extend your code and find ways to do things more efficiently.
My harvesters and builders were standing in front of the energy source if I didn't use up the energy in my spawn. Blocking the harvesters or builder and upgrader. My creeps didn't get anything done over night. My colony almost died, because the builders blocked access for the harvesters, So I could not create new creeps to replace those who died of old age. Now they park at the spawn, when full, allowing free access and depositing the energy as fast as possible when needed.
My builders were first programmed to repair buildings with the least percent health. Result: Move to building (wall) repair for one tick, move to next building. In the end it was horrendously inefficient, as the builders were mostly just moving back and forth in my cell, painfully slow. A little modification et voila, way more efficient.
Right now I am looking for my first prays. Yet I need to find out, how to actually efficiently fight them. Like: How only brake a small hole into their wall, walk through end get the actual objectives.
I love this game. I would have preferred Java or Python as ingame programming language, but well, beggars are not choosers. :D

So the Awesome, potential turnoffs and the improvement points. The game is still in early access, i trust most the improvement points will be fixed:
Awesome:
- Programming! And real programming, not some simplified version.
- Persistent Multiplayer World. And the world is regularly expanded with to accomodate new players

But yeah, great game overall! Will update review if something drastically changes :)

There are many games out there that claim to improve your brain; increasing memory retention, attention to detail, improve problem solving and prodding creativity.  This game claims nothing of the sort but it could do so and be fully justified.
It is not a game for people that dislike thinking about problems in depth or just want some light entertainment.  There are plenty of other games for that, rather it is a game that lets you stretch yourself and feel like you just got a tiny bit smarter for each new challenge that you solve on your quest to evolve your domain.
I would reccommend this game to anyone interested in general programming, computer science, engineering, logic and World Domination.
If you want to IMPROVE (not start from scratch) your knowledge of Javascript, this game is for you.
If you want to build autonomous rovers, this game is for you.
If you want to study data storage and retrieval, this game is for you.
If thinking about pathfinding logic keeps you awake at night with excitement, this game is for you.
If you like to plan out contingency scenarios, this game is for you.
If a book on genetic algorithms sits dog-eared on your bookshelf, this game is for you.
If you secretly harbour a desire to eliminate all life on the planet via murderous AI, this game is definitely for you.

With Finding Paradise being the sequel to in both mine and so many other opinions, one of the saddest games ever created, To The Moon, there was definitely an extremely high standard this game had to meet. Not surprisingly however, Kan Gao has yet again created another masterpiece, worthy of as much praise as the last game. Through the perspective of both Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosaline, you are again thrown into a not so distant future where people in the final days of their lives have the option of having their memories altered so that whatever dreams or regrets they had in life can artificially come true, ultimately letting them die happy, or as seen with the name of the game, help them to "Find Paradise". Such a premise for a story is evidently unique beyond words, and clearly is already a very emotional topic, and yet the journey that is created through the amazing story that accompanies it for a topic already so special makes it such a powerful and moving game.
As someone who rarely cries, I have no shame in saying I bawled my eyes multiple times playing this. The story was perfectly executed once again, with Kan Gao and everyone at Freebird Games creating such an emotional journey traveling through the mind of another dying man that if it were a movie, it would receive numerous awards. While I could go on endlessly about the story, the biggest factor that many people probably already know is the music. Whether they were trying to get you to cry, feel extremely freaked out, or even cracking up laughing, in each and every scene they hit the nail. They had me tearing up in parts of the story just due to the music alone. If you are going to buy the game, do yourself a favor and spend the few extra dollars to buy the soundtrack, it is a great investment.
One last thing I wanted to mention was the gameplay. While both To The Moon and Finding Paradise both play out almost like a movie, Finding Paradise introduced something that To The Moon didn't have as much of, and that is both humor and gameplay. I was surprised how much I was laughing at some of the bizarre and funny encounters that constantly occured throughout the story, something that wasn't nonexistent in To The Moon, but definitely was much less. At first I thought it might take away from the level of other emotions the game would have, yet of course through the exceptional story telling and music, my fear was completely unneeded. And with the added gameplay, without spoling anything, all I can really say is you need to see it for yourself.
Overall, I would consider Finding Paradise an extremely worthy successor to To the Moon. While I think the music for To The Moon is my personal favorite, I found Finding Paradise to be a better game overall, something you absolutely won't regret picking up. If there had to be one thing I found wrong with the game, the only thing I would be able to come up with is that there is no in-game screenshots

WTMG's Heidi Hawes writes: "While the premise of this game is very similar to To the Moon, I was happy to see that it wasn’t a direct copy of it. It starts off with the doctors trying to figure out how to please their latest client Colin Reeds, the main protagonist of A Bird Story. His request is fairly simple, he wants to feel like he’s lived a full life, but without changing anything major from it. Alright, maybe it’s not so simple. With that, the doctors are off trying to reconstruct his memories so they can make his dying wish come true.
I was elated to see that Finding Paradise was able to take the few shortcomings of To the Moon and improve upon them. It offered a bit more variety with the gameplay, although it was still a heavily story driven game that holds your hand through most of it. The puzzles that were once so easy my four year old could solve them, have now been replaced by a new puzzle system that gets increasingly harder and more creative as you go. The few new hilarious minigames were a welcome addition as well. While the story in this one wasn’t quite as poignant as in To the Moon, it was all around a much better and more enjoyable game and I cannot wait for the next episode."

An update of a classic that is undoubtedly true to the original.
New 'n' Tasty is a brilliant way to relive the classic Abe's Oddysee, without ever feeling that the game has drifted too far from its roots. The puzzles and locations are all the same, with a few minor tweaks to fit in with the graphical updates. It's incredible to go through old, recognisable locations that have been updated with beautiful graphics for the present day. Every location, consequently, looks both new and familiar.
While this is a faithful update, there are a few tweaks and new additions. For example, Abe now has a health bar which you can replenish by chanting around birds. Playing into this, you now have three difficulty levels to choose from. Sometimes you can take advantage of the fact that each "screen" from the old game is now part of a single, long level; this sort of thing allows you to mind-control the Sligs when previously you couldn't because of those floating probe droids were on your "screen", but now you can move just out of range of them.
The game is not without its flaws, however. Even on a single playthrough I came across a few bugs and glitches. Occasionally you might be doing an intense platforming section where you can't stop moving, but you will abruptly grind to a halt for no reason. Such an instance, especially when you are being chased, will lead to instant death. Additionally, some of the controls can get a bit fiddly. The game's instance on you pressing the jump button and then the direction a split second later can either result in your jumps being poorly timed or Abe simply grabbing onto the ledge above him. Finally, you might find occasionally that when you try to trigger something integral to a puzzle, nothing happens. It's a shame that the game was thoroughly bug-tested prior to release, but fortunately these glitches are few and far between, and hardly game-breaking.
A quick note should be made about the claim that there's three times as many Mudokens to rescue in this game. While this is true, the extra rescuees are all in the same locations as before. All you have to do is shepherd the same group to the same location. The only thing that's different is the number of prisoners who jump through the portal: this doesn't make the task any trickier or add anything unique that wasn't in the original. Please don't think there's three times as much content, because it's the same as it was before. The extra Mudokens add nothing.
All in all, this is a wonderful way to see a *true* graphical update of a classic game. The entire world is re-imagined without ever stepping too far from what you remember. They built the game from scratch, but they never left the original drawing board. The world feels a lot more connected than it did previously (especially when you can see locations you've already visited in the background), and they managed to do it without "ruining your childhood". I'd recommend this game for both fans of the original and people who have never touched and Oddworld game before.

Having finished the game here's my review based on gameplay, story and art.
Gameplay:
I didn't encounter any bugs. Movement was smooth. Level difficulty as the player progresses is acceptable.
The game focused more on player reaction time rather than puzzle solving skills. Overall an average gameplay.
Art:
The game's art is good but not great, to be fair it showed promise at the beginning, however nothing of the same followed until the end of the game. With a title like Color Symphony I'd imagine the game to have more creative art.  Well at least the artwork per level shows consistency throughout the game however I digress that there's nothing really eyecatching.
Story:
Again at the start of the game the prologue showed promise as we see a glimpse of the world we get to play. However during gameplay the only resemblance of any story progression was a few lines on the background shown on every other level. No character development, very simple goal, weak conclusion. It might be too much to expect an engaging story for a platformer but the prologue really showed that there could have been much more.
Overall, this is an okay game to play if you have an hour or two to spare, It's decent for a platformer game, there's worse games for sale on steam and this is at least free.

First of all this game does not deserve the mixed reviews it has received.  I've been a fan of CRPGs since the days of Might and Magic.  Maybe it's the nostalgia of the Dark Eye ruleset that reminds me of games like Star Trail, which even with its flaws I love. I cannot understand some of the complaints I've heard here. I find the battle difficulty perfect. I know this may turn some people off, but I love it. I typically play all of my RPGs on the hardest settings. I play this on normal. There is an easy mode if you need. It's understandable. That said everytime I'm frustrated I put it down, come back to it later, and succeed.  I will say that I restarted once because given the difficulty I was unhappy with how I had planned out my characters. Let me also say that I am happy there was not a "respec" option.

Cons:

Uninteresting and simple models/textures for armor/characters
A few bugs, some graphical, at least one gameplay
Note: For those complaining about the RNG, please remember that the mother of all RPGs D&D is a dice game. Get over it.

I remember when this initially came out awhile back that people were going on about the darkness of the anti-heroes, the crudeness of the dialogue, almost juvenile humor, etc. Maybe years of playing the Witcher games have heightened (or is that lowered) my tolerance bar, but nothing in Blackguards even raised my eyebrow. In fact, rather than being the EDGY ANTI-HEROES that seem be everywhere these days, it was kind of relaxing to find out that my party were just a bunch of losers, with a lazy, whiny main character, a dwarf who is possibly nuts and most certainly an arsonist, a philandering wizard, and that's just to start with. Rather than choices that are downright eeeeeevil, you mainly get the choice between being a cold-hearted pragmatist or a bit more charitable, which works great. Voice acting was quite good for the price and the type of games, and the graphics, well, they are what they are, I don't mind (honorable mention goes to the fire effects which may be the prettiest I've seen in ANY game at ANY price tag.)
I didn't find the combat to be as intense, strategic or engaging as Original Sin, but it was satisfying enough. The lauded interactive elements were for the most part useless when the surest, easiest strategy (on Normal, anyway) was to fall back, put my tanks in front of my glass cannons, hop the former up with all the buffs I could lay on, and let rip. But the game would fairly frequently throw a curve ball to shake things up; some fights have limited turns before you lose an optimal victory condition, others force you to move forward with ever-spawning enemies or poison gas. There was enough variety that it never got too repetitive or boring, though obviously some of the fights are going to feel annoying or unfair, or leave you way too open for the revenge of the RNG demon.
Conclusion: I feel no rush to play this again, but I have no regrets buying it in the first place.
