Evoland 2 builds on the premise of the first game - they're as related as any given Final Fantasy titles, so don't worry about missing any story elements. Evoland 1's big gimmick was jamming an elbow into your side every five seconds and going "REMEMBER THESE MECHANICS???" while haphazardly including things like load times because HA MAN AREN'T YOU GLAD YOU DON'T HAVE THOSE ANY MORE??? EvoLand 2 has put that on the wayside in lieu of... jamming an elbow into your side and going "REMEMBER THESE GENRES???"
Evoland 1's issue was that the 3-4 styles felt unpolished. Evoland 2 takes that to all new heights by dragging in a new type of game genre every five minutes, ALL of which feel unpolished. And even if you do find yourself enjoying one of these genres, it will never show up again.
Stylistic choices are inconsistent (UI elements are always in the same style, even when they don't match the style of the era). Story elements are seemingly never explained. The game plays like a cross between a Wario Ware game and one of those "50-in-1" game systems you get for $10. In at least one part, poor storytelling or bugs in tracking quest completion lead to vague, unclear directions as to what you should be doing. Some 'puzzles' are incredibly obvious but tedious (In order to progress at one point you must use one portal to go to the present, talk to one person, use another portal to go to the future, talk to one person, use the same portal to go back to the present, talk to the first person, talk to a third person, then go back to the past - that's the entire puzzle).
If the creators wanted a demo reel to show that they could make any type of game, then this certainly succeeds in that regard. But as a game, it falls flat in many ways.

While sequels to underrated games seldom salvage the series, this game did markedly better in terms of story-telling than its predecessor, enough to merit my statement anyway, as I was very critical of Evoland '1' and its lack of depth. Evoland 2 retains its core mechanic of being able to flip between time zones, although again often limited by story progression, but actually fleshes out each time zone with differences in areas, characters, themes, and mechanics, which was very refreshing to see. The protagonist, as while as your party members, now have stories and motives, and
ones at that.
The story revolves around a boy (Clink 2.0) sent through time for initially unknown reasons, and his journey to discover his origins and how it links to the fate of his world along with his companions and their varying roles. As you can surmise, the premise is still fairly vanilla, reminiscient of Ocarina of Time, thematically anyway, but the gameplay towards that objective is what makes the game truly unique: It samples various genres and their evolution through video game history, including Puzzle Platformer, RPG, Runner, Top-Down Shooter, Turn-Based Strategy, and others, even some as foreign to the norm as Brawling, Match-4, and a surprisingly well put-together card minigame (at least superior to the blatant Triple Triad clone of Evoland '1'). What surprised me the most were that many of these changes to play didn't even seem forced (some more than others), and saw seamless incorporation into the plot. In any event, it's definitely not a game you see a lot of out there, and is clear the devs put a lot of work into making everything fit into place.
Ultimately, Evoland 2's message saw implementation a lot smoother than the first one, was a genuinely fun experience to puzzle through and collect everything for, and more often than not, an actual challenge, in blatant contrast to everything that made up Evoland '1'. I applaud the developers on their handling of this title and would recommend it to any of my friends and colleagues. If they decide to do a third installment, I'd be in full support.

All players are on one server, on one big and it's basically a realt time strategy game. You harvest resources to upgrade your controller, which allows you to build more and more advanced buildings. Those give you access to more advanced Creeps which will be more effective at working and fighting.

Do you code for fun? Do you enjoy learning programming languages in your spare time? Or do you want to learn Javascript but you are really not looking forward to slogging through a hundred coding examples in a five pound book.
Screeps is an RTS where the only interaction you have with your creeps is code. You write every line of code that governs their behavior. That defensive tower? It won't shoot if you don't program it to. Those harvester creeps? They won't mine energy unless you code them to move over to the mine and harvest it every game tick.
The tutorial gets you through the basics, but beyond that it's all up to you. You can guide your creeps by laying down construction sites for them to build (assuming you wrote the code to have them build!), drop flags to guide their behavior (if you wrote the code that has them do something with flags!), and modifying their memory so they know what role you want them to have (if you wrote the... yeah, you get the idea).
I've spent far more time in Screeps than this indicates because I've been doing most of my coding in a separate IDE. They even have hooks to allow you to pull your code directly from Github. This is a game by programmers, for programmers. Unless you already know about callbacks, inheritence, hashmaps, profiling and a lot of other coding constructs (or you are in this to learn them) then this is not the game for you. Beyond the basic tutorial, there is no handholding. It's all your code, and the unforgiving universe.
The MMO portion of the game has a separate monthly fee for normal CPU amounts, but you get 10CPU just for buying the game. This is enough to operate one or two rooms of creeps... to grow larger, you will need a subscription, or be very good at optimization. If you don't want to participate in the MMO side, local play and the ability to run your own server are planned but not yet complete (as of the Early Access release).

I've been following the development of this game for quite a while and playing for a few months now on the web client, and supported the campaign to bring it to steam and opensource it in the future.
Let me first get one thing out of the way: If you are no programmer, AND you have -no- interest in learning a programming language (JavaScript in this case) whatsoever, no interest in learning to code, this is not the game for you.
But If you want to learn JavaScript (or already know it), this game is brilliant though. While it does not teach you JavaScript itself (you will need to make an effort yourself to learn, though there's good online courses for it like this one:
, but it provides a platform to experiment on, and exposes you to a rather modern style of JavaScript development via NodeJS, it does not require any complicated setup, and it makes it excitingly fun seeing the fruits of your work in front of you, not just immediately, but also over the course of weeks and months. It will give you a great platform to experiment though. You will write a few simple lines of code, and suddenly a little virtual creature called creep will walk across the screen and start harvesting energy. A few more lines, and it'll bring it back to your Spawn. A few more lines here, a few more there, and before you'll notice you will have spent hours, days, weeks coding your perfect little empire, optimizing it, trying out various strategies and ideas; you'll have armies of little creeps working on harvesting energy,  increasing your controller level, harvesting and processing minerals, defending your borders, trading with your neighbor or even waging wars against that other, more annoying neighbor.
And ofc, even if you are already experienced with JavaScript, there's always something new to learn and try. Experiment with Grunt to prepare and deploy your scripts, write out-of-game tools to interface with the game, plot charts for the performance of your little creeps - there's always something to do : )
The game also has a great, incredibly helpful and patient community, answering questions in the game's forums or the dedicated chatroom, about the game as well as about programming in general, giving tips, sharing experience and even sharing code. Forge alliances, or start wars, it's up to you.
One last thing: You will probably not get it right the first time. Maybe not the second time. You'll scrap your code and start over. Or somebody attacks, wipes you out and forces you to start over. Thats okay. The game can be tough. It certainly isn't always fair. We all went through that. Think about the lessons learned, not so much about the progress (though you will keep your global control level forever, so you'll never loose everything). And each time, you will do better than the last time. And it will feel so good to get there.

This was a game I found lying around my computer desk as a kid. After my first experience playing Quake II, which you can check that review for the experience, I had no idea what to expect from Quake III except greatness. It could have been a new single player, an enhanced multiplayer, really anything. But the word Arena was the next word I saw on the disk. I was a pretty smart kid, so I knew it was going to have a badass multiplayer. Little did I know that it was going to be ALL multiplayer.
So I booted up the game after installing it and started watching the intro. It showed some guy shooting down things and running out of ammo. The guy runs away and then decides to rush in. Immediately, I was a little unimpressed. After the Quake II intro, I was expecting awesomeness! Now it was just showing a cliche FPS sequence. Then, after diving towards the enemies, something unexpected happens. Time freezes as the guy is being teleported to some unknown place. This is where id Software did NOT disappoint! After being teleported, it then shows some gameplay of what I was going to be playing with random letters zooming out. I watched the gameplay and knew it had to be awesome. Then, the legendary words filled the CRT monitor.
I was hyped. I could not wait. So I went to the options to peek around and noticed there was a better Player Setup screen than Quake II. You could actually see who you were choosing before you picked them. MUCH better than having to scroll through the different models in Quake II to pick your character. And yes. Before you ask, the same customization of Quake II with being able to play as many different characters is avaliable here too. After picking this weird alien thing named Flisk, I immediately went into the game.
The graphics looked really nice. I was gazing upon the room I was in and noticed all the little details in the room. My eyes were like a kid in a candy store. The textures popped out like flowers in a field. The graphical detail was legend, and everything just seemed amazing. Then I noticed the mirror in the room. I gazed at my reflection and loved the little details on my character.
Another thing I noticed was the sudden announcer coming through my speakers. "WELCOME TO QUAKE III ARENA!!" I had never heard such a thing in a video game before. It was really mindblowing at the time. I then decided to test fire the guns I had collected. The machinegun sounded like a more powerful version of the one from Quake II, and the Shotgun sounded like it was the most devastating thing in the game. I decided to go outside the room and see what was going on around the map.
I immediately ran into Crash, the first enemy opponent in the game. She's like Doomguy except she's a girl. I shot her down with my shotgun and noticed that she talked to me in text like she was a friend in real life. Wow! Talk about advanced! I never had a character talk to me in text like that. It was something really special at the time and it's something games just don't do anymore. It's kinda sad, but I can see why.
Alright so the gameplay. Well, it's a shooter that is a heavily polished version of Quake II's multiplayer. Even the single player is just a bunch of fights with bots. Nothing really special, but it's good practice. The weapon balancing is something id wanted to do in this game and it really works well. Each weapon has its own use, just like the single player in Quake and Quake II. The Rocket Launcher is good for if your enemy is mid range, while guns like the Lightning Gun and Machinegun are great for long range attacks. The Shotgun is definitely used best at shorter ranges because of the more realistic spread this time around.
The gunplay isn't the only thing you'll want to learn in Quake III. Movement is definitely a really important skill to learn, especially if you plan on playing online. Since the original Quake engine had some bugs that made advanced moving techniques that are real useful in multiplayer possible, they decided to embrace those bugs and make them part of the physics of the game. Things like Bunnyhopping, circle jumping, and the infamous Rocket Jump are just a few examples of techniques that made Quake III very famous.
Overall, I gotta say that Quake III Arena is to FPS games as Super Smash Bros. Melee is to fighting games. The really complex formulas and techniques that were present in the original Quake are improved and embraced in every way imaginable and the multiplayer community is still really strong. There was even a Dreamcast port of Quake III designed with Keyboard & Mouse controls in mind due to these special techniques that also has cross-platform capabilities with the PC version! Definitely get this game and enter the Arena!

This game absolutely rocked the FPS world back in the day. As a young pre-teen, I played my sports outside, did my homework and when I could, I'd jump on the PC to play this. If you have played Unreal tournament, it may ring a few familiar bells while playing this. If you can tolerate old graphics, you'll able to enjoy the gameplay.
What is Quake 3 : Arena? It is a first person shooter (FPS) multi-player focused game with fast pace featuring players duking it out for in front of a race called the Vadrigar. All the player movements are normal (four directional + strafing) with the addition of jumping. Mouse button 3 will allow the player to zoom and C will let the player crouch. Throughout the map there are items available for pick-up in which the player can press enter to use them. The basic strategy back in the day was jumping up and down and strafing while shooting. Playing the game today after so many years seems players have really figured out this technique and it's almost near impossible for me to hit them. Most servers are decently friendly (for n00bs as well) but some servers have some very good players. Most FPS's will demand a lot of attention from the player but this FPS will keep you moving due to paranoia. Non-stop movement is recommended.
The AI within the game is actually a formidable opponent. Upon first playing the game, I had some serious trouble beating the first level. I got back on the horse eventually and was able to ride to the next tier. One player mode will have you square off against stronger and stronger opponents the more you progress. The weapons in the game are outlandish in design and style while having their strong and weak points. Some weapons will benefit the player from a long range while some will demand a shorter range. The BFG10K is a plasma based weapon that can fire rapidly. The gauntlet is a short ranged melee type weapon in which the announcer will announce "humiliation" if an opposing player is killed. The gauntlet does not require ammo. The lightning gun fires a beam of "lightning" and is useful for groups of opponents. The railgun fires a hot slug rounds at a high velocity. It would be better to use this gun from a distance. The plasma gun obviously fires burst of plasma but is slow regarding it's firing rate. There is also a rocket launcher (that is pretty self explanatory and is my favorite weapon as it can make players bounce or explode). The last two include a machine gun and a grenade launcher. All the guns are fun to use but players will find their own style which work for them.
There are items scattered throughout the level and respawn after a short amount of time. The first item includes a red armor icon which has the most defense out of all armors. The yellow armor is half as good as the red and armor shards (pieces) will increase your armor by increments of +5. Besides armor, there is health around the map available for pickup. The blue health orb will replenish your health to a maximum while an orange health orb will only do half of what the blue can do. The small gold and green health orbs are the smallest units of replenishment. Also included are power ups. Power ups include a blue icon which quadruples the damage you deal, a red regeneration icon in which when you receive damage your heath will regenerate, a yellow icon which doubles your speed you fire your weapons, a purple icon which allows you to jump at unbelievable heights, invisibility (which is self explanatory) and a battle suit that can protect you from literally anything from the environment (lava, water + splash damage from opponents). Additional items include a personal teleporter (which will transport you into a random spot when in trouble), a medkit which can be activated by the user, in-place teleporters which have a pre-determined destination, jump pads which will launch the player and acceleration pads that will launch the player in the direction they are facing. Don't face the wrong side or an edge when approaching such a pad!
As I've said, this game is big time multi-player focused even though it has some single player events. There are differing game-modes to keep the player engaged : Free for all (where everyone plays for themselves), team deathmatch where two teams compete for the highest "frag" (kill) score, tournament mode which is one versus one ending after a set time and lastly, capture the flag. Capture the flag is played on maps in which both opposing sides have the same map layout (to keep everything fair).
This is a good game for hardcore FPS fan's while the casual gamer may find the graphics and gameplay lacking due to the difficulty. I would consider this one of those games where you really have to take the time to perfect your skill to get the most joy out of it. I've been playing the game for around 4 hours at this point and I'll be honest...  I don't get the bad rep this game is getting...  The characters (so far) are well voiced, the story, although fairly generic, is decent enough and the combat system is decent.
I will admit, I bought the game as a part of this weekends sale, so got both Blackguards 1 & 2 along with a bunch of other games for about £12.  I've been tempted by both of these for some time now, but was put off by the reviews and the price.  So far, I have found these to be unfounded.
I dove straight in on character creation rather than have the system do half the work for you and I am learning it as I go.  There's a lot to choose from so I just went with basics at least to start with.  It looks diverse enough to branch out later, which is always nice.
Sure, there is a large element of RNG, but look at XCOM...  That game has continually devastated its players by repeated 95%+ shots missing at the, single, most crucial shot of the game.  I can't count how many times in that I have missed that said shot and the mission suddenly went to hell.  This is no different, though I have yet to encounter anything so drastic, but it's still early days.
I can certainly see the game getting repetitive after a time, but there seems to be a lot more variation than XCOM in terms of attacks you can do, especially when you take in to account the spells.
I would say that this game is definitely recommended to fans of TBS games and also to those of strategic fantasy games.  I would also definitely say that this game 'should' be recommended.
To set 'not recommended' as others have because it's niche is just a tad overkill tbh.  If they aren't interested in a game just because it's a TBS or fantasy, then why are they looking at it in the first place?  It's a moot point.

This game is a very special kind of misguided.
- It takes the stance that the player should be learning the mechanics exclusively through negative reinforcement and repeated failure.The exact opposite of what a modern game with a complex ruleset should do. The tutorial gives you all the non-relevant details. It tells you where to click, instead of how things work.
- If you already know the pen-and-paper DSA rule-set, you'll understand how things work. But the system is too convoluted. It does not translate to a single-player on-screen experience in a game that is exclusively about combat, not a full role-playing experience. The game does not properly communicate the 'relevant' deatils well enough. And it displays misleading stats that do not take 'effective' numbers into account, but just some pre-stage calculation that is irrelevant. If you turn on the detail log, you'll not get any more insight in how things work. Instead, you'll just notice that the rolls are very likely rigged. I could sit with a real twenty-sided die all day and would not come up with a sequence of results that much skewed towards failure on my part. Four failures in a row on that special attack that uses 7 arrows? Get used to it. On the other hand, you'll see that the enemies, especially in the later chapters are rigged to basically almost never fail. Towards end-game the mechanics of the game work solely against you, never in your favor. The enemies are rigged so the game stays 'challanging'. That includes NPCs with impossible armor/resistance stats, quasi-teleportation of certain mobs 'at random', so your positioning ends up good or bad 'at random', etc.
- The difficulty is based on the QA guy having finished a level. With a perfect party build, knowing all events and scripted enemy behaviour up front. Sometimes, If the RNG was playing along. What sensible game developers would have made the 'hard' mode is 'normal' here. You're going to be restarting battles a lot for reasons you have no control over. The 'retry' button pops up a confirmation dialog that's borderline mocking you: 'Do you really want to repeat this fight?'.
- For a tactics game of such a slow pace, the outcome of a battle relies way too much on rng chance. So you're playing that last arena level in chapter three with endless enemy respawn? Pray to god that after twenty minutes of sitting through the tedium of that convoluted level your key char is not double crit-hit by a small mob after two consecutive misses of ninety-five percent to-hit blows of his own. Thanks for playing. Please sit through another twenty minutes of tedium. If the game is generous it will crit your key chars just ten minutes into a level, so you don't have to pointlessly replay as much. Some levels are crafted to the execution of a pretty tight plan. RNG does not like you in a key moment? Have fun restarting. Single failures or mistakes spiral into catastrophic failure way too quickly for this to be fun. There are random actions enemies can perform, especially casters, that can keep your entire team in a perma-stunlock long enough to reduce you to mincemeat. In essence: the random element is too strong on quite a number of encounters. An in this game it means: half the time you have a chance, half the time you don't.
- The story and dialogue is jar-droppingly incoherent and outright stupid. Why did they bother to have the dialog spoken, I don't know. Bad voice acting of a minimalist script makes this an incoherent mess. Barely manages to convey the gist of what is going on. Sometimes not even that. My bet is they were afraid of writing, because the masses apparently do not like reading through a story. Well. Now the story makes less sense than the plot of 'Suicide Squad'.
- Combat levels are hit and miss. The ones you'll remember are mostly miss. The devs want you to fail certain levels at least once, but preferably multiple times. And since you can't save mid-battle, and have to restart from scratch, it all nicely 'extends' play time, you know. No way to speed gameplay up either. See that tentacle animation of it coming out and going back to water that it does every time? Good thing we have 7 of them on-screen, so you can watch a pointless pre- and post- animation every time one of them does something.
- Props for the devs trying to change things up a bit with some 'creative' missions. It's not well done though. Example: there's a mission where you need to 'sneak' past a patrol. Basically stay out of lit areas and run from cover to cover in bushes. Guards don't see you if you stay hidden. Guess what happens when one of your characters has the 'attack of opportunity' skill, which grants them a free attack when an enemy tries to pass by them? That's right, the oblivious guard passes your char by the bushes, and the attack of opportunity triggers automatically, so your char takes his spear and skewers the guard passing by. You can't turn it off short of giving the chars in question ranged weapons. After you 'retry' the level of course. Because you messed up, obviously....
- If they wanted it to be difficult but rewarding they should have gone for bigger combat areas, better weays to utilize terrain, and more opportunity for player agency. They designed the levels to be played in a certain way. You deviate, you lose. You find out the hard way (by losing a lot) what the designer's idea of 'solving' a level was. Your ideas are not wanted, and there's no freedom for you to come up with anything anyway. You're railroaded, because the levels are too small, too cramped, and thus you have very few choices and the enemies have very few choices. So you work on some details, and hope RNGesus is with you. Then you restart the level, because you lost again. There's levels where at a certain point a certain spell must be successful, or you lose (due to limited turn constraints). I've rarely seen such incompetence in level design. The 'hard' levels are designed to be 'clever'. They're definitely not designed to be 'fun'. This is a game, it should be fair, transparent in its rules, challenging, and rewarding. You could make a point a that it is challanging. But not on its own merits. It's merely challenging because its unfailr, intransparent and unrewarding.
So. No. I can't recommend it. It's a wrong kind of hardcore. The game goes out of its way to dish out frustration by witholding information, or just screwing you over at the last moment of a long level with a sequence of 'unlucky' rolls. Good strategy/tactics games are easy to learn and hard to master. This one is hard to learn. Up to this day there's a debate on the forums as to how the to-hit system even works, because dev's explanation is inconsistent with what we see in-game and the game certainly does not tell you how it works. And there's too little freedom within the levels to really master anything. You solve a level/puzzle each time around it's 'interactive objetcs', whose use is often mandatory. And then try to deal with things you can't possibly anticipate to happen, but hey, the QA guy managed once and he said he had fun playing, so it must be good. Thumbs down for not thinking about how to present content and how to communicate mechanics. It's almost as if player frustration was their goal when designing this. Too bad, because at its core it has nice potential.
Remember the frustration of dealing with the Bed of Chaos in Dark Souls 1 for the first time. Then imagine adding a random element that insta-kills your character the moment you step throught the boss door seven out of ten times. Then add the insult of the game communicating to you that it happens only one time in twenty as a sacrifice of sorts, and that it's just you being unlucky. If you're into that kind of thing, go ahead and buy Blackguards. It has about a dozen or so levels that are pretty much like that.

So having finally finished the game, time for a quick review.
Eh, just about. It's regularly on sale for £2 or £3, and I got 70hrs out of it, so on that basis you'd be a whiny little ♥♥♥♥♥ to complain.
Eh, just about. It's a classic TBS affair. The storyline's OK, but gets kinda convoluted throughout the game so by the end, you've pretty much lost the plot and stopped caring. Something to do with a Whisper...? Anyway.
One big plus is the characters and writing. They're generally a likeable bunch and have good banter between them, and often their conversations raise a chuckle.
Progress is extremely limited - you won't be working your way up through half a dozen better and better sets of gear as you progress: in fact, once you've got a complete set by around chapter 2, you can pretty much forget about upgrading any more. So if you're a loot junky and love waiting for the loot windows at the end of every fight to see what shiny new gear your heroes are getting, you'll be disappointed.
Having said that, if you simply enjoy the basics of TBS combat and love moving your guys around a hexboard and using your new skills/spells to smash zombies in the face, you'll enjoy yourself.
It's not the best TBS out there, but it's not awful. The thrill fades throughout the game so towards the end finishing it off becomes as much a chore as a pleasure, but at 90% off there's no reason TBS fans shouldn't have it in their library.

Chrono Trigger and FF3/6 were the main standouts towards realizing what the developers were after, since those there the two games I was most involved with during the time frame. It worked like a charm. Very nice job. I often found myself dreaming to experience my more youthful days once again, when such games hadn't yet lost their sheen through the tarnishing effects of time. To experience a fresh game that paid this kind of respect towards the era was an absolute delight.

Awesome zeldalike with references to other genres and gaming culture. The game plays well and the story is neat. A few hickups here and there (my game froze like 3-4 times during my 24hr playthrough), but still it has so many fresh ideas, time travels and the design is really beatiful that I can overlook that. I didn't bother to hunt achievements because you have to backtrack alot and play the ingame cardgame quite often to do so. Still, these are doable as well.
All in all, I can recommend the game to everybody interested in the genre, you won't regret buying it.

I liked the first Evoland. There was an interesting idea behind the game - to show the evolution of RPG genre. It was short and fun game.
The sequel, however, is worse. The main reason is the attempt to stretch the same idea from 3-4 to 15-20 hours. It didn't work. I don't see this "evolution" suggested by the name. For most of the time it is the same game, in three different graphic styles. Boring game, I must add. The story is average, the characters are bland, there's a lot of NPCs with uninteresting dialogs we must click through, fighting system is also poor. And puzzles require using special attacks, which have recharge time - this slows the game in a very frustrating way.
But after few hours of playing, there is some diversity. Game switches genres, one moment you play strategy game, the next is Guitar Hero. One it's bullet-hell shooter, then it Street Fighter. While the ideas are interesting and quite fun to see, after laughing that you will be playing Street Fighter now, you must play rather mediocre Street Fighter clone. Yes, some of those minigames are really enjoyable, but not really worth spending so much time to get to them.
To summarize: it's rather boring RPG with some interesting ideas for minigames, but the execution of them is average. The concept of the game is good (but not as innovative as it was in the first game), but it failed against the attempt to make a full game out of it.
one word : 素晴らしいです

Also there's still no form of map or quest log, you're going to be incredibly lost if you ever take a break for a while & even then, most times you're left to wandering around town trying to figure out which house you havn't been in to find the quest person
So if you're longing for those old rpgs that make little sense & at least half the game is padding quests then go for it, the whole evolving gameplay thing barely makes an appearance as every time it evolves is basically an entire part of the game & it drags out a lot
Spoiler, you will have to do mindless tedious tasks to gather 500g or so before you can leave the town & think about progressing past the first phase
Also I've never been more angry at a support character that isn't an escort
tl;dr If it wasn't padded to all hell it might've been a decent concept

There are two things I enjoy doing in life - playing video games and programming. This is a combination of the two. I've always enjoyed tower defense style games, which this is. In terms of the game, I don't really know what else to say; if you enjoy tower-defense games, MMOs and enjoy/want to get into programming then this fits all of those criteria with ease.
So, on to the elephant in the room. The subscription model. In an era where subscriptions have almost been wiped out. I think subscriptions are heavily outdated and expensive, however in this case it is justified. After all, this game is clearly going to have a fairly small niche playerbase, and they have to run servers powerful enough to run everybody's code 24/7, so relying on income from sales alone is impractical.
I also let the subscription model off for a big reason. Once the game releases from early access (1-2 months from now) the devs are open-sourcing the server and allowing anybody to host their own. In doing so, the subscription model is removed and you can try your AI against friends with as much power as you like (or have).
The developers also seem to be very engaged with the community - due to its relatively small size they are able to respond to the majority or forum posts and many suggested features are added.
For those who are put off by the standard MMO playerbases, this one is pretty civilised. Because they're programmers and not 12 year olds screaming into their microphone.

This game tries to build on the ideas of its predecessor. Instead of just progressing through the different eras of gaming Evoland 2 has a storyline that connects the change in graphics with time travelling. Unfortunately I had to quit when I reached the 3D era. The controls and the camera are a mess in 3D. It is poorly optimised and incredidly frustrating and sluggish to play. The eras before were okay and had their fun moments but no era really differs in gameplay and the 3D era does not improve on combat at any means. It just gets uncontrollable.
The major problem I have with this game is that its main premise is so poorly executed. Yes, you timetravel and suddenly everything looks like a Gameboy game and that is cute and all but why doesn't the music change? The textboxes and alerts don't change as well and when you get some items they are presented in high res, no matter what. Other than that there is no change in gameplay whatsoever. Every era has a side gimmick like Jump'n'Run parts or a fight inspired by fighting games like Tekken but it is always halfbaked and poorly executed. Combat stays essentially the same (it just stops working in 3D) and there is almost nothing going on with the perspective changes because changing your perspective comes with a change in the worlds timeline so areas just look different anyways. There could have been interesting puzzles or secrets where a change in graphics is necessary to reach certain areas but these instances are incredibly rare and not really worth mentioning.
It just feels lazy to me. There is so little attention to details in a game that could have been fun. Don't get me wrong, there are some fun and interesting parts but they always feel lacking or somehow tacked onto the main game. I always had the feeling I was playing an introductory chapter but somehow the game never gets interesting and instead throws minor gimmicks at you so you don't quit out of boredom. Other than that the plot is nothing special or interesting, it's just an excuse to keep going in the game and a halfbaked explanation why you switch graphics. The game could have worked better without its main gimmick and even then it would just be a mediocre action adventure.
I would recommend the first Evoland if you want a similar but more focused experience but if you play neither you won't miss out. Evoland 2 is all over the place and doesn't know what it wants to deliver.

First things first, I have many more "hours on record" than will show on the review, I've been playing in the browser for several weeks now. Actually I'll let my github activity chart speak for me:
On to the review. There is nothing else to compare this game to, it is a shiny gem sitting all alone in the genre it just made up. As the description talks about, your job is to program an AI to do your bidding in the world of Screeps. You are not alone. There are other AIs inhabiting this world, some programmed for evil, some for good, and some with tons of bugs (mine). If the idea of of a RTS MMO where you control your units, base, combat, and resource gathering 100% through code intrigues you, then you are exactly the type of player this game was made for.
Pros:
-Completely new game concept that appeals to programmers or people wanting to learn programming
-Friendly community to pester with questions
-Well-documented API
-Balanced game mechanics that rewards more seasoned programmers without punishing newcomers
-A chance to be a clever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with your coding skills
-Best way imagineable to learn Javascript, if you've been meaning to
Cons:
-Pricing structure might be a bit confusing, subscription is likely needed for MMO play
-Early access game, occasional bugs, mostly cosmetic
-Pretty steep learning curve that won't be forgiving for casual players or those who aren't really into programming
Just a word about the pricing. Basically you are paying to have your code run 24/7 on a remote server. In light of this, the 10 free CPU is fairly generous and would be enough to have a smaller-scale operation in the game world. Half of the fun is optimizing your code, so it would be possible to participate and enjoy the MMO from that angle. But if you want to be a kingpin in the MMO world, you are going to want a subscription, plain and simple. It isn't like Guild Wars where you buy once and have lifetime access AND be on the same footing as everyone else. I think the devs could be a bit more clear on that.
If you don't know Javascript, you are probably wondering if you should even try. Learning Javascript was actually the main reason I was interested in this game. I can't think of a more engaging way to learn a new coding language. I wish the had a game like this for all the languages I wanted to learn/maintain. There are nicely padded novice areas where you can start and learn at your own pace.
If your main interest is the RTS elements and you are hoping the coding thing won't get in the way, you'll probably want to avoid this game. You'll easily spend 1/3 of your time in a text editor/IDE, 1/3 observing the game world, and 1/3 in the IRC chat asking questions or looking things up in the API. If that actually sounds FUN to you, get this game right away.

I can not tell you properly with words how good this game is.
I will try however and I should start, as everyone, comparing it to old school RPG titles. Unlike recent RPG-called titles from this century —mostly made for the new generations of players, with little or no brains needed at all to solve quests—, Divinity: Original Sin looks like a true role playing game reminiscent of the old ages but with very cool new ideas —some of them unique— and fresh graphics.
The main characteristic, typical of Larian games, is the freedom to do almost everything you want: the game is classless, so you can choose a warrior in the beginning and later on you can change your mind and provide him with some spells or range skills, if you like it, when he level up; this way you will end up with four characters, two of them from the start and two more later on, with a combination of skills, traits and talents that fits you. You can interact with almost every item in the game: doors, chests, barrels, pictures, chairs, etc, and you can open them to look inside or destroy them if you prefer, or even take them and move them from one place to another. You can also choose if you prefer to talk to every NPC and solve quests, trade with them, or killing them if you like it, or even steal their items and loot their houses. Every action will make the villagers approach you in different ways, turning hostile to you or being polite instead. And if you don't like to trade with NPCs a lot you are able to craft your own gear and even spells if you choose to do it with the immense amount of ingredients and tools you will find everywhere.
What makes this game unique, and a gem, is a combination of the role playing part with the interaction between characters —even yours!— and its combat system. Divinity is not a combat focused game, it is more a conversational and exploration RPG title; however, combat is also very important and this is not a real time one, it is a turn-based combat system with action points mechanics that forces you to think about your resources, the enemies, and the environment; so each turn you can use your points to move, drink potions, attack or cast spells if you got enough points for them, or if you prefer you can reserve some of your remaining action points for your next turn, for example if you want to wait when the enemy is far away from you and later on you want to hit him two or three times in the same turn. The best part of the system is, no doubt, the chance —and mostly the need— of using the elements on your favour. It means you can cast a rain spell on your characters to stop them from burning; you can also cast rain on enemies, make them wet and then cast electricity spells for extra damage and stuns. You can also use ice spells if enemies are wet —state than come from your spells or from real rain itself!— to freeze them. You can shoot (after throwing it for example) an oil barrel with a fire spell to make it explode and damage the area, or just hit it with your arrows to make it pour the oil and later on cast fire on it if you wish. You can make an ice barrier to protect, wait until enemies are near it and then fire it, making it water and causing enemies to stumble, and then electrify them. You can combine elements to create clouds to avoid being a target. You can stealth and stab enemies too if you have the right character to do such a thing. You can use barrels and things of the environment to take cover, to protect you and to avoid damage. You can also try to flee if you find the situation too chaotic for your taste. You can... well, you can —and you should— do all these things if you want to survive, because combat is not always an easy task on this game.
For all these things I must say this is a heck of a game; I have not THAT fun with a videogame probably since some decades (I'm absolutely for real here). It's also true that there are some things that are not optimal and need improvement. Among the negatives, there is the camera movement, the slow pace of the game sometimes when you need to go from A to B, and the bad interfaz mechanics when you need to equip gear, change items from character to character, sell something or look at the items you got, or pick them. This is not a noob-friendly game; aside from the little dungeon tutorial at the start, you will find little or no help at all and you will find lost yourself if you are not used to RPGs games. However, asking in the forums will help you; there will be trolls, true, but overall the community will end up answering your questions and solving some of your starting problems, I'm pretty sure.
But if I take all these things together and put them all in a balance, I have to recommend this game to every player in the world. If you are an oldschool gamer you just can't pass on this. And if you are a new player and you didn't play or didn't even know any of the games other guys are mention, you have to give this one a chance and compare it yourself with the new RPGs. I promise you won't be disappointed.
PLUS you have also the Enhanced now, which add more quests, balanced skills, graphics, controller support, camera movement, subtitles in some languages, full voice actor and help with some of the issues the game got before. And even more difficult settings, with a new one with permadeath and only one savegame for massoquist tastes.
Harder, better, faster, stronger.

Quick number rating is on top. Detailed review is in bottom.
As you read this review, keep in mind that I'm heavily comparing this game to "To The Moon" as it is a sequal to said game. If you think that's unfair, so be it, but it's a pretty good benchmark by which to judge "Finding Paradise."
When I rate the game, a 0 is abysmal, 5 is average, 10 is near flawless.
So, my To The Moon benmark is -
10/10 Story
9/10 Soundtrack
3/10 Gameplay
0/10 Controls
Overall - 9/10
Compared to that, here's my Finding Paradise rating -
8/10 Story
10/10 Soundtrack
4/10 Gameplay
0/10 Controls
Overall - 8/10
STORY (What you're here for) -
I get what Kan was going for. I really do. And I appreciate the theme he was trying to drive home. It just didn't resonate as hard as TTM's story did. That's not to say that the story isn't good. It's emotional and interesting. But it could have done a few things better -
-Abstract theme.
Rather than being a story that delivers a message, Finding Paradise is a message that cloaks itself in a story. The story and characters take a backseat to the message Kan is trying to deliver, and the story suffers naratively for it.
-Convoluted, not complex.
The story loses a lot of the steam it builds up during the first half by pulling a "twist" out and undermining one of its characters (Faye) rather signifigantly. The best way I can describe it is that "simple" goes a long way. TTM pulled a twist with one of its characters, but that twist was built on a simple premise, memory loss. Instead in FP, we get a Matrix/Fruedian-esque explanation for the twist that confuses the player more that anything. And like I said, the character's twist isn't even really that complex. I saw it coming long before the game revealed it in its "AHA!" moment. The plot tried to squeeze a harder payoff from this than it actually earned.
-Side plot with little payoff.
Throughout the story, a sideplot develops with Watts. It is given neither a resolution nor an explanation, yet takes up a signifigant amount of time. I understand it will weave its way into the sequels, but that's no excuse to leave it narratively weak in this entry. Just because this is part of a larger story doesn't mean we shouldn't get a decent resolution here.
-What did Colin want?
I'm still confused on this one. I get what he says he wanted, and what he truly desired and all that, but I still felt as if his own wish undermined the purpose of the whole story. I can't say much beyond that without diving into spoilers. I just feel as though the plot's theme could have been expressed better if Colin's motives were more clearly fleshed out towards the end. Kind of like Johnny's wish, and how it becomes more clear what he really wants in the end. And just to make it clear, I don't believe the story intentionally made Colin's desire unclear for creative purposes. Where TTM hit a home run in pulling the rug out from under you and giving Johnny's true desire impact, FP comes just short of squarely hitting the ball and leaves the player a little confused.
Despite these issues I had with the story, it still hit enough emotional notes to be satisfying. It is still great, but not as brilliant as TTM's story was. Where TTM was a narrative puzzle where every thread fit perfectly together, FP has a few rough edges and out of place pieces, but it's still a great story with an even better message.
SOUNDTRACK -
Even better than TTM. They weaved the soundtrack into the story even more, which I appreciate. Kan outdid himself with the game's music. Bravo.
GAMEPLAY -
. . . . better than TTM? That's all I can really say, and that is not saying much at all. When I say "better" I mean it's more present and less frustrating, but it still feels in the way, like a roadblock that's not really part of the game. It feels neither intergrated into the story, nor fun or interesting to ineract with. At least there's a lot less frustrating traversing due to the smaller enviorments compared to TTM.
CONTROLS -
Awful. There's no excuse. Moving is a pain. Controling characters is a pain. Characters will often move where you don't want them to and interact with objects you have no intention of using. The interface is still annoying to navigate despite being bare-bones. It's like Freebird Games learned nothing from the complaints TTM got. Seriously. Fix it for the sequel.
SUMMARY -
Pretty good. The story could have been better in comparison to TTM, but if TTM didn't exist, this would be a 9/10 or 10/10 easy. Soundtrack was even better, I can really tell Kan learned a lot between TTM and FP. Gameplay is still more of a nuisance than enjoyable and the controls are abysmal, but we're all here for the story anyway. Again, biggest gripe is that the story tried to pull something that it thought was complex only to be worse of than if it would have just stuck with the simpler narrative it was building up in the first place.

I'm a big fan of this game so far. I've been playing PC games heavily since about 1990 and I follow a lot of indie games. This one is a highly immersive survival/builder. You survive, shoot, board, invade, build, farm, fly, and so on and it has a lot of potential as a great sandbox game. I just wish the multiplayer was more of a sandbox, but currently it's more of a faction vs faction experience with PvP zones. That may change. There seems to be a lot of changes and the team seems motivated to complete this project. The shooter experience, if I were being honest here, is not as good of an experience as most other shooters, but does contribute to the immersion of the game and is just a part of it. The storytelling and universe backstory is also very dull and could use some serious creativity. There are also some poor translations, although many of their developers are very well spoken in the forums. I believe the developer may be German in origin. One this that it does have is the visuals. It is an absolutely gorgious game, regardless of the low quality graphics. I've always felt that good developers can make even poor graphics work better than other developers can do with newer generation graphics, but that graphics aren't even that poor and as the game developes I see them being easily upgraded. The community is also strong and more of a creative and design-oriented type as they share their creations. I've even seen some groups from past sandbox games like EVE Online play on the servers. The dinosaurs on alien planets were a little weird at first, but I'm a sucker for dinosaurs and such, so I dig it anyway. I'd be pretty excited to see a Mawsonia Gigas in the ocean, or the like.
If you like immersive environments and science fiction, then I strongly suggest this game. Please try it. I'd really like to see more support for these developers. Now, after 189 hours, I think I need a break from this game, but I WILL be back soon. :)

This is without a doubt one of the best games released this year so far, and one I expect to see on many people's Top 10 lists at the end of the year.
This is an unforgiving platformer. It's VERY easy to die in this game. This makes it incredibly satisfying when you precisely navigate through the many obstacle filled areas, but also very frustrating when you make progress and die only to respawn where you were a few minutes ago, having lost all of that progress.
You can make save points nearly anywhere at anytime, but this takes energy and there is a short cooldown before you can make another. Through upgrades you can shorten the cooldown, and cause save points to restore you health, among other things.
Mobility in this game is probably its strongest point. You start out very limited in how you can move, but are constantly acquiring new ways to travel and overcome obstacles you couldn't before. This makes back tracking not so tedious, as there is almost always an upgrade you either missed, or couldn't get to coming through the first time. Jumps are precise, and moving around feels great.
Every inch of this game is brimming with beauty. There were many times when I was simply breathtaken with how gorgeous some of the locations were. The music is fantastic too and kicks in at all the right times.
10/10. This may very well be my game of the year. You would be doing yourself a disservice by not playing this game.

THE SOUNDTRACK.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a short game. I was able to beat it after about 8 hours of non-stop play. Still, that’s a fair deal given the price. The experience is worthwhile.
If you’re looking into this game and like what you see, do yourself a favor and get it. Play with a controller if you can.

I like the visual design and concept of the game.
Being a stealth game, it forces the player to avoid confronting the enemy, but you can still get out of it if there is only one guard.
A some-how workable cover system, body hiding, muffled landing, poison, door peeking, secret passages, alterate vision, putting out torches,  typical system in a stealth game.
The skill system lets you decide what style you take, but a more stealthy playstyle is favored.
Here comes the bad partS.
1. The damn bugs
There's a bug type enemy and they are the most annoying thing I've encountered in the stealth games I played. They are supposed to be blind and can detect the player if the player is moving in a loud fashion.
WHY THIS DOESN'T APPLY TO THE GUARDS? the guards yell like there is no tomorrow, literally hugging the bugs, I even throw dead bodies to the bugs hoping they will be distracted.
But no, it seems like the bugs are not only blind, but also racist to goblins.
When I sneak past them, they are aroused.
When I kill someone, they are aroused.
When I kill someone with a supposed muffled kill, they are still aroused.
The worst part? You cannot kill them if they are directly facing you and attacking.
2. Muffled kill
You are a goblin, with a dagger, the master of shadows.
You can approach someone unnoticed and perform a muffled kill.
So your victim's friends cannot hear his last cry for help.
BUT the master of shadows don't know if you let the body hit the floor, there will be noise.
So your victim's lifeless body hit the floor and sometimes flop like a fish on dry land.
Basically the surrounding guards will still be attracted, just with a smaller radius and after you kill the person.
Although the game want to make sure you have pay for the more stealthy way to kill,
I think the muffled kill is taking too long.
Come on, I am approaching the guard from behind, a swift slice to the throat while covering his mouth would be enough.
Our goblin friend like to climb on men's back, make out with them, then kill them with a "shhhhhh"
YOU SURPRISED THE GUARD! JUST KILL HIM FOR CHRIST SAKE!
3. Skills
So I like to kill people, in games of course, and that's why I like to get the killing related skills
While the drop kill works like a charm, the ledge kill seems to be not working for me
I'd prefer some skills to let you carry out tasks faster, i.e. lock picking, muffled kill
4. Poison
Goblins somehow cannot poison without sound, and guards like to hug their water source/fruits
So most of the time you would need to use a clone to do it for you, then destroy it before the guards kill it
and sometimes the so-called accident kill will still make the guards search for you or simply calling you out
I don't know if that's something I did wrong or just a bug, but its so inconsistant.
All in all, not recommanded for someone wanted to enjoy a stealth game

There is not a lot of variety between each level and you go back between the same locations often. Great stealth have very memorable and distinctive levels and that’s what prevents a stealth game from getting boring. A change in location, a change in objectives, a change in gameplay and styx fails on all of these. All the levels feel like a mish mash, it just feels like a mess and all the backtracking to the same areas you have already been through doesn’t help either. The gameplay feels the same from start to finish, they add new enemy types to make the game more difficult but all it did was make the game more frustrating. I didn’t care for the story at all I found it boring and I didn’t care for the characters and their turmoil’s. The stealth gameplay can be satisfying when you sneak past an area undetected and that’s the best thing about the game. It’s a hardcore stealth game, I like that there is a lack of offensive options so as a player you rely much more on not been seen and it’s a difficult game overall. If you like stealth games it’s worth trying out you might like it more than I did.

This game is a Half-Life 2 version of Left 4 Dead. And it is,dare I say,harder. NOW! I know I haven't played L4D,but I've got a feeling it's easier.
The hitboxes on the zombies can be sketchy.
The guns deal damage kind of ok,however! However,the zombies apparrently have deadened nerve sensors so instead of dying when taking a shotgun blast to the face(at a range of about 11-20 ft.),they continue to charge at you until you've unloaded about two or three shells into their faces.
The speed of your character varies with your health and shields.
Say if you have full health,you will outrun/run circles around most zombies.
At half health,you'll run a little slower.
At low health,you'll move at a slow shuffle.
If you're at low health,you have little-no-chance of a sucessful mission. PERIOD. This is if you are by yourself,though. If you have a team,or are playing with someone else you have little-to-a-little-less chance of survival.
"Why such negativity about low health? You can always shoot all the zombies." Ummm(back to the guns on this) Yes. You CAN shoot the zombies. And die because one saw your backside.
If a horde comes,you'd better hope you're NOT in a corner. That is THE ABSOLUTE WORST place to pick for a defensive position. "Why?" you ask again. Because. The zombies are not I repeat NOT to be taken lightly at ALL. They will rip you limb from limb with no sweat on their brow.
The zombies are arranged like so:

The Regular zombies:
These zombies have Arthritis,or something. Still deadly as heck? Yes. Can they run? No. That's why I made the bad joke. They do not go as slow as the Soldier zombie,though.
The Sprinter zombies:
These look exactly like the Regulars except! These can run. They usually start running towards you when they hear gunfire. When on mid-to-low health you need to watch it for these. They will cut you down fast. Fast is what they do.
The Soldier zombies:
These soldiers have been infected. They wear body armor,so that should tell you how easy they are to take down. They are the most powerful zombie in the game. They are slow zombies,about as slow as you with low health. BUT! you need to watch fo them when at full health. They will put you six feet under quick.
NOTE:being hit by zombies will slow you down temorarily.
When playing! Remember! You have Three objectives from my observation. #1:Plant the bomb. #2:Get to the extraction point. #3:TEAMWORK! TEAMWORK,TEAMWORK,TEAMWORK! Teamwork is IMPERATIVE! IMPORTANT! TOP PRIORITY! Without teamwork,you get nowhere except six feet under. Teamkilling is you digging your grave faster. Splitting up can be,too. Going solo is a death wish. Try to get a team together. Join a server with people on it.
Go solo,you die.
Go commando,you die.
Go CoD(thinking you're invincable 'cause of Black Ops Zombies and crap) and guess what? You die.
Without a doubt.
You will die.
A lot.
Get this game if you like zombies,teamwork,or one heck of a challenge. It's a fun game,don't get me wrong here. But it's not easy at all. Be prepared for your screen to have the following coming across it "Mission Failed".

I understand a lot of people are liking this game, and I feel like I would too. So let's start with what I liked about the game.
It's a platformer. Honestly, I just love platformers, and puzzle games excite me when I play them because I feel smart about solving the puzzle, and satisfaction literally washes over me as I beat a hard level.
The music was actually pretty nice to listen to, although it felt like it was just one song looping, it's a decent melody to follow while you're traversing this world.
The concept, as I'll state later as I get more into this, is incredibly fascinating and I really love the idea of manipulating colors to create platforms or make them disappear, and it's not just platforms; everything is made up of colors, specifically Blue, Green, and White. To play the game, you change the color scheme of the background to, as I said, make platforms and other things appear that are a different color of the background. A bird is one of the enemies in the game; it could either be Blue, Green, or White, and whatever color the background is, that bird will either appear as it is a different color, or it will not exist if you change the background to the same color as the bird. This, to me, is an incredibly innovative concept and, while not the most impressive, still pretty nice that someone even thought of this.
I did just call the concept a gimmick and, well, it's working. I'd be hooked if... there weren't some blaring problems. Now let's get to the parts I don't like.
I could not stand to play this game for more than 10 minutes at the most. It's going to take a lot of reworking to be considered a good game.
Right now, it's an amazing concept performed incredibly poorly. I might not be a game designer, but I know quite a bit of what it takes to make a good game, and the only thing good about Color Symphony is the concept, the music, and the level design(at least most of the time, but then again most of the levels I've played fabulously incorporated the controls of this game, no matter how much this game frustrates me); and yet, the controls are horrible.
The jump is fixed, which is a problem, especially when the boxes that determine if you're standing on a platform are terrible, as I've found myself to be stuck on the side of a platform, unable to jump or walk, and having to change the color and fall to my death.
In quite possibly every platformer, you'd control the height of your jump the longer you held down the jump button. I feel like a lot of this game would be made bearable if you could at least do that, among the many other things that need to be reworked, such as some of the level designs. While I said that they were great and that they incorporated the original intention of this game nicely, some of the levels, while beatable, didn't take much thought. What it did take, was changing the color multiple times to see if there's a platform, only to find a bird literally dive bombing you from inches away, a dog sitting right next to you and immediately biting you, and so on.
Another problem with the jump is the double jump feature. While it is pretty cool and sometimes saves you from when you would have taken a hit or died, if you wait too long on your initial jump, you lose the ability to jump a second time. Again, if you could double jump whenever was needed and not on a timer of some sort, the controls would be much more tolerated.
You can only take about 3 hits from absolutely anything in this game, and while you do regenerate your health, it takes way too long. I feel like that a part of the game is pulled away because you're so focused on regenerating health just so you can take another hit, meanwhile you have to change colors because a bird is coming for you and it's the same color of the platform you're standing on. If you change colors, you'll fall, possibly to your death. If you jump, it'll just fly vertically and attack you anyway. This needs to be reworked and thought over.
While I enjoyed this game, the simplicity of the controls mixed with the complexity of the level design was beautiful, and the music was nice, this is just too far from being a good game. I hope there's a big update on this game that the developer is working on, because I'd honestly love to play this game all the way through. It's just too much of a hassle to play at the moment.
That being said, I don't recommend this game AT THIS POINT IN TIME. If there's a big update changing at least the things I complained about in this review, I know I'm giving this game a solid 8/10.

Ok I originally had a rant but I've since decided to take this a more logical way.
The steam version you get a lifetime 10 CPU limit. This is good for a small group, one or two rooms and that's it. If that's all you plan on doing, which you can reach within 30 days, then you're good. However to go beyond you will need to pay a subscription fee.
Now - you can also get a 30 day 30 CPU limit demo which again, is more than enough to get up and beyond the 10 CPU limit and warrent the purchase of the subscription.
Thus, purchasing this is a waste of funds. Go to their site, try the demo and if you enjoy the game, pay the subscription. You get nothing else with this at this point and your money is better spent elsewhere.
The reason for the downvote is that features were promised, and not delivered in the time they were promised. These features were the sole reason I purchased this version since I already had a subscription on their site. Now, I feel ripped off. But read the logic for yourself - it's solid advice.
** Edit ** Changed to up vote
The reason for the change is because the personal servers are now available and you are no longer forced to pay a subscription to play the game. As it is, the game is really fun and a great way to get into programming. Now that it's as it should have been from day one, I can recommend it once more.

Stealth RPG like no other game I have played.
Lord of the rings-esqe stealth monster game. You play Rakash, a monster with the ability to clone yourself, turn invisible and climb around a medieval world filled with horrible humans and evil elves.  I was immediately at home with the controls having played Assasin's creed.  Moving in three dimensions around the dungeon-like tower is intuitivie and easy.  Evading the humans is not so easy, and once they spot you its almost certain death due to your relative weakness and the fact that they call for backup.  It has a quick save feature on F5, now there's a novelty (Quantum Break developers, you know who I'm talking about) and I used it after almost every kill.  Not that you have to kill anyone if you are clever enough to evade them; that was just my playstyle.   I think that's the best part of the game, the fact that you can use a variety of playstyles and still enjoy the game.
The impossible end of game boss (again Quantum break, take note!) was also blissfully missing, challenging, yes, especially if you were low on resources when you got there but definitely doable.  You can also replay missions at any time in the game so you can collect all the skill points before the end of the game if you are happy to do some grinding.  Often the second play through was actually more enjoyable as you can go around like a pro having learn't all the shortcuts in the map.
This game was a bit of a punt for me as I was not aware of it before I bought it but its well worth the money.  This one being older than the latest one is also cheaper so I recommend buying it first to cut your teeth on the Genre before tackling the second one.  All in all a surprisingly good game.

This review is about 70 hours in and I've since built bases, SV's, a single CV, and a hovercraft. I've also visited several planets.  Currently running a private server with a small group of friends. Here's a quick summary of some of the more major points I have.
Positives:
Building system is extensive and relatively user friendly. It takes a couple tries, but once you start to recognize how the blocks fit together it becomes a lot of fun. Futher, there's a lot of modification you can do as you grow as a player to improve your various structures.
Reaching new planets and seeing their overall terrain is fun, as well as space travel. Though there are similarities, I feel that each planet presents it's own strengths and (albeit minor) drawbacks. Though this doesn't go without saying that much of the exterior features, resources, and POI's are a little too similar.
The games logic system is sound. I like that there's so much to consider when building a full size base.
Negatives:
The game is designed with PVP in mind. I am much more a Co-op PVE player which means that combat is relatively repetitive. Most of the primary interest points become redundant to take over, and the thrill of raiding a base like a bunch of space pirates starts to wear off after the third or fourth go. I really hope that this feature is addressed in a future update. A greater challenge via AI, wildlife, and varied races/planets would add a lot. Further, one turret will protect your base and is rendered relatively useless as soon as you take down the planets drone base.
After warp capability, there is little in the way of challenge. It's relatively easy to prepare for a new base placement, and it can take as little as 10 minutes to set up a temp base that will provide everything you need to survive. This takes away from the excitement and thrill of landing on an entirely new planet, because we already know exactly what to expect. Varying requirements would help keep players surprised and add a challenge.
Overall: I have really enjoyed this game so far, and am very eager to see what the devs release. Currently, as soon as warp is achieved, the game becomes somewhat redundant and really takes a turn toward a casual playstyle, as opposed to one of constant survival, risk, challenge, and danger. On the bright side, and there is a major bright side, it takes a while to actually achieve warp, and it's wildly fun getting there. The game is well worth the $20 for the content received and has SO much potential to be something truly great.

This is without a doubt one of the best games released this year so far, and one I expect to see on many people's Top 10 lists at the end of the year.
This is an unforgiving platformer. It's VERY easy to die in this game. This makes it incredibly satisfying when you precisely navigate through the many obstacle filled areas, but also very frustrating when you make progress and die only to respawn where you were a few minutes ago, having lost all of that progress.
You can make save points nearly anywhere at anytime, but this takes energy and there is a short cooldown before you can make another. Through upgrades you can shorten the cooldown, and cause save points to restore you health, among other things.
Mobility in this game is probably its strongest point. You start out very limited in how you can move, but are constantly acquiring new ways to travel and overcome obstacles you couldn't before. This makes back tracking not so tedious, as there is almost always an upgrade you either missed, or couldn't get to coming through the first time. Jumps are precise, and moving around feels great.
Every inch of this game is brimming with beauty. There were many times when I was simply breathtaken with how gorgeous some of the locations were. The music is fantastic too and kicks in at all the right times.
10/10. This may very well be my game of the year. You would be doing yourself a disservice by not playing this game.

I am playing this for the second time. First time I played a mage and now I am playing a dual sword-wielding woman. There is definitely good replayability here. My old computer crashed a lot when playing this game, but it seems to be running fine on my new computer. I recommend a more modern machine when playing this game. Check the sys requirements. Wwhat can I say about it? Some of the battles can seem impossible. Save a lot. Not just a quick save, but named saves too. I like that many of the battles have to be repeated with new strategies. You will need heal spells, potions, poisons, nets, traps and some good strategy. Try to figure out how to get the overhead perspective to work because sometimes WASD camera control just won't do. I have a trackball mouse, so sometimes I can't see all the enemies or my PCs' positions. For regular mice, it should be the scroll-wheel to zoom all the way out. I like the spell effects. Complicated level up system with lots of points to spend from attributes (which cost the most so save for these) to special abilities (need to find a trainer) to weapon skills and spell strength. It's based on The Dark Eye, a German pen-and-pencil RPG that is more complicated, can you believe it, than D&D and very popular throughout Europe. Con: can be confusing how to finish some quests as they lack location markers and you will need to remember in which cities certain trainers are and the merchants that sell the equipment that you want. Overall, I find it more enjoyable than frustrating and it is a good turn-based tactical experience. Plus the voice acting is better than you'd expect. Pick it up on sale. Note: some poisons that are listed as lasting "whole battle" may not. Weapons with a magic bonus do not hurt magical creatures. When a wizard is wounded some spells will have very low chance of success, especially debuffing spells. Bandages often do not heal wounds even with high score in the healing talent, so visit a healer for wounds as needed.

Known for old-school point & click adventure games such as Deponia and Edna & Harvey, German developer Daedalic took gamers by surprise when releasing Blackguards – a tactical turn-based RPG based on The Dark Eye tabletop ruleset.
While the story sells itself as a dark narrative where you play as outlaws, it’s rather cliche and heroic. The Dark Eye ruleset is the true drawing point. While some rules where cut, such as most non-combat talents, it remains a solid and complex (if rather intimidating) classless system, offering ample freedom when creating your character. It’s a joy for hardcore players, but very poorly explained for newcomers. Sadly, the forced party members end up limiting some of your party building possibilities – sometimes even forcing a restart.
Blackguards knows its limitations and uses some unconventional design choices to compensate them, betting everything on its battles – cities are presented as simple animated backgrounds with stores and NPCs to talk with, exploration is limited to a 2D world map full of icons, dungeons are but a semi-linear sequence of battles without rest and the story is told via simple cutscenes, with an occasional decision to be made. This leads to an unique “Western Final Fantasy Tactics” feel, and while the game first hours are very linear, it later opens up to a wide range of interesting side-quests.
Daedalic’s background as an adventure game developer is felt here in an unusual way. There are no random battles in Blackguards, meaning that every encounter happens in an unique arena specifically designed for it, often with unique challenges or tactical puzzles. There are traps, time limits, holes that spawn enemies, movable and destructible objects, healing orbs, falling chandeliers, mechanical blades, flying dragons, swamp gas, giant tentacles, mind-controlling plants, draw bridges, collapsing passageways, a giant cage on a crane, etc.
There’s not a single RPG out there that offers so many interesting combat scenarios. This alone makes Blackguards a must-play for any tactical fan – or RPG designer.
Unfortunately, the game stretches out for far too long (40 to 60 hours), and the limited variety of enemies and equipment result in a rather stale second half of the game. Still, fans of Tactical RPGs will have a blast.

This could be a good medieval title some day, but since last year the game has had almost no population, tons of problems with lag and disconnection, hardware performance issues, and nothing added interesting enough to attract people back to it. The combat could be fun if the lag was sorted out and the rubberbanding could stop just for a day, but that seems to much to ask after waiting a year I have given up. The current "building" system is not what was pitched when I bought this, and as the game gets older nothing useful gets done. Maybe next year, maybe not.
All that aside this game has some redeeming features. The medieval world looks and feels nice, though the performance of the game is a little weak. There is a timed arena that pits the different factions against eachother for fun, anyone who is online is invited to join. The world map is fairly large, and has plenty of AI threats to deal with.
There are a few quests, but it doesn't take long to rip through them. Then the goal becomes more about exploring and killing what you find to finish levelling up while helping your faction take over and defend points of interest spread across the map. The crafting system is a little overwhelming but also a big part of the game as gear can be difficult to obtain otherwise.
Combat feels pretty good, when it isn't lagging. You can block, counter, kick, and all the fun things you would expect, but it rarely works right. This needs the most work on this game, and I think more people would be interested in trying it again.
Building currently is limited to upgrading the points of interest after you have taken them for your faction. While this isn't a bad idea, what I read about when I first bought this years ago was the ability to build houses and castles in the open world. Hopefully that still happens.
