I picked this game up during the Thanksgiving sale. I do not regret it. It is a throwback to the glory days of mmo's in my opinion. Where skill,  NOT gear, marked the measure of a player. This low/no magic medieval based pvp-centric mmo is exactly what I feel the mmo-verse has been missing for a long time.
Do you like a sense of danger while exploring? Do you miss the days when venturing out of the pillowy confines of your starter town was a risk-reward double edged sword? Enjoy streamlined combat that is easy to pickup but takes considerable practice to master? In Gloria Victis YOU can make a difference to swing the war in your factions favor regardless if you like solo, small group or large scale pvp.
How does a player driven economy sound that's fueled largely by crafting? How would you like to NOT have to depend on RNG drops from some heavily farmed instance/boss to bless you with that 1 item that will make/break your entire build? In Gloria Victis there are no false RNG walls to self improvement, only your desire to push limits and attain a more powerful mastery of the detailed (detailed, not tedious) crafting system.
This game is on it's way to greatness. The development team works hard to implement feedback from the community and to take feedback under careful advisement.
The game itself is quite PVP-centric, if you're looking for world bosses-raid bosses-dungeon bosses etc, with fancy yawn-inspiring mechanics you may end up disappointed. In Gloria Victis the most powerful boss you may ever encounter is an adversary from another faction, a cunning ruthless player who perhaps caught you off guard and looted your newly crafted sword sealing his/her fate as your newfound nemesis. Revenge is sweet and a powerful motivator. Gloria Victis features an innovative partial loot system which encourages players to know how to replace what they wear via crafting.
Is this game 100% polished? No. There are issues, it's Early Access after all. However, since it has been out for quite some time as a newer player I can say that the bugs/issues I've encountered pale by comparison to the bugs/glitches that plagued major triple A release titles during their BETAS and even at launch such as Elder Scrolls Online.
Some of the issues I've seen thusfar... a few bad meshes scattered throughout the world (which is beautiful by the way).
Occasionally if you aggro a mob while harvesting a node it can prevent you temporarily from swapping to your main weapon though I've never been put in any jeopardy of dying as a result of that glitch.
The new Treasure Chest system (which is rewarding and really encourages exploration) I've noticed the "E" to interact with the chest can stay on the screen after you've looted the chest... this goes away simply by hitting "E" again.
There are occasional pathing issues of some mobs, and if you have a high ping they may seem a bit out of sync (i.e. an aggro'd mob is walking toward you and then kind of moves in from a different angle.)
That's the majority of the issues I've seen thusfar. None of them break the game (for me) and overall I'm having an absolute blast playing and discovering the world.
There is no cash shop. There is no pay 2 win. It's on sale. The game needs more players. Buy it, it's worth every penny and developers like this deserve your support more than some massive company that couldn't care less if you're satisifed with their product.

Best enjoyed in local versus mode despite its lack of a "shared/splitscreen" official Steam tag.
Nidhogg is a simple concept; You kill your opponent you get to move forward progressing level screens, he kills you, he gets to move forward. First one to reach the end screen their designated direction wins. This makes for a great tug of war, insane comebacks, and thrilling grudge matches. They tried to give the combat some nuance with the ability to hold your fencing sword at three heights (plus throw) but like any basic player vs player combat it comes down to timing more than anything. All the technique in the world isn't gonna stop somebody from timing the perfect roll or jump to run right past you. And that's where the game gets interesting. Besides the beginning stalemate for the first kill, combat only hangs on the "defender". Once you get your kill and control the ability to press forward, that's what your focus is on. Many times its better to just get past your opponent and continue your run rather than engage. It really levels the playing field and makes it fairly easy for anybody to pick up and enjoy. Then you toss in four levels with decent variety and things stay interesting enough for a competitive sitdown.
With the advent of in-home streaming, HTPC's, etc. Nidhogg finds a comfortable home in the living room to get the competitive juices flowing with friends and family on the "bigscreen". I'm a fan of local shared/split-screen games on the PC that are done well. And while utterly basic and simple (and thus probably overpriced) this delivers pure fun. Wait for a sale, but if you like making temporary enemies with friends on the couch, this is good stuff. Recommended.

First to quickly note: My recommendation isn't that you don't play it, afterall it's completely free. It simply means whether or not I would go
to recommend it and why. Of course you can overlook most of the problems I've experienced with this game since it's free and probably has little to no budget but they're still problems nonetheless which I feel shouldn't be overlooked in a review.
Color Symphony is a platforming puzzle game. In it, you switch between three colours to avoid or reveal like-coloured objects which can range from birds, dogs, spikes, platforms, doors and more. As you progress from door to door, the levels become harder and more complicated.
In general, it's a great concept that shines at the start. As you progress though, the limitations begin to show and, along with poor physics and collision detection, turns enjoyment into frustration. The cause can be any of the following and more:
Once you die, you start back at the entrance to the level, which is forgiving at first but eventually as the levels become longer and the whole game becomes trial and error it becomes necessary as no hints are given as to what to expect beforehand.
As far as I played there was only one music track. Though it's a good track, being the only one in the game, it gets repetitive. Visually, everything is plain and generic with random props placed here and there in the background but, like the music, there's no variety and it gets boring fast. The visuals to however give the feeling of being in a void which is likely what the game is going for.
So to summarise, Color Symphony is a great concept which shines in its simplicity but gradually becomes more and more unfair and frustrating as it progresses.

Quake 3 Arena isn't really an expected sequel of Quake franchise. It actually throws off single-player portion fully and focuses on mutliplayer part, which was quite wise as of that time. Arena-styled Deathmatch was still hot and at the peak of interest, you see. It came out in 1999. It's notable that in same year Unreal pulled off same trick, coming out with Unreal Tournament.
It also had ports to Dreamcast and PS2. Dreamcast is awesome, supporting keyboard+mouse, 4-player split-screen, had online multiplayer and had new awesome music that PC doesn't have. PS2 version didn't had online part, but had improved single-player, with some story, from what I know. Didn't check out that one yet, but it has different final boss.
As you expect, it has usual technical problems nowdays.
Game doesn't support widescreen by default. But you can look up Community Guide on Steam, one explains how to set it up easily.
Steam Overlay is conflicting with this game as well. If you try to immeditly play at default setup, you will be horrified by all the graphical flickers and glitches. You have to go to game's system options and disable "GL Extension", after that it should be fine.
Though, some computers will still experience crashes here and there. In this case you will have to disable whole Steam Community for this game. Bai bai overlay.
I think that auto save from Team Arena expansion may erase Quake 3 Arena save. Goes both ways. So be careful with that one.
As for multiplayer community, it's somewhat alive. There are some servers with some players. Most often you will meet servers full of bots. Other times it will be pro players who will rip you apart.
So, what can I say. Q3 is a classic arena, where you spawn, you stock up, you encounter, you restock. Or respawn. While strafejumping and bunnyhopping like a chicken. Everybody starts the same, they spawn in random spot with no good weapons. After that you have to grab all the goodies on the map. Weapons, ammo, health, armor and powerups. Stocking and restocking is quite important, having more armor and health than opponent will put you into superior position. If you are good at shooting and maneuvering, that is. Health and armor over 100 slowly drop down, so you want to make use of it. You also want to be the first to grab the respawning powerup, which is announced by subtle sound. Pro players time it in mind. Remaining powerups drop from defeated players.
And when it comes to duel, you should make sure that opponent will not get to timed powerups and big bonuses. It's called "Arena Control". It'a also wise to sometimes not to encounter the opponent.
It also has some physics exploits like bunnyhopping and harder to pull off strafejumping. Thankfully, bots don't use them.
Weapons are designed to be balanced with each other and to be useful in each own situation. It's mostly a tried and classic combination weapon set, of rocket launchers, shotgungs, railguns and such, so people who wanted a gun that ricochets around walls and turns enemies into ice cream critized them heavily. They work really nicely though. Railgun requires at least two hits on a row for average opponent, which is always better than usual instakill of sniper rifles in other games. Shotgun is good even for medium distance and just gives off a nice hitscan punch. Rocket Launcher is universal, good for splash damage with huge direct hit damage. Good for rocketjumps too. Really, it's great to see that the game took more balanced weapon approach of Quake 2 and tried to combine it with faster pace of Quake 1.
Level design is great too, with nice astethic. It's either sci-fi base or more of gothic-hellish red style. Like Quake 1 style, but more careful and even more evil at times, it's great. Has enough verticality. Just nicely done, with all the curves and corners. It also has some interesting "platforms in black space" levels, though those are the worse bunch as far as balance goes. Too much open space, railfun users be happy. Gets even worse on the level which has many lift-platforms, making it all look quite messy. Otherwise, nice layouts with nice looks.

The in manual says that mysterious race Vadrigar teleported the greatest warrior of all time into arenas for their own amusement and they can't be fooled by Death, combatants just respawn. in the end you will beat current champion Xaero, who's spirits will leave the body and it will turn into statue. Did I tell you that bots actually have a bit of behavior personality and favourite weapons?

So, Blackguards, either loved or hated it seems.
I wouldn't go in either direction. To me this is a solid Combat RPG with a pretty decent story and excellent voice acting. The characters are a bit stereotypical, though. There's your hero, the crazed dwarf who sees dragons everywhere and the macho mage, as well as some other characters I won't spoil now, but their backstory and motivations aren't that much better. Still, they managed to make this into a more interesting story than Dragon Age: Inquisition...for a CRPG it's more than you need.
Be warned though, this is NOT a traditional RPG, you will NOT be exploring a huge world, you will NOT have hundreds of different dialogues and quests and choices. There is quite a bit of that but it's not the main focus. Quests are usually: go here and do that. And by go here I mean "click on the overworld map to move to one of the interactive points" or on the city screen. This is how you navigate the world of Blackguards, you click a POI on a map and your party moves there. This is either a city in which you can further navigate different parts of said city and speak to people, buy stuff, heal and rest. Anything else is mostly combat.
Combat and gear in general are pretty in depth. There are different types of weapons which all have advantages and disadvantages and must be learned to use. So your spear wielding barbarian is no good with a 2 handed sword for instance. To improve a certain aspect of a character you have to spend AP. You can spend AP for pretty much everything: ranged combat, specific weapons, magic resist, hit points, detecting traps, healing wounds, improving spells, movement points, etc. Like I said the system is pretty deep. Special weapons also have special attributes that you need to factor in. Maybe a weapon does less "attack damage", but has a +6 fire damage value, increasing it's effective damage again. You need to do the math in your head, though. There aren't too many unique weapons though so not that big of a deal. Of course there is also armor and set bonuses as well as magic you need to consider.
Once you're happy with your characters' equipment you can do battle. On the easiest difficulty most battles can be won at first try. On the harder difficulties, however, the game becomes rather difficult and potentially frustrating. And I think this is why the game has "so many" negative reviews. The combat can be unforgiving and you can't save during a battle. Battles also last forever. Do you like Heroes of Might and Magic? Yeah, like that in the late game. One battle can easily take up to 30 minutes, esp. on higher difficulties. There is of course also a random element in hit and crit chance. There is no 100% hit chance, only when an enemy is prone. And even then I needed to roll x, which I did, and still missed. I'd say that's a bug. Oh, apparently the chances are decided by dice and not actual percentages, so beware of false security. There's a handy battle log though.
Overall I feel that this is a pretty good product IF you are looking for this type of game. If you want Dragon Age or Baldur's Gate, don't bother. This is not that.

I'm writing this review just after I have beaten the story once, after 18,5 hours of gameplay. Which I consider a decent length, not too long and not too short.
Now, first things first: Styx is not a game for the casual player. If you like mindlessly running about in Assassin's Creed with no real difficulty to it, then stick to that hot garbage. Styx is challenging, you have to think about which route to take, who to kill first, how to move in between all those enemies while staying unseen. Which skills do I want to take into the next mission? What playstyle do I wanna use (yes, you can follow multiple playstyles and the game encourages trying them out or playing through it multiple times or replaying missions)? You have to manage your resources well.
But all that is incredibly fun. When something works out you feel accomplished. And in between the missions you get to see nicely drawn cutscenes and that's where I get to the best part about Styx: Master of Shadows:
The STORY! God damn, I would bet every single one of you that it is absolutely impossible for you to predict the story, it is so fresh, original and just awesome.
So if you like sneaky games where you have a really cool character who swears a lot and speaks his mind, while experiencing an awesome story, and do not shy away from a nice challenge, then go ahead and play this game, you shall not regret it.

It takes either an extremely good game, or an extremely bad game, in order for me to take the time to sit down and write a review. And with "Ori and the Blind Forest," I would feel ashamed to not give this game my support.
Out of the many games I have played throughout my life, this game is, by far, one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. And I am not just talking about visually. It is pure gold not only due to its superior visuals, vibrant colors, and breath-taking graphics, but due to its sound as well. I'm not even talking about JUST the music. Even the SOUND EFFECTS are golden. Like the little noises Ori makes when you receive damage, use special skills, etc. The integration of music is astounding too. For example, when traversing throughout the world, the music that plays in accordance to your location and the progression you've made in the story flows and transitions fluently and smoothly, granting you a much more immersive experience.
I don't just like this game solely because of it's beauty, though. In addition to my concurrence with individuals who state this is a form of art within a video game, I would also like to inform you that this game consists of even more value than that. In addition to the colors that gracefully lather themselves onto your screen, and the melodic harmonies that caress your ears, this game is fun as hell, too. The gameplay you will experience is smooth, satisfying, and keeps you from wanting to take a break for very long periods of time.
Lastly, and one of my favorite things about "Ori and the Blind Forest," is that the game is definitely reminiscent of Metroid, as well as The Legend of Zelda. As I was unlocking new skills throughout the game, I couldn't help but notice the experience I was having to be resemblant of "Metroid Fusion" for the GameBoy Advance system, which I absolutely loved playing. And the little fairy-like creature that follows you around everywhere and offers you advice/guidance while playing this game reminds me of Navi, from "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time." These aspects found within "Ori and the Blind Forest" only strengthened and intensified the positive experience I had while playing this beautiful game.
This game is an extremely hard-to-find masterpiece of a platform game, and it should be played by anyone and everyone it appeals to.
TL;DR
-One of the best platform games I have ever been lucky enough to come across and get my hands on
-BEAUTIFUL graphics
-BEAUTIFUL music & sound effects
-Extremely immersive as well as emotional story
-Entertaining, satisfying, and all-around fun gameplay
-Rekindles nostalgic experiences found within previous titles such as "Metroid" and "The Legend of Zelda"
-Essentially the best $20 dollars I have ever spent
Purchase this game and play it, because if you haven't, then you're missing out.

The visuals of this game are in real stark contrast with the game mechanics. Everything looks very nice, but when it comes to the combat, skill system, rest periods and so forth, the game begins to feel like it was drafted twenty years ago.
It's just so inbalanced. The classes are not in balance. The attributes, skills, talents, weapon talents and special talents (I probably forgot something) are not in balance. The cost of items and services - compare for instance provisions, healing, bandages, potions and taverns - are not in balance.
The game is haphazard inside and outside of combat. You may begin a series of events only to notice that there is no way to return anymore. There are unforeseeable series of battles, and failing one may set you back an HOUR of progress. Failing even one spell might flip the situation completely. Putting all points in a single weapon talent can screw you up, because, well... find it out yourself.
But all this got me thinking. Are we too pampered with forgiving games? Perhaps. Here's a game that you can seriously break by playing it wrong (or right, in a good way!). Here's a game that requires putting those annoyingly flexible talent points into right places. So begrudgingly thumbs up for this one.

I was a big fan of the original Thief series back in the day.  I was really excited when I heard that Thief would be returning and really disappointed when it didn't (another game bearing the "Thief" name showed up instead but had little resemblance to the games that laucnhed it - that's the topic for another review, however).
I then stumbled onto Styx: Master of Shadows.
For my money, a good stealth game needs to provide several key ingredients.
1) Light and dark are your bread and butter.  If you're hiding in the shadows you should be harder (but not impossible) to see.
2) Sound can help you and hinder you.  Hear a guard coming?  Hide.  Or run too fast and you alert those guards to your presence.
3) Choose your own path.  I'm not just talking about whether you choose to kill guards or not, I'm talking about having multiple routes to your objective.  There are some areas of the game that become linear, but for the most part you usually have multiple avenues.
The game is not without its faults.  Some later levels reuse the exact same locations as earlier ones, with the difference being you have to make your way from what used to be the end of the level towards what used to be the beginning.  As well, there are a few of the bonus challenges that can be hard to complete due to glitches in the game.
Overall, this game definitely gave me that old school Thief feeling of creeping through locations unseen waiting for that perfect moment to dart past guards with their backs turned.  If you're looking for that old school feel, forget the "Thief" reboot and go with Styx instead.

The most common offender is cutscenes, particularly the transition from the Underground to Mean Street North. Some are never able to move past that point, others can reload the game and move on. I was able to get through it, but whenever I attempted to use the camera item I immediately crashed to the desktop (even just staring at the ground, so it's not a weird issue with draw distance or loading lots of art and textures), and have since given up further attempts to make the game work.
The community hub is filled with similar reports, and these issues have never been resolved by the developer. There is a thread reporting some success by
just to make the game work correctly, to give you an idea of what a poor port this is. On top of these problems, the controls feel clunky and this version of the game removed co-op, leaving you to deal with the occasionally frustrating and clumsy AI controlling Gus.
If you're able to look past the bugs and serious functionality issues, and not run into any sections that block progression, the game itself is an average platformer with lots of collectibles, but nothing particularly special. If you really want to play it you should stick to the console versions.

This is exactly what I wanted from Evoland's sequel. The game is not perfect of course, but the developers overall did a good job: a longer game with much more game play variety (and references) and a good story. So I'd say:
PROS
+ Everything that was great from the first game is still there
+ They removed the "boring" parts from the first game (JRPG and ARPG)
+ A lot of new game styles added. Loved the shoot 'em up and the bejeweled ones!
+ Decent card game, even if a bit too basic
+ A couple of songs are really good
+ The story is nice and also pretty dark. You'll only get some hints of this at the end, but there are some solid theories around the internet that helps understanding it. All in all I'm not convinced the story makes perfect sense, but you don't really have to think TOO much about it. It's time-travel stuff after all
+ Best aspect: it was in a low price bundle :3
CONS
- I had two separate issues with the future: it's incredibly bad optimized (i had several video and audio lags, and my laptop is pretty decent) and it has some bad hidden secrets (hiding chests and levers in spots where you simply can't see them because you can't turn the camera around is not particularly good)
- The fact that you encounter the smith that forges the best equipment in the game so early is a bit meh. Ofc you can't have the complete set until the late game, but having the best sword after like 1h of game is a bit disappointing. I would have placed all the orikon ores in the last stage of the game or something like that
- I know that making 61 different cards is not trivial, still, I didn't really like the power creep aspect. For example some "hard" to find late game cards (Largo Le Grand, Nawi) are worse version of cards you got much earlier
- I also know that making a time-travel story without errors is really difficult, but there are some times when the events seems a bit off. Like, the time-travel interaction worked in a specific way till that moment, and then happens something that's incoherent with the previous behavior
- The fact that the skills with which you interact with the puzzles have a CD is sometimes really annoying
- The Sylph forest dungeon is one of my worst gaming experiences
- Why are secret stars so oddly distributed? You can get like 25/30 in the first 6h of play, and the remaining 5 in the following 10h+
Some of the cons are really just nuisances, but still. The price on steam might be a bit high (ty HB!), but for me it's a solid 8.5/10

7 or so hours in and I've made my thoughts on this thing. Note that this review contains spoilers on gameplay, but not story.
1). I enjoyed the opening few hours of the game, it's quite cute, the storyline has potential and the artwork is nice.
2). The music is repetitive but good.
3). The story thinks it's cleverer than it actually is, but I like the little side plots and how the characters change over the timelines.
4). Very often throughout the game you get sections which change the gameplay dramatically. These are the weakest parts of the game IMO. Spoilers if you don't want to know. In the time I've played, I've played a stealth section, which was fine, a top down shooter which was easy, boring and went on for far too long, a street fighter thing which just sort of happened, and a bomberman section which was boring, frustrating and went on for ages. You fight a boss in this mode, and she takes the bombs away from you half way through. This makes the boss fight a lot easier, as she simply kills herself with the bombs like you've been doing for the last half hour.
5). There are filler sections in a town, and these are cute but again go on for far too long. The timelines storylines mean that you actually go to the town several times, and twice you need to crawl through the town, talking to everyone very slowly, going to each building, solving easy and tedious puzzles, find hiding children by pressing action on everything (which you have to do twice), and playing a restaurant server mini game.
As someone who hasn't really played these kinds of games before, I might not be 100% the target audience. However what I can say is that I got bored and frustrated a lot. The core gameplay is nothing special, but the graphics are colourful and the story vaguely interesting. However, the many other games within the game are pretty alright at best and are just plain frustrating at worst, and overall detract and add filler to what would otherwise be a pretty solid 7/10 game.

Subject to change, but first impressions are decidedly mixed. Graphically it's not bad, though the lush environments look better than the moonbase and interior, though the tutorial places you squarely in the least appealing environ from the outset. The keys used are minimal in most cases, which is a good thing, but with a few extra random keys thrown in when you find yourself wondering if a small context sensitive popup would have been more friendly instead. The crafting system is clearly intended to have some logical design, but falls short and I find it to be very unfriendly. When you find yourself mousing over non-descript images trying to find what your'e after crafting, clicking through tabs, then repeating to find components, it's not ideal - I would have preferred some text to help on that front. It comes across from the outset as the sort of game that if you're used to it, it's fine, but doesn't feel friendly enough to encourage new players to stick around.
As far as the tutorial is concerned, it's not too bad though you might feel a little like meaningless tasks are being thrown at you. Having been asked to make some planters etc, mine bugged out, and I found myself, 4 planets later, without enough materials to make more, and the quest log still asking me to make 3. That said, it's early days and an alpha so be a little forgiving - feedback and bugs are all part of the alpha "job" so should be expected.
In regards to change, personal thoughts are I'd have rather seen the tutorial place me on the surface after an "accident", with a handful of events occurring and a few meaningful tasks to accomplish. I'd have rather seen much more limited crafting options on the menus (ie remove the stacks of other options) initially, building up to others and revealing them only when unlocked - via a more natural feeling progression system for skills. Best not to drown new players in buttons and clutter and build up tech / knowledge.
Aside from that, shows some promise and will spend some more time on the weekend getting to grips with it. For now, it's still a slightly shaky tumbs up.

This is the kind of game that's hard to review. It's not because of anything in particular, but more so the fact that trying to describe what makes Finding Paradise so special without spoiling even a minute detail is nearly impossible. It is an emotional rollercoaster that gives incredible insight into one man's life. It is a philosophical debate wrapped up into a series of key questions. It has plot threads just present enough to make you wonder what else there is. And it is just in time to be on my personal favorite list of games for 2017
Finding Paradise is, at this moment, the best thing that Ken Gao has made thus far and it makes me excited to see what is next for Freebird Games.

I know I'm in the minority here, but I liked this more than To The Moon (and I loved To The Moon).
First of all, while I like the premise and plot of both To The Moon had some painfully bad dialog at times. In Finding Paradise each character has their own voice instead of everyone sounding like the same nerdy teenager. It still squeezes in some comic relief video game and anime references, but handles the much better this time around.
Second, while it has a few action scenes, they don't feel completely broken like in To The Moon. The puzzle minigames also felt like less of an interuption.
And third, the story hit much closer to home for me. I figured out what was what they were going to have to do at the end, even before the childhood friend was introduced. But the specific way those events play out hit me much harder than I expected. Near the end I was like, "So I guess this game won't be sad like To The Moon..." and then those damn onion ninjas caught me off guard. Wow, this story can really make you think about life, love, memories, aging, motivation, truth, and dreams. To The Moon is great, but it's just so specific and sappy where this feels like something most people have experience with.
If there's one fault, I didn't find the music as completely awesome as To The Moon, but it did catch me surprise how much the main theme had grown on me by the end.

My Favorite movie.
R.I.P. Brandon.
The night before his wedding, musician Eric Draven (Brandon Lee) and his fiancée are brutally murdered by members of a violent inner-city gang. On the anniversary of their death, Eric rises from the grave and assumes the gothic mantle of the Crow, a supernatural avenger. Tracking down the thugs responsible for the crimes and mercilessly murdering them, Eric eventually confronts head gangster Top Dollar (Michael Wincott) to complete his macabre mission.
The following scenes were completed after Brandon Lee's death:
-Draven first enters the apartment after digging himself out of his grave: footage of Lee walking through an alley in the rain was digitally composed into the scene where he walks through the doorway. Computer technology added drops of water to the door frame to make the water on his back not seem out of place.
-The shot of Draven falling from the window was made by digitally composing Lee's face (complete with simulated blood) onto a body double.
-The scene where Draven puts on his make-up was filmed using a double. The face in the smashed mirror was Lee's, computer-altered to fit the shards. The image of Draven walking towards the window with the crow on his shoulder was a double with Lee's face added during lightning flashes.
-When Sarah visits the apartment, we never see Draven's face as it is a double.
James O'Barr stated on the Crow DVD that when he met the movie's executives, they originally wanted to make this a musical staring Michael Jackson. He immediately laughed uncontrollably thinking it was a joke, only to find that they were quite serious. It was only until Brandon Lee and Alex Proyas came on board that the movie took a more serious role.
"So spake the Cherub, and his grave rebuke. Severe in youthful beauty, added grace. Invincible: abash the Devil stood, and felt how awful goodness is, and saw virtue in her shape, how lovely. Saw and pin'd his loss, but chiefly to find here observed his lustre visibly impaired, yet seemed"

I have tried nearly all of the Medieval/survival/crafting games out on Steam, and this is the one that I havent refunded.
Of course in its current state of development there are aspects and mechanics not finished or fully implemented, but I was pleasantly surprised to find that the game is fully playable, and enjoyable.  The game is littered with dozens of different resources which can be crafted into hundreds of items and components. Recipies for crafting can either be learned through character development, or purchased from specialized smiths/tailors/merchants. Gathering the necessary ingredients for any given item is sufficiently challenging, though can get tedious if you arent the patient type. The actual crafting system makes sense and is easy to grasp.
My experience with the playing community has been mostly positive, without much of the toxicity that you find in games like Rust.  For example, I wandered into enemy territory searching for Pyrite to mine. A player from an opposing faction took offense to my trespass and swiftly buried an axe in my back.  Possibly realising how hapless and lost I was, the player tracked me down afterward and gave me my helmet back, which he looted from my corpse. It was the first peice of armor I ever made, so I was quite attached to it.
Of course there are glitches, bugs, and sometimes laggy episodes, but the developers seem far more engaged in seeing this through to a finished product.  In my opinion, the worst part of the game is that it needs more players.  Give it a try.

7 or so hours in and I've made my thoughts on this thing. Note that this review contains spoilers on gameplay, but not story.
1). I enjoyed the opening few hours of the game, it's quite cute, the storyline has potential and the artwork is nice.
2). The music is repetitive but good.
3). The story thinks it's cleverer than it actually is, but I like the little side plots and how the characters change over the timelines.
4). Very often throughout the game you get sections which change the gameplay dramatically. These are the weakest parts of the game IMO. Spoilers if you don't want to know. In the time I've played, I've played a stealth section, which was fine, a top down shooter which was easy, boring and went on for far too long, a street fighter thing which just sort of happened, and a bomberman section which was boring, frustrating and went on for ages. You fight a boss in this mode, and she takes the bombs away from you half way through. This makes the boss fight a lot easier, as she simply kills herself with the bombs like you've been doing for the last half hour.
5). There are filler sections in a town, and these are cute but again go on for far too long. The timelines storylines mean that you actually go to the town several times, and twice you need to crawl through the town, talking to everyone very slowly, going to each building, solving easy and tedious puzzles, find hiding children by pressing action on everything (which you have to do twice), and playing a restaurant server mini game.
As someone who hasn't really played these kinds of games before, I might not be 100% the target audience. However what I can say is that I got bored and frustrated a lot. The core gameplay is nothing special, but the graphics are colourful and the story vaguely interesting. However, the many other games within the game are pretty alright at best and are just plain frustrating at worst, and overall detract and add filler to what would otherwise be a pretty solid 7/10 game.

Ultimately, this is a game that I would recommend, but there are some simple factors about it that bothered me and I felt could have been handled better.  I'll start off with the positives first though.
Starting off, this game wasn't really what I had expected from the trailer and description.  I thought it was going to be much more linear, with a clear progression from early eras of video gaming to more advanced graphics and gameplay styles.  You would more or less just steadily progress and level up through 8 bit to 3D graphics.  However, the plot is more dynamic than that, as you will bounce back and forth steadily throughout the game, which I thought was more engaging than what it could have been.
One area I find difficult to cover is all of the different styles of gameplay that wind up being covered through this game, as it isn't a clear good or bad thing in my view.  On the one hand, it gives a nice slideshow of various popular games from the 80's and 90's, letting younger players get a taste of what gaming used to be like and giving a nostalgia trip for those of us who grew up in that era.  On the other hand, these transitions can be quite jarring, with some areas being more tedious or boring for people who don't find themselves liking a particular style of game, especially since none of them are skipable.  I certainly wasn't a fan of sneaking through the jail myself, but each section only plays out for so long before you wind up beating it and not needing to deal with that style of gameplay again in the play through.  Plus, since there are three levels of difficulty, that can be adjusted at any time, any unbearable sections can be played on an easier difficulty to speed up the process.  These shorter tastes of various game styles can be a downside for those who find themselves enjoying a certain style of game mechanics, but they can always go to the original game series for more of the same.  I would ultimately call this a positive because the developers clearly took plenty of time recreating these game mechanics and did a fairly good job at it.  Nothing came off as a sloppy rush job, none of the segments felt like the developers were just putting in that style of gameplay because it was quick and they didn't have to try.  It seemed like they wanted an honest recreation.
I was quite pleased with the card game, as it was pretty well designed considering it's only an extra collectible to earn in the game.  I won't delve into the full details of how the card game works, but I would say that it came off as one of the more fun parts of the game for me.  The strategy and attributes of the cards are simplistic enough that it takes little time to figure out, and once you start building up a decent deck you have what you need to win without needing to play the strongest or best cards.  The developers might consider building up a full, stand-alone card game sometime because what they have here is a decent foundation.  One slight complaint is that it takes a while before you can start playing the game, which is strange since it is played throughout all of the time periods.  Not sure why they waited so long before bringing it into the game.
The story is certainly not what you would normally expect from this style of game, with it being pretty clear who are the main pro/antagonists.  However, even after clearing 100% of the game, I'm still a bit unclear on the exact timeline of the game's events.  If you like some ambiguity and uncertainty in a plotline, this would be a positive, but if you prefer a more clear outcome this wouldn't be for you.
Something I would see as more negative in the game was some of the pacing of collectibles and items in general.  Early on I was finding collectible stars fairly quickly, but throughout the rest of the game they became much more spaced out.  Might have been nice to not stack so many right at the onset of the game.  Placement of some items also seemed kind of odd, like when you get access to the library and find a chest of maana right in the middle of the room.  Seemed strange that nobody else would have opened it or left it there for some unspecified reason.  I think the worst offender was the Stone of Time.  When you first acquire the item, it seems incredibly important and mystical, and all it achieves at first is to create a set of stairs up a short cliff.  I swear the characters could probably stand on each other's shoulders and pull each other up to get the same result, and until the climax of the game it serves no other purpose.  Kind of a buzz kill considering what needed to be done in order to acquire it.
As I played through the later portions of the game, traveling through time and going to specific areas in order to do so, I learned that there were items I could have been using to make it go by much faster and more simply.  However, unbeknownst to me, I was taking a very inefficient route because the way I just so happened to be exploring in the game led me down a less effective route.  Considering that I left one of those devices, thinking it to be broken and useless, when I wanted to take it with me and would have been useful had I been able to, it was annoying that the game hadn't been set up so you would get that item earlier through a linear part of the gameplay.  All it did was cost me some time, but it was still annoying to find out about that lost time later, especially since it adds up very quickly with how the game transitions between time periods.
Again, I would recommend this game, and am actually curious about trying the first one in the series, though reviews indicate it's not nearly as good as this one.  I do hope they make a sequel at some point, whether it does or doesn't tie in to this storyline, as I'd be curious to see where they would take things from here, both plot-wise as well as with the gameplay aspects.

Old but still golden.
Fallout 1 is the first entry in the franchise (duh); so you most likely already know the deal. It's the post nuclear war era in the South West of the US and you are a vault dweller emerging from a generation that has lived their entire lives in these small underground shelters. What awaits outside this haven is a world of bandits, mutated creatures, and small establishments conjuring up semblances of civilization amid the corruption and turmoil that emerges from a society with barely a semblance of law and order. Towns are guarded by sheriffs that are barely holding back crime and base human instincts; the ruins of Los Angeles has given birth to decrepit buildings used as housing by gangs and crooks at the outskirts.
It's sort of like Detroit
At its core you get the same Fallout experience the newer generation is accustomed to: quests (both main and sidequests) and RPG elements that allow you to distribute points across many skills that are used for either combat, speech and character interactions, and world interaction. The staple VATS system is used as a turn based combat mechanic whereby you can target specific body parts of enemies.
First, the good: the base Fallout experience is quite good. The world remains unique to this day and the writing, plot, and lore still hold up in creating something intriguing that keeps you playing and exploring. The claymation style has outlived time and maintains its eye-catching flair both in the large maps and especially with the characters that have animated faces during conversations.
Anyone who knows me knows I appreciate good, coherent, sensible writing in my games with sound logic behind every element, and with this title I have no complaints which is not something that occurs often. That's honestly a tremendous compliment because video games, in general, always have faulty logic and plot holes-
Japanese games.
But here's the bad, and there will be a common thread here which is summarized in one word:
The isometric view makes for some nice looking maps when zoomed all the way out and displayed in high resolutions;
duckduckgo it.
But damn is it
. When walking behind buildings you get a circular shot that allows you to see through buildings and at your character, but it's rather small. Some buildings have their doorways away from the camera so you might actually miss some character interactions because you assume its just an empty building with no doorway. The camera angle presents a few problems if facing a lot of enemies in tight areas, which results in targetting specific enemies a hassle.
The menu and manner of interacting with the environment relies on right clicking and holding your mouse button to bring up a menu. It's not difficult to understand, but again, its unorthodox and unintuitive. And don't interact with anything when weapons are drawn; your character goes through a small animation to put his weapon away for every action. A time waster.
To be fair, this game was made around the mid 90's; try playing the original Doom and not a sourceport for comparison. But that doesn't mean its not worth bringing up, rather what is commendable is that such an old title still maintains relevance and a flair of uniqueness more than two decades later. Enough to warrant a playthrough - few things outlive time, after all.

If you have only heard of Fallout starting with Fallout 3, then it's time to go further back if you enjoy original lore.
Interplay was an amazing company who first came out with Wasteland (EA published originally) and with not being able to obtain the rights from the publisher moved to creating a spiritual successor.  Fallout is born.
This game is a pretty straight forward turned based RPG but it's the story telling and the writing in general that really has always gripped me with this game unlike Bethesda's try with Fallout 3 (though they tried).
It has an open ended world with hints on where to go next if you interact well enough and decide to go the path.   You can find help such as Ian and dogmeat but others are out there if you seek them out.  It's actually another part I like about Fallout is the freedom you have to explore.
And I mean explore!  None of that "sorry you need atleast this % skill to do that" except locked areas.   Even with locks though Interplay doesn't necessarily stop you from trying, just you risk breaking the lock. With so much freedom also comes choices and their accompanying consequences.  Even if the effect isn't instant, word of mouth spreads like fire in the wastes.
Replayability is there as you can change your skills to play differently, such as have fun raising your outdoorsman skill and see what random encounters you may run into!   Some are very helpful and others are clever jokes.   With the main story out of way if you follow a different path and play like a detective with finding hidden items or exploring different areas you may have passed up,  even talking to npcs you overlooked, you'll flesh out more of the lore of Fallout.
The original is highly recommended and is why I rated it as so in that sense.   This copy by Bethesda though has me shaking my head because it's mixed for those who played Fallout in the US.   That's right, this version is the UK version.
Back in 1997, Interplay was not politically correct in the states and had many situations in the game that could shock some folks.  The biggest one was children in the game which could be killed.  For doing such an act you are known throughout the wastes such a reputation and makes dealing with many npcs in the future a bit uneasy.
With children in the game though they played different roles and in one area in impaticular, The Hub.   Spoiler here but the kids in the area are thieves and they run up to you and run away as if they are playing only to realise something is wrong when checking your inventory and notice items missing.
Interplay was seeking a realistic gritty wasteland but not every country felt it had to be so realistic that you could kill anything that breathes.  So in order to sale the game internationally they had to make changes.  For UK, Interplay had pulled all scripts involving the children which broke code so the children sprites would not even show.
So while its definitely not a deal breaker, if you do wish to have the complete original game, you'll need to look up how to add the scripts back if Bethesda didn't touch anything that is.  It's relatively easy to accomplish.
I still have my original copy of Fallout when it was still published by Interplay themselves but with a free copy being on Steam I figured why not.   Other than being the UK edition of the game, it still holds as a recommended title to any RPG fan.

So, I have this to ask of you. Why haven't you gotten this? Have you at least tried out the demo? No? *Smacks you upside the head* Go try it! It's a gore filled, bloody as Hell (No, wait, it's Orks. But oh, how they bleed.), and it's a VERY simple control system that'll have you taking on Hordes of Orks in maybe a minute after the start.
And speaking from my experience on the 360 version, the Online is INCREDIBLY fun (Though I was limited due to buying the game used), and, believe it or not, I could find people. Yes. Actual people. In ALL the game modes I had. Exterminatus, Versus, the likes. Even though I was level 5 most of the time, I was doing a large amount of work for my team, keeping them well placed. I can only wonder what I would've been like at a higher level, with more weapons... <3
And then I get to the campaign. It's a camping trip gone astra- And I'm going to stop there. No, it's a typical Warhammer 40,000 story. Orks, suddenly, *Censored*. Whoah. Since I'm still new to the series, it caught me off guard, but, hey. It's still well done. The final fight is a gory mess of blood and fun and gore. But that final game movie, it's a painful one. The people in Warhammer 40,000, especially Space Marines, are♥♥♥♥♥holes. No bars hold,♥♥♥♥♥holes. GLORIFIED♥♥♥♥♥holes, them Space Marines are. But somehow, Relic has, once again, created a sort of relate-able glorified♥♥♥♥♥hole who has a heart of light (Or so we may think, depending on how you take the game.), and is a good character for the 40,000 universe. Upon arriving to the first Guardsmen outpost, he tells the lead Guardsman there that they saved themselves, and told him to rise. Captain Titus seems to treat Guardsmen as a form of little brother. It's very amusing to me.
And oh my Emperor, the music. The music is very much, to me, the highlight of Space Marine. It's an absolute blast to listen to, and every second of it sends chills down my spine. It's like listening to Dawn of War II's "The Green Horde Rises" in 19 songs, ESPECIALLY "A Hero's Legacy". Holy crap (That plays during the end video, before the credits).
Over all? I'd recommend getting it while on sale, but get it. It may not be your cup of tea, but try the Demo out. The two levels included (Well, level and a half because of the SHEER size of the Jump pack mission in game) are essentially copied and pasted out of the game itself. They give you a basic understanding of how the game works, and plenty of ways to test your skill.

Ever wanted to be a Space Marine? No, not one of those weakling Blizzard knock-offs from Starcraft... a true Angel of Death? Well this is the game for you!
Relic Entertainment, as usual, does a fantastic job here. They know the Grimdark Warhammer 40,000 universe very well, and have crafted the game with the love and care of the most ardent 40K fanboy. And boy oh boy, have they delievered for the fanboys (and newcomers!) here.
Gameplay can be sumed up basically as a 3rd person action melee/shooter hybrid. Built on the same engine as the Darksiders games, think of that game, crossed with Relics superb RTS Dawn of War 2, and you have an idea of what Warhammer 40,000 Space Marine is like.
There is alot of fun to be had with this title. With a great Singleplayer Campaign, PvP Multiplayer and Co-Op Horde Multiplayer modes to try out, it is good value for money too. The only real criticism I can lay on it is the lack of dedicated servers for the multiplayer, which can sometimes result in a bit of lag in some matchups.
Finally, if you have previously read any reviews by critics comparing Space Marine with Gears of War, then you can safely regard those critics as fools from now on. Because, apart from being in 3rd person and including chainswords, there are very little similarities. Also, anyone claiming this game has stolen its chainsaw concept from GoW, will be summarily executed for heresy. (Warhammer 40K has had chainsaws for over 25 years!)
To sum up, this is a must buy for Warhammer fans, and a great entry point for everyone else not yet acquainted with the incredible setting that is Warhammer 40,000.

I have never been interested in stealth games. I never saw the point, why wouldn't you want to rush in cry havok and let slip the dogs of war?! Why sneak around and avoid confrontation constantly saving and loading to erase tiny mistakes? The interesting answer provided to me by Styx is simple: because you don't have to. Styx is actually tremendously powerful, and near the end of the game when you've awakened most of his latent abilities you are capable of walking directly up to someone and murdering them in broad daylight in full view of their comrades with them barely registering a disturbance. The reason you do not do this to every hostile on the map is simply because you don't need to (although you can). It would be a waste of time and resources, and that's not what you're there for anyways, be a professional. After having exhausted myself on action hero type archetypes constantly tasked with saving the world, it was a strange bit of relief to play a character that was not a sculpted from marble and powered by selflessness.
Learning to play stealth games is no walk in the park and not for everyone, but I could not have asked for a better introduction to the genre. The original Thief series is far to old to be enjoyed properly and the level of polish Styx ships with is enough to assure a returning customer. The difficulty and challenges presented by the game ratchet up smoothly so that by the end you feel incredibly powerful but not overpowered, you still can't just run up and pop elites, but the tools and options you have to dispose of them become more accessable.
Many people cite Styx's unlikeableness as a reason they could not immerse in the game. But you aren't supposed to be cute and cuddly, you aren't superman, you are Batman. Striking from the shadows because you have complete mastery over them not because you have to. You are out for yourself because everyone is trying to kill you and there is nothing worth fighting for. You become embroiled in matters of tremendous consequence not because you are heroic, but because you want something for yourself. Ultimatley it is all just a game, even to Styx.
9/10

Those who played “Of Orcs and Men” will surely recognize the main character of this game, Styx the Goblin, as he is trying to make his way to his goal deep inside a tower-like fortress inhabited by both human and elves.
To safely navigate this treacherous environment and discover the truth behind your mission you will not only have to use the abilities granted by six skill-trees but also stealth and infiltration techniques. Mastering these is the key to your survival as Styx is fragile and he won't survive a face to face encounter with the battle-hardened soldiers of the tower.
All in all this title combines an interesting protagonist with a good storyline, great atmosphere and above average gameplay to create a hidden gem of the stealth genre. Just try it and see for yourself!

Let me get the bad out of the way first before I start flattering the game.
This game has a lot of bugs, a lot. None are game breaking but they are there and they are annoying.
1)Enemy patrol vessels "ghost" for hours and hours where projectiles pass through them and they don't fire and they get stuck underground and you can even fly your ship through them like they are "ghosts".
2) Sometimes when you exit your ship in space you get cold and have to return to warm up in a powered on ship but occasionally you don't "warm up" and freeze to death.
3) In certain larger SV's when you exit the♥♥♥♥♥♥pit and turn your jetpack off you fly into the ceiling turning upside down and even pass through the ship at times.
4) Turning your jet pack on in a ship somehow shuts the ships gravity off and makes the interior zero G.
5)Enemies sometimes fire through walls.
Now those are just a few bugs and surpisingly the game doesn't crash, in 44 hours I have had no crashes.
In terms of gameplay spawning ships(larger ones) is annoying. You can only spawn them on your bases and some are MASSIVE and you need to spawn them on the surface area of your base and this can be impossible or irritatingly delicate in early game. I found a enemy patrol vessel base with a large landing pad worlds away and took it over and that was a fix for me so keep that in mind if you are having trouble.
The saving system can be broken. If you load into a save then exit the game the game erases that save and replaces it with one where you exited. So if you load in and say lose a ship and want to load your old save it is gone so then you exit to load a new one and it keeps erasing and replacing and pushes you back in terms of progress. There should be a set autosave and cancelling the game with task manager doesn't bypass the wonky autosave either.

There's crafting, base building, mining asteroids, escavating crashed ships by digging them up, portals to insane planets, unique wild life, parasites that infect you and go through stages of evolution before killing you, disease, warp jumps, massive capitol vessels you can dock fighters in, lasers and plasma, underground bases, and almost everything is customizable! This game is a nerds wet dream and yes, I am a nerd!
It is what I would imagine Star Citizen would be if they hadn't wasted 10's of millions of dollars on a 20hr single player campaign and motion capture with Gary Oldman. If you have a itch to fly through space and get into dog fights or raid a massive cargo ship blowing a hole in it's side and raiding it or just enjoying the hum drum and nitty gritty of maintaining a large vessel and traveling the stars with "Space Oddity" blasting into the void then Empyrion is for you!

I break down this review into several parts, each about one facet of the game.
The building is this game's strong-suit. The array of different blocks is not very high, but many of the blocks are actually lists of blocks, which have somewhere between 5 to 50 different variations. So, there is a full cube, a half cube, a half-cube with top corner slanted, a half sphere, a thick cylinder, a curved cylinder, and so on and so forth. It really added a lot of fidelity to the things I built, and it was fun to do too. The rotation was simple, though it did take a bit of getting used to. I spent more time building a base than anything else in this game, even though it was pointless from a gameplay standpoint.
On top of the raw building blocks themselves, there was quite a robust logic system. Though I only saw 4 different types of input sensor (tripwire, motion detector, manual lever, pressure plate), the logic was handled through menus, rather than crafting and placing objects in the world, which gave a lot of freedom for how to make a system work. Motion sensor, configured to sense a player in my entry hallway, and then this would turn on the lights in my base, for example. Another sensor outside on my landing pad would detect when I had left my base, and automatically power down non-essential systems to save power. Speaking of power...
Though the building was largely fun, it is not without it's drawbacks. The base & vehicle building system all use a 'power' mechanic. This consists of a fuel tank, to store fuel; a generator, to burn fuel and create power; any number of things that consume power, such as doors, lights, thrusters, weapons, and storage crates. Storage crates? It apparently takes 1 unit of power/min to have a storage crate in your base. Or each tile of an elevator, even when not in use. Or a decorative chair. Or a lever that is doing nothing. Not 1 power/min tp use the storage crate, or 1 power/min to lock the storage crate, but 1 power/min for it to simply exist. These little things really add up, and make the power system confusing and opaque as best, and downright frustrating at worst. Additionally, the storage crates and elevators
when your base is without power, so it looks like they didn't need the power anyway!
There is a power management screen, where you can see your fuel reserves, power generatrion capability, and things that drain power, but it doesn't show
that drains power on the list, including the aforementioned crates, chairs, or elevators. So, attemping to track down a power hog is a crapshoot, if you aren't intricately familiar with the (sometimes hidden) power costs of each and every thing you ever put inside your base. Never mind if you are playing co-operatively iwth others, who knows what THEY added to the base that is secretly draining all your power for no discernable benefit. A chair? TWO chairs? Better add on a second power generator for all those potted plants they decorated with! This encourages a playstyle of having 2 bases on top of each other: the base full of passive things that work fine even without power, such as doors, elevators, chairs, plants, and storage crates, and then a second base that contains all the things that actually need power. Doing this will save you tons and tons of power, but it's extremely metagamey and finnicky, and is almost certainly not intended by the developer.

I never left the first starter planet (Akua), because I never realized how easy it was to travel to another planet, at the time. As has been explained to me in direct messages, al you have to do is build a small vessel (SV), and then fly into the sky until you reach orbit. However, this planet is quite pretty. It has some snow-capped mountains, some serene beachy lakes, and some generic forests. However, the interesting part of the exploration was in the world-gen structures and locales. There were neutral NPC villages, a trading post (with a link to some sort of space platform), abandoned mining complexes full of evil mutant looking things, and various other hostile locations. It was fun to explore these places, and see what they had in store. If the combat wasn't so bad, exploring would have been even more fun, instead of just a pain in the butt.
In this game, you start with a basic crafting station. It can craft some stuff, but it takes time to do so, and it's fiddly, since you have to manufacture all the sub-parts yourself. After you progress a bit and set up a base, you can produce an intermediate crafting station which requires power, but can produce all the intermediate recipies automatically. This is a great timesaver, but ... it kinda makes the point of having all the intermediate recipies pointless. If a tube costs 2 iron, a motor costs 2 tubes, and a door costs 10 iron, 2 tubes, and 2 motors... whats the difference between just costing 20 iron (or whatever) to start with? Why do all these stupid bobs and bits which you never touch even exist? Sure, you COULD craft them by hand, but let's face it; you're not gonna. It's too inconvenient to do so, so they might as well not exist.
There was a somewhat neat-looking player advancement / tech-tree which allows you to unlock more recipies as you level up. By and large, however, I had enough points to unlock everything I could possibly want as I leveled up, so it wasn't too interesting in the current game state.
A weird mix of models from the early 2000s, with post-processing effects from modern days. The enemy models look like something out of Deus Ex (the first), but the firey exhaust streaking out of a cruiser's thrusters is gorgeous! The weapon models look like generic unity store assets, as well as the sounds. This is always something that can be changed later, and doesn't detract too much from the overall game, but it definately looks dated at present.
To recap:
9/10 : Building
0/10 : Combat
6/10 : Exploration
5/10 : Crafting
5/10 : Graphics

I understand the negative reviews. The ruleset is complicated, and even more jarring perhaps to those used to D&D attributes and rules. That is why you should do as the game suggests and play on Normal difficulty and use the Basic (pre-made) character if it is your first time and unfamiliar to The Dark Eye. That's exactly what I did, and by the time I play a second time, I'll know enough of this convoluted system to choose a different class and choose my own stats.
It's a really fun strategy RPG, with an emphasis placed on usable objects on the battlefield, and unique battle maps. Every fight seems to have a "hook" to it. You will, however, spend hours looking at the manual, in-game tutorial and rules menu, and ultimately guides to explain what the hell is REALLY going on.
Talent modifiers to aid failed skill checks; Damage types as diverse and odd as Infantry, Piercing, Fire, Bashing and Magic (No, there is fire magic, it's just, well, the system is weird, OK); 3 separate attribute checks just to cast one spell; finally figuring out what the ♥♥♥♥ Armor Rating and Encumbrance really mean. This is for all the true OGs of CRPGs.

First and foremost: this is NOT an RPG.  It's a party-based tactical combat game with RPG elements.  If you start with that understanding, you'll avoid the disappointment that many players have encountered.
The game is about figuring out how to beat a series of scenarios.  Sometimes it's about how you use abilities and items, sometimes it's about using the environment.
It's not a perfect game, but it's fun.

This game is a lot of fun as long as it caters to the kind of roguelikes you prefer playing. What I mean is that this game, while being very strategic with currency, elemental resists, attack stances, etc., some people looking for, say, another ADOM or ToME might be dissapointed with a lack of variety in equipment and attack methods (i.e. you will be in melee 90% of the time; there appears to be no spells in the game aside from wands at the moment). Classical roguelike elements like cursing and identification exists, and this game features a corruption system that is somewhat similar to ADOM's (albeit a lot nastier and dangerous in this game).
Currently there are 5 classes (3 of which are locked for hard and higher difficulties) and they are generally pretty unique and interesting. For instance, you can play as a spirit that can't use items or talk to NPC's but possesses the ability to possess and completely control a monster that's close to death. Gameplay and strategy appear to be largely tied to the classes and their playstyles at the moment, so I suggest doing some reading (or better yet, watch a video) in order to determine if this game sounds like it'd be fun to play.
Overall I'm very pleased this is an actual roguelike with strategic depth, and not a twin-stick shooter "roguelike" the genre has been flooded with in recent years. I Recommend this to anyone interested in the former, as it has a lot of potential, in my opinion. More classes and more variety in consumables would be a good start for the game to improve, I think.

This is a fun game, which unfortunately suffers from some issues and problems. Personally, I'd rank it as "decent." I found it fun - then again, as a 40K fan I would probably find any half decent game set in that universe fun, so the following is to be taken with a pinch of salt.
The single player campaign is decent but relatively short. The plot is a bit bland (same concept we've seen so many times) but the way the story is actually set up and executed is ok, I guess. No big problems (regarding breaking of immersion) there.
The basic premise of the game is 'go from point A to point B' while slaughtering everyone in your path. Because of that, the gameplay tends to get a bit repetitive after a while. The final boss (fight) is disappointing, seeing the whole story is basically a huge setup for this encounter. One of the mini-bosses along the way was actually harder than the end boss.
The levels are unfortunately a bit generic. There's nothing really wrong or out of place, mind you, it just seems to be lacking that 'lovingly hand-crafted' feeling. For a large part of the campaign, the levels tend to feel kind of empty. This might seem like a bit of a given seeing the levels are basically large or small arena's in which you fight hordes of enemies, but as you can imagine it doesn't really help with the repetitiveness. The servo skulls (audio logs) add some much needed atmosphere, but are basically a drop on a hot plate in this regard.
Multiplayer is fun, but often rather laggy and sometimes kind of buggy.
Hardly anyone plays the DLC's (Chaos Unleashed and Dreadnought Assault) anymore, so buyer beware.
Versus can be very fun, and the classes (tactical, devastator, assault) feel balanced. Playing this mode will net you xp through which you will level and unlock armor perks, with which you can improve your loadout. In versus, you will also unlock weapon perks for the same purpose.
When starting out in MP, the gameplay tends to feel a bit clunky and requires some getting used to in order to get the hang of it. Needless to say, against other human opponents there generally isn't much room for error. Thankfully, this is something that is easily alleviated with a bit of practice and experience - but it does require you to bite the bullet first.
Exterminatus is great fun, but there's some problems here as well. Sometimes either you or the enemies get stuck in the scenery, which in the former case means you're pretty much a dead weight to your party and in the latter case means that the wave will never end. There's also some issues with the Weirdboy on the later waves of Hab Assault.
There is also no way to see what loadout your party members have selected until after you've entered the game (and selected your own loadout), at which point you cannot change your own loadout anymore until after the arena ends. Without proper communication, you basically have to guess which loadout to take, and if you guess wrong, you're stuck with it for the duration of that arena. This isn't really a problem in the earlier waves, but for the later waves good communication is key.
Exterminatus also grants you xp, through which you can level and unlock armor perks (similar to versus). Playing this mode doesn't level your weapon perks, though. To obtain those you have no other option but to play 'versus' against other players.
While for me that didn't prove to be a problem (I like versus), it's a bit silly to have to play a multiplayer mode you theoretically have no interest in playing for a couple of hours in order to unlock the weapon perks you wanted, just so you can use them to play the multiplayer mode you wanted to play all along... Don't really see the logic there.
Despite these issues, though, this is actually a decent game. It's just that there is a lot of room for improvement. It could have been a good game (or even very good) with proper polishing and vision, but unfortunately falls a bit short of that mark. Still, I would recommend this game to anyone with a more than passing infatuation with 40k.

Fallout 1,
after all what Bethesda threw on us and so much critique I've seen on how it's all worse than the original game, I must say...
Fallout 1 feels a lot like it was created by a company under Bethesda, install the unofficial patches before you play it! (I didn't, I wanted to see what the original game was like with all it's flaws).
First on the good experience (I can see why the players compare New Vegas to it) - The story, variety of the outcomes/choices and dialogues are excellent. I like the turn-based mechanics a lot. The graphics are good enough for it's time and the overall look could be compared to the excellent Commandos or Robin Hood with much better mechanics. Although, there isn't an option to gear up companions with a better armor, but it forces you to plan your fights carefully, I see that more like a plus, it's never boring or repetitive.
And why it feels like the game has something to do with Bethesda?
The unfinished programming and improper beta testing. You will often bump into a situation where you can't say or do something you obviously should have, sometimes the game itself point out the outcome of the action, but nothing happens. There are quests, that can't be finished due to the missing NPC's or dialogue options, some of them directly influence the ending outcome, what is really bad. The game also don't recognize some important actions related to some towns and leave you with a bad ending for them. Most of this was fixed by modders (or so I've read), but the original product is overall unfinished.
Finally I would definitely recommend the game, it just isn't, for it's vanilla version, such a perfect game as portrayed by the fandom. They had to fix it themselves.

After playing Fallout 3 and New vegas for so long, I wanted more. The Gameplay was intimidating for me at first because it didnt play the same as the newer ones but when I finally got the hang of it I was hooked.
Not even sure where to start.  The game is repetitive and uninteresting.  Gameplay gets super boring quite quickly.

Where should I even start? The campaign mode is terrible. It has 3 levels, all of them which have a 10-minute long obstacle run that inevitably gets boring, frustrating and repetitive, followed by a boss fight that can be ended in as short as 15 seconds if you get some lucky shots and if you attack right off the bat. Besides the campaign mode, the current version offers survial mode, which is basically an endless torture of the same repetitive patterns of enemies and obstacles, the only difference being that bosses appear every 60 seconds.
I'll be blunt about the mechanics: they just look like the developer/s wasted more time on prolonging the idiotic obstacle runs rather than actually working on the diversity of the game. The only things you can do are move left, right, and a tiny bit forward and attack in 2 ways: the normal, projectile attack and the whirlwind attack, which needs a second or so to charge and makes you invulnerable for a short period of time while also killing enemies in a very short range around you. That's literally the whole game. I wouldn't be bashing the lack of diversity of the game (it's normal in a game made in unity and with a cheap price tag) if it weren't for the awfully long levels.
The enemies you will encounter are gargoyles, some banshees, wolves (most annoying enemy), and skeletal hands randomly placed in your path, while the bosses are cheap nicknames given to Nosferatu (The Phantom), The Headless Horseman (The Horseman) and Dracula (The Count, if I'm not mistaken), which have the same pattern of attacks over and over again, the only thing distinguishing them from the normal enemies being the increased number of hits required to take them down. A thing that I quite liked was the art style, I have to say that it turned out pretty well in my opinon.
I certainly think that the game can be improved a lot and that an updated version with some fixes of the minor bugs in this one and added content (might as well have a bigger price, but I think it would be worth it) would have a pretty nice succes among the indie lovers. I can't reccomend it in its current state, maybe only for the trading cards and achievements (it will be a pain in the a** to get them all, trust me), but I do certainly hope that the game is not left unattended by the devs.
TL;DR: A cheap game that might be worth getting at first glance, if you're looking for a couple of achievements (which are quite frustrating to get) and 3 trading cards, then go ahead, you might be satisfied with the purchase. But if you are looking for a nice little indie game for you to kill some time with, this game is certainly not what you're looking for (at least in its current state)
