Lots of negativity on this title and i got curious as we know sometimes even bad publicity is good publicity no? It was on sale at 85% off so i thought no big loss if it's as bad as the haters say it. From hard to win, to hard to control, to exit bugs and what not, this game has taken a lot of undeserved flak and by extension, the developers. Didn't really want to buy it at first since i already got 13 but the heavy discount made me want to try it for myself and see what all the fuss is about.
First, lets talk about the one race (Termas de Rio Hondo) which was exceedingly hard; i got 8th place. Incidentally, that is acceptable for career mode since the team's objective for this round is only 15th place.
Funny that this video haz got more views than my other MotoGP14 videos in which i did well, go figure :D
Ok, on hindsight, this poor position may be due to the default setup for the bike which usually seems to be set to fail / lose for every track. It's not really bad per se but it's a safe setting that doesn't allow you to push the performance to it's limit. Furthermore, i did not experiment enough with all the setups nor retried the race too many times so maybe i could've done better.  This explains the frequent difficulty in handling the bike around the corners or poor top speed or poor acceleration when you go by the default setups but the above example is an extreme exception. Most of the tracks so far has been quite easy to master. As of this writing i've just completed the 8th round of the Career mode (TT Assen in The Netherlands) but it's not uploaded yet due to having exceeded my daily upload limit.
IMO the developers want the players to fiddle with the setups to get the best results and learn in the process rather than hand-hold them all the way to the last race of the season with optimal setups for every track and every bike. Furthermore, as the bike gets upgrades, the optimal setup will need adjustments.
The only problem as far as i can see, a minor one at that, is the inability to save custom key bindings. As for the much gripe about difficulty in winning, there's one other oft overlook aspect; bike upgrades. Initially career mode is tough to win even against easy AI. I thought the AI somehow cheated but really, as a newcomer to the sport, no one expects you to win a podium finish. Besides, a new team is likely to have sub-par bike components and inexperience in bike setups so it's a realistic scenario you're put through. You're afterall an unproven rookie rider so don't expect the top teams to take you in.
So what about the exit bugs? Well in the beginning i didn't encounter it until i went into the Career mode. So the claims that it occurs in the Career mode is true but only half true. You see it only exists in full-screen (fs) mode. Not sure if it occurs in all fs resolutions but since i started using windowed mode, i've never looked back. You can see for yourself in this video and also in some other videos of mine that exit is possible in Career mode; just need to press Alt-F4. ( ok shameless self-promotion here :p )
As for the complaints about the lack of in-game graphic options, well there's some options you can set in the launcher. And if you need more tweaking, you can use manual override in the graphics driver app. For sure the options are not as extensive as in some games but it's enough to allow balance between performance and image quality. A note about graphics quality; many people say it's dated. Maybe so but if you compare the in-game graphics of Losail night race in the rain and the real-life video of the same which you can find in the unlocked video in the Multimedia feature of the game, you'll find that it's a surprisingly accurate rendition of the actual scene; surface reflections and all.
In summation, this game is thoroughly enjoyable - just give it a fair chance. As of this writing, i've already put 34 hours into it. Nothing to complain about really and no game breaking bugs. If you're afraid of savegame corruption just make a backup of the savegame directory which can be found in C:\Users\"your username"\AppData\Roaming\Milestone .
Final note: The
which was present in perhaps all previous MotoGP and SBK series has been removed from this version so you'll have to find your own interesting portion of the replays yourself.
Verdict: 7.5/10 Would be 8.5 if the developers didn't skimp on graphics options or game features present in previous iterations. Highly recommended if you don't already own 13, recommended if you're a fan of the series or if you're like me and just want to find out for yourself what's all the hoopla surrounding this release.
Unrelated side note: Of all the motorcycle games from Milestone, the one i like best is really Ride just 'coz the scenery is varied instead of just typical track layout. If only Ride has a massive open-world map like Test Drive Unlimited 2 then it would be perfect !!! Either TDU3 needs more motorcycles or Ride needs more open-world. :D

A few yeras ago 10tons made a game called Crimsonland, a 2D arena shooter.  They took the same engine and added a whole bunch of features and made Neon Chrome.  They've now added a bunch more features and changed some things around a bit and made a new game, Time Recoil.  I mean JYDGE.
It's the same 10tons engine we know from its antecedents but with more structure.  There's no procedureal generation this time and you don't get randomised starting gear.  Missions aren't randomised either; there are three difficulties, each with three objectives.  I found it much easier than Neon Chrome but I already know what I'm doing.  The major difficulty in Neon Chrome is the beginning: if you make it past the first boss, chances are you'll go the whole way through.  The bite sized format of JYDGE removes the false starts and lets you make constant progress.
It's funny how giving it a new name allows so much more acceptance.  Had it been called Neon Chrome 2, people would be complaining about everything which is different, others complaining that not enough has changed.  SPAZ 2 got loads of bad reviews saying it's nothing like SPAZ 1.  So 10tons dodged a bullet there and JYDGE is judged on its own merits.

All 10tons games are amazing and this one is no exception.  This is the most polished game of theirs that I have played.  Very solid twinstick shooter experience.
If you liked Crimsonland or Neon Chrome, you're most likely going to love this one.  Biggest differences with Jydge are more secret areas, and support for up to two players.  Oh, and more polished ;)

JYDGE is a top-down shooter for twin-stick or mouse/keyboard (my preference) control. You play as a badass future cop; each mission starts with your flying police vehicle hovering onto a scene and letting you loose to go after various objectives, such as kill particular targets, collect evidence items or free hostages. Missions don't typically last more than 5 minutes.
Missions are not randomly generated - there are 18 maps total, and each map comes with 12 objectives each (3 per difficulty level, you unlock the harder levels as you progress). The objectives ensure variety in gameplay - some objectives require full rambo style gameplay ("kill everyone within 30 seconds"), while others require stealth ("don't be spotted" or "no kills"). Other fun ones are "survive X seconds", or "melee weapons only". Sometimes it's possible to achieve multiple objectives in one run, but more often you will repeat the map at least once for each objective.
There's also a huge variety of items that are progressively unlocked - a total of 14 fire modes (rockets, shotgun, sniper etc - these all have infinite ammo btw), 25 fire "mods" (increase fire rate, shoot through walls, faster reload etc), 15 special weapons (stun grenades, remotely triggered C4 explosives, turrets etc - these have limited ammo for each mission), and 35 "cyberware" gadgets (more armor, invisible in the dark, faster movement etc.) You get to choose one or a few items from each of these categories before each mission to match your playstyle and objective at hand.
Missions can be repeated as often as you want, but a few things will have permanent effects and affect subsequent repeats: Some "bosses" will be dead permanently when killed once; unlocked doors will remain permanently open; and credit chests can only be opened once (you need credits to acquire all those items).
The sound track consists of a few tracks of energizing electronic music, it can get repetitive eventually but overall I enjoyed it.
The game seems pretty polished, not trying to be anything it isn't and not taking itself too seriously; a great experience overall if you're into these kinds of games. I probably got more fun out of this than Hotline Miami (which I also enjoyed very much). Compared to that one, this is a little less twitchy and also a bit less violent probably, although the graphic style here isn't quite as unique. Anyways, I'll definitely be checking out other games from this developer (10tons) soon.

In Jydge you play as a Jydge. Just one. A mass-marketed model made to dispense justice or the nearest approximation. A robotic cop that's also a judge that also terminates, connect the dots.
Made by 10tons Ltd, who have done about 10 billion other twinstick shooters, it's a twinstick shooter! You twinstick and you shoot. All the good stuff. It's objective based, so you tackle new objectives each map - free the hostages, disarm some bombs, and shoot some targets. On the way you shoot everyone.
Now this might look like Neon Chrome 2, from the aesthetic to the gameplay, to the destructible wall tech (which is great, by the way), takes place in the same universe, features ads from it, yeah. Honestly it's tied in with just about every other 10tons game, they all make an appearance either in the lore - the lore that doesn't matter - or as a secret item or whatever. I didn't notice any absences.
The main difference is despite being advertised as a roguelike (roguehate?) there is not a single procedurally generated element in this game. Maps are static, enemy placements are static - some stuff just has to be done once per map and carries over but else what you see is what you get.
Jydge is a better game for this alone.
All the maps in this game are fantastic - they're varied, they're intricate, they're memorable, they love you like your parents don't, and they don't get boring over the playthroughs and difficulties. You've got plenty of enemy variety, and learning routes around the levels is integral for getting "medals".
Apart from getting the ending (there's a dumb morality system, by the way - it doesn't matter and the plot is stupid the end) the real idea of the game is to get all 216 medals across the difficulties - difficulties that completely remix the levels and change your objectives completely - for the sake of getting them.
This is fundamentally pretty fun. It's a process that's carried by the gameplay.
Now it starts off slow and forgiving - just ambling around with your starter rifle taking down starter mooks and threatening potplants, but the variance in playstyles that you can make viable - and have to, to get the Nightmare medals - is all there. Stealth, Tanky, Hotline Miami 2.0, Pet Summoner AI Build with MLG strats, and just hitting things with your gun - none of them are bad.
Well some of them are. Until you get all the Cyberware, Mods, a couple of upgraded weapons and specials, and get to experiment with them. Then they're not.
Course getting all that requires all buying them then upgrading them, which you will not do. The economy is just bad, like 2007 [economic depression] bad, it's a total mess. You have to spend tens of thousands of credits to fully upgrade each weapon, credits that you just won't get. You'll get the 4 fully upgraded special and weapons, you'll get all the mods and cyberware, and after that you're not getting jack.
Get used to your tiddlywink selection of weapons. Unless you like grinding.
Overall, though - great game, great aesthetic, and great sense of justice. If you're after an action game that's fairly easily paced and gameplay that lets you play around with, I absolutely recommend this.

BlackGuards is a turn based RPG with party combat and grid battlegrounds . It is not open world game but rather simplified system where you move around towns and map by clicking on images .There are some sidequests and text based choices that can effect quest outcome and impact later in game . At the start you will be able to customize your character in depth with skills but cosmetic options are lacking .
This game has a lot of issues but I was able to overlook those because the core gameplay is fun and challenging . I will go over some negative points that people mentioned in reviews to give some feedback .
-Beginner's trap?-
There are several events in this game that can force you to start over if you did not manage your resources properly . You can end up in a position where you can't win a fight and can't go to previous areas to level up on side quests .  Auto Save will not help so you should keep 2 more save points .I don't think that it adds any fair difficulty but I like games that do not hold my hand .
This game is extremely hard because you can't always anticipate what happens . Like you may need a speed buff for a mission but you never got it . There are many fights where I had to go back to get the right skills and come back (which is not always an option) . If you are a casual gamer there is a chance you might get stack because you did not build characters correctly .I am seasond RPG player and this was the most unforgiving game I ever played .
-Permadeath on Party Characters-?
One of the characters in your party will die ( forever ) This is a scripted event so you won't actually loose party members by diying in combat  . It is kinda cool to see a game have the balls to do that but for obvious reasons not everybody likes that . You can potentially waste some gold by buying equipment for that character ( I think you get it back but sellback value is not the same ) The real problem is that you may waste some of your Skill points thinking that you can rely on this character for a specific role .
- Too much Luck -?-
In this game Ranged,Melee and Spell attacks have % to hit . Luck is a big factor early on  . Eventually you can upgrade skills high enough to where you will hit 90-100% so it has to do a lot with how you level your characters .
Dodging is frustraing early in game but not a fair criticism for RPG because it adds depth to character builds . However there is a luck element to using items from iventory which can be avoided by save/load ( so that mechanic just wastes your time )
-Very basic loot System -
Loot in this game is not exciting to say the least . You get a 3-7 damage weapon and 10 hours later you get 4-8 weapon .It keeps number values low which is good because it makes fights less gear dependent but I would prefer something better than just common white trash as you would call it in other games .
Rewards for Side quests are very unbalanced . Some quest chains can take 2-3 hours and you might get the same reward as the 20 minute quest . There are some specific quests that give uniqe weapons but there is no consistency with legth or difficulty of the mission .
I also should address god awful inventory weight system . This game kinda requires you to carry a lot of gear especially toward late game but you never have enough inventory space . Like entire game I was between 90 and 100% full . You constantly have to find items to remove even though you do not have that much junk .
-Pros ?-
Challenging tactical gameplay
Good variety of different stages and objectives
Text choices that impact later in game
Spells that gain new effect at maximum level
Decent voice acting and some good jokes .
Score: 7/10 . I am really enjoying the unpredictable and unforgiving nature of this game . Perhaps it is a bit unfair  to new and casual players but it is fantastic for someone who does not want the game to hold your hand . At full price I would not recommend it to everyone but on sale you should consider picking it up if you like turn based party RPGs .

Gloria Victis is a game that starts bad.
At the first few levels the game is quite boring and feels grindy but as you level up and you start to participate in PVP events you will realize that this game is actually quite fun, with your character becoming stronger and easier to control.
If I had to compare Gloria to two other games it would be Life is Feudal (but wayyy less grindy) and Mount and Blade (but being more similar to an MMO).
PROS:
- Has a combat system similar to M&B (and in my opinion could actually be better).
- Has a partial loot system (for example, when you kill someone you can take a few of their items).
- No cheaters (in 51 hours I haven't seen or heard of any cheaters).
- Frequent major updates (just last week guild-controlled bases were added).
- You can always get pvp action, even if the server is near empty.
- Good graphics.
- Performance has been significantly improved (I always get near 60 fps on high even though I use an old system).
CONS:
- Very small community
- Desync is a bit of an issue
- Map design is good, but the placement of NPC's should be overhauled.
- Lacks creative freedom when it comes to base building (but you can make a completely unique crest that hangs from the walls of your base, for example I can even make my family crest from real life).
Honestly, sometimes Gloria feels like a MMO / Survival game hybrid and I love that.
I eagerly await the next updates and I can't wait to see what the future has in store for Gloria Victis.

Because my friends, of two reasons.
The GAME BALANCE. It is so broken i cannot even believe it. Some fights are so unbalanced i had to actually lower the difficultry to Normal to beat them, which i never ever did for any game in my life. This because you are put in situations where you just need luck to make it out alive.
And Luck is the real master of this game, not skill nor strategy. Just pure luck. RNG (Random Numerical Generation) (What determines % of success or failure of things) is so determining in the combat that it just rules over everything. In other turn based games there is RNG of course, but also other factors like strategy, formations, class builds, level are critical to win a fight, but not here in blackguards, not at the same level.
A single random critical, or spell failure (spells can FAIL casting, yes you got it right), or a random miss with 99% chance, or again some trap which activates randomly decides to turn just towards your party and wipe it out with a blast of fire.
All these things can make a fight fail. Random chance upon chance upon chance upon chance. Not even in Vegas there is so much gambling.
This more than a game of skill is a game of luck. I have many many years of experience in all kinds of RPGs but i just cannot take it anymore. I find myself by now to repeat fight over and over and over again just to get a fight where the RNG favors me, where traps do not activate on my team, or on the target i have to protect, etc, and make me fail after a well planned strategy.
Do yourself a favor, go and buy Divinity Original Sin, that's a turn based game made right, not this disguised slot machine of a game we have here.

Styx is pretty good. I'm glad I bought it.
I always compare stealth games to Thief 2 which was first person. In Styx you get to see your character most of the time. I don't know why I need to see him, but because I do, the camera, my viewpoint, is about ten or fifteen feet back but it can swing all around him. That means that at the end of a hallway I can swing the camera around in Styx and see what's on either side of the end of the hallway I'm on if I take the time and go through the somewhat nauseating and time consuming camera moves. This would not be possible in Thief 2, but in Thief it wasn't necessary and peeking wasn't nauseating or time consuming. Everything was quick and agile. You didn't level up agile, you just became agile when you familiarized yourself with the controls. In Styx if a guard gets close enough you get locked into a combat orbit, which is just weird and unrealistic and annoying. The camera gets very nauseating and I often lose sight of what's going on because of narrow areas which are common. This was not a problem in Thief as there was no combat orbit. If I planned I could always jump into a canal and swim away or jump onto a climbing rope and climb out of reach and sight. Also, in Thief I could become a better swordsman. I sometimes enjoyed the swordfights in Thief. In Styx I usually just watch Styx get killed. Styx can't run fast enough to get away most of the time and fighting is awful. There are still skills involved though.
Thief had rope arrows and rules for sticking to the rope. You could run right through the rope without sticking or you could jump onto it and grab and climb like an olympian with a little practice. You had a great bow in Thief and you could sink multiple rope arrows to get where you wanted to go. You could douse torches with water arrows and fire explosive arrows and arrows that didn't drop as well as normal arrows. The bow was an incredible tool. Styx can walk up to some torches and douse them or he can throw sand at them from range.
With Thief you could download about 500 fan made missions that were better than the original. Probably you could easily get 3000 hours of fresh gameplay with all the missions as well as help from a well organized community. Styx might give you 25 or 30 hours of good gameplay, much of it seems to be copied from Thief. Thats a hundred times more content for one low price. No free to play schemes that are bs.
I liked the guards better in Thief. The Styx guards aren't funny and neither is Styx. Thief had the eye, which you could throw and then look through it as though it was your eye and then you could pick it up. In fact you had better pick it up because if you didn't it was gone. This added gameplay. Styx can whistle to attract enemies. Most of the time it gets Styx killed. Thief could fire a noise arrow, which would attract enemies to where it landed. This added gameplay. Imagine being able to fire a noise arrow in Styx at the spot where a chandelier would impact. If you had multiple noise arrows you could lure guards from all over to that one spot and then drop the chandelier on them. In Styx I tend to just wait for someone to be standing below the chandelier. Its cool but not as cool as luring lots of enemies to the place they'll be obliterated. Also, in Thief you could lure one baddie that was an enemy of another baddie and they'd kill each other.
Styx has some beautiful levels and dizzying drops. Styx can poison fruit. Thief couldn't. Sometimes the guards would take the fruit, but other times you could spend all day trying to get the guards to eat the fruit, but they'll never do it. Its almost like there is just an obvious spot here and there where they want you to poison guards in Styx.
The bottom line is that its been almost twenty years since Thief came out and yet it did so many things better than Styx and yet Styx is still a pretty good game, one of the better games I've played this year.  Back then games were made by enthusiasts that were discovering and creating things as they went along. I think they created their own engine just for Thief. These days most games seem to be using the same engine that is adapted a little and full of conventions. The ambiance, the feeling you get from being in the two worlds is different, but familiar.

I was looking for a nostalgia kick without breaking out my SNES. I played Owlboy and the recent Shantae game and left wanting more as both were around 6-8 hours. While both were fun, they lacked depth and I beat them with relative ease.

I did not play the first Evoland game but I don't feel like I am missing anything. The story in Evoland 2 feels self contained and rather straightforward. The way the story progressed along with the time jumps feels interesting. You have a real sense that you are traveling in time with the generation jumps. The only moment it was really jarring was when you went to 3D for the first time. The depth and camera angle doesn't feel right at first and takes time getting used to and that first dungeon can be brutal at times.
As far as the story is concerned, it's nothing immaculate to write home about but it is compelling enough to finish the game and play through to conclusion. You will likely sink ~22-25 hours into the game and it really opens up little over halfway. The references and throwbacks are welcome for a chuckle but Evoland 2 easily stands on it's own. It's secrets and puzzle solving are fantastic and the real time action elements are well balanced. Playing this game on it's hardest difficulty, I only felt frustrated with two points of the game.
The only real complaint I have is that it tries to do too much. The time aspect of switching generations is great but the implementation of other genres is where it drags. It throws every type of genre into the game from SHMP to side scrolling brawler to Bomberman. Some it does better than others but there are a few genre types where it is a slog to get through. Most of the time it's for a boss fight or a specific instance but others you are expected to play through long sequences in a completely different genre than the standard real time action. I like tactics games, don't get me wrong, but the section in Evoland 2 is so long to get through that I felt weary and thankful I completed it so that I never had to play that section again.
If genre switching and generation switching sounds interesting to you, you will likely find this game a great throwback to your childhood NES/SNES rpg days. Get past the nostalgia and Evoland 2 certainly can stand on it's own with the minor flaws of just trying to do too much.

The game presents a very good concept, however fails to execute it. The changing of colours to move around the levels and solve puzzle like stages is entertaining, however each stage feels either rushed or unfinished. The art for each stage is lovely but the issue is that there is not enough of it. The stages themselves also feel a little buggy and the number of leaps of faiths required to finish the game is not impressive since you rely so heavily on colours to find out what objects are in the stage. The controls, being simple, do make navigation easier, however. Another issue is the audio of the game. The soundtrack does not suit the game at all and in being repeated over and over again it becomes very boring, making the game feel very boring. It's also too hyped up for the game, attempting to make the whole game feel "epic" but instead makes it feel sloppy, as if the developer didn't have time to bother with a proper soundtrack. Then there's an issue with the game story and universe. There's no proper explanation as to how the protagonist can use his "colour changing powers" in this world, nor is there a proper explanation of what this world is. The odd sentences scattered throughout the game in random stages don't offer much insight, if anything they tease a possible storyline. The protagonist himself appears as some mysterious figure, however in this attempt he just seems like the usual angsty character that has been executed poorly, turning into another bland character that doesn't leave any special mark in your mind, unless his mark is meant to remind you just how lame he is.
Overall the game was a nice concept but executed everything badly. It is a shame because I did enjoy the colour changing aspect and the artstyle but that was about it. If the developer ever decides to make a game like this again then I hope these issues are addressed and improved in the future. It may be a free game, and that is also a plus side, however that's no excuse for it to be a bad game.

If I was to put this game into a genre, it'll be a point n click adventure with heavy narration and themes. However, I feel like that's definitely not enough to describe how much " Finding Paradise" left me in wonder and awe.
-For a game that only took me 5 hrs to play, it felt like I was actually unfolding someone's lifetime worth of memories.
-Everything from the whimsical characters , to immersive plot, everything about this game is an experience.
Note: I haven't played a bird's story, nor did I know that it was a continuation. So do play that first then experience this :)
The order would be : To the Moon, Minisode 1 , Minisode 2, A Bird's Story, Finding Paradise. The minisodes just add a bit more depth to the characters and the Sigmund Organisation etc :) ( I'll update again if I'm wrong)
-Absolutely astounding mix of delicate and whimisical characters , a lot of character development
-Would you sacrifice a lifetime of memories , for a new set? Or maybe, just to fufill a dream?
- What can you do when a compromise between decisions need to be made?
- What happens when there's a blurred line between dreams and reality , where your dreams can come true?
Simply, you play as the agents from Sigmund- Classic O'Neil and eloquent Dr Eva Rosaline whose goal is to fufill one's final wish at his/her's last breath. That itself isn't a spoiler.
To do so, you travel back to their past and witness the events of an individual's life unfold. All the emotions felt, all the causes and consequences and "what ifs" revealed in plain sight. It's a surreal experience, to be able to wander through and see why and how the client became who they in their present moment.
- Simple click and point , discovery game.
- The goal is to find memory orbs and links to be able to "unlock" a memento.
- Puzzles involve a lot of switching and matching- The Difficulty definiterly increases
-It's highly philosophical :)
- Depending on the situation, there may be a set of combat options but nothing too grand ( fun easter eggs to be unlocked too, without spoiling ofc :))
-Pixel Art - Beautiful nostalgic and calm art.
- At times, the pixels can be really detailed too :)
- Reminds me of the classic snes games like zelda, chrono trigger :)
- I'd describe this as natural sounding music. Everything goes so well with the scenes
-Loopable themes - Piano :)
- Really serene orchaestral music
- Transitions to Epic Music occasionally.
- We learn about the client and his/her life through symbolism and interaction with mementos.
- It's basically filled with symbolism, to each of their own :)
If one was to abandon all their regrets or chased their "what ifs" , what would become of the current form of themselves? Simply, it would cease to exist.
This game is purely about acceptance of what is and isn't, but I'll leave that to you to judge.
I promise you, if you're wandering around, unsure of what to make of your current life, or even just want a surreal experience through another pair of eyes, then I strongly recommend "Finding Paradise".
P.S. To the Frosty that gifted me this game, you're a legend. What a lovely Christmas present, thank you  :)

Install OSP. The instructions suck, but all you need to do is take 4 of the files that start with "zz" and put them in q3base. Not the one with "server" in the name, that one will make it so single player games don't work. Now if you open console with ~ you can type "/ch_crosshaircolor 1" for example. I think names work too, like Red or Blue. Some servers don't like OSP. If you want to play on one that kicks you, take those files out. Keep the entire OSP folder in your main Q3 folder.
Other important settings:
\rate 25000
\snaps 40
\cl_maxpackets 125
\com_maxfps 125
\com_hunkMegs 128
\cg_drawTeamOverlay 1
\cg_noProjectileTrail 1
\cg_enemyModel "keel/pm"
\cg_enemyColors "iiii"
\cg_trueLightning 1
Make sure your mouses polling rate is 500 or less or your gun will get stuck firing sometimes, or not fire at all occasionally.
If it keeps forcing your Game Key to Upper Case go into the games directory in Q3base and edit the key file with a text editor. Make it lowercase - save it - then right click the file and go to properties - make it read only. It may still ask for your key after a match but it's just a glitch, ignore it. As long as it doesn't do it BEFORE a match it makes no difference.

Jydge is a very good top down shooter. For a relatively cheap game it has extensive customization system which allows for a large variety of viable gameplay styles. There are 35 perks called cyberware of which 4 could be equipped at the same time. You could opt to go guns blazing with perks that deal damage or debuff enemies or you could take your time and choose perks that facilitate stealth gameplay and anything in between. Additionally, your weapon can be extensively customized with 14 firemodes and 15 special firemodes as well as perks of its own of which it could equip 3 out of a choice of 25. Essentially, as you customize your gun it becomes a different weapon, you could have automatic rifles, shotguns, rocket launchers and sniper rifles among other things. The weapon sounds good and is satisfying to use.
In terms of level design in Jydge, it is quite good with distinct, hand crafted levels. The levels come in a variety of themes and feature environmental destructibility. There are 18 levels in total which may seem like a small amount but the replayability in this game comes from challenges. The challenges come in 4 tiers, Normal, Hardcore, Grim and Nightmare with 3 in each tier for each map. What I like about those challenges is that they force you to adapt and experiment with your playstyle. The game also comes with some secret areas which contain collectibles which either provide small bonuses to stats or introduce interesting visual effects.
All in all, if you are a fan of top down shooters, Jydge is a must buy game, it delivers in both the amount and quality of content.

The only thing Jydge is missing to be an absolute 10/10 is a few more missions and maybe a scenario editor so people can set up their own.
It's a top-down shooter which supports everything from gung-ho Touhou-esque bullet-dodging through stealthy assassinations and sometimes even completely non-lethal approaches.
You essentially play a shameless Judge Dredd/Robocop crossover in a crime-ridden, neon-lit metropolis where you gun down bad guys, save innocents, collect evidence and cause ridiculous amounts of property damage in the process. The music's great, the art is simple but expressive and the controls are good. About the only issues I could pin on the game is that some of the weapon options are considerably less viable than others(and a few are so OP they were basically all I used throughout the game) and that it could maybe use a bit more content from the devs.
The addition of optional objectives that are sometimes bone-hard to pull off help provide the game with some longevity if you're the sort of person who likes to challenge themselves by getting all of the optionals. But some of them are an exercise in frustration since they A) require a very quiet and methodical approach to a mission, for up to five minutes, and then B) can be failed at the very last second of those five minutes because one guy saw you out of the corner of his eye or you got grazed by one bullet.
So even though I'm pretty completeist, I have to admit I did NOT get all the optionals, on any of the game's four difficulties.
All in all, pretty good game, with the only extensive source of frustration being that getting the soundtrack requires either dealing with a very broken site or getting Neon Chrome and using its modding tools to rip open Jydge's files to extract the music.

First Impression Gameplay:
Fan of Hotline Miami?  Enjoy character and weapon upgrades?  Dream of becoming Robocop?
Well, then perhaps JYDGE is right up your alley.
JYDGE is a top-down rogue-like shooter, where you can upgrade your character between missions.  You take on the roll of some kind of futuristic robo-cop, beating up thugs and criminals alike.
The art style is fun to look at, the audio is good, and the gameplay is fun.  What more would you want in a game of this genre?
Anyways, I'm about 25 minutes in, and I found this game to be quite fun.

If you grew up in the 1990's you may remember an indie game called "Oddworld: Abe's Odysee". This game was centred around a small blue guy called Abe who, along with the rest of his friends, was enslaved and worked for cruel Glukkon bosses with sadistic Slig supervisors. These creatures were often subjected to being beaten or shot in a day's work (and if the went on strike, I bet it was worse). One day, Abe finds out that the managers are planning a "New 'n' Tasty" product. This new kind of meat? Abe and his Mudoken friends! So you have to possess sligs (and make them go boom), get up close and personal with the local wildlife, (who are just as friendly) and whistle and fart (yes, fart) your way through temples and puzzles to get Abe and his friends out of Rupture Farms.
The game from way back then was amazing and it has been remade, rebuilt and ressurected. It is such a visual treat as it conjures up the old nostalgia of the original game but with a "next gen" make over. Graphically stunning, new features are welcome (such as being able to "Quicksave" which was only released in the spin off title) and leading more than one of Abe's friends at a time) as well as new puzzles and things to discover. If you loved the original game then this is a must have! And for new players, welcome to Oddworld, just be careful of anything that moves as even your environment is out to kill you!

Ah, Abe's Oddysey. I remember being 11 years old when I first got it, back when begging our parents to buy us a video game was a hard sell. It's very rare to see a nostalgic game redone from the ground up, and yet stay faihfully steadfast to its core. Right down to each individual platform and puzzle. Of particular note, are the cutscenes. Obviously they're FMV's and not rendered with the game engine. Infact, I think they're the original cutscenes from the PS1 game upscaled. And if I'm right, then it really does show how timeless the art design is, since it can stand with games of our current era.
One thing I have noticed with these nostalgic games, and this is more interesting than it is a negative. These nostalgic titles actually feel shorter than they did when I first played them. Like, I don't remember the escape from Rupture farms being as short as it is, and I'm not sure what it is, whether it's the camera angle, controls, or instinctive muscle memory being triggered again.
Regardless, I can't recommend this enough, whether you're a new player or going on Nostalgia like me. 10/10 would yo yo yo yo again.

For the next five minutes or so, I stumbled my way through the game, blinded by the river coming out of my eyes. I don't even know how these game developers managed to reduce me to this in such a short amount of time. I blame the soundtrack.
Once I finally managed to pull myself together, I was struck by the lovely art style- something I had heretofor been unable to fully appreciate in my sad, sad state. And then came the actual game. The controls feel very responsive, and the animations are smooth. I don't pretend to be an amazing platformer, but I think this will provide an adequate challenge for most players. I somehow managed to die 24 times in the first two hours- the struggle is all too real for me- but despite that, the nerd-rage never reached its peak. Once again, I look to the music. (It's quite calming, yet at the same time, it leaves you tensed for the next moment some story element comes to rip your heart out and leave you a sad, salty puddle on the floor.)
In conclusion: 10/10, would die again.
UPDATE: Reading back over my review, knowing what I know now, I can't help but laugh in despair. Oh, sweet summer child. Dying 24 times in two hours? If only I had been able to maintain that ratio! 7 hours in, and I have now died over 400 times- most of that on one specific segment. Tears are in my eyes as I write this. Please, for the love of all that is good, do not underestimate this game. Let me be an example to what happens to those that do. (Still 10/10, but would actually prefer NOT to die again. Please, God.)

For the first ten to thirteen hours it scratched an itch I didn't know I had, only to become an irritating sore as the game's systems tired themselves out through overbold repetition and dubious direction.
Some complaints that may resonate with the potential player:
- The game lacks a reference for where you are in the story, and unless you're following along the copious dialogue very attentively you're going to get lost. I used a walkthrough from about halfway through: I cannot recommend this highly enough. If I did not acquire a walkthrough (mostly for each levels' checklist) through the Steam Guides page, I wouldn't have finished the game.
- You won't get an item (a short-range radar) that informs you of whether or not there are collectibles in a given level until far into the game. This means you stand to be backtracking onto levels you've already scoured in the name of completionist achievements, often just to double check. Because of the short range of the device, however, you practically have to replay a lot of the awkward gameplay variations - yuck. There is very little justification to this: one is ultimately still navigating puzzles and learning a levels' layout even with the radar, and the player shouldn't sink 10 minutes exploring only to realise there's nothing of value.
- The item menu overlaps with a dialogue: when the character is asking for something quite obvious, and you - button mashing your way through the dialogue to get it to a reasonable pace - will be offering your conversational counterpart the first item in your inventory often.
- The last few achievements are off. I can't imagine anyone having enough difficulty with the game that they would reach level 30 'naturally' - I had to watch stuff on my second monitor to filter out the grind. Disappointing. Most of them are on point, however, spaced neatly throughout the story.
At times, it's great. The writing often flows and the humour isn't as heavy-handed as some other meme masterpieces littering Steam. The developer is clearly reverent of their referential material. At other times, however, you'll wish you were playing the games its referencing: leaving Evoland II, I find myself with a strong desire to play BioShock, revisit Professor Layton and conquer a Beat 'Em Up.

Nidhogg is a small game developed by an indie developer Messhof. While the game isn’t the longest one I have ever played, it is definitely
I have played in a long time. You can literally spend countless hours playing the local multiplayer against your friends. However, if you like to play with your friends, then this game is for you, but if you do not like the local multiplayer, I still recommend that the game is not very long, this needs improvement.
In Nidhogg there is only one objective , kill your opponent by out-stabbing them by using only three sets of stances, high, middle and low. While it may sound simple at first, the game is really hard to master, and sometimes it gets a little bit frustrating when you get stabbed couple times in a row. After you kill your enemy you have to run to the right in order to advance to next level, the enemy can do the same thing, the first one being the easiest and the last one. I don’t know what’s the point of that but It’s kind of hilarious and random.
As I have said before, the single-player consists of 17 AI opponents, which is great but the same can’t be said about the level variety, there is only 3 or 4 different levels which are re-used during the 17 battles in the single-player. I really wish that there was more variety in level design, maybe we’ll get them in later updates.
The art style is what I love the most about this game, the player animations are also worth mentioning because of how smooth and realistic they are, and also it feels really satisfying when you stab someone.

A gritty action experience befitting the setting of Warhammer 40,000.
Being a 3rd Person Action experience immediately makes it stand out from the rest of the competition.  With an excellent mix of brutal melee weapons and satisfying guns,  Space Marine excellently pulls-off hack-and-slash gameplay while still being a shooter.
The campaign mode is average, pitting you as an Ultramarines captain fighting against the Ork hordes and the Chaos heretics and Daemons.  The variation is little and overall, the campaign is not truly inspiring.
However, the game shines when it comes to multiplayer.  With basic multiplayer and a wave-based co-op mode, Space Marine breathes much needed life into generic multiplayer modes.
With heavily customizable loadouts and being able to play the roles of Assault, Tactical or Devastator, Space Marine allows players to tailor their loadouts around their playstyle and the needs of the game itself.  With it's unique Dreadnought Assault mode, multiplayer gets hectic while an entire team is faced with a machine capable of wiping them all out.  Space Marine's multiplayer is also blessed with decent lag compensation and speedy host migration (< 10 seconds).
Space Marine brilliantly executes a fusion of Hack-and-Slash and Shooter and brings  this brilliance with it into multiplayer, but unfortunately presents an unispired single player experience.
7/10

I got this game a couple days ago ($10), finished the tutorial yesterday.  The tutorial is admittedly complex simply due to there being much to learn, but not insane.  Movement, personal health, resource gathering, crafting, piloting, combat, building, and other stuff I've not even touched yet (social), but be patient with yourself, make use of all hints, and save the game often so you don't start from scratch each time.
Building I've not tried yet but great potential.  I'm a Landmark orphan so to me any building system is going to pale for awhile, but there is a huge library of stuff to craft and snap together Lego-style.  I'm cautiously optimistic.
Movement is pleasant and feels very realistic with nice touches of graphic subtlety.
Survival with food, health, O2, etc. seems just enough without being terribly annoying.
Resource farming I'm not sure of yet. Too little experience yet.
Crafting can feel initially complex with so many choices, especially if new to such stuff, but its bark is worse than its bite by far. Lovely to have many options and hopefully many more in the future.
Piloting/movement is simple once you get fuel, oxygen. Yet to try combat. Nice range of vehicles from scooter to hovercraft to small and capital ships. Eager to see what I can come up with.
Combat so far has been shoot from a distance but very large selection of various weaponry each with advantages and disadvantages.  Like real weapons from Saturday night specials to rocket launchers, mines, and more.
Wrapup: For a game trying to include so much I didn't feel as though it was too ponderous.  I've been playing on my laptop and even at fast [low] resolution with a trackpoint I've found myself immersed.  Of course, the challenge of playing a new game blind factors in, but I'm looking forward to my next step:  choosing a server, jumping in, and looking for a place to call home.  Worth the $10 already.  I think this ones' for real.

This game is more than a HD remaster. It overhauls the entire game with a complete redo of the graphics and a lot of minor changes to every level and the cut scenes have all been redone aswell. The game looks amazing, the atmosphere of the original setting is fully intact, if not more so. The game doesn't exactly have a "lot" of "new" content.
By this I mean, if you are buying this game to experience a brand new story or a reboot of the original game with a completely new story, this is not it. This is basically just a modern version of this game. In a way it feels inde rather than AAA. The story is largely the same with maybe a few tweaks that I noticed, but those feel more like things that the original game never patched rather than add-ons to the story. Although I think all of the oddworld games existed before patching on consol was common place.
The levels are, as I remember pretty much the same in design, just minor tweaks, and branching paths that lead into new levels. All of which are VERY nicely designed and range from easy to "I'M going to throw my controller if that damn saw kills me one more time!!" in difficulty. The challenges feel SO VERY satisfactory, especially if you take the time to figure it out yourself making the next playthrough that much faster. The awards feel pretty good when you get them, though I wish there was more. I still feel like Abe deserves some kind of upgrade tier feature, so as he progresses further he gets more powerful, you do in a way, but only with the chanting power.
When I got this game originally It wouldn't load, but support from the dev's and the community helped me resolve it in about a week or so of buying it. Playing in windowed mode seems to be preferrable on my machine, and the 360 gamepad works very nicely with the game.
Either way, this game is worth any price below 15 dollars!

I hope that this isn't a sign of a trend that this series and its "remakes" wont be charging DLC for every single little thing that is just outside of the main story line. I get charging for Abe to where scrubs, but not the Alf Escape.
Overall the game is a 7.5/10 for me.

I almost didn't buy this game. I was in the mood for a good twin stick shooter and bought Neon Chrome. This was simply an impulse buy based off the discount you got for buying NC. I'm SUPER glad I did.
I don't usually devote too much time to little indie titles like this one because they tend to get old quick, but Jydge left me pleasantly surprised. Although it's not a huge game 10tons has packed a lot into this one. The wide variety of weapons and items lets you experience each level in a new way over and over again. At first it's pretty basic, but as you ramp up the difficulty and unlock new items your playstyle can ((and will definitely need to)) change through each incarnation of each level.
Some of the challenges are crazy difficult and at times I found myself thinking 'That will just never be possible.' ((I'm talking to you 'Thinning the Herd' on Nightmare)) After a few dozen tries and a few choice words I always managed to find a set of items and strategy that eventually worked out. This game is loads of fun and I never for an instant regretted my purchase.
I've seen a lot of people upset over levels being locked behind a prohibitive amount of medals and while I get the arguement I didn't have a problem with it. If anything it pushed me to explore new strategies and helped me to get more out of the game overall. The devs have since patched in an option for that though and I think such a quick response speaks pretty highly of them
There are a few small gripes:
1. The stealth mechanic can be a little wonky at times.
2. Some of the items and weapons in the game have little or no use, ((could just be personal taste though))
3. Civillian deaths rack up even when you don't finish the mission ((ie. die or quit)) and that sucks pretty hard when there is an acheivement and something else I thought was pretty cool attached to a low civie death count. There is a way to decrease it, but it can be time consuming or simply not an option I'm willing to choose.
4. Really feels as though there should be a tracker for loot chests and elite enemies and you for sure should be able to choose whether or not you want elites or locked doors to respwan.
My biggest gripe however is that it left me wanting more. I did everything there is to do and I'm just super sad it's over. I can't wait to see what they do with that gigantic world map!
It's a fast paced good time and well worth my money. Yours too.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a fairly short metroidvania action platformer, but well worth the time and money. The unique and gorgeous art style left me staring at the scenery several times, along with the character design, incredibly detailed animations and the wonderful soundtrack.
The gameplay is solid, controlling very well along with upgrades that add a lot of motion and variety in combat. A lot of the upgrades are fairly basic things always seen in your usual metroidvania platformers, such as wall jumping and double jump, but their implementation is done very well, giving full control to the player and along with the great level design and a good difficulty curve, allowing for some challenging moments that do not feel unfair for most part. The few sections where you get no checkpoints can be a bit annoying, as you need to react fairly fast and often it just ends up being trial and error, although there aren't many of these sections and they provide a good challenge. The main problem I had in combat was just that sometimes, things would get fairly hectic and flashy and it'd be difficult to tell what is dangerous terrain and what are enemy projectiles, and what is safe. This didn't happen often enough to matter much, though.
The game has a mechanic where it allows you to place save points at your own will, at the cost of some energy. Early on, you need to be a bit mindful of where and when you place save points, as your energy stock isn't very high and is also required for other things. But as soon as you get a few more Energy Cells to upgrade your maximum energy, you'll essentially be able to save as often as you want, which takes away a bit of the difficulty. But as you choose where to use these save points, along with some of the experience upgrades that can help with the cost of the save points or even make them heal you a little bit, it's up to you how challenging you want it to be.
The experience/leveling system is fairly basic. You can get upgrades that assist with your damage, or upgrades that help gathering collectibles, or some other miscellaneous ones. If you try for 100% completion, you'll probably have almost all experience upgrades, if not all of them, by the end of the game. I finished the game missing a single upgrade.
The map is quite large, but the world and its areas connect very well, letting you traverse from one corner of the world to the other fairly quickly, especially as you gain more upgrades. This is really nice if you go for 100% completion, as you won't be wasting all that much time backtracking to get to previously inaccessible areas. Collectibles include the basic things - Maximum health upgrades, energy upgrades and experience points. As they are fairly simple items, revisiting areas is only really worth it if you're having some difficulty or if you're going for 100%.
The biggest issue I had with the game is related to this aswell, 100% completion - Two sections of the game are inaccessible after you complete them, so if you missed anything in them, no matter how little, 100% completion may become impossible. In addition, once you finish the game, your save file is locked as "completed" and you can no longer return to it, forcing you to restart the entire game if you missed anything. The game does warn you before you enter the final section, that there is no return after entering. However, there are no warnings for the other two sections and the point which they become locked also sort of comes with no warning or indication. This left me with around 96% completion all around, which was a little disappointing once I saw I could no longer access my save file.
Overall however, Ori and the Blind Forest was an incredible experience, and is definitely one of my favorites of the metroidvania platformers genre, and perhaps one of the most visually pleasing games I've ever played.

Not a particular amazing game, but enjoyable enough and some cleverly designed scenes here and there prevent you from tackling each and every battle with exactly the same old strategy.  Comparing the number of pros and cons, it's a really impressive game; but one of the cons just happens to be super important to me, bringing the game down to just decent instead.
CONS
The game can basically be broken down into four parts: cutscenes; inventory/ability screens; towns/shops; and battle scenarios.  Each of these is actually very well done.  But it leaves the game feeling a bit hollow simply because you don't get much of a feeling of exploring.  You move around the map by clicking on dots.  You move around submaps by clicking on dots.  Even the towns/shops just feel like clicking on dots.  They shouldn't, because they're much more visual, but the game just builds that feeling of dot-clicking into it, and you can't shake it.
The inventories get messy.  Weapons and armour can be seen separately, but everything else is all piled up in one section with no sorting options.  So when you're looking for healing or mana potions, be prepared to go through page after page of poisons, traps, buffing potions, throwing weapons, and EVEN all the 'quest items' - new and old, jumbled up with them.
PROS
The cutscenes are well done, the plot's interesting enough, and you really feel like you get to know the characters.
There's a good number of abilities, categorised in some interesting ways.  Most importantly, the spells have enough variety that you can really explore a range of different strategies.  Even within typical categories like direct damage or buffing, there's still variety.  (Potential SPOILER examples:
The variety might take a little while to sink in, because at first it looks like 24 spells with 4 levels of power each.  But within the 4 levels for each, most have at least one significant change, so it's actually more like 48 spells.
The options for non-spellcasters are more limited, but still allow for some good variety - especially since you can have up to three weapon sets; and/or make use of traps and throwing weapons.  It's hard to do early on, but each route you take eats up experience points, but this ultimately allows you to do things like: (a) Carry a giant two-handed bashing weapon for massive damage and quick battles, but be ready to switch into sword and shield if you need more defense and accuracy.  (b) Run around with a two-handed pike-style spear, but pitch javelins and poison bombs at your enemies before they get into melee range.  (c) Mix up archery and fencing.  (d) Go all archery, but set traps - especially stunning or slowing traps - around you when melee fighters look like they're going to get too close.  (e) etc, etc.
The weapons and armour are pretty bog-standard for an RPG overall, but are just varied enough.  The expense might seem frustrating at first, but I enjoyed the way it made me mix and match parts more often, and set different characters up with different equipment sets.  And when there are all kinds of traps and poisons and buff potions, etc, as well, it feels like you've always got something new to pick up.
The combat!  At first it looks like each map is going to be a matter of big vs small, wide vs narrow, and empty or covered with traps or blocking environment.  That'd lead to a bit of variety, but eventually you'd work out a couple of strategies that you'd just use over and over again.  But soon enough, you start seeing unique twists (some are repeated a couple of times; some are just used once).  There are plenty of them, and they are what really make the game worth it in the end. I have wanted to love this game. I really, really have. The character development system is complex and has a depth rarely found in RPGs. The story and choices are a combination of dark and darker, and yet there is no shortage of humor in the game. Having said all of that, I do NOT recommend this game for the casual gamer who enjoys RPGs. This is for the hardcore gaming fans who want to spend hours agonizing over points spent in skill and character development, only to find that you have to start over because you lack core abilities in your characters to survive. Further, the combat system is ridiculous. You get a wizard at the beginning of the game as a companion who has an ~80% accuracy range - however, in my experience, his spellcasting is weak at best, and backfires most of the time, and at often critical moments. Unfortunately, healing is also problematic because it uses an entire action (turn), and so by the next round, you may be down more health points than you were before you healed. Following me so far? That's good, because on top of that, you can count on being outnumbered and outmaneuvered in nearly every battle.
I could go on to wax poetic about the ineptitude of the combat system and the way the developers correlated character development with combat in a way that is clear, but I think you can get the gist of it from above. I have to quit playing this game because after too much time trying the same battle over and over again to rescue some baroness who loves the less than useless wizard companion I have, I am going to retire this game entirely and quite playing it. It simply lacks any enjoyment for me at this point. I think the game designers have a lot of work to do to create a product that I would ever consider purchasing again. I feel cheated of my money and my time.
Oh, and you don't have the option of really grinding your characters up to par, either. There are a set number of quests and side quests, and you spend those character development points at your own risk.
Again, there may be a market for this to hardcore gamers and some others, but it is definitely not for the faint of heart.

I honestly took a long time to play this game (I knew I eventually would as I love turn based tactical RPG), because of all the mixed reviews.  Regardless, I can't believe how much fun the combat in this game is.  I'll break down some key game concepts that might persuade you to buy or push you away.
Good:
-Amazing character development using a deep system of random dice rolls and old-school board game elements
-Hard battles (some are pushovers) that make you think or have to re-do because of a single screw up
-Deep turn based hexagonal board-like combat involving traps and the environment
-A Baldur's Gate style of map minus the exploration
-The game really focuses on the battles without the fuss of wandering and exploring (ie. not an exploration game)
Bad:
-The story is not bad, but one shouldn't be getting this game for that reason
-The itemization and game mechanics are a bit complicated to understand and required a lot of Google searching
-Linear story and no exploration
If you are looking for a game that focuses purely on the tactical turn based combat, then this is truly it.  There is no wandering and exploring with your party and discovering secrets.  The world map is like Baldur's Gate, however, when you visit cities and places, you are either transported into a combat situation with some cutscenes or visit a town where NPC's are static screens filled with innkeepers, healers, merchants, etc.

Don't bother getting attached to characters or strategically saving points to spend on a worthwhile skill.  You can lose them without any notice, having wasted opportunities to use those points to get you through certain battles.  Cardinal error.
Some fights are designed to be artificially punishing.  I haven't used the word 'cheap' since I played Nintendo in the 90s.

I'm a fan of games that try to do something new with an MMO structure, and this game definitely tries that, with massive PvP battles that you can get into pretty early on and a combat system that is at least interesting and different from any other MMO, if nothing else. The game has some good ideas, but it fails to capitalize on them with wonky controls, and a UI which isn't very user friendly, making for a fairly awkward experience.
The game is also very poorly optimized, with framerate drops happening left and right on even running on low graphics settings on a moderately powerful PC that can run a lot of other current titles.
On top of that, the writing is also somewhat poorly translated into English. It's not the worst translation I've seen, and of course, this could be overlooked if the rest of the game was great, but it's just another thign that adds to the game's overall awkwardness.
It's a shame a game with such neat ideas is currently just not very much fun to play. Every moment that I was playing it, it felt more like a chore than a fun experience. A lot of other MMOs also tend to fall into that category in some respects, but the difference is, in those games you're repeting tasks... in this game, it's just a chore to struggle with the controls, as well as struggle with the frame drops which makes everything less responsive and sluggish.
In it's current state, I wouldn't reccomend it to anybody. For MMO fans, there's plenty of other better games for you to look to. For fans of multiplayer medieval combat games, you should just check out Chivalry or Mount & Blade, both of which have a similar style of combat, but done much better with more responsive controls, but unfortunately without any kind of MMO wrapper.

I thought this would be a small, indie, pixel art game. Only one of those three is correct.
Evoland is, in essence, derivative of the Legend of Zelda games - this is apparent in the design, attack animations, level design, world map, potions - hell, the whole lot would be massive grounds for lawsuit by Nintendo if it were closer. However, in its own way it blends parts of all of the old LoZ RPGs with humor, wit, fourth-wall breaking dialogue, and absurdity that could only be inspired by Earthbound, which makes it original in its own way. The art style changes from Final Fantasy to Stardew Valley to Pokemon Red/Blue to oldschool 8-bit. The music isn't fantastic, but it is relatively period accurate to its base works.
Some would call Evoland 2 a parody of the RPG genre, but I argue that it's an exploration of how RPGs have changed over the years and a homage to games that nerdy 20-year-old guys are nostalgic about despite having never played them. It's shallow, full of wit, and charming, and never hands out the answer to a puzzle - there is no easy way in Evoland 2, much like its source content. I personally give Evoland an
and definitely would recommend it to anyone interested in the genre. I will warn you, though, the default keybinds are a bit odd and the game never tells you what they are, so just set your own when you first boot up.

Oddworld: New n' Tasty is a remake of the first game in the Oddworld series and while I hope this heralds both future remakes and new titles from the world of Oddworld, there are still some flaws with the intial game. First, the platforming sometiems has to be a hair trigger of a difference to make it through and you need a lot of patience to execute some of your movements or you will die. I played with a controller and there were times when I wanted Abe to do a forward jump, only to have him put a single toe on a mine and blow up. The Quick Save feature is also flawed, as while it is handy, you will be using it over and over again for dificult parts so you don't have to go back to a check point; good idea, but there are no save slots, you just get the one quick save. Alright, just have to be smart with your saves then, right? Well, it isn't so easy; you will be quick loading time and time again, which means pausing and gonig to the load option; problem is between resume and load is the quick save button; accidently press that in a moment when you're not dead and bam, quick save messed up. Luckily, the only time you will need to load is after a death or you fudged up a rescue, jsut becareful not to accidently hit quick save in the menu unless you actaully mean to. The deaths in this game are amusing at first, but if you die a lot, sitting through them can be grating; falling down a pit is the worst because you have to wait for Abe to hit the buttom before your checkpoint loads or just load a quicksave while you're waiting, but its still annoying.
The charm of Oddworld and the puzzle/platforming are still quite exccelent, making you think in new ways to figure out how to deal with a situation or even finding your own way to with enough creativity; it does allow deviations from the set method of problem solving, so one person's solution to a problem could be different from another's solution. Despite the negatives, I had fun, just skip the DLC level Alf's Escape unless you really have that itch for more.
7/10, for those who like a good puzzle platformer.

A decent remake but for one thing: the game's entire atmosphere gets ruined by the Mudokons' and Sligs' comic mutterings. In the original, Sligs were silent and focused killing machines and terrifying, and Mudokons were sentenced to toil silently. The tone was oppressive, serious, and frightening in a good way.
Now sligs patrol complaining about their paychecks and lunch, and the Mudokons make jokes about super shiny floors, finally getting their own brush, and another day in the office. The entire atmosphere's gone, and there's nothing we can do to recover it as players.
I completed the original a couple of times and loved it. The fact the remake included these voices is a loss, and I can't keep playing it, and in a puzzle with a few Sligs and Mudokons they're all complaining and joking enough I can't even think straight.
Would become an excellent remake if there was an option to shut the voices off, or they simply weren't there to begin with (they shouldn't be). Alas, they destroye the atmosphere and it sucks.
I recommend against getting this remake.

This game invoked such a feeling of nostalgia - I played the original Oddworld games on my PSX, and thoroughly enjoyed them.
The game follows the adventures of Abe, a Mudokon, and drone working for Rupture Farms.  He stumbles across a secret he'd rather not have found out about, and his mission is to rescue his fellow Mudokons.  Killing a few of his captors along the way doesn't hurt either.
There is challenge in this game, and I'm pretty sure I picked up the 'Kill Abe 25 different ways' Steam achievement very early on.
The new graphics really are great, and small changes like finding trapdoors for secret areas, rather than just disappearing behind some barrels were nice touches.
I highly recommend this game.  If you played the originals, this game will remind you why you loved them so much.  If you're new to the franchise, prepare to fall in love with Abe, and his sweet little stich-lipped face.

Let me preface this review to say I have not played Neon Chrome, nor do I agree 100% with what a lot of the negative reviews seem to have a gripe for with this game and its style of progression. I have just finished the last level of the game to give you an idea of where I am at.
First off the setting is fantastic. You are basically a robotic version of  Judge Dredd, placed in different scenarios ranging from rescue the VIPs to murder the crap out of all of the bad guys. The game feels best with a PS4 style controller I've found (well any controller with 2 sticks at least) as you will be using one to aim and one to move. The controls feel very fluid and fun.
Now each map has three different objectives and up to three difficulties (you unlock the two remaining difficulties over the course of the game). Completing an objective gives you a medal. These medals are basically your form of progression as they unlock new levels, new skills, new weapons, everything (then you use money to buy those unlocked items). If you stick to your play style you should have no problem making it through to at least the first half of the game. This is when you probably need to take a look back at the medals and see where you need to get them. A lot of people seem to be complaining about the ones where you exit in __ seconds. I feel like this is specifically a design choice not to make you a speed runner or care about time as much as its making sure you have put the money toward making sure your character has the power to deal with running through the earlier levels rather than making it to the next level and thinking its ridiculously hard when in reality its because you've invested poorly. I completed most of those for the first chapter just to make sure I could and did a few stealth missions from those as well. Aside from that I did not do any more of either of those style medals for the rest of the game, I just didnt need to, there were enough medals to unlock the remaining levels.
The game is definitely not easy but I love that it has some difficulty. But here are a few tips for while you go through the game:
- In the first half of the game do NOT just go and buy every weapon that unlocks. Stick to something you like and upgrade its damage as much as you can. For instance I went with the laser as my primary. That beast can rip through multiple enemies with a single hit and if you have the Vampire trait on your gun you get +10 health for every enemy you kill with it making crowds easier to deal with since they become a roving health kit (just dodge their bullets of course! not that it matters as much as you will be healing quick).
- Don't forget about your specials! They can do some ridiculous damage on enemies especially elite enemies. Not only that but can help with the environment. Dont have a key or hacking ability to open this door? BLOW IT OPEN!
- Use the environment to your advantage. Don't run through that hallway full of enemies, go into the bathroom next to it, knock a hole in the wall behind one of the enemies and let them trickle through as you rain death upon them funnelling themselves into the room.
- Keep running into a problem with a type of enemy? There are probably multiple ways to resolve that. You'll run into melee enemies that just run up and bash the crap out of you and many are pretty powerful. You could buy the Bull Bullet perk, which hits them back for every hit of your projectile, OR you could max the crap out of your weapon and kill them early. Do what makes the most fiscal sense for you now, later in the game you will have more than enough money to unlock whatever you want.
Closing thoughts: I loved this game. It scratched the itch that the Crusader games left decades ago and has been festering. The only negative I have is wishing the game was a bit longer. HOWEVER thats not to say I didnt think the game was worth $15 for a game that took nearly 8 hours to complete (not 100% of the medals and unlocks of course). This does make me want to buy Neon Chrome however!
UPDATE: So after finishing this review I went right over and bought Neon Chrome. I honestly think Jydge made much of the gameplay and aspects of Neon Chrome easier than if I had just started with that as there is a lot of cross over with some enemies, objects and abilities. In the end I defeated Overseer 1.0 in 5 hours and on my 4th asset.

Other than movies, it is hard to make me cry at a work of art. I am not claiming it in a masculine undertone, but instead in the methods that work of art impose through a major amount of text. Whenever I read a novel, I never find myself in the verge of tears over an emotional scene. It may, persay, get my heart in a sort of drowsiness, but that's about it. So when I say that I had big droplets coming down at the end of this game, I can safely declare that such a game is a complete masterpiece.
The concept is already incredible and hard to think about without posing the ethics, the correctiveness, and the technical aspects of it, and regardless, it is still something worth talking about at any given moment. This sequel kicked off just like the original, with a new twist in the mechanics of the machine and an explanation behind said mechanics. Everything ties together and you can tell that Kan Gao is not ♥♥♥♥ing around when he writes his stories.
Apart from the side-story with Sigmund Corp., the story itself begun simple to me, and I already had expectations for how it would turn out. Of course, the genius of Kan made you believe certain events would happen, when in reality, it was something completely different. Truthfully, Kan Gao knows how to correctly write a plot twist, and even more, how to write a plot twist that is subtle, but predictable and not spontaneously ex-machina.
The ending of the story punched me into a muse of thought that shifted itself into one of emotions, and before I knew it I began to cry at the complete melancholy that was this story, this game, this experience.
Finding Paradise is a work of art that cannot be compared easily to other scientific works, but instead deserves a spot at the very top of those of the genre. So much was left for me to think in only four hours of playing it. Truthfully worth every penny, every minute, and every bit of space it uses to convey its story from thought to thought.

It's Call of Duty In Space!  Nothing more, nothing less.
The campaign looks like an ordinary CRPG nowadays, let's say Mass Effect. The only difference is - you don't have the dialogue wheel, but still there's gear customization, few things you can interact with on your star-but-not-star-destroyer, perks, and you can choose which and when to start side or main missions. Somehow this makes CoD: IW more of an RPG game than a lot of CRPGs. If you like those things set in the future, go for it.
Multiplayer is CoD meets Titanfall - double-jumping-wall-running-fast-paced-shooting-things. It's not the best combo, but it works. There's a lot of things to unlock and work towards to, if someone likes to be regularly rewarded and grind those levels - here you go. The profile and character customization are an overkill, those shiny and badges with gifs, crazy colored weapons just look like the beginning of the internet. Just close your eyes, hear the modem sound and go for an adventure in the 90's...
Is it worth buying? If you'll get your hands on it for 10$ or less - it's worth the price.

A great mid budget game that comes to revitilize a stagnated genre that has failed its core audience for years. This is not an action game with stealth elements nor is it a stelath game that here and there relies on combat. This is a pure infiltration, assassination and thieving game. Combat is the bare minimum and enemy encounters in the open should be avoided at all cost. In stealth games less is more and the fact that combat in Styx is basically three functions makes the game shine in every other aspect. In addition the game has a well written story in a low fantasy setting with a pinch of moral ambiguity and some dark locals and levels. Styx himself is a well written protagonist with great voice acting and animation that truly represents how a golbin should act. This fluidity of Styx's movement goes hand in hand with the verticallity of the level design and the variety of his weapons and skills to create a great hardcore experience. However, Styx is far from perfect, all of its shortcomings are created from the fact that this is a mid budget game. Animations at times are rough, the AI may hiccup and some textures feel too generic. Although these shortcomings are mostly product of nitpicking over tiny details. In conclusion, Styx: Master of Shadows is a diamond in the rough. A game that can sit in the same self  with Thief 1, Thief 2, Tenchu, Splinter Cell and all the other great games that defined the genre. Fans of the stealth genre will love it but everyone else that occasionally meddles from time to time with games like Dishonored an Assassin's Creed will find difficult and non-forgiving.
