This right here is an underrated gem from the pitch black depths of steam. Initially I was very skeptical considering the first Evoland lasted only about 4 hours and was horribly linear. I liked it, but there was something missing... a great story!
Luckily this time around, Evoland 2 got it right! The story lasts between 15 and 25 hours, and many new mechanics have been added (trading cards, time travel, power upgrades, etc). There’s plenty of game-related references and fun easter eggs that should please any experienced gamer, and there are some TV and Anime references as well!
Evoland 2 is blessed with a great story about time travel and it's consequences, through which you’ll meet many different characters each with their own backgrounds and ambitions. There’s a big world to explore, minimizing the linearity that plagued the first game. Each of the time periods feature their own beautiful, hand-crafted pixel or 3D graphics, different styles of gameplay, with soundtracks to match! Hack and slash, turn-based strategy, Bejewled-style match 3, beat-em-up, you name it. Many more waiting to surprise you!
In terms of pacing the game had some problems with 2-3 areas dragging on for far too long and I had to look up some puzzles, but beyond that there’s little left to complain about! I couldn’t find and bugs or real problems throughout my playthrough.
Evoland 2, A Slight Case of Spacetime Continuum Disorder uniquely combines so many different genres and ideas in a way that no other game has really done before, and i can recommend it to anyone who is interested in an RPG/Hybrid that is doing something that no other game has done yet. Solid gameplay, a great story, and videogame history all over the place; what’s not to love about that?

Holy smokes this game is huge. 20+ hours during which you don't even need to grind since it's content packed and tries it's best to remain fresh? That's pretty impressive.
The first Evoland was just a short, metadevelopment joke using the player's nostalgy to show some puns and not-that-good, grindy gameplay. Evoland 2 is actually like a real, complex jRPG with a lot of variety, detailed setting, developed characters and epic, well planned story (which unfortunatelly is cliche as heck and very predictible).
Some parts of the game have decent depth while the others only touch the surface of other genres and give you just the general taste of them. It's impossible that you'll find each and every one of these game modes equally interesting since you may find here almost everything - logical puzzles, CCG, tactical RPG, sidescroll platforming, Pong, Bomberman-like levels, shoot 'em up, bit 'em up, god-damn guitar hero... The only part I really missed was the one which would include a good storytelling, but you can't have everything.
Attention to detail is very impressive. Not only the game uses multiple camera views and graphics from various periods, but most changes affect the controls as well and each area looks different depending on which timeline you visit it. It's difficult to not get even slightly attached to the land you try to save from Epic Danger. The music is mostly lovely (check out the "Magi's Theme", it's fantastic) and you can visit most-if-not-all areas if you want to chase the collectibles.
There are, obviously, some problems. For example, sometimes your character gets blocked in a weird glitch and you have to reload the game. The thing I hated the most, however, was the dad-joke'y humor. 90% of the jokes are references and they get lazy and boring really fast. Here is an example: you see a picture and it has a "blue hedgehog" on it. That's the joke. If you find it hilarious, you will laugh your butt off while playing this game, but if you are like me and you need something more than "oh, that's something I recognize! lul!", you'll roll your eyes a lot.

It's a lacklustre console port. If you can get past that then please feel free to read further.
The game is 'good' and probably the best bike racing simulator I've played, and as a biker I buy them all. The physics engine is generally pretty decent, the bikes themselves are faithfully modelled and of course its nice to have the Dorna permissions to include the full roster of teams and rides. But that's it.
The game is built on a clearly dated engine that has reached, if not passed its end of life cycle. I'm playing on a fairly competent machine, i7, 16Gb, GTX670, SSD and the game performs poorly with frequent stuttering. Garage scenes are particularly ugly with massive screen tearing and corruption when selecting the bike to confirm which developments to complete. Very poor.
Racing is generally good. There's a decent sense of speed and simulation going on though the sound of the bikes is pretty off. AI is generally perfunctory at best. They ride and do what they're supposed to do though have no real character; you can certainly tell that it is algorithm riding the bikes.
However the biggest negative is the startling fact that this is a poorly optimised console port and Milestone hasn't done anything to even attempt to hide this fact: No graphics options, poorly optimised UX (for PC), No way to Quit to desktop(!), no way to save custom controller configurations...
Milestone don't tend to patch their games. I don't expect any of these issues to be addressed.
End of the day I waited until the game was on sale before buying as I'm fully aware of Milestone's track record and history with respect to their games and support there on in. I paid GBP 14.99 and feel that I have a fair value for money at that price proposition.
Summary; it is a 'good game' for an unambitious console port with the usual trappings of what that entails. Don't buy at full price!

This game is far from optimised for the PC platform. We've been waiting for a patch to fix many bugs, major and minor, since June, and so far we still have a game working at 75%.
The community support from Milestone has been terrible since the launch of this game. Communication has never been their strong point for titles like MotoGP, WRC, etc, which I suppose is equally as bad as their efforts to release games which are worthy of being retail releases.
Perhaps one of the biggest gripes I have is the limited video options you get with this title. As per usual in a Milestone game, you cannot change the video settings in-game; the launcher is where you have to make your changes, and once you're in-game, that's it. Not only that, but the options you actually get to choose from are dire, and the game, even when bumped up to the highest settings, looks tacky for a PC game. I wouldn't consider myself that much of a graphics snob, but there's a line you cannot go back over once we're into a new generation.
There's a good game in here somewhere, but it's surrounded by problems, from stupid to complex. Therefore, I won't be recommending this game, neither will I be recommending any Milestone product until they pull their finger out to improve 1) the quality of their games for release, and 2) their general customer support.

A huge downgrade from 2013, the Graphics are awful. There is no option for AA, and everything looks fuzzy. I still have to force quit out of the game, half the time it doesn't save my game or controls. There are big inconsistency between qualifying and race lap times. The bikes sound more like a lawn mower then a superbike. Not to mention the UI for the game is still terrible,

The game provides a very reallistic riding experience, especially with TCS off. Very demanding controls but once you learn how to handle the powerful bikes you can go much faster without TCS. The graphics are decent, no clipping, jagged edges, etc on my machine running it at full settings. However the game is plauged by several technical bugs that have no business being in a finished game. The control schemes do not save after exiting the game so if you change the controls you have to do so again every time you start the game up or they revert back to default. Also the game has no exit button. Sometimes alt + F4 works but sometimes you get stuck with having to force close the game with the task manager. I personally have never been able to connect to the online portion of the game even for uploading race times. The game has a lot of potential but really falls short and it feels like the developer just rushed it out with little to no testing. Very dissapointing after spening $40 on the game. With that said, avid moto gp fans will enjoy the authenticity and the actual racing mechanics but the game has very little depth to keep you interested after a season or two. I can't honestly recommend this game to anyone other than die hard racing fans who might at least get some enjoyment out of it.

I'm sorry if this isn't a very technical review, but I just got done playing and wanted to gush. This is seriously one of the BEST recent games I've played. I didn't know much about this going in aside from how simply gorgeous it looks, and for $20 I figured I'd take the plunge. Man, I'm REALLY glad I did.
Okay, so first off, you're going to notice that the art is, bar none, the most beautiful looking thing ever. I want to say that it kind of invokes a Ghibli sort of feeling, but that's not really doing it justice because that doesn't even begin to explain it. The whole world seems alive with its painted style. Colors are vibrant, sounds are immersive, and oh my GOD the soundtrack is moving.
It really helps out the story, too. The tale is emotional and well-presented, really doing a good job of tugging at the heartstrings without feeling too cheesy or tryhard. It isn't a particularly ORIGINAL story, to be fair, but it's just executed so well that it doesn't matter. All of the characters work really well, especially the antagonist. You really get a sense of dread and panic every time this giant black owl swoops down. It's crazy.
Graphics and story aside, the game controls amazing. Moving and jumping around feels awesome, and each new upgrade you find makes you want to go back over everywhere you've been just to see all the new things you can do. Progression is smooth, and you can explore the game at your own pace or try to speedrun and probably have fun regardless. It's not an EASY game, either. Unless you really know what you're doing, prepare to die a bunch. It's not much of a problem, though, considering that you can save at any time just by holding down the corresponding button, assuming you have the required energy. You die, you're dropped right back where you last saved without missing a beat.
That being said, I DID have one problem with the controls. There's a ground pound move you can do by jumping and pressing down. Fairly standard, I like the ability, but it felt like it was a bit too sensitive. I found myself dying more than once because I was holding a direction at a slightly downward angle, causing me to fall right into traps and get frustrated. I never stopped playing because of it, though, so it's not really that big of a deal.
All in all, this was an EXCELLENT buy. The price is logical and you'll get a lot out of your money with this. Seriously; give it a try. You won't regret it.

Now that I finished this game, is time to review it.
When I heard about a tactic turn-based strategy game, about some blackguards (that promised some bad guys doing bad things!) with RPG elements, and I saw the game was in my steam library, I said: "Yes!"
But... that was a big mistake.
The story of the game has a good start: A mystery. A murder. Are you guilty? Are you innocent? If you are innocent, who is the true murderer? Why can't you remember nothing?
And with that, you get out of prison to live some adventures.
The characters are charismatic and with personalities of their own. The world is full of life, but most of the secondary missions are only valuable for the Adventure Points (the XP of the game), and they are irrelevant to the story.
The game has a few plot twists and they are not bad at all, but before reaching them you will probably exhausted. The problem is that the ending is... well... is HORRIBLE. It is the ending that you can expect, but is displayed in a really awful and strange way that makes you think: "I really finished this game to see this?"
The gameplay is good in the beginning, but when you are more or less mid-game you will probably be sick of being poisoned. And that's only the start: The machine abuses the use of poisons. You will probably hear every turn "Poison!" or "I am poisoned!" or "I hate poison". Also, some special combats in Act 5 are never explained why are this special or why the special rules.
As many other tactic turn-based games, probabilities are really important. That means you can have a lucky day and impact an almost impossible shoot, or a really unlucky and fail all your 98% chance spells. But, as always, it seems "50%" means "1/2" to me and "1/10" to machine, as I never impacted an attack under 20% and usually failed things of 70-80%, 95% or even 98%. In a game where every movement, every action counts, this can make you sick really fast. Also, the enemies are as if they were taken out of Matrix, because they can dodge easily and usually all your attacks.
So, well, unless you really want to be poisoned EVERY combat, lose your patience failing your 98% chance spells and being parried attacks that shouldn't be parried, and playing a lot of hours to receive a half-cooked last Act with a fast ending as closure, you probably shouldn't play this game.

It's just... bad.  The visuals are average, with bits of them bordering on terrible.  The story and exploration are linear, and the story itself is just plain boring.  The voice-work is just good enough to point out how comically bad it is.  Towns are bland and lifeless.  Combat is stagnant, and shows no complexity.  Even if you buy Blackguards on sale, you likely still won't find the time to sit down with it.  There just isn't any single thing exciting enough to make up for the blandness of the rest of the game.  Nothing to draw you back in, after the first time you've played.
It's well done from a mechanical standpoint - The skill trees are well thought out and balanced.  There's just nothing flashy in them to draw attention, and the execution becomes poor when you see your character dully performing their moves and abilities with passable graphics and poor weapons/equipment.  Blackguards is a pen-and-paper RPG adaptation that never really got past the pen-and-paper bit.  More of a visualisation of some DM's real-world tabletop setup that would seem much cooler set up with cardboard on your buddy's gaming table.
If you're hellbent on playing Blackguards, I hear Blackguards 2 is actually worth the time.  It's on my list of 'soon to play' games, so I'll put up a review ASAP.

Alright, so aesthetically this game is wonderful. The multi-colored silhouttes and epic background music had me ready to go. The mechanics, however, ruined the playablility. I kept trying to play and got pretty far, but I got to the point where it didnt seem physically possible to proceed and I rage quit. The problems seem minor on the surface, but become increasingly difficult to work around and increasingly frustrating. First off, the double jump is really touchy- if you wait too long you lose it and if you go too soon you're distance is cut, which all too often leaves a tiny window for a perfect jump. If you had the ability to see ahead you might be able to plan out the jumps, but thats not an option. On the topic of jumping, hitting your head into the low ceilings cause you to swiftly fall, which cuts your margin of error even futher. The enemies aren't horrible to deal with, except for their knockback, which is basically a death sentance since there is very little ground. The only time running into them is a real issue is when you are stranded on an platform of the same color,  which forces you to jump far before you are ready. Couple this with the quirky double jump and you can't help but wonder why the bottomless pit isn't filled to the brim with corpses. But wait, there's more! Even if you get your perfect reaction time going you'll find there are a few delays--if you change colors quickly you'll find its not instantaneous, and enemies have a short moment to hit you even with the color change in effect. When the basic method for solving the "puzzles" is broken you know you have a problem.  Also, the MAX bar is useless except for a few puzzles where the game basically forces you to use it, and it feels so unsatisfying to use. You have a super short period of time to use it and sacrifice most of your hp, and it takes too long to change each color as i mentioned before so you spend half the time turning them off.
The biggest thing about this game that gets to me is that there isn't time to do "puzzles", its more of a reaction time game. The saws that appear by proximity are the best example of this. You can't plan, just run fast and hope you don't die, and when you do you have to revise and run again. There are many games that pull this off well and in a satisfying way-this does not, mostly on the basis of the levels being too long and redoing these parts is frustrating at best.
If you play this game, enjoy the music and visual elements, and good luck.

This game has a really nice concept. You go through a series of platforming levels making obstacles and platforms appear and disappear by making them match the background colour. The graphics are very simple but they work well for this game. The problem is that the mechanics and level design are not as polished as they should be and instead of becoming about skill and reflexes it seems to be a lot more about trial and error.
Some of the main problems I have encountered have been really weird hit boxes that kill me before a collision or after I've changed the background. Making obstacles appear and disappear starts to become frustrating when you're standing on a platform, change the background and are instantly killed by an enemy appearing over you with no way to counter it. Random deaths are not good in a game.
You can also die instantly from revealing platforms in the same space as you. That does make sense but becomes a problem with the game levels being much larger than the screen and no background visuals to judge distance. The only way to jump from one platform into an invisible box with no references on the screen and the screen moving to keep your character centered is by luck and many attempts. This problem could be easily solved by making the character smaller and the levels tighter. You won't lose anything but it will make platforming easier.
It's a nice concept for a game but the levels are poorly designed lending itself to trial and error.

I found the game to be quite fun starting out with it ,but as time went on it just starts to decline until it just became a chore to complete. By the end of it all, there are more cons that outweigh the pros and it just makes it an overal unenjoyable experience.
I'll start with level design. I find the leels to be similar to dishonored where you have a large area with multiple ways to approach a situation andcollectibles to find. But there's a lot that Styk misses out on. First off, the collectibles are very spread out and hard to find, having small coins that are hard to spot where there are 30-40 on each level. These levels are already really long so I imagine it being a huge pain to actually go out of your way to collect ALL the coins, although you do get more skill points for doing it (I think). The levels are also made in a way where it's best to avoid enemies often instead of taking them all on, as there can be about a hundred enemies per mission. The biggest problem with level design is that halfway through the game, they make you go back and do EVERY LEVEL BACKWARDS. I'm not joking; you have to go from the jail cells all the way back to where you did the first mission and it's HALF THE GAME. You go from A  to B, and then back to A. This makes the game way longer than it should be (took me 20 hours to beat the game, started to get tired after 15).
The story is ok. I can't really explain my issues about it without spoiling it so I'd say skip this paragraph if you haven't played and are reading reviews. For a long time I had no idea what the full objective of the game really was; just something to do with the heart of the tree because "Styx" couldn't remember much. I was actuallyreally interested at the plot twist halfway through when you find out your playing the clone and that the real Styx has been giving you orders the whole time. But then it started to get confusing because Styx and Rakesh (I'll just call the clone Rakesh since it's what Styx refers to him as) look and sound basically the same other than some scars on Styx's face. It took me the rest of the next mission to figure out if I was even playing as Rakesh or Styx, and even then there were some inconsistancies (such as when Ozkan frekas out when you return to the hideout, despite the fact that you've been working with him for 3 or 4 missions [Also they say multiple times that he's blind but he's suddenly able to see Rakesh]) The end was also anti-climactic. No boss fight, just kill a couple of clones and then it's done with a cutscene. Very uneventful conclusion between the scuffle of Rakesh and Styx.
Gameplay. As I stated in my first paragraph, I did enjoy the ability to have multiple ways to approach a situation. There were some glitches with hitboxes (especially the ogres and amber cockroaches, they need to be fixed badly). I like the ability to have a skilltree as well, but I feel that the entire 'kill' skilltree is unnecessary as it's all something you should already have as abilities when starting the game; being able to pull people down from ledges, attacking from above, attacking from around corners.
By FAR my biggest issue is with enemy types. As the game goes on, more and more enemies are introduced to the game. Enemies in a stealth game should provide a new challenge without becoming more difficult, so as to not make the game too challenging. This can make it so that certain options may not be feasible to get past a section due to a new obstacle. What does this game do wrong? HALF THE ENEMIES IN THE GAME CAN KILL YOU IN ONE HIT!!! I'm not even kidding. Enemies that can kill you in one hit are; Knights, Ogers, Elves, Crossbowmen with poison arrows, and amber cockroaches (they technically can since they're melee attack can chain you and you can't excape from it). Enemies that CAN'T kill you in one hit; Standard Guards, regular crossbowmen, clones, workers of any sort, doomed, and possesors. This makes it so that even if you're playing on the easiest difficulty that the game can be INSANELY hard. Especially by the last mission where they have almost only elves who can one hit you AND sense you without needing to see you.
I find it hard to recommend this game to someone. If you get it on a good sale then it might be worht picking up. I payed ~$5 for it and I did have some fun, but it was stressful by the end. There seems to be a large lack of tesitng done to evaluate the game before release, especially in terms of bugs. It might be a reasonable to get this when it's on sale, but I can't give it a thumbs up when it's at full price.

Styx is one of those games that you can just tell that it needed a sequel to polish it up enough to be great. (I have yet to buy said sequel but I will next sale.) For the most part it’s a pretty solid stealth game, but as mentioned in a lot other reviews it is not a modern stealth game. Modern stealth games like Dishonored and Mark of the Ninja tend to give you a good deal of freedom in how you play, Styx pretty much demands you to be much more cautious, getting into direct combat with more than one enemy is practically a guaranteed death sentence even on Normal. You need to pick off enemies one by one, avoid them entirely, or get the heck out of dodge. The controls are a bit wonky, the enemy pathfinding is laughably bad at times, and towards the end of the game you pretty much have to savescum because good luck trying to run away. The game also probably should have been a couple of hours shorter, because it starts wearing out its welcome, especially because you do the past four areas in reverse. It also has a final boss fight that could probably be pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you haven’t been upgrading your abilities. Despite these flaws it’s still a fun game, the level design is expansive, giving you a good deal of options and while you go through each area twice, they change things up enough so it’s not completely samey.  The writing overall is just okay, but the plot has an actually clever twist.
Overall, while flawed, Styx is still a quality stealth game. Definitely looking forward to Shards of Darkness considering that it sounds like it’s an improvement.

When I saw that the creators of Neon Chrome made this, I was really excited and picked it up, but after playing it a bit, I became very dejected and disappointed.  My issue with the game is that progression is tied in with earning "medals" for completing specific objectives per level, and the medal curve becomes so steep to progress it becomes tedious to keep playing trying to get every little thing done the way the game wants it done.
What I really LOVED about Neon Chrome is the freedom and flexibility to complete levels the way you wanted to, such as clearing the whole floor or running right to the elevator to avoid death, and the way random chance created a new experience every time.  Jydge is the opposite experience, where each level plays out the same way, and you're forced to learn it and replay it as many times as it takes you to get enough medals to progress with either gear or the story itself.
Although I really enjoyed the setting and aesthetic of the game, I find the way progression functions to make the game a tedious experience.

New 'n' Tasety really captures the essence of Oddwold: Abe's Oddysee, but in 3D!
The gameplay is exactly the same 2d platformer, and everything is right where I expect to find it (even if it loks a bit different), but the areas aren't divided into small screens - each area is one continuous ...err... area.
But what about these Sligs, you ask ? well, good question. As far as I can tell, as long as you cannot see them, they cannot hear you, and you cannot take possesion over them. (well, actually it's OK if you can just barely see them).
One thing that I think was lost here is that Sligs can no longer run off screen when you chant before you take possession of them, which is a shame. (I did play the game on normal difficulty, so I may change that last bit after I finish hard difficulty).
Another new thing is difficulty levels. On normal difficulty you get 10 HP, so it's easier to escape Sligs that are sooting you in the back. I will certainly try out the hard difficulty soon.
There is one thing that I feel is a bit off, but I just cannot be sure - it feels like you have more freedome in Abe's position, and it feels like I sometimes die because my position was off a few pixels (opposed to Abe's old tile-based position). But again, it's just a feeling, so I may be wrong.
All in all this is a great game, and I recommend it to all Abe's Oddyssee fans and anyone who likes a good puzzle/action platformer.

Oddworld: Abe's
is the seventh game set in the Oddworld series that has spanned across 20 different platforms to date. The Oddworld universe and the beloved main character Abe's first appearance was on the Sony Playstation in 1997, which released to immense critical acclaim, winning multiple, much deserved game of the year awards and was instantly projected into the rarely achieved elite status as one of the best games ever created. Fast forward 18 years and the initial title Abe's Oddysee graphically speaking didn't age well whatsoever, yet the gameplay of course has still stood the test of time.
With that being said, can the newly developed Abe's Oddysee: New and Tasty ressurrect what was once considered a pinnacle of the industry and return the franchise to it's past glory? Can developers Just add water do this with grace, remaining faithful to fans as well as the series roots that built them? Let's take a deeper look into the Oddworld Universe once again and see if Abe's Oddysee is still as endearing as it was all those years ago....
Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee
is a reimagining of the 1997 platform/puzzler classic Abe's Oddysee. Here you take the role of Abe, a pleasantly delightful award winning janitor, who discovers his glukkon overlord employers at Rupture Farms, have decided to attempt to increase their profit margins by using your species as the ingredients of their new food products.
As Abe, you attempt to escape, while freeing as many of your fellow mudokens as possible, you will encounter an assortment of challenging situations that are each more life threatening than the next. With locals, visually each more awe inspiring than the next, you'd be hard pressed to not be impressed with the care taken in recreating this beloved classic.
Developers, Just Add Water have managed to not only recreate the experience many of us grew to love years ago, but have reimagined it by such great lengths that simply calling it a remake is doing it a great injustice. For fans of the original or simply fans of amazing gaming exoperiences, Abe's Oddysee: New and Tasty is one to remember!
Many as well as I, consider the tale of Abe and his oddysee to be heavily influenced by Stanley R. Greenburg's screenplay Soylent Green. Although there are substancial differences between the two, the general principle behind them both are quite similar.
In Abe's Oddysee
, you'll establish a relationship with your lovable protagonist within mere minutes, as he walks across the screen happily buffing the floors of his workplace and as he continues down the halls, by chance, he discovers the shocking truth, in regards to, the gukkons plans for the frightening future they have in store for his mudoken race. As you continue your journey, you'll truly want to see Abe to his safety, so he can live to see another day and that is incredibly rare achievement.
During your journey, you will encounter a differing mix of platforming and puzzles both of which are excecuted to perfection. I simply can't find anything to gripe about in terms of gameplay and must commend Just Add Water for their skillful recreation.
Abe's Oddysee: New and Tasty, like the many other platforming classics that have come before it, shows why this genre during the 80's and 90's was considered the measurement to which all other genres were judged. Precise movements, challenging scenarios and a multitude of other gamplay elements that bring it all together creating a seamless gaming experience. It's exactly these reasons why the platform/puzzler genre is one of the most difficult to successfully design. You must make each gameplay element mesh, unbeknownst to the player, without them ever feeling forced and Abe's Oddysee
nails them all without blinking an eye.
Abe's Oddysee is something to behold, especially so while being played at high resolutions. The 3D models, environments and well...everything was crafted with care and detail. There's simply not a thing in this universe that isn't a sigt to behold. The art style is ageless, as well as original still to this day. There aren't many worlds that resemble anything close to the Oddworld games and in this day and age of copy/paste to succeed, it's fantastic to know that artistic experiences like these can still exist.
In regards to optimization, Abe's Oddysee
runs amazingly smooth and across the three workstations I've tested it on, each experience at their respective resolutions were simply magnificent. A fantastic port, filled with just enough graphics options to make the PC gamer happy. Directly below, in the screenshot, lists the available graphics options.
Resolutions can be selected up to 4K and can be achieved by systems of moderate hardware resources, all easily at 60fps. Yet even at lower resolutions of sub 1080p, Abe's Oddysee is still a breathtaking experience. So overall, if someone were to complain, they would simply be rustling up problems that don't exist in the games coding. They would lay within your system and not that developers lack the ability or excecution to bring you a successful product, because they did and a grade A experience at that, did they bring you.
This is something that shouldn't be overlooked when judging the Oddworld games, specifically one's with Abe as the protagonist, due to the vocal nature of his gameplay. The sound in New and Tasty adds so much depth to the experience, it simply cannot be overstated. Without Abe's hello's, follow me's, whistles to name a fwe, the game just wouldn't have the same effect.
Aside from aiding the character development and gameplay elements, the other sounds in the game add quite a bit of atmosphere, making you feel that this world is genuine at every turn. From ambient environment sounds, to the sounds of enemy sligs firing away with their weapons as you evade their attacks, each and every element comes together to create a living breathing world.
Although, the Oddworld games aren't known for their replayability due to their linear nature, they are still very much so games that you would revisit from time to time over the years. With that being said Abe's Oddysee: New and Tasty is no different. A classic experience that, once purchased, you have the privilage of re-experiencing again and again throughout the years. Yet, this time I foresee Abe's Oddysee standing the test of time for a much longer duration than the original, due to the immense amount of effort given by Just Add Water. With that being said, it is without a doubt that I beg you to buy Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee
for your own benefit, because this is a game that truly must be experienced by all.

is beautiful, heartfelt and a worthy follow-up to
.  The light puzzle and exploration gameplay serves to illustrate the story of a man's life, wishes and regrets that shows a keen understanding of human nature.  As a sequel, it improves on the original in length, gameplay, art/graphics, and humour, while also telling a different story.  Despite the multi-year wait I was happy, and recommend it to anyone who likes emotional narrative-driven games.
The gameplay divides into three types: periodic simple puzzles; exploration; and some more arcade-like mini-games later on.  In this regard it follows its predecessor, but I found all three elements improved.  The puzzles are simple, but varied with new mechanics introduced throughout.  The exploration sections divide up the story, and serve to draw attention to the relative importance of different events in Colin's life.  The arcade sections are simple and silly, but fun and less frustrating than the
equivalent.
Away from the gameply, the art design is good and the music excellent.  The humour also hit the mark frequently, one area that I felt was much improved over its predecessor.
also avoids the sequel trap of telling the same story with the names changed.  This has its downside;
was noted for its emotional sledgehammer, but here the story places greater emphasis on mystery and humour.  But it also knows how to play your emotions when appropriate.
Despite my references to the previous game,
is a stand-alone game.  To those unfamiliar with the SigCorp Universe, this is a satisfying introduction.  Old fans should find this a worthwhile continuation.  I only hope we don't have to wait another six years for episode 3.

If you're a fan of Moto GP or motorcycles in general, I'd say you'll get some decent enjoyment out of this.  It's a shame it's really the only game in town.  Let me say up front that I really do like this game.  That said I do have my fair share of gripes with it.  It seems to perform better than 2013, but for a "last gen" game, there really is no excuse for the occasional frame drops I get.
Also, the AI is very weak, seems like a step back from last year, which wasn't great.  The AI is so linear with no personality whatsoever and are basically on rails.  Come to think of it, I am almost a season in and have not seen a single crash (that didn't involve me).
Also the difficulty is basically useless.  I want to win, but I like a challenge so, like last year, I turn it down a little until I get in the groove and then crank it back up.  However, even on medium difficulty I have issues, but it's more the inconsistency of the AI.  I can go out blind folded on Free Practice, Qualifying, and Warm Up and set the pole by 2 seconds, but on race day, certain tracks, the AI will then go out and out lap you by 3-4 seconds!  Also, I have noticed if the AI is in front of you, they are very difficult, but if and when you manage to get past them, magically they suck horribly and will fall far behind you, whereas if you do not get the position back quickly, they will continue to pull from you and there is little to be done about it.
The AI also appears to be bound by a different, more lenient set of physics laws as well, as they are able to hold corner speed that you cannot dream of in general.  Hold tight lines and accelerating faster at full lean, while you're picking the bike up and cannot keep up.  On that same note though some tracks with open fast corners, they always are extremely slow which allows you to blow by them.
Anyways, even though this review must sound highly negative, I do enjoy the game, and it offers plenty of fun to be had, and I will continue to keep playing and getting better.
Side note: does anyone play this online as I can never seem to find any active lobbies?

Turn based tactical games are a genre that I'm very much into, I play a lot of Chaos Reborn on a daily basis for the PvP side of it. Consequentially I often find that with story driven turn based tactical games that the PvE battles are a let-down, I don't think an AI can generally replicate the engagement that comes from playing against a human opponent. But I tell you what, Blackguards comes as close to it as I've ever found. There's a real wealth of variation in the battles that occur from; small skirmishes, arena fights, fighting withdraws, chase downs, there's all sorts. The developers of Blackguards have really gone out of their way to keep the fighting fresh. As a result this is one story driven turn based tactical game that I can see myself replaying. Just taken on their own the fights are a lot of fun.
I think the one caveat that I'd give is that this is a game where it's worth checking out what happens to certain characters in advance. I’m not going to give anyway any spoilers here, but making your party build based on that knowledge does make a difference to the overall effectiveness of your party by the end of the game.

Finally a revive of the stealth genre. With only little imperfections here and there it's an unforgetable ride. No nursing, lots of freedom, outstanding level (or should I say - world) and sound design, solid graphics*.
Controls:
Smooth, precise, no automation allowing a great deal of freedom of movement. People complaining about it are usually accustomed to Assassin's Creed type of aids or plainly didn't grasp the introductory tutorial of Styx. After few hours I'm looking like a Quasimodo returning from a ballet lessons!
Good camera movement BTW. I've never seen a serious clipping or obstruction problems with it.
Story/world:
Mature fantasy world with interesting, original twists. Again, mature and non-trivial!
AI:
A little bit short-sighted and quickly dropping the hunt for you if you manage to run away after being detected but aside from it. A solid work.
Game mechanics:
Like a well-selected orchestra!
Initially I thought that some elements I've seen in the trailer are misplaced and that I won't use them. So wrong. Everything has its place and purpose and everything has its limitations, avoiding boredom and making a specific item too commonly used during gameplay. A stealthy run through a guard-crawling level on the highest difficulty level will leave you thinking you're a god :) It's all hard work, patience, planning and execution all put together.
Good representation of Styx's limitations. A jump 15 meters down and you're a goner. It's not anime...
Audio:
One of the biggest selling points of the game. Apart from repetitive dialogues of the guards that is. The soundtrack should be sold separately! Well done and, as with the story and world design, a great deal of originality.

Just play up until mission 4 or 5 as the final chunk of the game is just the previous levels with tougher bad guys. Also get it on a deep sale, like pocket-change-cheap kind of sale.The gameplay is alright and is at its best when playing on the higher difficulties as it disables combat and forces you to engage in stealth 100% of the time. There's a good level of verticality and multiple paths implemented throughout each level but the character controls very awkwardly as he feels extremely floaty and unpredictable, making jumps a random chance affair, save before taking leaps of fate over bottomless pits. The game also has a funny habit of being unable to properly highlight shaded areas. You could be smothered in shadow and be visible or standing in a well-lit surface and concealed by darkness. This isn't a huge problem but it makes sneaking inconsistent in areas reliant on visual detection. The final level of the game is honestly where the game challenged me to recommend this and it's what broke me and made me uninstall it. It's one of the worst levels in a game, period. Between the elven enemies who can detect you very quickly without having to look at you and the final 'boss fight' being an unbalanced, horribly designed and all out clusterf*ck, you'd be well applauded for simply making it that far. I could not finish the game as the final fight forces you to engage in combat, the game's most underdeveloped feature that is actively discouraged by how pointless and just awful it is. Like I said, deep dirt cheap sale for this one. Once you've done mission 4 or 5 just reinstall Splinter Cell. Thief or Dishonored as this game is too dull to be stretched out for 13-15 hours and would have been an easier recommendation if the story was just 8-10 hours at most, cutting out the final 3 or so levels.

Where 'Of Orcs and men' had a more tactical game play and light roleplay elements, the story had been spot on. It had actual well written main characters, especially Styx.
This game tells you the story of Styx and his beginnings, lightly touched upon in the first game.
After just finishing it, i can say i stuck around for mainly that.
The gameplay itself is pretty decent. Though the controls may be Jank at times and the Ai can be weird (maybe due to all the Amber they take, i dunno). Think assassins creed but less good in terms of mechanics. there is no automatic ledge walking and if you want to drop down a ledge, oh boy is it fiddly. The bug enemies are the worst. Blind but the slightest movement triggers their hearing and they rush onto you to inspect. If they find you, it might as well be game over. Like most enemies, enough will stun lock you and end your run. The bugs are fast enough to simply do that themselves.
You revisit a lot of areas and there is actually a lot to explore. Very time consuming and especially hard on a 'no kill' run.
There are in fact multiple ways for you to complete a map and ive even done speedruns on them.
If you want the best experience, get a trainer and cheat in all the skill points for all the abilities off the bat.
Tl;DR: loved the story, jank assassins creed controls, big levels that you revisit.

I'll admit that I've never played the real Warhammer 40k, but I've read enough material on it to know that it is one seriously well created world, and this game does the franchise justice. Space Marines are hardcore, in your face, beat you down tough guys and this game does everything right by placing you in the middle of hordes of enemies, fighting them off using unigue firearms and melee weapons, like the infamous Chainsword. After one fight you will literilly be covered in gore and loving every minute of it.
What's kind of suprising is how active the multiplayer aspect of the game still is. Admittidly the game isn't very old, but you'd think players would have migrated on to other games. Yet you'll never have trouble finding Classic Capture matches, even if you might experience some lag and host migration isues. This may be bacause the MP is kinda fun, with 3 seperate classes, all with different loadouts and tactics and the ability to switch whenever you have to respawn.
Sadly, while the game's director had a further 2 games planned, odds are that we'll never see them for sale as THQ was auctioned off and SEGA now owns the rights to this series, so if we do see any further 40k games, they'll probably be RTS's like Dawn of War rther than continuing the chronicals of Captian Titus of the Ultramarines.

Bit.Trip Runner was designed by someone who likes listening to music and jumping in videogames, but unfortunately they just decided to smash the two together and call it a day without htinking about the implications. The music in Bit.Trip Runner is synchronized with the game, so when your character jumps over an obstacle, a note plays, but the note plays when you clear the obstacle, not when you start the jump, so if you're musically inclined and start to jump with the rhythm of the music, you'll always jump too late and have to start over at the beginning of the level. Basically, if you can carry a tune, you're boned, because the instant you try to become one with the beat, you lose.
One of the best rhythm games i've ever played.

This is great fun, and particularly recommended if you're looking for a less daunting, more linear story-driven turn-based RPG.
It's perfect for busy people who perhaps have less time for too-open and deep an experience:

- Fairly linear, especially for the first half of the game (it opens out a little in Chapter 3, but even here it is still really just about having some choice about what order you do the quests and fights).
- Great story, with a central mystery, and lots of believable twists and turns; it takes you to lots of interesting locations and has you meet a range of engaging characters.
- Good voice acting nearly throughout - only a few weaker performances. The main heroes and villains are all voiced very well.
- Some great characters, such as Zuraban, the womanising socialite, Niam, the drug-addicted lost soul or the gold-loving dwarf. These may be fantasy archetypes, but the interaction between them often takes you to new territory, and is often funny.
- Fairly deep (but not TOO complicated!) skill tree and leveling up system.
- Good turn-based combat, and challenging if played on Hard.
The only criticism I have so far is that there seem to be just a few areas that are a little unpolished - for example, you can skill up you 'traps' detection and disarming ability, only to discover that there is no actual mechanic to allow you to disarm traps. And yes, I've searched the forums! In the end, there are other ways around it, so it's no biggie!

The overall mechanics of the game are very familiar. Collect experience (action points) and use it to buy upgrades to your character. The battles are all turn based so you essentially get a number of action points per turn with which to move your character and perform a single action. Not being used to this type of game I wasn't too sure I would  like it but I ended up really enjoying it.
The graphics are pretty nice, not spectacular, but nice, The voice acting is a little ropey but doesn't spoil the game.

I have waited for a decent MotoGP game. I did not buy the 2013 version when I read of the problems.
This year, even though people were reporting similar issues, I caved in and bought MotoGP2014, hoping I could sort the controls out for myself.
Well, the game is FANTASTIC, but it is ruined by a few problems.
I cannot exit from the game - Can a game developer seriously forget to put in an exit button? Or if there is one, make sure it actually works? I have to CtrlAltTab. Even then I have to restart my pc every time, as the app continues to run in the background and cannot be closed from task manager.
I cannot map my G27 buttons. It simply will not recognise them properly, no matter what I do. I have plenty of experience in mapping keys and buttons & can usually find a way with these things, but this has severe problems - it MUST be fixed by developers.
I cannot get my mapped keys to save for next time.
So overall, I am trying to play a really promising game using keyboard, which makes precise leaning of the bike extremely difficult.
I DO NOT recommend buying this UNTIL these issues are fixed. Sorry Milestone, but I really hope I can return and change this to a positive review very soon if a patch fixes these basic errors.
EDIT: 4 mnths later I have decided to change it to a thumbs up. I stand by my review and I am disappointed in the lack of proper fixes by Milestone - they have let themselves down as there are lots of unhappy customers because of this.
But the truth is, I enjoy the game, and I use a workaround to get race v qual pace working correctly.
I just have to put up with the annoying ctrl Alt Del & retsart pc every time I want to end the game.
And I am using an xbox controller which is ok as long as I follow a set method to avoid losing my bindings.
So for the fact that it's enjoyable and unlike other games I will actually come back to this game from time to time, I have decided to give a thumbs up.

Many people were worrying about this game having the same story as in To The Moon.
And it is! But it has completely different point and message.
And it is beautiful
It may not be as harsh as To The Moon, but it doesn't intend to be. Instead the story focuses more on the other idea and greatly describes the power of our brain.
Unfortunately the downside is of course much weaker story in general. The game offers more shenanigans around Sigmund Corp, and I can get that a lot of people will not like it. But the game still does it, in the smoothest way possible, without trying to enforce anything onto players in an obvious way (even though it is deeply connected to the moon, its minisodes and A bird story)
An upside? The story will still force you to think and brain-storm the plot as you play through it. A different plot, that is, maybe not what would To The Moon fans expect, but it's better this way than repeating itself.
All in all - it is a must play for anyone who touched To The Moon. You may even dislike it a lot on the first half of the game, only then to get punched for thinking everything is gonna be simple and clear.
If you haven't played To The Moon - I would strongly suggest getting that first. And perhaps on mobile device, since that version is more polished.

Let's be frank, this game is definitely one of the worst I've ever seen on Steam. Among the very few good things about this game is the creativity. You can't shoot or jump on enemies, instead you can only change the background color. But by doing so, all enemies in the same color will disappear, and landscape in different colors will also show or hide accordingly, as seen in the preview video. It's a pretty good idea, never seen before in a platforming game.
Aside from that, the pictures that tell the story at the beginning are very nice. The music is also very nice.
And then everything else about this game is horrible. I don't even know where to start - yet I have to start somewhere. Well, let's start from graphics. While the storytelling pictures are good, the in-game graphics are horrible. Big chunks of pure colors everywhere. The whole screen is about 4 or 5 colors - that's even worse than the 8-bit games. Yes having few colors is not bad, but it has to be accompanied with a fitting art style. Things have to be flat, big, straight, simple and abstract. Look at Windows 8 or iOS 7 for examples. However when things are drawn with fine detail and very thin lines, as in this game, people would expect some Renaissance style artwork - full of colors that look realistic. Having the hero in complete black is okay, but it doesn't match with the art style elsewhere. Refer to Limbo on how to draw a good-looking hero in full black.
The in-game UI also looks wrong. Somehow it gives the feeling of a Flash game, not a PC game. On closer looks you can actually see aliasing(or sharp pixels?) everywhere, on the hero, on the landscape, and on the health bar. I mean, WTF? This is not a 3D game that burns graphic cards, and yet it looks worse than one without anti-aliasing? This game's graphics look as if drawn with Microsoft Painter. Even pencil sketches will look better.
As for the sound, the music does sound good, but all the sound effects are just childish and random, especially the strange "hah" that occurs everytime the hero jumps. I don't ever remember playing any platforming game where the hero shouts whenever he/she jumps. Well, except for New Super Mario Bros. OK if you insist on making that sound, it'll be a lot better if they recorded multiple samples and randomly chose one to play at each jump. When you are hit, the sound played sounded exactly the same as that sound of slicing someone with knife in Counter Strike. And same sound also plays when you die of falling, although you aren't sliced by anything. I hope I'm just mishearing this.
And control, oh my god. It sucks. Sometimes you can change background color while jumping, sometimes you can not. Sometimes you can pull a double-jump, sometimes you can not. Whenever you get hit, the hero starts flashing, yes that's common, but the frame rate drops drastically. I didn't know making a shape blink was such an intensive task. And good luck if you fall into spikes, because sometimes you can jump out while blinking, sometimes you can not. The health bar also acts very strangely. Sometimes you regain HP by standing still, sometimes you do not. Sometimes you lose only about 1/3 of HP when hit, sometimes you lose about 7/8, and sometimes you lose all of it just by falling onto spikes. And by the way, if you fall below the map, the hero can fall for about 1 whole second beyond the border of the screen before he dies.
So after all these flaws why do I still give it a recommended? Because it's free! Although I've seen other far better free games, this game is still worth a try. For about 5 minutes. Have enough fun changing the background color around, and then feel free to delete this game. All in all, this game feels extremely childish and uncompleted. It looks more like an unfinished student project than an indie game that dares to come to Steam.

This review is based on 2 hours of gameplay. Code was provided by the developers free of charge.
Jydge is a cyberpunk, objective-based twin-stick shooter that takes inspiration aesthetically and thematically from Robocop and Judge Dredd with some Hotline Miami and Neon Chrome thrown in for the gameplay. It does a ton of unique and fun things with itself and it's not afraid to crank up the challenge but the biggest flaws come into it's replay system.
Gameplay:
In each mission of Jydge you have a primary objective and two secondary objectives to complete. Once you complete an objective you gain a medal. Medals are used to unlock new missions & upgrades. The upgrades give a strong customization sense to the game as you will need to upgrade your weapons, armor and even upgrades in order to beat tougher missions and blitz through older missions to obtain all the medals. You can upgrade and busy new upgrades that you have unlocked through money which is obtained from opening item boxes in a level, collecting dropped cash from enemies and – you guessed it – getting medals.. This means that you will be redoing a lot of levels in the game.  Aside from that, the gameplay itself is pretty solid. There's a good variety of weapons and equipment to interact with the environment and all the enemy types which include mini-bosses. There's destruct-able environments, hack-able areas, small holes to sneak through and dark spots to hide in, all depending on the equipment you are using. AI is also solid. Enemies might not be hyper smart but they aren't ready to die. They will react loosely based on sight and sound and they aren't eager to run single file at times into your gunfire, sometimes hesitating.
Sound & Visuals:
The sounds are awesome. Weapon effects are pretty solid but the strongest point of this game audibly is its soundtrack. You get this orchestral, epic, robo-cop esque music in the title screen and on the map but in game you get this cyberpunk soundtrack that varies from sounding like rap to a rave to a combination of both and an orchestral feel. It's pretty dope. The weakest part of the game are the graphics. They don't really grab you or pop out. Thankfully, the game does run extremely well and makes up for it even further with a lot of environmental detail and colors to make everything stand out a bit more. The game looks dirty but in a good, appropriate way to match the tone of the gameplay.
Content:
Once you complete the first act you unlock hardcore mode which unlocks a new set of 3 medals to acquire for previous mentions you have beaten. Thankfully, hardcore mode switches up the secondary objectives as well as the enemy types and placement of objectives. The biggest issue with Jydge is that some medals are nearly impossible to acquire all at once and completely impossible to acquire on your first try for some missions. It's not very frustrating to get two levels on one mission but to get all 3 is where the frustration sets in, meaning you will need to play the level again just to get one medal and that's not counting doing that level for a 3rd/4th time respectively on hardcore mode. So even though there is a lot of content on the surface the game has you repeat it a lot. To the point of grinding for cash. I'd say the game is 4-5 hours long if you don't count replaying a mission more than once but you do count hardcore mode. So at the very least you do get 6+ hours if you like replaying levels and it can be fun to blast through older levels with decked-out gear. The unlocks keep you going to try new things and the game does have a diverse set of levels to go with it. There are even secret levels.
Overall, this is worth checking out if you enjoy twin-stick shooters or have been looking for a good one in a sea of mediocre ones. It's biggest issue is the replay system, as it's not used as a way to increase time at the players will. Instead it's mandatory and by the time you're done you don't have a desire to play it all again. However, if you can get past that it's a lot of fun and the aesthetics will keep you going through those tough times.

I usually don't write reviews but I enjoyed other shooters from 10tons like Crimsonland, Xenoraid and of course Neon Chrome with
JYDGE being in the same vein as the latter. This game has been described as a "thinking man's top down shooter" somewhere and I agree. There is plenty of mods and toys for your character and their gun to unlock - which in turn gives you different ways to tackle each level. Most of the architecture is destructible and the guns (it's really just one, which you configure to your liking before each level) and gadgets are fun to use. Enemies patrol, react to audible cues and require line of sight to engage you, which allows for a few fun tricks and a stealthy play style - if you like.
There's some 18 levels in the game with 4 difficulties each which slighty change layout, enemies and objectives. Achieving different main and side objectives ("exit the level in 20 seconds" "don't get spotted" "rescue the hostages") will unlock further levels and equipment. They also challenge you to use different play styles and keep replayability up.
There's plenty of top-down shooters but only a few are truly great and 10tons' games are among them.

I loved this game. I ended up binging through the entire game and the level-based DLC in about 4-5 days in short 1-3 hour bursts around bed time or when I had time to relax. It was very remenisant of games like Eufloria and Osmos in its play-style and core mechanics and just as addicting. The levels were well balanced, providing a decent amount of challenge and almost all the achievements were obtainable (if you're an achievement hunter like I am). The only hard achievement to get is the "Conquerer" one but that is attainable if you replay the game over again (possibly on a higher difficulty?), DLC included.
The DLC for this game also actually worth getting. Each one give you 50 more levels with all new mechanics. Although the "Mutations" DLC added some new types of organisms to take over and use, it felt like more of the same base game levels, not that that's a bad thing. As for the "New Life" DLC, now THAT was amazingly worth it. The new enemy mechanics and power-ups provided a whole new level of difficulty and made the game feel fresh and new.
The "Color of organisms" DLC didn't feel that worth it in my opinion since it's just different colors for your main organisms and it made me a little sad to see them charge for it since Eufloria let you do that for free.... Also, after playing the base game with the original blue/red colored organism, I kept getting confused any time I tried a new color scheme.
I HIGHLY recommend this to anyone who loves challenging puzzle games or just wants an interative experiance to zen out to; it's a game that caters to both. The DLC prices are a tad high but considering that the base game has 72 levels and each DLC pack that adds levels had 50 new levels each.... it does seem a bit more wrth it. I love love LOVE this game and can't wait to see more from the devs, whether it be other games or DLC (it's super worth getting them, I promise).

My bike sim experience includes SBK 2011, SBK Generations, Motogp 13, and now Motogp 14. All are Milestone titles. The SBK series was extremely well polished, great sims, included lots of features, and I enjoyed them thoroughly. The Motogp series, OTOH, has been a bit of a disappointment.
Motogp 13 doesn't include SBK standard features such as telemetry data and ghost in time attack mode. Motogp 14 is more of the same. Also, in the SBK series, you had to be extremely careful not to go off track because you'd lose traction if you were on the throttle or brake in anything but an upright position. In Motogp 13, you can pin the throttle while fully leaned over off-track and you'd never have to worry about losing traction. Motogp 14 is more of the same.
Motogp 13 had a few bugs but the main one that affected me was the online play. Connectivity through Raknet was horrible. Motogp 14 chose to go with Raknet again so I'm not holding my breath when it comes to multiplayer. Another bug in Motogp 13 was that enabling vsync in-game would cause choppy frame rates. Motogp 14 again has issues with choppy frame rates, remedied somewhat through config.ini modifications, but looks like a step backward compared to Motogp 13. While the replay mode in Motogp 14 looks stunning, in game is a different matter as the lack of anti-aliasing makes for blocky imagery that looks like low-res textures have been upscaled.
Another disappointment is the inclusion of more bugs. The controller settings are not saved, forcing you to reinput your settings each time you restart the game. Also, if you play the career mode, the quit option is not accessible, forcing you to use CTRL ALT DEL to quit the game.
That being said, I really enjoyed the helmet cam view in Motogp 13, and thankfully Motogp 14's helmet cam retains the same enjoyment. Motogp 14 has also tweaked the physics, limiting your ability to the slide and brake during cornering bringing about a less arcadish experience.
Motogp 13 felt like a beta version that was sold to consumers. Motogp 14 feels like more of the same but with even more bugs and graphical issues. A recurring theme of recent Milestone titles appears to be to release untested console ports that force consumers to wait for patches that may never come. While I can find enjoyment in the game, after consecutive releases that have been full of bugs, I've lost faith that future releases from Milestone would be any different. I'd love to see another developer take a shot at Motogp.
Purchase at your own risk.

*disclaimer*
- I am a solo player, i don't like multiplayer, thus i didn't play at all to multi and my review is based solely on the single player campaign.
- Yes i am aware that BF's multiplayer is so ****** better but, once more, multiplayer hits me one without moving the other.
Sooo, that said, , i'll be straightforward : i loved this game and it is a good game but i recommand to buy it only at discount price !
** Pros :
- The setting, i loved it, classical Mars vs Earth or colonies vs old world.
Kinda feels like a mix between Starlancer and the Expanse, minus the aliens.
- Ethan, i mean .. Ethan ! I hate toasters, i hated them in MEs, BSG, and so on but Ethan is so well written and so far from the regular "killzzz all humanzz" that he feels like the most fleshed out (no pun intended) character of the story.
- The graphics. They are good, with gorgeous sceneries, nice skins and very good animations (heyhey Bioware).
- Fighter craft missions : i really liked flying a F22 lookalike in space with semi realistic newtonian model, drifting between structures/asteroids.
- Spacewalk missions, nothing like infiltrating an enemy capital ship hiding in an asteroid belt, throwing away enemies with your grapple or fighting on a hull with mag boots !
- Realistic weapons, all hail kinetic energy and boo the lazors because they are cheap SciFi and the devs didn't fall into the trap !
** Cons :
-  The campaign is very short and this is the reason why i said to buy this game on discount : 11 or 12 hours only to finish the campaign doing all (i don't think i missed any) side missions.
- Enemy motivations ? Beside "killzz all Earthlingzzz" i didn't catch any, maybe i missed ? Not even a "colonial fools !" !! I mean nothing, absolute zero ! It is a waste of Kit Harington's talent.
- The music ! I know there is music in this game, i've read about it but sincerly i don't remember it, at all.
- Few months after its release the game is still plagued by the infamous crash at 1st mission loading screen : c'mon devs, can't you fix the anti-virus exception with a patch or you just don't care anymore and let players handle it by themselves ?
** Conclusion : A good "hard" scifi shooter, but very short so buy it only with a very good discount !

So, Kan Gao mentioned before that Finding Paradise and To The Moon were intended to be two sides of the same coin. By this point, I understand what he means. There are a number of really cool contrasts between Finding Paradise and To The Moon, and I found Finding Paradise to be much more polished, well-written, and personally, more engaging than To The Moon. (This is not to say that I disliked To The Moon; rather, that I liked Finding Paradise so much more.)
What Finding Paradise did well: the entire game just felt more polished as a whole, both in terms of mechanics and in terms of writing (though presumably, part of this can be attributed to the fact it's the second game.) I liked the story a lot more as it felt more relatable, and the banter between Neil and Eva was sharper and more on point; I also appreciated the amount of development Neil got (and to a lesser extent, Eva.) I liked the information portioned out to us about SigCorp, the machine, and whatever is going on with Neil, and learning more about Roxie and Robert was lovely, though I get the sense that some things have transpired in the interim. Finding Paradise also nicely advances the meta-plot, with continued hints that something is--not quite--right with the world as is given to us.
I like the branches as well; clearly, this is not a 'choices have consequences' sort of RPG, but I like how different choices offer you different insights into the shared world and situations of Finding Paradise.
Finding Paradise has heart. It's a different kind of heart from To The Moon -- it's not about love, but about happiness, regrets, and loneliness. To that extent, I find it much more relatable.
Issues: I found it strange to introduce a mechanic to swap between Neil and Eva -- it's a great mechanic, and I like it, but why introduce it if we can't use it except at the beginning?
Still, would recommend and am eagerly anticipating (what, in 2023?) the next installment :P

Pros:
-Jack of all trades: the game as promised delivers tons of different play styles as you progress through the game, from tactics, to platforming, to shoot’em ups, to fighting game, to playing bejeweled and more the game is packed full of different play styles.
-Universe building: although the story may not be the most gripping and kind of generic the universe that is built around the story is very enjoyable to explore. Seeing the small bits of lore connecting across the world is one of the best parts of the game.
-Good time travel: although somewhat tedious in the way you have to transition mechanically through the ears, however the plot related time travel  is done very well. You get to see how the actions of characters affect the world and how you’re action can change it for the better or worst. Going back and forth between places to see what’s changed and what’s new gives the player purpose to explore.
-References: sometimes you’ll find something subtle in the background of the game and smile to yourself as you recognize something that isn’t made obvious and could be missed by other players.
Cons:
-Master of none: although the game throws everything possible game play style at you it is obvious that not all of them will stand on par to your expectations of that style. Many of them fall short, feeling like weak imitations of the genres it’s trying to portray. So if you’re favorite genre pops up it may not be realized to it’s full potential.
-Story and characters: since it’s an RPG the story and characters are rather important and in this case the cast and story here are more or less rather generic. Not to say that any of them are annoying or badly written characters it's just you’ve most likely seen this story with similar character in other games.
-The word puzzles: the word puzzles are dense and annoying, you can’t go back to reread what the npc said so you have one shot at getting it right otherwise you gotta listen to everything they said. Now if you forget something, guess what, you do it again. I found it better to just brute force your way through them rather than trying to solve them.
-References: there is a point where references can go too far and sometime it’s hard to tell where the story starts and the reference ends. In addition to that the game might make the player want to play the referenced game more than Evoland 2. For me that happened with music which was just a bit too similar to Final Fantasy, which made me want to play that each time I heard it’s familiar tunes.
General Thoughts:
Evoland 2 is a decent representation of older games wrapped in a neat package of Zelda for it’s core game play and Chrono Trigger as it’s theme. It doesn't do everything perfectly but it creates an enjoyable world in which one can sink in around a dozen hours and come out satisfied from it. It’s not going to be for everyone, and there definitely are better games out there in each of the genres the game tries to portray. However if you’re feeling like you want a short game that’s whimsical and has a charming world, then hop on in and you might find yourself enjoying some old taste of gaming.

Some weapons can only be crafted from other mid-grade weapons, which aren't craftable at all. I've never seen them drop. Don't know if they even exist.
Once completing the game once you'd be unlikely to want to play again. You only made it to the end due to good luck. No skill will change the outcome of your game.

Early Release Review, Early Release Review, Early Release Review....
Just so you get the hint that this game is not done yet.  This game is a survival sandbox set in space with the beginnings of a story element tied into the tutorial.  The game has been in developement for a while and continues to get regular updates.  Most of the time these updates are either in direct relation to suggestions by the gamers that play it or part of a larger development scheme.  About once every three of four moths they will tweak the re-balance, but unlike some other games they aren't trying to make a perfectly balanced game before its finished, becuase you know adding stuff usually breaks things...
There is a lot to work on on this game, the enemies are fairly single minded killing machines, the economy is set-up for multi-player and frankly gives single players a giant f-you. (single players cannot sell items, only buy them).  And the building mechanic takes a while to really get the hang of.  A lot of the physics in the game are "broken" but again, thy aren't done with it yet, and often times these things get fixed...eventually. (UPDATE: They recently added a sell items capablity - see they are trying to make the game better)
So why bother, becuase this is a gem that is recieving polish, constantly.  The original form of this game was "neat", and started as a PvP across the galaxy battlefield, but during development the single player aspects sort of blossomed.  Now the game is starting to pick-up steam (see what I did there),  and frankly is not looking to slow down.  What before was a concept is starting to finally pull together into a cohesive idea.
Are there issues, yes.  Minig is one of the largest issues with the game.  Many players long for the original days of giant balls of ore in the ground, frankly, I like the new systems better because it is more realistc, but it's still wrong.  Ores run in viens, long connected lines that snake around underground, not little clumps in a somewhat localized area, yes there would still be cutbacks and corners (get over it gamers mining isn't done in straight lines it wanders a bit), but there would be less periods of rock, rock, rock, rock, hey look ore, rock, rock, rock, etc.  Also, enemy spawning is sometimes...erratic...  In the outpost there are two spawners that drop enemies under the building, they can shoot you, you cannot shoot them, yeah, that's a little unfair.  But for all it's warts, there are some really cool ideas.  The idea that each vehicle has its own niche in the world is much more developed than the earlier concept of, "all I need is a capital ship and something to steer it into..."
I hope they continue to develop this game along their current lines, if so, this game will be a must have.  honestly now, it's my go to time waster.   7.5/10

I've previously stated how much I hate games like Dirty Bomb as I'm not really into the whole "gritty" side of first-person-shooters and whilst I can confirm that Codename CURE is better than that broken mess I still cannot get over how disappointed I am with this game on the whole. If there is one thing that I think is as redundant as the conventional FPS it is the conventional FPS with zombies.
Codename CURE is a decent action-shooter at best and a cliche catastrophe at worst. I enjoyed it, especially when playing with friends, but it really doesn't compare to many of the other Half-Life 2 mods-turned-standalone-games like GMod or The Stanley Parable.
Let's start with the positives: it's a fun game with replayability, decent graphics and passable loading screens. It is purely a multiplayer game with multiple servers that you can join and different difficulty levels. Thanks to the "connect" code found in games of this type it is extremely easy to hook up with friends and play with them and the number of options, maps and styles of play in conjunction with its half cooprative, half competitive nature makes for a different experience each time you play it.
Despite all the coolness that radiates from this standalone mod there was a familiar feeling that crept up when I played this game for the first time: Codename CURE is not a good game. Constant lag and bugs made the experience unenjoyable and although the modelling was well done, the textures were bland and the lighting was sporadic. Aside from the technical issues, I still found a number of questionable design choices. Firstly, zombies come in swarms and soak up bullets like a sponge soaking up water. This wouldn't even be so bad if the framerate wasn't so awful and there was actual indication on what is hitting you and from where. It also doesn't help that your character moves so slowly and is made even slower when he is hit. Basically, if you are cornered, you're screwed. You get a defensive punch to use whilst your gun is reloading but it is over-powered and thus the developers made sure there was a delay between each hit. To feign variation, the game allows you to choose your class and whilst some characters have different scroller-click items to use they all play the same. You could easily get through a level with two pointmen and a supporter or even three pointmen. Whatever appeal there is from this mechanic is short lived for the reasons I've already mentioned but the desperate attempts of the developer to make this game varied are even more blatant when you can clearly tell that there are superior classes. Oh, and the music is SO REPETITIVE!
So, to summarise, Codename CURE is an enjoyable experience. It is completely free and fun to play with friends. But I can only recomend it to those of you who are into hardcore FPSs. Otherwise, this is a flawed experience with too much praise given where it isn't due.
