Disclaimer: This is a review of the Single Player Campaign only. I'm not big on CoD multiplayer. Also, I have finished this title previously on PS4, so please disregard my playtime as of the time I'm posting this review.
So, I personally LOVED this game's campaign. Trust me, this was very surprising to me as I had previously not really loved a CoD campaign in forever. Some were quite decent, like Advanced Warfare, and some were horrendous, like Black Ops 3 and Infinity Ward's very own Ghosts.
I was quietly optimistic about this game though, I actually liked it's reveal trailer. I thought it looked cool tbh and had no issue with the futuristic setting. In fact, I really liked that the vehicles, suits and weapons etc (absolutely fantastic weapon models btw, some of my favourites in any FPS) and thought they looked believably developed tech-wise from where we are now.
The game has that bombastic, Hollywood blockbuster CoD feel to it, but it also allows more player agency than any previous entry in the series. In between main missions players are able to branch out from the main narrative and perform side ops, these allow for new weapons to be added to your arsenal and upgrades and new cosmetics to become available for your fighter jet, the Jackal. Many of the side missions, and main missions for that matter, allow you to fly this awesome bit of kit and it's a lot of fun, and nowhere near as "on-rails" as CoD usually handles vehicular traversal/combat.
It's a really nice touch and makes the game feel far less linear than other entries in the series.
The title looks absolutely exquisite for the most part as well. Sure, the engine does show its age here and there, and some textures don't stand up to close scrutiny, but overall, the presentation is almost always consistently excellent. I'd actually say Infinite Warfare looks routinely spectacular. Character models and facial animation is another area the title excels, perhaps only bettered by Advanced Warfare in the franchise.
The story was enjoyable from beginning to end, and propelled the action appropriately. The antagonist is a little one dimensional but honestly, who cares? Your protagonist and his crew are a likeable bunch, in particular the wise-cracking robot Ethan, and the story actually has some surprising moments of gravitas that I definitely appreciated.
In summation, I liked this title quite a lot. I cannot comment on multiplayer as I'm not qualified to do so, but the single player was a big win for me. I think it's unfortunate the game didn't get the reception I feel it deserved. Speaking for myself, I found the campaign in this title 1000x better than the manure that was Battlefield 1's campaign. Which was, in my opinion, such a boring collection of disparate stories cobbled together to form a fairly forgettable whole. It looked good, but that was about it.
Performance wise, I have it maxed on settings at 1440p and running at an almost constant locked 125fps(the SP max refresh).
However, I highly recommend Nvidia users do not use the most recent driver; 384.76. This driver was initially tanking my framerate hard, and was in some sections dropping as low as sub 20fps! After investigating, I found this was an issue many were experiencing. Rolling back to 382.53 seems to have completely remedied this situation and performance is buttery smooth

Bike control hasn't improved, still no proper XB360 controller for PC, exiting the game currently requires CTRL+ALT+DEL and Task Manager, tyre grip still isn't modelled, bike setup is still childishly pointless because it does so little. I'm a big fan of MotoGP but how on Earth Dorna Sports can let such a potentially fantastic license be ruined by such inept software development is beyond me.  Milestone claim to have fully revamped the game engine but the evidence for this is painfully absent.

Easily a contender for game of the year, it has just about everything but the best possible graphics to make it a contender.
Story is interesting, plenty of twists and turns to keep the player hooked.
Music is very varied, and the many song tracks fits in to just about every area you visit.
Gameplay is a obvious 10\10 in my opinion, where as the story progresses, the game changes the fighting rules to hint at several game classics like Double-dragon, Galaga, Bomberman and MANY more!
Nothing is really too challenging or too simple, there are plenty of areas to explore, side missions and a few collectibles to get to improve your equipment and if you get stuck in the story, its not too challenging to find out what to do next.
Only negative for me was the time you spend traveling between locations when you get stuck either with the main story or trying to collect 100% of the items.
To sum it up, this game is very good and has something for just about everyone that aren't too narrowminded and focus purely on graphics. A must-play title without any doubt.

Don't be fooled by any of the screenshots or the presumed premise. The only way you will enjoy Evoland 2 is if you like the idea of an RPG inexplicably switching genres to a different half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥knockoff every half hour.
From Zelda-style top-down action RPG to side scrolling 2d platformer to Professor Layton to Metal Gear to Bullet Hell Shooter to Canabalt to Mega Man to Bomberman to Street Fighter to Chrono Trigger and more; the game's gimmick is regularly switching between play styles meant to homage other titles, but none of them are done particularly well. Every mode change is a mediocre imitation, designed to tickle nostalgia when you recognize the franchise, but not implemented with the finesse that made the originals enjoyable. They're frustratingly bare-bones with watered-down mechanics, and frequently drag on far longer than they probably should.
Many of the instance levels are poorly designed in terms of pathing, and either ridiculously easy or unfairly difficult; you'll either pass them effortlessly, or die 20 times before you figure out what the designers intended you to do. Likewise, enemies and obstacles will either barely scratch you, or kill you outright. At least they're generous with the autosave points, because manual saves are not allowed, and many areas can be vague and punishing, especially to gamers not schooled in the flavor at hand. With all the easily-missed collectibles, a walkthrough FAQ is practically required for completionists (and those who despise mandatory brain teaser puzzles.)
Gamepad controls across the board are dodgy even with a 360 gamepad, and it's practically unplayable with a keyboard. Under the hood are glitches galore, with nagging collision and hit detection problems cropping up at the worst possible times, and each new style change bringing its own unique issues. I experienced at least 6 instances of the game getting stuck in a scripted event and forcing me to either suicide or restart to get it to work again -- twice during boss battles! They couldn't fix the rampant bugs or polish the gameplay, but they sure give you an achievement for talking to a girl dressed as Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite. So, y'know, priorities.
Technical presentation aside, the visuals are excellent, if only because of the surprisingly numerous variations in theme, and the music is pleasantly appropriate. The story is your typical fantasy adventure trope, weakened by having to shoehorn in the constant gameplay changes and 4th wall nudges. I guess the nonstop LULZSORANDUM gag references probably appeal to a certain demographic who likes seeing Tomb Raider, Dragon Ball, and Dalek cameos, but I got tired of them pretty quickly. The writing is humorous enough on its own, when it's not trying so hard to wink at the player.

BATMAN: ARKHAM CITY REVIEW
Sometimes reviewers can't see the forest for the trees. When I finished Batman: Arkham City, I immediately cataloged what I thought it did wrong. It tossed in too many villains and didn't flesh them out, it clearly tried to replicate the Scarecrow stuff from the first game and didn't do it as well, and Batman still moves a bit stiffly when simply walking around. When I formed the list, I found myself disappointed with the game. But the days rolled on and I couldn't stop playing -- in fact, I only wanted to play more. The hundreds of things Batman: Arkham City nails outweighed my nitpicky problems. I realized Batman: Arkham City is a brilliant game.
Fans of the Batman: Arkham Asylum will immediately be at home in Arkham City as developer Rocksteady took the core gameplay, refined it, and polished it. You brawl with one button, counter with another and leap when you feel like it. Batman's got a slew of new counter attacks -- including the ability to take out several attacking enemies at once -- and the ability to use nearly every gadget in battle with a hot key system. Even though the system can seem simple (that's if you ignore the combos and multipliers) the diversity in the attacks and battles keeps it interesting. I wanted to engage bad guys instead of sneaking past them. Maybe it was the promise of more experience points and the upgrades they unlocked, but it probably had more to do with wanting to see Batman dislocate another elbow.
Rocksteady kept me on my toes by peppering in special enemies. Guys with stun rods, armored outfits and broken bottles all have to be dealt with in very specific ways. I needed to assess threats and engage situations like Batman would. I don't know if I can express how awesome that makes a comic nerd like me feel; after years of hypothesizing how Batman would beat Character X, I now have to do it to survive.
Feeling like Batman made Arkham Asylum a must-play, and Arkham City continues that tradition. I felt like I had the upper hand when I walked into a room where the enemies outnumbered me 20 to 1 because I could drop a smoke pellet, use freeze grenades to take enemies out of the game and basically kick♥♥♥♥♥ Five gunmen with hostages didn't scare me because I knew I could disappear into the shadows to string them up from gargoyles, punch through walls to take them down and glide kick them over railings.
This feeling of empowerment carries over to bosses, which is weird at first but makes sense. No boss in Arkham City really gave me a challenge. In fact, they're all a bit easy. Mr. Freeze had me stumped for a while as once you use an attack on him you can't use it again, but then the Bat-computer just sent me a cheat sheet. (Although, disabling hints would've eliminated this moment.) That specific instance was no fun, but overall, the joy of Batman bosses is the journey to them and not the fight themselves. The Penguin will never challenge the World's Greatest Detective.
Arkham City isn't an open world like Liberty City; it's more like a hub world with a bunch of dungeons like The Legend of Zelda or a bigger version of Batman: Arkham Asylum. You can't go into every building, but as you explore, you're going to find you're kept from discovering some of the 400-some Riddler Challenges until you double back with new gadgets. As you unlock the game's dozen side missions, you have to search nooks and crannies for murder victims and political prisoners in distress.If being Batman sounds good to you, expect to play this game twice and have the second time feel light years better than the first. New Game Plus unlocks after your first runthrough of Arkham City, and it carries over all your gadgets and shares your Riddler Challenge data. It also doesn't erase your original game's progress – it lives in its own section of your save. Historically, I despise playing games more than once. I know what's around the next corner, so where's the fun in it? Well, I adored Batman: Arkham City's New Game Plus. The difficulty is amped up, the enemies are more diverse from the get go, and the reversal indicators are turned off.
New Game Plus takes the training wheels off and forces you to be Batman. When Batman enters a fight, he knows how to win; he just needs to execute his plan. That's you in this mode. You already know what's coming, you just need to execute your 45-hit combo, dodge explosives and save the day. This left me feeling more like Batman than ever before.
Challenges rooms return and have been given an update since the days of Arkham Asylum. There are a dozen combat challenge maps (take out the four waves of bad guys) and a dozen Invisible Predator challenges (sneak around and silently eliminate all the bad guys) and each comes with three medals to earn. All that is standard, but Arkham City offers up Riddler Campaigns. These link three challenges together and apply gameplay modifiers like low health, time limits and so on. There's even an option to make your own Bat-exams. These challenges mainly serve to point out how slow my version of Batman is, but I'm glad they're here. They help hone my skills and provide leaderboards to chase and keep me playing.

SUMMARY: 8 stars out of 10.  A solid and highly enjoyable RPG!
PROLOGUE: I show as having 88 hours playing this game, as of this review.  I probably actually was playing for 80 hours of that, for ONE playthrough. I am methodical and slow, so most of you whippersnappers who like to cut to the chase will likely finish in 40 hours or less.  I saw a lot of complaints about this game having spikes of frustratingly high difficulty, so I played the EASY/NOVICE setting, which I believe gives more Adventure Points (AP) than the other settings.  In retrospect, I can understand the complaints; but I never had that problem, maybe because of the easy setting, maybe for the most part because I pushed off what I suspected would be the tougher fights until I had more skills under my party's belts.  I ended the game with 1300 ducats (enough to ditch EVERYTHING the party needed and buy it all back again), lots of poisons, potions, provisions, projectiles, traps, and other stuff I never seemed to have the need to use.  I used one potion, and that in the second to last battle.  Perhaps on NORMAL difficulty I would have needed more...
REVIEW:  This game has a main storyline which is fairly linear, but the available sidequests (and locations they open) make it feel less so.  The RPG character development system is versatile and refreshing: You can mold your characters by earning and using AP to buy levels in any of a myriad of basic traits, talents, weapon talents, special abilities, and (for magic users) spells.  You get AP by fighting battles and completing quests.  You do not get enough AP to turn your characters into super heros; but, if you do most of the sidequests, you will get enough to make them excellent in their chosen specialty (magic, melee, ranged) and solid in a second specialty and/or support.  One word of caution: this is not the game for those who want to destroy waves of hapless foes with giant fire or frost balls.  Using magic to buff teammates (and/or debuff enemies) will carry the day.
There are approximately 180 fights available in the game, for those who wish to seek them all out, with plenty of tactical variety and some light "in-fight" puzzle solving.  In all but a few cases, the game clues you in to what is needed to make a fight easier.  For those few where they fall short, there is the internet: I used it about six times.  There were about three fights I elected to replay because I failed or did not like the outcome.  All in all, I found the combat to be satisfying.
Some have complained of running out of ammo (the shops do not re-stock arrows and bolts); but I ran two archers and one crossbow, and did not come close to running out.  I think someone relied too heavily on "triple shot" and "rain of arrows," which skills none of my characters learned.
The storyline is nothing to write home about; and the ending cutscenes/wrap-up is lackluster.  But the character voice acting, approriate interjection of humor, and plot intrigue that is played out was, in my opinion, quite well done.
Replay value is modest.  The plot twists and intrigue are a lot of what pulled me along the first time.  Your party characters are a mandatory set of (up to) five characters, only one of which you get to roll from scratch, and even HIM not entirely (name, gender and appearance are all set for you).  After almost 90 hours on record for my first run, another one (this time on NORMAL) will have to wait until I am up for it.  But, for the pittance I paid for the game (got it on a deep, DEEP discount), one run was overwhemingly worth the price!
EPILOGUE / HINTS (which some might consider slightly spoilerish, but I will not give away plot.)
-- Screw the game's advice:  Roll your own character from scratch the first time.  It is almost impossible to fail if you buy in as a magic user and start him out good at SOMETHING.
-- Take magic, unless you are dead set on a heavy melee fighter.  the 500 AP cost might seem like a lot, but it is a pittance over the course of the game, compared to the advantages it gives.
-- Continuing this line of thought, a dedicated heavy melee fighter is probably not the best choice, as you will eventually end up having two excellent ones foisted upon you.  You will be much better served with a magic buffer/healer who is good at bows.
-- All your magic users should be good with staffs, or possibly daggers.
-- Study spells carefully before trying to achieve high ranks in them.  For most spells, level 4 is not worth the cost.
-- Hammer Blow (HB), coupled with level 3 "Standfast Catlike" buff is OP.
-- The level 3 buff "Move like Lightning" (or some name llike that) is OP.
-- A fighter simultaneously buffed with level 3 Lightning and Standfast, and also using HB, is beyond OP for most fights.

Hello here is my review for Jydge.
Jydge is a top down shooter with role playing? elements. You have a campaign with 4 acts. Each act has 4 missions. You choose the missions on a city map or in the drop down menu. Each mission has a normal and a hardcore mode to unlock. You progress through earning medals in missions. The goals for earning medals are like "do not take any damage" or "do the mission in 20 seconds" "open all containers".  The more medals the more missions, weapon mods and cyberware you unlock. Then you have to buy the upgrades with credits earned in missions.
Cyberware are upgrades for your character. There are 28 cyberware upgrades in the game. More health, stealth in shadows, 20% more speed, a riot shield, take less damage etc. Your character can have 4 cyberware upgrades at a time.
There is only one weapon in the game, the gavel, but you can upgrade this universal weapon carrier with different mods and firing modes. You have a main attack and a special weapon attack. Special weapons are things like rockets, spider bots, stun grenades. You can have 3 firing modes in your weapon.
There are 15 special weapons in the game.
There are 25 firing modes in the game.
The gameplay is fast and furious. You can play gun blazing or more tactically. Killing lone enemies sneakily. For some medals you need a clever plan to succed.
The hardcore mode is a little harder but not unfair. The missions get seriously hard to the end.
If you like top down run n gun shooter like Smash TV, or Neon Chrome, or Crimsonland you will like this game. For crimsonlands veterans it is perhaps a little easy.
The game is only 400 mb big and runs very good even on older machines. The game visuals are simplistic but you are here for the gameplay. The enviroment is completely destructible, except thick walls.
Thank you for reading, i hope my review was informative.
Have a nice day.

Skyhill is a roguelike post-apocalyptic horror game in which you start on the 100th floor of the Skyhill hotel and must explore your way down to the first floor. Each time you move from room to room (on each floor there are three rooms: the stairwell and two rooms on the left and right) you lose one hunger, and there is a chance you'll encounter a mutant to fight in turn based combat. You craft weapons, upgrades, medical supplies, and food from the things you scavenge from rooms. Throughout the game you discover newspaper clippings, photos, notes, and lost cell phones (that give clues urging you to go to specific floors) that hint at a deeper story going on in the background, which I find quite intriguing.
The game has a pretty intuitive interface, and you quickly learn which enemies to fight and which to pass up. If I had any suggestions for improvements, I'd say I'd like to see buffs attached to prepared food or medical supplies.
All told, it's a fun, creepy, and atmospheric game that packs a lot of challenge but isn't cheap about it. When you screw up, it's often because you overestimated your combat prowess or overextended (or misuse) your resources. I can see myself playing a lot of in the future. It has lots of replay value in that there appears to be a secret ending that you can uncover if you're lucky or persistent (or both).
9/10, will play again!

I was rather excited about this game and wanted to like it, and for a while it was an enjoyable novelty, but that novelty very quickly wears off when you realise firstly how pretty much every aspect pales in comparison to the original and secondly how sloppy and glitchy it is in places.
As linked elsewhere in the negative reviews there is a youtube video comparing the original and remake that sums up these issues pretty well. With all due respect to Lanning he obviously had to refamiliarise himself with the Abe voice, but it shows, a lot, I'd put this down  to him being so out of touch with the original game but I think it just ties in the direction of the dialogue in general and how it tries too hard to be comical and cutesy and just doesn't have the same passion poured into it. I miss the sound Abe made when he plummets to his doom, his chanting noise, the sligs and mudokons are even worse, constantly babbling silly lines to themselves, which makes the plight of the mudokon slaves less harrowing and the sligs a lot less menacing. The old Oddworld games really are a classic case of "less is more" in both audio and visual, and I don't think Just Add Water really got that when making this game.
Which leads me onto the visual elements. As pointed out in said youtube video, this game is a lot flashier, colourful and luminescent, especially in rupture farms, where there are flashing lights and expensive neon signs everywhere as well as a permanent luminscent smog everywhere of varying colours. The screen is full of bloom sources throughout, not hard to see why they opted for hiding in steam vents in this game as the brilliantly designed screens of pitch darkness and shadow in the original just don't exist in this game.
There is also the issue of the graphics capabilities, it's times like this when you realise just how overhyped next gen hd graphics really are. With films perhaps visual quality really can be reduced to pixel resolution and frame rate, but with video games you still get terrible shadow graphics, polygon issues, and things being simply a lot less crisp and perfect as a result of being moving and £d as opposed to pre-rendered artwork. As for frame rate, this game has a serious animation issue with anything that involves fast travelling, be it doorways or wells, Abe's animation just fast forwards everytime and it's just plain sloppy.
The controls and mechanics are a lot worse on this. There is no single button for jumping forward, so you end up walking into mines all the time unless you time the button combo perfectly, Abe is always hesitating on the edge of platforms which gets very annoying, and because they have hugely dumbed down the act of jumping up and climbing down you seem to only need to be within a yard of the precise spot. This seems like it would make things easier, but not if you need to crouch down for any reason, you have to practically move to the other side of the screen to prevent Abe from just dropping down a level instead.
I quickly realised after giving this game a reasonable chance and appreciating the amount of effort put into reviving it for the modern HD generation, it only served to make me want to play the original, every level, every screen. Nothing comes close to the character and atmosphere of the original, it feels more like a generic child oriented platformer in many ways like Munch's Oddysee.
My advice to fans of the original: Don't bother, stick to the classics. My advice to newcomers: Just buy the originals anyway, they're dirt cheap to download on either steam or console and have aged brilliantly.

After completing Ori and the Blind Forest I can say with absolute certainty that it's 'one of those' games, and by that I mean it's easily one of the best games I've played so far this year. For a Unity engine game, the controls are perfect and require a good degree of mastery to 'get' how the bash mechanics work, which you'll have to pick up fast if you want any hope of getting through certain parts of the game without dying.
The art style makes any screenshot you see of this game look like art in its own right, but in real time, everything moves. The cutscenes are in-engine and mesh perfectly with playable events: sometimes you don't even notice it's your turn to take part in the story by how well it does this.
The sound design is possibly the strongest example I've seen where the sound completely integrates with the game, and allows you as the player to relax where no sense of urgency is required, and forces you to the edge of your seat when events unfold and require you to perform at your best in order to get out of a sticky situation. Kuro, the not-so-friendly owl not only comes across as formidable, but fearsome and impossible to even contemplate ever attempting to take on, and her cries and screeches have you desperately scrambling using every skill you've learned to get out of her way. Amongst all the other things going on, she comes out clear as day to let you know she's coming, she's coming fast, and she's coming to kill you.
As for gameplay, this is a hard game. You'll die, a lot. As I said above, you'll need to master all the abilities you learn if you have any hope of getting far in this game, and sometimes the puzzles will have you completely perplexed as to how to get around them. Ori controls brilliantly, and the game responds to you extremely fast, a given considering some parts of the game require you to be precise with your movements as you scale the forest from its marshes to it's very peak.
I'll admit that the difficulty in some areas might put some off, but the sense of relief you get from clearing them is worth the effort (and the many deaths). Is it worth the price tag? Absolutely. I couldn't fault this game in any places, and the only thing I'll say is that the gorgeous artwork doesn't always help you find your way, but I think that is partly the point. You are exploring a place you've never been to before, no one has ever traversed. There are no arrows to help you navigate, and sometimes you have to think out of the box to get around. There are many senses of accomplishment to be had here, and they are all yours for the taking.
I have no problem recommending Ori and the Blind Forest, especially if you're in to metroidvania-style titles, or even just to get sucked in to a world that has been painstakingly perfected from art to sound to control. I'll be keeping a close eye on Moon Studios from this point on.
Edited: Just a quick mention on the story front as I didn't earlier but didn't think I needed to. While there is a story it is minimal, and very remeniscent of Disney of old which is a good thing: It's not the length of the story that is key, but how it unfolds. The story is not told to you, but shown through the very heavy use of animation that would make anyone a fan of animated movies glow with glee. Ever felt like you wanted to leap in to the screen and help a loved character in trouble when watching any Disney movie when you were a kid? With Ori and the Blind Forest, you have that power and it feels awesome.

Stealth game with a fantasy setting.  The story follows a foul-mouthed, drug-addicted goblin named Styx as he tries to get into the Heart of the World Tree.  Language content not appropriate for younger children, violence content is typical for games in the genre.
The game is all about stealth.  You have multiple options for dealing with enemies (avoidance, distraction, clone ambush, etc.)  There are multiple paths through most areas, although sometimes the safer alternates (i.e. paths that stay away from all the guards) can be hard to spot.  I also enjoyed the strong "vertical" theme in level design.  Often avoiding guards means climbing up and over, which I found fun.
Combat, no doubt.  The combat system is difficult to handle - I basically gave up and outright avoided combat for a long time, until my skill purchases made it more feasible.  Even when I could do it, I found it tiresome.  However, a good stealth game encourages the player to avoid combat (and detection of any sort) anyway, so I didn't mind this drawback too much myself.
The story is grating at times, but it comes together in the end.
If you like stealth games, you ought to at least try it.  Unfortunately there doesn't appear to be a free demo for Master of Shadows, as there is for the sequel (Shards of Darkness), however, as I write this, Master of Shadows is on sale for about $6.00.
If you're into stealth games that really emphasize the "stealth" part, this one is worth playing.  If you're on the fence, wait for a sale.

I personally love this game, but I think most of the criticisms are valid.
I don't want to spoil the game, but as you've probably gathered from reviews and whatnot, the gimmick of this game is that the game bounces from different graphical styles and entirely different forms of gameplay seemingly willy-nilly.  It's something of a love-letter to video gaming history.
If this game had hit all its marks it would be absurdly great.  As is, I still absolutely love it, but that comes with a number of "buts."
What holds it back is the very thing that makes it charming: the gameplay shifts.  For me personally, right in the age group that it's targeted to, and somebody that grew up with a wide variety of games, I loved every second.  If you suck at shooters, though, or suck at platformers, or have no rhythm, etc... the game is going to probably going to force rage-quits because a genre-shift to a genre you don't like becomes not only a difficulty spike but an exercise in frustration.
My personal experience was that the genre shifts flowed very well and maintained a reasonable difficulty curve throughout, but perhaps I was one of the lucky ones.
Not all of the genre-shifts are perfectly executed, and it takes a fairly wide range of abilities and trope-knowledge to roll with the changes so to speak.
For the right type of gamer this is an easy 9.5/10 game, with the flaws easily overlooked because of the sheer scope and fun of the whole ordeal.  For others, I imagine it will forever remain partially completed after a genre shift becomes a sticking point that does nothing more than♥♥♥♥♥♥people off.
I absolutely love this game and highly recommend it, but the whole concept of it prevents it from having universal appeal.

After sinking a lot of both fun and VERY frustrated hours of time into this game I would recommend it to almost anyone to try out.
The characters are pretty sub-par and generic most of the time. The real strong point of the story though is how it uses Time-travel. It's actually a very clever use and carefully constructed story plot. Probably one of my favorite stories using time travel.
The game starts out pretty linear but opens up quite as bit as you get more items and dive deeper into the different ages. There are A LOT of pop culture references, poking fun at pretty much every type of game style it tries to mimic. The game shifts as you go through changing genres to a lot of old classic games a few newer ones too. The change in genre can create sudden difficulty spikes as you're effectively playing a whole new game.
But this gets me to one of my first and probably biggests frustrations with the game. Some of the these genres are just the worst to play depending on who you are so you'll struggle to get past specific points in the game because you don't like a particular type of game. It's actually kind of a good tool to figure out what type of games you prefer now that I think about it.
The only other issues I have with the game is how repetitive the music is. The soundtrack isn't very big so some tracks repeat a lot or just aren't very long tracks.
But over all I think it's a very unique game and experience. Kind of a piece of art, not trying to be gimicky just trying to make a silly playful unique experience using the concept of time-travel as a key story part and a means to fairly smoothly transition to all these different types of games instead of making it feel like a series of mini-games
By no means a 10/10 best game ever experience, but an interesting one if you want a change in pace from today's trend of gaming

As fun as the actual experience is, I HAVE to give this a negative review. Why?
Google "Skyhill: Is Accuracy Bugged" to see my full rant.
Apparently, whoever designed this game has a poor grasp of statistics. You are the dungeon crawler who must fight through hordes of monsters. Your accuracy decreases slightly with a string of lucky successful hits, and increases with an unlucky combo of misses, in order to 'balance the game'. Your dodge chance is directly dependent on your dexterity. Sounds fair, right? Well, monsters have a base accuracy of 100% while you're stuck with an initial 80%! Your dodge chance is a pitiful 2.5% that increases only by 0.5% with each point in dexterity, at 4 points per level and an expected max level of 10 at floor 20 that only means a pitiful 22.5% dodge chance when you finally reach the elite monsters, and you need to spend points in other stats to use your strongest weapons (See, there are some pure dexterity weapons but they don't gain attack power from your other stats like a multi-stat requirement weapon does)! In addition, in order to progress, you must successfully hit multiple times, which usually demands you hit more times than you miss, which causes the balancing system to lower your accuracy significantly the lower you descend, while the accuracy penalty for combo hits is outright nonexistent for the increasingly difficult monsters!
In short, (A) the monsters have a clear advantage over you in their unerring accuracy, and (B) statistically, you are expected to lose accuracy over time, while the monsters keep high accuracy because your dodge chance is low and will always be low even if you invest a serious number of points into dodge! They don't tell you this in the HUD or tutorials and as a result your rolls start getting increasingly unlucky, especially when you try repeatedly to use a move that is indicated to have 50-50 accuracy but is acutally like 10% from all your good rolls accuracy debuffs, until finally you crash and burn at the bottom despite all the powerful stuff you found!
Excellent game ruined by horrible mathematical error, someone PLEASE remove the damn accuracy penalty!

I thouroughly enjoyed this game, even if my hopes were low. Great character customization, great battle mechanics, and most importantly this "just one more battle feeling" made for a wonderful time sink.

In brief: fairly linear hex-map RPG with good character system and decent storyline. You'll enjoy it if you like that sort of thing.
Blackguards is an old-school gaming experience dressed in modern threads, a pen-and-paper RPG brought to life on the PC. The graphics are appealing, animations smooth, sound effects satisfying and voice acting mostly good. You take the role of an assistant to a noble family who gets into trouble at the outset and goes on the run, and your attempts to unravel what's happened ultimately take on a global significance. The story, chiefly told in cutscenes whose animation is best described as economical, follows a fairly linear path, but a wealth of subplots and sidetracks provides a pleasant illusion of free movement which probably won't convince today's open-world gamers.
Your character is provided with several sidekicks and you marshall and move your party on the world map. Movement is essentially the selection of locations and passage of time is not tracked. In towns and similar locations you'll find traders, trainers, inns, healers, and the like, as well as NPCs who advance the plot and give you quests. Party management is done through the stat sheet and inventory of each character, and true to the RPG that gave birth to this game, the system is satisfyingly deep and complex. Your decisions about character development will win or lose you the game, and new players should take note: it is possible to build a character badly and it's very difficult to undo this once you've done it, so take the time to read the manual and the in-game character creation notes (which don't appear in the manual and are very useful).
Quests and plot advancement almost always involve a skirmish, and it's these hex-map clashes where you'll spend most of your game hours. It's clear that a lot of thought has gone into skirmish map design: in some cases it's a straight fight to the death, but often there are environmental factors to deal with and in some cases the map is a puzzle which you must solve to win. In fact you can think of every skirmish as a puzzle which must be solved, as enemies differ in their capacities and susceptibilities and you must apply the right tools in terms of weapons, spells and equipment to prevail. That said, the game depends ultimately on the roll of the dice, so luck is always a factor. Fortunately death isn't permanent and so long as you have the last man standing, you'll walk away with your party intact.
Some reviewers have complained of the game's excessive difficulty. At the time of writing this review I've completed the game on Normal difficulty and have clocked up over 80 hours of play. I think I saw every skirmish there was to see, well over a hundred in total, and more than half of those I completed first time. There were only a handful I had to attempt more than twice. The final battle is difficult, but so it should be – my only gripe is that the plotting, or perhaps the scriptwriting, feels a bit wrong at the end, but YMMV. If you find yourself stymied by a skirmish, see whether you can go elsewhere to level your party up a bit; if not, it's very likely that you're either missing something important in the skirmish (always check the interactive objects) or you've taken a serious misstep in character building. Be careful not to spread XPs too thin on your characters: you can't take all spells and weapons to the maximum in the course of the game, and you do need some top-level skills and spells by the end if not by the middle.
Two things bothered me about this game: loading times, and the ending. My system isn't top-of-the-line but neither is this game, and I saw far too much of the loading screens for my liking (Mengbilla in particular tried my patience quite a bit). The ending... without spoiling things, I was surprised to see essentially the same cutscene after winning the final battle that I'd seen when I lost it. I'm unsure if your choice in dialogues makes any real difference to the way the game pans out, and online chatter suggests that a lot of players were left confused by the denouement. I can't honestly recommend that anyone other than a genre purist buy this game at full price, but if you see it on sale grab it and give it a try, and be sure to get to the top of the bow skill tree as early as possible!

I have seen many games go from Alpha to Beta to final release. Likewise, I have seen some games go from Alpha to failure. I have been disappointed, and I have been satisfied, but with a game in Early Access, I have never been so completely astonished.
The team behind Empyrion - Galactic Survival is hands down the most active and responsive team behind any pre-release game on the market. They frequently participate in the forums, taking player suggestions and beautifully implementing them in the game. They also release patches almost daily based on player bug reports, and, over the course of just a few months, have brought the game to a state of stability you don't often see in Early Access, particularly considering how buggy and clunky the game began. They have also added many new features that have improved not only gameplay, but quality of life.
I find myself so absorbed in exploring, and in building... I can only imagine what the game will be like when some of the more lacking features are rounded out. With almost 100 hours invested in this project, I can safely say that I have not been disappointed.
I must note, before you blow me off as starry eyed, that Empyrion is not without its flaws. It is, after all, in Early Access, and is inherently imperfect. There are many bugs, many features need to be added, and existing features need to be balanced. The combat AI reminds me very much of the original Doom, without the ingenuity that came along with that era's limitations, and, among other things, mining for resources feels very scripted at the moment.
However, it has been extremely promising to see the developers accomplish as much of their goals list from earlier this year as they have. They have done much fixing and balancing and adding of features to answer the community's needs. I wait with baited breath to see, and vote on, their next goals list.
I am pleased to say that if Empyrion's progress continues as it has, and procedural generation and interstellar exploration pan out, as well as the game's combat mechanics, it will find its place among my favorite games of all time.

The best way I've found to describe JYDGE is "top-down reverse Payday".
You play as a JYDGE, one of many robotic(?) Lawbringers protecting the city of Edenbyrg from crime. Your JYDGE is extremely customizable through the use of various Cyberenhancements. Lights Out and Shadow Blend turns you into an invisible force, killing everything in your way. Pick up Giant and Extra Armor, and you become extremely difficult to kill, and can tank pretty much anything. Cyberenhancements aren't the only custom option, there are also Special Weapons like Rockets, Turrets or my personal favorite, the Pyschoactive Darts that cause enemies to explode violently after killing every ally in sight.
Then, there are several different basic weapons. Shotguns, Ion Balls, Lazyrs, Snypers and even a Mingyn, all through the Gavel MK 1, probably the most badass gun ever. And that hammer on the end isn't just for show. Certain weapon mods (which also affect your fire) can improve this Gavel, making it explode on impact, or turning you into a bullet deflecting Jedi.
So JYDGE is extremely customizable, but do the levels allow for it? Of course. The levels are almost perfectly designed so that sneaking, guns blazing, and any other playstyle are accounted for. Each level also has 3 medals that you get for completing tasks in each one, that encourage a variety of weapons and enhancements. Furthermore, each level has 4 difficulties to it, that change the layout of enemies and the medals for each one.
Is the game perfect? No, not really. The story is really bareboned, though I must mention that there are various endings depending on how you play. But I'd like to see that quality amplified. Oftentimes the enemies don't seem that interesting. They look like Runescape Characters, with their hair color denoting their strength. The bosses especially are just like the regular enemies. I wish there was more variance here. But, with 18 levels, 3 medals, 4 difficulties, and a ton of weapons and modifications, JYDGE is definitely worth playing.
Seriously though, the melee deflect is so fricking cool! When do I get a mod that changes the Gavel into a lightsaber?

Jokes that don't work, unclear mechanics, and obvious padding make this a horrendous and frustrating slog.
The writing in general is very on-the-nose and obvious, and it's hard to derive much humour at all from it.  Most of it revolves around "hey, we're paying homage to this old game, do you remember this game?"  The premise of the game is fine, but I feel it would work better with fewer gimmicks and less mugging for the audience.
The game plays like a standard overhead Zelda clone, with a brief sidescrolling section à la Link's Awakening.  The gameplay is good, and works well, for the most part.  The worst part of it is a forced stealth section, which includes the player getting a cardboard box to hide under.  This is where I had a major problem, since it wasn't clear that the box reduces the sight range of the enemies as well as allowing you to avoid patrols by standing still.  I was stuck here for a while until I accidentally found out I could walk in front of enemies with impunity.
Everything came to a head in the first major city, where you have to do boring tasks that would be obvious filler content in any other game (except here, where it's probably a "tribute" but it's still just as boring), while your party members complain about them the entire time.  It's not fun and it's not pleasant and it's not witty.

The levels are completely redone from the ground up and you can tell how much effort went into each reimagined design. Many of the original puzzles and set peices are kept, while others have multiple tweaks and additions.
The original '97 title gave you 99 Mudokons to save or kill.
This title gives you 300 Mudokons to save or kill.
That should give you a little idea on how much extra content JAW has put into this game.
They added difficulty settings: Easy, Normal and Hard - being the closest to the original.
They added new mechanics such as throwing bottle caps and flint rocks for distraction/puzzle solving and changing the control scheme to fit the feel better - I.E., mainly changing your move button to the analog stick for a constant run. Oldschool Oddites need not worry, for
to slow down and get to hoppin' like back in the day.
Support the Dev's and they will continue to release ODD content, which is absolutely wonderful.

Color Symphony is a puzzle-platformer where you can change between 3 colored background, changing to one of the colored background will dematerialize all the elements of this color while materializing the 2 others colors.
You play as a vampire/dark elf/something who got blinded (literally) by his friend(s) and send to hell (which is apparently a large USA city in black and white). The plot of the game is to go back to your friend(s) for revenge.
In each level, you need to go to the door to get to the next level and you will be facing colored eagle, dog with 2 heads,  tentacles and sawblades you can mask them by changing to their colors. The first levels are easy enough, even if you get hit because you have a regenerating health bar. You also have an ability which use like 60% of your health to be able to combine all 3 colors to hide all colored obstacles but it's really useless because you switch colors all the time and you need to wait for the ability to wear off and the only time you really need to use it are too obvious (like 3 differents colored sawblades or tentacles on top of each other or in a row) making this skill worthless.
After a while, the levels become more difficult but still challenging until the worst idea in a video game : Colored sawblade that appear when you are near them, which make the invisible coin block from Super Mario World like a blessing to play with because they are often located in the air, right above a bottomless pit, right before the exit, which mean you have to jump, get hit and die because you weren't expecting it and that not the worst, that would be too easy, you just need to come back and switch to the color of the sawblade to go through, right? Well no because their colors are randomised every time you got near them, so you need to be on your toes and press the right color because there is a slight delay before you can switch again and by that time, you would see your character get hit with a big recoil Castlevania/Megaman style where you can do nothing before you land and going in the bottomless pit and wait 2-3 seconds before your character die in it before you get the continue screen.
If you didn't stop here (I wish I did), the level design become more and more dickish with the introduction of leap of faith through a vertical shaft with sawblade you cannot touch or you will go flying into a pit, or where you can't see the platform and have to guess where it's going to be.
IF you didn't stop here (I mean, come on, it's like platformers have regress with this), you will have to do pixel perfect jump on 8 pixels girders with your character's hitbox of 4 pixels wide which is right in the empty space between your shoes.
IF YOU DIDN'T STOP HERE (We are back to bad NES games with this), you will have to jump into a colored inclosed box, which mean you have to jump into it, select the color of the box making it invisible, pray you get into the box and switch back to an another color to make the box solid again and if a pixel of you is inside an object, you get one-shot, even if you have all your life. Also, those boxes love to have sawblade on their side, making it more hard and less fun.
(What is wrong with you?), you will have a final level with a cathedral on the background, no enemies, no jump to do, only go right, have a line of monologue and you get treated to a 5 images credits with reuse pictures from the intro, making it one of the worst credits I have ever see.
In conclusion, this game had a kinda neat idea gameplay-wise, but run out of idea to work with it and made the game really frustating to finish. The music (There is only two tracks, one during gameplay and one during the credits) is meh, not bad enough to want to mute the audio but not good enough to put it on my MP3. I also wonder why this game is on Steam when it's obviously a flash game you see on various websites.
TLDR : This game is basically a flash game you find on Newgrounds or Armor Games, play for 5-10 minutes and have a good impression of it or try to beat it and see all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level design and wish you didn't played this game.

There are three levels divided up into eleven stages and a 'boss' stage, in between each stage is a challenge stage where the real high score hunting comes in as it's relatively easy to unlock each one through normal play, as the path the game takes puts the gold blocks required right in your way.
As a game, it's relatively simple. You automatically run forward and have to duck, kick, block and jump through a stage full of obstacles. This sounds very shallow in depth, but the patterns introduced can be a bit of a shock to encounter at first, but are satisfying once conquered. The game is all too aware of how long you hold the jump button. This belongs among games such as Super Meat Boy and Jamestown - Difficult without being punishing, but satisfying when finally beaten

♥♥♥♥ this boring game. Orks are the tool of unimaginative game designers, and monster closets haven't ever been fun. In this case, they wore out this game's already short welcome. The weapons and inventory system is stupid, all the melee weapons are the same, the story is for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and War from Darksiders handles significantly more like a space marine than Captain Titus. I know Chaos Marines happen later in the story, I don't have the time. I quit halfway through, and I'll come back once I play everything else in my collection.

Even if you're not a Warhammer 4K fan, Space Marine offer quite a bit of fun as a FPS. Unlike the plethora of shooters out there, you cannot simply wade in through your enemies, scything through them, as your opponents are generally quite hardy. Adding to that, although this is in the future, weapon cooling has becoe a forgotten art, as your weapons will quickly overheat.
In single player that is not so much of an issue, as you can simply duck back behind a wall, have a smoke, and then resume at your leisure.
In multiplayer, however the pace is too frenetic to pause, and as a result, the default choice for most players is to go melee.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun, and with a good team, should be able to support each other. Unfortunately, multiplayer is where the game is really broken.
The game works on a round robin hosting basis, which means each player will get the chance to have a chance to play with no lag. Sounds good in theory, but quite often you will be in mid attack, and the game pauses, whilst it changes host. When it resumes, it doesn't wait for your client to update, so you'll often find yourself, or in some cases, the entire team dead.
With the respawn timers being so long, if that was your hosting segment, then you get to sit it out in a (lag free) death timeout. Which is quite a big game killing experience. LAN however, would be ideal for multiplayer.
Good enjoyable game otherwise.

Ori, And The Blind Forest is a fantastic game.
I felt I needed to write a review after completing the story, and I will summarize it in a few short bullets.
Pros:
-Wonderful story, The story while a little cliche and sappy is very well writen and goes along with the exploration of the game very well.
-Combat, The game not only uses multiple forms of combat, but incorperates it into the game so that you must use it to complete puzzles and progress through areas, which I think is a brilliant idea.
-Movement, The game is based around movement. You need to dodge your enemies and often times use their attacks against them, and it is done so smoothly I am honestly impressed.
Stunningly beautiful, The reason I bought this game was out of impulse just based on looks alone, I had seen it pop up in my recommended for you list and took a look, and it was awesome, I'd taken another look, saw it was a platformer with a good story and bought it right away. It looks fantastic, no more I could say about it.
Cons:
-Lack of Knowledge, If you werent paying attention to a cut scene, you can kiss 10 minutes goodbye wondering where to go next. This game has a lot of problems with the lack of indication on where to go, which some might argue promotes exploration, but regardless it can get to the point where its just frusterating.
-Combat again, I said combat was good, but only for your character, AI are often predictable, which some would argue are necassary due to the use of combat to complete areas in the game.
-Difficulty spike, When playing the difficulty ramps up from very, VERY easy down to ludicrus levels. The final area I spent a solid 10 minutes on, due to the low timer that I had to complete that area, and a lack of indication on what to do.
Summary:
In all I would recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a platformer, or a good story, but you'd better pay attention, or you may get lost.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a great game, good enough to satiate 2D platformer / metroidvania players. Of course as you will expect there are plenty of power-ups and skills, the leveling system and skill tree are simple but fun, every skill really help you out, I mean, there is no skill that you will feel is not worth spending your points in it. You really want all of them, and it keeps you playing and leveling up.
Apart from that of course, there is the fantastic gameplay and how smooth everything is put together. Monsters are very well designed, each of them have their weakness but they can deliver high amount of damage to you if you are not careful or approach them with the wrong tactics.
The 2D world is good, there are plenty of secrets and hidden caves to discover containing more HP, Energy, XP, Map fragments and even skill points. The design of the 2D world and the background are amazingly smooth, sometimes you will not even see Spikes, because they match and blend so well with the background, so you need to be careful out there. The difficulty of the game is just fine, it can be extremely hard at some point, for me that is fine, because I really don't like games that are too easy, specially this kind of games.
What I like the most is the game saving feature, it is well implemented, I think that is a great idea to save the game using energy, that makes a challenge too because you can create your own checkpoints, but at the same time, you can run out of energy and not be able to save your game for a while until you recharge your energy, so you need to think how to manage your energy carefully.
Unfortunatelly, there is a annoying bug in the game, that can cost your save data, and you may have to restart the whole game, that is why I don't give this game a 10/10. Regarding the bug, you can search here in the steam forums how to solve that, there is a player fixing save files at the moment, but no official word from the developers yet as far as I know.

What it brings to the already dense Metroidvania genre is topnotch all around: The tight controls, the diagonal and motivating difficulty curve, the breathtaking artdesign and orchestral music, the sympathetic characters and heartwarming story; Ori and the Blind Forest is - despite relying on established formulas - a unique experience and a mustplay for every fan of 2D platformers.

PROs
* Well, it's fun
* Decent amount of content
* You can set up your perks and your equipment for each level separately
CONs
* Well, it's gets tough, especially if you want to speedrun. Expect Hotline Miami's cycle of rush, shoot, die, rinse, repeat.
* You're going to wish for more diverse enemies at some point
* Despite gamepad support, you're better off with mouse/keyb if you want to hit targets with smth other than a shotgun.

Astonishing. Ori and the Blind Forest is at its core a Metroidvanian like many others, but the execution is just impeccable. Never before have I been so awed by 2D graphics as here, this is truely one, if not the best looking platformer ever. It goes beyond pretty screenshots too, because nearly everything animateable is animated, and they feel so fluent and impactful that it really enhances your immersion in the world. The music is also of very high quality throughout the whole game, absolutely gorgeous.
The gameplay itself is bizarelly smooth. I don't think any other platformer I've played can compare with the smoothness and joy it is to move Ori through the world. Again, the animations really help with enhancing this. Combat is not the most interesting in the game, though enjoyable, but given the relatively short length I never felt like it was an issue, especially when you get the super fun Dash ability!
Many people talk about its high difficulty. I personally didn't experience this so much, but I noticed friends of mine were really struggling. For me, the difficulty was high enough to keep being challenging and rewarding while only very sporadically getting to the point of frustration, but with the great pacing of the game this was never a lasting issue.
While this is without a doubt the best action platformer I have ever played, it is not without its flaws. While the art invites a great story, this is unfortunately not the case, riddling in boring cliches such as finding 3 elements and "save-the-world syndromes". There really isn't as much narrative to the game as you would expect from it at first glance either. The prologue and ending are the only moments where the game tries to pull your heartstrings, but I couldn't see either as particularily emotional. It also never dares to provide narrative content that is more challenging, unfortunately.
Furthermore, the game is at no point truely innovative. While it surpasses them, the game clearly shows its inspirations, and at no point truely adds anything new to it. However, it's an example that crafting a game with such love and attention to detail can be one of the most impressive works of the last few years.

JYDGE is a top-down twinstick based in the Neon Chrome universe. If you liked that aesthetic and like the concept of Judge Dredd, then you'll love the feel of this game. The game makes you a JYDGE; what makes them so fun is the way they handle the law and their customization. You can try to be stealthy or just run in guns blazing. Your JYDGE has lots of loadout potential; there's loadouts for the JYDGE themselves, mods for the gun itself, and lots of different ammo types and special weapons to choose from.
Levels aren't Roguelike though, they are hand crafted. Same goes for the buffs/mods, you get them in a specific order instead of random drop.
I had a lot of fun running around and shooting enemies while avoiding getting shot. This game does Twinstick very well and I enjoyed it a lot.

I played the first Evoland and while i didn`t liked some of the later features, over all it was a good game.
Evoland II on the otherhand... well...
l can honestly say: I have never played a game, that made me so angry and frustrated in so little time.
While i have to admit, it`s VERY unfair of me to judge this game so harshly after barley 2 hours of gamplay ( out of approximately 25-30 hours), i can not and do not want to play it any further.
CONS:
1. Backtracking:
While there wasn`t any "real" backtracking in the first 2 hours, there was already some kind of uncrossable passage ,which i presume, could be crossed with a new character or new artifact... later in the game.
Backtracking is a completely normal elemten in RPGs, but it´s still a huge turn off for me.
2. "helpful" partymembers:
Would the partymembers not join you, but instead teach you a technique and leave, there would be no change gameplay wise, at least not to the point where i gave up frustrated.
3. Finas horrible character:
________(SPOILERS)________
She charges alone into the forest, because "she can take care of herself" and almost gets killed by some LOUSY mushrooms.
She more or less commands the amnesiac, probably still weakend protagonist to kill a huge, powerful beast almost alone.
Right after that fight, she carelessly reads some old inscriptions from the now activated ruins and - oh surprise - something bad happens.
We as player do not know, what our protagonist thinks about demons, but we do know and every normal human in Evoland II should know, that demons very likely do not like humans.
So what does the super brain FINA do, as soon as the duo meets a young, very obvious demon, who is hunted by some guards?
Fina helps the demon... because she feels sorry for him/her? ( i dont know if he/she is a boy or girl and frankly, i dont care)
It`s hard to see, because of the art style of the game, but we can assume, that the demon is frightened and exhausted from all the running, but even then the demon is able to push a few grown, strong, armored Guards away from itself, so its very safe to assume, that the demon could and probably did hurt or kill some humans, which would be a very plausible reason for a demon and why he/she is followed by the guards.
________(SPOILER END)______
These were not the only annoying moments with her, there are more. Probably a LOT more.
It feels like Fina is forced upon the protagonist to show him the way the developers wanted the player to go...
Which would be more acceptable, if Fina wouldn`t ask for your opinion so very often, just to ignore the answer, if she didn`t liked it.
4. Unreachable Content:
Just an example, there is a dungeon and almost at it`s end, you will find a locked door, behind said door is a chest.
There are two ways to go, and if you choose the way, which looks more important, but ends more or less in a dead end, you will see another chest. If you choose, to loot that chest, suddenly the dead end opens up, also the way back is closed up now... and if you still want that chest behind the looked door, you have to either restart the game or hope that there is a new game plus, because the game autosaves and even after quiting and reloading, you still can`t go back.
Even though you could skip through all the dialogues until this point and reach this rather early point in the game, i really did not want to re-play all the "wonderful" scenes with fina...
PROS:
1. The Artstyle:
What i was able to see in the first 2 hours, looked like a gorgeous pixel-art game.
I especially like the face of the Protagonist. Just this look, like he`s dead inside, every time he has to put up with the horrible treatment Fina puts him through...
It makes him so relatable ^_^
2. The Puzzles:
They are good i guess. Not too hard, not too easy.
My Conslusion:
I HATE Fina. With the burning intensity of a million stars.
In my opinion, she is a horrible character and a very cheap excuse to force the player on a certain way.
If it wouldn`t be for her character or the fake-opinions, i could probably enjoy this game a lot more.
Backtracking is maybe not such a big part in this game, can be overlooked.
The "helpful" characters probably are very useful in later stages of the game, this point can also be overlooked.
The unrechable content is pretty stupid in my opinion, but as far as i know, it would be just for an achievment, so who cares ?
Right now, i would not recommend this game,
but like i said before, it`s not fair AT ALL of me to judge the game this harshly, when i only played such a little portion of it, but maybe someday, when i am extremely happy and need something dim this happiness, i while get back to this game, endure Fina and try to beat it.

Blackguards is a turn-based combat focused RPG, that will most likely frustrate you a lot with the amount of dice rolling in it!
My opinions won't really add much to the discussion, as they're mixed... like almost everyone else's. Also, I'm farily new to the genre, so the min-maxing aspect present in the attributes and skill-trees in the game don't really appeal to me, yet (mostly how of ignorance, but anyway...).
I really like RPGs in general, but I'm not one to read up on the game's numerous systems to learn what the optimal builds are -- I like to shape my characters as I please, leading to some interesting, fun, but not necessarily good decisions. I've done the same in Blackguards and will admit that, for the
part, it went alright. I played through Normal mode, and never got truly stuck, which was my biggest worry.
Many people complained about reaching an unbeatable point in the game because they had a sub-optimal build. Maybe they were either playing on Hard, or I've simply been fairly lucky in my decision.
I will say that there were lots of details in the game that I simply did not delve into -- potions (offensive), traps, etc. Those didn't seem all important in any of the battles in Normal.
Anyway. It's tough. Some of the battles were infuriating, missing 3x in a row when I had a 90% chance to hit, having some periods of extended battles that far overstayed their welcome, etc.
But I did enjoy it quite a lot. Until I finished the 3rd Chapter, that is. Then the game offered nothing new.
The game is very linear, although it opens up a bit in the 3rd Chapter, giving you quite a lot of sidequests. The following 2 chapters barely have any of those, which felt strange.
It seems like the focus of the game was only the 3rd chapter, the other ones being mostly to build it up or simply carry the story.
The story was pretty bland, and the sidequests weren't too interesting either. Gameplay-wise, it's almost a pure combat game. You move from battle to battle. Other than battles, you just go to cities to buy equipment/heal/train, and get sidequests. Sidequests simply lead you into more battles. You never explore anything, never really find emergent gameplay or anything of the sort. It's very, very combat focused.
But hey... I really have very little to add that would be in any way meaningful. I want to talk about one thing exclusively -- and that is how opaque the game actually was! It was one of the biggest sources of frustration, for me.
Sometimes, the game pushes you into extended battles. Battle after battle after battle without an opportunity to heal, restock, change equipment, etc. These, of course, are a much bigger challenge -- especially because, if you do poorly on one battle, you'll carry that penalty onto the next one.
These battles felt extremely tense, to me. Sometimes they could go on for 2 hours, even if they were just 2 or 3 battles. The game is very slow paced, and a mistake can cost you quite a lot of time, which is frustrating. And the game often likes to pull tricks on you that it never pointed to. They're unwelcome surprises.
This is one side of it. The other, happened in the end of the game. After the
, you're lead into a serious of battles, but you
heal and re-equip between them. What you
do, is buy anything. Every healing potion, equipment, etc. that you can use is what you've taken with you.
There were a few problems here -- first, you had no idea how many battles there would be, so you couldn't really judge. Second, what the game showed you was very misleading, by having it spread over 2 "pages", but only showing you the first.
Basically, you're expecting x battles, and suddenly, after wasting most of your potions, you're shown that there are actually twice as many. Well,♥♥♥♥♥♥
Thankfully, the game wasn't tricking the player and ramping up the difficulty artifically -- on that second page, there was a healer and merchant that was essentially a safe point. And that was a very nice thing.
The problem is how the game never communicated that beforehand. Every battle I fought felt that much more frustrating because a small mistake seemed like a colossal one.
Arguably, that the feeling that the game was trying to carry -- I doubt it, though. In this case, it was simply a case of bad communication with the player, it seemed. And similar issues happened throughout the game -- often leading you into "extended battles" without warning, and the like.
For me, at least, it's a huge source of frustration, to have to "judge" something without information. Especially when mistakes can cost hours.
So yeah. That's basically it. The game is a huge "tension" without the "release"...
Regardless, I enjoyed it. I'm not a hardcore player of the genre, so my appreciation is certainly different. It was a good challenge! There was some frustration with the dice-rolls, but overall, I'd recommend it to anyone who is looking for a tough turn based rpg.

I can sum this entire game up in a sentence and a half. A three or four layered pile of stat sheets that serves to slightly improve your chances of besting the RNG gods on a turn by turn basis. With the odds against you.
If you think this is a dark, or pessimistic way to sum the game up, I can tell you that that is actually the nice way of putting it. To the list of gaming sins this game commits you may a redundant and unrewarding item system, the most difficult to navigate skill system I have seen since the sphere grid in final fantasy X (which is mainly out of your reach anyhow, seeing as it depends on trainers which appear at arbitrary points in the story), multiple attempts at large scale battles which quickly descend into long lines of infinitely spawning enemies dog piling on your phalanx of heroes, percent chance failures on pretty much everything that mean any well laid plan can come to a deadly end at any point in your game, and a difficulty curve that pretends all the random the dice wielding percent chance jockeys whom designed the game smashed into every nook and cranny of the game does not exist at all.
The end result will leave you hitting the (restart battle) button on the second or third turn of each attempted play because your warrior's power attack whiffed, which you immediately realize means you won't be able to kill the enemies quickly enough to keep up with the level. Assuming none of the heals whiff (yes, your heals can whiff to, about 33% of the time in most cases), which is also a death sentence. I could go into the ham fisted attempts at interactive levels, mysterious and all around dumb line fo sight mechanics that let bows shoot a seemingly infinite distance but leash spells at just a few tiles, impossible side objectives, and lack of actual counter play and tactics, but my ranting would fill three pages.
All this is a shame considering the clear level of effort and passion that went into designing the graphics, story line, and characters, who despite being completely archetypical adventures manage to characterize themselves wonderfully though they're well developed connection to the adventure is set in. If half the effort that went into all that were part of the game, this would likely be a tbs to the caliber of dynasty tactics or r-type command. Instead, you have either a slightly better version of fire emblem, or a slightly worse version of final fantasy tactics, both of which are mind bendingly boring and tediously frustrating to begin with. If you enjoy either of those than you richly deserve this.

Buy this game. Get it on sale, get it at full price, and get a copy for someone who has an appreciation for complexity in storytelling.
If you've never played To the Moon, there are two things you should know: (1) you don't need to play To The Moon FIRST in order to love Finding Paradise, but (2) you should play To The Moon (and its two free DLC minisodes) anyway for the complete narrative experience.
This is a complex, surprising, unpredictable, emotional and rewarding story. This is one that lives just as much in your mind as it does the minds of the characters involved. When the credits roll, and you begin to think of the implications of what you've beheld, you start to realize that the impact of the events which transpire can't help but continue to impact the characters in meaningful ways that we may never get to see, but we can confidently conclude what "it all means."
JRR Tolkein resolved to create a work that would make the world a better place by simply being a good thing within it. He penned the world of Middle Earth; this was his contribution to improving the overall net worth of our rock floating through space. And improve it he did.
Kan Gao and his team have done something similar; they have taken the medium and used it to bring their audiences to emotional highs and lows with enormous skill, insight and charm. Innovative isn't the word to use here; wisdom, vulernerability and "heart" are more appropriate. If aliens ever invade our planet and have to decide whether the human species deserve to continue to exist, they will likely conclude that we don't - however, Freebird Games will certainly tip the scales in our favour.

The game has Great mechanics, and I do really like it, but at the same time, Your skill doesn't matter. How good you become at the game doesn't matter.
Its random chance as to how far you'll actually be able to progress.
For example. I got the Hammer sawsword (or something like that), basically a weapon that does 28-33 damage per hit (supposed ot do more, but didn't have the stats for it), and I got it fairly early on in the game. For example, a starting weapon, a Kitchen Knife, does 3-5 damage per hit. Enemies have 20 health to start. And yet, even with an insanely powerful weapon to start, I still died before I passed floor 65. Because almost no food was spawning. It had nothing to do with how strong I was, or how my skills were distributed, I just had zero food, and so couldn't really recover health, since I was loosing 11 per room.
And that's why I'm giving this a thumbs down. Because, for me, a game where you cannot use skill to win, and instead MUST rely on luck to win, strikes me as bad game design.
However, I know this isn't a negative for everyone. So if you don't mind having to rely on luck to win, by all means, go for it. For me, I'm done with the game.

I own the PS4 version of MotoGP 14 and have been enjoying it despite the 30fps lock on the refresh rate.  I decided to pick up the PC version so that I could let the game stretch its legs a bit with the extra power of my computer.
Unfortunately the PC version is very obviously playing second fiddle to the console version.  The graphics options are extremely limited (extra fx and hi res textures) though you do get to change the refresh rate and vsync.  The graphics while in the garage seem a bit strange, as if they are being rendered at a lower resolution than the 1080p which the main game runs at, and the textures in the garage are also very low resolution and blurry.
There are other oddities, such as cut scenes and replays being locked to 30fps.  Being able to exit the game to the desktop is glitchy, sometimes you get the option to do it and other times you have to kill the game from the task manager.  That's a pretty obvious issue that should never have been allowed through the QA process.
I am able to unlock vsync and run the game approaching 120fps but it's very stuttery, the only way to get the game to run smoothly for me is to run it at 60hz with full vsync and this seems to remove most of the problems.
Thankfully, the actual game itself is great, the racing is fast and furious and the handling superb.
In essence, it's a great game but a poor PC port, there aren't even any options for AA.
Despite the reservations I have about MotoGP 14 on the PC,  I'm still thoroughly enjoying it as the base game itself is excellent and the Career mode is really fun this time around.
Whether the game is for you or not depends on how you feel about slightly shoddy console ports.....

The bikes and riders are well re-created and they look the part, but the graphics are lacking in the environment department, textures wise. Flat grass textures in this age of graphics is pretty much inexcusable. This said, the gameplay is quite solid and I have had no real issues with it. Controls on an Xbox 360 controller feel much better than they did on the last MotoGP game I played (MotoGP '07) and since then, rather than having to create a team and choose a bike to ride, they've made vast improvements on a progression through career mode, very much akin to the F1 and WRC series of games (especially WRC as they are the same developers) where you join real-world teams. Apart from being a blatant port to PC, it's pretty good so far.
