After checking into the hotel, I decide to watch a bit of television. My plan to unwind is abruptly cut short as the newscaster reports that the city has been attacked. I look out of my penthouse window and I can just see the first impact. A huge mushroom cloud appears on the horizon. It’s something we never expected would happen. Nuclear war. But it’s not just ordinary nuclear weapons. These bombs apparently contain biological agents that turn people into horrible mutant abominations. I try calling the cops, even the front desk. No reply. After a while, my food runs out and I realize that I have to leave this place if I want to survive. But I have also been hearing strange noises. I suppose it’s better to go out there and try to survive than die of starvation.
Skyhill is a 2D point-and-click game that places you in the aftermath of World War III. People have turned into mutants and your objective is to try to escape from the hotel. The problem is that you’re stuck in the penthouse of a hotel with 100 floors. And the elevator is out. You have to make your way down, floor by floor. The layout of each floor is exactly the same. The central area is reserved for the staircase and elevator with one hotel room to the left and another to the right. Your first priority is scavenging for food. The protagonist has a hunger bar and a health bar. You lose hunger points every time you move from one room to another. If your hunger bar goes all the way down, the health bar is next. And if that one hits zero, it’s game over.
The key to Skyhill is exploring rooms and picking up food and various items. Your penthouse acts a base of operations. You can return there whenever you want in order to craft or upgrade items. Every five to ten floors you will be able to fix a small section of the elevator. The elevator can take you back up to your penthouse or upper floors that you have already visited, but it won’t go down. You have to use the staircase and repair the elevator bit by bit until you reach the ground floor. You may be tempted to just go all the way down without exploring hotel rooms, but that won’t get you very far. You’ll either die of starvation or you’ll encounter a deadly mutant. Preparation is important.
As you gather various items, you will be able to use the workbenches in your penthouse and craft weapons, medkits, and other items. The crafting system is intuitive and easy to understand. You can also combine multiple pieces of food to prepare meals that provide more hunger points. You can also upgrade these workbenches in order to unlock more elaborate meals and weapons. If you’re running out of health and don’t have any means to heal yourself, you can use your bed and go to sleep. This will exchange hunger points for health points. Just be sure that you have food to restore those hunger points. Upgrading the bed will make it more efficient. Sometimes you will be awaken by nightmares or strange noises, which will affect how many health points you were able to restore. To mitigate this effect, you can choose to upgrade your doors, so you can feel perfectly safe while sleeping.
Once you enter a room occupied by a mutant, a fight will ensue. The combat system is turn-based. You can just click on the mutant for a basic hit or you can go into the battle screen. This will enable you to choose where you want to hit the mutant. For example, hitting the head will deal more damage, but the chances of missing are significantly increased. That’s pretty much all there is to it, the combat system is very simple. That can actually be said about all of the game’s systems. The exploration, level design, character upgrade system (each level you can choose to upgrade damage, speed, dexterity, and accuracy), crafting system, combat system – it’s all relatively basic. However, I still found the game rather enjoyable. Roaming through the hotel, looking for that one elusive item you need to craft that badass weapon is actually pretty interesting.
After each playthrough you will unlock passive and active perks that you can enable at the start of a new playthrough. Choosing a different combination of perks does provide a slightly more different experience, but after several playthroughs, the simplicity of the design and systems in place is going to start to wear very, very thin. The truth is that the design and gameplay simply cannot sustain more than a few playthroughs. You will not only feel like you’ve seen everything there is to see, you will actually see it all. There are three different endings to shoot for and that is where you will have completely exhausted the content of this game. I have to say that the endings are rather unexpected and well done. However, as everything else in the game, the storytelling is rather rudimentary and not particularly involving.
Skyhill sports a very nice, clean art style. The interface is also simple and intuitive. You always know what is going on around you and what items you are missing for that weapon that you want to craft. The sound design isn’t that noteworthy. There’s barely any music to speak of and the sound effects are entirely unimpressive.
This is a slightly odd call to make because I did enjoy Skyhill. This is a good foundation. But it needs to be built upon. There is simply no denying the fact that the design and gameplay systems are too basic. Roguelikes need to support many playthroughs, all of which should provide a different experience. Skyhill simply doesn’t succeed in this task. However, it is still an enjoyable romp while it lasts.

I was a bit suspicious at first, judging by the looks I thought this would be another typical "play 20 minutes and be disappointed" indie title.
Boy, was I wrong... you can see from my stats how many hours I've actually played this game. :)
The concept of the game is fairly easily outlined.
You move between floors and rooms, fight monsters, consume food to balance your energy level, consume medical supplies to balance your health level, craft meals and weapons and occasionally find trivia pieces that help describe the circumstances surrounding the game; call it a story, if you will.
You start on floor 100 of a hotel, and you need to get down to the ground floor to escape.
You can walk down the stairwell or, as soon as you find the keycard, use the elevator to move about.
Each floor consists of a stairwell and two rooms. Some rooms contain useful items, others are entirely empty.
In some floors' stairwell or rooms you might encounter monsters that need to be fought, in others you don't.
Some rooms may be locked and unaccessible, but you can find or make keys to return and open them.
Not all locked rooms are worth re-visiting and unlocking, except for the achievement, some contain nothing at all.
On some floors, the elevator doors or some electrical box will be broken.
You can't do anything against broken elevator doors, but you can repair broken electrical boxes.
In fact, you HAVE to repair the electrical boxes in order to use the elevator on and below the current floor.
While you're moving about, there's a fairly basic leveling system that should underline your progress.
You collect experience points (XP) by fighting monsters, when you level up you get to distribute a few ability points.
This, to me, does not seem to affect the overall gameplay experience, but mostly controls which weapons you can use.
Having a high accuracy level still means that your guy can miss up to 5 turns. In a single fight. In a row.
There's a basic crafting system involved - basic, because it's not very deep or demanding.
Most weapons can be crafted, some can only be found (golf club, machete).
Some food and health items can be combined "on the go", but most things (weapons, meals, etc.) can only be crafted in the room on floor 100, so you will probably need to constantly travel back there in order to craft things or meals.
Actions cost "food points", energy if you will. Changing floors or rooms uses 1 point, going by elevator uses 2 points.
Some food types can be combined to more interesting ones. But beware, some combinations only give you +1 additional food points, which means it's better value consuming the two items right away (or waiting) rather than spending food points for traveling.
On your way down (and up) you'll come past different types of vending machines: crafting items, food and medical stuff.
You'll occasionally come by coins, these can be used to buy random (mostly not very helpful) items from those machines.
Hints:
Make sure that you build a kitchen and upgrade it as soon as you can. A better kitchen gives you access to better recipes, you could for example eat 4 items with 5-10 food points by themselves - or combine them into one tasty 65 point meal. Even taking the 4 points for elevator travel up and down away, that's still a worthwhile gain.
You can not "dodge" or evade monster attacks, and you can not apply medical items (Medipack, Painkillers, etc.) during a fight sequence, but you can flee and leave the room or change the floor. Although monsters may attack you an additional time while you do so, it still gives you some extra breathing time to heal. After healing, you can return to the monster which is still as weak as it was when you fled and finish it off.
Don't forget your bed! I can usually complete a run without going to bed at all, but I've more than once ended up in "the lower floors" with ZERO health items left, no Medipacks, no Bandages, nothing. Not even Alcohol and Rags (combine into Bandages) or Coins to spend on medical vending machines. Retreat to your bed and heal, it basically turns food into health and can get you through.
Some monsters can "infect" you, which will drain your health points pretty quickly and won't stop without medication.
To avoid this, always be prepared. As soon as you come across Antibiotics and Mutant Blood vials, combine them for an antidote right away rather than using them to craft Painkillers or what it is. You can always recover health in your bed, but it won't get rid of the infection. It's better to have 4-6 antidotes ready, rather than looking for one when you need one.
Upgrade your Workbench once, maybe twice if you have nothing better to spend your materials on. Don't bother upgrading more. All it will do is give you a larger variety of weapons, but not necessarily stronger ones.
I'll end with the things that bother me, devs pay attention:
One run can take several hours to complete, especially if you're doing well. Being a casual "work night" gamer I don't always have 4 hours in one go to spend. It's a huge PITA that I can't save a game mid-play and then return to it the next evening. If I have to leave the game, for whatever reason, all my progress is lost. PLEASE, dear devs, include a possibility to save games.
The success of the game mostly depends on nothing but bare luck. I see no value in leveling up, except that it helps get access to better weapons. Having level 13 or so speed and accuracy will do nothing, the guy will still miss up to 5 times in a row -- and this is with up to 96% hit probability, not just "aiming for the head". When you're down in the lower floors, this can mean sudden and unexpected death. Oh so many times I thought "this is going pretty well", stocked with lots of food and medipacks... encounter one of the "long ones" and wham, all gone to waste because the guy misses and misses and misses and misses... *sigh* PLEASE again, dear devs, DO SOMETHING ABOUT THIS.
There aren't a lot of cut-scenes, one at the beginning and one at the end, but catogorizing them as "music" is quite enfuriating. I tend to play my games without background music, or with the music turned all the way down. Not because I wouldn't appreciate the work that went into the soundtrack (I'm a musician myself, so I do), but because it distracts me from the gameplay. So... I turn the "music" down in the options dialog, and now the cut-scenes are turned all the way down as well. It's either "music at full blast" or "can't hear the cut-scenes". PLEASE once more, dear devs, make the volume of the cut-scenes independently configurable, or at least control the cut-scenes' volume with the gameplay volume.
These things are NOT challenging, encouraging, action-enhancing, thrilling, entertaining or anything else.
They're just plain annoying.
The startup configuration dialog offers the ability to set up 2 additional attack types and a jump command... either this is preparation for a coming update, or it's a bug.

Pros
+ Tactic and varied combat, with lots of maps and strategies
+ Fully voiced, good dialogues
+ Many different weapons, spells and items you can use during the fights
+ Shady characters, not your classic heroes
+ More content than I expected, with a lot of sidequests
+ A real challenge if you want to go into the hard mode... or even normal difficulty
+ One of the best dwarfs ever
Cons
- Some fights can be really hard compared to the rest of the game
- Learning curve? More like learning wall
- You won't understand how combat works until you've failed a lot
- Game controls feel a bit clumsy sometimes, you may end up casting heals on yourself instead of the intended target

- You may find yourself trapped... if you built your characters wrong, you won't be able to survive to certain parts of the plot and may even need to restart everything. I'm thinking about you, Nine Hordes...

I, as many here, am a big fan of the Oddworld series for a long time.

Starting with the good:

-The adaptation from the fixed camera to side-scrolling was amazing. They way they adapted the gameplay worked really well.

The bad:

The both bad and good:
- The ragdolls of dead characters are sometimes weird, but so funny.

I played the first games, and loved them as a kid, now that I am older I found out about this re-make and was skeptical. I have to say this is one of the most faithful recreations I have ever seen, so long-time fans rejoice and enjoy. For those who just want an interesting platform game I highly recommend it, here is a quick list of the pros and cons purely related to the gameplay.
Pros
-Initially controls were a little "odd" since I was using xbox controller with joystick isntead of d-pad for movement. Over time I found it to be MUCH better and smoother translating to a highly responsive reactions that felt natural.
-Gorgeous scenery, great ambiance, everything seems to have a personality now, the mudokon and slig banter is a welcome addition.
-Chapter select shows mudokons rescued and allows you to go back to each one to get 100% saved without having to restart game.
-Quicksave'quickload is true to it's word. Not only is it fast but you will find yourself using that feature frequently getting past a few parts without having to restart from a checkpoint.
-Addition of bottle caps to throw to distract enemies is a welcome addition.
Cons
-Since it was released for the playstation first it isn't terribly optimized for PC, you can't change the graphics much and controller can't be modified (although keyboard can).
-While things seem to be redesigned there are not too many new areas, however if you purchase Alf's Escape there are some great new areas to test yourself in.

This game will never die.  From 1999 to the present, this game has been at the heart of Esports throughout.  After Challenge Pro Mode Arena (CPMA) was released the competitive community divided.  Since then, the game's popularity has seen a steady decline.  Currently, there is only a small crowd of hardcore fans that still enjoy this game.
Around 2007-2008 a new iteration of this game came along as a free-to-play web version named QuakeLive.  Download QLPrism (standalone browser made specifically to run QuakeLive) to fully enjoy.  As a pro-subscriber in Quakelive you can spawn servers to run all kinds of fun gameplay from simple duels to team based games and now Quakelive even includes Race mode (Quake3 DeFRaG Mod).  Quakelive is constantly updated with new content (gametypes, maps, custom options) making it the most comprehensive Quake ever.
Quake 3 is one of the most enduring games in all of FPS history.  The gameplay is dynamic, engaging and unique.  If you are a fan of fast-paced, deathmatch style gameplay, Quake3/Quakelive is the ONLY game for you.  Takes years to master, takes seconds to become addicted.
Currently, there is some debate over whom the G.O.A.T. (Greatest Of All Time) of QuakeLive is.  The greatest contenders for the title include the two finalists of Dreamhack Winter 2013, the Belarussian "Cypher" or the American "Rapha."  Other names through the years include American "Zero4", the Swedish aim master "Toxjq", and the notorious Russian "Cooller".
In the end, I see the competition for this title always coming back to the two:  Cypher or Rapha!  After the latest Quakecon and Dreamhack tournaments in 2013 you can see why!!

A stunningly beautiful game with some of the best, most calming music I have heard in a game. The HUD is about as minimal as possible in a game, and the gameplay mechanics are very easy to grasp.
Ran into the issue of the abilities not displaying all the possibilities, which briefly got me stuck late-game. For a squishy fellow, Ori fights pretty well.
Had a blast with the abilities, and certainly enjoyed the climbing and Burst jumps. The world drew me in, and I desire to see more. I want to see more about the cultures, the environment, and Ori herself. Make a movie/series. :)
I was impressed with the world's design. The developers used the immediate foreground and the background to GREAT effect, making the world feel more open, rather than a sidescroller. But seeing the terrain displayed in such a way made me want to climb everything, and go anywhere in full 3D controls.
The one glaring issue I have witht he game would be the boss cinematic fights. While they were cleverly designed, the game does punish you for every mistake, and my wrist feels like hell because of it. It was easy to rack up near 100 deaths in the first and final boss fights as my hand locked up.
All-in-all, I would certainly recommend this game. Short and sweet, but challenging. I am baffled that the top three people on the leaderboard cleared the game in 2 hours with 100% complete and ZERO deaths. I need to go back and play it with a controller next to see how it compares tot he keyboard and mouse.

Hover Cubes has a genre that I would normally not consider my cup of tea, mainly because I'm not that much interested in action / sport related games and also happen to suffer from motion sickness.
The early access serves on first sight as very polished proof of concept, that lacks only a few things I could imagine on my wishlist. I found it a bit confusing in the beginning to learn the controls for example.
However, if you approach this game with a bunch of friends, Hover Cubes opens up a way more complex and tactical dimension beside scoring within a good time frame. As you probably saw, the cubes act as bridge elements that make the puzzles possible to begin with, however, other players can of course interfere with your strategies, which lead to a bunch of super fun cups, both from the players and spectators perspective.
The motion sickness element is something you should consider, however, I actually avoided it, by playing on very low graphics and doing breaks in between.
All in all, I feel very positive about the current outlook of this game. I voiced some concerns in this review (Mainly tutorial aspects and motion sickness), however, I doubt that the communication of gameplay elements can't be improved and given that this game is an early access title, it has established a solid foundation already.
I tried to keep this review as objective as possible, however, I enjoyed a free copy so you might want to consider that too.

This guide is made for people who are not sure if they should buy Evoland 2. I will give you the con's and pro's. For the people who cannot be arsed with a lot of reading, I have a TL:DR section on the bottom.
Con's
- Difficulty has a spike close to the end. I felt a sudden increase of difficulty and that might be a problem for casual players.
- In my entire playthrough of 20+ hours my game got stuck 3-4 times whilst my computer was fine.
Pro's
- Game takes 20+ hours to complete, if you are aiming 100% it will take you 25+ hours. A lot of content!
- Story rich, loved the entire story with ups, downs and plot twists. The ending was amazing and gives feels!
- The audio is amazing. The retro tunes give you a nolstalgic feeling to those legendary games back in the day.
- Graphics are very innovative. They change depending on the situation. It really gives more depth to the story.
- The controls were excellent. Played it with a xbox controller and I had no problems whatsoever.
- This game made me laugh a lot. Great humor and tributes to famous games/anime from way back.
- Genre? This game has a lot. The main genre is that of the legend of zelda. Puzzles, hacking and slashing, buying upgrades, leveling up, collecting items, etc. But the game also gives you a taste of other genres whilst playing through the story. Think of playstyles like: Megaman, Streetfighter, Bejeweled, Fire Emblem, Guitare Hero, Bomberman and the list goes on. You even have a card game in it :D
TL:DR
Evoland 2 is an indie game that is well worth 10 bucks. A lot of content, funny, great secrets and one hell of a story. Even though the game doesn't have the "overwhelmingly positive" review, I still think it deserves as much. If you are not sure if you should buy the game and liked the pro's... BUY IT! You will 100% not regret it. The devs did an amazing job and I cannot wait for Evoland 3!

The only RPG I completed before (besides Evoland I) has been Chrono Trigger, so this game, which has a time travel theme attached to it as well as a nostalgic melting pot of gameplay genres, interested me.
Some might find it too easy, but for a casual player like me, the difficulty level was mostly okay. I also found the story interesting, however I really got into the game once the characters went in a lab which reminded me the apocalyptic future of Chrono Trigger. Before that, I didn't have some reference such as Pac Man and found the game lacking the originality of Evoland I, with its basic features added one after the other.
If there is a thing I missed in the game, it's perhaps this "basic" humor which got me interested in the first of the series. Still, Evoland II is a good game standing on its own. Yes it is borrowing a lot (some seem to think too much) on cult videogames, but the story is less a patchwork than I feared and it flows nicely. There was also originality in the game (who thought Candy Crush could be a multiplayer game?). Besides, in art, everyone is inspired by their predecessors...

Evoland 2 is in fact a full fledged RPG. It's to Evoland what Portal 2 was to Portal. Evoland 2 takes the concept of playing through all the eras and genres of gaming from the first one and expands on it. It integrates the various genres/eras of gameplay seemlessly into the plot. It adds way more genres of gaming than the first.
As with Evoland, Evoland 2 pokes fun at itself and the games it derives from. There's also plently of references to classic shows and movies. Good 'Ol Arcade mode provides enough challenge that makes it difficult, but still fun to play. The time travel aspect is really well done as there is a lot of small details that you'll notice that either have changed or make sense once you play farther into the game. There's so much more depth to tin this game than one would expect.
All in all I put in about 33 hours in the game to 100% it. The story mode will run you about 22 hours if you don't care for all the items and mini games. Getting everything is a good experience and enhances the game, but not necessary. This game is more than worth the $20 it costs. There was no moment where I wasn't having fun, even in the frustratingly difficult moments.

Absolutley adore this game. Evoland had a good concept of showcasing the evolution of video games through the ages, but Evoland 2 took that concept then wrapped it up with a gripping plot, challenging puzzles, parody humour, better mechanics, and standards that would have made the original game a heap better (like a consistent health system). I find that I easily lose interest in games that keep you doing a lot of the same stuff. This is why Evoland 2 is such a godsend. Just when I was getting bored, I'd run into an event that would completely change the style of play (temporarily). There were so many different play styles and minigames: from turn-based, tactical RPG and real-time stratergy to pong, pacman, space invaders, 2D platforming, mortal kombat, and the ever precarious Game of Cards. Just to name a few notable ones... Not to mention the default, classic Zelda-esk play. Of course, it can have some drawbacks if there's a particular game you are poor at (for me, the 2D platformers were very agrovating -looking at you, Mt. Alpha- and I barely completed the guitar hero, the one where you have to keep ahead of the edge of the screen or you die, and the bullet hell sections by the skin of my teeth. That being said, I do feel more appreciative of the latter two now that I've had some practice).
The plot was good, although it didn't leave much space for theorising after the game - if you spoke to all of the NPCs and saw all of the cutscenes. I managed to piece the majority of it together pretty well by the end.
The graphics were spectacular in every time. Some of the puzzles were a bit easy. Some of the puzzles were a bit hard (the Sylph forest...)! The humour was just right. Music was nice, though I think that I may have had enough of it for now, having just listened to it for 34 hours... Mechanics were nice and easy to use.

First off I didn't play the .6 version that everyone loved so much. Apparently, this game is getting review-bombed by them. Those people like spawning in fully functioning 30 gun carriers out of their pockets AT ANY TIME instead of a realistic shipyard or base. They complain that they have to mine out large nuggets of ore from the dirt instead of different colored dirt... ...in the dirt. I don't even know why people are complaining about mining anyway. this is one of the few games that I have seen that makes mining easier and less grindy as you level up. You can literally build a vehicle and strap a bunch of drills on it to tear through the ground. Mining not your thing? Then just drop an auto miner down and come back later to pick up your ore. The recipes are changing, yes. They made it so that you have to choose whether to use expensive guns that use rare ores for ammo or stick with the conventional stuff that uses the cheap ammo. It seems the devs are trying to make it so that not everything becomes obsolete. They are also experimenting with the rolls of tanks vs ships vs carriers. The old guard is complaining because they have to change the way they play the game.
Anyway, the game is good but is buggy. The animations are garbage but for the most part, combate is acceptable. Hopefully one day we get more enemy types that do more than run right at you to pummel you to death or run right at you to shoot you to death. Some of the enemy types are strong for no reason (spiders of all types and shotgunners that Snipe you). Graphics are really good for a *voxel-based game*. How much fun you have is very much based on the scenario that you're in. I had a lot of fun in the new singleplayer scenarios but in a lot of "custom" multiplayer scenarios, they seemed to not have utilized a lot of the new space-based stuff that has been coming out.
PVP is well, not great. large ships create a lot of lag and there are a LOT of exploits right now. They need to add some sort of shield system to limit the effectiveness of Death Cube designs. There needs to also be some sort of detection if your engines are enclosed and hidden to stop people from unrealistically hiding them.
This game has a lot of potential. If you don't get it then at least keep your eye on it because it can only get better.

Pros:
Visceral combat system with two popular PvP modes (capture point, team deathmatch) emphasizing teamplay. A blast to play with friends, if a bit anemic to play alone. Still active enough to have games running most of the time. Armor customization is detailed, even if the colors do not provide the large RGB spectrum like Dawn of War. But the amount of armor pieces, patterns and color combinations means that you will be hard pressed to create the same thing as another player unless you do it on purpose. Though not free of flaws, many of the early ones have long since been ironed out.
Cons:
A play-once campaign, with no supporting DLC to keep you going back, trains new players the wrong way for PvP. Anemic DLC adds very little to the game other than a small spattering of maps, unplayed modes, and an expensive lineup of unique armor that cannot be completely picked apart for custom outfits. P2P connectivity provides the constant, irritating spectre of lag and host switching. The graphics were already pushing middle-aged when it came out, but the animation and design made up for that. Nowadays, you'll either not mind or it'll drive you bonkers.
The game's been out long enough that it has some fairly entrenched players that can be an overwhelming challenge to newcomers. And with obsessive veterans comes the abusive verbal treatment seen in many communities that have been destroyed by it.
Other thoughts:
People disagree on the weapon balance. I've used them all, and I think each one is fine, with distinct strengths and weaknesses. The exception being the axe, which is neither as fast as the sword nor as strong as the hammer, striking a balanced surpassed in utility by both alternatives.
The community itself is hit-and-miss. While most of the players are amiable, there are a few grudge-bearing sour grape obsessives who will spend hours striving to verbally troll you out of an enjoyable evening. Like in most other online games. But since there isn't really any community control, simply block or don't respond.
The game does have cheaters, but they are very rarely encountered. If it isn't something lag-borne like being shot through a wall, and is instead obvious like plasma cannon teleporting to high ledges to release charged shots, then teleporting back to safety, then you'll know for sure.
And since this game now has defunct support, there is very little chance we'll see any more content for it, or even a sequel.

While not as good as To the Moon, this game still manages to be its worthy successor. It wasn't quite that emotionally devastating and impactful (I'll explain why later in the spoiler section), but on the other hand it has improved quite a bit in its presentation. The character animations, for example, are great, plentiful and surprisingly detailed. You can tell that the success of To the Moon allowed the devs to spend more resources on them. With To the Moon, it felt like it was made in the simplistic ways of RPG maker out of necessity. This time around, it feels more like a deliberate artistic choice. The music is beautiful as well.
Still, I'd definitely rank To the Moon above Finding Paradise and here is why:
It could be that that was the very intention. After all, most important life decisions aren't really that dramatic. They too just kind of happen, often without us realising it. And I really get that Kan Gao wanted to say something different with this game, something else than "just" another great tragedy, so I don't wanna be too critical about it, because I very much enjoyed it. However, it did left me feeling little bit lackluster in the end so there's that.
To the Moon was 10/10 for me, Finding Paradise is more like 8/10. If you haven't done so yet, go play them both (and A Bird Story). You won't regret it!

Blackguards is a RPG with a decent number of dialogue choices. The story has its ups and downs and early it is a bit confusing because they throw alot of unknown terms at you and and most of them you will only learn halfway through the game. And the end is kinda lackluster in my opinion.
The combat is turn based and the battles are mostly diversed since some can have puzzle elemnts others can have a few stages and so on. And your choices along the game influences some of the battles you have.
One of the biggest problem in the game is the amount of stats and character builds you can do makes the game way to difficult and players that dont understand how the game works in that regards can completely screw their games and be forced to start from scratch. The game does a really poor job of explaining how the overall stats work and the only way to learn about them is looking at help menu and read it or go to the manual.
On the positive side when you learn to make a proper build your mid-late game characters can have quite impressive abilities and power, the high level spell effects are rather impressive.
Also it is worth mentioning some of the achievements don't work properly or don't work at all.
Overall I liked the game however the high learning curve that can really punish you is something that only some people can tolerate. And the game only really offers a couple of playthroughs in terms of story and in regards to builds I dont think that people will play purely on the interest of seeing builds with diferent weapons, the spells are nice but they will not make the players play the game again just to see their high level form.

Stumbling upon the store page for Oddworld: New ‘n’ Tasty, I bought the game upon a whim. I’d remembered an “odd” series of Playstation platformers and thought to myself, another day, another HD remaster. Anyone could be forgiven for thinking that. For all their care and attention, games are at risk of repeating themselves to an audience whose familiarity with the very subject is the game’s own greatest weakness. It’s a wonderful thing, to see a game rendered so beautifully, and there are many HD remasters which have proven successful and proven that they provide an experience that is richer, deeper, and more satisfying than the original. But dragging the gameplay of yesteryear into the high definition of today begs the question – is that how we used to play? Are games really that different?
Oddworld has always been an outlier. Originally developed for PlayStation, Oddworld was both a revelation for its story, GameSpeak and its charming mix of beautiful CG and challenging 2D puzzle-platforming, but how it kept to a gameplay model which had been quickly discarded to create dazzling 3D worlds for gamers to run around in. A year since Super Mario 64 and the well of 2D platformers had just about dried up. Games were easier, and gamers demanded more stunning environments than ever before. The world of Oddworld is a mirror to our own; a satire on capitalism, environmentalism and the natural order. Driven by this theme and not the technology as so many other games were made it a far cry from its competition and a risky proposition for any publisher. If anything, its message, if it indeed has one, is all the more relevant than ever before.
Which brings us to the game we stand before today. New ‘n’ Tasty is a ground up recreation of Abe’s Oddysee, and like the very best of remakes, it changes and challenges what you know from the original game while giving you a new experience. Everything is new, from the character models, backgrounds and cinematics, nothing has been re-used from the original game. New ‘n’ Tasty is the rare treat in that the developers have used new tech to recreate and enhance the experience. Gone are the flip-screen backgrounds, they now scroll, and this is a major feature that adds greatly to the gameplay.
The story starts with Abe, a lowly slave toiling away in “the biggest meat-processing plant on Oddworld”, Rupture Farms. Stumbling upon the organisations plans to literally turn him and his fellow slaves into the next product, he decides to break free, and along the way, saves fellow workers and discovers his destiny. As a feeble and everyman character, Abe is unique in that he has no real powers, doesn’t wield weapons and uses the GameSpeak system in order to help his fellow slaves to safety.
As a creature, Abe is difficult to love. His very alien look fits well within the game, and he is emotive with large eyes and powerful body language, but it is the GameSpeak system that requires you to talk to fellow slaves, or possess enemies in order to progress that provides the most satisfaction. The storyline breeds hope that the Mudokons are not a forsaken race and that Abe is the “chosen one” that will lead them all back to their natural roots. The mudokons fit in well with a cast of characters each as bizarre and unique as the last, with paramites and scarabs trying to eat you while enemy sligs and their ravenous slogs are out to kill you. The gameworld is a brutal one for a powerless mudokon, but with GameSpeak, the power is literally in your hands to rise above.
Challenging as it may be, the gameplay isn’t too difficult and most gamers should only find the rare frustration. The addition of checkpoints, and a quick save gives you more of a safety net than you probably truly need, and there is a good variety of difficulty settings. The difficulty curve ramps up hard towards the middle of the game, and gets quite difficult towards the end, but the challenge is mitigated with the satisfaction of success.
And even two decades on, the levels and gameplay remains surprisingly engrossing and just as riveting. Abe’s travels through the bowels of Rupture Farms, the harsh security of the outer walls and into the natural wilderness from which the Mudokon belong is still a compelling journey. Deadly puzzles await you from various meat grinders to vigilant security guards, mines and perilous drops, and death always seems moments away. New ‘n’ Tasty remains a testament to the solid design of the original, and it has been recreated in excellent detail.
Still, not everything old is new again, and some minor details have been trimmed to make a more cohesive package. Even so, New ‘n’ Tasty is a relatively lengthy challenge, it took me around 8 hours to complete, and upon completion I had only saved about 60% of the 300 Mudokons, with many remaining hidden.
Overall, New n Tasty is a testament to how a remake should be done. It enhances the original game while also sticking to what works. New ‘n’ Tasty remains a honest-to-goodness platform puzzler with a story to tell and a world to embrace, and remains something unique in a world of “me-too” gaming. Well worth picking up.

This game is pure beauty. Every aspect of it.
The artwork is incredible. Just look at the screenshots.
The soundtrack is simply brilliant, the sort you can listen to for hours.
The story can bring a tear to the eye in the first ten minutes.
If you don't think games can be art, Ori and the Blind Forest is my rebuttal.
Moving swiftly from aesthetics to gameplay, the game is difficult. VERY difficult. It starts out simple enough, but soon teaches you that any mistake can be your last, with a vast amount of enemies who will not hesitate to crush, shoot, spike, ram, and generally injure you in any way they can. Still, despite the diversity in the opponent's ranks, Ori is far from helpless. With the help of a little ball of light named "Sein", Ori can shoot enemies, charge for a powerful explosive blast, leap from wall to wall, and through enemies, even redirect the opponents attacks them!
as you progress through the game, you will increase your health, your energy pool, and can spend ability points to make yourself stronger. You can make your attacks hit multiple targets, shoot faster, deal more damage, that sort of thing. You can make health and experience orbs fly toward you (TAKE THAT. The game feels very quick-paced, and the movement feels very fluid, and natural, making for an exiting, very enjoyable gaming experience.
If I had one complaint, it would probably be the controls for the "bash" ability. I find that it can sometimes be a little awkward to aim, often sending me in the wrong direction, that said, I can be rather clumsy, and I am new to the game, so I am fairly certain I will get the hang of it with time.
Anyway, drawing this review to a conclusion, this game is a visual masterpiece, has an amazing soundtrack, and is a game I would recomend it to anyone, so long as you don't mind a challenge.

I usualy dont write reviews... I'm not even sure if i ever did ^.^ but I've been reading through the existing reviews and wanna offer my own opinion:
First of all I just wanna adress some of the negative reviews. While I could see alot of reasonable and correct arguments, as usual there is once again that big group of people, not understanding how EA works and people like that simply gotta stop writing any reviews at all x) Yes, there are alot of bugs right now. Yes, it often is quite laggy which can affect pvp combat and yes, there is some lack of endgame content, which basicly is completely oriented on PvP. Yet as already said, those are the same arguments people bring up while talking about an EA game. Those issues will be resolved the closer we get to the games release. Of course as an EA game it can fail before it even gets released but we are not pesimistic are we? Oh, you are? Then u might aswell get out now! Just kidding :P There is always a risk but so far the devs hold on tight to their project.
Lets get to the positive aspects of GV. The developers tried to build a realistic envirement and the game has a very special atmosphere. There is a spark of fantasy here and there but enemies like a spectre or giants limit themselves to be special bosses or part of an event. Most things you will encounter are either humans or animals, be it a dirty little thief which you encounter in the beginning or a leader of an entire army which requires a big group just to reach his position.
The combat system is still very clunky yet much more interesting to me than the average mmorpg. Its moves, blocks and kicks to break an enemies guard remind strongly of games like chivalry or mount & blade (can't say that for sure, didnt play it, just seen videos). Also at the time of me writing this review there is a highly anticipated update in its polishing phase which is expected to solve that clunkyness and other issues regarding combat and put a real flow into your battles.
PvE at this point offers a decent amount of different enemies. Drops can be quite rewarding, as even a little henchman has a good chance to drop a weapon or a piece of armor that is actualy worth wearing. Keep your eyes open for chests and crates in bigger camps or near special enemies, as they can hold good crafting materials and occasionaly some pretty decent gear. You don't have to wait until you reach max lvl (100) to encounter bosses which of course usualy yield a better reward than their minions. Of course once you reach a higher lvl you can take on bigger bosses which will can drop high end gear or even the much more desired recipe's to craft high end gear yourself.
PvP is a huge part in this game. Basicly the whole endgame at this point as soon as you reached max lvl and stocked up on high end gear and found all the crafting recipes you are interested in. Fight for your nation to take over outposts and even castles. Holding those will benefit all of your brothers! During peak time there is a good amount of people attacking and defending said settlements. Trying to tear down gates or walls, burning farms or on the other side positioning a solid shield wall on the frontline while the back rows and archers on the wall put pressure on the attackers. But dont be reckless! if you die enemies players have a chance to steal some of your items for a short period of time.Not everything, dont worry, but maybe 2-3 of your most precious possesions. Then again... you can do the same ;)
In addition, there are the "valley of death" tournaments where the two nations fight it out on an arena like map followed by a PvP focused open world event. Both the tournament and the following event dont allow players to be looted so... just go full berserk if you want to! :P
The crafting system is quite deep and time consuming. Other than in most mmorpgs, you have to do every step to the finished product yourself. You dont just take a steel bar and turn it magicly into a sword. You gotta put work into it! I personaly love it, others hate it. Simply a matter of opinion. Make sure to use the correct kind of work station to ensure the best possible product.
One thing about the developers. I'm not one of those guys who watch over their shoulder but my experience so far is, while they might not be the most experienced developers, those guys put hard work and their hearts into this project. They listen to their community and try to solve issues that concern us while pushing the game further and further and that is something I rarely encountered and admire!
So, if you understand what early acces games are and the risks and problems they bring with them I can definitly recommend you Gloria Victis!

I've been following GV for awhile now - waiting for the right moment to jump in and try it. With the recent sale and the upcoming animation update I decided it was time. So far this has proved to be a very good decision.
GV has its problems. Worst is occasional de-synch. One time the enemy retreated through the gate and closed it and even though I did not follow on my screen they killed me on the other side.  Falling through stairs can make getting to the capture flag in towers tricky. In combat there are times when what you see does not match the result - no damage when you seemed to hit someone being the most common.  Also pings are higher than I would expect.
That said combat works. Fighting the AI is often fun due to the Mount and Blade style skill based combat. If you fight badly versus multiple npc's you can get you♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked whereas if you do a good job the same fight can be an easy win. Combat versus players is really fun. Player skill is huge. Staying focused is crucial and good tactics make a huge difference in fights. You can win outnumbered 2 to 1 with lower level character just by being cautious, using the fortifications and npc's, and picking your moments to be aggressive.
GV has a huge edge over many other pvp game because it provides combat environments which work with a wide variety of numbers matchup's. Outnumbered 3 to 1 - fight defensively using fortifications and/or npc's to strengthen your position and provide opportunities for your enemy to over reach and leave themselves vulnerable. Outnumber your opponent - go on the offensive and attempt to take locations while they use the defences to try and counter you.
Most MMO's separate the player base out over a huge power curve. In GV a low level character with decent gear can kill a level 100 character with some smarts or luck. This helps the game bring players together for entertaining pvp rather than separating them out the way most MMO's do.
A huge part of why the pvp works so well is that the game encourages you into conflict from very early on in your experience. Castle and village combats see messages sent out to everyone to let them know a fight is happening and there is generally time to get involved if you want to. A constant stream of world events draw the two sides together into conflict over locations. Due to the nature of the objectives being fought over wildly uneven forces can engage in pvp using npc's and fortification to balance the conflict.
You can join GV and get into pvp in your first few days. Unlike other games you won't feel massively underpowered so long as you can fight smart.
The crafting system is very detailed and a bit overwhelming at the start. That said it is very rewarding when you get to the point of being able to make your own pvp gear so that losing a your armour/weapon in pvp is no longer such a problem. The relationship between crafting and pvp, more places you control the bigger bonus to crafting, draws you into the pvp game and doesn't let you settle easily into being a pvp adverse carebear -something many other games encourage you into early.
So far it is a very promising game and has the potential to be one of the best pvp MMO's ever. Let's hope the new animations patch sorts out a lot of the problems.

Honestly, a good Rogue-like should not be 90% luck. You can be the greatest tactician of all time, but some games will just refuse to give you anything to work with; all of your gaming skills mean nothing when what little food you get is rotten, you can not craft that antidote for the eternal poison, and the game thinks that kitchen knife from the third room is the only weapon you will ever need or should have access to.
Skyhill is pretty much one of those Rogue-likes. The playtime is entirely dependent upon how far the game feels like letting you go. Stats give such pathetic bonuses that leveling up feels pointless once you're accurate enough to reliably hit enemies ("Yay! I got .2% extra dodge chance and plus .8 damage on my stick!"), and you will constantly be relying on the RNG to not give you impossible requirements for fixing elevator panels ("Oh yeah, five floors down and I definitely built a generator with all the supplies I don't have, game.") so you can make those frequent trips back to your apartment to craft everything that requires you to be there or to heal up after one enemy crits three times in a single battle. Eventually, a merciful roll of the dice will just give you an easy but slow grind straight to the first floor via handing out plenty of medkits or crafting supplies.
Story? After the very first newspaper clipping, I called the easy "twist ending" that you can get, and I'm certain any other player who has read a few books or seen anything shoveled out of Hollywood in the past ten years will predict it as well. The other potential story lines are not really stories at all due to having so little content within them.
I bought the game on sale and I still feel like I wasted my money. Once you've had a successful run to the end, there is probably not going to be much drive to do it again unless you love speedrunning luck-based games or just want to waste time with a mouse-only game.

And there's multiple endings too, if you're engaged enough to want to look for them. All in all, if the trailer interested you, go for it.

Warning: This review is full of spoilers from someone who did not get spoilers ahead of time to know better.
If you're going to get this game, get it on sale. It's not that the game is bad, but that it simply too minimalistic, and I'm not talking about the art style--which is one of it's main good features. There's simply not that much to the game itself. It's a point and click roguelike game that admittedly tries but fails to achieve the basic aspects necessary regarding those two styles to make it worthwhile here. With the only options being to go down the stairs or to one of the two optional side rooms to ransack or kill the monster then ransack, it's too tedious to be enjoyable as a roguelike.
A point and click game needs strategy, which the option of where to hit monsters and what item you're going to smack them around with simply doesn't offer. But above all, it must have a good narrative. And that's what we're missing here, which is also quite possibly my biggest issue with the game, which is why it confused the hell out of me as to how this game got an award for it.
Spoiler alert: The initial narrative here is that you're stuck at the top of a building when nuclear war hits and the monsters start crawling out of the woodwork. You as the protagonist have to work your way to the ground floor while crafting tools to bludgeon things with or to fix the broken elevators/lights which inexplicably stopped working for all but the top five floors, and to cook up food because apparently you're an anemic who can't go from one room to another without suffering hunger pains for it. Not a bad premise in and of itself, but the execution is poorly handled.
The story can branch off in three different ways, but all are jumbled together in the course of the playthorugh that they contradict one another, and none actually contribute to the gameplay. From this, you get three potential endings, all of which are depressing and none of which are in any way original twists to include when they're all a few years past "done to death". The "twist endings" become pretty obvious early on depending on where you find the randomly generated plot-specific items that relate to them, and ultimatley lead to a slow, drawn out crawl through the samey, boring, tedious levels making up the rest of the building before you finally receive the ultimately unsatisfying confirmation of them.
Ending one: You're crazy.
Ending two: You're crazy and you murdered a bunch of innocent people along the way. You monster.
Ending three: You're trapped in a computer simulation a la The Matrix but without the graphics or Keanu Reeves powers to make it worthwhile.
So in no version of the storyline is anything you're experiencing real even in the context of the game itself. It should say something when even the game is showing how pointless it is to play it. Even worse, all of these endings are detached from the initial narrative and disjointed from the gameplay itself. What about all the little background hints that suggest there is more going on than what is in this man's head? Nope, all equally pointless and of no real value to the game or story within it because even in the game, none of it matters.
If I have to give the game credit for anything, it's the art style and the initial concept. I certainly liked the crafting system which was a main reason I was drawn to the game, though the random luck of what items I could find in a single playthrough to even try to make anything worthwhile made it more annoying than anything. Some of the earnable perks weren't worth it, though they could add an extra sort of challenge to the game even if it does nothing to really enhance the gameplay itself.
Ultimately at this point, I have to say I don't recommend getting the game for full price. It was fun at first, but quickly became tedious and lacks replay value that would actually have me WANTING to play rather than feeling obligated to do so just to get two other comic-style pages showing potential "what if" scenarios that still leave me feeling just as confused and unsatisfied as the first.

The first video advertising Skyhill on the Steam store page makes it seem a lot more fun than it actually is.  I expected a game that would make me think more about the choices I had to make to survive.  I expected more dynamic gameplay (especially from a roguelike).  I expected more replay value (especially from a roguelike).
In reality:
* The gameplay is repetitive.
* In most cases, the decisions you make are obvious.
* The fact that it's a roguelike does not make one playthrough that much different than another playthrough, which means ...
* The replay value is next to nil.
I guess the one positive thing about the game is that the crafting is kind of interesting.  However, you can only perform most of the crafting on the top floor, and, at some point, you're likely to be low enough on food and far enough from a working elevator that the cost of making your way to the top floor simply isn't worth it anymore, meaning better weapons, parts used to restore power to floors, etc. are not craftable for the rest of the playthrough.
2/10.

Very fun game, with a great storyline, takes everything good about Arkham Asylum & builds on it.
The open world is well designed & is used to serve the story well.
There are more side missions & they mostly focus on Batman being a detective, instead of just scanning collectables like in Asylum.
I thought the Clayface animations were great, like watching the T1000 turn into liquid metal for the first time in Terminator 2, the Clayface tranformations were actually cooler than my imagination.
Catwoman as a playable character is most excellent. The devs did The Cat right with great animations & moves that fit the character perfectly. For example, in at least one of her counter animations, between grabbing the guy's arm & throwing him to the ground, she slips him a kiss on the lips  -- totally something Catwoman would do! And the "beatdown" combo is actually more fitting for Catwoman than for Batman.
Arkham City has more world-building details put into it (beyond the unlockable background stories). There are lots of little easter-egg-esque details put into the locations that add richer realism the small section of Gotham you get to play in. And there is foreshadowing in an exchange with an inmate at the beginning that you will only recognize on a second playthrough, & only if you've completed a certain side mission. (Spoiler: 1st play "Bruce Wayne, you're on my list. Bang!" LOL that guy looks like Adam Baldwin. Wayne meets Jayne, haha. 2nd play "Bruce Wayne, you're on my list. Bang!" Lol It's the guy who looks like Jayne agai-- OMG! That's Floyd Lawton!)
Some of the "inmate conversions" are pretty entertaining, especially the guys trying to play rock, paper, scissors with three people ("Gun beats paper!" "No, no! Stick to the rules!" *guy does a thumb up gesture* "What the hell is that?" "Dynamite!" "No dynamite either!") & the goons guarding the church ("You think the rumor is true?" "That Harley used to be a dude?" "What? No! I meant that Joker is dying!" "Joker's dying?").
The Harley's Revenge sequel story is fun, & ties up the end of the main story nicely.
I do have some negative observations:
The combat controls can be a bit sluggish sometimes, especially when trying to use the "special combo moves", & large battles tend to devolve into button mashing & spamming gadgets to get through rather than being the skilful system the devs were obviously going for. Arkham Asylum also had this problem, & it holds the combat back from its full potential.
Talia al Ghul is very...um... "plain looking". She's supposed to be very beautiful & alluring (and in the comics she is), but [in the game] she isn't even pretty, heck even the female paramedics you rescue from Riddler are better looking than Talia. Her father is a psychotic madman & she's a manipulative witch with an abysmal personality, the only thing she has going for her is her looks...and not even that much in this game.
What the hell does Bats see in this woman? He'd be better off with Catwoman!
And speaking of the Cat...
The Catwoman story is thin, Selina could have had more missions & more interesting missions. The timing of the Cat "episodes" is a bit off... one ends seemingly mid-conversation, with Cat tied up by Poison Ivy. After a lengthy bit of Batman & the main story, after we've almost completely forgotten Cat's storyline, we get the next Cat episode which finishes her convo with Ivy... are we supposed to think that Cat was just hanging upside down for x hours?
The Nightwing content is... non-content... very disappointing. Nightwing isn't available to play in any story missions, only the challenge maps, and he isn't even voiced; he doesn't even get a clever quip for the challenge map intros. The "default" character model has a god-awful "emo" hair style...it makes me want to beat Nightwing senseless myself. There is only one alternate skin, the Animated series version, which is better than the default emo-hair version, but they could have at least included George Perez's original custume design, which would've actually made Nightwing tolerable to look at. When playing as Nightwing, his "detective mode" has a "radar circle" animation going around in the corner; it indicates nothing, it's just an annoying visual distraction. There is no reason to even bother playing Nightwing, except to get his medals for 100% completion, which is not worth it, IMO.
Robin at least gets voiced & gets some nice story missions In Harley's Revenge, but like with Nightwing, the character design is a mistake. The default is the stupid "Damian Wayne" hooded costume, even though Robin is supposed to be Tim Drake, & the alternate skin is the Richard* Grayson animated version, even though Robin is supposed to be Tim Drake, and the other alternate skin is the stupid "Red Robin" costume. Whaaaat? How about the mid 00's Tim Drake costume?
(* lol D!ck gets censored...it's original meaning is only a nickname for Richard (Richard -> Rick -> D!ck) not a swear word people, really)
The second set of "AR" missions is annoying & pointless, at least the first set of "AR" missions gets you a nice upgrade, but the second set gives you no rewards & isn't worth the frustration of completing.
Just like with Asylum, getting 100% is a pain & not really worth it.
All in all, however, the negatives are only minor imperfections & don't really hinder the enjoyment of the game.

Absolutley adore this game. Evoland had a good concept of showcasing the evolution of video games through the ages, but Evoland 2 took that concept then wrapped it up with a gripping plot, challenging puzzles, parody humour, better mechanics, and standards that would have made the original game a heap better (like a consistent health system). I find that I easily lose interest in games that keep you doing a lot of the same stuff. This is why Evoland 2 is such a godsend. Just when I was getting bored, I'd run into an event that would completely change the style of play (temporarily). There were so many different play styles and minigames: from turn-based, tactical RPG and real-time stratergy to pong, pacman, space invaders, 2D platforming, mortal kombat, and the ever precarious Game of Cards. Just to name a few notable ones... Not to mention the default, classic Zelda-esk play. Of course, it can have some drawbacks if there's a particular game you are poor at (for me, the 2D platformers were very agrovating -looking at you, Mt. Alpha- and I barely completed the guitar hero, the one where you have to keep ahead of the edge of the screen or you die, and the bullet hell sections by the skin of my teeth. That being said, I do feel more appreciative of the latter two now that I've had some practice).
The plot was good, although it didn't leave much space for theorising after the game - if you spoke to all of the NPCs and saw all of the cutscenes. I managed to piece the majority of it together pretty well by the end.
The graphics were spectacular in every time. Some of the puzzles were a bit easy. Some of the puzzles were a bit hard (the Sylph forest...)! The humour was just right. Music was nice, though I think that I may have had enough of it for now, having just listened to it for 34 hours... Mechanics were nice and easy to use.

Perfect sequel. The main dislike I had of Evoland 1 is that it was too short--5-6 hours of excellence that was over too soon. This game takes around 25-30 hours to 100% casually (5x longer). This game contains a much greater mix of genres and game references than Evoland 1. Where Evoland 1 had you picking up chests to "upgrade the game" and give you better graphics, music, etc., Evoland 2 changes graphics based on the "time period" you're in which is a nice touch. I won't spoil the plot for you--it's "more like a big ball of wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey ... stuff." You'll have fun, and you'll enjoy the many references.
One of the really great things that I hope they're sticking with moving forward is that where Evoland 1 was inconsistent and your stats didn't travel from the switches between turn-based and action-based, in Evoland 2 your stats carry between every genre, and leveling up and getting better equipment makes each genre you're playing in easier. There's an awesome persistence to it. Also, most of the genres seem to come with an easy-to-find and follow "cheese strategy" if you're having difficulty beating it.
Lastly, this is one of the few RPGs I'm aware of where you can't actually miss anything permanently. You can always go back and get it (some things you'll have to wait longer for than others). One more cherry atop this excellent game.

My opinion of Empyrion so far is that it's a pretty good game. It's not easy, there's a steep learning curve of commands, figuring out mechanics, asking tons of questions in the community, finding a multiplayer server with a decent server size, watching the occassional youtube video, and so on. There's lots of learning and grinding to do, so if you like those things - a creative/survival game with a space/sci-fi theme, you'll probably like this game a lot.
More polished in my opinion than games like Interstellar Rift, right now, but it shares a number of similarities, except that while ISR is entirely space based, you get to roam the planet and set up bases and enjoy that sort of thing on a planetary level. I found nothing so far that beats the enjoyment of flinging yourself around the planet riding a Hover Vehicle (HV). They can take so much abuse and are multi  functional. They're only usable on planets, but they are great for covering distances, combat, and mining. Space Vehicles (SV) are good for going to space, warping to different solar systems, and combat. And CVs are good for warping to different solar systems farther than 15 AU (longer range than SV), as well as transporting SVs and HVs with you.
I've quite enjoyed playing the game so far, learning about it's ups and what it could improve on. One thing I think it could improve on is if you could add the CV mining drill to the ship's hotbar and access it that way. Instead right now, you have to access the CV's control panel "p", select the "devices" tab, scroll down to the mining laser and "Access" it.
The blueprint system reminds me in a lot of ways of Ark with unlock levels and a points based spending system. Points of Interests (POIs) can be looted, destroyed, taken over (if you destroy the "core" block in the base, you can even deconstruct the whole thing and get all the materials from that. The POIs on the multiplayer server I play on (shout out to HWS NA
, if you want to join me on that server), respawn every 3 hours, or so. So even if you take down a POI, it's not gone forever.
I hope you decide to give the game a shot, and maybe I'll get to see you on HWS!

EGS is an ok game. The idea is good and for the most part is present in the game. However, the animations are absolutely horrendous and at times... laughable. I understand the game is in Alpha and fully expect them to improve, but at this moment in time they are just trash. This includes player and NPCs.
The planets are coming along nicely in terms of visuals but they still feel a small. Do not expect Space Engineers sized planets.
Sound design within EGS is what I would call barely functional. From the badly looped and clipping engine sounds to the player effects. The whole sound design needs to be redone ASAP as it really lets the game down.
NPCs of every type in this game look like asset flips bought from some 3D model store. There seems to be no flow with the art style when it comes to them (meaning it looks like they have been purchased from many different artists as cheaply as possible). This may not be the case, but if they are created in-house then this problem is worse.
Flight mechanics are simple and minimal. Your ships have no weight to them in the feel of flight. You can turn on dime in a huge capitals. Fighter flight is just as bad. It just feels that any ship you fly acts like it's on ice!
I love the idea of the game and the Devs are really getting the game in a good state. Gameplay is ok and exploring is fun. It's just clunky and a bit grindy. You spend 40% of your time in inventory/crafting menus.
This game is in Alpha and as I said, I expect the game to get a lot better and even in its current state, there is fun to be had. It's the aesthetics of the games so far that let it down by a big margin.

A fun, creative, and exciting game. Immerses the player in a cellular world where you struggle for dominance of the cellular pool.
I loved playing it and loved the feeling of crushing my enemies when I have a large number of cells to control.
There are 3 bugs that annoy me somewhat:
1. When you have a large number of cells, it sometimes happens that one of the cells just decides to wander off and no matter what you do, you cannot control it. It simply wanders off into enemy territory getting itself killed.
2. This also occurs when the game has progressed a bit. When there are loads of anti-bodies on the map, the commands have a massive lag when interacting with them. They sometimes respond in 6 - 8 seconds after you have already given a command. This makes micro a horror.
3. The antibodies sometimes go smoothly around corners in the map and other times they get stuck in the terrain rendering them pretty much useless.
I am mentioning these bugs to drive at a point. The game is small and is not a technical masterpiece. What I mean by that is that you don't need to be a master RTS gamer to play this game. There are simple mechanics and the game is made to have fun, not to be extremely competitive.
That being said, I really enjoy playing this game. I feel that it would be a pleasure to complete it and at the end I would definitely recommend it to others.
A passable phone app, maybe. It is pretty, at the very least.

*I am not a professional review writer. I just love video games, and here is my opinion.*
First of all, do not play this unless you have played To the Moon and A Bird Story. If you do not, some of the dialogue and plot will not make sense.
I absolutely adore To the Moon. A Bird Story and the minisodes were also lovely. I found Finding Paradise inferior to these. Yes, the soundtrack is gorgeous, the art is beautiful, the dialogue is engaging and comical, and the story has some heartfelt life lessons.
However, the plot did not affect me at all. I absolutely bawled throughout To the Moon, but I did not cry once during Finding Paradise. I could not relate to the main character. The plot twist made me think, "...Really? Are you serious? An old man with ...... That's just weird."
By the end of the game, I absolutely hated the puzzles when activating momentos. They became more complex and tedious, thereby ruining the player's immersion in the plot. The puzzles in Finding Paradise felt like road blocks, whereas in To the Moon, the puzzles were simple and felt more connected to the story.
(Also, the game ran very poorly in regards to lagging. That might have been an issue with my own computer, but it was quite annoying and nauseating. It especially became a problem during the combat sequences which were clever but completely frustrating and out-of-place.)
Overall, the soundtrack, art, and dialogue was beautiful. When the story finally came to a meaningful moment, I did not even pay attention because I was so enraged by the immersion-breaking puzzles and combat.
However, I will always recommend To the Moon and support the developers because it is a masterpiece. Unfortunately, it is nearly impossible to make a sequel on par with a masterpiece.

Great graphics and framerate, cross platform support (albeit so-so but playable  performance on LInux; tested on a 550-Ti; I blame Unity.) Although it is a very good remake, I felt that the game is not as "solid" as the original, rather than making a good/bad list let's just compare the game to the originals thoroughly.
Original: 10 hours (saving almost all the 100 mudokons)
New 'n' Tasty: 8 hours (saving 159(52%) of the 300 mudokons; but it wasn't long since I finished the original again)
Expect roughly 10 hours on your first run if you've never played the original, 8 hours if you recently did. You will want to play this game with a controller, if you didn't know. Any PS style or Xbox style controller should be fine. (Or maybe the steam controller?)
-
The atmosphere is lighter than in the original Oddysee (think back to the atmosphere of Exoddus; it's more like the atmosphere in that game) besides the more brightly lit, warmer colored environments, the voice acting played a big role in this, the voice actors were trying to make comical voices whereas in the originals everyone sounded more depressed, especially the protagonist. As a fan of the originals I did not like the new slig voices, that's what stood out to me the most. As for the mudokons, most of them sounded the part. I hear that for teh lulz they had different voice actors for most of the mudokons in the game. For someone who never played the original (or played it ages ago) this may not really matter, but a lot of the original fans liked the game for the dark atmosphere.
-
Chase camera (instead of stage camera) this was a sort of "get with the times" featuer, but the stage camera was a very important element in a lot of the puzzles but most noticably what bothered me I will mention next.
-
Sligs can no longer outrun your chant, i.e. when you would try to possess sligs in the original games, sometimes they would run outside of the stage you were positioned in to escape your chant, in this game the equivalent would have been to run outside of your field of view, but sligs are unable to do that (and this sometimes looks incredibly awkward) the up (or down) side of this is that it makes the game significantly easier at some parts.
-
Sligs don't instantly drop dead when shot anymore (slogs luckily still do though) this was all for a feature so that you could keep shooting them until they explode. They designed the levels so it wouldn't pose a problem (at most you're shooting 3 sligs at a time) but in Exoddus where there's more of them, this would be a bit bothersome for sure.
-
Some puzzles were changed or removed, new ones were also added here and there. Unless you knew the original like the back of your hand you will rarely notice this.
-
Health system; since there is now health in the game you can survive some fall damage and shots from sligs this time around (it's an easier game) however there is a hard mode which brings this closer to the original, but I noticed one major flaw in this hard mode which is thatin the original, your health (which only affected bats and bees and similar minor threats) would regenerate to full in a couple of seconds after you have not been taking any damage (or transition between stages) and of course when you die. There was no visible health, it was just a "how many hits you can take from this thing before dying" sort of thing. For players that didn't play the original, play on normal and everything will be goody goody,  But for others you will probably only notice this annoyance if you play on hard when you are in the paramonian temple where you need to jump between some swinging rocks and bats will attack you once you make the jump (I was stuck for a long time) I'm gonna report this as a bug though, so hopefully they will change it.
-
Controls are rather different now and there is no "legacy mode" for the controls as is. By default now your character will run instead of walk (unless you use an analogue stick to walk) this I didn't like at all, but luckily there was an option in the menus called "button to run". Similarly the jumping button in the originals would jump forward, in this game it jumps straight up unless you are running forward. There was also an option to fix this called "sideways hop" which brings us very close to the legacy control scheme with the exception of (of course) the speech which is now bound to the D-Pad insteaad of a complex mix of shoulder and main buttons, this I considered a non-issue though. My biggest complaint after setting the options right was that running was set to the lower left shoulder which on xbox style controllers is a trigger button, triggers are a pain in the neck to hold down for extended durations but I struggled through it (although i would have loved an option to switch it around so that sneaking and running would be on L1 and R1 and throwing and alt-speech would be on R2 and L2, it's more convenient and makes more sense to put throwing on a trigger button than a regular one.
-
Quicksave system; this was in the Exoddus games but not the original Oddysse game this one is based off which brings some minor implications. Overall I liked the quicksave system in exoddus so I liked the concept of having an quicksave system in this game, however it wasn't set up as elegantly as in exoddus, in exoddus you could quicksave, then next time you'd die you'd respawn where you quicksaved.  In this game you will always respawn at the last checkpoint when you die unless you specifically load the quicksave after you die either by accessing it from the menus or holding down the select button (which is also the quicksave button). In other words, quicksaving could have been better implemented, but at the very least it was implemented which is good enough.
-
Ragdoll effects, in the original games you either blew up or turned into a steaming pile of meat when you died (yes it was funny) now instead of getting that "steaming pile of meat" effect we have ragdoll effects, but I really miss that sound we always got when we died in the original, the "steam" sound . It was totally silly but it was one of these things that was actually funny about the game. I guess it's mostly because this game is 3D and the original was 2D that they couldn't keep it in this one but the ragdoll effects are very generic and I didn't feel they added anything to the game in the end so I would have preferred something totally stupid like what I described over the ragdolls personally, but it's a minor thing.
-
Soundtrack timings are not as good as in the original (and I also could swear that there were some missing tracks, but it might just be that some tracks weren't always played when they should/would have in the originals) I also noticed that sometimes sound effects don't play (clearly that's a bug to be fixed though)
-
You can't always carry items between stages whereas in the original you could.
-
UXB (Toggleable) Mines are more difficult (While they all follow the same pattern in this game; the time to press is different than in the originals in the way that you have to super precisely time it just a millisecond before the long green beep, in the originals you had to press it as soon as the beep sound is heard, rather than before it is actually heard)
-
That's pretty much it for the comparison to the original. My only major complaint is that the slaves don't sound that tormented, and besides the times they're beaten on-screen, they don't look that bad-off (there isn't blood all over the floors and walls like in the original; as I said before, lighter atmosphere)
Definitely an epic game, and if you haven't played the original jump right in on normal difficulty and enjoy it! It's the most 3D side-scroller I have ever played for sure.
I'd love to see an Exoddus remake as well!
