Rescue your fellow Mudokens in this remake of the classic platformer.  This game has been built from the ground up using modern graphics and level design while still retaining a lot of what made the 90's game a classic.  With some very minor technical problems, the only negatives I could find while playing through this a few times were related to my adoration of the original, a game that I count as one of my top games of all time.
You play as Abe, a meat factory slave who discovers that his species are next on the menu.  You now to escape and discover you have a much larger part to play.  The game is littered with secret areas and Mudokens to save.  Of course you don't need to save anyone, but you will be rewarded with a darker ending and will also miss out on what makes the game challenging...saving every single Mudoken.  You have 300 to save and some are hidden away in the most unlikely places.
The game looks gorgeous, perhaps too much bloom, but gorgeous nontheless.  Part of the charm of the original was just how detailed the backgrounds were and how gritty the world seemed once you stopped to take a look.  This has gone in the remake, but  you can see instantly that a lot of love and care went into the creation of this world for this remake.  However, the game has been changed in terms of how seamless each environment connects to the next.  It may sound like nitpicking, but I honestly prefer the originals single screen approach.  I took each screen as its own puzzle and New 'n'  Tasty makes puzzle solving more irritating than difficult.  You will wonder if that enemy can see you or if you are allowed to chant without taking a single step back.  It looks seamless, but it doesn't act it and this leads to some minor frustrations with certain puzzles.
The use of a quick save has made the game much easier, but for new players I think the game will be difficult anyway.  The game has been made a little easier in other ways; no deaths from high falls and of course an easy mode.  These are personal disappointing issues and I would still recommend this game to veterans of the series as well as newcomers.
The game can be played with a keyboard or a controller.  Personally I can only comment on the use of the keyboard as I never planned on using a controller for this.  The keyboard controls are solid for the most part and the keys are mapped in a way where you can play one-handed throughout most of the game, leaving your other hand to scratch yourself or read a guide if you are getting frustrated.  As for the controller, I cannot see how playing this type of game with an analogue stick is comfortable!  A d-pad or keyboard always seemed the best option, but that's just personal opinion.
The game itself retains some of the charm of the original, it is an admirable remake and, despite it not being as atmospheric, difficult and charming as the original, it is still an excellent puzzle platformer by todays standards.  Its existence does not diminish the original and it is still quite beautiful, quirky and slightly strange.  If you have never played the original before, or haven't played it in years, then I highly recommend you pick this up and spend a few hours in Oddworld.

A masterpiece of a game, marred by a handful of terrible design choices. The art and music are second to none. The controls are decent, though not without their quirks. The gameplay is very challenging, but (by and large) in a good way. Strong level design, with rewarding secrets add to the sense of accomplishment. The story is genuinely emotional, albeit on a (good) Disney-movie level. All in all, I would recommend.
The 'bad' comes in doses of unnecessary frustration; there are times when the graphics or UI kill you, and that's simply inexcusable for a game that put in this much effort to its visuals; I'm referring to a number of times when your character, hazards you need to dodge, and/or enemies are lost, obscured by foreground art or UI elements like "You got a Thing!" Also, the pickups and projectiles -- which both typically go flying at your character -- look extremely similar on my monitor, making knowing what to dodge challenging in a way that's probably not by design.
My biggest gripe is that there is at least one point in the game where you've got to escape something that's happening. This segment is terrible. First, it's simply too long for the level of difficulty; the number of things that are out of your control that can go wrong is just too long. Second, the primary mechanic you need -- an air dash -- has finikey controls, and an internal time limit, making for very frustrating losses. Third, it relies on the actions of enemy AI (it uses projectiles as it's 'anchor'), which means when the AI doesn't do what you hope it will, you die. Fourth, you don't ever really get 'ahead;' any time saved by skillfully navigating a segment is instantly negated when you reach the next segment, so the pressure is artificially eternal. And fifth, the foreground elements are constantly obscuring your character, which is miniscule on the screen to begin with, meaning that you essentially have no idea what's going on a chunk of the time. I haven't finished the game, but segments like this have plagued games since there've been games, so maybe it's not such a big deal. Just ... be ready.

I didn't hear much aside from a review I read on Gamesradar about this and it seemed interesting, though I was still a little shaky about hadning over $20 for it. Now after finishing it I can confidently say that it was $20 very well spent.
It plays a lot like Metroid where you have to explore an overworld overcoming obstacles and defeating enemies along the way. As you aquire more abilities, the world opens up to you more. The gameplay was easy enough that I didn't get frustrated, but challenging enough to keep me interested. The best feature the game had I would say is the checkpoint system. If you're in a safe spot you can use some of your stored power to save and create a checkpoint, inadvertantly allowing the player to set their own difficulty in a way. Don't like repeating the same four easy obstacles to get to the one that's holding you back? Create a CP and keep at it. Think checkpoints are too easy? Don't use them and be hardcore like that. The game doesn't push you to use them one way or another.
The most challenging parts are certain section of the game where you have to overcome a series of obstacles within a given amount of time due to certain events. This can get frustrating to less skilled players, but for me it was a nice challenge. It made me use every skill I had learned up until that point and use them together, something not every game remembers to pull off. These areas are kinda like your boss fights, since in the game you're overcoming the environment as well as enemies.
The story and art in this game are both simple and beautiful. It's one of those stories where few words are said, but much can be felt when watching it unfold. The characters didn't have to say anything for me to care about them, and most of them didn't. The graphics in general also complemented the game well. This is a colorful and diverse game visually. It all takes place in a forest, but sometimes it goes into caves, inside trees, over mountains, and into swamps. No two places are the same. The wrap it all up with a nice and neat, the soundtrack is great. Sometimes I just fooled around listening to the music playing instead of getting where I needed to go.
I had a blast with this game. It had a great story, great gameplay, great visuals, great soundtrack, and best of all a great price. For me this was well worth the 20 bucks.

I had been waiting for this game since last year's E3 and it was everything I had hoped for. I don't want to describe the game in detail because discovering it for yourself is part of the joy of experiencing this game, because although it's mechanically a videogame, it hearkens back to a time when videogames transcended their shells and were more than videogames; they were experiences - experiences that we don't see quite often anymore.
A videogame 'experience' these days might mean a game that tries to feel like a movie. This is not what I would call a good videogame-experience. A good videogame-experience is one that tries to invoke something from the player as opposed to telling a story and bringing the player along for the ride. Not only is Ori and the Blind Forest such an invocation, it's a celebration of one of the greatest eras in videogames: the 16-bit era.
I hope you fall in love with this game as I have.

Finally something different! Infinite Warfare is the best in the series since the originals, bringing the series into the future is a great idea, it was time for a change as games like this were getting repeditive and lacked content. Infinite Warfare is almost 3 games in one package, as you have the normal FPS mode with amazing battlfield layouts, then you have the new and amazing "Space combat" taking off from the ground and into space, and then we have the Zombies DLC which is also Amazing, this game also has the best graphics around and I often find myself just stopping to admire the scenery. A lot of the enemies are robots instead of boring old human soldiers and they require tactics to destroy, like the excellent ability to "Hack" the enemies and take control of them! theres nothing cooler than being able to hack a robot and suddenly be inside it on the other side of the battle looking back at youself and taking out the enemy from the inside! after a certain time limit you can then self-destruct taking out as many enemies as possible, you also have the ability to call in a gunship to attack chosen groups of enemies, and you also have "Spider Grenades" that when thrown unfild into a mechanical spider that seeks out the enemy and then crawls up their legs and attaches itself to them before exploding. I'm generally a little bit dubious about the whole "rogue-like" phenomenon, but occasionally you encounter a game where it's handled exceptionally well.  Monstrum and Darkest Dungeon both come to my mind, and now I can very safely add Skyhill.  Why am I so dubious of the rogue-like phenomenon you ask?  Because I'm a firm believer that 98% of the time, what makes great art great art - whether the art form in question is music, movies, books, or, yes, even video games - is careful and meticulous DESIGN.  Because rogue-likes, by their very nature, add in highly randomised elements to determine the mapping and what-not of the game in question, the likelihood of such games being "well-designed" becomes greatly compromised.  Having said all that, it is my relief to announce that SKYHILL IS A STAGGERINGLY WELL-DESIGNED GAME.

I guess it's maybe a bit like improvisation jazz music...occasionally, it rocks, but for the most part it emerges as little more than a sloppy, communal WANK.  But when that chaos somehow all pulls together - bear with me, trying to keep the "communal wank" metaphor going - then something magic can happen.  That's precisely what the makers of Skyhill have pulled off here...MAGIC.  It's deceptively simple, but hard as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  You'll "get it" in very little time at all - the combat system is straightforward, ditto the crafting system, and anything and everything else you care to mention - but it's designed in such a way that you will almost certainly die multiple times before you beat it, even on Easy difficulty.  This is partly because progressing through the one hundred floors of the building unlocks "perks" which you can choose between at the start of a new game, without which you're really not liable to make it all the way to the bottom.  There's also a learning curve, such as one which led me to prioritise achieving certain things (such as crafting certain weapons) as soon as possible in order to improve my chances in the long-term.
I dunno...maybe to super-seasoned rogue-like/RPG-lite gamers out there this would be little more than a grind-fest, but for me personally it required the gradual accumulation of a STRATEGY to get through the ♥♥♥♥er.  And, of course, luck also plays a role...but it's always going to in this genre of gaming, let's face it.  But it's still pretty darned "fair" on the whole, in my humble opinion.

Overall, I really can't imagine how this could have be any better designed, and it's just challenging enough - but also just "hey, at least I'm slowly making progress" enough - to be a really fun and addictive little game.  I hit it for five hours' straight the first night I played it, and that's a rarity for me, to say the least.  It's also nice to have a game which is a bit of a "dungeon-hack", minus the dungeon (though the horror setting is only liable to be "scary" to your grandmother, but it's still a tone and atmosphere which I personally prefer to the usual "light fantasy" fare).
Oh, and for all the value-for-money people, there's four difficulty levels, as well as innumerable weapon crafting options, selectable perks which significantly change gaming strategies, and a hefty♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of achievements to aim for, so even at full price no one needs complain about longevity of gameplay (I mean sure, it might get a tad repetitive eventually, but all you people seem to enjoy forty to fifty hours of mindlessly shooting and looting the same stuff in Borderlands game after Borderlands game after Borderlands game, don't you?)!

Definitely one of my "games of the year", even if the ending is a bit on the lame side (no big challenge or boss fight or anything...you just walk out the front door of the bottom floor of the building, and somehow end up in a cut-scene on the ROOF)!  Luckily the game isn't really about the "story", though, but rather the EXPERIENCE...and a very, very enjoyable and compelling experience I've found it to be.  Let me put it this way:  Now that I've conquered the Easy mode, I'm already itching to beat it on Normal, and no doubt the higher difficulties after that.  If that's not the definition of a well-made turn-based game, I'll be darn-♥♥♥♥ed if I know what is.

Verdict: 9.5/10.

Full Review:
I always feel like horror lends itself very well to roguelikes. The implicit terror of slinking through halls clutching a sharpened spoon and half a roll of twine and unsure of if the next room contains one of the Seven Knights of Hell or a new set of pants lends itself very well to pants p******. Uncertainty is terrifying, and the variance of a roguelike leads to more nail biting moments than a game about caveman manicures. As a result, there are a fair share of “horror” roguelikes, or at the very least games claiming to be as such. Most forget the psychological elements of horror, and even superlative games like The Binding of Isaac forego adult storytelling for cartoony poop jokes and flies.....

Skyhill is an addicting survival game.  You start at the 100th floor of a building and need to work you way down to the ground floor.  Each floor has rooms you can loot and maybe even a monster or two that you need to kill.  There is crafting in the game as well.  To get to the ground floor you need to watch your health and hunger.  Replayability is there too, as everything on floors changes from game to game.  How many floors can you make it down?

All you want to do is to have a quiet evening in a VIP room at the top of a hotel, and then someone had to go and bomb the city. Thankfully you have a room with a bio-shield that will block the harmful radiation or poison that is now spewing all over the town. There's only one problem, you see you're going to run out of food, and when you do that you are going to have to venture out. So you have to ask yourself one thing, can you make it out of the hotel alive?
In the game of SkyHill you are going to be forced with that very question. The thing is once you are out of your room, you might as well try to get out of the hotel. There is one slight problem though, you see the VIP room is on the top of the hotel, a hotel that just happens to have 100 floors, so to get out of there alive you are going to have to go all the way down.
There are two statistics that you will have to pay attention to ABOVE all else, and that is your Health and Hunger. If you let your health dip below zero, well then you are dead. If you let your hunger dip below zero, well your health starts taking a hit. So you will have to balance your food intake as well as your medicine intake. Don't take too much at any point, but don't take too little that you will fall prey to the monstrosities that now hide within the building.
There's not much I didn't like about this game. There's challenge galore, you will never play the same game twice as the building is randomized on every playthrough. I will tell you this, though, your hunger will slowly increase through EVERY room that you walk through, and it will greatly increase when you are trying to fix something without the correct materials.The good thing is that you there's only always 3 rooms to a floor. You have the stairway/elevator hall, and then a room to the left and right. Be careful when going anywhere in this game because enemies can appear in ANY of these rooms. Oh and on a side note don't get to♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when you discover that there are rooms that have nothing in them, or that appear to have something but turn out to be empty.
For the completionist out there one of the main reasons why you are going to continue to come back and play this game is that there are collectables hidden in the game, and of course you have to collect them all. For those who are just looking for a one run type of experience, I'm going to warn you now, even if you make it to the bottom and get an ending, you're probably going to want to play again just to see if that's the ending that will always happen.
So here's the deal, are you looking for a solid game that deals with mutated human beings, some of them that you hope you only see once in the game (I'm talking about the lady mutant, once you see her, you'll know you don't want to EVER see her again)? Are you looking for a game that has crafting of weapons, food, medical supplies, and upgrades to the crafting areas so that you have access to more stuff? Are you looking for a game that if you play your cards right you will HAVE TO play from start to finish? Well this is the game that you have to have on your radar. There's no other way to say it, this is a good game, and there's only 1 flaw that irks me to no end and that is that sometimes you consume more than 1 piece of food or medical supply when you are trying to decrease your hunger or heal yourself, but it doesn't happen all the time, and the way I played the game it actually was never truly a waste. So here's the score, this game gets a 9.3 out of 10.

SKYHILL is a kinda-zombie survival game with roguelike elements. You start at the top of the Skyhill building and have to fight and scourge your way through 99 floors back to possible safety.
VISUALS
Simple but solid 2d. I'm not too fond of the art style, but after a few hours I got used to the character model and enemies. The building itself, the rooms really, look quite allright and post-apocalypticsy. Intro and outro are made in a comic book way and are rather meh.
AUDIO
Simple and not annoying. The background music is plink plonking, the sound effects are very basic, but you don't need more. Nothing much to say here really.
GAMEPLAY
The premise is pretty simple, it's turn based, you can move one room at a time, each move costs food, food can be found. Each encountered enemy has to be killed if you want to pass through. You can find medpacks to heal, if your base is upgraded enough you can also heal by sleeping there. The base can be upgraded to allow for building new weapons, items or cooking better food. There is permadetah and the game can be very random, but that's not necessary bad. It's a roguelike after all.
All in all I had 10 or so hours of fun before I managed to get to the bottom for the first time. There are three endings, so there is some replayability. Recommended.

I believe everyone has to play this game. Really.
This game is like a love letter to a lot of classic games and I truly believe you'd be missing out on something if you didn't play this game.
Unlike Evoland 1, this game did everything perfectly. No jokes were dragged out, no freature/gameplay element overstayed its welcome... Everything was portioned just right. The music was really great, too. If you've played Evoland 1 and avoid this one because of it-- Don't. This game is so much more better, trust me.
At its core, it's a Legend of Zelda-esque adventure game with time-travelling elements. But as you advance in the game you'll soon see that this isn't everything this game has to offer. There's a little bit of everything everywhere: Tactical RPG, RPG, Platformer, card games, .. and much more that I don't want to spoil.
Most "genres" are only introduced once, and like I said, never overstay their welcome; as quickly as they come, they also go. This was made very well in my opinion, I believe certain moments in the game would have lost their charm if they happened over and over again.
The story isn't random at all and it all makes sense in one way or another. I wouldn't say the story was really great as there were some things left open that were never explained, but there's also a lot that didn't need an explaination as you could figure it out yourself. All in all I'd say the story was well written, even if it had a few plot holes.
Lasty, I can just say this: I rarely find games that make me want to finish them as soon as I start playing them. The game was well-paced and was very interesting from start to finish. I binge played it and I regret nothing. It was an amazing experience that I truly believe everyone should experience for themselves.

Sky Hill is great for a lot of reasons, but it has a few things I would like to see changed. I shall list them for easy reading:
Pros:
-Looks very nice, the art style and graphics are well suited to the gameplay and concept
-Music and sound effects are appropriate for the situations you find them in and are original; No Wilhelm screams here
-Controls are simple, straight forward and respond well
-I really like the concept of starting at the top of the building and working your way down to the ground floor to get out. It's an interesting take in a game genre that usually involves you starting at ground floor and either going up a castle or down into a the dungeon. The idea of being trapped in a building full of windows is a cool twist.
-This game is difficult, but after you unlock a few perks and get familiar with the gameplay you can get further in each attempt, which is exactly how it should be.
-Crafting is solid and well thought out, there aren't many arbitrary items, everything you come across can be useful
-Enemies are well designed and all stand out from one another. You'll need a different strategy for each one which makes the combat a lot of fun
Cons:
-I've encountered a glitch where sometimes I will get a lot of artifacting. My computer doesn't quite have the grahical memory the game recommends, but I've played many other games where I don't meet the exact standards and the game runs just fine. Thankfully, the artifacting seems to only affect the background and if you have the interactable object indicator on, then the little eye symbol will show you which boxes of colour you can pick up. Strangely enough, even with this glitch the game is still 100% playable and is actually pretty funny; like playing on a SNES that's acting wonky.
-The accuracy seems to be a bit off. When I have an 80-85% chance to hit an enemy it seems a lot more like 70% from the amount of misses. That problem scales as well; at 50% chance only can hit an enemy 1 out of 3-4 times, which can truly screw you over. This should be looked at in the next few updates as it is the most annoying part of this otherwise great game.
TL;DR:
If you like RPGs, Rogue-likes, and crafting, then this game is right up your alley, I would highly recommend it.

tl;dc version -
Literally Auralux with mobile bases... most of the time. Several levels were almost explicit copies at that. Granted I don't blame them for copying Auralux given I found Auralux to be amazing myself.
If you don't know Auralux, in a nutshell, it's a strategic numbers game: outproduce your opponents, defend your cells, destroy/capture other cells at vulnerable times, repeat.
I'd recommend the game, despite everything listed below if it were free or at least a maximum of $2. I may be stingy but this game is not worth the listed $9 in my opinion given I'm fairly certain that anyone that's done enough Unity tutorials could clone this game in a fairly short period of time, excluding the graphics.
On a positive note though, when you post a bug in the forum, a fix is usually made available the day of.
Full Review -
The controls don't really seem very "mature", last I checked the circular selection does work but there is no indication for it (can't see it like you can with the square). Sometimes the cells simply stop responding and just start doing their own thing, wandering off. Sometimes the cells ram each other so much that it's like Unity's 2d physics engine gives up and lets them overlap. Once this happens you cannot regain control until they separate OR you tell all your cells to move to a certain location. You also cannot tell your cells or "antibodies" to regroup in the same location they are currently in (they have a wandering/flocking ai meaning they meander around if given the opportunity)
The graphics are really nice to look at but when you're working to beat the level, you're generally not paying attention to them so for me with a game like this, while they are nice, they are also kind of rendered pointless since you don't have time to appreciate them. I'd rather have the time spent on graphics spent elsewhere.
Sadly the game becomes highly repetitive after a while given that after you beat the levels, the only thing you have left to do is max out your cell's abilities via the evolve menu. With differing levels of upgrades (purple being the best so far) it seems alright until you realize that the only level (at least that I've been able to get) are white (the lowest) from levels you've already beaten.
The AI difficulty is increased by giving the other cells more of a default advantage over you (i.e. they produce antibodies generally a lot faster than you and have better armor) along with having them generally target you over any other cell even when there are 4 other types all around them and you're not strategically optimal. Presumably these disadvantages can be countered with personal upgrades via the evolve menu but with only getting white's it turns it into a massive grindfest.
There also seem to be levels beyond the last level listed but you can't access them without continuing to play without stopping after the end. I'm not sure if this functionality was intentional or if those levels are only being tested still or if these are the levels that are suppose to be "exclusive" to any DLC they have or might have in the future.

In many ways, Arkham City is a massive improvement to the first game in the series. The graphics are better, the villains are generally more intriguing (e.g., Mr. Freeze, Mad Hatter), and the gameplay has been refined with touch-ups on the controls and gadgets. Your grappling gun makes you feel like Spider-Man as you swing through the city, so backtracking never became too annoying.
Arkham City, like its predecessor, is equal parts stealth, action, adventure, and fighting game. It blends several different game types in order to prevent repetitive gameplay. However, the story isn't as cohesive as it was before and the side content became a chore to finish due to its lack of integration with the plot (AKA Riddler trophies).
That being said, Arkham City's a solid game all around that should take you anywhere from 12-20 hours (not including the challenge maps). While some of its content didn't appeal to me, there's more than enough for Batman fans to engross themselves in.

Just take my inability to seperate myself from being in-game and doing♥♥♥♥♥♥as the surest measurement of how captivating the game can be. Mentally you should invision 5 well written and worded paragraphs detailing everything that makes this game a fun experience, and gain a general sense of my enjoyment of the game so far.
I'd be doing a dis-service however if I didn't mention that the first couple hours can be confusing, things in-game have explanations that can lead you to assuming the wrong thing --
-There is a difference between a ship core and a ship starter block. You can use a core to claim a structure if it has no core already or you successfully destroy their core. Ship starter blocks are similar but you cant use them to claim existing structures.
-Numerous flaws with quests in the default scenarios i.e.
(one instructs you to capture an alien ship. it doesnt indicate which one, but specifically it means a particular CV in space. Of course you can add more thrusters or more RCS (gyroscopes) to change the way your ship handles, but the physics of making a banked turn mid-air are off a bit. Inertia is a present feature but the physics feel slightly flawed (too much "friction") I mention the above phtsics oddities but in all seriousness, they're things you get used to that effect everyone the same, so they aren't game breaking or unfair.
So, take the above 3 grains of salt, and the following advice:

3D MiniGolf is a simple mini-golf game for 1 to 4 players boasting just over 50 courses and a few game modes.
-4 player co-op
-cheep and simple
-Glitchy physics, especially the ball physics
-the game doesn't shuffle the players to prevent 1st player disadvantage
-the music
-lack of variety. No moving obstacles, little differentiation between holes
-quite a few holes that can be easily hole in one'd
Overall maybe someone could have a bit of fun with this over an afternoon with some friends but It's a pretty limited golf experience. Maybe if you're really into golf and party games and are looking for a budget game to fill a few hours but otherwise probably best avoided.

Overall it needed just a bit more polish before release. Maybe it can still happen?
Pros:
- The graphics are pretty good.
- The layouts of most holes are reasonable. I've seen mini golf games that have holes that ramble on and on, this game generally does not suffer from that.
Cons:
- Alt-Tabbing out of the application causes it to freeze and makes it unable to be switched back to. It then has to be killed through Task Manager. This is the most annoying flaw with the game and pretty much makes it unplayable as a casual game where I am switching back and forth between playing and doing something else.
- Par for each hole seems rather arbitrary.  A hole of a particular difficulty may be presented as a par 1, but a later hole of similar difficulty will be par 3. I wasn't even sure why the par existed until I reached the second course, because the first course had all of its holes at par 1 (which made it the most difficult course to attain 100% gold medals).
- The game was way too easy/short. I gold medaled all 54 holes in under 2.5 hours.  That's an average of less than 3 minutes to master each hole.
- The physics are occasionally glitchy, especially around hills.  When a ball moves from a slope to flat ground or vice versa, the ball tends to skip unnaturally along the ground, killing momentum and spamming the ball collision sound effect.  Also, sometimes a ball can take several minutes to come to rest (this was most noticeable on course 3, hole 5, right at the tunnel exit where 2 downhill slopes seem to meet).
- Each course only has a 5-second loop of music, occasionally fading to... the same 5-second loop of music.  This gets very annoying after a few minutes.
Overall the flaws tend to cancel out the good things about this game. If I could give it a neutral rating, I would, but since there are better mini-golf games out there, I'll say meh to this one. If the flaws could be fixed, this would be among those better mini-golf games.

Pros:
Hex-based tactical combat
Lots of character customization
Points system for leveling skills
Environmental effects such as setting bushes on fire, slipping in puddles, or knocking stalagtites off the ceiling of a cave
Cons:
You will likely hit your opponents maybe 10% of the time. You have a hit percentage ranging from 0 to 100. This is based on your skill with the weapon, your attack stat, and the level of the creature you're attacking. This does not take into account their ability to dodge or parry. A character (opponent or ally) can parry the first physical attack against them each turn. They can dodge any number of attacks per turn. So, if you have a 90% chance to hit, it is then further reduced behind the scenes by their dodge rating, and again by parry if they have not yet been hit. If you have anything less than say, 80% chance to hit, it may take you dozens of turns to end a battle that could have ended in like 6.
Enemies at the beginning of the game hit every hard, and rarely miss. You can increase your dodge and parry ratings through skills, but at character select you can't exactly make it huge. This would be fine, if it weren't for the fact that enemies can quite often hit for 10-15 damage, while your character only has about 30 health. Early game you only have 3 party members, and very often face off against 5+ enemies. It's easy to get swarmed, so using choke points is a must-- at least it would be if the majority of the levels they put you in weren't open rooms.
Cover doesn't seem to do anything. One of the earliest tips you get is that you are harder to hit in partial cover, and even harder to hit in full cover, like behind a tree. Archers have no trouble hitting you from the full length of the map behind full cover for 5-8 damage a turn, and it will take at least 2 or 3 turns to be able to reach them.
Some quests/scenarios are outright impossible if you try them too early, and the game has no qualms about sending you to your death. A good example of an early scenario in this game is facing a Wood Troll (like a treant). It has a ton of health and does a lot of damage (like 15-20 per hit), but it's slow and in a gaseous swamp. You can stand in front of a gas pocket and  use a fire spell or torch on the gas to explode it a few times to win the fight. You could do this at level 1 if you wanted, but an uninformed player would try to rush it and die quickly.
A bad example is later on. You fight some dwarves in an arena. They have a lot of health, do a lot of damage, and can move as far as you. You're *supposed* to use the same method as the Wood Troll. Stand in front of the mace trap before it activates, lure the enemy into it, and do most of the damage through the trap. My issue is I was underleveled, and there was no way for me to know this until it was too late. The enemy dodged 100% of my attacks, knocked down a character per turn, and the melee dwarf hit for 15+ damage per turn plus 5 poison per turn while 2 of my characters had ~30 hp, and one with 46. The melee dward also parried the trap that was supposed to deal the damage to him each turn, so he was functionally invincible. I tried at least a dozen times, looked online, and saw the only real way to win the fight is to ignore the mission until you had another party member and were a little more leveled. Looking at my saves, I had one auto save right before the fight, a quick save right before the fight, and a manual save about an hour and a half prior (Which isn't the game's fault, but frustrating nonetheless).
You can't level skills without finding a trainer, even if you meet the pre-requisites to unlock it, or had the option to learn it during character creation. If I don't spend at least one point into the mend wounds ability at character creation, I cannot learn it until much later when I find the right trainer. I would understand for some skills, but for the basic levels of some passive abilities or skills it doesn't make much sense.
Overall, the game is difficult for the sake of being difficult, but not in a way that self improvement can make it any easier. Unlike an action game like Dark Souls, dying isn't always the result of you ♥♥♥♥ing up. A lot of the time, it's because a creature rolled the highest it possibly could 3 turns in a row, or all 3 of your characters missed every single roll 3 turns in a row. If you're okay with restarting a mission over and over just to beat it, or to avoid getting knocked down and started on fire before your first turn, go for it. If you're as easily frustrated as me at a game where RNG is the core mechanic of the game, avoid it, even for $3.00

I have 725 hours in game and decided i would write my first ever steam review. I have played this game since its release on steam even though i purchased the game initially off their website before steam release.
I have had a lot of fun playing this game yes there are issues with this game but the devs have been making strides in the content they are bringing out from way back when there were only two events to kill brandon and ragi (world bosses) to where we are now with multiple events to help newcomers level up quicker and contend with the big boys.

General pvp and combat although the current system has its issues which the developers are aware of they are hard at work finalising their brand new combat overhaul which will hopefully fix a lot of the main complaints about the game. But the current combat system is very skill based knowing when to block, attack and kick to stagger your opponents is tricky to get used to at first but over time you will get better.
Guilds are a large part of this game aswell joining a guild preferably one that has a discord or a teamspeak is very useful as most help new players and teach them the ropes of the game, i recently joined the midlander guild called LEGION sorry for the caps but that's how they wrote it, but in doing so i have been apart of some of the greatest pvp sieges and fights in my whole time on this game the chaps really know their stuff when i comes to this game and have been helpfully to many newcomers.
Many people ask whether to buy this game or wait i would say buy this game learn the ropes of how to play it level up abit and see what this game has to offer they are bring out an update soon that will make massive improvements to the game's mechanics and overall feel yes the player base is small but thats allowed some great communities to be formed.
I hope you have found this review some what helpful and has made you consider purchasing gloria victis.

Ori and the Blind Forest is one of those rare, magical, mysterious, and fantastical games that feel like they whisk you to a dreamlike world far away the very moment you start to dive in. The vivid color, graphics, animation, lighting, sound, atmosphere, and enchanting music all synchronize harmoniously to create an amazing and surreal experience that feels half like an animated movie and the other half a compelling game that invites you to explore and discover what dark and captivating secrets and challenges lie in store for Ori in the immersive forest of Nibel.
Ori is a 2D platformer that uses a familiar tried-and-true Metroid-like mechanic of unlocking abilities and powers that allow you to access more of the forest areas that couldn't be reached before. However, even if that's not usually your typical game genre and gameplay of choice, there's a lot here that makes Ori feel refreshing and unlike anything you've played before. Also, the challenges, puzzles, and enemies you'll face are tricky but fair. The game also rewards you the more you step up to the challenge to dive further into the fantastical world around you and explore every nook and cranny you can. Dying is also more of an inconvenience than a serious frustration, just so long as you remember to carefully Soul Link (a unique way of quick-saving) often.
In all, this game is absolutely worth every penny of the $20 and makes you feel glad to be born in an era of games like this. You can tell the creators of this game put a LOT of extra special care, attention, and dedication to every detail, aspect, and component in this game and left no piece of it carelessly forgotten or hastily neglected in their effort to make it the absolute best and most captivating experience they could create.
Do yourself a favor and take the plunge. This is an enchanting and very immersive game that yearns and definitely deserves to be explored by everyone looking for a mystifyingly imaginative, sentimental, and mystical escape. Step away from the glut of first person shooters, zombie games, and simulations for a while and give Ori a chance to take you on a visually incredible journey and adventure that stays with you even after you've stepped away from the game.

Skyhill is great. It's a roguelike, 2D, turn based, dungeoneering type thing. You're a dude who booked himself into a VIP room in a hotel, then an apocalypse happened. You have to fight your way from the top floor to the bottom floor trying to maintain your health and keep your hunger levels down along the way. You can use the hotel lift to get back up to your Room, where you can sleep to heal if you're running low on medical items and make other improvements to the room that allow to to craft more complex foods (which replenish your hunger by more points) and build more complex weapons and medical supplies.
The mechanics reward careful thinking and efficient resource allocation but the turn based combat does involve an element of luck. You might not always find good food or medical items and you can't rely on anything. Even on the easy difficulty it's a fairly challenging game. I think it'll take me a few attempts to get much further than floor 50.
I did get my key for this game free in a giveaway the developer did on the fly during one of Dodgers Twitch streams because Dodger was playing Skyhill at the time. I have to say, the devs are really nice and I'm so happy this game turned out to be a lot of fun.

This game is just purely awesome. It delivers on every possible aspect. Of the core parts - it has very decent gameplay, which involves a big variety of genres, it has a good story which despite involving time travel for once is actually interesting and engaging, together with from-retro-to-modern visuals and a similar style soundtrack they complete the atmosphere of the game. All the humor and references I found rather non-intrusive, there's no Magicka style overload of this stuff, it's rather moderately spread out.
If you've played Evoland 1 - this game looks exactly the same except this time developers didn't forget to make an actual game out of the core idea of the game. Evoland was cool but it was a bland nothing, a short series of minigames mashed together with a joke of a story. This one is a complete continuous game absolutely worth playing.
Other technical information:
- gamepad recommended
- bugs: few
- playtime: took me 30 hours to do all but one achievements, main story only would probably be around 20 hours, overall depends on your engagement in side-stuff like collectibles

Where to begin...
I'll start by just saying that the first game was miles better. That game was a tight and well-thought-out experience, which is a phrase that does not apply to Evoland 2.
Let's just get this over with.
The good:
>the soundtrack was alright
>the game mechanics were solid and worked as intended most of the time
>it's 20 hours of content for 20 dollars
>the time travel mechanic was done decently
>some of the genre shifts were pretty fun, like the Gradius and Double Dragon clone modes. The Fire Emblem clone mode was pretty fun, too.
The bad:
>it's 20 hours of♥♥♥♥♥♥ /SPOILERS I'm exaggerating a bit, but the story is just constructed in an infuriating manner. I understand that part of the game was trying to be Chrono Trigger (RPG with world map, time traveling mechanic, and a journey to stop a catastrophe at the turn of the century), but this lacks the nice execution that CT and games like it had. The problem is that barely anything is explained (through showing OR telling) or built up to. The "villain" Ceres is kinda just there and you really only learn that she's planning on doing something that you don't really want to happen (arguably I'd rather have had her succeed, really) a few minutes before she starts to do it, and you never really get any exposition on her at all. She's a demon-human hybrid, right? Where/who are her parents/creators? How did she learn of the happenings of the story/gain the awareness to hatch a plan? Why is she doing this? Why does she expect Kuro and co. to assist her (she's visibly surprised when she learns that you don't want her to destroy everything). /END SPOILERS
>everything takes so damn long to do
Walking around in the two sprite-based eras is so SLOW. I don't think I've ever played another RPG where I was just silently screaming for the character to "PLEASE JUST UNLOCK A RUN BUTTON." When you get your "airship" (which was a huge relief), walking around the world map becomes a lot easier, so that's nice, but then if you want to time travel you have to go to specified locations on the map, get out, go walk a few seconds to an obelisk of some sort, cycle through (instead of directly selecting!) the eras to go to the one you want, and then walk back out to the world map. See, in a better game like Chrono Trigger you could just, from your airship, select from a menu what time you want to go to and perform a 4 second animation and just BE there. These alone taken in a vaccuum are fine; I can get past them, but when you put it in a game where all the story points are sandwiched by huge filler sections of just going from point A to B, it gets very frustrating very quickly.
>the gameplay's not very fun
See this is where Evoland 1 shined, because it almost never let its gameplay overstay its welcome because it was ALWAYS introducing new mechanics. In Evoland 2, the majority of the game is the same, VERY basic Zelda-like action-adventure RPG, and you would think that, of course, if the game's going to be mostly all one style of gameplay that it would at least be good gameplay, but of course that's not the case. There's one attack and three different charge attacks depending on what buddy you've got selected (of course not applying to the Double Dragon clone section, which was decent). In Zelda, at LEAST you had some sub-weapons to play around with that were pretty interesting, and none of them had an annoyingly-long cooldown time that scaled with ability strength that could reach something like 15 seconds. There was honestly no damn need for a cooldown at all for ANY of the abilities. The chargeup time was "balancing" enough! It's not as if the game is particularly hard to begin with (which is fine, but really at some point I was expecting to get a powerup that would make my partner abilities feel more useful)
>the setting is bland
All there is to say about that one, really. I was hoping we'd get to travel to a more far-future time, but instead the whole game sticks with this very generic high-fantasy-to-low-modern theme. The whole "smug" thing was really interesting, and I was hoping that the game would take it and the implications of using it SOMEWHERE but, again, Evoland 2 just disappointed me. I don't know what I expected at that point.
>I hate the story/ending
This is completely subjective, but the ending was terrible. It'd be fine if it were just one of several endings, but hell it's NOT EVEN A DOWNER ENDING, it's just a NOTHING ending. Nobody's happy; nobody's even SAD. The game just ends with a decent boss battle and a montage of very confusing, vaguely happy and/or melancholic scenes of the characters. You never really find out what on earth is going on with Kuro (though it's easy to guess some parts about him, he and Fina are mostly a loose end), and in the end, you've basically just screwed everyone over, because that's what your "destiny" is. No, Kuro's sudden character shift and flood of memories in the Lab scene is never properly given its due OR explained.
Don't take this the wrong way; I'm not asking for a Golden ending (though that would be nice); I'm just asking for ANY ending besides the garbage that was at the end of this game. I don't even care if it's a downer ending; at least that'd satisfy me. HELL, it could be just an alternate scene if you lose to the final boss that says, "you failed to save Time" or something like that. Anything besides that atrociously-poor ending that we go. "Oh but what if it's trying to make a comment on the futility of it all and how destiny runs our lives," you may ask. Well, sure, that'd be fine, too, if it were executed properly. It's not; I assure you.
>the referential humor sucks
It really does. There's a right and wrong way to go about this. LITERALLY putting the LITERAL (and I mean it; I have no idea how this dev did not get C&D'd) Hyrulian shield as your ebin Zelda reference in a shop or making an achievement referencing a 2006 meme or doing almost any of the things this game did is the wrong way to do this. Y'know what game did it better? Evoland 1.
>the characters are not developed well
I'll say that I cared about Fina and Kuro pretty well by the time the game ended. I even cared about Menos and, heck, even Dalkin. Who's Velvet, though? You know, that party member that's with you for most of the game? Do you ever find out anything about her other than her Magi/Archaeology interests? Do you find out her motivations? Her backstory? Her personality? No, not really. What about Ceres? No, not really. The character development is lopsided and even if a character is well-developed, the game doesn't DO anything with them of note. Once you figure out that Kuro and another character in the story are the same person, that's pretty interesting, I'll admit, but beyond that nobody is really used for anything interesting, which really saddened me.

This is basically a Galcon-clone (i.e. a barebone RTS reduced to 1 building/1 unit) with the novelty of slowly moving your spheres around the playfield and 'autoattack' to upgrade the bases (2 times). The macro scale has been changed to micro, and we have cells+hormone molecules setting instead of cosmic theme. Victories give you upgrades for movement and defence. The scenery represents primordial soup vessels of various forms with neutral fungi on walls, it looks and feels quite atmospheric and convincing. It's also got stunning minimalistic visuals at close view, some sort of scalable vector graphics with really pretty lighting effects. In this regard I can compare it to Tulpa and Raeticon.
The downside here is the clunky Unity engine with UI shortfalls.. some will argue that Unity's totally allright per se, they say even Wasteland 2 is made on Unity, so it's just the devs can't use it properly. Maybe so, frankly speaking I hate W2 anyway.. and I don't know sh!t about engines' programming. But I definitely know when my clicks won't register occasionately and the active zones won't work near the screen edges. The interactions starts to feel uncertain and you can easily imagine what it turns out to be in harder lavels - a ragequit fest!
Anyway I really liked everything about this game except its technical basis, 100% advise you to get it for mobile, but I have to downvote it as a PC game for not passing my extremely high quality standarts!

VERSION 7.0 AND UP_
First, I have not used the multiplayer so far so none of this applies to that.
This game so far manages to combine aspects of:
- No Man's Sky, in the fact that the scenery is quite well detailed and pleasing to look at, especially on akua.
- Survival games, in the fact that you do have to hunt for food, cook it, find your own resources, and you may even encounter hostile drones and other threats. Being an exploration game, the emphasis on survival is not as heavy as other
survival games, but it still seems balanced enough that I don't need to constantly fret and worry over it.
- I don't remember what game had this, but instead of using a voxel system to mine resources (or just mess up the scenery to your heart's content) this game seems to actively displace terrain in a way that is much closer to actual digging, only considerably faster for obvious reasons.
- Space Engineers...is the first game that comes to mind as you can make hovercraft, fighter vessels, capitol ships, and base structures, and so far they each have their own uses that makes them distince. Hovercraft move fast across the land and are good at traversing rough terrain, and can also have mining equipment, as well as both manual weapons and auto turrets. Small vessels are often fightercraft, and as such do not have turrets, but are small and relatively cheap to manufacture. Capitol vessels are always quite large, expensive, and near unstoppable if you design them correctly, and can even hold smaller vessels within.
Pros so far:
- The planets have landmarks, some of them hostile, and are quite varied, giving you a reason to explore, and to be cautious.
- Beautiful environment. Enough said.
- Combat is simple yet functional and satisfying with a variety of basic weapon types, that being an assault rifle, pistol, shotgun, rocket launcher, even a minigun, ect.
- A blueprint system allows you to design a base or vessel in creative mode then build it quickly and passively in your survival game without it being too cheaty or instrusive.
- Ships are distince from one another. Each part has it's own health rating, function, ect, and they can be shaped in a variety of different ways to suit your creativity. Also some parts can be upgraded cheaply.
- Survival elements are not too instrusive, but do make sense. Planets without oxygen require you to have oxygen in your suite, you need to eat food, ect.
- Loot boxes in hostile landmarks often have rare and valuable loot that often cannot normally be found on the planet you're on, giving you a reason to assault them.
- Planets often have several unique mobs that may or may not be hostile and are more insteresting than your standard pallete swapped enemies with a few new parts you would normally see in such a game.
- A farming system with visually distinct food types with different uses (emergency rations...EMERGENCY RATIONS!).
Cons so far:
- The tuturial needs some work, especially when you accidentally put all of your bio-fuel into one device when you need some for another and the game refuses to explain how to get more.
- Mob behavior is still relatively simple. Passive mobs don't react at all until you start shooting. Hostile mobs charge right
at you the moment they see you. Sometimes passive mobs that are not involved in the fight take it upon themselves to attack you if they are close enough to the gunfire.
- In game knowledge base still simple and doesn't seem to update. Monsters that exist on the planet may not be in the database at all. Will probably be expanded in the future.
- Solo missions (that are completely optional) don't seem to function correctly at this time.
- There are some clipping issues when exiting a ship after orientation of ship has changed, sometimes getting you stuck
in a wall, though console commands can fix this temporarily. This usually happens only in space and only with small
vessels that are constructed with a hollow internal cavity in mind.
- If you accidentally catpaw and shut off the power, all of your plants die instantly, fortunately, they grow pretty quick. Also the game doesn't tell you this, but in order to make plants grow (besides using a grow light, and plot, the basics), you must create an airtight enviornment that may or may not need oxygen in the base.
Neither good nor bad:
- Enemy bases are constructed in a way that encourages you to go in on foot, but if you have ridiculous amounts of
explosives on your ship, you can just blast your way into the interior of the base, fly your gunship with hardened steel armor in, and mow everything down. Some enemies bases you don't even need to blow stuff up (akua moon).
- The game doesn't tell you clearly how to use the warp drive. It is rather frusterating to figure out initially.
- Credits can be used to trade with neutral aliens, but so far are not very useful and hard to find, plus you can just take everything that isn't nailed down and the aliens won't care at all.
- The planets don't seem to be procedurally generated and there is only a limited number (10-30 I think) so far. Still, each one is visually distince and gives you a reason to explore.
- Mob infighting doesn't seem to be a thing yet. It needs to be. Please. Not enough games consider what that would add to the gameplay experience. (this is neutral because it is a personal preference)
In summary, for twenty dollars, this game is pretty fun even in single player. Even in early access the game is very much playable and there is alot to explore and do, plus I love flying around in hovercraft. If you wanted No Man's Sky except with a reason to actually explore and travel, get this game! If you aren't into survival or exploration, this game is not for you.

A simplistic, bare-bones minigolf game that suffers from really bad physics, stiff controls, dull gameplay mechanics, numerous bugs, and strange interpretations of minigolf rules and terminology.
+ It's a no-frills, straightforward minigolf game (sorta)
- The ball moves and feels like a weightless ping-pong ball
- The wall deflection angles are really wonky
- No camera free-look controls, zoom, or map to plan shots
- The swing mechanics are not fun and require no skill
- The single music track loops quickly and gets repetetive
- "Par" for every hole is a hole-in-one!  What?!
- Strange boundary mechanic and ball drop rules
- Numerous bugs and odd design choices
I've been looking for a nice, straightforward minigolf game without all the wackiness and superflous zany things that usually are often put in to "spice up" the core game.  3D MiniGolf, on the surface, looked like it might fit that criteria.  Unfortunately, the terrible ball physics and lack of ability to plan shots really detracts from the experience.  I think a simple two-click swing mechanic could have worked OK in a simple minigolf game like this if the ball physics were at least somewhat realistic, but as it stands it just feels like you are smashing a ping-pong ball around in some alternate universe where momentum and deflection angles do not exist.
Additionally, for golf/minigolf enthusiasts, the strange use of terminology and rule interpretations make the game seem like it was programmed by someone who has never actually played a round of golf in their life.  Things like par for every hole being a hole-in-one make it impossible to score below par.  The use of the term "par +1" instead of bogey or just flat out a number of strokes.  Strange boundary lines on the actual green which if you don't cross you have to drop your ball again from the start.
While I respect the idea and ambition to create a simple, straightforward minigolf game, this one needs a lot of work and refinement in order for it to actually be any fun to play.
Golf With Your Friends, also available on Steam, is an excellent alternative for those looking for a simple yet well-made minigolf game.

The holes are all standard mini-golf setups.  Most holes are either a complete miss where you just hit restart or a hole in one.  There aren't really any par 2 or par 3 holes where you try and get below par.  You are pretty much just shooting for a hole-in-one on every shot.  This doesn't work very well for this kind of game and doesn't really encourage you to try this playing against someone else.  I played practically the same game 10-15 years ago.

In general, I simply can't recommend this game. Some people will be able to enjoy it and you should think about whether or not you fall into that category as you read my review. There are several things that need to happen before you can enjoy this game even a little. You need to be able to tolerate "low budget / low quality" games, really simple "gets the job done" physics (which really don't work that well) and you need to be able to enjoy the mere act of "pocketing the ball," since any other features are essentially non-existent in this game. You may be able to enjoy some local play with friends or family, but I could imagine most people would look at you funny if you tried to make them play this game.
Detailed Review:
-It's a mini-golf game at its core and despite its poor physics, features and general quality there don't seem to be any game breaking bugs or flaws. Despite aiming being difficult due to the camera, the ball will almost always go where it should.
-There is a diversity of courses which offer [very] minor changes to standard courses, giving you a bit of variety as you play through a tournament. But, IMO the courses are mostly uninspired and far too similar, plus some of the obstacles are pretty iffy when combined with the low quality physics.
-There is a tournament mode where you can play against AI players on various difficulties, but the difficulty / AI (like the physics) is there just to "get the job done" and doesn't feel like it's actually dynamic on how the players are arriving at their scores. Even on the typical straight-line hole-in-one hole there were AI players taking over 6 shots to "pocket the ball" and defaulting to a score of +7, which is rather silly.
-There are challenge modes where you can play a course over and over until you get a hole and one. It's kind of a neat mode except for the fact that it really highlights some of the problems with the game. Every single hole in the game has a par of 1. That means, unless you get a hole-in-one, that you are over par for that hole. This is the main reason that so many of the courses feel almost identical when played since they're all basically one and done, where you're aiming right down the middle of where you need to go. It also contributes to a less enjoyable experience since you're constantly reminded that anything above a hole-in-one is above par, and thus essentially a failure.
Ultimately, this game is worth a shot if you can pick it up for $1-2. It's an almost certainty that it really isn't worth your money, even at that cost, but for mini-golf nerds like myself, it isn't really worth passing up for only a buck. Like I said, there isn't really anything insulting/game breaking in the game, so you pretty much get exactly what you'd expect from a game that you only paid a dollar for.
At >$2, don't ever, EVER buy this game. Seriously, don't.

The game starts off well enough but I eventually had to quit.  I was getting so frustrated I nearly threw my mouse through my monitor.  Blackguards is presented as a game returning to the core roots of RPG strategy goodness.  Just check out the multiple videos from Daedalic above for all the stuff that sounds so great about this game.  What is presented sounded awesome to me but in reality my two attempts through the game turned into a frustrating slog from one scenario to the next.
I got hooked on the story from the start which turned out to be a prison break.  Nothing ground-shakingly new here but it worked for bringing three main characters together and launching them off on what was to be a quest to save the world.  The cut-scene interactions just propel the story forward, but did contain some humorous dialogue.  City/settlement locations are really just screens you click on to visit the tavern/shop/quest giver, etc.  Again, nothing earth-shattering for the genre but where this game was supposed to shine was in the combat.
And the combat on many of the levels was excellent.  Some of the scenarios were very challenging and I truly felt good when I had achieved victory conditions.  You certainly cannot simply build up your characters and then rush through everything.  Planning was necessary.   All that was great.
Specific building of your characters is crucial to the point that if you build them wrong, you will find that the difficulty spikes.  Character building is handled through allocating skill points.  There are a lot of options (FIVE screens worth) and very little in-game guidance on what to build up first.  I am sure most players will do what I did and end up resorting to the forums and walkthroughs to know how best to maximize their points.  It should not be this difficult or nebulous on building up your characters - especially with this many options.  The game reminds you to save often so you can go back to an earlier time and rebuild if needed.  But that still stings a little knowing that you lost that progress and will need to make it up.
But then the game started throwing out some curve balls on the scenarios and I found myself needing to restart certain ones again and again.  These levels were often fronted by a cut-scene dialogue that had to be clicked through again and again.  I just do not understand why they couldn't simply start the level with your characters on the field.  Many of these levels had special rules or situations that were not made apparent until you played them.  So you learned the "special" rules through failing at the level and had to try again.  And again.  And again.
It does not help when the game chains scenarios together without a way to rest in-between.  You may find that by the end of the 2nd or 3rd scenario you are completely out of potions/health/magic/whatever.  And you may need to not only restart that level, but perhaps go back to a prior level so that you end with enough health/magic to be successful in the next one.  I could see the game doing this on hardcore difficulty for those who really enjoy upping the difficulty, but I just wanted to veg out after a hard day at work.
By the time I was into the gladiator fights in chapter 2 I realized something.  The. Game. Was. No. Fun.
I am recommending a pass on this one.  If you do buy it, wait for a nice Steam or bundle sale.

For players of the original games it can take some time to get used to, oh and do yourself a favour and select the 'forward hop' option in the controls menu, it will make your life a lot easier. The new ragdoll physics are something that troubled me, there are no set tiles like in the original so it can be hard at times to judge the distance between your face and a meat grinder or live mine. Ledges can be trouble at times during the Elum jumping sections and there's an autostop when you get too close to the edge when standing.
The Shrykull uses confused me too, there are times when you're free to blow up everything on screen and times when you have the power but can't use it because you need a Slig to complete a puzzle.
I haven't played Alf's Escape for long because the level design confused me that I didn't get very far with it at all.
I was expecting an easy ride so I first played on hard but quickly had to switch down to normal, they've added enough that it really does feel more like a reimagining than a simple remake which I approve of a lot.
I'm really anticipating an Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus re/make/boot/imagining and I'm excited to see if there's plans to make a new Oddworld game too.

I've spent quite a bit of time in this game and here are my impressions:
The Good:
-Non-lock combat with directional attacks and simple block mechanic
-Variety of playstyles: a heavily armored knight wielding a greatsword, a light-armored two-handed axe user who flanks the enemy, or maybe even a deadly but vulverable archer?
-Partial loot system makes getting kills rewarding but getting killed not a game-ruining experience
-Leveling is relatively easy and quick: there are quests scattered around the map and "world events" that bring many players together for great XP and loot
-Crafting is a worthwhile profession: it can make you lots of money and allows you to make the best gear available
-Speaking of that, recipes are lootable but require craters to use them to create armor and weapons. This creates a strong trade economy.
-Devs are dedicated and extremely active. Usually a patch per week that fixes a multitude of bugs and adds some new features.
-Sieges are fun. Really fun. Seeing the banner fly over the (newly added!) keep after breaking down several gates and fighting the player and NPC garrison is very satisfying. Defending a castle against superior numbers and winning is great and even losing can be rewarding - you'll go home with bags full of loot!
-Graphics are ok. Nothing to marvel at but good for an MMO. They are improving slightly as new graphics settings are added.
The Bad:
-Animations are a bit odd (especially jumping) and can sometimes be a bit glitchy. However, new motion-capture animations are promised to being coming in an update soon.
-The weapon balance isn't too good. Two-handed axes do insane damage, while greatswords are only viable if you're wearing heavy armor and need to conserve stamina. One handers are generally bad and are only good when a shield is needed for a formation or when facing large groups at a chokepoint. Spears fill a useful role for stabbing through gates and standing behind shieldwalls.
-Player counts on some servers are low (Russia, SE Asia, and Oceania mainly) but US and EU servers are always very populated.
-Community is generally helpful and positive, but there is some turmoil among the many guilds (which has sometimes led to civil war and teamkilling)
The Ugly:
-THE DESYNC: The desync is sometimes insanely bad, to the point where the location of an enemy will be shown to you with a one second delay, causing none of your hits to connect and blocking to be almost impossible. This isn't always a problem (most of the time the desync is fairly minor) but it's most annoying when playing an archer. The desync fix should come soon with the new animations.
-The optimization: This being an early access game, some lag is to be expected. If your system isn't too up-to-date, don't expect good framerates. Now that I'm playing on a 1070 and a 6700k I get 60-70 FPS at 1440p ultra, but on a laptop with a 940m I was getting 15-20 at 1080 on minimum/off settings. The game is constantly getting small performance bumps though.
-The faction system. Players can create characters of both factions and switch between them easily. This allows enemies to create characters that teamkill and open gates to make taking castles easier. This ruins the game for everyone.
tl;dr
The game is fun with good base mechanics. The combat is a highlight and the devs are hard at work, releasing patches frequently. The lag and "spies" can be game-ruining experiences at time, but the lag issue is already being addressed.

Gloria Victis plays on the game type that has been seen many times. You can easily compare it to Mounted Blade, Conan, Life is Feudal, and Mortal Online. You can expect to be thrown into a medieval era conflict between two factions (although they claim they will be releasing more later, along with a larger map). In the character selection you can only be male (Female is promised to be released later) and can select your starting gear (character type) and assign a small amount of attributes.
Although the Ismir starting town is quiet beautiful, the Midgard starting town is a typical castle With everything scatter to fit inside the walls. There is a moderate amount of crafting that can be done, although you will quickly find that the time it takes to reach the level to craft the gear you need will result in you crafting thousands of lesser crappy gear (no matter what resources or level you are) and have wasted weeks.
The first hour of killing random people, with no back story as to why, that are scattered randomly (and respawn within 5-10 seconds) you will probably not notice the current major issue with the game. Although considered desync, you may have 200+ FPS and are ping below 20ms and still find that your opponent will be able to back-stab you while being in front of you. You might be able to shoot arrows through them and inflict no damage. You might have 10 of your friends help you gang up on one person and find that even though you have them completely surrounded, they are able to block in all directions at the same time.
Simple mechanics for this game are broken, such as; opening a door may launch you into the air causing damage to your player. Respawning in certain towns will cause you to be stuck on top of a tower where you have to jump and lose half your health to get down. Selling items may cause them to be stuck in your inventory after being sold (until you restart the game). Prices for items sold by merchants may or maynot be 10 times the listed prices. Just to name a few.
Major mechanics for this game are broken; Being a game that is based around combat, where the combat system is not only flawed but downright unplayable. (This video gives an example;
While the promised overhaul to the combat system appears to be a possible fix to some of the issues, this game has yet to reach it’s claimed Alpha phase of development. TL; DR version:
I am keenly aware that Skyhill does enough right to merit a recommendation. However, I am going to give it a CAREFUL recommendation at the current stage and the current price. 15€ is a tad high for what this game is. It needs some more content, methinks... For now, anything from 33% off or more would make it an easy buy, as you will absolutely get your money's worth.
Longer version:
In Skyhill, you are a businessman on a short trip who decides to rest in the best Suite of a large luxurious 100-story hotel during a time of war. During his stay, one of the warring sides (and obviously the losing one), the Confederates, launches a biological weapon at your location that turns everyone into mutants or zombies. You survive, but soon the hunger drives you out and you need to find a way to survive and go to the ground using all the resources you can fnd at your disposal, or die trying in this post-apocalyptic rogue-lite game.
So let's take a look at what the game does well, and what poorly.
The GOOD:
1. Lots of rooms to explore and loot - you will have over 190 rooms to explore and loot throughout your adventure, contaning everything from food to stuff you can use as weapons or consumables, or to save for later for crafting.
2. Upgradable stations - in short, your suite is your fortress. You can improve it in a number of ways. You can create better weapon building or cooking stations, fortify the door and fix up the bed so you can rest better and regain health.
3. Lots of items to craft and use - the amount of weapons to make and use in combat is amazing - and it pays to note that some weapons can also be upgraded to better versions by using the core weapon(s). The devs really went overboard with the craftables be it weapons, food, or stuff you can make on the fly like bandages and medicine. The system really forces you to think whether you should use a certain item or save it for later. And about that...
4. Decisions you make when it comes to craftables matter - being a rogue-lite with a randomly generated loot, it is always a huge decision whether to use a certain item or not, as god knows whether you'll find another one of those. In the end, when all falls into place, knowing that you've made the correct decisions is extremely satisfying.
5. An RPG system that ties well into the weapon crafting - you have 4 skills that can be improved throughout the adventure and govern various types of combat - strength (the ability to wield powerful heavy weapons that do the most damage), speed (the ability to wield fast weapons and also get faster with improved chance for 2 action per turn), dexterity (the ability to wield weapons based on agility and dodge in combat) and accuracy, which improves you chance to hit.
6. Starting and unlockable perks that make your playthroughs vary a lot  - from the ability to always go first to being extra lucky or have an extra ration or a medkit in your backpack, picking different perks during the various playthroughs will let you experience the game from a different perspective.
7. Great combat - as a consequence of 3-6, the combat in this game is really good, and the outcome of a fight always ties into every decision you have made so far, be it wrong or right. And talking about decisions, you can also manually target various parts of the enemy body to inflict more damage at a higher chance to miss or less damage with a higher chance to hit. Just remember to run away when things go bad... No need to die heroically when you can still live to fight another day.
8. Mini quests to keep you occupied while exploring - from finding keys to open various rooms to discovering cell phones with messages on them, you always have someting to look for as you search the floors of the hotel.
9. Good game aesthetic for a rogue-lite - while I wouldn't put that on the top of the list, I still appreciate how the game looks for a 2-D one.
10. Great replayability - the combination of perks, stuff you find, character build you make, and the little quests always make for a different experience the next time you boot up the game.
And now let's take a look at the BAD:
1. To counter #10 of the GOOD, even though a good number of parts of the game feel differently based on the perks, skills, weapons and stuff you pick, you ultimately do the same thing over and over again - find loot, craft, eat food, make weapons, open rooms, fight, survive, and hopefully get out of the hotel alive. I, personally, finished the game 3 times in my 5 hours of play, and sadly, I couldn't shake that feeling upon leaving the hotel...
2. The RNGesus can make or break your game, unless you like to invest heavily in accuracy so that you wont miss too often. Or, of course, you get stuff that doesn't fit your character build at all... Or not enough food or medicine... or other stuff... you get the point.
3. You can lose games through no fault of your own - in true rogue-lite fashion, victory through correct actions is not guaranteed. You may not find the stuff you need to get you set up properly, or you can get attacked way too often and die, and so on and so forth.
4. I didn't exactly enjoy the music... while it undoubtedly fits the whole experience, I eventually muted it and played my own.
5. Once you unlock all the perks, dying does feel like a true game over - until you unlock every perk, dying is ok and always lets you try something new the next time around. But once you unlock everything, dying is just that - death, game over, force restart.
Conclusion:
I am keenly aware that Skyhill does enough right to merit a recommendation. However, I am going to give it a CAREFUL recommendation at the current stage and the current price. 15€ is a tad high for what this game is. It needs some more content, methinks...For now, anything from 33% off or more would make it an easy buy, as you will absolutely get your money's worth. Why?
Easy. If you are a huge loot hoarder like me, like exploring, improving and seeing the stuff you do matter, this game is absolutely the right one for you. However, if you get easily irritated by loss, bad dice rolls, or games that expect you to play them for a bit to learn their quirks, I would stay away from it.
