Disclaimer: I received a digital key of this game free.  My comments and reviews are my own.
Gameplay Video:
In this game the end happened and you are, possibly, the only one left in the entire city.  The rest has become mutated creatures out to kill and eat anything that is not them.
Each floor has a lobby and 2 rooms.  The lobby can be the host of some nice goods like vending machines.  But they also hold power boxes that need to be repaired if the elevator is to reach any floor below that one(including the floor the power box is on).  The rooms can carry more resources than the lobbies and may hide subquests you can take on for extra experience.
But the mutants are in the building.  They want to kill you.  Take whatever weapon you can find(even if it gives less damage, it's better than going bare-fisted) and kill them.  You can let that weapon fly or go for a more 'aimed' approach.  But accuracy is vital.  Should you miss, death will be one step closer.  Once you have slain enough you will level up.  This will give you stat points that can give you an edge or make that weapon you are wielding a lot more potent than it is.
But remember: dying is normal.  As you die you will gain perks that can also give you a push to escaping Skyhill.  The passive has benefits but also have a cost.  For example: you can be impervious to food-poisoning but hunger will be much more lethal.  There are also active perks.  Some are single-use while others require you to wait before using again.
It's a good thing that home base is a VIP room.  Access to this allows you to upgrade various parts of the room.  Improve your workbench for better weapons.  That bed, as damaged as it is, can be turned into a five-star comfort.  That door doesn't look safe, but that can be alleviated.  Home cooking can be a dream come true if you bring the right components.
The graphics are simple but well designed.  Enemy animations to walking down the stairs in fast-forward.  The music also adds to the somber feeling of the game.
This is a lovely game.  If this interests you, but you are on the edge try the demo.

The main problem with this game is there is too much of not enough.
The game has turn based combat - but there is barely any strategy to it other than picking which dice to roll. There is nothing actively happening in these fights to make the player feel interested. All you feel is frustration over your health ticking down when there is nothing you can actively do inside or outside the combat system to better yourself.
The game has RPG stat elements  - but they are probably the lamest, most simplistic I've ever seen. Leveling a character is so linear and obvious that it shouldn't make a player scratch his head any longer than 5 seconds to figure out what path to take (largely dependant on what weapon the game's RNG decides to give you early on). There isn't even any defense ratings for character or monsters, making the whole weapon/damage system feel hugely simplistic and unrewarding.
There's a crafting system - it's pretty bread and butter. The actual items you can create and variety isn't too bad really. But the way the game plays out just makes it another aspect that falls to the side as unrewarding, plagued by RNG happenstance, and rather pointless. It's true you will need to use it to some extent to make it to the bottom, but I doubt you would need to invest in much, which is good considering there is no active way to get materials you really need. In other survival games, you have areas that have greater or exclusive chances to wield certain items. This game it's all at the drop of a hat, and it completely makes the player feel void of any real sense of achievement, because they never feel like they are actively surviving.
The premise of the game sounds super neat - but in reality it's such a hollow rendition of what the game promises on paper. You have to escape a hotel from the 100th floor and get to the bottom. When you realize that each floor has two... yes, two rooms on each floor, I think that's when it kicks in how lazy, barebones and unadventurous this game really is. I'm also not sure what hotels these developers have been to, but this building barely even qualifies to be a crappy highrise in Newham.
In the end , this needed to be fleshed out, in all areas, by a factor of 10. The price of admission makes it clear that they're not even shy (or are perhaps ignorant) to have made such a minimalist and lacking game.

I am so torn on writing this review.  One thing for sure, it is very original.  It could be so relaxing, it could be so soothing, it could be so awesome.  Let's just say it is so close to those three things.  What is holding me back from a thumbs up is the controls.  What they are is frustrating as heck.  The best way to describe the game is as an organic RTS, so for the movement of your objects I expect that to be sloppy and flowing.  The controls are so simple, yet so botched in implementation.  You control two differnent things, an organism(s) and the anti-bodies that it produces.  You left click on your organism to select it and right click in the direction that you want it to go and it will most of the time meander in that direction, bouncing off stuff it hits.  That is the organic sloppy part and it moves like it should.  The anti-bodies you control by left or right clicking and whle holding in the mouse button create a bounding box around the anti-bodies you want to move.  Once you do that the selected anti-bodies turn a brighter white and then you left click on the target you want them to attack or on a point you want them to move to.  Your mouse wheel zooms in and out pretty much centered on where your cursor is and moving the cursor to the edge of the screen pans the map in that direction.  Pretty standard stuff.  Where the controls fail is in the implementation.  For the next part of my description please note that I play in full screen mode with a dual monitor setup.  If you move the cursor to the very edge of the screen the panning stops, you have to have the cursor about 1/2" from the edge of the screen for the panning to work.  If you go to the edge of the screen and the panning stops, your next action can't be to start a bounding box, it just fails to start the first corner when you push either mouse button.  You have to release the button and start again, usually when you do this you move back to or pass through the 1/2" from the edge of the screen and then the map starts panning you away from where you wanted to start your bounding box.  As far as the edge of the screen that abutts the other monitor, there is no stopping the cursor at the edge, if you move the cursor outside the screen and onto the second monitor and as soon as you click the game minimizes.  There is also the frustrating act of trying to select your organism, sometimes you have to click it several times to select it and make it active.  I think what happens is that at times when you single left click you actually select a single anti-body that is over top of the organism. (and there are hundreds of anti-bodies at times).
Bottom line is that this game is good as it is now, and if they fix the controls so that you don't have to constantly fight the interface, it would be fantastic.  The sound track is almost hypnotic, the visuals are awesome fractals that grow and pulsate as your organism(s) grow.  With the controls, when things are busy on the screen it is just a frustrating mess.  On a scale of 1 to 10, the game as of now is a 4.9.  Fix the controls and it is 9.5+.

A fantastic step up from Evoland 1, Evoland 2 goes from being an appreciable parody of games, to a full interesting action adventure game in its own right. While the basic idea is the same (homage to game, full of mini games, genre sidesteps, and references), the characters have dimension, and an actual story exists beyond being a big reference to JRPGs.
Graphics changes are handled through time travel now, with the future being more modern graphics, and the past being as far back as Gameboy graphics. Random encounters are gone, except for one area that makes "random encounters" its genre-gimmick, and even then, it's done in a better way than the first game did.
The game really has everything. Off the top of my head after beating it, I recall the following: top down zelda style, sidescrolling zelda style, megaman, old arcade donkeykong, bejeweled, guitar hero/rhythm game, top down shooter, sidescrolling shooter, 2d fighting game, bomberman, JRPG turn based combat, final fantasy tactics/fire emblem strategy RPG combat, double dragon beatemup combat, MGS style stealth sections, and a card game reminiscient of Magic: the gathering. I'm pretty sure I missed a few in there somewhere. There's also a few puzzle-y sections that call back to Professor Layton style puzzles.
The game is a joy to play through, and without spoiling it, the time travel is handled extremely well without being hackneyed, paradoxical, or full of holes. The story in the end does leave a little bit to speculation but otherwise ties things up nicely.
If you liked 1, 2 will blow you away, and if you didn't like 1, I sincerely recommend giving 2 a chance, just because it feels like an actual game rather than as a parody of one.

The first Evoland was an odd beast. Although it lacked depth, it was generally fun and interesting enough to travel through the different eras and see what the game would throw at you next.
Evoland 2 seemed to have taken this criticism to heart and try a little harder to develop it's characters and story to be a more solid game in it's own right. Unfortunately, this is exactly the reason it falls down: rather than having it's own quirky charm, it's just a collection of worse versions of other games. Because of this, the cracks stand out all the more. The professor layton puzzles are a very good example of what I mean. Because it only copied the PL games at the most basic level, a lot of important functions are lost. This turns the library segment from a fun homage to frustrating slog. The addition of a simple note system like the PL games, could have mitigated a huge amount of this frustration. With the longer and more memory heavy types of puzzles they chose to include, you are expected to keep a huge amount of information in your head. This makes trial and error or simply looking up the answer far more effective, which your game should never allow.
The game is also very buggy. I have encountered numerous glitches within the first couple of hours, for example:
-Character models bugging out
-Audio distortions which blow out my eardrums
-Enemies getting stuck or ending up places they shouldnt be
-Lag and slowdown in certain places
-Crashes
And a lot of general weirdness like speeding up several times the normal run speed when leaving a building.
To wrap this up:
- The graphics are passable but not good
- Soundtracks are okay, but loop too quickly and start to get on your nerves
- Hitboxes are inconsistent and weird. Too many times have I been hit when I shouldnt have been, and not been hit when I should have been
-A lot of information isn't conveyed very well to the player (if you forget what you were last doing, you could be spending a very long time figuring it out)
- The characters are pretty bland and the 'choice' joke is beaten to death.
- The humor is not as good as the first game, and the references are about as subtle as an anvil to the face
I feel like Evoland 2 lost sight of what made the first game interesting. As it is, it's just an inferior copycat of better games. Each part of the game just makes me wish I was playing those games instead.

Report after one permadeath game: nice little classical roguelike that doesn't feel dumbed down.
Right of the bat you face elements like digging through the level and freezing water to advance, dynamic poison gas clouds that expand and shrink around vents, enemies with dangerous abilities like making you dizzy, that you can't just bump through mindlessly. Quite refreshing compared to other "lite" roguelikes where the first few levels are devoid of any challenge.
This is still simpler than a "full-fledged" roguelike as there is no item identification, inventory space is very limited with barely any management, and there seems to be very few item types. It seems that you only get four spells and keep them for the whole game.
Each level I saw had a locked monster zoo, an orb you must push into place for a strength boost, an altar to remove curses, and a merchant. It's pretty neat as it allows you to plan for what you want to do, but it might get repetitive in the long run. The environment for the second level was quite different from the first though, so the game seems to have avoided the "generic same wall tile for 10 levels" syndrome.
All in all, recommended, and most especially if you never tried a real classical roguelike like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, Nethack, TOME, Brogue and the like, and would like to get a taste of what they can offer without learning a lot of keyboard commands.
If you're a fan of classical roguelikes this is a must play. If you're new to the genre this is a great game to introduce you without sacrificing depth. 10/10 cant recommend enough

This is a true roguelike that is in my opinion worth the asked price, and is worth a look if you're a fan of the genre. It bears some resemblance (in terms of gameplay and feel) to dungeon crawl stone soup, and angband, though much more graphical and streamlined than either of those games. It's nothing like caves of qud, cataclysm dda, dwarf fortress, and etc, so don't expect anything like that, it's purely a dungeon crawl style of roguelike. That being said it's executed very well, it seems alot more fair and easy going at first than all of the previously mentioned games, and therefor would be good for beginners to the genre. The UI, controls, and inventory system are alot more simplistic/streamlined than most other roguelikes as well, you start off with a low number of inventory slots, and a few equipment slots (armor, and weapon). It has a bit of a puzzle/strategy feel in terms of the gameplay as well, which in that regard reminds me of brogue, the gameplay is bottlenecked to the tune of focusing on strategy and skill, in contrast to some roguelikes that revel in tons of details and situational role-playing charm. I recommend watching a video of the game or two before buying, but overall I think it's a sound purchase for fans of roguelikes.

This is a good, stripped down tactical combat based, classic-era style roguelike. What I mean by this is that it's a straight out dungeon crawl in the style of the original Rogue, but remarkably simple in design. The original Rogue was wonderful but owing to it's early origins on mainframe computers, suffered from over-complexity in it's UI.
This game is perhaps a touch over-simplified, in comparison. That being said, this was clearly a design choice, one clearly made to focus purely on tactical combat. In that aspect, the game seems pretty solid so far.
I've not been playing roguelike games for a long time, but in that period I've pumped hundreds and hundreds of hours into them, and played loads of different ones, and many different types to boot.  I must admit I've not really touched on too many of the 7Day roguelike competition entries yet, and I suspect that there you might find many more examples of games of the type that Curse of Yendor is attempting to be. With that in mind, I thought it'd be good to try out this kind of short-play roguelike a little more.
When it comes to these "coffee-break" roguelikes, my benchmark is the superb Brogue by Brian Walker, which I consider to have one of the best thought out game designs ever: not just in roguelikes, but in video games in general. It's balance and replayability are pretty much unmatched in games of it's type. So far, I've not played Curse of Yendor a huge amount but I feel I've gotten my head around how it's likely to play now. It doesn't have the same depth as Brogue, owing to the design choices over the limited magical set: they are two very different games in style, but comparisons can be drawn in that I can clearly see that each game chose it's design in order to create a certain type of experience, rather than play to the old school crowd. In this regard, I think CoY comes across very well.
It's not a very deep game, with regards to the variety of things you can do. However, the game's tactical play more than makes up for this, I feel. Having a limited set of commands really works to it's benefit: if you're going to go for minimalism, keep it really minimal! CoY is a success in minimal design.
My one request would be an ASCII mode. I know it's probably not so popular with the mainstream Steam audience, but I'm not so keen on tilesets as I find they distract me from the game mechanics. That being said, the graphics here are colourful and meaningful, and they're growing on me!  The interface is quite clear and has a sort of late 80's Atari ST feel to them, which helps a lot considering I'm an old bugger who digs that kind of aesthetic!
This is worth the money, I feel, and I'm looking forwards to playing it through to see whether it gets any deeper :)

Empyrion could be called mine craft in space but there is certainly more of a game here than just building things. At its core you use cubes that can be used in a variety of shapes to build bases and ships to combat both players and AI to gather resources or meet objectives in small basic missions that can be done by yourself or in groups.
While the interface is a bit clunky and the ships themselves lack a physics grid, meaning capital ships will have to be motionless to roam about on or a seat must be taken to prevent falling out of the ship.
Over all constructing things is simple as is making blue prints to reproduce later however the build tools are still a bit clunky and hard to use for me and there is no ability present to replace lost blocks, only repairing damaged ones. So heavily damaged ships are usually left abandoned with the core removed to be rebuilt again from scratch.
Over all the voxel used in the game is one of the better examples i've seen. While there is no impact damage or crumple physics like in space engineers you are free to manipulate the terrian rather easily.
A decent array of weapons and a rather solid prefab list of ships and bases exist for those that would rather not spend hours building make sure there is a good balance of action with this survival game.
Planets also are rather diverse with different terrians, hazards and even gravity which is a nice touch and might force changes to ships to over come these issues.
Over all its a good co-op survival game though with a weaker single player experince. I would like to see more officail servers but the verified ones seems to be pretty good for the ones i've tried.
It still has work left to be done to come onto its own but this is game certainly does what starmade does but better with more pleasing graphics.

I love mini-golf/crazy-golf, and had high hopes for this game. Unfortunately, while it was fun for a short while, the bugs and limited courses get boring quickly.
UX
The actual controls are okay, but there are long delays between responses where you aren't sure if the game registered what you are trying to do or not. Restart on the challenges should put you back ready to take your shot, but puts you back before the preview of the course, for example.
Also, there are bugs where sometimes you put the ball in the hole, but it lags for 20 seconds, then registers the stroke, but either puts the ball back where it was before your last shot, or hides it beneath the ground, both forcing you to restart.
COURSES
The 18 courses available are great for a tutorial, but once you get into tournaments, it is disappointing to find out that those 18 courses are the only courses in the game, and you play them in the same order everytime. The game needs a lot more variety of courses, and many more difficult challenges.
SUMMARY
There is a little fun to be had here, but the game still needs a lot of work. I woudn't recommend buying this on it's own, but if you get it in a bundle, it's worth a little play.

While less of a game and more of interactive media, the story of "Finding Paradise", and it being a follow-up of its excellent predecessor "To The Moon", has been masterfully written. There are moments where there are lapses in the story to compensate for silliness, or so it would appear until you reach the ultimate goal [no spoilers provided.] Everything related to the humour of the game, excluding the very beginning, plays into the necessity of explaining the ending, and at nearly every turn you will find something that will shock you as a revelation of something you had likely previously viewed as either insignificant or minute in its complexity as part of the story.
This is gaming that has been steered away from the 'game' aspect, and more towards the story teller's side. This is not a bad thing innately, because there are games that do this in much the opposite manner, but if you are looking for something that's treated as a game where everything is explicit in its results immediately, you are at the wrong place. "Finding Paradise" is, at its core, a refined cinematic work of art. Feeling as though it lacks smaller facets of investigation on a personal level unlike "To The Moon", it still catches on with its linear figure and reducing the amount of general confusion that was accompanied by some parts in previous series entries.
Only thing, again mostly spoiler free, is that the title is misleading to the actual story telling that is provided, because you do not necessarily go looking for Paradise, but that's a minor caveat of interpretive art. All-in-all, Finding Paradise helps tie in new pieces of this beautiful series, and I can scarcely wait for the next entry to grace us. If you like story telling, or liked "To The Moon", buy this as soon as you can...

The name itself suggests the game is much more expansive than its predecessor, Arkham Asylum. The sheer size of Arkham City leaves you with so much to do and so much to discover. Whether you're beating up gangers, tracking down leads to crimes, collecting trophies, completing challenges, or just pushing along the story, the game never really seems to have a dull moment.
To achieve 100% completion is...tasking to say the least. I found myself falling out of enjoyment and forcing myself to accomplish meticulously mundane tasks that became nothing more than a chore. However, if you are indeed someone who wants the absolute most out of a game, Arkham City most definitely delivers.
The combat system is nothing new if you have played Arkham Asylum, save some new techniques the game has added to your combos in an effort to diversify the combat. However, after taking on enough groups of gangers, you will quickly find it is not diverse enough.
I thoroughly enjoyed the two main villains in this game and the direction they took the story. I absolutely did not expect the ending to go the way it did and, if I am being honest here, it left me devastated and shocked. What's more is I love the number of classic Batman villains that made an appearance and most of your favorites all of substantial roles to play in the mischief and mayhem across the city. There are even plenty of side quests that cross paths with other famed villains of the Batman universe. Furthermore, the sidestory and character swapping with Catwoman is an unnecessary but much welcomed device within the game. It doesn't hurt that they made Selena Kyle smoking hot.
All in all, this game was very much enjoyable and absolutely worth every penny. I loved Arkham Asylum and this game improved on everything that was integral to Arkham Asylum.

This game is not bad. However, it is overpriced for what it is.
When you first start playing the game is fun, however after half an hour or so it quickly becomes repetitive and it will seem as if your success is very random and there is no real skill involved.
In fact this is not entirely true - to have any hope of completing the game you need to make good use of the crafting system and you need to be strategic to survive. Once you start paying attention to upgrading your room, crafting weapons and cooking food the odds start to shift in your favour and for me the game then became fun again.
Unfortunately you'll have to figure out most of this stuff for yourself as the tutorial is pretty lightweight  - I didn't realise until I'd played and died a few times that you could sleep, upgrade the bed and various other items in your room etc.
Once I started to formulate a strategy I did enjoy the game again - I think a lot of people give up before they ever reach this point though because the game doesn't really emphasise the importance of crafting, sleeping and so on. A lot of the perks actually make things worse too, which can be frustrating, so choose wisely.
Gameplay is based far too overtly around probability - I sort of didn't mind that but a lot of it is trying to be clever by offering perks that on the face of it sound good but aren't or vice-versa, which really is a way of making you die more often and lengthening the game. There are perhaps eight or ten different enemies and several of them are variations on the same creature.
Now I've beaten the game there's really no replay value left in it. For £5 or less I'd probably recommend it if you enjoy roguelite games - it will entertain you for a few hours if you don't get bored before the strategy elements start to crystallise. At over a tenner I'd save your money and wait for it to get cheaper.

By all rights, I should love this game. It plays like Legend of Zelda with JRPG elements, and the gimmick of each era having different graphical quality's very well executed. Although I'm going to play this game to completion, I'm probably going to delete it after I'm done. Even though I'd still recommend it to others, I'm not sure that I like this game, at the end of the day.
My main complaint lies in how many minor glitches, such as the main character "hovering" on slopes in the 2D portions of the game, end up causing major gameplay consequences. These end up ramping up difficulty in ways that I don't appreciate, and take the fun out of playing.
My other issue stems from the characters themselves. While it's admirable to play with gaming tropes, merely lampshading them does not a clever story make. The characters lack... well... character, and their dialogue tends to find the longest route to say something simple.
Something that leaves me ambivalent are allllll of the mini-games spread throughout. They're neat, they're stable, but there're so freakin' many of 'em. I wish some of that detail went into the main gameplay, like... I dunno, a dash/dodge feature or some more complex combat options and equipmment. You get what amounts to a lllllot of games just in this one, but man... I really would have liked more focus on the primary gameplay.
With that said, I can't fault the creators on this project. The world they've made has a lot more detail than a lot of the Adventure/RPGs on here, and the treasure hunting's pretty snazzy (I just wish there were more treasure to hunt!). It's packed with little nods and references, and you get the feeling that the people who worked on this game had a good time doing so.
Tentacle Wars or another similar flash game is more fun. This didn't do much for me.

This is a rouelike. Sometimes called a 'true' rougelike or a traditional rougelike. Anyone who has been playing the genera long enough will know that thanks to the word Yendor in the title.
If you enjoy classic rougelikes, the older ones. Nethack, ADOM, Angband and so on, this is definitely something to look into. The sheer amount of terrain and terrain interactions with your spells is worth it. Often turning even simple encounters into odd yet engaging environmental puzzles.
If you're not into traditional rougelikes? Check it out anyways. It has a fairly good tutorial (that you are supposed to die in) and it's a touch' stripped down' from some other traditional rougelikes. It's a top down fantasy turn based adventure where you control a single character. Death is permanent and you have to start over each time you die. Which sounds frustrating but... well, it is. That does not mean it isn't fun.
While Curse of Yendor does pretty much all the classic rouge like stuff, it does it with style. A solid persistent story with a villain that you begin to feel a relationship with. Turn based single character control combat. Spells. Equipment. Risk vs reward gameplay, lots of weird fantasy monsters all with different weaknesses and strengths.
Of course, you'll die, a lot. That's kind of the rougelike thing. However, it's at least in my experience, YASD way more than anything else. As in, Yet Another Stupid Death. Where when I die I look back ten rounds of the game and see, oh, no, I died because I decided to try on this heavy armor in an unsafe area.
If you're an old hat at rougelikes this one is a solid continuation of form that has perfected environmental interactions with an interesting and detailed weakness and strength chart for weapons and magic. If you're new to rougelikes, this is not a bad one to put your money on and see what the fuss is about.
Dying and having to start over from scratch isn't for everyone, but the knuckle dragging intense experience that can come from it is often worth the trade off and this is one of those games that will give you that kind of experience. Just be sure you know what you're getting into.

A very nice little roguelike - the UI is quite clean and usable once you get used to it (much better than Dungeonmans, which I love but you're always fighting the UI and graphics).
Mechanics are much clearer than in Dredmor - you can almost always guess, or should have been able to guess, what weapon type or magic type some mob you haven't seen before is vulnerable to.
When you start, it'll feel too lean - OMG, only 3 classes, only three spare inventory slots, no potions, not a huge map?  But it opens up - you can find inventory slot expansions, for instance.  There are lots of different terrain types, lots of little environmental puzzles, and it's great fun to just blow up the map with your earthquake spells. You'll find out the maps are just the right size - by the time you're tired of this level it's time to move on to the next.  And each of the 3 classes is very survivable.
There's also a continuing 'plot' - not a heavy one, but there's a goal, and antagonists who will torment you over the levels...   Hell, it's well worth the asking price!  If you're bored of Dredmor, Maj'ael, and Dungeonmans, this is your next stop.

The Curse of Yendor is a simple but tactical-like roguelike game that you must make sound decisions.  Do I attack the mob while my health is low and try to get the treasure, or do I go somewhere and rest first.  Each run through is random, so if you are not careful, you may die on floor 1...or die on floor 5.  And the loot is randomized as well.  It's a nice little game to play when you don't have hours of time to invest.  And it's always fun to see if you can beat your score from the previous game.  If you are into rogue-likes, I recommend it! :)

I highly recommend this game, both as a coffee break roguelike and as a game you can sink your teeth into. If you are a roguelike fan, you need to try it.  I have no doubt it will inspire future games.

I mean, just when you think you are getting the hang of things and building up a powerful character, along comes some necromancer who decides to cast a fear spell on you that sticks.... And at that same moment, a room full of monsters was opened up. Oops! Time to die! The perma-death option makes it so much more fun.
One tip - you can freeze lava with your ice spell. It takes a moment to figure out how, but once you do, it'll open up some nice areas.
This is an indie developer that really deserves community support. He continues to make fun games for inexpensive prices. Let's help him pay his bills so he can continue adding more content and making more games!

In short (TLDR): Fluid gameplay with mechanics that synergise well. Addictive, one more go vibe. I recommend The Curse of Yendor to all RL fans, and to anyone interested in trying out a roguelike for the first time.
A bit of context: I play a lot of RL's ranging from more traditional titles such as DCSS & Angband, to Cogmind & CDDA. The Curse of Yendor is modern roguelike with a traditional feel. I have been playing the game on Itch.io hence the low play count in Steam. The gameplay is fluid and feels much akin to DCSS and Brogue in terms of pace and ease of use. There is full keyboard control which is greatly appreciated (full mouse control is also available).
The game mechanics aren't complex however synergise well together. While simple to play the game still requires some tactical awareness and timely use of spells and items. Like any good roguelike you can die in a turn if you're not paying attention.
There appears to be some updates with the Steam release (which are available on Itch.io too), so existing owners may want to give this another go.
The game is addictive and fun. Recommended.

Instead of trying to be an expansive dungeon simulator, Curse of Yendor offers a streamlined experience that focuses on moment to moment tactical choices. On that note, players of DCSS should feel right at home here. Different enemies will have resistances and weaknesses that must be exploited for success. Progress through the dungeon feels meaningful, with bad choices being severely punished (on the Insane! difficulty, anyway). CoY allows you to manipulate the dungeon environment through spells to accomplish your goals, which is a concept that I really wish was utilized more often in this genre. You do this through fire, ice and earth spells - each of which  has different effects (spreading fire, freezing liquids, causing cave-ins, etc).
Definitely a fun and polished game, and has earned itself a place on my roguelike rotation.

Empyrion could be called mine craft in space but there is certainly more of a game here than just building things. At its core you use cubes that can be used in a variety of shapes to build bases and ships to combat both players and AI to gather resources or meet objectives in small basic missions that can be done by yourself or in groups.
While the interface is a bit clunky and the ships themselves lack a physics grid, meaning capital ships will have to be motionless to roam about on or a seat must be taken to prevent falling out of the ship.
Over all constructing things is simple as is making blue prints to reproduce later however the build tools are still a bit clunky and hard to use for me and there is no ability present to replace lost blocks, only repairing damaged ones. So heavily damaged ships are usually left abandoned with the core removed to be rebuilt again from scratch.
Over all the voxel used in the game is one of the better examples i've seen. While there is no impact damage or crumple physics like in space engineers you are free to manipulate the terrian rather easily.
A decent array of weapons and a rather solid prefab list of ships and bases exist for those that would rather not spend hours building make sure there is a good balance of action with this survival game.
Planets also are rather diverse with different terrians, hazards and even gravity which is a nice touch and might force changes to ships to over come these issues.
Over all its a good co-op survival game though with a weaker single player experince. I would like to see more officail servers but the verified ones seems to be pretty good for the ones i've tried.
It still has work left to be done to come onto its own but this is game certainly does what starmade does but better with more pleasing graphics.

Their target audience can be hit dead on with this game, however it wasn't originally marketed that way.

The game is somewhat overpriced for what you get. If you buy it during a sale, may be worth it as it's a decent casual game.
In essence, it's a simple rogue-like game that relies heavily on RNG, i.e. luck. I had a few games that I needed to restart after a few floors as I wasn't getting any items. The best perk I have discovered is "Total Mess" as it guarantees that you get an item every time you search (which is very VITAL), although you do lose an item randomly every 10 actions, which can be really irritating if it's your primary weapon. The strategy is to leave as much junk as possible in your inventory, while consuming stuff that you do need so that they don't randomly disappear. Another strategy is to put as many points as you can in accuracy while still having sufficient points to carry a decent weapon.
Storyline is very thin, and not very satisfying. Gameplay wise, although it's quite fun, there is much room for improvement. Go ahead and read some of the other negative reviews, and you will get a good idea of what it is lacking.
Overall, a 6/10.

The game is pretty much decided on how quickly you can spawn your antibodies, then zerg rush enemy spheres. It seems to be somewhat based on Eufloria, with some differences.
First off: gameplay is slightly different, since the cells (planets in Eufloria?) move. That's a nice idea, but the implementation is odd; it involves lots of clicking (and re-clicking) and dragging, and cells actually bump against each other and then gently drift away.
Second: it's a lot less complicated. There's simply not much to do. After getting the basics, you expect some extra game elements, which don't exist. Perhaps the AI could become more challenging, which it doesn't. The same strategy actually works for all levels!
Third: there's a 'upgrade your cells' - feature included, which seems a failure; it automatically means you're the fastest and strongest cell out there, which lowers the difficulty even further!
It does look somewhat nice, but there's not much graphical content. I can't say the music is good, because it gets really repetitive, which is quite an accomplishment for a game that's about two hours long.

What is this? And why is it so addicting?
Maybe because it's similar to an online multiplayer cell-based game but it doesn't have a learning curve like a brick wall. Or maybe because it's just a super fun little game. It's not exceptionally long, it's not exceptionally revolutionary, but it's darn good fun, and addictive enough to have you keep coming back.
Granted the game slows down very quickly once you're waiting on the last few high level upgrades and aren't getting much to fuse together, but at least it's not a wait or pay mobile game so you can grind out that upgrade if you really want it without maxing a credit card.
But in all seriousness, buy this game (it's really not expensive) and have fun.

Bought Curse of Yendor on a lark with all this extra cash I've got now that Marvel Heroes doesn't want my money any more (BUE bleh).
Yendor is a turn-based rogue-a-like with charming early Ultima graphics. Under the retro hood is a lot of gaming goodness. Besides the usual monsters, loot, vendors, keys and puzzles, there are some surprises.
The procedural, modifiable, tile-based terrain system is what sold me on getting CoY. If you get a pick you can chop through stone walls, or take them down with an earthquake spell. You can shoot thorugh barred windows. You can freze water. Reeds block missiles, but if you cast fireballs in reeds, you can catch yourself on fire. Run away!  Destroying the right tiles will weaken the big boss later in the game. I'd love to see a game with triple the variable terrain types as CoY, but for now, this is a lot of fun.
CoY has a clean interface, rebindable keys, multiple difficulty settings and even permadeath for you machochis- er, purists out there. Fortunately, permadeath can be turned off if you have other stuff to do in your life than lose your character right before the final boss fight and have to start over. Best of all, the grind does not feel grindy yet, so here's to many hours of happy hacking.
The Curse of Yendor is a classic dungeon crawling RPG. Choose between a warrior, rogue, or wizard, and make your way through procedurally generated levels.  Overall, a very simple and fun roguelike.

Saw this game off and on. Reviews went back and forth. Game has been in development for a long time. Still Alpha.
Decided to Finally take the plunge anyway.
First Impression was a very rough and unfinished (obvious because of Alpha) band-wagon game just trying to throw some stuff together and half-heartedly be in the mix of the survival, craft, open-world game craze.
My Son hopped on with me for a LAN Server game.
WE ARE HAVING A BLAST.
At first I told myself this is a cheap product. I was wrong.
Yea, enemies need to be smoothed out and their movement sucks. But the shear amount of what I'll call "isolated complexity" going on is incredible. What I mean by this is no, there is not background trading, world affects, faction relationships, universe political or local/global leader influences yet. But WHERE the player is active (Points of Interest, Villages, Capitols), there are several events taking place....
Ex: Being on some random planet, no clue what to do. Getting killed by basically everything. Can't even Imagine that we could actually build something and go to space at some point. Find a POI ....in this case a random Communication Hub with some Radars and Cannons. Die about 30 times trying to get inside. Running around feeling like kings looting it after such a dismal start. An enemy freaking Dropship comes and drops off Alien Assassins to kill us. Realizing we can destroy the Base's Core and REPLACE it with our own to now OWN it and now the same cannons the were killing us moments prior, are now shooting down Drones that were sent to destroy our newly claimed home.
In this game, you live and learn. And the fun is figuring it all out.
We spent hours making what we thought was an awesome home. It was all wood. (By the way, the combinations of shape designs you can have makes for some of the best base/vehicle building I have seen in a survival game.) We were happy to just survive an entire night for once without dying. "Warning: Drones have been sent to destroy your
Yea. Our base was shot to hell as we fought bravely with our pistols to defend it.
Then we realized we were mere ants to the world. And we learned how to make better materials, and stronger everything.
Even the mining is pleasing. You literally can dig your own cave or tunnel network.
The possibilities this game allows you to pursue is incredible. Hell, there is even a gun that lets you change color and texture of blocks! And I'm not saying just from Blue to Green. There is some complex textures that even "power on" when power is applied and glow with circuitry design....oh...and did I mention there is even Custom Signal Logic you can do within your Custom Built Base or Ships (there are different classes of vehicles that allow to travel different distances as well) that allow you to control entire network by switches you install.
There are a ton of features to balance. Oxygen, Temperature, Food, Armor, Radiation, Ammo, Repairs, Power, Fuel. All while trying to make your base, vehicles stronger and better.
And yes.
Eventually you can build something (or select a prefabricated design if you aren't comfortable going custom yet) and simply takeoff, and fly up.....into space. To a moon, an asteroid, another planet, another system, and blow up or land at even more POI's along the way or spaceships.
I hope the development continues.
As for the "Grind" issue. My Son and I had no complaints.
Within a few days of gameplay, being complete beginners, on a Hard Difficultly setting (except enemy difficultly...PS...currently all this does is increase their health to the point where it will take fun out of the game due to the insane amount of ammo it takes to kill the simplest things.) we have taken over a few bases and JUST got into space with our made spacecraft. Heck, they even have technologies that make your tools better and more efficient, and automated bots that can assist you in gather resources.
Supposedly this was easier to do before. But the amount of effort required as the game currently plays created an atmosphere of excitement and anticipation to accomplish space travel. It was rewarding and satisfying.
We couldn't even fathom doing so when we first started. There was plenty to learn and do just being on the surface. And doing so, while knowing we could "leave" all the while if we learned how, and built our way to success, made for an amazing experience.
Ya there is weird crap that happens and some things that don't make any sense. But it doesn't detract from the experience really, or leave the player feeling too jaded.
Devs. Keep it up.

One of my favorite games of all times. Where Rayman lacks, namely story, it shines, while not being that far behind gameplay-wise.
First and foremost, it's beautiful. The art is stunning, the music is wonderful, and overall it's very pleasing to all the senses.
Gameplay is the area where it's hard to assign a single score.
All areas are one huge seamless level and it's great, because it makes the world more real. It isn't static, it evolves as the game progresses. There're many interesting areas with fun gameplay. In one area, the ground keeps changing. In another area, gravity force changes direction as you move. But most fun parts, at least for me, are escape sequences where you have to run away from something or someone chasing you very quickly. They remind me about some levels of Rayman or Fly'n.
On the other hand, killing very similar enemies which respawn the moment you move off-screen is annoying (in some areas more than in other, often enemies can just be skipped). Backtracking through the whole map to collect new items, because you can reach more items with a new ability, is annoying. Not being able to replay certain areas is annoying (will be fixed in the Definitive Edition). However, most players are unlikely to encounter all this — no one forces you to collect every single item or explore 100% of the map.
There aren't any innovations, but it isn't something I'm after when I'm playing platformers. What really matters is fun. And there's plenty of it.
The game is difficult just on the right level — you'll never hit a wall of difficulty, but the game expects you to get better at playing over time, to learn new skills, to perfect your moves. Expect to die a lot, especially if you aren't hardcore player (I'm not).
(removed text)
Nevermind, the story is touching. After playing five or so times, it still gives me goosebumps, so complaining about little details at this point is absolutely silly.
For those who care, achievements are good. Some are story-based, some are collection-based, some are skill-based, and some are extremely difficult which very players can complete.

A bit underrated game about stealth and infiltration set in a dark, fantasy world.
I had this game on my radar for a while mostly due to the fact that it looked good and featured a goblin like main character in a Thief like world. Didn't know too much about the gameplay before diving in but I've seen mixed reviews. In the end I must admit I very much enjoyed the game despite some flaws and a bit hard difficulty level.
Styx: Master of Shadows is a third person stealth game. Set in a world that reminds the one in the Thief series but a bit more fantasy and bright. But the general feel is pretty similar - at least for me.
The story starts a bit slow and is a bit confusing at first. It's hard to make out exactly what's going on. But it comes around somewhere mid-game and when it starts making sense it starts to reel you in. And despite the rough start of "ok, this one is not for the story" I must admit it hooked me. Without giving anything away - you play as a goblin like creature trying to infiltrate Akenash tower in order to steal the heart of the tree. An amber producing tree. The amber in this world is a sort of drug and an extremely valuable thing. The story follows your journey through the tower while you seek to access it.
The visuals are pretty nice. Levels are well designed with a multitude ways you can approach certain objectives. Sometimes you get to travel the same area twice and doing so from different starting points is a very unique experience not often found in other games.
Audio layer is also well designed - the voice actors did pretty decent job and the soundtrack fits with the gameplay. Nothing breath taking but absolutely fine.
One thing to note about the gameplay is that it's pretty hard. I've struggled with first levels before figuring out there is quick save functionality which I would strongly advise to use. Without it - the auto-save spots are so rare that getting trough meant replaying up to half an hour of level progress. On the other hand learning the level layout made travelling through it all that much easier and satisfying. Even with the quick save - the game is still pretty challenging and though. I don't think I've achieved a "no alarm" or "no kill" or any other of the achievements for a single level of the game. It's not hard enough to discourage from playing though.
The game gives at your disposal a set of abilities. You can upgrade them between missions through experience points. You get them by completing secondary objectives and getting achievements. From the lot the most notable are amber vision - which is sort of night vision with benefits, invisibility - though for painfully short time and clones - can be useful at times although didn't find all that much use for them. Overall they're a nice addition though I've relied mostly on sneaking, moving between covers and quietly killing off guards.
Aside from that you have to manage your consumables - you get two health potions, two amber bottles - which are used for the above abilities and two throwing knives - probably most useful thing in the game. You can replenish them between levels or sometimes pick up along the way though they're all pretty scarce commodity and thus so much more valuable.
The game is fun. Although being very difficult it's really fun to play.
It has some flaws as mentioned in the beginning - of which two are most note worthy. First is the ledge detection and jumping. It takes time getting used to it. It's not very polished and can lead to a lot of trouble while trying to perform a tricky jump. The second problem lies with AI. While the enemies behave quite good and pose a challenge - the NPCs are terrible. Most of what they do is stand and shout. Even if no one is coming and you're murdering one of them just in front of the other. Makes up for a silly moments.
Overall I really did enjoy the game and would really recommend it to any stealth loving gamer.
Interesting take on the stealth genre. Killing is fun and satisfying, and so is tricking enemies. Complete stealth, at least for me, is incredibly difficult, so play on Easy if you need to.

Quake III Arena (1998) is a memorable classic in my opinion. Consider this game if you enjoy classics and fast paced FPS gameplay. Even though I think Quake Live is a clone of this which makes it pointless to pay for this.
Quake 3 Arena combines FPS gameplay with extreme speed of reflection and extreme-pace gameplay. As with old games, the game does not have much variation and no customization in comparison to today's games, but can still be a great fun.
The gameplay consists of players; humanoid shaped hitboxes that move at a very fast speed without penalties, with a weapon selection including a rocket launcher, a railgun (one-hit precision killer), a shotgun and a few machine guns. The game modes at least include DM, TDM and CTF, not sure about others.
The gameplay is just about maneuvering and shooting very quickly and precisely. When you die, you respawn right away and the insanely fast fun continues.

With no exaggeration or hyperbole, it would be 100% objectively correct to say that this is the absolute greatest competitive multiplayer shooter of all time. Anyone who says otherwise is simply wrong, and should probably kill themselves to save the embarrassment.

This is where it all began, the birthplace of the Arena Shooter genre. Insanely fast-paced, it pushes your skill to the limit. There's no place for overly complicated tactics or stupid gimmicks here, it's just pure, raw skill. Can you rocket-jump? You better learn quick then.

How would you feel when you are unable to proceed because you do not have the required abilities to deal with the enemy?
You could say, tough luck, it is your own fault, because you made the wrong choices.
And I grant you that.
But how can I make the right choices when I do not know the strengths and weaknesses of these abilities? And how can I foresee that the story seriously impacts the functioning of my party?  At two moments in the game you will be inflicted with a setback that unhinges your party's fighting power. Once, one of the party members gets killed because the story is written that way. And at another time her replacement, a magic user, gets robbed of her ability to do magic and so thousands of points sunk in developing her magic powers becomes nullified with one stroke.
So you might expect that the game takes this into account, but not at all: you cannot undo your choices nor does the game allow you to make up for the loss of a valuable party member.
This then, in a nutshell, is the problem with Blackguards..
This game is very much like searching for keys to doors, while you do not know which key opens which door, you do not know if a door leads to anything useful, you do not know when or if you will find the key or the door to which it belongs and you might find  that the keys and doors disappeared before you actually could make use of them.
So what is left is to go back to an earlier point in the game and find the right keys to the right doors: make the right choices. And unfortunately you might have to go a long way back: perhaps all the way to the beginning.
And then another issue pops up.
Blackguards is  basically a tactical battle simulator in which the battles are linked together by a thin storyline that gives the battles context. You will find that many of the common characteristics of a roleplay game are underdeveloped. For one, your party members are a given and so are their classes. Do not expect that you can build your own party.
Furthermore there are few choices in equipment so your party will be running around with the same armor and weapons for long stretches.  And while many places have shops, you will only visit them to restock your supplies.
But the crucial issue is that the story is simply too linear. While at some point you can select what to do first, you will be unable to change the storyline in any significant way. And because the story isn't really special at all, redoing this game just so you can change your characters is not enough of an incentive to go through the game again..
Even as a tactical battle simulator the game leaves much to be desired. For instance you are unable to determine the setup of your party members. More often than not the game gleefully shoves your more vulnerable members, your magic users, in the front line.  Hilarious is the ability to set traps. You have almost no time to set traps, let alone set the traps that actually make  difference. The traps are expensive, the relevant skill requires a massive amount of points and you have only a very limited amount of traps.
In addition some battles confront you with a special setup that is pivotal to the battle, often without explaining to you the specifics. In one battle, for instance, you will be able to make use of automated flamethrowers. But the game doesn't explain this to you, nor do you know what the impact is until you have seen their effect and you figured out how to operate them. It therefore requires you to redo the battle at least once.
Some battles are practically unwinnable until you achieve a certain level, or develop a certain ability to a certain level.
Is it all bad then?
Actually no.
When I went through the game the first time I actually was entertained. The game uses what I call the fall out principle. The fall out principle is that you start out as a nobody and then gradually start to make a difference when the story unfolds. This is the reverse of what you might call the dragon age effect in which  it is clear from the start that you are a special person destined to make a difference.
Personally I prefer the first angle to the last.
Also the characters are amusing, even though, or perhaps because, they are so cliche. The remarks of the Naurim, the grumpy dwarf, are pretty funny and in line of what you might expect from a dwarf: a fighter who distrusts magic users and elves.
The story, although linear, has a few twists and also there is some emotional connection as it involves a friend and later on a family member. It isn't also clearcut that the enemy is actually bad and it leaves things fuzzy  for a long time.
So it seems to me that if you go once through the game(using a game guide to form your party) then you might probably be entertained.
Verdict:
Blackguard is a nice filler when you are in between better games. Pick it up when it is in the bargain bin and around five dollars or euros or less.
(Note: steam doesn't allow for a meh score at the time of writing this review. This game most certainly belongs to this category. I gave it a thumbs up just because, when choosing between the negative and the positive, i prefer the latter).

Almost every aspect of this game is lacklustre, with a few exceptions.
I can only say I've truly enjoyed the game's single-player mode, which was extremely short, lasting around 9 hours from start to finish. The story and characters were relatively uninteresting, (even by Warhammer standards) however the game had much better and more consistent mechanics in the singleplayer than it had in its multiplayer and co-op modes. Enemies in the campaign were at least scaled reasonably, and there were a few interesting set pieces at points that were fun to play through.
This is probably the most horribly balanced non-F2P game I've ever played. The multiplayer is built with a rock-paper-scissors type system in mind, however, instead of rocks, papers, or scissors, all classes and weapons are instead nuclear ICBMs, leading to almost every weapon seemingly killing you instantly. Also, the game sports a totally-not-copied-from-CoD leveling system, where you become stronger than other players because you played longer and therefore have better perks to one-shot them with.
Exterminatus (the co-op mode) is really good at first, especially with friends, however it quickly becomes old after continued playing, and is plagued by many of the same problems the rest of the game is, such as various porting issues, and what may be the worst netcode ever made, even by console standards.
The difficulty scales schizophrenically. One moment you'll be gunning down hordes of weak ork Slugga Boyz, the next you'll be lying dead, surrounded by 3 huge nobs and 20 scar boyz, each scar boy having about 3 times more total health than you do. It gets to the point where the enemies get tough it will be literally impossible to beat them unless you have a very well coordinated team, and a specific cookie-cutter loadout for your squad.
Overall this game is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥, except for the singleplayer and the armour customization.
Oh, and most of the DLC is overpriced ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. 10 dollars for 3 ♥♥♥♥ing maps? Are you kidding me? THQ can go ♥♥♥♥ themselves with a rake.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a visually stunning platformer featuring an outstanding soundtrack delivers an immersive and emotional story. From the get-go, players go on an abrupt emotional rollercoaster ride before fully taking charge of Ori.
Gameplay-wise, the controls are very straightforward, controlling Ori through the lush terrain. Running, jumping and using the Spirit Flame is quite easy to grasp. However, the only gripe evident so far is Ori's wall jumping ability. Climbing up isn't the issue but leaping from the said wall to another wall can be quite frustrating even if it was timed perfectly. It's not impossible to do but simply frustrating.
Other than simple mechanics, the game features a straightforward skill tree. Each ability is unlocked using an Ability Point. As expected, some abilities require more than 1 AP to progress.
Ori and the Blind Forest overall is a solid game that's worth having in player's libraries. For players who love immersive environments featuring a deeply haunting but mystical soundtrack and a well-devised story, this game is clearly designed for you.
In conclusion, the game was definitely well worth the wait! Highly recommended!

Simple, yet really captivating roguelike point'n'click.
Though don't be fooled by it's simplicity - game's plot and usage of it's mechanics gets deeper and deeper as you go down the stairs of the Skyhill hotel...

The survival mechanics is why you'd want to play the game, as while the combat mechanics aren't anything to write home about, the rationing and risk/reward of attempting to find equipment does uniquely stand it apart from other games in the genre. It's hit a specific niche: if you like roguelikes and survival mechanics, this game may be up your alley, as it does that rather well. But that's if: if neither of those sound entirely interesting, then the games lackluster sound design and mechanics that could have gone a step further or two really won't make you play it in the long run, especially considering the repetitive nature of the runs. The lighting does stand out in the visual department, and I enjoyed my time with the game even when I'm not necessary a survival mechanic fan at times, but it's the home run hitter of the genre: if it connects with you: you'll be playing it for hours and hours. Or you'll strike out.

Review copy provided by developer
Described by the creators as a point and survival game Skyhill sees your character survive a nuclear apocalypse and after eventually running out of food and supplies having to venture out from his protected penthouse on the 100th floor with the intention of reaching the ground.
The main mechanics of the game are managing both your health and hunger as you travel down each stairwell with the option of investigating both rooms on each floor. Every move you make uses up one point of hunger so sensibly navigating the games rooms is essential.
Another key mechanic is the games combat. As you meet an enemy you must select your weapon and then choose which body part you are going to attack. Different body parts have a higher percentage chance of missing but equally harder to hit parts do significantly more damage. This turns the combat into a logic puzzle as you get further down the building and the enemies get harder and harder.
In order to help manage your hunger and health there is a well fleshed out crafting system to allow you to craft food, resources and weapons as well as a level up system with a simple set of stats you can add to.
As you descend you unlock access to the elevator that allows you to travel back up to your penthouse and improve food and weapons. It also becomes important to use you Penthouse to sleep and regain life especially on the higher difficulties as enemies become harder and first aid kits become scarcer. This works by increasing your health but reducing your hunger bar meaning you are generally starving when you awake.
There are a few issues I have with the game to do with balance. I will say that with each play through there is an active and passive ability to help you that you can choose at the start. Some are more helpful than others with a particular overpowered favorite of mine being Bulimia which reduces your hunger loss by 50% but makes it possible to take damage when you eat. Equally there are a few weapons that are easier to gain than others that are very powerful the clock work axe being a good example of this.
Now I am not usually a fan of roguelikes but there really is something about Skyhill that grabbed me and would not let me go. As you progress you are drip fed storied through articles you find as well as some key bits of information about side plots that only become apparent through multiple playthroughs and alternate endings.
Having completed the game relatively easily on easy and just about on normal the hard is proving difficult and the currently locked nightmare mode is about as far from seeming possible to me right now as it could be.
All in all Skyhill is a very original roguelike game that is different from anything I have played before and is well worth your time. Games take a reasonable length and it never outstays its welcome with subsequent playthroughs drip feeding you more and more of the games story.
Cannot recommend it enough though, fantastic game.

EDIT: I have added further comments below.
This game isn't particularly fun or difficult. To clarify:
Yes. It's a roguelike. You start out without any passive or active abilities, and you have to "learn" them as you re-live your life.
I started the game in normal mode, and made it down to floor 59. That's almost half way to the bottom on my first go-around. That's unheard of in most roguelikes.
The battle system and enemies lack any particular flair. Called shots make things interesting, but there's not really a point if there's no advantage in hitting a specific area. Yes, striking a monster in the head will cause more damage than the torso, but why not have a chance to stun or blind? The same goes for limbs: why not a chance to decrease enemy strength or cause accuracy to fall?
Missing the ability to equip your character with any sort of armor was confusing. It definitely made things less interesting when it came to decisions about what I would attempt to upgrade.
Finding food and health objects is not necessarily difficult. The first time I decided to head back to the VIP room was because I wanted to see about crafting a weapon. I didn't even know that you could use the bed to rest and trade food for health. Strangely, sleeping off your injuries isn't really a great deal compared to just exploring a few floors to find some more health items.
The crafting system is more interesting for sure. As you progress in the weapons you can make, things get even easier.
The mechanic of entering a room and clicking on objects became boring and repetative. Coming upon a locked door didn't really make me frustrated, because I knew I was only missing out on the contents of a single room.
Control boxes found on some floors require tampering to ensure that power goes to the floors below. I found this the most interesting aspect because it was the only challenging question I had to deal with: do I want to try fixing this thing? The answer was always "yes", and it felt like 50% of the time I could do it on the first shot. I never attempted to use an item to fix the panel. It seemed like a waste of time.
Item drops are notably sparse aside from basics like food and health. A weapon above a basic killing implement was never dropped during my game. That is to say - I had a few weapons drop, but they were far surpassed by the things I had already created for myself.
No, I did not give this a whole shake. Yes, I only played for about two hours. No, I don't want to continue playing - the game is boring, and I have better things to do with my time.
Oh, a few positives - the voice acting in memoirs left behind seemed to be mildly engaging. Unfortunately, grasping the full scope of the situation was not something I really felt was necessary. Especially since your character doesn't really have a dog in the fight besides "I am in the top floor of a tower. I would like to leave this tower."
The crafting system is interesting. I could see it going far, but armor would be a welcome addition. Further, the ability to create almost anything required with wood, rags and scrap metal is kind of odd.
There's also some flavor text notes left on walls and corpses which seem to hint at a greater story arch.
This game seems like it would be better suited on my phone, and played specifically while taking a long dump. Paying rapt attention to the goings-on are not necessary, and there's not really much of a decision-making process when it comes to playing the game. Will I explore both rooms on this floor? Yes. Will I continue down to the next floor? Yes. Rinse - repeat.
If I were to recommend something to the developers, I would recommend somehow increasing the size of the floors beyond two rooms. Missing out on a room due to a lock is a non-issue. I have no idea what I missed by not entering those rooms, and even after I found keys to go back and find out later, I didn't. Finally, I am not sure if I missed it, but a map would be useful - something to see if I can get back to a locked room.
**ADDENDUM**
A note to the dev team: dive deeper guys. This game was on training wheels, and I can tell that you definitely tried. I did not experience a single bug. The art work was great. The animation was smooth. The sound and set design were great. The concept was engaging, and I am a HUGE sucker for rogue-likes. This concept pushed all the right buttons.
Yes, I was disappointed, but that's alright. I want bigger, better, more complicated stuff from you in the future. I want you to succeed. This was a good idea. THIS GAME WAS A GOOD IDEA! I swear to god, if you create an R-rated version of this with more complicated features, I will be back.
**SUPER ADDENDUM**
This is addressed to Broshan:
Making the game more difficult would have made it more of a challenge, but it wouldn't have changed the fact that traversing floors was more of a chore than it needed to be. A quick way to improve this specific game would be to at least speed everything up - have a keyboard command to just retrieve all items in a room. At least then you can get done with everything immediately instead of going through the chore of clicking on separate room components.
Because of the floor construction, there was no complexity. There are almost no choices to be made in a direction of travel. There isn't even an inventory system - your character has pockets that can hold everything, and there's no need to leave behind some items in order to store or keep others. Again - no choice to be made; just take everything you can click on. You can't save inventory items on the top floor because there's no need to. It would be  logical for a game like this given you have a safe room which you can effectively return to at almost any point.
Roguelikes in particular suffer when you lack the ability to make informed decisions. It feels really good when you make the right choice, and are duly rewarded by the game's mechanics. On the contrary, it feels like you are on rails when nothing you do necessarily affects how the game progresses. No one wants to feel like that when playing a roguelike.
Yes, tweaking aspects of the game are necessary pertaining to item drops, but that is a drop in the bucket. The issue I am attempting to indicate is more systemic. This game needs an adult version. One with real choices, massive rewards, and crushing defeats.

I can't give this game a thumbs up not because it's a horrible game, just because it's not enough for my personal liking.  Too much randomness in the procedural map layout, and way too much luck involved in the core fighting elements.
It's a decent game for what it is, but I'm just left feeling a little too bored playing this game after only about 20-30 minutes.  I wish it had something more, I dont know.  For a game like this with so much randomess determining the outcomes, maybe I want to see some dice being thrown and see those numbers either coming up 'hit' or 'miss', but this game just leaves me feel like something is "missing".
You start off the game in the top of a 99 floor hotel.  You can use the elevators on each floor once you find a VIP card by searching dead mutants you kill or searching searchable items you find in the rooms.  There is no WASD or even arrow keys, its all mouse driven and point-and-click.  Point and click items to search or rooms to walk into.  Every action has a result typically success or fail which is really all based on randomness, and perhaps your characters "skills" in fighting.  Still it all just feels like a bunch of dice rolls to me, and very little in the way of strategy or puzzle solving.  And that's where this game fails to deliver for me in the game satisfaction and overall challenge.
It works well enough and might be fun for some people to play, but again to me.. it's just lacking either a real satisfying level of strategy or in showing us the dice rolls that determine our fate.  I don't mind games of chance, but for a game that involves this much luck with every move, somehow I think it might help to see the dice rolls on the screen.
In the end, I cannot give this game my personal thumbs up even though the game works well enough.  It just lacks enough engagement in the players choices to make it satisfying to me and therefore fails to deliver a high enough level of enjoyment while playing it.
My score is a 60% and I think there are much more fun games out there of this style and at or under the same price.

SKYHILL is a turn based action-RPG pitting you with the task of escaping a 100-storey hotel by descending from the top floor to the Lobby.  You're set up against increasingly difficult mutated human beings in hand-to-hand combat using either found or crafted weaponry.  Mutants are not your only difficulty as you are faced with a hunger bar that depletes for every room you move from, causing starvation and eventually death if you can not sustain yourself.
You're granted a "VIP Card" early in the game which allows you to use the central elevator, so that you may quick-travel between floors or to the VIP room itself; an absolute need since walking up each floor will cost you your difficult-to-attain hunger bar.  The central elevator however is in a state of disrepair, requiring you to find or craft the necessary parts to fix it as you progress through the game.
Your VIP room is your hub for healing yourself by exchanging an equal number of hunger points for health points and allows crafting of foodstuffs and new weaponry.  SKYHILL does not contain any armour at all, so you are going to take many damaging blows as you complete the objective of reaching the Lobby, making hunger trading for health a must-do.
Ultimately, the game is unforgiving, even on Normal difficulty making it difficult to play for those easily frustrated.  Although you may die often, depending on your level of descension, you will unlock "perks" for future playthroughs.  These perks give you a bonus (and some a detriment) for your character.
Sadly the game is not very long in length (Beat the game on Normal in 5 hours after 5 playthroughs), and the random generation does very little to supplement the game (The tower is always 100 stories, different mutants are found in generally the same depth, the only randomism that kicks in is room loot quantity and contents along with attack rolls).  Therefore there is very little replay value once the game is complete.  Difficulty levels also seem to only adjust mutant hit point values: On Normal a standard 'clawer' has 20 HP where it has 22 on Hard, as an example. I failed to notice if anything else is adjusted between difficulties.
In conclusion, I found SKYHILL to be very addicting and entertaining for what I did play!  Always getting just a little further each time, developing new strategies and trying out different perk load-outs until I found one that I liked ("Total Mess" perk is extremely overpowered.  Every lootable container and creature corpse contains an item, where regularly it's more of a 50/50 of a container having an item or being empty.  The downfall of the perk is every 10 turns you lose one random item, so once you get going, the worst that could happen is you lose a really good weapon or your VIP card).
Definitely a fun game in my opinion, and that's why I recommend it.  Would be significantly better with extra replay value (Modded content, different size floors or rooms, additional challenges or story, etc.) - as now that I've completed it, I have very little inclination for beating it again on a higher difficulty.
