I am writing this review to those who are purposely bombing this game's reviews, because of complaints. Reminder: You are playing an EARLY ACCESS GAME. Therefore, bombing the review section because of one update THAT WILL BE CHANGED IN THE FUTURE is somewhat childish.
I played this game for some time now. as you can see from my total hours. For the record, any reviews under 100 hours will not be nearly enough to create the most accurate review in my opinion. This game has gone through huge changes this past 5 months. The developers are trying new things and seeing the response. Not everything will remain permanent, we have been shown that before.
Onto the game stats now...
Based on the NEW terrain. I would say it's pretty good. It's fun to go into space, see the different Nebulas, then go into a moon or another planet and look at the new atmosphere and terrain features. Almost every planet is unique and they have different difficulty settings applied to them as well. You can find unique structures lying around the planet, raid and loot them, take over them for yourself, then shoot it peices if you felt like it (and if you had the ammo). You can find enemy bases and do the exact same thing as well. When you are in space, there are space stations in certain locations and you can trade items there as well. You can also be attacked by Capital Vessels of varying levels now, this occurs when you build a base that has enemies on the planet.
I haven't spent the time trying to do this, but you have the ability to make a custom scenario and even publish it to the workshop. This is not done in-game though, I believe the developers posted a certain way to make scenarios correctly. DO NOT CONFUSE THIS WITH CUSTOM SETTINGS FOR THE MAIN SINGLEPLAYER MODE, what I mean here is that changing the world settings for a scenario before making the world, is different from the scenario creation itself. Aside from that, players have already published custom scenarios, and the developers have been applying a couple of them to the main game! The same goes for player-made Bases and Ships. so if you get bored of playing the main singleplayer scenario, you can try out another player-made scenario. There are other things as well, but I'm not trying to spend 30 minutes writing a review.
- Graphics: I would say they are alright, but I am not using the strongest of computers either, so it can definitely look better if you have a more beefy computer.
- Combat: It's simple really. The more complex battle situations will happen on PvP servers where you are fighting other players or higher level AI base locations.
- Grinding: It's a slight rough in the beginning, especially if you are new and trying to figure out how the game works, but once you understand how the game works, then grinding will be reduced to a simplicity.
- In-game Console: Yes you can press the amazing " ` " key and see the console. There is quite a bit you can do here.
- Building Bases: Gather the resources necessary and you can build pretty much anything, I have built (still unpublished creations) all types of bases, both from underground, to space, and on the surface level bases. They have much use but can be hard to build on planets with poison gas on them.
- Building Small Vessels and Capital Vessels: I have been CONSTANTLY SURPRISED as to what I can replicate, customize, and shape. I have see many different techniques that ship builders are using to define their ship with. If there are limitations to ship bulding, I would say it is ones creative ability.... and the 250x250x250 ship size limit. HOWEVER, building a ship larger than that is a horrible idea anyways.
- Bulding Hover Vessels: These are your ground vehicles of Empyrion, they hover above the ground and move around with rockets pushing them. As I said with the flying vehicles above, there is just as much customization to be done here.
There are players who are not specifically stating where certain issues are happening. I have seen one player talking about how he lost vehicles because they fell of the map, etc. He was mentioning about MULTIPLAYER. Not the SINGLEPLAYER mode. There are servers which the PLAYERS can make, and load/create their own worlds there. Some of the servers the players make are EXPERIMENTAL! You simply CANNOT blame Eleon for the fact that a PLAYER made a server that has bugs on it. THEN AGAIN, some of those bugs were cause by Eleon, so who is to blame? It depends, and I'll explain. I have played on the Homeworld Server. Excellent server by all means. There were bugs on it that Eleon had caused from new updates, but the Server owner had the ability (because he is a skilled individual) to fix some small problems on his own. Some other bugs had to be fixed by Eleon. So it depends on the Server host to make sure that the server remains updated, and that certain problems are reported and fixed by Eleon.
End of review.

If you like stealth-games, then this is definitely one of the better titles around. Particularly if you like adding some fantasy-elements to it all.
You have your missions, connected to an overarching story, and there are multiple ways to go about accomplishing them. You can sneak through them, fight your way through them, or backstab your way through them. If you are the overarchieving type, there are also plenty of secondary quest objectives to pursue. In what other game will you get the objective to steal a guard's pet kitten?
Styx himself also gets upgraded throughout the game, which you get to choose depending on your play-style. It is great fun launching a goblin from the tope of a ledge only to have him land silently by "landing" his knife in a guard below.
The game has its glitches, such as guards getting stuck walking into each other or bodies bouncing away as they land. Most annoyingly is that there are places you cannot access until you return to the same map in a later mission... but the game does not tell you that. Instead, you are stuck wondering how to get in there.
However, all in all Styx: Master of Shadows is a very solid effort.

Ever since I learned about the Battle of Thermopylae (The battle depicted in the movie "300") when I was in high school, I took to creating my own little chokepoint battles in doodle form when I was bored in class (Read: Most of the time). I would draw bases, heavy units, and split teams between Red and Blue (Per my pen colors). After that, I would draw dots as the troops and feint lines marking their "shots" while X-ing out deceased troops.
I found a game like this on Kongregate and that was good fun, and now I'm happy to drop five dollars in what is basically a graphical representation of my imagination, circa ~2005.
This game is basically what was going on in my head, only depicted as "Cells" rather than armies.
A great in-between game, not something you spend an entire sitdown session doing. It's great during loading screens, queue times on your chosen MMO, or simply find yourself with not much to do the hour before leaving for work. I wouldn't fault anyone for getting it on sale but if you're like me and use the 1 dollar per Hour metric of gaming quality, then this will likely do the job.
The only fault is a very brief learning curve when you figure out that the best strategy is charging up your beginning cell, avoiding conflict. If you can make it to a level 3 cell before your enemies do, then you're pretty much set as you'll have all the pixels you'll need to both defend yourself, and begin absorbing neutral cells. I've cleared several levels by doing this with only a couple of times I would refer to as "Close calls".

New 'n' Tasty is a finer cut of meat; more visually appealing, brighter color, not nearly as gritty, and the toughest parts have been tenderized to perfection.
It doesn't reinvent Abe's Oddysee, in fact some things still gracefully show their age, but it does add some very welcome new features and mechanics to make it much more enjoyable to replay or experience for the first time. Even on hard ("classic") mode, it's more forgiving than the original and it can be completed allot faster due to better gameplay progression. There are no new areas in the game, just a larger amount of Mudokens to save, The art style is sometimes too bright but the character of the world and significance of its message are not blinded in the least. The environments might have less grime, but they are more varied and interesting while still being equally dominating in scale.
New 'n' Tasty definitely isn't without it's own bugs and a few things can use some tweaking (like the hard mode meat-saws and most of Scrabania). But those are all fixable and don't ruin what is ultimately one of the best, most faithful remakes of a classic. I sincerely hope that the superior Abe's Exoddus is given the same treatment; just get rid of the steam-vents and bring back the heavy shadows, please.

is a medieval fantasy turn-based tactical RPG based on the Dark Eye tabletop RPG. Framed and tortured by the one you called your friend, you make your escape with a few other prisoners, trying to find out the truth behind the accusations against you. This review takes into account the Untold Legends DLC.
: Nice game with enough mechanical depth to offer a variety of gameplay styles: rather than level-based progression, you spend adventure points on anything from attributes, weapon skills, spells and perks and determine exactly how specialized you become with your various talents. The story isn't of a great hero, but of someone who won't leave a mark on history, making your way in shady towns and accepting questionable quests, especially in the multiple side quests added by the
where you must take stances on subjects such as slavery. Graphics are good enough for the genre, tactical maps are clean, most of which have interactive environment elements you might use against your foes if they don't use them against you. The game is sufficiently balanced, and even with the occasional difficulty spikes, you can jump right back in the last encounter to try things differently.
: Many will find the depth to be a bit too much, scrolling through 5 pages of skills and perks will make it hard to figure the best way to optimize your character. There is a limited variety of equipment, especially armor. The story is pretty linear and not all that complex. The odds of success aren't mushed, so 95% chance of success might still miss, multiple times, in a row, which will frustrate anyone who isn't used to rolling dices. The music is somber, and sucks life and excitement out of the game whenever you're not in a combat situation.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you

A much more interesting game than the Dawn of War 2 Battle Arena series. Interestingly, this game goes even further from the original table-top squad-based Warhammer 40K game. Space Marine (or as I call it, "Gears of Warhammer") uses solely an over-the-shoulder 3rd person view that changes the perspective of the series once again. It also one of the first WH40K games to peek into the daily lives of humans who are just plain civilian workers.
By stripping away the remaining aspects of squad-based play (your two support characters are fully AI controlled) the game certainly feels more intimate. The art design is great, successfully evoking an Imperium planet with enormous architecture and spacious levels.
But the gameplay is pretty basic and strictly linear. The only standout aspect is the jetpack you get to use for a limited period only three times in the game. The combat gets a little predictable, but enemy combatants make good use of cover. At the end, the final Boss level is both ludicrously difficult and laughably easy. With one single specific weapon choice you either are unlikely to finish the level or it's far too easy. It's a strange thing.
Is this game for you? Depends. If you're a real fan of the source material then, yes, definitely. If you like a base-building style (like the first Dawn of War series) or Battle Arena style (as in the DoW2 series), then this game is not for you. If you're looking for original gameplay, then it's not likely you will find much to inspire you.
And even then, I still recommend it because it's kinda fun.

I have mixed feelings about this game.
Although it claims to be an independent game and not part of a series, there were some jokes and references back to previous games so it helps if you've played the previous ones. However, I find the plot to be a bit too unrealistic in the way it includes superhero and supernatural elements. I think the charm of To The Moon lies in the simplicity of the story, but how it is still relatable and touching. There are a lot of cucumber references, which I also believe relate back to To The Moon, and although funny I find them to be used a bit too frequently.
I like how they added the element of changing between two character perspectives, since it improves the gameplay experience and it reminds me of the game Rakuen (which was created by one of the composers for Finding Paradise and To The Moon and inspired by the two). The game builds up suspense very well to get you hooked and provided 4 hours of gameplay, so I think it’s well worth your money. Although I listed a lot of criticism above, if you’re looking for a sequel to To The Moon, then this is it. Finding Paradise will take you on a crazy ride and although it didn’t suit my taste, the game is well made and most of my complaints relate to my personal preferences.

Where to start... To sum the rest of this review up, this is the best Batman: Arkham game. It features CHALLENGING (at times) combat and boss fights. For Solomon Grundy alone I needed to die six times. (On normal mode, of course.) You get to swing around a large, albeit lifeless, city and choose whether or not to take down groups of criminals. Specifically, some pros to this game are:
1. Amazing combat and ambush techniques, not to mention gadgets.
2. A large world to roam around (and lurk) in.
3. Tons of playtime, lots of levels and missions to do. On other games, I find random unfounded side missions tasking and not worth my playtime, but here, I was engaged and ready to find everyone from Deadshot to Hush.
4. Great graphics and animations, that went smoothly and made skirmishes fun to both engage in and watch.
Of course, there are, like any other game, downsides to playing. Here my main three qualms are:
1. While the combat and boss fights are stupendous, I found myself both bored with the repitition of the same moves and controls, and struggling with late game boss and gang fights. I understand that they are supposed to be hard, but sometimes I really wanted to ragequit.
2. A couple of problems with the thugs in the city. There's no motivation to take them on, because there's no one to save, (there is zero civilian population), and the fact that you can hear them talking using your radio ALL THE TIME, because the game automatically tunes in when within, maybe, 100 meters.
3. Weird controls that were hard to get used to in the beginning- sometimes the counter button doesn't work, so you get sucker punched when you were pressing it, and the awkwardly selected CTRL that you use to crouch. It is out of the way,  and totally unreasonable. When I have my hand on WASD to move, I don't want to have to slide my pinky under my finger and try to get it in time to slide. (If you dislike the CTRL button being used for crouching, use the launcher in the files to rebind it to E. That works fine.)
To wrap things up, this was a fantastic game with a huge prescense, with some pros and cons, but, overall, is definitely the best Batman game. If you like great graphics, engaging characters, amazing action scenes, and wonderful open-world exploration, choose this over any other Arkham game.

Chambara is a local multiplayer first person pvp game where you have to fight each other in small arenas with a two-color art style where you can hide in the color of your character.  Since it can only be played locally at one PC, be aware of your friends, they can just look at your side of the screen and know where you are despite your concealment.
- Local play for 2 or 4 players, either 1v1 or 2v2
- Nine different maps, each with its own theme and 6 color combinations to choose from
- Smooth and precise gameplay with wall jumps and shuriken throws
- Fast forward recap of the last round played
- An option to close your eyes so your teammates can’t find you as easy since looking on your part of the screen won’t help them anymore
- Various customizations options
- Minimalistic design that is pleasing to look at; was running smoothly on my rig
Chambara is a solid recommendation for local couch meetups with friends and people who enjoyed Screencheat since it’s a similar game. I would love to see different weapons with different mechanics to them and maybe some more maps in future updates.

Until now I never knew the pain of watching my girlfriend run me through with a guitar as she used her bird form to dash across a black and white city-scape to which I then exploded into maple leaves... Thank you Chambara my life is complete.
TLDR: video first impressions and extended gameplay.
Chambara is a local co-op brawler in which you play samurai birds fighting in high contrast maps with only a main weapon and a throwing star to claim victory.
First off: this is a wonderful local co-op game and has every right to stand along side games like overcooked, smash bros and towerfall in anyones line up of competitavce local co-op party games. My sole critique of the games is that its lack of an online multiplayer mode will hurt the longevity of it on a playform like Steam. Chambara is also available on the PS4 but Steam and the PC are not traditional local co-op platforms so this game may see rough long term returns.
Aside from that the gameplay, handling, sound, visual, combat, and general feel of the game are superb. You controls are fluid and intutuive. The combat is fast paced and rewarding for clever play, and the visuals are gorgeous. The use of negative and positive space put this games asethetic into another category on its own.
If you are looking for another local co-op when entertaining guests this should be a game you seriously consider.

The idea behind Chambara is as simple as it is brilliant. A local multiplayer game in which trying to catch a glimpse of your opponents' side of the screen is pretty much mandatory and it's not cheating (or you could consider it as cheating, but you still have to do it if you want to have a chance) and you have to build your strategy around it, aware that your opponents will do the same. The game mechanics are entirely focused around this core idea making the title both very accessible and quite challenging if you're facing a more experienced opponent. The art style has been seen in other games but it's still pleasing. I'd recommend it if you have the right people to play with.

SKYHILL is a randomly generated roguelike where you must manage your resources to survive in a postapocalyptic skyrise hotel. You start at the top and must work your way down, fighting mutants and jerryrigging fuseboxes to keep the lights on for protection.
If love does not exist, humph, my god, what am I feeling? if love does exist, what is it on earth? If love is good, where does my sorrow come from?

Skyhill is a procedurally generated point and click Roguelite in which you descend through 99 levels of a hotel collecting resources and weapons a long the way or craft your own with the materials you find.  As you go you will encounter different types of Mutants or Zombies and clues as to what’s actually happening in the world your character lives in. Level up to progress and make it to the bottom floor or die.
The game has a great aesthetic complete with some fully voice acted comic style cut scenes and it’s simple, streamlined interface makes the game incredibly easy to pick up and play. The only drawback is the price point. If you’re really itching for a roguelite point and click with some good story this game is for you. If you have a passing interest in the genre better to wait for a sale.

What I liked about the game was the visuals. They weren't bad. The dogfighting was decent, and the bombing was decent as well... When I could take off. That was an odd issue that I came across. With the large aircraft, it was nine times out of ten impossible to take off from the carrier. I find that to be a huge problem. I tried everything I could think of to take off, but maybe the physics engine was just off enough to make it near impossible. I understand it was hard to take off from a carrier back then, but not impossible. I double checked my controller, that was fine. I tried every way to keep the bird in the air after take off, and the one time I did I couldn't climb at all above 20 meters... for three minutes straight. That tells me the game might have a large issue.
Besides that issue, the game played rather well if you don't have to take off from the carrier. The Zero was a fun plane to fly, and I liked the SBD. The ability to switch aircraft was a nice addition to the usual flight games. Graphics were good, sound was good. All in all, the game has some promise.
What I would like to see changed so that I would recommend this game is the addition of a graphics option in the menu. I usually turn on VSync to help the game run smoother, and I would like to see how the game worked with the graphics running on ultra compared to low.
So, save your money for now, and maybe wait for a few fixes for this game. Unless it hits five bucks. It's worth five bucks.

Occasionally the ai will launch coordinated attacks, but by that time you should have snowballed enough to just roll over their cells ignoring your own losses and win the level.
Tactical advantage in moving cells consists of saving minute amounts of time by moving close to neutral cells you plan to take, and past that the only time you'll move a cell is to stop it moving after the AI bumps into it.  As someone who played all of the Phage games, which are free by the way, this one is a disappointment with its faceroll difficulty and dearth of tatical choices.  As an added bonus, there is no strategic value in letting antibodies sit idle at all.  Ever.
The fastest way to clear levels is by selecting all antibodies and doing one task at a time, overwhelming enemy and neutral cells, while the constant stream of antibodies flowing in the spaces between your cells neutralizes almost all efforts to attack you.  Biowall makes it even easier by limiting the area you have to mouse over to select all of your antibodies.  This all being said, its atmosphere and music fit the overall theme of low difficulty and make for a relaxing experience.  Except when the AI bump into you.

I've put in a good amount of hours on this game.  It's interesting at first, but it quickly becomes repetetive.   The entire premise of the game:  Grow/acquire cells.  That's it.  No depth.  No massive strategy.  It's grow-and-conquer.  If you're not fast enough at circling your antibodies and getting them to beef up your cell, you won't be able to get anywhere.  Eventually, it's about overwhelming your computer opponents with the number of cells/antibodies.
Some levels have a bug that allegedly was fixed in a prior patch but still persists -- your cell(s) can get stuck in the cell walls.  Ditto for opponent's cells.  Sometimes your cells will overlay with another cell, and you can't click either.  If your cell gets stuck in a wall/overlayed, you can't move, you can't send out antibodies, you have to restart the level.   This makes for an infuriating gameplay, especially at higher levels.  I've lost several games in one high level because my cell keeps getting stuck in cell walls.
Responsivity of the cells: You will click and point for your cel to move.  Nope!  The cell likes to make up its own mind if it may or may not move.  Same for the antibodies.  They'll move when you don't want them to, or they'll not move when you've given them an order.  This bug appears about ten percent of the time in any level.
Finally, the game  only has so many levels.  There's no random 'map' or unlimited play.  Once you win the game, that's it.  You're done.  You can restart, but, what's the point now that you know how to win every map?
I'd like to recommend the game, but the bugs and repetition aren't worth it.

I love the Oddworld series. I own all of the games in the series, and in fact have bought Abe's Oddyssee four times - once for Playstation, once for PC, once on
and again on Steam. Now I've effectively bought it a fifth time in the shape of New'n'Tasty.
First of all, it looks absolutely stunning. JAW have managed to capture the look and style of the original game whilst bringing it bang up to date - the new character animations are gorgeous, background effects really add to the atmosphere, and the 3D effects work without being distracting.
Sound wise, it's a great improvement. Higher sample rate, more dynamic music, and yes! Lorne Lanning voices Abe again. In addition, there is a lot more dialogue so there's less repetition when talking to characters.
JAW have also added many of the improvements that appeared in Exoddus - you can now Quicksave rather than relying on checkpoints, and an "Everybody" option has been added so you can move Mudokons en-masse.
The levels themselves are similar without being exactly the same - there are extra secret areas, and many sections of the game are longer with more screens thereby meaning that knowledge of the original Abe won't guarantee success here.
So... all in all, a great update of a modern classic!
No. Whoever designed the controls for this abomination deserves to be put through the nearest meat grinder. Abe is slow and unresponsive, with a lethargic, lazy feel to the character, where every action has an artificial delay put into it, which you have to account for when moving between dangerous objects or defusing mines. I find it next to impossible to manage complicated sequences of moves, as the game will suddenly decide that I'm not holding down "Run" after all, and Abe will start walking, inevitably resulting in his death at the hands of a Scrab.
In addition, the controls have become needlessly complicated. Rather than using UP+DOWN to move elevators, you now have to USE it first. Rather than UP to go through doors, you now have to USE them. You now have dozens of extra controls which were completely unessential in the original, such as the ability to check your health (huh?). Despite having over 14 hours of game time with Abe, I still get my fingers knotted together trying to manipulate the character into doing what I want him to do.
Also, the flip-screen mechanic has been replaced by a standard side-scroller. This would work for a new game, but unfortunately it's just too different for Abe. In the original, if a Slig was on the same screen as you, on the same level, and facing you, he could see you. In N'n'T, that isn't a guarantee. They have a certain distance they can see, represented by a red cone. This isn't exactly intuitive for people used to Abe, though perhaps it'd be acceptable to newcomers. The "Anti-chanting" drones also behave differently. In the original Abe, if there was one on the screen with you, you couldn't chant unless you destroyed it. Now, they switch on and off depending on the distance you are from them. So you can find yourself unable to possess a Slig because you're one-step too far to the left or right from where the game wants you.
Worse of all, the game is no longer tile-based - they've gone for a traditional hitbox based collision system, which means that a lot of the old game mechanics no longer work. You can try bunny-hopping over three mines by holding down the space bar - the first two will work, and the third will fail because you're two pixels out. In the original Abe you could effectively "bank" motions by pressing the next button whilst Abe was between tiles - this was essential for many of the harder puzzles, to ensure there was no wasted time with him stood still - you could get him to jump up to a ledge by pressing space just after he leaves the previous tile. None of that works here - it feels like a completely different game.
So, unfortunately, no. Whilst it may look and sound like Abe, it doesn't in any way feel like Abe. What we have here is something like a fan-port done by somebody whose seen the original game but never played it. Which is ludicrous as apparently JAW had the original source code to work with! Five million dollars this apparently cost. I think at least four of that went on the graphics.

I would first like to pre-face this review by saying that I bought this Deluxe version and Blackguards 2 as part of the Daedalic bundle for £9.99, making each game in effect worth £4.99 to me. Based on this price I think Blackguards is definitely worth it. The full price of £29.99 is however WAY off the mark for the amount of game you get (hint: not much)
Despite me finishing the game in 40 hours, it is a very combat focused where pretty much every event you’ll encounter will be a fight. Whilst this is fun to begin with, as a lot of battle maps are quite interesting, after 20 odd hours it just got tiresome. After every cut scene, conversation, exploration, etc I knew I would be fighting something. So you can imagine my utter delight when after defeating the final boss, the final cut-scene was just that a cut-scene!
Outside of combat there is unfortunately very little to the game, hence I only recommend it at a steep discount. There is no exploration to speak off, the town screens are static and the story kind of gets lots amongst 180 fight scenes you’ll have to slog through.
I also have a few gripes about the story, but these could just be personal preferences. For example, I don’t see how this is a “dark” story as it seems very much like any other RPG where you-are-our-only-hope-to-save-the-world story (spoiler: you save it). Also this games is called Blackguards and makes the point of your character being an outlaw. I was picturing more of a vagabond, a mercenary on the run, or some petty thief down and on his luck. What I wasn’t expecting however was for my character to be buddies with a PRINCES whilst chilling at a home of a COUNT in the first “memory” cutscene. Less of a BlackGuard, more of a Brodude! Also in this game you have no meaningful choice – it really just railroads you along the main story-line with some side-quests where you have a choice between killing guy A or guy B... with no impact on main story-line.
A lot of negative reviews about this game are regarding the dodgy RNG, and whilst I have encountered some odd miss on a 95% chance, I have never experienced a 3 in a row miss. If you read the manual and understand how the rules work. The % you see isn’t the % to inflict damage, but rather to do an action, then the enemy gets a couple of saving rolls – parry / dodge. So you might have successfully rolled an action, but then the enemy might have rolled a saving throw and so all you see is your guy missing or spell fizzing out.

Don't judge this game by it's screenshots or cover picture, as they make the game look like a crappy, thrown together mod that only took 30 minutes to make. I can assure you that it's not.
What makes this game great is the fact that it is so simple yet at times complex. The game uses a class system, with different primaries, secondaries, and equipment for each class (assault, sniper, support, ect.). This is one of the ways that the game can get complex, as some equipment helps the team (ammo box, sentry gun), while other classes have grenades or molotovs. The guns are surprisingly satisfying, well designed, and have the ability to ADS (something valve seems unable to program). There are 3 zombie types: "Fast" zombies, normal zombies, and "Tank" zombies (I won't explain them in detail because they are pretty generic zombie types).
Since the game runs on source engine (It's a Half-Life 2 mod) the menu is similar to HL2. This also means that there is a myriad (many) of user created maps and gamemodes.
Being on source means you also get HELLA FRAMES. I'm getting over 100 frames on high settings using onboard graphics! Just imagine what a Nvidia GeForce graphics card could get you!
Another thing to note is that through using the console, you can change your playermodel as you rank up in certain online servers. As you rank up in these servers you get access to playermodels such as Steve, Creeper, and Enderman (Minecraft), Bugs Bunny, ect.
Lastly, this game is 100% FREE. There are no microtransactions, DLC, ect.
And by the way, If you don't like the game just move on (it didn't cost you anything).

Did you like the original Evoland? If so, you're bound to like this one as it mostly plays like the original but with a bit of stank on it. However, this doesn't come without some negatives. Firstly, the concept of an evolution of the Zelda-ish/RPG type of games seems to have been forgotten in exchange for a evolution of all games. For example, you'll have to fight a fighting game battle right after doing a shoot 'em up style mini game.
The game also isn't a steady evolution like the original. Instead you jump between different time periods, each with their own console aestetic (i.e. one time period might look like the original game boy. Another would be in full 3D). This causes the game to lose a bit in the terms of a natural flow. However, it makes enough sense in the plot that it isn't that distracting.
Overall, I'd say the game is worth a play though if you're into Zelda-esq games, and don't mind having that style interrupted for random mini games every so often.

Evoland 2 is a really great homage to RPGs, which I strongly recommend to fans of this genre. What makes this game unique is that it includes all sorts of gameplays and aesthetics. You have Zelda-like action-rpg gameplay, classical turn-based gameplay, tactics gameplay, and so much more that is not necessarily unique to RPGs (e.g. beat'em up, shoot'em up, side-scrollers). The graphics and the music range from what you would have had on an old gameboy to a more modern cartoonish 3D style. The screenshots on the store page will give you a good idea. It is a carefully designed game, as the developers really captured the feel of these different generations through their unique art style. The music is really on point !
What I also liked about the game is that while it is very nostalgic and includes many references to really great games dear to me (such as Chrono Trigger), it still has a very modern touch with funny gameplay from more recent games. I don't want to spoil anything because the inclusion of these gameplays was such a nice contrast with the more classical things. As with most RPGs you have collectibles (cards and stars), and one thing I liked is that nothing is permanently missable, so you can always go back to some place to find your last missing card.
If one really has to find a flaw in this game, it would be the fact that all these gameplays end up being rather superficial. What I mean here is that since most sections of the game offer different types of gameplays, you won't "develop" your characters the way it is usually done in a traditional RPG. There is character progression to some degree as you do gain XP and can unlock a few abilities, but not in an in-depth way.
To conclude, this game is a no-brainer if you love RPGs in general, but if what you are looking for are in-depth mechanics and complex character progression, you may want to try something else. Note that the game takes around 20 hours to fully complete. I would also recommend playing the first game first, not because you need to have played the first one to understand the second (they are stand-alone and unrelated), but because the first one is simpler and less elaborate. Therefore, if you play it first, you will appreciate the second one more because you will see how the developers took their initial ideas and improved upon what was already a really good game !

While Blackguards has interesting characters, visually appealing backdrop and a good amount of character customisation. It is linear in nature like most tactical RPGs, it is still engaging enough to keep you playing.
What could of been an exceptional tactical RPG, is heavilly mared by the skewerd RNG.  Enemies with ludecrously low hit chances will regularly hit, while your group with ludecriously high chances to hit will miss quite often.  This simply plays out this way the entire game.
Many of the enemy hits will impose effects but you wont resist them because of penalites of unknown oragin making the skills you developed to resist them, meaningless.  Likewise Enemies will constantly resist your statuses because aparently you dont apply the same penalities to them.
This would be fine for the most part if enemies did similare damage to your group, sadly they typically will almost always do about 50% more, leaving you to scratch your head wondering why.
In general enemies will always be better than or equal to your group in combat, even if they happen to be some merchant or alchemist they will be exceptional warriors none the less.  They also wont give you the gear they are using (aparently that vanishes in a puff of smoke when they die)
Again this woud be fine through the use of tactics.  However the RNG issues will often destroy the best tactics you can bring to the table.
Plenty of places have traps everywhere and the non-enviromental ones will let the enemies happilly walk over with without triggering them.
At the end of the day unless you are happy to ignore the RNG issues and vague information on many of the combat aspects, I cant really recomened Blackguards (hopefully the second one has improved those issues).   Even then best to get it on a 75% off sale.

Crafting is overly cumbersome. There are redundant and worthless steps that don’t add any depth, only frustration to the crafting system.
Inventory is broken. Universal banking (small map and limited slots) combined with extremely limited storage space makes for a terrible mess of objects and junk. Your character can have more inventory slots than your bank.
Limited fantasy game that demands you carry nearly all your belongings with you in your backpack… Fine, so I can’t use magic, but I can carry five thousand oak logs with me everywhere I go… great.
Universal banking with ultra-limited space is worthless. The map is tiny, transporting goods would add to the value of conquering territory. If your faction loses control of a town where you have junk stored, you may be more inclined to join up and regain control of said town.
Localized banking would add to the value of towns and territory. It would make sense to keep the majority of your smithing supplies in the mining town, and your farming supplies in the farm town. But that’s not the way it is. You have a universal bank that doesn’t have enough room for your smithing or farming supplies.
There is lag.
Hit detection is crap.
Collision detection is crap.
Looting is crap. When enemies loot your items they stay in your quickbar, and I experienced a shield animation that wouldn’t go away. After I relogged the shield animation was fixed, but when I misspressed the quickbar number for my bow (my bow was also looted) it appeared from nowhere. Even though my item was looted, I got it back from an empty quickbar location. THEREFORE, items may be duped in this game.
The default field of view is crap. Enemies and players appear from thin air (20ft range).
What year is it? 2017? Ya… I’m happy to report harvesting resources in MMOs hasn’t changed since Ultima Online. Click and wait…. Click and wait… Static resource locations and timed respawns – BORING!
NPCs are worthless. They do nothing and add nothing to the game.
Buildings are worthless, you can’t interact with anything. Might as well be an empty field of grass within city walls, at least then we wouldn’t have to run around pointless buildings to get from one gate to the next. Why even have houses inside city walls if I can’t do anything with it or have one to put my things in?
No player building, no terrain modification, no destructible environments at all… Completely static environment.
Combat is no better than Mount and Blade… what year was that game released?
Overall, if you change the inventory/banking system I will amend my review. I’m sure that in time, all these other shortfalls will be addressed. But I can’t stand lugging around so much♥♥♥♥♥♥in my backpack!

I didn't try the online multiplayer, but I imagine it would be decent. The gameplay is very fast-paced. I had some matches end in about 17 seconds, and others lasted 5-10 minutes. In essence, the game's goal is to get to the other side of the map by killing your opponent and/or running away from your opponent. If you get the last kill, then you control the scrolling of the map. You can run, throw your sword, stab your opponent, slide your sword up/down/in/out of your opponent (requires skill/practice), somersault, crawl, jump, and punch your way to victory. The multitides of techniques used to win the game vary by player. With only 4 maps, the game feels a bit bland, but the maps differ in layout and provide different strategies in order to win. There are also some game tweaking options to provide some variety to your multiplayer matches. I didn't play with them yet, but they seem interesting enough to try out.
I bought the game on sale, and would recommend obtaining it that way. I didn't feel like spending $14.99 on it, but if I didn't have it by now I may have done so. It is worth the money, especially if you have a friend or two and want to have an impromptu tournament. Or even, if you have a problem with somebody: settle it in Nidhogg.

Codename CURE is a military themed, team-based, co-op shooter set during a zombie apocalypse. Players choose one of five soldier types: Pointman, Assault, Support, Engineer or Sniper each with their own primary weapon and either grenades or gadget.  Take on a mission from one of two modes; objective (bomb escape) and wave survival.  Pick-up health, armor and ammo as you move across 5+ official maps. Its made using the source engine and is free-to-play.
+ Its free.
+ Most bomb-escape maps are fairly long and the more interesting of the modes, especially as towards the end player must reach the objective before the timer runs down.
+ Objective maps have a few dynamic elements to randomize the path the team will have to take.
+ Swarm AI tactics used to good effect
+ Nice use of ambushes  to mix-up the action.
- Only a handful of official maps.
- Bad gameplay dynamics.  Survival = kite to stay alive.  Escape = run and outrun the rest of your team so they get swarmed and spawn is kinder for you!  Its gamey!
- Survival maps are small and boring.  Player-base also seems incapable of playing these effectively.
- Dated graphics.  If you dont like source inspired gameplay then this is not for you!
- Some ad-sponsered servers.  Sometimes causing PC to lock-up!
- Friendly-fire plus a player-base with too many immature griefers does not make for fun co-op.
- Vote abuse mostly map changing for no reason other than getting bored or bad impatient players who die too quickly!
- Some servers with lethal lag in my experience.
- Does crash but very infrequently.
* Action is fast if fairly limited and repetitive.
* Only three types of zombie; Armoured who are strong, runners, who are fast and grapple and shamblers who are slow but mass to overwhelm.
* Some servers have bots so you can at least play if no one else is.
* Nice range of achievements from; kill x zeds with y gun, complete maps on z difficulty to, complete n survival waves.  One achievement seems semi-bugged but does trigger eventually.
* There are tactics to employ but these are either gamey or limited; i.e. block doors with support crate, run in circles to avoid being overwhelmed.
Overall Codename CURE is a simple yet enjoyable game. Gameplay dynamic is similar to other games that have wave survival or objective modes.  The quality of map design is varied enough to make each outing a different experience.  The difference in perks also adds to the dynamism between each soldier type.  I enjoyed playing it but it will have somewhat limited appeal simply because there are better or more modern games out there.
Essentially for me the whole experience can be reduced to a few days (40hrs) of source-engine style, zombie killing fun.  Its free and worth a few hours of some beer induced fun with friends.  However Im afraid that there are a good amount of griefers in the player-base which can ruin the experience unless you move to another server or get lucky!

Although I didn't play the first installment, I must say Evoland 2 got me hooked IMMEDIATELY and for GOOD.

With more than one wink of the eye to Chrono Trigger's time travels, Evoland 2 will make us journey through the different eras of gaming, bouncing from 2D/2 colours graphics to full super-deformed 3D---exploring many MANY kind of gameplays along the way, from strategy to action, from turn-based to---is that Guitar Hero!? O_O
The game, its enjoyable story and really various gameplay are sure to keep any RPG/adventure lover hooked for a good 30 hours, if you intend to explore and find EVERYTHING---and if you are old school gamer you KNOW you will explore EVERYWHERE xD
To add to the pro side, a very well crafted soundtrack---a bit repetitive in some tunes but definitely top notch in others, expecially the ones that incline to rock/metal/folk.
The achievements are not border-line insane to obtain for someone that would like completition without going crazy---you can easily do it in a single playthrough (:
As well as a card game that I just loved to death xP Triple Triad was too tough for me ^^" the one in Evoland is just the right thing c:
So go out there and enjoy catching all the references to videogame/anime history ;D

Rocket Wars is mostly local-coop game, where up to 4 rockets fight against each other at the same time. There are 3 different modes (deathmatch, survivor (like deathmatch with limited lives) and nuke king, which makes one ship much harder to kill and other players should take it down).
Now, first thing: what I like about the game is the
. The menu items, the pick-ups, the ship movement: all of this is well-animated. The flat design fits the game well and you can see that each aspect of the game received lots of attention and was done right. In this type of games, it’s important for music not to distract you and not to get repetitive / annoying, and I must say that the music in Rocket Wars fits this description.
The controls are also smooth and ensure the good experience while playing. I’ve played with gamepad and had no trouble navigating. The gameplay is intense: there’s a burning star at the center of the battlefield, players spawn on the sides, fly around and fight. If you fall into a burning star after someone pushes / shoots you – you die, which adds an extra layer of tactics when it comes to positioning.
:
There are 12 different ships that get unlocked, each has somewhat different stats. I did not notice a huge difference when picking something different, so it felt like it did not matter but it’s there and it influences the game much more as you get better at it. There are some pickups: special weapons that can be used a few times, but there aren’t many of them. I think less than 15. There’s also only one map, so content is somewhat lacking.
The game also lacks online multiplayer, and I seriously think that online mode would make the game much more fun and engaging. I’ve played a few singleplayer games: the bots are not that bad, especially in the beginning, but after some time they become pretty predictable. Am I going to launch it in single player again? No. I’ve tried playing with a friend and it was OK, so it’s a good option to have and I’m probably going to play when someone visits me, but it definitely won’t be a first pick game like Towerfall or Move or Die. I suggest waiting for 50% sale before grabbing this one: at the current state, the game just lacks content to justify the asking price of $7.99.

Rocket Wars is a fast-paced local multi-player game. Destroy your opponents as you navigate a 2D ship picking up powerups and shooting your main gun.
-Gameplay-
2-4 local multiplayer action as the objective of the game is to destroy your opponents ships.
Rocket Wars is a simple game with 7 different game modes:
Deathmatch- First person to 10 kills wins
Survivor- Last person standing wins
Nuke King- Whoever is the Nuke King the Longest
Team Deathmatch
Team Survivor
Team Nuke King
Freeplay- Practice mode
-Graphics, Sound & Artstyle-
Honestly, the overall look and feel to this game isnt anything special. It has a very arcade-esque style that fits the gameplay.
-Price-
The retail price is 7.99 USD
-How many hours estimated?-
The one feature I have not talked about is the progression leveling up system that Rocket Wars has, with 12 unlockable spaceships all with distinct stats. With this in mind, and the ability to throw bots in any match, I think this is well over 10 hours of gameplay overall.

Coupled with colourful, stylized pixel-art - and a soundtrack that's unconventional, but incredibly catchy - I have a hard time complaining about any of

However, it suffers from the same problem that a game like

is painfully vacant. But where a game like
is making strides towards things like community building and online play,
has already moved passed them.
So, while I recommend
to anyone looking for something easy to pick up, challenging, visually striking, and relatively cheap; they'd better be prepared to play it alone.

In a short summary, this game significantly exceeded my expectations. I came to the conclusions that since the game was delayed and the time lapse between To The Moon and Finding Paradise was such a vast amount of time, that either the game wasn't going according to plan, or that they were truly perfecting it. The game ultimately fufilled what I requested from the last game - I felt the gameplay lacked enthusiasm from me, basically the same, find the memory cues, which are very fun because for me I love puzzles. However, I was delighted to be able to play as Neil Watts and go full-out battle mode. Other than that, the game fulfilled my expectations, plus an addition of more suprises that makes me want to come to the conclusion that these are my favorite RPGS of all time. Sure, portal will challenge your brain and make you laugh, or Undertale will pull at your heart strings, but these series of games, despite seeming so small, are extrodinary. (Also, I'd like to briefly mention, I NEED TO KNOW WHAT'S GOING ON WITH NEIL?!? In a more professional tone, the mystery and suspense left behind from these little hints at a bigger picture truly make me crave for more. You've cracked the code, Kan, you have all of us waiting in suspense, in the palm of your hand so-to-speak, and you could do anything....) Furthermore, my only imaginative request would be to see a spark of interest as a significant other between Neil and Eva, but that might be a bit perposterous. In conclusion, thank you Kan for all of your dedication into making such an alluring (in a good way:) franchise of games, and thank you Laura for the most beautifully composed songs.

Finding Paradise story is more a sarcastic view on sigmund's service with specific cases, however that does not implying sigmund's service is anything related to moral value or human ethics, is not like what people always deem "escaping the reality just to feel good" kind of thing. I have played Air Conflicts: Secret Wars and I have this game too, but somehow I just can't get into this game.
Basically, this simulates the Pacific Carrier Wars between US Navy and Imperial Japanese Navy of WW2, where you pilot planes from either side on various missions featuring rather arcadish controls.
Graphics are actually quite good, with multiple views: cockpit, follow-cam, or forward-no-cockpit. For planes with rear gunner, you can go there too. Planes suffer realistic damage when hit. Flak will put holes and ragged edges to your control surfaces and wings, plane will start to smoke, and so on. Ground detail is also quite good, with all the terrain features very visible, and structures easily seen. Sound is decent.
The game gives you a "play in a team" feel by giving you several AI squadron mates. However, they don't seem to do anything. Instead, you can switch to them (swap planes) and fly them when your plane ran out of bombs or whatever. Then when you jump back out that pilot will fly back to carrier to rearm and come back out.
However, the controls are horrible. I don't think it's my gamepad... which is a Xbox360 wireless only a few months old. I can't seem to stablize the plane to do the bomb or torpedo runs. The plane just bounce left/right/left/right as if my controls are lagging. After prolonged play all the planes want to nosedive (lost calibration). This doesn't seem to affect dogfighting much as planes are always going all over the place, but for stable bombing this is impossible.
Furthermore, there's no explanation on bombing or torpedoing. Nothing in the manual.
Missions are extremely long, as you are supposed to experience very bit of the battle. Instead of 3 different versions of battle from 3 different POVs, you will play all three... First you launch as fighters to sweep the sky of enemy planes, and bomb a few AA sites. Then you go in as dive bombers and take out structures and fuel farm. Then you play as torpedo bombers and torpedo 2 cargo ships just off the island. When bombing and torpedoing aren't working, frustration sets in.
Somehow I just can't enjoy this game.

Although it's not the best stealth game I've ever played, I deeply appreciate the amount of effor that went into making this game feel unique. As far as the levels go, I found them to be pretty well done. There's a lot of verticality, so you have many different ways to get to your objective. One thing I found a little annoying was that they reused most of the levels in the 2nd half of the game, although they did try to make it different by giving you a different entry point/objective in the map. I still found these levels fun and they definitely get harder the further you get into the game.
Gameplay wise I found it to be pretty engaging. Sneaking around was the best part although I felt like you weren't a good selection of tools to do so. You got sand, which you could throw at torches to put them out, and then you got knives in order to kill someone from a distance. That was pretty much it, so the gameplay kinda got stale the further in the game you got because you never got anything new.
The story for this game was actually quite different. I wasn't expecting what I gotta give Cyanide props for pushing the boundries. Now it's not the most amazing story in the world and certainly wont win any awards, but it does try to do some new things.
Overall I feel that this game should be in the library of anyone who appreciates a good stealth a rather interesting little protagonist. No. No no no. I'll tell you why.
The start is awesome: stunningly beautiful animation, amazing music. The puzzles seem alright, as you try to learn the game mechanics.
Then, you get to a part where you have to jump from wall to wall while avoiding thorns. Here is where you will see for the first time that not any failure is allowed. This could be okay because beating that part makes you feel like a king, but as you finally reach the top you'll get bombed. It happens, so another 100 tries later you are on the top again and you avoided getting bombed.
First thing you think about is setting up a save. This is not possible because that mechanic is on cooldown. Then you try going left; you drown (or get eaten by fish).
Another 100+ tries later you are on top, avoided the bombs and, as you don't want to drown again, you go right. You kill the mobs there, jump to the next branch... miss. Guess where you end up? You got it right! Right back at the wall jumping.
The thing is, grabbing the wall feels like RNG fest, and so does the jumping in itself. Even though I really set my mind to it for a few hours learning every little bit there is about the jumping/climbing technique, it depends on the game whether your speed/grabbing lines up.
At some point I got afraid to explore, while in a game like this and with these graphics exploring and looking around should be the number one thing you want to do. Maybe it's a keyboard-mouse kind of thing, but the controls don't feel consistent at all. In a platform game this is insanely frustrating. That from a person who can sit for hours upon hours staring apatheticly at the screen trying to get this done.
It was a beautiful experience, but it sure ain't fun. It's too linear to go some other part first and try again later, so if you can't get past a part you'll just be stuck with a worthless game.
If you like frustrating, this is your game. If not, I'd advise you to try something else.

This is the first time I've tackled and completed a visual novel with multiple routes, as I am used to kinetic novels.
And after completing all five heroine routes, I have to give out my final judgment.
We've all seen stories of people who are both complete strangers and (former) acquaintances, gathered together by a single goal or objective. In this VN, it's the glider and the push for the Morning Glory. Seeing them becoming the greatest of companions while also trying to conquer their own personal demons is a thing of beauty.
Of all the characters, Kotori is easily the best one. Her character arc is symbolic of being a bird trying to free itself from a metaphorical cage. And that's as far as I can tell without handing out spoilers. Her personality is well-rounded, too.
Of course, there are two issues with this VN: the wonky translation quality (especially glaring in Ageha's route) and a lack of an English dub. I personally don't mind the removal of H-scenes, anyway (there is an all-ages PS4/PS Vita port in Japan only). To fill in the void in the second clause, here's my hypothetical English cast list.
Max Mittelman as Aoi Minase
Xanthe Huynh as Kotori Habane
Kira Buckland as Amane Mochizuki
Faye Mata as Ageha Himegi
Shelby Lindley as Asa Kazato
Carrie Keranen as Yoru Kazato
So what do I really think of
? Seeing as it was praised back when it was first released in the Land of the Rising Sun, I can easily why this story is as beautiful as the sky hovering above us.
Good job, MoeNovel. Now let's see the Soaring Club ally with MacGyver!

Graphics / Visuals: 10/10
Sound: 10/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Overall: 9/10
Now, I grew up with Oddworld as the core of my gaming life. When I was a child, I played Oddworld morning, noon and night. Although I could never beat Scrabania back then, I have since grown up and was able to beat it eventually when I got my own PC and was able to play it again. When I heard that JAW would be remaking the original, I was HYPED. And for good reason.
The visuals. OH MAN THE VISUALS. The original had some stunning backgrounds and designs and concepts, but they just cannot hold a candle to New 'N' Tasty. This game is visually stunning. And no other word can describe it. Just when walking through RuptureFarms in the first level, my breath was taken away at how different everything looked, yet everything was still based on the first game enough so that I knew exactly where I was in comparison to the original. Dear God this game is pretty. The lighting and skyboxes are amazing, which matters more in a 2D game than in most other games, but at the same time, they didn't cut corners with the foreground environment, either. It is obvious from beginning to end that the environment design is something that has been meticulously slaved over, as a chef would slave over his special dish, from start to finish.
The sound and music in this game is based, again, heavily on the original. Gamespeak has been redesigned and improved, which is a huge mercy. One of the most annoying parts about the foriginal was having to shepard Mudukons one at a time to portals. Now, you can simply get all their attention with "All o' ya!" and run them to portals in one trip. Sligs and Mudukon slaves now chat idly while working, which is a refreshing touch and one that gives every character a little personality. If they'd maybe put in more lines for a bit of variety (since hearing "If only I had a bomb~" from ten different Sligs was got a bit tedious towards the end), then that would have been an amazing addition. The music is much crisper and better than the original, too.
As for gameplay, this is where the 1/10 is deducted. Abe, this time around, feels far less rigid and more alive than he did in the original. While sneaking, he'll check his surroundings, his movements are far more akin to an actual living creature; when standing still, he'll rock slightly. When running, he'll take a little time to build up speed. These things are things a dedicated fan will instantly notice, and it'll make them smile every time. The controls, however, were ever so slightly clunky in my experience. I had more than a few deaths with Abe moving too far forward or not breaking into a run quickly enough (The part where you have to lead the bees to Elum), and with Abe deciding to hoist up to the level I had just jumped down from, instead of hopping to the other side, which happened more than a few times. Though both of these are changable in the options makes this partly my fault, but I do think they could have pointed such things out; it would have made playing through the game significantly easier.
Overall, this is a stellar game, and one that truly is worthy of the "Oddworld Inhabitants" seal. It doesn't just beat the original; it blows it out of the water, like a son inheriting his father's factory and then turning it into a Fortune 500. This game, Just Add Water, is that Fortune 500, and for anyone who played and liked the original "Abe's Oddysee" I say:
"Why haven't you brought this yet?"

While I haven't gone through the entire game yet (still working on a Hard 100% clear), I think the rather high price tag might warrant another review for people skeptical about the game.
- Performance wise, I've had little issues before or after the patch. Prior to the first patch's release, the worst I had was the game crashing on me twice during a transition from one area to another, but I haven't experienced FMV hiccups nor any general play issues even with max settings. The sound has been acting a little odd (hurr) after the patch, though, often cutting out at certain points like when several mines explode at once. It's not big, but it's noticeable.
- As someone who hasn't experienced the PS4 version and its possible issues, I've had little problem with the game compared to the original Oddysee... in more ways than one. Some may argue that the sterile, dark nature from the original is lost in the colors and bloom here, but I think there's still very nice environmental design that still highlights the industry vs. nature idea going on between the game's major settings. The new voice work can be rather goofy, though I think that falls under the more subjective argument against Oddworld's change in tone over time more than anything.
- On its own merits, the game still remains as clever and charming as I can recall (yes, even considering the changes in tone). The keyboard controls have been great, save for some time to adjust to more precise movements in the beginning. The ability to call multiple Mudokons together is nice, but I think there are moments where it shows that they didn't intend for it to work that way, forcing me to stick to single Mudokon greetings. Quik-Save is perhaps too nice; instantaneously loading to a save point can really diminish some otherwise tense challenges. It also bothers me that chant suppressors and certain chant possession moments are harder to gauge due to the lack of screen transitions, but it hasn't emerged too much to be a consistent issue.
Is this still a good game? Definitely. Does it outplace Oddysee? Not exactly, but I think it's a great complement. Is it worth $20? It depends. It's well worth a try to see Oddworld reimagined in HD, but the difficulty and tone are not going to be the same. I liked it enough to spend that much, but others might want to wait on a sale before stepping back in.

This game looked very promising in the early screenshots and descriptions.  Unfortunately, it turned out to be quite boring.  The character development system is neither interesting nor diverse, especially in the early levels.  With such a small party size and limited abilites, success in the early to mid-game battles is more about dice rolls than about planning or clever tactics.  In a party with only one caster, healing is so much more important than damage that it is rarely wise to cast damage spells (except when environmental effects more or less demand it). For a party with two casters....well good luck.  Although there is a dearth of solidly enjoyable tactical, turn-based rpgs, I can't recommend this game to fill the void.

First: Blackguards isn't bad or good.  It's just extremely mediocre.  If you're into D&D alternatives and dig X-Com, it probably won't waste your time.  But I can't recommend it for most people.
The character customization is surprisingly lacking, despite the illusion of choice.  There are twice as many attributes as a D&D system, but they all just sum together to increase your attack, dodge chance, initiative, etc.  There are only a handful of combat abilities to use, so there's not a lot of choice as far stabbing/shooting.  The magic users are more nuanced; there are a ton of spells, each with 4 tiers, so you're constantly weighing the cost/benefit of those.
Combat itself is very similar to X-Com or D&D 4.0: you get either a move and an action, or a double move.  This all occurs on a hex-grid, and most maps have some sort of interactable element to spice it up.  They do an admirable attempt to differentiate the levels, but you will take place in about a billion combat scenarios, so a lot of them inevitably feel repetitive.  You'll probably be skipping side quests by the end out of boredom.
The plot is pretty linear.  There are batches of side quests that open up at various points, but none of them augment the main plot line at all.  It's your typical RPG "save my daughter" or "escort my caravan" kind of stuff.  You become enslaved and forced to fight in a gladiatorial arena at one point, so that's pretty neat.

Excellent follow up to the great To The Moon. Very emotionally charged story with some wonderful characters and dialogue that concludes in a way that probably touched me more than its predecessor did. The music is beautiful in its simplicity and has a welcome return from Laura Shigihara, who provides the vocals for the ending song. Kan Gaos unique humour still shines but like To The Moon it can slightly mess with the tone in one or two places, though it doesn't detract from the overall experience. FInding Paradise is the perfect example of why you don't need tens of millions of dollars in development costs to create a game that's both fun and manages to connect with you on an emotional level. I recommend buying it and playing in one or two sittings; You don't need to play To The Moon to enjoy the sequel but I would suggest picking it up beforehand to ensure you get the most out of it.

-Besides the main plot (you are two professionals altering the patient's memory), this game's story does make it worthy of a stand-alone sequel.
Negatives (and this is a stretch):

-Any new mechanics (besides the mementos mini-game) only exist for a few minutes

Another simplified (but enjoyable) riff on air combat from Games Farm, "Pacific Carriers" seems to leverage a lot from "Secret Wars." As in its predecessor, this game stays fun because of its core combat mechanics. Because each encounter can unfold with slight differences, there's an inherent "microvariety" that keeps the game from becoming too repetitive. Also, the combat allows for quick rewards that can keep you hooked.
The game isn't flawless by any means. Every once in a while, you'll run into an objective which has an unclear solution. There are also some issues with difficulty spikes, especially when squadron members are shot down before you even get a chance to make them useful. Also, the Japanese campaign seems to have a strange overabundance of "intentionally unwinnable" scenarios. If you know a bit of history, you can see these scenarios coming, but the way they're handled in terms of gameplay can be a little too vague at times.
(Also, the graphics engine seems to struggle disproportionately when you fly through partially transparent features, like smoke.)
"Pacific Carriers" is rather more challenging than "Secret Wars," especially since midair collisions have been implemented. Enemy fighters seem perfectly happy to simply smack into you, and you'll probably have a number of frustrating experiences where a squadron mate flies into you. On the flipside, I felt like this game allows for just that much more nuance in the flying, with working the throttle being much more meaningful than it was in "Secret Wars."
Like its predecessor, this game has the potential to provide you with a gleeful and interesting romp through a number of air combat challenges. You do have to suspend your disbelief a bit, and the level of polish isn't quite "AAA," but it's plenty good and worth a look.

To start things off, I've always loved these fighter planes-esque games (e.g. War Thunder, Pearl Harbor). AC:PC was honestly the best game on my joystick that I've ever played (other than Star Wars: Rouge Squadron). Two separate campaigns in the WWII era, having the choice between Japanese and Americans were very interesting. Upon initializing the mission, you'll notice that every mission is taking off from an aircraft carrier (duh!). And unlike most single player campaign mode fighter games, you aren't the only one in the sky. You've got a whole squadron behind you (or in front, I'm always in the back) and the best part is that you can switch planes like how you switch players in FIFA. The pilots also have a ranking system e.g. Private, Captain and added skills to them depending on rank. It gets emotional when one of my starred pilots die in combat. The overall dogfighting is very fun and engaging, but when it comes down to missions, not so much.
Yes, there's two campaign modes, but all the missions are very mundane; some just bore me to death, literally. These include trying to spot an enemy carrier that's off the coast for 3 minutes, attempting to dive bomb a radio tower because your fighter planes ran out of ammo, or trying to kill the rest of the enemy squadron with one plane left. Not to mention that the flak cannons on the ground do insane damage. Aim is quite hard with a joystick (you can play with a keyboard, but it still doesn't help the aim) and the bombs/torpedos take some skill to land unless you're literally right above the enemy unit. However, that still doesn't take away the fun of things.
What I really enjoyed most was bombing ships. I love bombing runs; going down an entire stirp of an enemy aircraft carrier brings me so much joy. Knowing you have air superiority against this bomber always brings me to rejoice my lovely machine guns. Also, you can specialize the weapons on the plane to the mission, making even greater firepower.
Overall, the game was very enjoyable. Missions were a pain, but atleast AC:PC got the basics down.

Wow! What a load of rubbish! It is atypical of me to write reviews, but this game deserves it! I am sorry guys, but this game just fails in so many ways. Its not all bad, but the bad is so very bad that it overshadows all of the good this game has to offer. So, in fairness, lets start out with the good.
First and foremost. I love the character. Styx is a fun loving, no holds barred, goblin pickpocket assassin with a mind of his own. After watching the intro videos to this game I knew I was in for a good time even if it didn't answer all of my prayers to a post-workday reprieve. What's not to love. He looks cool, he moves cool, and he even uses foul language. My kinda goblin man. The story... really who cares. I have never played Assassin's Creed games for the overarching tellanovella that it turns out to be. At a point these games are about killing your marks in stealthy and creative ways. This is not to say that the story is bad per se. It is just a little lackluster and does not really peak interest or drive character development.
Second, I would mention the environments. The developers did not dissapoint me on this front. At one point I was up upon a high perch looking down into what i can only compare to an M.C. Escher portrait. It was phenomenal. The camera movement around the environment was even better. I had near perfect scope of my marks and I could see the path to the level's end. So far, what more could you ask for?
Lastly the perk tree, for what few hours I did play the game, seemed reactive and I could follow along with the developer's idea of where the game was headed in terms of the new and interesting subterfuges that Styx would eventually be able to perform. So what went wrong? How did this seemingly good game go bad?
So, sadly, this is where my interest was smashed by some overwhelmingly repulsive aspects of the game. Now I realize that this may be a bit harsh to the developers, and I do apologize for what I am about to say. I also realize that this game was released back in 2014 and I am keeping that in mind when I am offering my opinion on this title. All that aside however, was it really necessary to make this game so clunky.  For an agile goblin assassin I would think that the game would  take into account, that instead of picking up the dead body in front of Styx, he would be more concerned about parrying an incoming blow from the living threat standing two feet in front of him. It would almost be alright if Styx was not so terribly squishy and that his parry ability had some indication of when he was going to be hit. Just a thought.
This, however, is not even the most rubbish thing about this game. The worst part is that, at a point, you must take your time with the game, plan where all of the bodies are going to be placed, and then, if for whatever reason you were either spotted by an enemy or simply falling off the nearest ledge, your save will take you back to the dawn of time. At one point in the game I had to stop exploring the wonderful map because it became unnecessary. It no longer mattered what beautiful game design was there. It was easier to simply run through the path that I had completed so many times before. It became a game of tedium. I no longer cared for the story because I figured hey, what the hell I bet by the end I will have listened to the game script 10 times over. Additionally, what now is the point of the relic peices. Gotta catchem all only really applies to pokemon and I am sure the dozen times I played through a zone i found them all at least once. So if finding the pieces is the difficult part why does remembering where they all are have to be difficult as well?
Styx in terms of control response reminded me of an all out brawler class in WoW. He felt like he lumbered about dodging into walls and inadvertantly pulling himself atop a ledge only to find his brutish self staring into the eyes of an enemy. All the while he seems to have no desire to GTFO when a squad of archers fires upon him from afar. He just takes the two shots that he can, and then crumbles to the ground like a true WoW mage class only to find himself respawning at what seems to be the beginning of the entire game every single time.
I realize that I am writing this reveiw 3 years too late and that they have already produced a new game which hopefully answers all the abundant and obvious issues Styx: Master of Shadows has. And yet I am still writing it. The game aggravated me that much! That I went back in time 3 whole years to criticize that which, to current standards, matters not. Yes it is that bad of a game. I have not been this disapointed in a game since I found out that "Watch Paint Dry" was never going to be released. I think the real issue here is do I want to buy the new game? I mean i probably will because I'm a dope. And maybe it will be better recieved now that my expectations of it have been torn down to the foundation. But really, where were the play-testers here? These are not complicated improvements to make. Surely I am not the only one that played this game for about seven hours and realized it was not worth continuing my playthrough. To review this game feels almost like my kid brought home a math test that he failed. It's not that my kid is stupid and can't do the math. It's not even that the math test was too hard. It's that he did not apply himself. I'm just left saying, "I'm not angry with you, Im just dissappointed." What's worse is that I don't even have a kid.
