Evoland 2 is a grand adventure game that has the feel of a JRPG without actually being one. It is a
step up from the original. If you haven’t played the original Evoland, I recommend not bothering – just skip to this one. It takes all of the half-finished ideas from the original and finishes them, combining them into a huge, story-driven, humor-driven, genre-sampling experience that will leave you feeling like you’ve explored everything that retro gaming had to offer.
The gameplay starts out resembling Zelda’s hack-and-slashing, but it doesn’t stay that way. In fact, I won’t even claim to pin a genre onto this game – it throws
at you. I wouldn’t dare spoil anything more than that. Half the fun is getting to see what crazy scenario the game serves up next. (And in case you're worried -- gone are the random encounters from the first game! This game has no random encounters at all, with the exception of one particular dungeon...)
Don’t be fooled by the constant barrage of borderline-plagiarism jabs and references to famous games – between them lies a decent, well-told story about time travel, nostalgia, war and politics, and the changing of eras. If you get immersed in the story, you’ll find that it occasionally drops thought-provoking details which keep you guessing and ultimately come together to paint a complete picture of what is really happening throughout history.
As a fair warning, this game has
slow pacing. Expect to spend 30-60 minutes in every new area.  Try to get immersed into the story and the world – if you’re the kind of gamer who wants to get things over with as fast as possible, you’ll probably get bored and annoyed with this game very fast.
As another fair warning, due to the genre-sampling nature of this game, you’ll probably encounter one or two areas you’ll absolutely hate. The genre-change areas go on pretty long (30-60 minutes each) but I enjoyed their length – they make the alternate gameplay feel less like minigames and more like valid representations of the various genres, something you’ve got to settle into and get a feel for before you can graduate from them. It’s a game about trying everything, so you’ve got to have a mentality of being willing to man up and complete an area even if you don’t like the gameplay – because what you don’t enjoy at first you might acquire a taste for in the end. (Although, if an area is giving you too much trouble, you’re free to switch the difficulty on the fly anytime you’d like.)
As much as I praise the game, it has its faults. It could have been a 10/10 game, had it not been for a handful of issues:
I give Evoland 2 a 7.5 / 10. It’s a bit rough around the edges and not perfect, but it’s one hell of an adventure! It's very much worth playing for fans of Zelda or retro gaming in general. I loved it; It made me laugh with clever references and fourth wall breaks, it really impressed me with its sense of story development, and it compelled me to keep playing just to see what would come next – just like a good adventure game should. Just make sure to go into the experience with a mentality of patience and expect a 20-hour game, and it might just leave you with warm, fuzzy feelings of nostalgia by the end.
(Achievement hunters: I got about 95% without a guide. The game includes some cool treasure-tracking features that make it much more enjoyable to find all the secrets than in the first game. However, a few secrets are unfairly hidden and don’t show up on the treasure tracker at all, and you might have to resort to a guide to find them at the end. It’s about 20-25 hours to 100%.)

No. No no no. I'll tell you why.
The start is awesome: stunningly beautiful animation, amazing music. The puzzles seem alright, as you try to learn the game mechanics.
Then, you get to a part where you have to jump from wall to wall while avoiding thorns. Here is where you will see for the first time that not any failure is allowed. This could be okay because beating that part makes you feel like a king, but as you finally reach the top you'll get bombed. It happens, so another 100 tries later you are on the top again and you avoided getting bombed.
First thing you think about is setting up a save. This is not possible because that mechanic is on cooldown. Then you try going left; you drown (or get eaten by fish).
Another 100+ tries later you are on top, avoided the bombs and, as you don't want to drown again, you go right. You kill the mobs there, jump to the next branch... miss. Guess where you end up? You got it right! Right back at the wall jumping.
The thing is, grabbing the wall feels like RNG fest, and so does the jumping in itself. Even though I really set my mind to it for a few hours learning every little bit there is about the jumping/climbing technique, it depends on the game whether your speed/grabbing lines up.
At some point I got afraid to explore, while in a game like this and with these graphics exploring and looking around should be the number one thing you want to do. Maybe it's a keyboard-mouse kind of thing, but the controls don't feel consistent at all. In a platform game this is insanely frustrating. That from a person who can sit for hours upon hours staring apatheticly at the screen trying to get this done.
It was a beautiful experience, but it sure ain't fun. It's too linear to go some other part first and try again later, so if you can't get past a part you'll just be stuck with a worthless game.
If you like frustrating, this is your game. If not, I'd advise you to try something else.

*SPOILER-FREE REVIEW*
I love visual novels and have played quite a lot of them, both through Steam and outside of it, and I have to say that I was pleasantly surprised by If My Heart Had Wings - definitely worth the money.
On a superficial level, If My Heart Had Wings has some great touches that make it feel very polished and professional, which naturally adds to the enjoyment of the gameplay.  The music is very nice and we get a couple of full vocal songs, which is a great bonus, as a lot of visual novels do not.  The visuals of the game are also really great, some of the best I've seen in a visual novel; there are a lot of animated scenes that, while relatively simple, really add to the moment and heighten the feeling of being sucked into that world.  If you put it on auto mode, it feels like you're watching an anime at some points.  The whole thing feels very high end, which is commendable considering I believe this is the first visual novel by this company.
I'll hit you with the flaws before we move on - there are some of the biggest translation issues I've seen in a visual novel.  In general, the translation feels natural and pretty good, and you can get immersed in the story without noticing anything, but after a while, towards the end of certain routes, it starts to degrade.  There are spelling mistakes and grammatical errors all over the place, random sentences come out really Engrishy while the rest of the translation had been fine, and at some points, people's sprites are labelled with the wrong name and people also refer to other people with the wrong name - sometimes, people's genders are switched multiple times throughout the story by accident.  In addition to this, on occasion, the moving visuals can be a bit janky.  So yes, there are major flaws with these aspects in a lot of places, and this can be really bothersome if that kind of thing affects you.  However, I personally found that these flaws paled in significance when faced with the enjoyability and emotional weight of the story, which I'm about to touch on, so even though there are technical problems, I would still whole heartedly recommend this visual novel.
If My Heart Had Wings knows how to tell a story.  Each route has its own funny moments, emotional connotations and genuinely relatable and enjoyable aspects.  There are things everyone can understand, and things that you've never experienced in your own life, so it's gratifying to watch these characters go through them.  There is a focus on romance, naturally, but it doesn't actually feel like the main event - chasing your dreams, hard work and finding friendship are the core themes of this visual novel, and they set up events really well.  I think the story was paced pretty well and I loved how the events changed with each route; huge events are changed, relationships are different and the whole outlook and success of the group of friends is altered depending on which route you take, and I love that.  After having played them all, it really gave me a wider perspective on how things could change and what was most important to both the protagonist and myself as a player.  The emotional aspects of each person's route are really well portrayed, and feel very genuine.  Also as a side note, I love how the story uses so much real world technical knowledge about the activities the group are doing and what they're aiming for - it makes it so much more believable and enjoyable because something like this could happen in real life, and the vast knowledge that these people learn that most people have no idea about really makes you feel like you're part of something special.
Also, because I know people will ask, this version of If My Heart Had Wings is fully censored.  The original had H scenes and slightly different events on routes, in fact one route is almost completely different.  I've read that you can buy and apply patches to restore this content, although it can lead to bugs in the game.  You could also download the original Japanese H version and get a translation patch, although it seems very hard to find.  A lot of people are boycotting this Steam release of the game because they feel it butchers the story.  I cannot attest as to which version is better, as I couldn't find a way to download the original, and I don't want to apply the patches as they seem too buggy to take a chance on, so haven't played the original.  However, what I can tell you is that playing this Steam version with no idea what I'm missing, I don't feel as though anything is wrong.  I thoroughly enjoyed this visual novel and felt like everything was perfectly fine the way it was.  Perhaps the original version is better, I can't say.  But I can promise you that if you play this version, you will have a really great experience with some memorable characters, hilarious moments, wonderful music, a story that constantly changes, and a plot that will really make you feel things.
In summary, I really recommend If My Heart Had Wings.  It was uplifting, interesting, funny and all round enjoyable.

Archers - You get 4 skills, 2 early on, extra damage shot, bypass armor shot and then later 3 arrows dps on single target (highest damage I can find in game) and then AoE rain of arrows. To the Moon is a 2011 RPGMaker game by Freebird Games.
It was a moving story about life, in the way that life has a lot of laughing and crying in it.
Since that game, there was promise of a "sequel" (although there is a considerable time gap between that game and this one).
As the years went by, we got little fun short stories like the SigCorp Holiday Minisodes 1 and 2, and A Bird Story.
Those are necessary to understanding the plot of Finding Paradise, as small as they might seem, it really is building up to something.
Finding Paradise is the sequel that fans waited 6 years for.
The most impressive quality of Finding Paradise is how it manages to tackle life in a completely different perspective from To the Moon; especially since it hit very close to home for me.
If you enjoyed Kan Gao's other works...This one is a treat.
I've been waiting for this game since 2011, and it did not dissapoint. Flawless art, music, and comedy as expected from Gao.

Many games can evoke emotions in their players.  We become attached to the characters we play as, seeing their lives, their trials and tribulations, their hopes and dreams.  But at the end of the day, it's rare that we truly FEEL for those characters at the most intimate of levels.
Finding Paradise makes you FEEL.
Just like To The Moon, the music is spot on, the graphics are appropriate (though I'd really like it if I could resize the window easily instead of having to play it stretched), and the storytelling is...'top-notch' feels almost like a disservice to how good it is.  This game is really a testament to the fact that you don't need AAA credentials, 4K visuals, and a multi-million dollar budget to create a truly beautiful game.
In short - if you liked To The Moon, you will like Finding Paradise.
And yes, I cried.  Multiple times.
Wow, just Wow.

"As we dream and as we grow
We have to learn to let things go
But let the wonder never fade
Though we've turned 10,000 pages
Flying high or stuck below"
A sequel to the masterpiece To The Moon and A Bird Story. Finding Paradise is a beautiful masterpiece. Like To The Moon, it really leaves you with many questions that all just snap together and hit you like a truck. Again, a story I will bring with me in my heart forever.
Thank you Kan Gao. Thank you for your amazingly creative mind and your way of telling these beautiful stories.

I have played this game a fair bit as well as a lot of others in the same sort of genre, but Empyrion is the game I always come back to. The majority of my hours have been in single player, but since about this time last year I have played only multiplayer (with the odd foray into creative mode to do some ship design).
For the new players, or people looking to get the game, I cannot recommend this game enough. When you do start out I would say play single player survival on easy mode first off and complete the ingame tutorial. Haven't tried the latest tutorial, it was recently updated, but this will give you a grounding in how the game works. Switch over to creative mode to get an idea of the build mechanics and then jump into mulitplayer.
The current version as of this review is 7.1. Prior to the 7 series of releases, i found this game fun but easy. Resources were cheap to obtain, leveling the character was fast and it never took me long to get a huge excess of material and start making my giant ships. With 7.0, they have rebalanced the resource requirements for items, changed up the recipes (don't rely on the wiki at the moment) and changed up the mining mechanics. It is awesome! It is now a good challenge to progress out of the starting worlds and I have had to plan carefully what I build with the limited resources available. One of the most important things to build early is an ore scanner to help you out.
In the later game, I have to be very selective about what I build as the new receipes for crafting have meant that a lot of resources have become 'rare'. To get my big CV's i have to plan carefully what I gather and when, but also it has added a lot of risk when i want to take these ships into PvP space.
All up, I love the 7.0 update and it has made this game even more enjoyable and challenging.
If you want a good survival game (challenge is mainly in the beginning of the game) and a game where you can build a variety of vehicles - small vessels, capital vessels and hover vessels, as well as elaborate bases and take them all out to fight then this is the game for you.
Do I wish there were some mechanics and blocks from other games introduced into this one? yes. But this is by far the most developed of those that I have played, has a good community and is continuously developed by the Dev's.
Get Empyrion today!

I have had this game for over a  year, played about 200 hrs and it is still fun to play now. Has a bit of a learning curve if you want to play on harder planets like Omicron. Any mistake you make there may be fatal and you'd have to start anew. But this is what makes it fun, balancing on the edge of failure and coming through in the end. It's a good survival game with some simplistic fighting mechanics but quite enjoyable regardless. The devs seem to know how to strike the balance so it's not boring and not frustratingly difficult. For example, in the beginning the spawn rate of hostile creatures is very low, to ramp up as time progresses, keeps the game challenging. Another example, you are not stuck with health packs, can apply local flora for a variety of symptoms, I find that both fun and practical.
Had a lot of fun hours playing coop with my 10yr old son. Last time we had to sneak past a planet patrol ship, carrying precious resources to the new location, diving underwater so it wouldn't see us. Almost ran out of oxygen there. Good fun.
There's not much grind, there are lots of opportunities to build stuff, loot and attack and defend. The game has not become worse in gameplay during the year of development, graphics has improved, and the devs are still actively hacking it. Multiplayer is mostly very solid, and very playable. Game is fast on a modern machine, devs keep optimizing it regularly.
From the cons:
A bit of simplistic tutorial, may put off some people. Simplistic fighting AI (predictable). Some scripted behaviours are too predictive, like the appearance of a troop support after taking down a drone. Might benefit from some randomness there. The unaccessable poles is weird (but not a deal breaker). Graphics is still basic in a lot of ways (e.g., terrain detail). Could benefit from more building block variety for both bases and ships. I personally am not a great fan of building stuff from cubes, due to the way the end product looks, but this could be fixed. Would be nice to have a way to mold the shapes in a bezier-like approach once the blocks have been put in place. This would go a great way to make things custom and varied.
All in all, a deep game with lots of crafting/fighting/looting, in a space setting. I strongly recommend giving it a  go.

This game has a huge amount of potential. They have made huge improvements to the game since the start of EA, especially in the last month or so. Completely redesigned settlements, group quests (events), a Glory/Contribution system, new player models and soon a completely revamped combat/animation system.
If you are not into PVP, this game is not a murder simulator, even though realm PVP and territory control is important. You can only lose a small number of items if you get killed and looted in PVP. If you are smart you can avoid most involuntary PVP altogether. There is plenty to do outside of PVP. Gathering, crafting, events, upgrading settlements and farming PVE mobs.
Crafting in the game is quite strong and detailed, with the best stuff all being crafted. Crafting is being revamped to make it less grindy with the introduction of "Mass Production" recipes, which address the time sink factor of crafting.
The devs of this game are genuine and hard working. They have released almost 40 major patches since launch and many hotfixes. They work a lot of late nights and weekends. They have a burning passion to make their game succeed. If you give this game a chance, you won't be buying into a project that will be casually abandoned like all too many EA games are.
So I have to give this game a definite thumbs up and recommend it to anyone who wants to see a refreshing take on the MMO genre succeed.

Admittedly I am not the best PvPer but at level 97 getting beaten by a level 20 whule the ping lights red over and over. That is a bit disconcerting. The crafting system is very eloborate and tedious. But that's ok. What isn't ok is that you have to hunt for recipe drops. There is no method for reverse engineering. There should be a method (with failure chance) to reverse engineer items found. The map is filling up as development continue and the game is certainly party necessity oriented. I see great things in the future but for now it is more a crafter paradise than a story driven or even open world game. Everything is beautiful but mundane. Some plot events need to be implemented and most of all I'd like to see the Merchant Bag which would allow you to have a bag where you store things to sell. Then, like the existing arena, have a seperate instance called market where players can enter and their characters interact like merchants do in game. As Is I give it 3.75 of 5 and rising.

Gloria Victis. First of all, this game is not forgiving in any sense of the word. It will kill you, it will steal from you, and it will do it over and over again. But you'll have an absolute blast while its happening.
This is a early access MMO developed with Unity, and it comes with all of the bugs and issues you would expect from that. That being said, I have never yet seen a team of developers more committed to releasing a quality title. Both for the fans that have support them over the (sometimes arduous) years of deveopment, and to the MMO community as a whole; which has been oversaturatred with lackluster releases, pay to win nightmares, and carbon copy cash grabs. This game is none of those things. Through regular updates and consistent communication with their players, the devs are creating an MMO experience that no other game can currently match.
It's a large, open world sandbox that does so many things right. Open world PvP with a focus on zone control and competitive events make for an engaging, and challenging experience whenever desired.  These central hubs for player vs. player combat do wonders for enruring the world never seems empty of action. The are similar events centered around PvE combat if the real thing is too daunting for newer players. And to top it off, there is an incredibly immersive and extensive crafting system waiting for anyone who is up to the task. Be a soldier on the front lines. Be a wandering adventurer who goes where the battle and the winds take them. Be a master crafter for a guild of warriors, ensuring they always have weapons and armor ready for battle. And why is that necessary?
I'm so glad you asked.
This game features a partial loot system. Meaning when a player dies, for a short window of time enemy players have the opportunity to loot a few items off of his body/inventory.  This system is implemented is a great way, and is honestly my favorite aspect of the game. It brings risk vs. reward to the table in a whole new way, and will be a major contributing factor to the heart pumping experience that this game's PvP delivers. You might loose that amazing sword you love using so much. But in the next battle, you might pick up an axe that delivers death even more swiftly to your foes. You'll never loose eveything, so getting back into the action immediately is never an issue.
So if this sounds like the MMO youve been longing for, or even considering, I highly recommend giving it a go, and seeing what the world of Gloria Vicitis can offer you. Happy slaughtering.

This is a kick♥♥♥♥♥stealth game. It's got some unique mechanics (creating a clone with limited capabilities as a distraction, throwing balls of sand to put out torches, turning invisible for a short time), but where it really shines is in pure, no-frills stealthy manuvering. A combination of rolls, wall-sidles and spry goblin leaps is all you need to surmount most challenges. Still, it's nice to have the oppurtunity to get creative now & again.
I adore the verticality in the level design, and I like that guards will be able to see you if you're plainly visible even if you're 20 feet above them. It's also neat that there's no piddly "indefinite knock-out" option for a nonlethal playthrough; meeting the "Mercy" condition means avoiding every enemy.
Speaking of which, there are some missions where getting seen by the guards fails the mission and boots you to a load screen, which it might as well do every time. Maybe if you aren't OCD about getting the "never spotted" bonus you wouldn't mind getting into a scuffle and running from the guards, which can be rather satisfying, but personally I'll just kill the guard who saw me to spite him and then reload. Two of the five upgrade trees are rendered totally useless in a no kills / no detections playthrough.
There's a lot of emphasis on the multiple paths you can take through the levels, which is true for the most part, but there are three to four sections where you can't progress until you find the single well-hidden chain of illogically-placed pointless struts you're supposed to jump along. What the hell did they put all these struts all over the place for? How much stuff did they need to hang on this random exterior wall?
Also, while the in-game graphics look great, the cutscenes and voice acting can get a little crude. It's by no means a dealbreaker, but I think the story they've told, which is excellent, could've been slightly better served by something a little more polished. But, y'know, it's an indie game-- what're you gonna do?
All in all, I've found it to be an enjoyable and satisfying experience that I'd heartily recommend.

This is actually a pretty good game. It does not present the most accurate or detailed portrail of the War but it is fairly enjoyable. The game feel slike it would be right at home on the Xbox 360 or Xbox 1. That does not mean its a bad game or it plays like crap o nthe PC but that it definitely is more of an arcade game based around conflicts in the Pacific then an actualy simulation of said conflict and its planes.
What is refreshing about this game that unlike many others that offer unlimited ammo and tell you where to go, and point to you what to do the game has limited resouces and actually requires you to think and pay attention. (Oh my gosh no way!!!). So during a patrol mission for example like mission #2 you are told to spot the enemy. You have to take off and actually look for them insead of the game pointing it out ot you. I understand that this mechanic for some of you might not be appealing but I find it a breath of fresh air in a world of games that keep telling me what to do to a point that I don't even have to engage mentaly anymore.
Another nice touch is that durring combat you have limited amunition. For example you might have 5 planes in a single engagement and each will  have 1100 ammo. If you happen to run out of ammo you are screwed for that plane and he might get shot down. What you can do is switch and take control of any of the other planes by hitting the back button on the controller. This is a pretty cool mechanic and quite fun.
The graphics are very good in this game especially the water. The game is colorful, the sky looks and feels beautiful and the planes at least the conckpits look good. When you dive you will see the cockpit shaking and hear some windsheer. Explosions look good and enemy planes behave, break up and fall apart in unpredictable and random ways.
I am playing the game on an xbox 360 controller. The game can also be played using the mouse and ising the keyboard. All control options allow for basic (arcaade) and simulation controls.
The music/score for the game is good although the few missions I have done so far a little repetative. It sounds like a movie score, being very cinematic. The game reminds me of a Michael Bay movie when in combat with the cinematic score, and good visuals.
I think that this is a good game and I am enjoying it then again I don't have unrealistic expectations n where everything is either great or♥♥♥♥♥♥and nothing in between.  The game is fun if you feel like playing a WW2 non hardcore sim/arcade game that deals with the Pacific theater.

i thoroughly enjoyed the story too: i'm not one for stories based on time because a lot of them use really greasy cop outs and even get confused within themselves but evoland 2 is one of the few that do it right (although the ending was very bittersweet). the power to travel to past, present and the future aided with maps in different art styles and with minor differences really works and makes the game feel three times as big, which is pretty hard to do when youre using the same map 3 times.
the mechanics of this game tells us the tale about older real games, some of which are forgotten and lets you live those moments again. Whether you've played a different array of games in the past, or if you're just getting started, this game is for you.

The story is well-written and rarely feels cliche. Game length is ~16 hours if you don't care about completion, and 21.6+ hours if you want to 100% it. It's enjoyable to 100% because the game gives you the tools to find the collectibles, so you never have to rely on internet guides.
In any case, I highly recommend this game if you are even remotely a fan of RPGs. If you can't afford the 20$ full price don't forget to at least get it when it's on sale!

White Haven Mysteries is a straight forward HOG (Hidden Object Game) that adds little new to the genre. There are a lot of HO scenes and very few puzzles. While there is no fast travel or map, each scene lets you know when you have completed all the tasks on it. While there is a fair amount of backtracking, it's not tiresome as the game is very short, taking just 90 minutes for me to beat.
The game sets itself up as a horror adventure and asks you to play with the sound turned up and the lights off, but there's very little horror and almost no jump scares. So a little disappointing.
The story deals with the subject matter of mental health but the conclusion is sudden and not very satisfying.
The graphics, voice acting, and sound are all average at best, but if you are into HO games, there are enough scenes to keep you busy for an hour or two.
Overall, it wasn't terrible and the biggest problem is that it is too short. I played through in one session and didn't have to save the game, so didn't run into the save game problems others are reporting. It's probably a game you should avoid unless you are a fan of the genre, and then plan to complete it in one sitting. I'm going to give it a positive review, for no reason other than it's not bad enough to give a thumbs down.

I enjoyed Blackguards. The gameplay is fantastic and the level design is great. Unlike most of the RPGs I played, this game is brutal: the heroes are either outnumbered or weak compared to the enemies and you have to take advantage of the environment in order to win. There are a few badly designed levels. For example, it took me about an hour to win the second 2vs2 arena battle, which was only possible with the help of the RNG gods.
There are a few weapon categories with unique features and access to a number of skills. My main character used a spear, but later on the spears look more like strange polearms. Wow, it has been a long time since I played the old "The Dark Eye" - Games. This game brought back some memories.
It has a nice atmosphere and is quite challenging. I really missed the roundbased RPGs, which is, for me atleast, revived in this. Sometimes you have to think ahead, sometimes you can just bully everybody down. Some fights are really stressful, while others are straightforward. The point is that almost no fight is like another one, each requires new tactics and strategies, atleast to a point. Of course you have your base tactics, which, in my case was a mostly ranged combat play style. But pure melee or multiple spellcasters sound interesting too. The good thing is that every character is can mostly do anything, aside the fact that only characters with magic potential can become wizards.
Another interesting thing for was the whole plot. Having played the other TDE games made it easy for me to fit into the world with its twelve gods, its mostly human based civilisation, with much prejudice against other races and of course its bright and wild country side, which makes this world a beautiful place. But the beauty in this is just a mask for all the darker happenings in this world.
All in all, if you love Roundbased Strategy, a good and detailed told story and funny, yet serious, characters, this game is for you. Just bring some time and patience, because the downside of this are the time consuming fights and the kinda missing background story of your secondary characters.

It should be noted that I picked up this game in a sale at a discounted price, my opinion is based on me paying about £18 for it rather than the full price. I think it is likely that my opinion on this game would change if I had forked out £30 for it.
I knew about Daedlic's point and click games like Deponia so I was interested to see what their take on a RPG would be like. As it is something that I almost expect in a RPG nowdays it is important to state that this game is very linear. If you are expecting something like Dragon Age you are going to be very disapointed (to be fair expecting all RPGs to be like Dragon Age will invaribly lead to disappointment). Also I think the game description is a bit misleading, you and your companions do have a slight criminal air about yourselves but at the end of the day it is standard save the world type stuff, nothing too ground breaking.
The game has three main views, the first is the world overview you use for travelling around. This is basically a map type view with marker locations for villages, towns, places of interest etc... To move around you click on where you want to go and jump to that location - so no player controlled wilderness exploration or anything like that. The next view is the "town view". This is pretty much a static view where you can click on characters to buy goods or obtain/advance quests. The final view is the battle view, this is a map split up into small hexagons where the player controlled combat takes place. These battle maps range in size, though none are particularly huge. They consist of different environments and obstacles that sometimes require a change in tactics for some scenarios. Combat is turn based attack and move type stuff with close combat with swords, axes, maces etc..., ranged with bows and crossbows and ranged with magic. The combat can get a bit repetitious but there is enough in there that it does not feel too much a grind.
You get to pick one of three classes for your main character, a mage, a rogue/archer type or a fighter. On levelling up you pick attributes and combat skills and there is the freedom to create hybrid classes by giving your archer some mage abilities for example. I did find though that each class tends to have one particularly powerful skill or skill combo that you will just tend to repeat in combat.
The game itself has a lot of good and bad points, it is quite a mixed bag but there is probably going to be something in there that does end up annoying you, it certainly is not perfect. How much that thing annoys you is probably the defining factor in whether you will ultimately enjoy the game or not. For me it was with the combat, there are some monsters which are only vunerable to one type of damage. However, ahead of the battle you do not necessarily know what type of monster you will be fighting so in my case I frequently had everyone inflicting either piercing or magic damage. That was my best set up given my characters, weapons and prefered skills. However, in some fights monsters will be invulnerable to piercing so you have to quit the game reload and re-equip characters with maces so you can inflict bashing damage. Nothing game breaking but it did really get annoying, you learn pretty early on to have back up weapons handy and make sure your party is at least a bit flexible. You can look on that as somewhat of a positive as my party was really not set up for those particular battles so it did add an extra challenge, making what should have been an easy fight a bit more difficult. I think one other problem that needs highlighting is the party make up. You have a limited number of companions that you can recruit, essentially there is one party for the game. You do not get to deicde if you would rather have a mage or a fighter in your party you get what your are given. I do not want to spoil anything but at some point in the game something happens that means that really to fill a specific gap in your party your main character needs to be a specific class. Luckily I chose this class anyway so it was not a problem in my play through. If I had selected a different class it may have negatively effected my opinion of the game.
On the positive side I liked the story (the ending is a bit meh but nothing too objectionable) and found the characters interesting with some nice back story and different personalities. By the end I found myself invested in the story and felt fairly satisfied with the experience on completion. You do get some "choices with consequences moments" that give you a sense of control over how the story plays out. My play through took me 26 hours and I pretty much did everything quest wise in the game.
I would recommend this game but I did pay about £18 for it. if I had paid the full retail price I would probably not recommend it as I think at that price some of the problems I have glossed over would have seemed a lot more annoying. My advice is to pick this up if you see it discounted as on the whole it is a relatively enjoyable experience. However, at full price there a lot better RPGs out there and I would be a lot less forgiving of the game's flaws.

A pretty dreadful experience.
Slow-paced and difficult, with too fine a stat/ ability granularity for how clunky and random the tactical combat actually is. The story was ok, just enough to give you a veneer of something to care about, but the beginning crisis was too cheesy and plot-holey, and everything that immediately followed felt really small, unimportant, and aimless. Game difficulty doesn't ramp well... as a starting player I felt always behind the curve, with crappy equipment and not enough gold to do much about it, and I spent more time redoing missions I lost than enjoying any sense of progression or accomplishment. The action wheel adds a lot of friction to the experience... it just took too long to do any action beyond the basic double-click weapon strike. Stores are weird... there's more stuff than I can afford to buy and more stuff available than I would even want, so it's an odd mix of too much/ not enough. As far as your character(s), there are too many skills/ abilities/ talents/ whatever and not enough information on what they are or do or what your starting levels indicate in terms of mastery... just too many knobs on one part of the game and not enough on all the others.
The VO was a nice touch and adds personality. The game looks good, if a bit stodgy.
But it's really just dreadful to play. The user experience just is not polished or satisfying. I like to have a good time, not a frustrating one.
Avoid, go play XCOM or Dragon Age or something else.

For those looking at the recent reviews wondering if you should buy this game, seriously read the reviews closely and pick between the ones that are probably sore because they don't want to invest the time to actually learn the game, those that bought the game and didn't read the fact that it was early access, and those that are actually reviewing the game.
I haven't played a huge amount but enough to see the bugs and the features:
Bugs most notiable right now:
* Some of the terrain is bugged where you will walk above the ground. This becomes a issue if you die and your stuff is on the ground but you are 30m in the air. This I haven't seen often but it's there.
* Structures being damaged behind large walls. Not sure if this is a bug or there is a physic that I'm not aware of that makes this make sense but yeah. If you have a wall and you notice it's getting hit hard all the time, don't place your stuff there. If it's a feature, it may be shock from an explosion. In this case, cool. If it's a bug, it should be fixed but for now, place your stuff smart inside your base or it's going to damage/destroy with too much attacking. This goes for your Small vessels as well.
* Transferring between planets. Every once in awhile you may crash between orbits from planet to space or space to planet. A safe way I've gotten around this is leave orbit, get to a moon or another planet. Before going out of orbit, log out and log back in. This should stop it.
* Some animals run around in circles like idiots however, this I've seen in other early access games. It's not a game breaker and I'm glad the developers are looking at other issues rather than something as small as this right now.
FEATURES:
* For those that want difficulty, this game can do that for you. Depends how your settings are or what server you decide to join. The game is a lot like EVE-Online with the PVP as well. Some planets are PVP and others are PVE. Server settings can be changed to eliminate whatever you don't like though so you can have a full PVP or a full PVE.
* Fully customizable. Don't like prefab stuff, you'll like this game. From the bases to the ships, their all yours. Not good at crafting or imagination though, they do have prefab structures and ships/hoover craft. They did a great job with allowing those that are creative to run wild with it but not so much to hold anyone back that has an issue with it.
* Similar to GEO-Engine back with red faction 1 days. The terrain can be manipulated. It's actually so much so that you can even build hovercraft to mine in to the ground. Get creative and work with it for awhile, don't give up. This is no small task, trust me. Think logically when crafting.
REASON FOR BAD REVIEWS (my opinion, of course):
* Many are from those that may not be use to survival sandbox games. They don't hold your hand. They are not meant to. With that said, the new tutorial (out 10/29) redesigned the tutorial. Don't expect to get on this game and be a master. You're going to f'up, your going to die for extremely stupid reasons, your going to loose stuff and you will more than likely loose your first base and ships due to poor design. Learn from it.
* Some I like to say are from man/woman children or those that don't actually have a reason to hate the game other than it's not another game. It's fine if it's not your cup of tea but it's another issue when you give no reason or you say the game is terrible because you can't figure it out. Again, read the above comment. It's a survival sandbox and not meant to hold your hand.
* It's not call of duty, stop treating it like it's another clone of activisons flavor of the month. It's also not space engineers, it's not ARK, it's not Conan, it's not Rust, it's not etc etc etc. It's Empyrion. It's PvP and PvE will be different from these games. If you like these other games version of said element, go back to them. It's okay. No one game can claim that everyone will like it. If you're going to hate on it, give a reason instead of "it's trash." Awesome review bud, probably should say why.
* It's an Alpha. The idea of an alpha is that you test it and give bug feedback. Of course crap isn't going to work. This is the point of an early access game. When you purchase it, you are willing going in to a game that is potentially broken. Is this game broken? Absolutely not, it has bugs but is fully acceptable to be played.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
I've played quite a few online survival games and so far this has been one of my favorite. Yes, it has bugs however, it's early access. I willingly bought the game expecting to float along with fire a weapon that wouldn't hit an enemy. I was surprised that a game in alpha status was actually working with bugs I'd expect to have seen in a beta release (which means it's almost there but still broken beyond what would be accepted in a final store release). For $9.99 or $19.99, this game is great. Do yourself a favor, take the chance to purchase this game. If you hate it, you lost $9.99/$19.99. Thats a trip to Taco Bell or dining at a restaurant.
Updated on 11/24/17 after 100+ hours:
* I have noticed that there are some instances where built structures and vehicles will drop through the world. If you are playing single player there are a list of commands to teleport objects to locations. If you are on multiplayer, you will have to contact admins to get it. This can be at fault of the server you are playing on or the game itself, it depends on what happened. Sometimes a restart of the game will fix this issue or a reboot of the server if you own it and can't seem to get the items to appear.
* There is several occasions where enemies will drop below a floor so you can't directly shoot them however, like mages, they can shoot you  making stealing their stuff quite the task. Solution is to blow it all up with more bullets. Seems to have worked well for me. (aka, this is a bug that is less frequent than it use to be and they are working on it. For now, you have to fix the bug by removing the issue... for the greater good of course.)
* Many reporting as a bug however, it's not. You have to turn your JetPack on in order to move in space otherwise you'll sit there forever just looking at your ship and depending on where you are, die due to freezing to death.
* In order to survive in some locations in space without a ship (how a lot of capitals are built is to build them in space) your suit must be able to withstand the cold. You can add resistance to heat/cold using an armour terminal and addons that you loot or purchase from NPC colonies/space stations.
* Hovercraft spins in circles for ever without stablizing even with the correct equipment. This one is an odd one as it's not the server, it's actually your client. You MUST restart the game, don't disassemble your craft, it won't fix it. It won't give you any errors when you look in the command console either, it just simply spins. As said though, just restart your game, it's on your end and not the servers end. It will fix the issue and you'll be on your merry way again shooting at stuff or mining large holes again in no time.

I don't normally do reviews, but this one certainly deserves one!
The first game was amazing, with the only con being that the game was too short.
This sequel I did not find out about until about a week or 2 ago...and I wasted no time in getting it. NO REGRETS! But anyway, time for the nitty gritty.
This game has a very healthy dose of video game pop culture references, even moreso than the first game. Not only references, but playstyles and genres! It has strategy, puzzles, side scrolling, fighting, running, vertical/horizontal shooters, CCG, and even rhythm games...essentially it's video game genre mash up.
One thing I can't really comment on is the controls, as I was playing with my PS3 controller the whole way.
PROS:
- A unique game, utilizing many different gameplay styles in one game.
- Tons of references to big titles/series (LoZ, FF, Super Mario, Chrono Trigger, MGS, to name a few)
- The story brings back memories for fans of Chrono Trigger (at least for me it does, and if you haven't played it...what are you waiting for?)
- A great game to introduce younger generations to the different arcade/console gameplay styles of the 80s/90s
CONS:
- Jack of all trades, master of none. It gives players a taste of many different styles of gameplay, but doesn't really satisfy cravings for any of them. Each gameplay style is very simplistic, so don't expect Fire Emblem level strategy or Yu-Gi-Oh level of complexity with cards. Every game referenced does their thing better than this game does (naturally), but no oither game has it all like this one does (yet)
- Story isn't very engaging and I would almost say the basis of time travel/global disaster is a little overused. However, it doesn't take away any enjoyment from the game as the primary appeal is the combination of gameplay itself.
Overall, I'd give it a 9/10. Very few games nowadays make me eager to play and more importantly continue to play until the end and this was one of them.

Attention Battleborn: this is what genre-blended is.
Evoland 2 covers a tremendous assortment of video games. With references and in-jokes to nerd pop-culture sprinkled throughout, you can see exactly what had the most impact on the developers as they grew up.
The breadth of genres and the game's excruciating length (SIXTEEN HOURS) unfortunately work against it at times. Several forays into specific games dragged on for what felt like an eternity--still others I could have done without entirely, or had them reduced sharply into a subtle nod rather than a whole hour long mode of shallow gameplay.
To make matters worse the game won't stop trying to take itself seriously like the classic Chrono Trigger. Nearly impossible when you're standing on a bunch of hilarious references to other games.
This game tries hard to be two polarizing things and it only goes so far. Evoland 1 is a much more precise package.

Having completed the original Abe's Odysee in 1997 when I was a teenager I figured that this would be a nice trip down memory lane, oh how wrong I was.
I underestimated my memory of this wonderful title. Having only completed the game once 18 years ago, it turns out I remember very little which makes this less nostalgia and more like an entirely new experience.
The developers have taken certain liberties with the gameplay. For example, there is now a selection of 3 difficulties with "hard" being pretty much the same as 1997 with Normal and Easy having varying levels of health. Other differences including a major overhaul of the controls. This is an especially welcome change from the original, which on PC is a keyboard only affair.
A lot of the frustrations from the original title have also made the HD leap. You will die a lot. But the saving grace is the quicksave feature. This is especially appreciated by those of us who are time poor.
I feel that some of the charm of the game has worn off on me now that I am bloody old. The intro sequence and dialog in general feels juvenile. And the precence of mild profanity and "comical" violence means that it misses it's mark in terms of target audience. I think this is important to mention because of the original game makers ultimate goals to offer environmental, social and political commentary.
The audio from the original is largely untouched but the voices have been completely redone with a substantial amount of new content. There doesn't appear to be any surround sound at play which I think is a missed opportunity.
Graphically, this is the best HD remake I have seen to date. It is somewhat faithfull to the original but the level of detail is far and beyond anything that would have been possible in 1997. It runs extremely well. Animation of the characters is well done but just like the original, transitions between actions is sudden which detracts from any sense of realism. This I think is a caveat of having a responsive control system.
Gameplay and controls are great. The game plays wonderfully and the changes made to the game work really well with the updated graphics and still fit well within the spirit of the original title.
All in all, fantastically done and well worth the asking price. Just a warning though, Abe will scare small children.

Not bad, but not a game I would recommend over the original.
This is certainly a new interpretation of Oddworld, I'll tell you that. Where the original focused on a sense of realism and grit, this has a more fantastical bent. It looks less like the iconic world we used to know and more fantasy. Some parts of the game benefit from the visual style, but for the rest, it hampers the atmopshere. It never makes me groan out loud, but it never impressed me. Abe had a distinct sort of feel that the graphics were a key part of, and they were packed with grit and more than a few punches.
This has none of that.
The game feels directionless more often than it should due to that issue, like the original elements and the newer ones are at war, and neither one seems to give any ground. Whereas in the original, it feels like you're navigating a facility, my reaction to the shifting of goals, "Instead of rescuing Mudokens, you're just going to swing on over here for a bit and platform it up," was that I was pulled out of the environment I was in to go to another one.
If this seems minor to you, it shouldn't. Oddworld became a cult classic due to the atmosphere the game presented, and that atmosphere is not preserved here. A lack of overall consistency contributes to an experience that feels like its lacking an overall flow, like it doesn't quite fit together properly.  It seemed like the team here tried to reinvent the original without understanding what made it so special or without injecting any of their own creativity to it to make up for what they messed up.
Perhaps this is a natural problem when it comes to newer games. The original Oddworld wasn't a graphical powerhouse and used single screens with careful attention to detail in each one. In a fancy modern game, I don't know how much of that can be replicated. It would be nice if they used the newer tools to their advantage to make improvements instead of making the game worse by not wanting to. Graphics is only one part of it. I love the camera. It could really add to the atmosphere of the game. Why, then, aren't the puzzles designed to fit it rather than the fixed camera that we used to have? Controls are more fluid than ever, but jumping is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I feel lost in puzzle rooms until I explore them, and oftentimes I die because I wake something up that I couldn't possibly know about. There's no context to the game, and it needs it.
I never died in Oddworld once due to a reason outside of my own inadequacy, but here, it's a regular problem, and it gets old fast.
Oddworld has never looked this good, but it's never been presented this poorly. New n Tasty is not bad, but every time I play it, all I think of is how the original did almost everything better. Its one trick is compelling, but that's all that it has over the original. Granted, it's a sizable benefit, but is it worth making the gameplay worse? I don't think so.
If you've played the original and loved it like I have, the fresh coat of pain provides a welcome reason to revist it, and despite all of the things I've dinged it for, nothing becomes a dealbreaker if you're an old-timer. If you're a fresh face, I'd recomend you play the original first and then give this a shot if you're still interested.

Styx Master of Shadows is a game made by Cyanide Studios. Fortunately, Styx is way much better and polished than Sniper Ghost Warrior. This game is focused on stealth, dont even bother engage to an open combat, cause it sucks♥♥♥♥♥♥ When you fighting against enemy, you only press one button, which is LMB/X/square (KBM/DS/XBOX360) to parry, after parrying for a few times, press it again to kill the enemy. Read below for a quick pro/con.
Pros:
- Good optimization, never had any problems.
- Good level design, this game urge you to explore to find shortcuts, useful for finishing the level as fast as possible to get the token. The map is quite big, some stage has secret rooms.
- Good AI, when the enemy spotted you, they will go to your last seen position and looking for you and then searching the surroundings, opening chests, wardrobes, looking under the tables, and even can lit the torch that you put out. I didnt see this kind of AI in Dishonored or Thief. Nice one Cyanide
- Good stealth mechanic. In this game, darkness is your friend, as long as you are in a dark place, the enemies cant spot you, or they might be suspicious at best. And the cover system is convenience, with one press of a button you can move sideways while in cover. And to add more challenge, the game give you two enemies that can screw your game, the bugs that has poor sight but heightened hearing sense and the elves. The bug is self explanatory, but the elves, they can sense your amber (why? play the game to find out), so staying too long near an elf, they will kill you in one hit (same as knight). The last few maps kinda frustrating on hard difficulty.
- The skills are pretty neat, like Clones. You can strangle a foe with it, bobby-trap a chest with it, or create a diversion with it. Sometimes it can help you in a dire times in story mode. The rest of the skills are generic.
Neutral:
- Graphic
- Story
Cons:
- 3rd person view, seriously?? A stealth game in 3rd person wont be as hard or good as in 1st person. Move the camera slightly, AHA! There is an enemy there. Not a game breaking, but its less fun for me.
- Invisibility and dark vision, most of stealth game has these 2 now. Dark vision is okay, cause it helped me finding the collectibles. But invisibility makes the game easy.
- Lack of gadgets, you only has dagger, sands and throwing knives.
If you like stealth game, give this one a try. This is a prequel of another game called Of Orcs and Men. Get it on sale though, the game is quite short. Thanks for reading this review, if you have any critics or advice regarding my review, feel free to write on comments.

I read many complaints about the immense difficulty and frustrating rng before playing Blackguards but when I got into it myself I found the complaints to be exaggerated though it's a subjective impression of course. The Dark Eye rpg system can seem strange to those who've never encountered it before and are mostly used to dnd-esque games but if one takes the time to study and understand the stats and skills and plan their characters the game will flow much more smoothly though there are a few missions that can feel overly long and frustrating.
The most underrated part of Blackguards is the writing I think. While the overarching story is fairly forgettable the characters and their interractions with each other and the world around them are a treat on many occasions and the humor feels fresh and I found it genuinely funny as opposed to meme-ish or pop culture reliant as is often the case. The game setting is gritty and reminiscent of the eastern regions in A Song of Ice and Fire (popularly know as Game of Thrones). It's a place where slavery and blood sports are considered the norm and the Poisoners Guild is the "most respectable" It's a great place for your band of greedy liars, violet thugs, lazy misfits and romantic rogues to have their adventure. I found the English voice acting for the main characters very enjoyable as well.
I won't go indepth into the gameplay rules since the game is a year old now and there's dozens of reviews and let's plays already. The system isn't perfectly balanced (is it ever?) and certain skills are not so useful to put it midly but it also offers a lot of flexibility in how you build your characters and it's satisfying to see your characters mature into serious♥♥♥♥♥kickers.
While Blackguards is a bit of a rough diamond I enjoyed my time with it quite a bit.

It is a good game. and I am recommending that RPG fans give it a try - but I think it's definitely an acquired taste!

I think this Blackguards has a strong base and may lead to a very good sequel.  The game is flawed though.  For a game that states:
"Your choice of spells, skills and abilities determine your battlefield tactics. Aggressive? Defensive? Tactical? It's your call how to tackle each challenging encounter! "
There is very little choice.  If you want an RPG where you can build your characters and team this is not it.  The game give you a very well defined group to play with.  It makes the game extremely difficult if you do not build your characters to a certain role.  The other characters are far enough down their progression that it makes little to no sense to try and change them.  What is so maddening about this game, is that there is a lot of really cool things you could do.  You are just not able to do them, because they game gates skills, and locks players into roles for you.  If the game just let you have 4-5 characters to build as you see fit it would be far better.
The story was fine.  The voice acting was ok.  The game is good.  There is no real choice in the game though.  No characters progression choice and no choice in what you do.  That is why the game falls short for me.  It is not worth the full price.
If you are looking for a decent game that has limited flexibility and is on rails this might be for you.   This game just falls way short of how it is advertized.

After 30 hours of playing the game I can finally give my opinion. As of my review, the Steam Patch 37 is out. I'm confused why this game has mixed rating.
I've been playing this game for a week now and I'm really loving. The setting of medieval style world with low fantasy is amazing. Music and the scenery is top notch and gorgeous. I love the classic old school feel of this game, my first two days made me think of Runescape somehow. The game has safe zones for both of the factions capital, no one can attack you there and after that it's pvp free zone. If you want, you can attack your own faction but you will be marked as a traitor and you will lose reputation (lots of it).
The game sure has it's problems (I will get to that later) but it's in EARLY ACCESS ALPHA and it's one of the most promising titles this year in my opinion. Crafting is simple yet deep and complex. One of the most relaxing aspects of this game is the gathering part and you can get XP & reputation by upgrading the faction castles. You will be XP rewarded with crafting too.
Combat of the game is good but also a problem currently. The servers have a little of desync sometimes, not always or every day. You have to time your blocks, you can stab another player from the side or circle him for a backstab. It's all dynamic and realistic. The Witcher 3 animation team is also working on the upcoming beautiful looking realistic animations for the game (can be found on YouTube, looks gorgeous).
PvP is the main aspect currently. It has it's ups and downs. Pros are that it's fun and can be rewarding if you get to loot another player and get something good from them. The feeling of a castle siege is fun and there's risks in it. PvP looting works in a way so you don't lose everything. You or the other player has a limited amount of time to loot something from you, spend it all by just browsing the bags and you might get nothing. Downs? Yeah well, as I mentioned the game has some desync issues and makes archery useless in some situtations. Because of the desync the players movement don't register always as you see them. They may be already on your side or back.
PvE is currently in under development, there's quests to hit you to lvl 40 (this game has 100 levels) and the rest is grinding mobs, PvP and upgrading castles which give a lot of XP. PvE is the feature I hope they add more content, I know public dungeons are on the road map which I'm excited about. More quests, just endless dynamic quests would be amazing.
The game also suffers from invisible walls which may or may not annoy you, honestly I don't mind. /unstuck command is your best friend if you get stuck in one or fall beneath the castle walls. Collision detection is buggy sometimes too.
There's still 2 upcoming factions for this game, mounts & mounted combat, boats & naval combat and lots more. This game has so much potential! I went with a risk and I'm surprised how good the game was. Community has some helpful players. Many of the high levels have randomly given fresh gear & weapons for me that I started doing it too by giving extra armor I had.
If you've been following Gloria Victis, I hope this helped you somehow. Remember that the game is in alpha.

TL;DR: The tutorial didn't help at all because the objectives flash for a millisecond and theres no way to find out what your objectives actually are. The game is a tedious grind for extremely little reward. The game doesn't explain the controls to you in any good manner and I found myself constantly looking through the controls to see what key did what. The game seemed interesting at first, but was not worth it to me at all.
My 2 hours of experience in this game:
Tutorial:
- Started the tutorial
- Slowly fell from the sky in an escape pod to some prefab structure
- I get an objective that I was barely even able to read in time.
- Continue following the tutorial for about 15 minutes up to where it tells me to put a oxygen generator in the lake. It then tells me to do something else, but like all the other objective windows, it appeared for half a second and I missed what it said.
- There was no other way for me to see what my objective was, so I quit and decided to figure it out on my own.
Survival:
- Spawned in on the same map as the tutorial
- Quit and changed the map seed because I want something fresh.
- Slowly fall from escape pod just like in the tutorial.
- Figured out how to use the drill and chainsaw.
- Put down my survival constructor and started making wooden blocks and iron ingots.
- For the next 20 or so minutes I looked through the crafting menus to figure out the game's process with getting better things, and I figured it out.
- Spent the next 20 or so minutes slowly running to 4 different ore deposits and mining the resources.
- Spent the next 10 minutes waiting for the constructor to make ingots.
- Built a Base Starter and started placing wooden blocks (which are freaking huge).
- Built a Generator and Fuel Tank. as well as an Advanced Constructor.
- Drone tries to blow my stuff up, so I shot it with a pistol with surprising success.
- I placed my Generator and Fuel Tank next to each other and fill up the Fuel Tank
- Generator won't start.
- Hint keeps telling me something like "Press N and click "Connect to Base""
- Hint was useless, I was extremely annoyed so I quit and instead decided to try Creative
Creative:
- Couldn't figure out how to open the creative menu.
- Spent little under a minute pressing every key on my keyboard until "G" finally worked.
- I wanted to build a Small Vessel.
- I filtered blocks for a SV and started building
- The blocks are extremely tiny
- Why are the BA blocks SO MUCH BIGGER than the SV blocks?
- I didn't want to spend 3 hours putting tiny blocks together to make even a decent ship
- Quit and refunded the game.
Like I said in the header, I could see how this game could be fun but there is a HUGE learning curve and the tutorial didn't do well enough in my opinion to explain anything. The objectives flashing for a millisecond in the tutorial didn't help at all either. Also, nearly none of the keys are explained to you and I found myself constantly pausing the game to look through the controls to find out how to use a certain thing.
I'm enjoying Empyrion way more than I thought I would. It feels like ARK meets Subnautica with elements of what No Man's Sky could have been, and aspects that I wish Eve had.

I wouldn't consider this a simulator if I was at gunpoint.  The flight mechanics are... rough to say the least.  The keyboard mapping is almost absent from what I can tell.  Flying by mouse, there are maybe five or so keys including a second primary fire button... just in case your left click breaks.  Taking off from a carrier I found myself rocketed abruptly upwards by some mystical force halfway across the deck and then when landing stopped about as abruptly as hitting a brick wall.  The voice acting in the campaign felt a bit forced and was empty of depth or feeling (especially in the Japanese campaign) and didn't really contribute anything to a storyline.  The missions are extremely repetetive as well (bomb a target, switch planes, bomb said target again).
On the better side, the game did have some pretty cool explosions and the planes burning out of the sky were as asthetically pleasing as it gets.  Bullet and cannon impacts in both soil and water are pretty well mimmicked although the auto aim defeats the whole purpose of WWII dogfighting.  Ships will sink if they are destroyed, which is nice, although I found it odd that the USS Arizona was capsized by torpedos and fully submerged in shallow water in about one full minute...
All in all I'd say this game is worth 3 out of 10 stars.  Would not ever recommend this to anyone looking for a "flight sim" despite what any of the trailers or pictures make it out to be.

I'm not a huge flight simulator guy, but this came in a bundle and I like to always branch out when I have the opportunity. Meh, if you've ever played a flight sim and realized that its only fun for a short while, well that's my recurring experience with the genre too. This game would be much more fun to me as a level in a full videogame (Like how GTA V has pretty detailed flight in their planes). Just the game alone doesn't have enough diversity for me, the idea that you are going to be doing the same exact specific thing throughout the entire campaign, makes it hard to enjoy.
On an opposing note, there are different planes and different weapons and different enemy targets that do mix up the levels enough to make it bearable. The first couple levels are actually fun until you try to fire some torpedoes (Those things will always be a mystery to me), and if there was a bit stronger storyline, I might be able to get more into it. Text scrolls across the screen and shows you a map of pearl harbor and other islands. Actually as I'm writing this, I'm realizing how terrible this review will be. I mean its obviously targeted at people who are into flight sims and/or war games enough to read a review about one written by someone who has absolutely no interest in either. So how about this, don't trust me, unless you are here because you also dislike war plane games and for some reason want to give them yet another chance. I'd say if this game is free or under $2 then you'll probably enjoy it that much. Otherwise, it gets old pretty fast.
The biggest problem with the game is the ever changing difficulty level. Rookie, the lowest casual level gets hard to the point where all of the backup planes with be blown up before you can even switch to them. Don't even get me started on the actual simulation mode (as opposed to controller arcade mode).  So to summarize this confused/confusing babbling: It keeps you somewhat entertained briefly and then get too difficult to be fun anymore. I beat the primary campaign and am leaving it at that.
Note: Again, I am not into this genre so take this opinion lightly.
Overall Score: 6.5/10 (The actual game play was done well)

Instead of a normal business simulation game such as ‘xxx tycoon’, Anime Studio Simulator, albeit sounding like what it names, actually possesses more similarities to a small visual novel game. The player interaction is limited to setting tasks at the beginning of every week of the three months the game spans across, as well as several multiple-choice decision points randomly occur. The story is interesting as for depicting how an anime is developed by a small group of people who have little experience but full of passion towards success in the anime industry.
I really appreciate the way it presents unexpected accidents such as accidentally mixing up the final storyboards with the draft right before the tight deadline. These make the story more true as blunders are inevitable during our daily tasks. It's always encouraging to find out that the characters finally manage to figure out the way to overcome the problems. The whole team never crumbles in the face of setbacks, which distinguishes this game from others consist of merely a series of success especially when you cheat in games.
The game is ideal for those who don't expect too much on the strategic management aspect of the game. Strategies are certainly required for achieving a perfect ending but generally, however you manage the studio, there are always situations out of your control according to the storyline. So, be prepared for frustrations and disappointment if you bought this game in the hope of expanding your studio into an empire business. That would never happen as your goal is to successfully bring only ONE anime into production.

This game is a magnificent achievment!
It is, in effect several games in one.  While you spend most of the game in the format of a top-down Legend of Zelda like format, the game play switches up as you go through.  Although there are seams, hardly noticable prompts to when the game play is going to change, they are minimal and not irksome at all.  In this game you get a top-down adventure game, a 2-D side scrolling platform shooter, a top-down bullet hell flying game, pong, snake, Pac-Man, Space Invaders, guitar hero, a 2-D side scrolling running game, a card game in the spirit of games like Magic the Gathering, Pokemon, Yugi-Oh, and others, a Bejeweled-like game, a turn-based RPG, a Street Fighter-like fighting game, a side-scrolling Double Dragon-like fighting game, and a tactical strategy RPG.  Did I forget any?  Anyway, all that in one epic game with an epic story and plot driven by time travel that is worthy of a Final Fantasy game.
Speaking of time travel, this game has an awesome mechanic where the further back in time you go, the more primitive the graphics get.  The earliest time period has old school Game Boy level graphics, then progresses to 8-bit NES graphics in the "past time era, then the next "present" time era sports 16-bit graphics, and the "future" features 3-D graphics.
Then there are the easter eggs.  I can't even begin to list all of the easter eggs in this game, but they are usually well done, and very tongue in cheek.  Some easter eggs are done such that I wonder how they are not copyright violations.  Some are obvious, others you will miss if you blink.  All will give you a feeling of nostalgia, if you are a nostalgic kind of person.
This is about as perfect a game as games get, in my opinion.  Certainly there are areas that can be improved, new play styles and graphics that can be incorporated into future Evoland instalments, but for what it is right now this game is a well-done, well-polished, monumental achievment.  The people who made this should be proud of themselves.

was the first HOG that I've played here on Steam, and also the first game that I've ever tried to review. Gosh, looking back to those couple of sentences that I scribbled and called as a review, I got embarrassed. I decided to run the game for a second time after a year - it's not that lengthy of a game anyhow - and write an appropriate review. I remember getting startled the first time that I've run the game, watching its eerie loading screen. I wondered if I've misread the description and bought myself a horror adventure instead of a HOG. Nope, this is a HOG nonetheless, and also a brief horror story.
Our protagonist is a young woman who finds herself in front of an abandoned Asylum called White Haven at the middle of the night. That's about it, that's all we know about our "Jane Doe". She doesn't remember anything. A little girl greets us at the front gate and invites us in for the doctor who would know what to do. As we step into the old building, the girl flees away and leaves us with a somehow distorted reality. Suddenly, a creepy voice that belongs to a young man echoes, calling us "his rats". Creeped out yet? I know I was.
Graphics and animations are fairly good within the genre. Background art works are cleverly designed to establish a unique atmosphere of "something's quite not right", and boy, do they manage to do so! The music is annoyingly creepy and background noises such as whispers, cackles and buzzing are always there to play you like a string. The atmosphere is the strongest feature of the game, creating the tension and thrill of the unknown successfully.
HOG scenes are usually quite alright. Nothing is too hard to notice, and items are always clearly displayed. But there are certain phases of the game when our character becomes "a bit off her head", then even HOGs turn into nightmares. Those games, I wouldn't ask for my worst enemy! Puzzles and mini games are not often, but the ones that we encounter are quite good. There was one puzzle near the end of the game, asking for us to arrange moon's phases in order as observed from earth. Quite neat, huh? Oh, fair warning: there is no map to track but the game tells you when there is nothing left to solve in an area that you are standing in, so backtracking isn't much of an issue.
I should say that I admire the effort put into making this game. It gives you a 3-4 hours of a HOG and a thrill that drives you insane alongside your main character. Does the ending worth it? Oh, I wouldn't know. It satisfied me enough, but I believe there would be people who'd call it a good story cut short. Maybe. We are used to unsatisfactory endings in this genre, so comparatively, it was great. Sadly, this is not the Collector's Edition, which would have a more complete story consistency, probably.
It might be important to mention that the game hails from Gogii Games, and their games are always either A+ or a big F. There is no in between.

The aesthetics are some of the best, if not the best, I've ever seen in any video game. Every background and foreground object is hand painted to awe-inspiring effect. This combined with the
adds up to be one of the most stunning displays I've had the pleasure of enjoying. On top of the amazing visuals and soundtrack, we have a heart-wrenching story to go with all this that will definitely leave at least some (me) in tears throughout.
Nestled within all this beauty is an exquisitely executed metroidvania platformer. Ori boasts fluid controls while still being extremely tight. It’s as if Moon Studios took the best aspects of Rayman Legends and Super Meat Boy’s controls with the result being a perfect marriage of the two vastly different titles. The progression of skills is steady and follows a logical succession. At first you’re barely able to jump over the smallest log, but by the end you’ll be nimble like the adorable little forest sprite that you are.
Above all else, this game is HARD. Maybe not as hard as some of the most infuriating levels of Super Meat Boy, but the inspiration definitely shows; be sure to save often because the last thing you want is to die unexpectedly and have to go through that hell again. Then again, maybe that is exactly what you want. In a market where it’s increasingly taboo to actually kill the player in a single player game, Ori has no qualms with killing you over, and over, and over again. That said, the deaths are never cheap or feel like the result of poor level design or other shenanigans; it’s abundantly clear that if you die, it’s your own fault.
I want everyone to play this game and love it as much as I do. I look forward to getting as many of the achievements that I can, no matter how difficult some of them seem to be.
To Moon Studios, thank you for delivering such an incredible experience. This is why I love video games. I can’t really express just how much I’ve fallen in love with Ori, Sein, Naru, Koru, and all the other characters in this masterpiece.
