FOR GAMERS WHO HAVE NEVER PLAYED OLDER ODDWORLD GAMES:
This is unique and amazing experience. The world is so unique, full with twisted dark humor. Basically, this is puzzle platformer, but not your regular type - this is a game where you need to save your friends from slavery in the factory via unique Gamespeak system. That means you have couple of words that you can use to talk with your friends, and they listen and behave based on your input. Now for your usual RPG this is pretty standard stuff. But this is not RPG. I've not seen yet any platformer that incorporates this system beside Oddworld games.
Second thing that makes this game unusual is protagonists ability to posses enemies. This opens wide range of game play approaches, tactics, as well as some really awesome situations. Now, possessing enemy is really simple - just one simple press of the button. Situations for that? Well they are more complicated. And that's part of the charm. To figure when to do something and in what order - this is Oddworld. Also each enemy type behaves differently creating sort of unique ecosystem. For instance - one creature is territorial, one pact based. Based on their behaivor, you need to figure best approach to avoid them. Now, beside things above - this is the game that also requires quick reflexes. But the game is always fair and it trust that you will figure it out. In the sea of games that hold your hand, this old school approach is much appreciated.
Trust me, new gamers - try this one. It's really unique even by today's standards.
FOR GAMERS WHO HAVE PLAYED OLDER ODDWORLD GAMES:
I can't stress enough, how long have i waited for a new Oddworld game. After Stranger's Wraith we finally got new Oddworld game and it's remake of the first one - the one which started whole insanity in this marvelous world.
This is not a port, not a remastered version. This is fully rebuilded game from ground up of the Oddworld: Abe Oddysee. And it's glorious. While playing it i constantly had that stupid kid like grin. I was all over in 90's again. I remembered special hidden zones, some scene design and some really awesome moments.
I've been shot, eaten, cut, electrocuted, beaten, killed on various ways. And i wasn't angry at all. I missed that in Oddworld games. I loved it, loved the patience that it required. Loved the puzzles. Incorporating everything in one seamless image works amazingly well, graphic are nice and i've beaten whole game 4 times with a keyboard - didn't have problem at all. They really put their hearts into this, and you can tell. This is still same old Abe's Oddysee but visually upgraded for newer generations, and you know what - it doesn't need anything more (well except follow up in a way of Abe's Exoddus). This is the same game that i loved for 20 years almost.
DLC - ALF ESCAPE
Just short comment since this is really new thing in this Oddworld. It's awesome, great spin on well established gameplay. Insted of saving bajilion friends, in this DLC you need ti save only one. Easy? Weeell, not really. Various types od obstacles appear and you need to take care of yourself and Alf at the same time. I really wish there are more of this levels, since creativity is there - level design is awesome and Alf grows on you by the end of the mission. Loved this part.
Lorne Lanning - you did it again. Really hope for remake of Abe Exoddus. Wish you and your team all the best.

1) if you have not played the original Oddworld Abe's Oddysee.. well i used to recommend the original too all the people that i heard never played it, simply because it was such a great game. a lot of people did not listen however, because it looked aged.
along comes New 'n' Tasty.
its a game where you play a mudokon called Abe, working in Rupture Farms, a factory where they process meat and use mudokon slaves to operate machines and clean. upon learning about a terrible new product, Abe decides that he needs to escape his familiar slave life, and take as much of his buddies with him.
using your brain to navigate the 2D platforms while your eyes can take in a 3D rendered environment (a bit like Trine), it is your job to guide Abe through various puzzle and actions scenes, where you have to avoid dumb gun wielding sligs, who are on the payroll of your now ex boss Molukk (who is a glukkon), while at the same time try and rescue as many mudokon slaves as you can find. other obstacles could be: electricity, Slogs (a bit like dogs though not quite), pits, falling carcass, saws and meatgrinders, the creatures that will eventually become the meat, bombs and mines, and the loyalty and gullibility of the Mudokons, as they WILL run into a mine/pit/electricity/etc if you just ask them nicely.
it is about a clumsy guy trying to stop an evil corporation from committing genocide for profit, as well as preventing to make already scarce creatures completely extinct.
the gameworld is a rich and dark one. it is an underdog story set in a world riddled with selfish people who think about nothing but ruling there business with an iron fist. it is also VERY funny at times, though that depends on how often and how spectacularly you fudge up.
new 'n' tasty also has a very fast quicksave and loading feature, which enables you to save and load while doing nearly everything. so even if you do fudge up, you will be right back into the action once you press f8 (takes less then a second), and if you quicksaved on the wrong time or place, you can always go back to the latest checkpoint by pressing f9.
2) if you have played the original its still great, though i have to warn you people. if you have played the original from start to finish, it won't bring back that feeling. why?
you already played this game, and thus know all the answers to the puzzles, know plenty of secret entrances and solutions, and obviously playing a game you already beat (in my case very thoroughly) will just be a nostalgia trip. a very good one though. i do know they changed a bunch of things, but not enough to bring back the  feeling the original gave me the first time i played it.
3) if that feeling is what you are looking for however, i propose you pick up Alf's Escape. the DLC features new puzzles and never before seen game mechanics where Abe has to guide himself and Alf through obstacles, sometimes on 2 different planes at the same time. the DLC difficulty is at least as difficult as the latter end of the vanilla game, so its a great way to continue to scratch the Abe itch, if you found new ‘n’ tasty on its own was not enough.
(a more in depth explanation of the Alf DLC: this entire DLC centers around saving ONE mudokon. this one slave called Alf follows you around for multiple "areas" while you have to navigate yourself and him, trying not to get yourself and your buddy Alf killed. he answers to the basic gamespeak commands just like all the regular slaves, but his obstacles are a lot more challenging than what most mudokons you rescue have to face)

TL;DR: Great game. This is basically Splinter Cell in a fantasy setting. I got about 60 actual hours out of it and 100% of the achievements (for once), so $30 is well worth the value.
Most of the bad reviews seem to be ignorant of the game mechanics or think this is supposed to be some combat-heavy game. For example, one person said, "There is no mechanic for dealing with armored enemies." Um, yeah there is. Drop a crate or chandelier on them. About the only thing you CAN'T kill is an orc (but they're placed as traps rather than as roaming enemies).
There are a bazillion ways to be stealthy in this game, and it's actually FUN to beat each level without raising alarms or without killing anyone, although you get different achievements for different play styles (e.g. the "Serial Murderer" achievement requires 200 kills, while the "Unseen  Unknown" achievement requires you to get the Shadow insignia on every level).
Someone else complained about maps being repeated - yeah, at different parts of the game you're heading BACK from where you went, and this time you're headed in the opposite direction with different enemies and challenges that still make the map different and fun (you might go OUT through a door, and later you have to find a window to climb through to go back IN, etc).
The only negative things for me were:
1. The voice acting / script is irritating. Your character first jokes about not farting (are we 10?) and later on is constantly angry and throwing out expletives about the most ridiculously-minor challenges. It just didn't sync up very well with the rest of the game, but since the character isn't constantly talking, it's okay...
2. Sometimes your character jumps onto platforms or hangs from ledges when you don't want him to (e.g. climbing onto a platform with a torch, which burns you). Doesn't happen often but when it does, it's a little annoying.
3. The map on the PC version doesn't have an indicator of where you are, so you have to sort of figure it out on your own, and it's a 2-D map, which can make it difficult to visualize things sometimes.
Aside from those items, I thought it was a fantastic game!

If you even remotely consider buying this (and if you don’t, why are you here?) you basically need to answer two questions:
1.        Do you like stealth games?
2.        Do you like (dark) fantasy settings?
If you answer both questions with “yes”, you can now go ahead and buy this game. The chance of you liking this game is around 95%. If you answer both questions with a definitive “no”, you can now look somewhere else. The chance of you not liking this game is around 99%.
The following part is especially for those who can only give a positive answer to one of the two questions and a negative or especially a undecided one to the other.
This is a proper stealth game. You cannot take on more than one guard in open combat at a time. Some guards (like knights in full armour) you can’t even fight AT ALL if they’re alone. Stab them from behind without being seen, avoid them or die. In the highest difficulty you cannot fight ANY guard in open combat. They will just grab you and slit your throat because you’re a small goblin and they’re trained soldiers or worse. So if you want a real stealth experience like in the old Thief games or are just looking for a bit of challenge, take the highest difficulty “goblin”. If you’re really you want the option to fight single guards in open combat you should know two things beforehand: The open combat system was only implemented so casual players could also make it through the game. This is not a light stealth game like the latest Splinter Cell or Hitman, so fighting is not the point of it at all. Therefore, the fighting mechanics did not get much love from the developers. You just wait for you opponent to reach back and then hit the block button. You repeat this step until your opponent loses balance. Then you hit the attack button and kill the opponent in a nice animation. That’s it. You can also dodge attacks with rolls but there is no point because you won’t get a chance to kill your opponent afterwards. This mechanic is not much fun to use, its nothings more than a last way out if you get detected by a single normal guard and don’t want to reload. If you’re detected by several guards or by one which cannot be blocked, running and hiding is your only option besides and reloading and, well, dying.
The intended way of killing guards in this game is to kill them they sneaky way without being seen before they feel your blade: Sneak up behind them and backstab them, jump at them from above and slit their throats, booby-trap a chest or closet, poison their food, let a chandelier fall on them or push them into the Abyss. Some of those ways are pretty graphic, while the game shows only blood and no excessive gore like cut off body parts, it’s still pretty drastic. Expect to see your goblin to pull the legs of guards and then stab them in the FACE multiple times like a maniac on a killing spree. Not everyone likes that, you have been warned.
If you don’t like this amount of violence, don’t like the unrealistic idea of Styx being able to kill hundreds of guards unnoticed or just want a real challenge, you can also play this game without killing any guards at all. That’s the way this game is meant to be played. Period. There are a handful of targeted persons you have to kill throughout the game for plot reasons, but that’s it. You get additional achievements for each mission which give additional skill points for completing this game without raising any alarm (so this basically means no guard ever gets a clear view on you) and for not killing anyone except distinguished target persons. If you play to get those achievements and turn off the markers for your goals/targets, you get the closest things to a modern day Thief game you can get. You can also add in the additional goals of having a time limit and to collect every collectible in the same run and you’re suddenly playing a hardcore stealth game with a significant (but fun) challenge.
The gameplay in general is rewarding and fun. You’ll be encouraged to look for new paths all the time and there is nothing like the feeling to cross a vast area packed with guards without being seen. The game is really good and giving you the feeling to play a master thief/assassin.
There is one thing especially important for stealth games and that’s level design. This is probably one of the greatest strengths of this game. It takes place in a huge (and I mean huge as in several miles high) tower which is build arounds an equally huge magical “tree of life”, which is harvested for its magical and highly addictive resin which is called “amber”, although it’s clearly liquid. The whole idea of this huge, magical tower with its distinct architecture mixing medieval and steam punk elements is just great and explains the verticality of levels in a very satisfying way. There are nearly always multiple, often dozens ways to get somewhere. Some are obvious, others hard to find. Some require a lot of climbing and jumping, others just precise searching. You’ll encounter some nicely detailed gimmicks and cleverly hidden secrets if you look for all the collectibles. Sometimes it’s really helpful to overhear the guards talking to each other; sometimes it’s funny and always immersive.
This brings us to story and atmosphere of the game. To say it in advance: It’s a double-edged sword. There are some really nice ideas in the game: The tree of life which is not only an interesting, mystic place of power but also the reason for exciting conflicts and schemes, amber addiction and trafficking, the tower with its great architecture, the unusual protagonist, elves like you’ve never seen them before, believably guards who actually behave like people coming from a mediaeval society, a nice plot twist midgame and instead of the usual good against evil there is just grey, more grey and sometimes pitch black here. You really get the impression of exploring a tower located in a really unusual, fresh and existing fantasy world. The problem is that you learn far to less about what’s going on. At the beginning you always wait for the curtain to fall and to explain more clearly what is going on but this only happens partly. Actually this game is full of good opportunities to tell great tales and to advance the interesting lore, but most of those chances are not used. I had a certain feeling that there has to be more, which sadly lead to some disappointment in the end because there isn’t. Also, the characters in the game are rather flat. They’re all pretty cliché, including the ever- swearing, grumpy protagonist who has not much personality beyond that.
The last main things about this a probably every other game is the technical side. This game is already a bit dated, so I won’t compare it to new games, because that would not be fair. But even if you consider the release date, the graphics give away the fact that this game was made on a tight budget by a small team. While the levels look nice if you do not look too closely, the textures look blurry up close. While the animations of Styx himself are pretty solid, the animations of the guards are mediocre at best. Another matter is facial animation, which are very basic and not lip sync. There are only very few cut scenes in the game, they often use comic slide shows without voice-overs instead. The voice acting on the other hand, is really well done. I’ve not heard a single line which seemed off. I would have wished for Styx to have a more alien, goblin-like voice, though. His voice just sounds like a grumpy, mean human, but it’s a matter of opinion if you think a Goblin should sound like this or not. The music and sound effects give no reason to complain.
Another important technical issue is the A.I. It’s rather mediocre. While guards quickly alarm their buddies if they spot you, they sometimes behave extremely stupid while looking for you. [continue in the comments]

Let me sum up the plot for you:
Generic harem protagonist and his harem want to build a glider.
That's it! It's an excuse plot so the protagonist has an opportunity to spend all day every day with cute girls.
The characters are as generic as they come and follow anime tropes down to a t. This doesn't have to be a bad thing; I for one love my tsundere and childhood friend archetypes.
BUT
The writing is poor and the pacing is some of the worst I've ever seen in a visual novel. The game manages to bombard you with literally dozens of hours worth of text without having anything resembling a plot, which is quite a feat. It's all fluff and fíller, meaningless slice of life dialog between characters that are just not very interesting. There's a modicum of drama in some of the routes but considering that you have to read through Great Wall of China tier text walls before you get there, I'd argue it's not worth it. Chances are you won't care enough about the bland stock characters anyway for it to have any kind of impact on you.
Also keep in mind that the game forces specific routes down your throat, which means you can't even pick your favorite girl in your first playthrough. Of the 5 waifuable girls, only 2 are unlocked right off the bat; to get on the fifth girl's route, you unironically have to finish the 4 other routes first.
For what it's worth IMHHW's production values (art, voice acting, soundtrack) are fairly high. Everything else is incredibly dull.

This game is a real gem. It's one of those games were you *think* you know what you're playing and then you realise the gameplay is just there to distract you from the real point of the game.
The gameplay is pretty annoying but it's a mixed bag for me. The tutorial gives you the *basics* but it doesn't actually SHOW you important details, specifically the fact that you can move the screen around in each area. I personally had a slight problem with it in that you had to press the buttons to move it just a little bit, as if it's on a grid-like system. It would've been nicer if you could have it slide along like on a bar but the areas are pretty small anyways. The game works in that you collect ingredients from three areas, throw them into your cauldron, and hopefully create the right golem. There are several villager types with their own immunities to certain golems. An issue I had with this is that, several times, I seemingly came *very* close to not being able to fight off villagers because ingredients don't come back, except for one method which requiresyou to sacrifice a 'stat' of your kit(inventory space, power word, or time). The developer assured me that there is always a way to fight off villagers, which makes me think that they generate the villagers based off of what ingredients you have available to you because otherwise you *would* be able to get stuck, especially since you can actually waste ingredients hypothetically. Another issue I had was time, because if you don't play with the time turned off, the game gives you a time limit from the second your begin your ingredients collecting, and it is *very* difficult to do it quickly in my experience, even with the time upgrade. It gets worse later on when you end up having bad remaining ingredients and the game just becomes unfun when you're constantly restarting the day, especially since checking the gate screen(to see the villager immunities) takes up time, which is very precious. Solution is to just turn off the time and enjoy the game, because otherwise the flaws of such a system shine too bright, unless you're able to handle it.
The story is

The first thing you should know is that
is a light visual novel at heart, with the titular golem creation taking a back seat as a framing device and mini-game.
The second thing you should know is that it's a
visual novel. I'm speaking as someone who
visual novels as a rule. Even the best examples of the genre are rife with clunky prose and atrocious pacing, and I simply don't have the patience for them.
, however, flows effortlessly, with smart prose and easy charm. It's a short, well-paced tale with some branches and genuine surprises, and shows that visual novels don't need to be densely-packed epics to be engaging.
The third thing that you should know is that while
has its share of glitches, the developer is extremely diligent about addressing them. During my playthrough I encountered a (game-stopping) bug, but I received a response within minutes of posting about it on the forums, and it was fixed within the hour.
Leaving glitches aside,
isn't without other issues. The mechanics are initially confusing, the interface can be unfriendly, and the golem-crafting is at best a diversion, and at worst an unwelcome distraction. The problem is that it has very little bearing on the plot - at least as far as I have seen, but I haven't seen all the branches - and seems to exist primarily to gate your progress. At several points I found myself thinking that I would gladly take the visual novel part without the accompanying gameplay. However, with perseverance, frustration gives way to understanding, and the challenge of building specific golems with runewords and ever-dwindling resources becomes an interesting affair in its own right.
As it stands, I recommend
on the strength of its charm and intelligent writing, albeit with caveats. With some quality of life upgrades my recommendation would be unequivocal, and thankfully, as at the time of writing, the developer seems dedicated to making the title the best it can be.
In the meantime,
is still well worth the price of admission. There are mysteries to solve, multiple endings and play modes to uncover, a creepy♥♥♥♥♥mirror and a bird who is more charming than he has any right to be. What's not to enjoy?

Golem Creation Kit didn't meet my expectations.  Watching the trailer I figured the game was something along the lines of a strategic RPG where you'd be crafting golems to do battle with some cool animations or, hopefully some tactical action.  I suppose that's my fault for not digging deeper into the description.   Yet even after settling in on the aspect of it being a narrative driven experience leaving the golem creation portion a bit sidelined, I still found several problems that eliminated any chance I would have fun with this.
The first thing that should be addressed for anyone looking to purchase this is the acknowledgment that there are some pretty serious bugs.  I encountered at least a few that flash the screen to a custom bug screen that I wasn't familiar with, but one that did have some more generic options like Reload, Ignore, etc.   The interesting thing is that it seems like it's built in to the game to facilitate the user resolving the issue to some degree as it has explanations for what could potentially happen upon selecting each option.  However, it seemed no matter what if I ignored a bug, things would stop working.  Only reloading (which goes from the previous save) actually seemed to have any value.  Yet, even with this, I came across a bug that prevented me from moving forward on an integral part of the game.  I would hit it every time and eventually one of the options actually crashed the game to desktop and no matter what I did, I couldn't find the game in the task manager to close it completely allowing me to restart it.  I understand that games, especially those newly released, can have issues... but the frequency and severity of what I experienced was more than I'm willing to deal with.
Aside from the bugs, there were also some issues in both the mechanics and how they're taught to the player.  First of all, the tutorial is brief and one of the more original I've come across, but it doesn't show you that one of the most interactive parts of the game, gathering materials for your golem, has a requirement that you navigate around each of the screens by right clicking and having the camera move to and center on that area.  I spent the first handful of golem crafting sessions picking clean the initial areas because I wasn't aware you could move the screen.  Yet even eventually discovering that, the game devolves into one of my least favorite genres of all time - the point and click adventure.  I've always hated clicking like crazy around a screen trying to find hidden stuff, and Golem Creation Kit will have you doing that very thing with the inclusion of a time limit.  So you're not only tasked with finding the invisible, but you have to do so before a timer ticks down and you lose.  Granted, losing essentially only makes you go back to the beginning of the day, but the most punishing part is having to sit through load screens and skip various dialogues each time you can't find the items you need or the golem doesn't come out right.
I think that I would have been more interested in the gameplay without the timer aspect.  With the game focusing instead on how to best make use of finite resources of certain types to make the perfect golem for the situation.  I found that most of the time, I'd just look at what sort of golem I'd have to create (avoiding what each round of villagers were immune to) and just haphazardly dumping things in the cauldron until it seemed like it might work.  Some of the outcomes were pretty hilarious, but more often than not I'd just make the same thing I'd made a few times before without much focus and it would work.
The one aspect of Golem Creation Kit that did interest me was the story.  There's enough mystery in it to make you want to keep progressing despite the bland gameplay.  With only a few characters, each has to establish themselves pretty significantly and they do a decent job at that.  If it wasn't for the addition of the game-breaking bugs, I might have been able to stick it out for a couple more hours to hopefully get everything resolved and end the story.   I think that, down the line, I'll either attempt to continue the game after some bug fixes, or go on youtube and find a 'let's play' that I can skim through for the meat of the story.
Golem Creation Kit's premise had a lot of potential in my eyes and I really wanted it to be more than it was.  Even though it got my attention with a quality narrative, everything else in the game felt like it couldn't stand up to a slight breeze.  In my experience, there are games out there that have great stories and also keep you engaged with the gameplay.  Go out and get those instead and let this one bake a little longer in the oven.  Maybe when it's half price and bug free it would be more worth the time investment.

Evoland 2 is truely a gem. It has a very varied gameplay which is basically copied from classics like Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy (Tactics), Zelda (even Zelda), Street Fighter, Double Dragon, Gradius, Super Mario. It also comes with a card game within the game itself. Lovely graphics ranging from the style of the really old Gameboy over SNES pixel styled to Nintendo DS 3D graphics. It has a marvelous sense of humour and so many reference to all sorts of other games. And it's got time traveling, which - let's face it - is always great in a video game.
The story is rewarding enough to keep you going. It follows a rather classic approach, gets much better throughout the game and towards the end becomes really intriguing. It is, however, somewhat dampened by an overhasty ending. It feels rushed and could have used some more polishing. It's lacking bits and pieces of dialog and character development that could have filled the gaps to make it truely memorable, but left the story end up being rather generic.
If you grew up in the era of the good, old SNES and know all of those games (or at least a few) you are going to have a blast with Evoland 2. At least I did. Some gameplay injections may feel a little forced, depending on your personal preference you are going to love some, others might feel annoying.
Overall, it is a lovely homage to what games used to be like and yet feels very fresh. The experience is a little clouded by the rather disappointing ending to what could have been a fantastic game. But this way Evoland 2 is "just" a very good game that will have you entertained and feel nostalgic for hours. 4/5

I found this game very enjoyable but a bit buggy. It's certainly still playable, but often the dialogue across routes gets mashed together (ie, you'll be discussing the casting for the mystery route but the discussion uses the character names for the action route) but I didn't find that adversely impacted my enjoyment that much. By far and away the most frustrating bug was that in each of the routes it skips over letting you manage your team's jobs for the week at least once, often twice. When I played the action route it skipped over week 9, on the mystery route it skipped both weeks 7 and 10, and on the harem route it skipped 3 and 9. I'm not sure if anyone else ran into this problem or if it even is consistent error, but keep that in mind I guess? I still had fun and managed to get all the achievements without too much trouble (to be fair, only the ones regarding the quality of the finished anime are particularly difficult). I got this in a bundle that cost (in total) less than half the steam base price, so YMMV in terms of cost/enjoyment ratio.
TL;DR: slightly buggy, but still a fun, short visual novel

While the concept of this game is great, the way it is executed could use some work. As far as the storyline goes, there are minimal choices that you can make, and much of the storyline is the same or similar regardless of what genre of anime you choose. The plot appears to be fairly linear, and I have yet to find any choices that really cause the story to branch off. Furthermore, I would say that the music is average, and the characters, while drawn quite well, seem to fall a bit flat at times.
However, if there is one good thing about this game, it would be that it is surprisingly difficult. Many factors throughout the story influence the characters in ways that you cannot control, and you can easily find a team member quitting or yourself bankrupt. Admittedly, I have yet to reach the "good" ending; I have reached a "bad" one only once, and have failed part of the way through at least three times. It can be infuriating at times, but it also guarantees more gameplay for those who are determined to unlock all achievements. A fair warning, however: going back through the story after you've either beaten the game or failed part of the way through quickly becomes boring. There is an option to fast forward through the "dialogue" and skip straight to the "choices", but it leaves very little gameplay.
In conclusion, I would not recommend this game. While it's difficulty could be seen as a plus, the lack of choices, the seemingly linear storyline, the average characters and soundtrack, and the lack of replay value do little for the game's value. If, despite all this, you still want to purchase this game, I would highly recommend waiting until it goes on sale.

I was a little baffled to see that this game had mixed reviews until I noticed some people mentioning an issue with the save file corrupting.  However, I played it through in one sitting and if you're willing to or want to use this for a single-evening playthrough, as I did, it is absolutely worth it.  The puzzles are simple enough to work through that it doesn't really require more than about 2-3 hours to finish (depending on your speed and whatnot).
The game does an excellent job with atmosphere and creepiness, sound and ambiance really adds to the setting, and voiceover work is quite well done (better than many HO games can boast).  The HO scenes are well done, with objects that can be distinguished from one another and nice clear scenes.  Puzzles, as I mentioned, are relatively simple but not so much that I felt like it was made for precocious kindergarteners.
The story is interesting, if not 100% original (but what story is nowadays?), and piecing together information via news clippings and journals helps keep the information trickling in as you go rather than spoon-feeding you chunks of information.  The end wasn't entirely unexpected but I felt like it was done well.  A few reviewers thought it could be confusing but it really shouldn't be, especially if you paid attention and read your news clippings as you got them.
At $4.99, it's priced reasonably for its length, and even better if you can grab it on sale.  I feel like it's totally worth it, even knowing you might have to plow through it in one shot if the save issue hasn't been patched.  It kept me interested enough that I didn't even notice how long I'd been playing it.

The story is set in a mental hospital called White Haven Mysteries. The main character wakes up in an abandoned building, only to find that she’s been drugged and cannot remember who she is. She needs to find the antidote to her illness as soon as possible, and all of this while a mysterious man taunts her with his experiments. She must figure out who and where she is. This is one of the common themes among horror games, but the story itself is not a scary one, though spooky enough to give you a couple of jump scares and a gentle thrill. There are interesting and unpredictable twists, meant to keep you absorbed throughout the whole gameplay. The ending ruins it a bit though - it is very abrupt and vague, letting you wonder what the meaning of the whole story was.
The scenes are beautifully drawn and the designers chose to lighten the dark setting with cheerful elements:  vividly colored flowers, white snow, gardens with green trees and joyful pumpkins. The ability to maintain a scary atmosphere while creating scenes that are both dark and radiant at the same time is what gives this game’s art a distinctive feature.
The ambience is even more emphasized by the spooky sounds and the scary little girl that happens to cross your path several times, singing “Ring Around The Rosy” in a creepy tone.
A downside of this game was in my opinion the difficulty of the puzzles – they were quite easy to solve and none provided a real challenge. However, a couple of the hidden object scenes reminded me about the early days of the HOG games, where all the items were arranged in a certain shape - I found those quite fun:
The game comes with a major flaw: for many people, exiting the game deletes the save files and the developers are not putting effort into fixing this issue. I quit the game several times and I didn’t get the error, but I did encounter this issue after I finished one full playthrough.
Unfortunately, the version found on Steam does not contain the extra chapter of the Collector’s Edition, so the gameplay is rather short: 2-3 hours on average.  I feel that the asking price is a bit too high for what the game offers, so I’d recommend picking it up during one of its many sales.

Oddworld: New 'N' Tasty is a remake of the original Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee that can make lots of gaming companies blush of shame. It was fully done out of scratch with gorgeous high definition graphics, new instrumentalization and sonoplasty (but still loyal to the original tunes), new voices, new and improved cutscenes, with additional difficulty levels, new and sharp controls, super smooth framerate, renewed (again, still loyal) level design... I actually found glitches but they are very very few and don't harm your gameplay. As a bonus, there's a DLC (bought separately) with a completely new puzzle named Alf's Escape that is a great addition to the game, offering a good challenge to veteran Oddworld players and to the new ones aswell. If you never played Oddworld, this game is an excellent start. If you already played Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee in the past, you're going to love to replay this in the New 'N' Tasty's engine. It is even more impressive to see that such a game of quality like this one is sold for a real bargain and with a real relationship of quality/price contrary to what the great majority of the game companies do. 100% recommended to every fan of platformers!

TLDR for the ADD out there: Did some stuff, broke some stuff, got stuck in a hole.
Purchased Empyrion as a comparison for Space Engineers.  Here is my first 12 hours of play.
Started with the tutorial which bugged out while trying to teach me about how to interact with the starting base.  Wanted me to open the control panel but when i did it would not progress to the next lesson.  Oh well, scrap that one and start a new game.  I found i missed most of the tutorial messages anyway as they flashed too fast while i watched the water in its unnatural fluid state anyway.
Learned that the drill likes to remove the ground beneath my feet over what ever is in front of it. Drilling while looking 'up' seems the only answer.
Gathered enough ores to make my first HV... yeah it took me a while to firgure out that i needed to purchase items form the tech tree in order to make a HV.  I am sure the tutorial would have told me this.  Also found that i could not make a meaningful HV until level 10 for drills.  I guess i will learn to make some drills by killing aliens instead.
Place the core block and grab some steel blocks to start shapeing my new creation.  Click once to place one block, place 5 blocks one level higher than where the ghost block was positioned. Firgure its a mis-click and try again, 7 times with the same result.
Slap a gattling on my HV and load up on ammo.  HV won't leave the ground.  Remove gattling and ammo, HV still grounded.  Turn HV off and on again, still grounded.  Check all components are attached and working.  Drive HV around dragging its belly on the ground like.... well, you have seen the vids ;-)
Finaly i removed the hover engines and placed them back on.  HV springs into the air ready for adventure.  Re-mount gattling and ammo.
Speed off in direction of nearest POI outpost and start turrent sniping.  Kill lots of alien scum and find epic loots and start dismantling the remaining turrents.  Learned that dismanteling stuff without one of your own cores installed only gives components instead of completed turrents.  Sigh and load everything into HV and prepare to leave.  HV stuck on ground.  Sobs quietly in the corner.
Return to base with ill gotten gains and noticed level jumped from 7 to 13!  Opt for a blueprint HV miner over my own design to save some time and limited ores remaining.
Thirteen minutes to make the blueprint and 11 minutes to figure out i have to paste it ONTOP of my base.  Yes, i did Google how to spawn the blueprint.  No, i did not find an answer.  I was on the roof to gravity and the interaction of me hitting ground with head.
Take new HV miner to an ore patch angled towards the ground and began to move forward carefully.  I should mention i have watched a couple of videos of people using HV miners, it did not prepare me for the bucking and flipping hell that was to come.  I will leave it at, it was not fun for me.
I was at the bottom of a hole that i could not get out of, approx 800m from base and the hover engines had stopped working so i could only thrash around on the ground like a... HV without hover engines on the ground.  Remember i am up on a mountain and the base is at the bottom.  Point HV towards base and press forward.  Now 100m from base and no idea if it is up or down from my current location.  Cannot get out of HV as it won't stop flopping around even without power.
Conclusion:
I really want to like this game, but i don't.  The only aspect i found enjoyable was raiding the alien outpost.  Even driving the HV around on open ground was annoying as you were tossed about by the slightest bump in the ground which is one of the reasons i am falling out of love with SE too.
So why do i recomend this?  For the potential i can see in this game.  It looks beautiful.  The amount of customizable blocks and textures makes the builder in me giddy with excitment.  The ability to raid POIs for goodies you can't make yourself makes exploation interesting and worth while on top of seeing another sunrise/sunset.
Sure i had a bad experience and lost 12 hours of progress but its early access and bugs are to be expected.  If you can't live with them, wait for final release and get Empyrion then.

Easily one of the most addicting games I've played in recent years, and one of the best early access titles out there. The devs are constantly working on new features, fixing bugs and and listening to player feedback. Obviously with it being in early access there are still missing features, placeholder models/sounds and bugs, however the small team are making massive progress and usually squash the game breaking bugs as a priority.
As always there are negatives, save games get broken by updates, new bugs pop up and sometimes the game mechanics seem a bit nonsensical. The dev team do listen and generally they give people the option of turning off annoying mechanics (weapon/tool durability I'm looking at you!). I understand that the game is early access and nothing is set in stone, so it's an annoyance when things change and suddenly you have to adjust to new mechanics, but that's just life in early access.
The main draw for me has been the building. It's in depth yet not a simulation. You won't be running wires or pipes but there are times where you need to think about where you place components to make your ship function efficiently. The game currently lacks any real kind of physics which is a shame and what has been implemented is kind of half baked but again, these are things that are constantly being looked at and improved. Planets are also not complete with the poles being cordoned off and the edges of the map being a teleport point essentially, but again these are things that are being worked on.
Overall I absolutely love this game and every update brings (mostly) welcome changes. The dev team is always on the ball and put a great deal of attention into making this a brilliant game. The Empyrion forums are a great place to get a glimpse at new features, provide feedback and see the wonderfully creative community at work.
I highly recommend it, but urge you to keep in mind that it's early access and that things can and will change. Expect that there will be bugs and missing features for now.

So the game is a lot like Doodle God; you can see the influence gained from DG in Golem Creation Kit.
The story is whimsical, doesn't take itself too seriously; and warrants a few chuckles every now and then but nothing too outstanding as far as I've seen yet; though the writer of the game has a gorgeous grasp on creative writing; you can really picture the scenes read out to you; as they aren't drawn.
The art itself is very hit-and-miss, a lot of the sprites are gorgeous, but a few feel very out-of-place and a lot of the text and spells are just downright hard to read due to the font choice.
The gameplay itself goes something like this:
The gameplay itself is nothing fancy, resemblant of old flash games where you would drag and drop clothes onto ecchi women.
The rush against the clock really keeps you on your toes, and you make some real stupid mistakes because of it.
Losing a level has no punishment, you simply replay the level, with the now updated knowledge of weakness of the mob type that defeated you.
Overall the game is a fun little time sink. The curiosity of the story and Kirby 64-esque mix-matching element game makes you want to try new nonsence and see what pops up.
The dev is also extremely active with us, wanting to do everything he can to work out the kinks in his passion project.
And I mean cmon it's like 5 bucks, that's a coffee on your way to work; the dev isn't asking much.
I do have to mention a negative though, as of a few hours after release; the click and dragging of objects (All of the gameplay) does feel laggy and unresponsive; but not everyonehas this problem. It's not gamebreaking by any sense but it is rather annoying and demorilizing.
This game definately deserves to be given a chance; but it isn't for everyone. If you didn't like games like Doodle God or those flash box click order games, might want to give this one a miss.

You don't have to know a lick about the storied Warhammer universe to take a crack at Space Marine.
Landing on the Forge World Graia (a planet utterly devoted to the production of arms and ordnance), you play Captain Titus of the Ultramarines, a particularly storied chapter of super-human soldiers in the Space Marine faction. You are accompanied by brothers in arms, the veteran Sergeant Sidonus and by-the-book rookie Leandros.
Together the three of you are tasked with stopping the Orks, an overbred horde of maniacal idiots, from taking Graia in ever-raging war for authority in the galaxy.
Gameplay is fundamentally linear and simple, but those rough edges are thoroughly buffed away with an arsenal of brutal and outrageously satisfying weapons backed by wild combos and an engrossing mythos. You won't be bored one minute of this ~8 hour campaign, and you're a fool not to try your hand at multiplayer.
Verdict: 8/10

This is a short visual novel with stats management where Yukari decides to pursue her dreams to produce an anime after graduating from high school and waiting for her university term to start. With her best friend Mayumi, two sisters Yuuko and Sumiko, Shunsuke and the initial investment in capital given by Yukari's grandmother, the team embark on a 12-week project that will put Yukari and her team's (and the player's) decision making and efforts to the test.
The game has plenty of save slots to replay a particular section of the game, 9 shown stats and 2 hidden stats which affect the quality and outcome of the anime production and the ending of the game and the option to skip and fast-forward already read sections. The game will require some familiarity with the expected activity Yukari and each team member can perform as it is fixed at each week as well as the possible bonuses and penalties given to each decision Yukari makes during various events. Certain random events will appear at different parts of the 12-week playthrough and certain decisions made can have variable effects. Soundtracks and overall game presentation are decent. Recommended when at discount as it takes less than 10 hours to try to produce 3 different genre of anime and attempt to reach the best ending in the game over 3 or more separate playthroughs.

This game has the barebones expected of a HOG; you get a vague story, lots of hidden objects to find and work your way through. The biggest problem with this one was it really had the potential to stick out as unique HOG (even without the expected bonus features you get with HOG's on Steam), in that it really drew into the horror/thriller world. The whole game was dedicated to scaring you and keep you guessing to the end. Unfortunately it doesn't keep the momentum going and the ending ends up being a plot hole on its own. Another missed opportunity, is the feature of hallucinations which really tied into the story but again never panned out. Solving puzzles to change the environment to 'reality' was really entrancing, but the game only used it twice (the second being only half-completed). This, with no replayability, is why I recommend the game, but only when its on sale.
This is a game where you tramp around a massive property, finding items to help you as you work your way through the story and the locations. It has sections where you have to find everything on a list (hidden-objects) or have to solve puzzles to proceed.
This HOG is one of the better ones I've seen, because it incorporated horror and thill so well, whilst many other games in the genre often skimp on. The hidden objects in the game are challenging but not frustrating and same could be said for the few puzzles you do find. Unfortunately, it has none of the bonus features that are now becoming standard on Steam, including trading cards and an epilogue. This game is an excellent example for a casual player and I recommend it.

White Haven Mysteries is a typical HOPA. It's mediocre in any sense possible. Why do I still recommend it? If you get it cheap enough - i.e., at a discount of at least 50% - you'll get yourself a fairly good deal if you like that kind of game.
In detail:
# It has the standard game modes: Quick hint recharge and sparkles OR slow hint recharge, no sparkles.
# The graphics are good, but not amazing. The HO scenes are clear, and the objects are big enough to be spotted.
# It's quite short. It took me just 2 hours to finish it, and I read every journal entry and didn't skip a single puzzle.
# The story is nothing new. A spooky building, a mystery to solve, a mad scientist - standard stuff. The ending was a tad confusing, but I believe I understood it.
(Note: I can't say anything about sound or VOs, as I played it muted. Also, I finished it in one sitting, so I can't comment on the corrupted save file issue.)

As a long-time fan of the Oddworld franchise and someone who played the original Abe's Oddysee back in the day, I can say with all honesty that is a great remake that does justice on most from the original game. The game, even though it has been built from the ground up, from scratch, plays very similar to the originall. Even though it has drifted away from the multi-screen cinematic playstyle the original had, it still functions with the same mechanics,
The gameplay is smooth and fun, yet still keeps its difficulty and is now tweaked to have three different difficulties to choose from for those that are new to the Abe series, familiar with it, or are looking to play the hardcore bare bones style of the original.
The edition of some of Abe's Exoddus features is a nice touch as well. One of the major gripes I had with the original was the checkpoint system, which is now much better, and even has the addition of the quicksave feature, allowing you to save at anytime, from Exoddus.
Overall this isa  pretty faithful remake. I would probably still say the original is better, since the game lacks a lot of what made the original great, but I do highly recommend it for any Oddworld fans.

For some reason though #MINI-SPOILERS# the end cutscenes have the traditional sprites. Looks much better.
The controls are also not as intuitive/dynamic as in the original (entering doors, jumping into whatevers no longer use "Up", but "Use"). You can no longer directly jump into the wells from an elevated position and there is some lag between stopping in front of one (or a door) and using it (at least for me). That's mitigated by the longer charge-time for Scrabs, though. You get used to it. Especially if you change the controls do resemble the original one more closely (important: sideway jumping).
Apart from all that, though, the game is awesome. Never would have thought that Oddworld's landscape could be translated as beautifully into 3D. Kudos!

This game is absolutely brilliant. I see myself playing through it again just to get all the achievements. That being said, there is one thing you need to know. While the game starts in happy-go-lucky way, it has 6 chase sequences that are brutally hard. Whenever you finish a temple section, one thing or the other is going to chase you away from there. I've been waiting a good while to play this game. To the Moon quickly became one of my favorite games of all time, so my bar was set very high for Finding Paradise. In a world where we are constantly exposed to stories that are recylced and lack orginiality, Kan Gao and Freebird games have once again found themselves a the tellers of a beautifully unique story. I cried at To the Moon, and darn if this one didn't make me do it again. You will wonder, laugh, ponder life, and likely cry in your experience playing this game. The characters are such great parts of this story, and work very well off each other.
Midway through the game, before one of the twists was revealed, I thought I had figured it out, and questioned whether I would be as touched by this one as it's predecessor. However in the final act of the game, it exceeded my expectations and became a very worthy sequal to a series with limitless potential.
Now onto less emotions and more gameplay. Similar style to "To the Moon", much more of an interactive story. Though they did throw in a slightly more complex puzzle system (still not difficult though, however it doesn't need to be) and there are a couple more instances where there is a minor form of "gameplay" which was fun in it's own way, allowing a little more variety to my experience playing this game.
I highly recommend this game, especially if you have played To the Moon. If you're new to the series and just browsing, make sure you play To the Moon first. If you prioritze storytelling, great characters, and excellent music thenI promise you will not be disapppointed.

That being said, you will probably not be interested enough to keep playing this on a binge where you spend hours on end.
The tactics style gameplay is pretty neato. That's... about all I can say about that part of the game. It doesn't really add anything to it or really borrow from some more advanced takes on it like XCOM: You've got area-of-effect attacks, you've to melee attacks, you've got ranged attacks. Don't expect to have any innovative takes on cover-combat, field of vision, and so on.
The characters are decent. Not really involved enough that I'd say I particularly cared about any of them one way or another, but not bland enough that I wasn't at least interested in seeing where they fit in the story. The character you kind of play as doesn't seem to really have a major stance on anything minus how you decide to direct his dialogue, but it's one of those games where you're kind of your own guy and you kind of aren't.
There's a lot of good side quests here and there that you are definitely going to want to do to keep yourself armed and leveled for the main questline.
As for the main questline itself, there's really nothing that much to it. The game tries to differentiate itself from other RPG-style adventure games by having the cast of characters be completely unlikely heroes. You, the main character, find yourself traveling with two fellows (a stereotypical and somewhat superstitious dwarf and a casanova mage) who collectively break out of a prison. From there, your party's membership includes a drug-addict elf whose pretty good with a bow (I think she's an elf at least. She's got the ears), a tribal dude who was ready to kick your♥♥♥♥♥before, and a childhood friend who ended up becoming an (alleged) nymphomaniac witch.
This seems like an interesting premise on the surface, but the game doesn't really apply itself that well. We don't really get much in on the character's pasts, and the interactions with the main character and the story are very limited. For a game that could've very well built onto a unique premise worthy enough of it being a constantly talked about title, the developers didn't really do much to apply themselves here, and I'm afraid that might still be the case for the sequel, Blackguards 2 as well (I haven't played it yet, so I won't judge).
So basically, this game is good if it's on a really, really good sale and you're already into fantasy and tactical games, but aren't looking for anything too innovative on either ends.

With the popularity of Dark Souls at the moment, difficulty seems to be the buzzword of the industry. This can be a great boon and imbues games with a sense of accomplishment and worth when done correctly. Blackguards seems difficult for all the wrong reasons, from an obtuse user interface to mindbogglingly poorly designed stats pages.
While I appreciate that any game coming from an existing Pen and Paper world will always have a higher step up for the user than most, Shadowrun earlier last year seemed to create a system both faithful and functional while Blackguards seemed bogged down in it's own mechanics.
The story is about par for course and the voice acting is quite refreshing, but it just seems like the clunky mechanics just get in the way of that experience and the difficulty wildly differs so much you bound between feeling elated and cheated every few minutes.
While people howl off the rooftops at the percieved "dumbing down" of videogames, sometimes it has a point. Parts of the design feel snobbish, as if it wants to pat it's faithful on the back and tell them how smart and clever they are while with the other hand swatting away the "casual, filthy masses". Blackguards needs to get down of it's high horse and reduce the barriers to entry that stop it from being the good game I know underneath is has the potential to be.

Did you ever play the cRPG mod for Mount & Blade? Well, this is like an open world MMO version of that. The combat isn't quite as polished as M&B, but it's getting there and is still under development. Gloria Victis has a great community and if you are the sort of person who likes to join in server-wide battles, defending and taking territory, you will be right at home. The game has a great system that calls you to help your nation whenever an event happens. Join or skip, it's your choice. You are not forced to fight, but if you do, you will be rewarded with experience and perhaps something a little more substantial (armor/items/weapon).
As for melee, your character's level helps, but you are still very dangerous as a lower level warrior. Attacking in packs, you can overwhelm the enemy. Even a farm tool can be deadly. You must manage your stamina well or you will be worthless in the fight. It takes some work, but if you spam the attack key, you will not last long. Shields are very useful as you can defend well without losing stamina.
Soon, a new combat system will be implemented with all new animations done by Geralt of Rivia's combat animator for Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. I am eagerly awaiting this update as I think this has the potential to rocket GV into the limelight. Kudos to the devs for landing such a great talent.
Archery works well and is very satisfying. You must account for gravity, distance and you'll need to lead targets. landing long-distance headshots are extremely gratifying and you are rewarded with XP for marksmanship.
Immersion is excellent. Moody lighting, great music and sound effects help to plunge you into this medieval setting.
Weapons do not have trailing effects. This is so nice since many games add these adn it completely breaks immersion to me. I hope they never add them (unless it's a fire arrow!).
Lastly, if you are at all curious about the game, search YouTube for gameplay videos and decide for yourself. It's a steal at this price!!

Easily one of the most addicting games I've played in recent years, and one of the best early access titles out there. The devs are constantly working on new features, fixing bugs and and listening to player feedback. Obviously with it being in early access there are still missing features, placeholder models/sounds and bugs, however the small team are making massive progress and usually squash the game breaking bugs as a priority.
As always there are negatives, save games get broken by updates, new bugs pop up and sometimes the game mechanics seem a bit nonsensical. The dev team do listen and generally they give people the option of turning off annoying mechanics (weapon/tool durability I'm looking at you!). I understand that the game is early access and nothing is set in stone, so it's an annoyance when things change and suddenly you have to adjust to new mechanics, but that's just life in early access.
The main draw for me has been the building. It's in depth yet not a simulation. You won't be running wires or pipes but there are times where you need to think about where you place components to make your ship function efficiently. The game currently lacks any real kind of physics which is a shame and what has been implemented is kind of half baked but again, these are things that are constantly being looked at and improved. Planets are also not complete with the poles being cordoned off and the edges of the map being a teleport point essentially, but again these are things that are being worked on.
Overall I absolutely love this game and every update brings (mostly) welcome changes. The dev team is always on the ball and put a great deal of attention into making this a brilliant game. The Empyrion forums are a great place to get a glimpse at new features, provide feedback and see the wonderfully creative community at work.
I highly recommend it, but urge you to keep in mind that it's early access and that things can and will change. Expect that there will be bugs and missing features for now.

Styx: Master of Shadows is a third-person stealth game by Cyanide Studios. You play as Styx, a goblin thief trying to steal the heart of the World Tree, a magical tree and the source of Amber, a liquid humans use as a drug and which fuels Styx's magic.
Styx is nothing but a small goblin, and most enemies he faces are at least twice as high as him. Because of this, some enemies can instakill him outright, and the ones that can't are still a pain to take down in open combat, requiring several parries so you can get an opening to kill them. This "combat" system, of course, means that against several enemies you're probably not going to get out alive, and the game really is just suited to stealth play. There's nothing inherently bad about that of course, unless you've got warped ideas on what a stealth game actually is.
You do have multiple ways to approach levels without being detected. Killing is a loud choice and even muffled kills are loud enough for nearby enemies to notice. Ghosting is supported by the ability to extinguish torches (though guards will notice it and light them again), and some magic powers. Amber Vision highlights objects, which is useful as sometimes objects are obscured by lighting. I tried not to use Invisibility but I ended up doing it to get through certain harder areas without being seen. Finally, you can create a clone and control it. It's a pretty fun mechanic as the clone can alert foes but then kill itself, making enemies return to an unalerted state. This allows you to access some places which are harder to access unseen.
The game has an upgrade system consisting of several sections. You can respec at your leisure to experiment however you see fit, and fully speccing certain pairs of sections unlocks special upgrades, such as Amber Vision letting you see through walls. The normal upgrades are nevertheless interesting, with stuff like aerial kills or upgrading your clone to be able to make a smokescreen or hold an enemy in place.
Overall the level design is pretty good and full of verticality, as you can jump and climb structures. The game is set in bits of a gigantic citadel, made by a mad genius-architect to protect the aforementioned World Tree. The gripe with the levels is once you reach a sort of mid-game plot twist you have to then go through the previous levels in reverse order. This is not as bad as it seems as the levels are now repopulated, and overall harder. The game presents a medium challenge until then (played on Hard difficulty) but the reverse levels do have areas which, as I mentioned, had me give up and use Invisibility (yes I do feel slightly ashamed.) It doesn't feel like too much of a rehash because of this.
This is a pretty fun game if you're a fan of the Thief games, or just playing games without getting detected at all.

I don't normally write reviews for any sort of game, but after playing through Finding Paradise, I felt obliged to.

To begin with, a basic summary of this game is that there is character that the story is revolved around, Colin, and he is on his deathbed and he hires Sigmund to fulfill his last wish. The thing is, Colin doesn't what he wants for his last wish as he feels like something is missing from his life but doesn't know what, so it is up to the workers of Sigmund, Eva and Dr. Watts, to traverse through his memories and figure it out by themselves.
I really like this game, as a matter of fact, I adored it.
There was the silly jokes that made this game and To The Moon so charming.
But then there was also the stuff that hit hard, the stuff that makes you emotional, and you have to take a moment and step back and appreciate how well this story is told as it builds this fantasy world that captures your attention and never once lets it go. But that's the beauty of this game, the carefully crafted way that the story is told that produces so many feelings inside of you that you even knew existed.
But there is so much more that makes this game endearing, so much so that you couldn't possibly describe in words, so do yourself a favour and play this game.

Infinite Warfare is an okay game; not amazing, not great, not bad, not terrible, just okay. It isn't the best CoD game out there, that much is obvious, and the best probably goes to Black Ops 1, Black Ops 2, World at War, or one of the Modern Warfare games, but what do I know. What I do know is that this game isn't amazing, but it isn't terrible either, just okay. Campaign is fine from what I can tell, Multiplayer is okay, and Zombies is good, even if they copied a lot from Black Ops 3 (like the Gobble Gum system and a lot of the lines of dialogue from picking up power ups or the famous "Fetch me their souls" which is in Rave in the Redwoods).
Multiplayer isn't as clustered or overpowered as Black Ops 3 with the infamous Brecci and D13 Sector. Speaking of, supply drops are much better in this game since you can actually get keys, not just Multiplayer, but from Zombies as well and you can salvage to just straight up buy varients, which for the DLC weapons, gets you the weapon; you don't have to unlock the weapon like in Black Ops 3, you just get one varient of that weapon or buy a varient using salvage from duplicates (and getting it from rare drops as a bonus like Cryptokeys) and you get that weapon.
Zombies, while it does copy a lot from Black Ops 3 and Teryarch in general, it's not bad. It's hard as hell, fun with friends, and gets you keys, so it's very worth your time to at least try it out. Zombies in Spaceland, the base Zombies map you get with the game is insanely hard, but the other maps do get easier (which is typical for most Zombie gamemodes). Plus it gueststars David Hasselhoff, Kevin Smith, and more to come with the maps. Also, the main bad guy is voiced by Pee Wee Herman, just throwin' that out there.
So, is Infinite Warfare a great game? No. Is it a bad game? Also no. It's just an okay game, it does not surpass the obviously better CoD games by no means, but is better than the obvious black sheeps in the series and most of the older titles, at least in my book. I say at least give the game a chance, if you don't like it, you don't like it, but that does not make it a bad game, it's just okay.
So, in my opinion, this game gets a 6.6/10 because 7 seems too high and 6 seems too low.

Short version: Bl♥♥♥♥guards is an average game which could have been a lot better without some of the bugs and a more intuitively developed story engine.
For those of you who remember the glory days of the genre with Baldur's Gate I and II, IceWind Dale amongst others, Blackguars might still be worth looking into. I enjoyed playing it, but I would also like to post a warning about some of things that knocked down the total score for me:
With the bad stuff out of the way, let's round things up with the more positive aspects of Blackguards:
it's an ambitious attempt at rebooting the genre (yes, I'm aware that there are several other similar games on the market nowdays) based on a popular tabletop theme. The graphics are decent and the voice acting is top notch.

Pros:
-Great mix of genres and different gameplay styles (depending on difficulty)
-Good Story
-The right amount of collecting for the extras if you want 100%
Con:
-Certain genres seem unfair at higher difficulties
Pros Explained:
This game is easily in my top 10 games of all time. Granted it can only be there because I've played most of the games that Evoland 2 references. The best games to compare the main theme / gameplay of this game is a Link to the Past or Oracle of Ages / Seasons. You solve puzzles by going through different eras in time while learning about the interesting story of the game world and how certain actions intertwine throughout the eras. One of the best parts about this game is that right as you are starting to feel like the gameplay is about to get repetitve, the game throws a curveball at you and has the area or boss fight in the style of a completely different genre. Evoland 2 will also have you actually laughing out loud at it's jokes and surprised by it's story. You'll most likely figure out each surprise before it comes up in the story but that didn't stop me from being surprised at the ending. Evoland 2 also has a fun, optional card game where you collect 61 cards throughout the game. The collecting never felt awful and the end game gives you a device to find all collectables.
Con Explained:
As you can tell from above that I love this game but there are some things that can get in the way of it being perfect. With throwing in different genres throughout the game, you are bound to hit one that you either don't like or one that is a lot harder then the gameplay you were just enjoying. Luckily, you can change the difficulty at anytime without penalty to your achievments so this isn't a deal breaker. I don't know the genre name, but in games where you have to move very fast in a side scroll without enough time to react to what is coming up, suck! A game that comes to mind is the lava level in Aladdin for the SNES. Like I said before, you can change the difficulty at anytime so if you start to feel stuck on a game type, change it down and then raise the difficulty once you are past that part.
All in all, Evoland 2 is a really fun game that I think anyone who likes multiple types of game genres, but mainly adventure, should buy when they get the chance. Here's hoping they make an Evoland 3 with even more genres and improvements on the genres that were already included.
PS. If you are like me and freak out that you missed something but are afraid that when you leave the area, you won't get the treasure, don't worry. All areas that have collectables are repeatable before the final boss.

When I think about what all great games have it boils down to four elements, interesting characters, well crafted narrative, great looking visuals, and immersive music/sounds. Gloria Victis is an early access game and they are still actively polishing these elements. However, what you get right now is so close to what most $60 dollar games offer, I can’t hesitate to recommend it. If you pick it up on sale then even better!
Gloria Victis is an MMO in which you choose one of two nations to join–the Midlanders or the Isimir. After customizing your character with a wide variety of options–which can be adjusted anytime– you set off in the world to fight over a rocky and grassy countryside filled with farms, towns, castles, encampments and hideouts. There are multiple servers to play on and your characters persist across them. They also plan on adding two more nations before the release.
When you set off into the world you can choose to fight solo, or in a party. There are level based scenarios which spawn across the world, along with outposts and cities which can be attacked and captured or reinforced and defended. Often these skirmishes involve NPCs as well as players. There is an emphasis on realistic medieval swordplay and I’ve heard that the developers have a mantra “No fireballs!”
Finding players to party up with is easy and many are keen to do so because there is a lot of fun to be had storming across the map in a group of 3 to 7 players and taking outposts one after another. Recently they have added PvP Tournaments where I’ve seen 15 to 20 players on a side in massive melee battles.  Immediately following the tournaments global dynamic events spawn and nations engage in sieging and defending selected towns or castles, or defeating NPC commanders that are protected by soldiers. They are working on even more dynamic events and world bosses which will appear in response to actions taken by players.
If crafting is more your thing then rest assured that Gloria Victis has a deep crafting system with around 8 different areas of specialization and just like fighting you can gain experience from crafting as well.
For those of us who understand the importance of supporting small studios who are trying to create quality games that aren’t just remakes of the same old formula, Gloria Victis is a breath of fresh air. Yes it still has some rough edges, but the team is dedicated to polishing them, they are interested in what the community has to say, and they are still adding more features and content. “Glory to the vanquished” indeed!

Gloria Victis should be used as an example of how an Early Access game should work. I'd like to start with saying that the game still needs improvement in the opimization but to me that is the only big issue. The Devs are very responsive to their community, they give updates on what their working on, and most importantly they actually update the game unlike many Early Access game devs.
For minor issues, some players accustomed to huge successful MMO's may find a lack of things to do for PvE but it makes up for it in it's amazing PvP, normally I tend to stay clear of PvP but in Gloria Victis they use a dynamic map system which causes shifts in territory as 1 faction raids the other. They also have a Tournament system which can earn you huge amounts of XP and I don't think any other game does better in making you feel connected and proud in your faction than Gloria Victis.
Anyone familiar with Mount & Blade will have no trouble learning the controls in Gloria Victis, while the combat system is NOT complete and still has a lot of work to be done (There's a patch coming out shortly that will add new combat animations) the combat is well enough that it isn't a chore to play and is actually a lot of fun. The best part of Gloria Victis in my opinion and many other players is the insanely in depth crafting system and AMAZING looking armors, from the traditional knight's plate armor to nordic warrior bear pelt headresses there is no lack of imagination and possibility in what you wear.
The progress this game has made in the past months alone is truley amazing and I can't wait to see what it will become by next year.

Now that I've had my Level 100 char to PVP with, I have to say that I'm a bit disappointed with this game, and, admittedly, I was pretty excited about it. I mean few games live up to a large hype, and that's understandable, but the simple fact is, that there is no way around the Nintendo SDK known as the Unity Engine.  The physics of this engine, even now, are quite immersion-destroying; you run downstairs quickly, and you simply float, as you do along railings, sidewalk edges, high walls, or even when you just hit the jump button; suddenly you are in space, floating at 1/4 speed, until you land again, where you are suddenly full speed again. Not nitty gritty virtual world, but silly game. This is not a bug, it's the engine, and that's just one example of many, so this silliness is never going away.
Which is unfortunate, because graphically, it is shaping up to be a beautiful game. The armor is fantastic looking, and the weapons are coming along nicely with the latest patches. So, unfortunately, IMO, what we have is yet another beautifully skinned, but not as much underneath as one would be led to believe, type of game. Of which there are entirely too many already.
The short answer on the PVP is that, like WoW, it is fun stuff (minus the magic, and you actually have to land your sword hits, which frankly is excellent for immersion and "pucker-factor"), but you still get a kind of temporary, lobby-based game type of feel at the end of the day.
If you are looking for a comparison, the easiest I can give is this: take a WoW-clone server, have the dev's try to copy the idea of Mount n Blade Warband, and you have a pretty good picture of Gloria Victis playsyle. Now this game is sort of hate-love relationship.
I did play the game with a XBox 360 controller on simulation setting
I did not play the multiplayer part.
It does have two different control modes: Arcade and Simulation, both for Mouse/Keyboard and controller.
Arcade is what the name suggests, easy controllable fast action.
Simulation, on the contrary, is much harder and more realistic in terms of flight dynamics. For this mode some training (like the training mission) is advisable. But even when using simulation, the game is still more arcade than some other games, so if you're a hardcore simulation fan, you won't miss anything here.
The missions are relatively straight-forward: Destroy that ship, destroy that many planes in XX minutes and so on.
I lacks freedom, but if you don't mind that, the air-action is doing fine.
There are however some boresome missions, like on the japanese campaign where you have to do some very precise bombing with limited number of planes (and bombs, that is). Here I needed several relaods of that single mission to make it in time.
That being sad, the scripting is still buggy; and I don't expect it to be patched any more.
In 2 levels the level border (you cannot fly too far away from the main objective) is set really stupid; I even had 2 occurences where I switched to another, previously AI-controlled plane, and instantly ended up in loosing the mission due to "leaving the battlefield"...
Overall, 60% of the missions are really enjoyable, the rest ranges from "nice try" over "boresome" to "annoying".
Also there is at least one real show-stopper bug:
After finishing the last mission in the japanese campaign, the game crashed. And looking up in the game hub, it seems not to be an isolated problem--
In general the game is not bad. It's entertainable for about 8-10 hours each campaign and there is a multiplayer part.
But I suggest you buy this game only if you don't mind some bugs, a more or less arcade-like flying style and relatively straight-forward mission design.
For myselfI don't think I wasted my time here, but if I'd payed more than 5€, I would be sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥due to the bugs and mission design flaws.
