Styx: Master of Shadows is a pretty decent third person stealth game.
The game is technically a prequel to Of Orcs and Men. However, apart from Styx himself and the overall setting there's very little in common between the two games. The gameplay is very different and the plots of the two games are only very loosely connected.
Styx: Master of Shadows is pretty much a pure stealth game. The combat is poorly implemented and fighting more than one enemy will usually get you killed. Generally this is not an issue, however, as Styx has lots of ways to avoid combat.
The stealth itself is solid enough at least. You have to stick to the shadows to avoid detection and any noise you make will alert nearby enemies too. Enemy AI on the other hand is not particularly good. Most of the sneaking is not particularly hard, you just need some patience to work out the enemies patrol routes and move at the time.
Level design is pretty decent too. There's usually multiple ways to reach an objective and the levels themselves are quite vertical. Unfortunately the actual locations are not that memorable and there's not a single level that really stands out. The game also reuses earlier maps quite a bit.
The final battle deserves a special mention considering how awful it is. All of a sudden you are forced in a small arena with minimal cover against multiple opponents. This kind of encounter has absolutely no place in a stealth game. I didn't have too much trouble with the fight myself, but depending on what items and skills you have available this battle can be extremely difficult and tedious.
Visually the game looks rather dated. The environments are passable enough but many of the character models are downright hideous. Some of the voice acting is pretty bad, too, and the lipsync is terrible.
Despite its flaws Styx: Master of Shadows is a solid enough stealth game. It is definitely not for everyone, but as long as you enjoy pure stealth gameplay the game is easy to recommend. It's not nearly as good as the early Thief games, but still much better than the terrible Thief reboot.
I played through the game on hard and found the difficulty level pretty good overall.
The good:
- Solid stealth gameplay
- Vertical and nonlinear levels
- Styx is a great character
- Interesting setting
The bad:
- Awful final battle
- Some control issues (I played with keyboard + mouse)
- Tedious insignia system
- Poor enemy AI
- Lackluster combat
- Weak writing and story
- Dated character models
- Some weak voice acting and terrible lipsync
- The clone system is rather fiddly and not particularly fun
The ugly:
- The game often autosaves at terrible times
- Lots of minor glitches and bugs
This game contains unfixed game breaking bugs and also does some major level recycling.

Styx is basically what happens if Assassin's Creed focused purely on the stealth aspect and used a set of open levels instead of a singular big open world.
I was thinking of listing the game pros and cons, but then I realized it doesn't really have any con. I mean, the facial animation and the use of artwork (instead of cutscenes) to tell the story is definitely not a good thing, but I think it's due the budget constraint more than anything else. And considering this isn't really a AAA game, those flaws are pretty darn forgivable.
I'll just list the biggest pros I guess.
+ Open levels with real multiple paths! I know the game advertises this as a feature, but I didn't expect players to actually have this many options. The level uses a good amount of verticality to achieve this.
+ Collectibles that rewards exploration! This synergizes really well with the open levels. Since you don't have to use every path to reach the goal, the game puts collectibles on optional paths to encourage players to try different paths.
+ You can actually finish the level and get all the secrets without killing anyone!
+ High number of playtime. Most missions take 90-120 minutes to finish, and that's not counting all the reloading you do in the game. The whole game takes around 26 hours to finish for me.
+ Surprisingly decent storyline. Cliche is definitely the furthest thing from the story in this game.
+ Much more.
All in all, if you're a fan of stealth game and don't mind a little platforming, then this game is definitely for you.
Think Assassin's Creed meets Hitman. Yup, that's what this game is.

I really tried to like this game, in spite of reading very mixed reviews. Alas, I ended up quite frustrated with a few aspects that are quite game (and immersion) breaking:
1. losing vital companions at crucial times makes party build options very limited. Essentially, once you figure out what will happen to X, you need to rethink your entire strategy for party build. This sometimes means restarting from scratch, or a very earlier save, as party build is very important in some of the encounters (especially the main ones)
2. lack of clothing for non-metal wearing characters - while there are several pretty good sets of armour for warriors, the (complete) lack of mage oriented outfits is a bit mind baffling. I could not fathom that no mage outfits EVER dropped, although you battle many mages wearing unique outfits. And none can be bought. As a consequence, you mage characters have to either wear horrible looking leather armour, or spend a lot of time buffing/running/dying. This is also important for...
3. almost 100% spell failure when wearing metal armour. I can accept offensive spells (cast outward) failing, but having a healing/self-buff spell have a <25% of success is nonsense. So playing as a battle mage/arcane warrior/cleric type role is pretty much out of the question
4. tedious battles - which can go on for a long time, with a lot of time sitting, and staring at the screen while seemingly endless hordes of critters/monsters/lice/etc. go thought their turns. Even tentacles get their own turns, and usually have a higher initiative than your party...
5. endgame decision disasters - going back to #1 - at the end game you find out that you are 'supposed to' have made certain vital conversation decisions with one companion, otherwise they will be lost, which as mentioned before, can be a disaster for the party.
So, if you want to play this:
a) read the guides and build a cooky cutter type that the developers had in mind, and
b) follow a pro-forma discussion template to placate one party member, or lose them at a crucial stage (or build with their loss in mind)
c) have a good book/magazine handy to read during battles, as you otherwise stare at the screen waiting endlessly

Blackguards is an tactical turn-based RPG game that brings some new soultions and points of view to the table, that are not always good.
(New feature - Simple city interface.)
If you remember Drakensang, Dragon Age or most other RPGs cities, large, vast, many NPCs, a lot of chests to look and barrels to smash for loot. Nothing like that in Blackguards. City is a simple one screen view with most important NPCs, merchant, healer, trainer, quest giver, tavern, the end. If you have business in the city it takes you about a minute to get it done and leave to get back to action. Some might like it, some might not. I like it, as it saves time, no more need to remember where was that cool merchant or a hidden pass etc.
So you may wonder how does this tactical turn base combat looks like.
(Character summary)
Before we get there you must know that Blackguards are based on The Dark Eye RPG pen and paper system. And character development is very much like in the pen and paper game. If you played Drakensangs before you will be very familiar with the system.
In most RPG games you have classes to select. There are no classes in this game. When creating character you select if you wanna be spell-casting able or not and then you build character on skills/spells you chose. In that this system is similar to Elder Scrolls. If you wanna be a warrior you can be a warrior, if you wanna be a warrior-priest you can be warrior-priest it's all based on how to chose your skills, not limited by class.
So characters have attribiutes that calculate their base stats like vitality, astral points (manna), base attack, dodge and parry. Attriubutes cost a lot of adventure points to raise. By chosing how to spend attribiutes you craft base for your character, if you invest heavy into strength, agility, courage and constitiution you will end up with a fighter with almost no chance to cast any spell. If you go for intuition, cleverness and charisma you will end up with solid base for mage with poor fighting abilities. You can also walk the path of average, but you must be careful and just select few spells and weapons to invest in those heavy.
Keep in mind that mages are limited by metalic armor - they will not regenerate astral points while wearing even a single piece of it and will have negative casting modifier, so a melee mage is a hard to play, but possible with correct spell investment.
Then are the skills. Skills are divided into weapons, talents (perception, traps etc) and spells. And in that game every weapon is another skills, so if your character is an expert swordsman (18 swordsmanship skill), when he will be forced to use an axe, he will be very poor with ti because he has no skill in axe, he will have very small chance to hit and large to be hit by enemies.
Skills make your characters use stuff. Skills are rated from 0-18. Spells and talents unlock bonusses at 8,13,18 levels. Here you choce which spells your character can cast and weapons to use.
At the end are special abilities - special attacks for melees, ranged and boosts for mages.
The better the special attack the harder it is to hit with it.
Original pen and paper game used three 20 side dices for skill tests, to make it computer game, devs changed that into % chance. So unlike dragon age it is not enough to unlock a spell to cast it, you must unlock the spell and invest points into it.
(Note on spells)
For me spells in this game are net design to be used mainly at blunt offensive magic. Spells play a support role in this game. You can cast offensive spells and they will do a lot of damage, however doing so will deplete your astral points in two shots so after your mage will not be able to do anything else than bash stuff with his staff.
(Note on weapons)
I really love games which make using axe different than using a sword for example. Blackguards is such a game.Every weapon type has it damage type (piercing for spears and fancing weapons, slashing for swords and blunt for maces). Every weapon type also uses a different skill. So if you wanna use few different weapons you must spend points on different skills. Different weapons also have different special attacks, you cannot make armor ignoring attack with maces, but you can make attack that tripples the damage with them.
(Combat)
Having explained the above. Combat is turn based in which your heros and enemies take their turns in order of initiative. On their turn everyone can move a little and make action (attack, cast spell, place trap, disarm trap, spot for traps, use item etc) or move further. You can hide behind objects or other heros to break line of sights of enemy archers to your mages as well, there is no other cover system.
Combat map is divided into small hexes for movement and there can be varius hazard spaces on the map like oil set on fire will deal you fire damage when you cross it, while mud can make your character fall down unless he passes bosy control test.
(Tactical combat)
By using combination on magic and physical attacks you must cripple and defeat enemies. Enemies will usually outnumber you as well and some of them will also cast spells, use healing potions and have special attacks. So this is where tactic comes into place.
Use your melees to block enemies before they reach your mages, or run to enemy mage to bash on him. Use obejects on the map and magic walls to block enemy movement and shoot them directly. You have options.
Cast damage spells to finish fight quickly, or same astral points for buffing and healing magic.
(Plot - Story)
Unfortunately game story is quite linear and not really involving. Characters are a bit shallow and the only one who really feels realistic is the dwarf who is fun and really combat oriented.
At few points in the game you will be stripped of your gear and forced to make through with given equipment untill you can regain your stuff. So it is goot to invest a little into maces(as you will usually end up fighting with a torch or a club) and offensive magic.
(Flaws)
There are some flaws to the game:
-Horrible mouth work. Unlike other modern games, the speaking animations here are just horrible, you will see heros open mouth like fish trying to catch a breath, it has no connectiong with what is being spoken.
-Very bad equipment comparison system. There is no way to compare one set of armor with another other than noting down the stats, changing set and seeing new stats.
-I have really no idea what in this game make it be 20gb large.
-Game does little to introduce players who are new to the difficult character creating and developemtn system. [there is good help&tips in the menu if you can spend a moment to read and understand it]
-Not involving plot and shallow characters.
-Not intuitive UI.
-No crafting system.
(Merits)
+Realistic when it comes to weapons and armors. Armors comes in sets, so it is no longer find best pieces, but you need to wear a complete set of armor to have best benefits. And I like it that way.
+Deep and difficult tactical combat. I like the games that are not easy.
+Quick cities exploration.
+You are not limited when crafting your heros, you have a lot of freedom in systems without classes.
Overall I would give this game 7/10.
I hope most of the flaws will be corrected in the upcomming Blackguards 2.

Blackguards is a good game but has it's flaws. Mostly I had fun playing the game.
- The difficulty of the game is quite easy at the begining but later on it becomes really annoying because mostly your enemies use spells that lower your move speed, attack chance and health. Also it will become quite impossible to fight your enemies if you don't finish all of the side quest.
- Interface/Combat  is excellent, but the controls are a little wonky and sometimes quite slow. There are some monsters that take up more than 1 hex ( places on the field) and it's hard to locate the spot to hit but it's not that bad that you will ruin your whole turn.
- Information is a little unclear  but after few hours you should figure it out.
- Loading screens. You will spend some time on loading screens.
- There is not much of different gear and weapons. Don't expect to find a lot of variety of great weapons, few of my characters had the same weapon from the 1-2 chapter to the end of the game. Also my wizards had the same clothes from the 1 chapter to the last part of the chapter 5.
- Opponents. There are a lot of different opponents and interesting ones. There are also opponents that are just frustrating you because they have have spells that lower everything (so yout hit chance isn't 95% but 45%) so they are hell to beat but when you beat them it's beautiful.
- Characters. All of the characters u play have different personalities that are unique. In some dialogues you can choose what your characters will say.
- Story. It's not a bad story at all and has some twists.
- Graphics. Some people might not care at all about graphics but I like it when the game I play has at least deacent graphics. The graphics are not that bad at all but when you talk to some people they will look totally different in the picture then they look in the game.
- Playability it depends on what difficulty you choose to play but It will surely have around 40 hours (surely more).
- To conclude this review I recommend you buy this game but on sale. You will enjoy it and be frustrated.

This VN is something I was looking at for quite a while. I tried it out on a demo long ago while looking for visual novels. I noted that it was on steam and put it into my wish list. With the dozens of games on my library and the several others in my wish list it got shoved into my back log. Finally during a steam sale I picked it up for less than $5. I decided to play it and I am glad I did.
This game is much longer than I ever expected 35 hours for the common and Kotori route and these routes are in one continuous run. There was no revisiting old saves or starting over for each route. This is One play through! ONE! 35 hours and there are several other routes to complete I feel like I stole this game. No wonder they ask $15 for the full price! It's even worth that and I'm a cheap person when it comes to my games. I did use Auto mode and I gave it enough time to read everything with a few seconds to spare, I don't read slow but not super fast either guess you could say I'm average. So your mileage may on this visual novel. I loved the auto mode though as I could kick back and read away kind of like an anime in a way.
OK the game itself. Having played a few visual novels maybe 4 or 5 this was a real treat to play. My first visual novel was Katawa Shoujo and I after that have always enjoyed them. This game is hard to review however, on one hand the art is stunning some of the best I've seen. The “movies” are a bit harder to call stunning as they are very primitive even for standards a few years ago. However you have to take in consideration that this is a visual novel so the engine was never designed to handle that well. I think they should have gone with hand drawn anime style cinematics instead of CG but that's my opinion and it's neither here nor there. The story is very well written mostly. There were many mistranslations typos and the like. I have not tried Ageha's route but I hear it's atrocious. There is a patch to fix this and remove the censorship but I didn't do it mostly because it didn't seem necessary to me. However it's an option if you need it. The music is fantastic. In visual novels you will hear the same music for hours on end. That can be a bad thing but I never got bored with it and there are enough tracks to fit any mood they are trying to convey. Some of the music I found myself whistling to at work. This is the first visual novel I have read that had voice acting and let me tell you it's worth it. The voice acting can really convey the emotions of the characters. There are so many voice lines in this visual novel I am surprised at how much work was put into it. Bravo to those who did voices in this game.
Overall I do not regret buying this game, on the contrary I regret not playing it sooner. It is a wild ride full of emotion and fun. This game does require some investment in both time and patience. There are times when the characters are explaining something that make you want to hit the skip button. Don't these things usually have some relevance down the line in the story. If you are looking at this as your first visual novel I wouldn't stop you but as Katawa Shoujo is free that one I think is better and a little more polished. However this one should easily be the second one you play hands down. Sorry this is so long but thanks for reading until the end. It's a phenomenal visual novel any person could enjoy

Finding Paradise is a shockingly well-written game, and since it's pretty much "the sequel to To The Moon" to the entire world, no one is really surprised.
Comparing it to its predecessor has been done a few hundred times already. They're both story-driven videogames about exploring a dying man's memories to change them in order to grant him his final wish, all done in RPG Maker XP of all things. I love you Kan, but you really gotta move that gear up someday,
While we're on the subject, the gameplay is awful. It's about moving your mouse over things hoping that your cursor turns into a magnifying glass icon so that you can make the story go forward ; and you have to do puzzles to move from memory to memory which I feel like I never really fully understood. Moreover, you can't change graphical options of any sort (not that I could find anyway, not like I looked hard) and the game assumes you're using a QWERTY keyboard and not an AZERTY one, which was actually a problem for me and my poor keyboard in some later parts of the game.
You might have noticed that I'm being harsh on this game. That's because in my eyes, there's little to criticize. Finding Paradise is absolutely amazing and I'm ready to talk about the great stuff, baby. Gaze, Internet Person, as my angry little frown disappears and I shower this game with praise like I shower your mother with one dollar bills on Friday nights.
The story is absolutely fantastic ; complex, but easy to understand, because it's told extremely well and the pacing is spot-on. The title screen itself managed to draw me in, then the game did not lose my attention for a second, nor did a single yawn escape my mouth. God knows how, since I yawn so much I probably consume twice as much oxygen as everyone else. And it's not because things keep happening and happening ; you're just always curious. What will the next memory be like? It's incredibly pleasant to learn more about Colin, little by little, and you really do get attached to him. If you didn't, which means the game wasn't incredibly human, the whole thing would fall apart.
Because that's this game's main quality : it's so goddamn full of humanity. The characters feel real and interesting, there's growth to their personalities, and the dialogue feels genuine : the writing is never forced, ever. Moreover, it's all very subtle. Everyone's heard of "Show, don't tell", but it feels like so little writers use it in gaming ; well not your boy Kan Gao, since his game is all about showing. You're shown who these characters are, you learn about them through their actions, not boring exposition. All the pieces are set for a very emotional gaming journey.
I've heard many people say, like for To The Moon, that this game has made them cry. It didn't for me personally, but that's mostly because Father fetches the belt if I feel emotions without his consent. Being the sneaky rebel that I am, that didn't stop me from feeling very sad or laughing with the game, and I can say that overall this is a very touching experience that little developers could pull off.
I suppose I also have to mention boring things like the quality of the music and of the pixel art, if I want to be thorough. But that's about it. I just wanted to contribute to that sweet "Overwhelmingly Positive" review score this game rightfully deserves. See ya.

I've said this before, but I'll state it again for the purposes of this this review: Very few things are able to drive me to tears, much less sobbing. To the Moon was one of these starring examples. I've been impressed severely by it's amazingly beautiful story and soundtrack... but that was the past... a memory if you will. Finding Paradise: The sequel to a story I had beloved so much. Is it able to hold up against the high expections set by its predecessor?
The story revolves around Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts - two scientists whose jobs are to investigate a patient's memories in order to do one last thing for them: fufill their dying wish. Today's patient goes by the name of Colin, who has a wish that is rather... difficult. The story - like that of To the Moon - is well executed. You will be laughing, you will be happy, you will be sad, you will be crying, you will be scared, but you will also be brave. Once again, Freebird - the devs behind this wonderful project - have once again outdone themselves! Finding Paradise is a masterpiece throughout the adventure! The characters are once again are amazing, although I do have a problem with the logic put behind a character near the end (and you’ll know what I’m talking about when you get to it), but I’ll let it happen because it did turn out really good anyways. Now if you didn’t play To the Moon, don’t worry. This game does a good job of catching you up without boring those who have already played the game, however, you will miss some references to To the Moon and apparently Bird Story also has a few references. HOWEVER! I still recomend you go and play To the Moon because you will seriously kick yourself in the face if you don't! You’re also probably wondering if Finding Paradise could possibly ever possibly beat To the Moon’s amazing finale. Believe it or not, the ending is on par with To the Moon, and you will be sobbing once again.
Now let’s talk gameplay. What happens is that you go around, collecting memory links in order to break momentos. Thankfully, the game does tell you if you’ve missed something and memory links are very obvious, so it shouldn’t be too hard of a task, but it still can be somewhat sluggish considering how slowly the characters move. Then, once a momento is broken, you must solve a puzzle to get past it. The puzzles of this game can be interesting, but they weren’t world breaking or anything. There are also a few mini games near the end that were interesting and kinda fun, but these aren’t the main spotlight of the game. But please don’t let these detract from the main story. These are the minorest of minor complaints, and I really don’t mind.
And now it’s time to talk music. The music - like To the Moon - is really well done. They have all added onto whatever scene is currently playing out really well. Also, Laura Shigihara makes a reappearance for the final song (you know, the one who sung “There’s a Zombie on Your Lawn” from PVZ or the ever amazing “Everything’s Alright” from To the Moon?), which by the way, you don’t need to worry about. The final song adds soooo much to the end (just like "Everything's Alright), and I know you’ll love it as well. I’m going to give you a tip: buy the soundtrack but don’t listen to it until you finish the game. You’ll thank me later when you start crying to the end.
There’s only one last thing to talk about: graphics. I gotta say, the art style may be the same, but you can tell that it’s gone through several improvements. There are now more expressions, zooming in, and now some objects actually sparkle, providing yet another helpful hint system. The visuals of this game are still good and do a very good job of telling the story.
In the end, Finding Paradise turns out to be an extraordinary example of a good experience with its amazing story and soundtrack. Though there are minor problems to be had, they pale in comparison to the story, and I could never let them get in the way. Overall, I loved Finding Paradise. It has managed to do what To the Moon could, even if To the Moon was an unbeatable story. Finding Paradise... might have even beaten To the Moon, but that will be a close battle to be sure.

I've been waiting for the release of this game since 2011 if I remember?
Now, four years later it is finally here and the wait hasn't disappointed me! I thought the "improvements" and changes would ruin the nostalgia and make it play worse in comparison to the original. Wrong! In fact, it plays better than ever before and still keeps the same atmosphere whilst retaining that same ol' nostalgia.
The new controls are certainly a massive improvement. Sections that use to be difficult in the original game are now relatively easy because of the new controls. This sounds like a bad thing? No, no. It's got rid of the frustrating timing issues that still exist in the original.
The graphics? They're beautiful, without a shadow of doubt. A lot of people keep going on how the original graphics are better but they're both very different artistic styles. The original used backdrops from pre-rendered scenes. The downside to this is that they were static so it couldn't add life to the surroundings. What you saw in the gameplay world was as much as you were going to get.
With New 'n' Tasty there is so much more going on in the world of Oddworld. You see mudokons in the background cleaning on the floor, sligs patrolling sections that you cannot see and not to forget the creatures of Oddworld living in their environment.
The only thing I do feel that needs improvement is the audio. I like the new richer quality sounds but they seem a tad off from the original. But this is a new game? Not a remake! Yes, I know :/ The original audio such as the atmospheric sounds were a lot more appealing. I could just turn off the screen and listen to them for an hour and feel like I'm in the universe of Oddworld. With New 'n' Tasty? I'm not really getting that. The audio needs some work, including the balance. Some things appear to sound louder than others and you don't really know where you are at points.
Overall the game is worth every penny and I would certainly recommend it to anyone. There isn't too much I feel that I can criticise about other than the audio. Everything about the game is everything I had hoped for it to be.

I was interested in seeing how historically accurate this game was, but couldn't get past the poor gameplay. According to other reviewers, it wasn't much. From the little bit I've seen of the game, it had a fairly simplistic view of the war and Japan. Quite honestly, it felt like the gang from Team America: World Police had a hand in the writing. I'd be intested in seeing the Japanese campaign, but the gameplay was much too boring - sometimes frustrating to actually bring myself to unlock it.
The keyboard controls are fairly simple. Hold Shift: go faster; Hold Ctrl: go slower until your engines cut out and you start to stall (good luck dropping torpedoes because you'll stall before you can go slow enough to drop them); Hold no keys: speed remains somewhere between stall speed and max speed; Hold Tab: Target cam (bonus points if you can spot the problem with this default); WASD: various camera angles.
If you're like me, you'll get bored once you figure out these basics and you'll be sitting with your head propped up on your arm trying not to fall asleep while you line up a shot with a slow moving bomber.
The game breaks a cardinal rule concerning the tutorial level. "The player cannot fail". If a player fails at any portion of the training level, he/she will have to play all the way through it again. At best, if a failure occurs, the game should commence from a checkpoint that's fairly close or the scenario should be designed in such a way that the player cannot fail easily. OK, my first experience with this game wasn't good - the game just crashed every few minutes, making it unplayable.
Now, more than year later I decided to give it a chance launch it again - and it's a miracle! - it worked! It still crashes occasionally, but it's pretty playable now.
But I'll stand on what I've said before. This is very different game compared to previous parts. Difficulty had been pumped up - even on easy level with arcade control mode it still very challenging. Developers decided to remove infinite ammo, and the planes are getting damaged faster. Switching between them is weird and uncomfortable. Even rosters editing is very complicated.
But the main problem of this game - you don't get the feeling of the battle. The ships are just occasionally shooting the sky, enemy fighters very rarely engage you in a dogfight. And your own plane is moving like it has some sort of "car speed limiter" option turned on, and whether you're gaining speed or slowing it down - it doesn't matter, it will feel the same.
The pro's would be huge amount of missions on two campaigns - but that's a pro for those who'll like this game. Nice graphics. Also, the game mostly stays true to history books - if some particular ship had sunk in WWII, it will sunk in this game too, no matter what you'll do to protect it.
My advice - buy "Secret Wars". It's much more entertaining.

Evoland 2 is a charming experience, but ultimately falls victim to its own premise of recreating the older style of games.
Many parts of this game are just tedious. One dungeon in particular, at the mid point of the game, combines difficult platforming, instant death spikes, and disappearing blocks in such a way as to remind the player why such things fell out of fashion in the first place. Other sections simply feature a great deal of unnecessary padding. Meanwhile, though there are RPG mechanics like a levelling system and currency included in the game, it seems largely superfluous much of the time, and there really isn't much advantage to attempting to "grind", as much of the game requires neither currency nor stats.
That said, the music isn't terrible, though it also isn't memorable. The characters are reasonably endearing, though mostly one-note. The story, while not breaking new ground, nor particularly deep, is harmless and relatively innoffensive. So, all in all, it does live up to its legacy insofar as that it is a thouroughly mediocre game, that manages not to do anything spectacularly wrong, but just doesn't offer much payoff for the amount of work it expects the player to put in.
It's just that, ultimately, that in itself winds up being disappointing. First of all, because the first Evoland really was quite creative and unique at its time, and it's a shame that the sequel seems to rest so heavily upon its laurels. Secondly, however, because so many other games have managed to take "old-school" gameplay, and mix it with "new-school" design principles to make some pretty amazing games, and it is therefore disappointing to see how little Evoland 2 does, compared to how much more it could have done.
Personally, I'd rate this game as a "Bargain Buy"...that is to say, pick it up on a good sale, or next time it's in a Humble Bundle, but there's probably something better you could find at the full retail price.

This is a turn based tactics game where you control (after about 30 hours gameplay) up to 5 heroes who walk between nodes on a world map in a very linear way and follow a more or less entertaining story (At least I found some of the dialogue mildly enjoyable). Some nodes are cities where you may learn skills, buy equipment, and get/perform quests, other nodes are quest nodes that may sometimes be skipped. Most of the time is however spent in  hexagon based maps fighting various bad guys.
The game has a lot of skills and stats that you may experiment with, but mostly it makes little difference what you chose to skill up (For spells any nuke will do, some early bosses are weak to fire, but it makes little difference for most enemies, a healing spell is pretty much required, you will alternate between those two and auto attacks for the whole game), and as most stats and skills are needed in the end anyway the customization adds little depth to a shallow game.
The major problem with Blackguards is that fights are mostly based on luck. Want to attack someone? Well, usually you have a 90% chance to hit (not bad, but that's as good as it gets unless someone is knocked down), but if you use a more powerful attack it might drop down to 85%, 70%, or 60% (based on dodge stat vs dexterity I think), further reduced with wounds that are randomly obtained when taking damage (I think your to hit chance can potentially go all the way down to 30%). If you manage to hit at all the damage dealt is then further randomed in a fairly large spread, and rarely it will crit for double damage. The damage is fairly high, so 3-4 good attacks is enough to drop most enemies and heroes.
This means that missing more than a few attacks will result in one of your heroes getting knocked unconscious, and the enemies snowball from there.
It's typically the enemies who get the good dodge stats, so while your heroes will mostly take full damage from anything that attacks them late game, your heroes will miss, miss, miss,miss, and miss some more as you watch them slowly die in frustration.
The game's "difficulty" slowly ramps up as you play. Every encounter is level (in)appropriate, so every fight is a challenge. Since spell damage is fixed your magic users slowly get weaker after their 2 main spells hit level 3. While this makes sense in a way you will never get to be satisfied with how much stronger your heroes have gotten. Enemies have about the same stats and skills and do about as much damage as the heroes do, so fights vary little in practise between various encounters.
The game could still be a mildly enjoyable grind with the above mentioned issues, but clearly the devs were obsessed with making the game into a never ending series of encounters by a power tripping DM trying to make your party lose.
I got through several unfair fights like Running past all the enemies who get to hit you for free for 6 turns to get to the girl before she's killed, shoot a giant tree with 150 hp to death with arrows that each do 1 dmg because it 2 shots everything in melee range, run through a basement filled with traps to get to the guy you need to kill before he gets away, kill the necromancer who's surrounded by unkillalbe skeletons that block your spells and arrows, and many many more. The straw that broke the camel's back for me was the fight against the tiger lilly where one of your heroes is turned against you, you have to run up to a plant that always has a 60% hit chance, is immune to magic damage, every turn one of your heroes is knocked down, and 5-6 tentacles you're not supposed to kill get to attack your heroes freely while blocking off healing spells you might want to cast on the hero being bullied.
I understand that something like this was necessary to make the game interesting, as the fights by themselves clearly aren't. With a different combat system these fights might have been fun, but in Blackguards you will just keep doing the right thing again and again untill it finally works and you get to go on.
So, TL;DR: Turn based fights heavily based on luck, little customization in practise despite the wealth of options available, you get weaker as you keep on playing, and gimmicky fights where the devs metaphorically throw your miss chance and weakness in your face again and again by setting up scenarios that force you into doing stupid things over and over untill the RNG gods decide that you may finally pass. If it sounds like your cup of tea then you will probably enjoy Blackguards, but I did not.

The gameplay can be challenging at times, which is a good thing. Completing certain chapters are really satisfying once you finally complete them. You have to be very precise in your movement in most cases.. and the timing on Bash can be crucial in situations of life and death! And whoever designed the dungeon where gravity plays a huge part, is a genius. Favourite part of the game hands down! Frogs on the other hand..
There's also leaderboards implemented, even for speedrunners! I haven't seen many games do this yet, and it's so awesome to be able to track your time against others without the use of external sources. Big +++ for this!
One of the only negative things I can think of right now is that once you complete a playthrough, you can't play in it anymore if you wanted to get all the collectibles. It does make sense story wise, so warrants for more playthroughs if you were eager for achievements! ;) Oh yeah, achievements. Whoever can legit get the Immortal achievement, even though they're most likely inhuman, deserve all my respect.
I haven't tried playing with a keyboard yet, but I can tell a controller is probably the best choice to experience this game at its best. This goes out to those having trouble with the lack of rebindable keys, although I do understand your pain!
So yeah overall a super big recommendation to play this game, you're missing out if you don't!

Hey guys
This is a review of the oddworld remake. I start with the long version.
So first off i want to say i really love the oddworld series. It was one of the first games i played and the more i played it the more i fell in love with it. The controlls where great the atmosphere was absolutely amazing. The dumb humor i loved every bit of it.
I was really hyped for this remake i thought to myself " This is gonna be gud. The same game with new stuff better graphics this is gonna be amazing.
A couple minutes in to the game i noticed that the controlls just dont work as they did in the original. The tile based movement was gone. Oddworld had a really good reason for this control scheme it worked with the game. The tile based movement was important to predict jumps or enemy movement in such a hard game. U allways knew how you will move. unfortanitly this is gone now. This remake shows perfectly why the original had to do this. It made a hard game fair.
Another thing was the screen based gameplay. If u havent played the original let me explain. In the original u mooved screen by screen it didnt scroll. Remember this is the PS1 it was well capable of sidescrolling. And the perspective was orthogonal for the most part. u could very clearly see when something in the background was right above u. In the remake i feel often that i cant really make out where the enemies in the background stand in relation to me. Are they behind me ? or is he directly above me. I endet up dying alot in the first two hours because i couldnt make out where he is or where i am.
Lets talk about button layout. Why cant i change anything ?. I really want to move with the d-pad this is a precision based 2D Platformer and the DPad just works better. We dont all use Xbox Controllers where the dpad is horrible i use a PS3 controller and i really want to use my dpad the stick feels unprecise and sloppy not to mention the deadzone issues the accidental up jumps and the way momentum works with it. It just feels wrong.
Is this easily fixable ? Yes. Atleast in the control department. I dont know how possible it is but give us a classic controller option. This would help massively. And sidehoping should be turned on standart. Took me while til i saw that.
One last point is unity... Unity time and time again has shown to not be kapable of runing graphicly intense games. Not to say they cant look pretty but they shouldnt be taxing. In the Emu sections where u have to ride the beast and jump around the framerate becomes too inconsisten to make reliable jumps and with the new movement which again is not tile based jumping cliffs becomes a real hassle.
and one last really personal thing. The game looks to bright for me the original seemed much more gritty and somewhat darker all in all. And bloom is a bit overdone
Overall wait a bit til some of these things become not fixed they arent broken but changable.
Short Version.
The old tile based movement is gone which leads to inprecise platforming. The perspective is sometimes really bad when it comes to judging where everyone is in relation to u. And u cant controll this precision based platformer with the dpad nor can u change the controll scheme or button layout. Turn sidehop on or punch youre monitor.
All in all i will give it another shot and i might start to like this remake. The dozens of frustrating deaths do to the new way of controlling the game. The overblooming "personal thing". The portions that are hard because i dont know where the enemy in the background is and the huge problems Unity brings and the way the camera moves somethimes
are just to much for me to bother with it right now.

Update the visuals, keep the controls, add a few fun things if budget/time/scope allowed it. That's all the developers had to do.
As is, New n' Tasty is wracked with poor controls and haphazard button placement. (Throw grenades next to talk? Yes, I might want talk you and save your buns or turn you into gibs. A tough call we all face) The aiming is also equally wonky- to throw left you hit right shoulder. To throw right, you hit left shoulder. But there is also precise directional throwing- which could have been done with a single throw button to hold down, aim with the d pad/analog, and release to throw- you know, like in a ton of other games. Instead, throwing is divided and mapped to FOUR different buttons- each with a limited throw arc. Coupled with how throws are mapped, the simple task of throwing (compared to the original) is turned into a messy ordeal.
Talking is also separated- “Normal” on the analog (Hello and Follow me) and everything else (six other commands- including the important “Wait” and “Look Out” Commands) mapped to different buttons. Again, the original (PS version) had an elegant solution- have them accessed by holding one of two buttons back buttons and press a face button for the command. Simple and fun.
The game also crashes when the pause button is hit. That may be fixed in the future- but it's a terrible way to start out.
I feel sorry for new players who never got to play the original- because Oddworld- Abe's Oddysee is one of the greatest games released in the 90's. It had great in scope, play style, difficulty, and story. A digital download can be found on a few modern consoles and the original PC game can played with a bit of software. Steam also has the original, however it is also finicky, so it may not be an option. Its also on the PlayStation 1- if that happens to be option for you. (Hey, PS2s and PS3s can read PS1 discs)
To see one of the favorite games marred by unthoughtful control mapping disheartens me. Maybe it'll get patched. Maybe not. Not a dev, I'm not sure what they're thinking.
But hey, at least its pretty.

First off I want to start off by saying that this game has potential. It's trying to achieve what No Man's Sky didn't in terms of building and multiplayer support. That's where the similarities end. (Full Disclosure: I played this game for a full 45-50 minutes before deciding to write this review)
Here's the Tl;Dr: If you're looking for a multiplayer version of No Man's Sky with the full polished experience, decent graphics, and no bugs or glitches... Turn back now. This is not the game for you. Here's why:
1. Optimization
I game on an Intel Core i7 6700HQ, 16Gb Ram, Nvidia GTX 970m GPU, and a Samsung 850 Pro SSD. Only when I turned the graphics settings all the way down (No SSAO, FXAA, Minimal textures, the whole gamut) was I able to reach near 60FPS with dips into the low 20's and 30's when there was a bunch of action happening on screen. That's not the worst of it, though. Try to do any quick 180 degree turns or jumping and strafing, and you'll experience frame drops, stuttering, and in some cases, complete game freezes for 1-3 seconds. This game is definitely in alpha stage and will need a lot of polishing and optimization before it will be able to run on anything other than a beefy machine.
2. Glitches/Bugs
I started the game in Tutorial mode, and that is where I encountered my first bug. As with any First Person anything game that I play, I died in the first five minutes. Respawn back in the escape pod that brings you to the planet again only to discover that the med kit and a few other items that I had first time around are now AWOL. This wouldn't be an issue, except that in order for you to progress in the Tutorial, you have to equip those items to finish the starting checklist. Oops. I was ok with this until I realized there were seemingly no other places in the worldspace to pick up another medkit, not even the shuttle depot I had found. With my health and hunger running low, I decided it was time to call it quits on that character.
3. Animations
If you're a perfectionist when it comes to animations such as walking/running/ADS/etc. then you're going to have a lot to complain about. I realize that again, this is an Alpha early release game, and I don't mind cheesy graphics and animations, I know several people that would cringe and say that the animations kill the mood for them.
Conclusion
If you want No Man's Sky only multiplayer with Minecraft-like crafting, then theoretically this is your game if you have the
1. Machine to run it with
2. Patience to wait for patches and updates that may never come (Initial Release Date August 5, 2015)
3. Patience to play with bugs
If you don't have these three crucial things, I would say that this game is not for you.

TL/DR: I REALLY like where this is going, great ambitions and concepts, but I feel it's held back by bugs, wonkey animations and more. Suggest to hold off on buying from now but to keep a close eye on it as it has great potential.
Originally, I eyed this game thinking it'd be an interesting game to check out, little did I know, today (Oct.24.2017) they are doing a 50% off sale so, why the hell not.
Like the description says, Empyrion Galactic Survival is an open world sandbox space game. Now as much as I'd like to recommend it, the feeling of this game feels... off. Might be chalked up to E.A.S. (Early Access Syndrome) but this game is like a overcooked pie, the outside is rough and burnt, but the inside can still be edible and even tasty.
Many complaints I have are pretty plentiful, many are issues the game has overall but some are personal which may not be of any issue to others. To start, there are bugs, ALOT of 'em too. A pretty big one i can point out is bumping into a motorcycle with your jetpack on can cause you to launch across the map like a north korean missile. Luckily this didn't kill me, but is a large nusance which may potentially end at some point with an unavoidable death.
Now along with that issue, there is optimization issues here and there, some pretty janky movement and more. For the more person issues, one that I find REALLY hard to put up with is the animations... those animations... I can understand its state as it is E.A. and most likely these aren't the final animations to be used but I do find them very hard to look past myself. Some of the ones that bother me greatly is the unsynced jumping animation and the very... questionable, reload and firing animations.
A small gripe I have as well is with travelling in planet atmospheres and using warp drives. Now main issue I have is instead of a very smooth transition, letting you see your ship and such warp or enter the planets atmosphere, it goes almost entirely white. Not sure exactly but it seems to be small loading sequences. This can be easily touched up by having a more smooth and natural transition but, I don't consider this to be a deal breaker for me, just personal preference.
I should get into the good since there is ALOT of good and I'd prefer not to tear a game apart that I believe can be an amazing game. Now the main things I like can all be summed up with is its concepts are REALLY interesting.
Some of these concepts such as temperature and radiation levels and needing to shower to clean yourself of contamination is a real interesting feature I don't think I've seen anywhere else. With that, the ships feel more... organic. Unlike another game I play, Space Engineers, the parts you can use and the functionality of many of these allows ships to feel more life like. Many of these details are actually useful, drawers and lockers store supply, showers help with contamination and much more. They even have details to the point of systems like your warp drive and generators giving off small doses of radiation which I love.
One other thing that was wonderful to see was that even though I griped about the white screen when using warp drive, I was still impressed that when I could see again, to find the skybox had changed. Instead of the black and blue space I was around before, I entered an area of space where the star shined red and everything nearby glowed red and felt very violent, this changed how I felt in the world and love seeing detail like this implemented.
There's much more good I could say, scenarios starting you on a space station being attacked by aliens, which are actually humanoid in shape and allowing you to engage in firefights as you make your way to a ship that is still docked to escape. Even having a full market system which even though I haven't tried it myself, gives off the impression that MP servers might have full on user controlled markets like here on Steam.
Probably the longest review that I've written yet, and feel somewhat sad of the tough love I'm giving this game. I can't quite recommend this game to be bought yet but at the same time, these features that are sneaking past the many issues keep me interested enough that I just can't refund this game. Even though I'm saying not to buy it right now, the price might be low enough for some to want to try and if not, I'd highly suggest to click the follow button so you can keep a close eye on this game.
I'm hoping to play some more, fight past the steep learning curve, and hopefully see this game improve to the point I can remove the majority of the negative points in this review and change it to a positive rating. I can tell Eleon Game Studios IS on the right path but I'm sorry to say that I just see myself recommending this game as of yet.

Dear the majority of those who have submitted negative reviews, look at the game in a full picture.
Gloria Victis has been in the making since early 2012, beginning with an already upgrading, and new system. Knowing that the team has been working on this, extensively, with more updates, new factions, and more land, you can't deny the amount of effort that they have put into the game. The graphics are beautiful, and I sometimes even stand in the middle of a forest, or swamp, and look at the magnificent detail. GV has outperformed many MMOs, and even being in Unity, that's even more outstanding.
Another part of the game that also surprises me is how they've introduced the story, so far, with the two factions, The Highlanders and The Ismirs. They made a description for them, describing their part and how they have come to be in Stoneholm, a continent divided with different control points, and environments. Many people can come over, and assist with attacking, and it feels like everything is so action pased. Although, knowing how large the map is going to become, and the population, expect alot more than just your average gameplay on any MMO. (even though their is lag, it is because of the large amount of players at one point, but this is only temporary and is unlikely)
None of this could have been achieved without the developers, and the assistance of the community. Unlike other games, the developers continue to improve on a game such as this, and don't let it rot like DayZ or Rust. I don't mean to bash on any other games, but Gloria Victis shines above them on many different terms.
You should get this game as soon as possible; you will not regret it.

I believe that games are an alternative medium for story telling, in a way that books are not capable of. The immersiveness that an interactive game puts one through places high standards on what one is willing to expect when playing through it.
Freebird's original game/novel To the Moon sets a very high bar in terms of story telling and the emotions it evokes for a simple game, which Finding Paradise once again uses the immersiveness of the video game/visual novel genre to craft an exquisite story
Understand that is its MAINLY a story driven game/novel that has puzzle elements imbedded within it.
the puzzles are nothing much, taking a few clicks here and there to solve.
if you are a person looking for a more stimulating puzzle challange without a need for a story then this game/novel is not for you.
for the bookworms like me, It is an exquisite visual novel, crafted in a fashion that is only achievable via the medium of interaction.
Placing you in the middle of it all, and having you follow the carefully crafted character creation, it brings together elements of animation, music and interaction to once again craft an unexpecting climax with a bittersweet conclusion.
the music is fantastically crafted to suit each moment, drawing upon old themes from previous games/novel as well as playing specific tongue-in-cheek jokes.
this game/novel itself is a roller-coaster ride of emotion, that would perhaps leave one with feelings of bittersweet love at the end of a long journey.
For those who are looking, savour the time to play this game/novel and do not rush through it. the story itself needs time to sit and sink into you, just like any normal story building a good plot.
One would have thought that To the Moon has pulled all the punches, and I was feeling rather fearful as to its ability to pull the same sort of emotional heartstrings as the previous game/novel did. But not this story.
Taking elements of the previous game/novel and building upon it, they have manged to craft a new story, plot and climax based on the same universe and some recurring characters.
As a story, I love it for its unique flavour of perspective that it provides, and specific questions that it tries to evoke in the player, just like every good story does.
Enjoy playing through the game/novel, and I hope that you'll be able to find some part of your own personal paradise by answering some of the questions that this game/novel evokes.

I'm writing this review really just because I feel like I owe it to the game and the developer, less as an actual recommendation to anyone in particular. If you have not played To the Moon, then you should start with that one. If you have, then you probably already know if you want to play Finding Paradise.
To the Moon was about a very sad-happy story of two people for the most part. Finding Paradise, while starting with pretty much the same premise, takes a bit of a different direction. It's really not about the people who you interact with in the game, but more about what the game has to say in general about certain aspects of life. As a result, it may not make you cry over the story like To the Moon did, but it may actually have even more lasting implications for your own life. At least it does for me. When I think of the first game, I feel sad while I recap the story of fictional characters in my head. When I'll think of Finding Paradise, I'll probably think of the lessons it taught me about my own life.
I've been playing tons and tons of games for way over 20 years now, and it's really weird to say that one of the best and most important game series is made in RPG Maker of all things. But it's really hard to think about any more meaningful games in my life than Too the Moon and Finding Paradise.
Huge thanks to Kan Gao for his work, I can't wait for the next one in a couple of years. And also thanks to Laura Shigihara of course, for adding to another absolutely beautiful soundtrack.

**SINGLE PLAYER REVIEW ONLY**
I bought this game very nervous of what the expect. I mostly wanted the Modern Warfare 4 Remaster, but since I got this thought I may as well give it a try regardless of the negativity it has recieved. I went in with low expectations and it turned into one of my new favorite games.
Story: The story is pretty straight forward; save the Earth from an enemy looking to take it over. But I felt like it was more than that because the story telling in this game was great. It felt like the story for this game could be a far off future when we can finally accomplish space travel on the large scale. I connected with the characters and was deeply saddened as the storyline progressed further. It should be noted that I love science fiction and this game made me feel like I was playing a blockbuster science fiction movie.
Gameplay: The gameplay is pretty standard and plays like any other Call of Duty game or FPS for that matter. The guns though were something that stood out for me. As much as I love science fiction, I am always concerned when I play a new sci-fi game when it comes to weapons. I don't like it when weapons go to futuristic that they don't seem realistic, but I don't like when weapons don't make a large enough jump from modern weapons to make them feel futuristic enough. This game hit a great balance of projectile and energy weapons with keeping them realistic looking. There are many space battle opportunities in this game as well where the player will pilot a Jackal and get in dogfights in space. At first, this was a lot of fun and I enjoyed it. Unfortunatly, after the fourth or fifth time, it started to feel like a chore and I didn't enjoy them as much anymore. I didn't outright dislike them, but the combat felt very slow, and I felt more disconnected with the characters and the story during those moments. Some of these missions are optional, and though I chose to do every one of them that I saw on the map, this obviously doesn't need to be the case for you. The game has a few moments where stealth is very much needed to complete a mission or get through an area easier. Though it isn't really required, going loud in these areas can be difficult due to the increased number of guys that show up all of a sudden. The stealth was nice to break up the run and gun, but was not necessarily implemented the greatest; but hey, it works.
Graphics and physics: I'm combining these too since they are both short. I played this game maxed out in 4k, so needless to say I thought the graphics were amazing. Some of the space scenes looked as good as some I have seen in movies, if not better. The physics were done much like any other game so they were nothing ground breaking, but there were some space missions such as one on an asteroid where the asteroid is spinning and it made me feel like I was on a giant moving rock. Now maybe this doesn't fall under physics, but the way it made that entire mission play, felt like physics were at play at all times even if they really weren't.
Conclusion: If you are looking for a good science fiction FPS, and are only looking for a single player story line to play through, then this is your game. I would highly recommend it to anybody looking to play this for single player only. I will not comment on multiplayer as I am one of the few that buys Call of Duty games for their single player and not multiplayer. Maybe that is stupid to some, but I have never been big on multiplayer in any game therefore it has never been my focus. Single player is what this game does do great though. My recommendation is to pick this game up on a sale as the single player campaign can be a little on the short side and definitely isn't worth full price just for a short compaign, but it's worth a play through at some point.
9/10 I will replay through this again for sure.

There are things I don't understand about Styx.
First of all, it's a Cyanide game that doesn't suck. WHOA! Holy crap. Vive la France! I'd say that all is forgiven, but the rest of their catalogue still makes that completely impossible.
Another thing I don't understand is why so many stealth games are basically about avoiding interaction. Wouldn't it be a million times more satisfying to play with a world and mess with its people from the shadows, instead of just crawling behind them?
I feel like I'm actively trying not to engage with the world, and it's made so much worse by the fact that probably the best thing about Styx is its level design and its art style. The world is gorgeous, and Styx the goblin thief is super neato, but it's a world that's basically there NOT to be touched, if the post-mission XP rewards are anything to go by.
And that's ♥♥♥♥ed up. That's a stealth game convention that we really need to move past. It doesn't have to be a murderfest, but at least let us screw with these people! Let's change their routines, let's pour something awful in their coffee, let's put some itching powder in their armor plate. Pull some pranks. Slap 'em on the♥♥♥♥♥ Just SOMETHING, other than walking past them.
One of the games half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempts at variation comes in the form of some very nasty bugs (unusually for Cyanide, I'm actually referring to insects) that are only sensitive to sound, so of course the way you beat those is by just moving REALLY slowly past them. I appreciate the inherent malice of challenging me to see how bored I have to be to willingly commit suicide by pest, but let's be real here, it's just a bad feature that's even less fun than sneaking past the oblivious generi-knights, the pissy orcs, and arguably quite badass-looking spellcasters.
Pound for pound it is a good game though. I'll recommend it. It's Cyanide, so you know things are gonna be a little off. The camera and the controls aren't exactly spot on, but they're surprisingly serviceable, and I've enjoyed myself so far.
... But I keep wishing I could engage with the world a lot more. I have vastly more fun killing guards than I do walking past them. It's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ idea that you can't have fun and be hidden at the same time, and I would've liked to see Styx forego that. At some point, someone has to understand that a stealth game should be about getting away with a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥unnoticed, rather than just passing through.
Once we get past that, we'll talk about all those stupid collectibles aimed at anal retentives with no desire to be entertained. Those suck too. If you want people to roam your world and see what you made for 'em, make it worth their while - don't simply rely on gamer OCD. It's being sloppy when you should be creative.
Finally, I just want it on the record that I dig that the plot is (initially) about stealing a tree, whose sap is basically heroin ("ember", wink wink, nudge nudge, knowadamean?) which is also the internet, because it is heroin that lets you hear peoples thoughts - Pretty much exactly like Facebook. TL;DR: The actual GAMEPLAY REVIEW is at the bottom of this post.
A really solid stealth game that i do enjoy a lot. I cant really understand some of the negative reviews here
( i think the game had mixed reviews when i bought it. Nice to see that has changed).
Due to that i just want to point out issues others had and what i think about them.
1. - The graphics
The game sure looks a bit older than it should, given it was released in 2014. But what it lacks
textures shaders and whatnot does not outweight the beautiful atmosphere of the tower. This depends on everyones
individual taste though i guess. I can see the "dungeon" like levels looking a bit too much alike, thats a bummer.
2. - The AI
That one is a bit tricky, the AI is in no way smart and thus lets you lure it into traps if you know how to do it. But i
think thats we wouldnt want that to be any different, as luring/dividing and killing enemies is what a stealth game is
all about. If the AI would make any sudden moves or not walk in a patern the game would be infuriating and killing an
enemy may almost be a question of luck. Sometimes the AI acts really weird though, doesnt go after you after
you made a sound, though clearly stating it heard you. On other times they see a corpse they shoulsnt see.
This however comes down to my major flaw with this game, bugs.
3. - The Bugs
I encountered numerous bugs in the game, that may make it unenjoyable.
One example would be that, when you load a game (e.g. quick load after you died) corpses may glitch through the
ground, eventually falling into the next floor and alarming the guards. Doesnt happen too often though.
What really bugged me was the fact that killing enemies "by accident" sometimes didnt work that well. as soon as
they find a corpse they get suspicious and draw their weapons. A work around is to send your clone out. As the AI
will suspect him as the evil doer, kill him and remain uncautios thereafter.
4. - The Controlls
This one is minor, as you get used to it. I do not know wther the game is a console port or not, but it sure feels like it.
I guess playing it with a controller would have made things better. Other than that its sometimes hard to pull of a
difficult jump onto an edge, but that felt more like a challange to me and ususally worked out after a few times.
Looking at the gameplay it is a bit annoying that you cannot "round" cover while hanging off a ledge. That was
especially surprising (and disappointing) as you cant do that while in normal cover.
THE GAMEPLAY REVIEW

The Game feels (disregarding the facts above) super great. If you enjoy stealth games i can really recommend this
game. The atmosphere and (VERY vertical) overall leveldesign of the tower is super great, despite the rather old
graphics.
The Gameplay itself offers some fresh touches to the game that sure was a little... Say "influenced" by Dishonored.
Due to your small sice you can hide under tables some shelves and other unique cover. Bumping into smaller Objects
around makes sounds and may alert guards, forcing you to move really cautios.
There is also the ability to create a seperately movable clone of yourself, to lure, distract, or even kill your enemies.
As an example you can make some noise and attract a few guards with your clone, make them chase you to another
room where your true self awaits to drop a chandelier onto the whole bunch.
The story so far is okayish, but ended in a really nice plot twist that may result in a really good story. Unfortunately
im not far enough yet to say more about this. Oh and you can collect♥♥♥♥♥♥and do sidequests, thats nice.
(Note that i have no idea about the combat system as i play on the difficulty wo direct combat,
e.g. get detected = your dead)

So should you buy the game?

If you do like stealth games and dont mind the issues above, thats a YES
(you may want to wait for a sale though, the game drops to 5€ (EU))

I have requested a refund for this game, which probably will not be granted because I have played for more than 2 hours, but here's hoping.
My advice to ANYONE who picks this up: DO NOT PLAY SURVIVAL FIRST. Go into creative, spend less than 2 hours there doing as much as you possibly can involving ships WITH a friend, and find the gamebreaking issues that make it unplayable before it's too late.
The reason I say this is that if you play survival, you'll play on a planet. Planets are generally functional. Generally. Don't dig too deep, or you'll fall through, but that's about it.
Then, after SEVERAL HOURS of gameplay, you
have enough resources to
build a ship. You'll learn that planetary flight isn't very functional. The only thrusters that fire automatically are the ventral thrusters. No other thrusters will fire automatically when facing into the ground, so if you roll left/right or pitch up/down while in flight in planetary gravity, your ship will simply start to fall.
This often leaves your ship behaving extremely unpredictably, as you're trying to compensate by firing the thrusters yourself and causing momentum to build up which the game interprets by making your ship drift in various directions unpredictably until you simply turn the power off.
Have no fear, though! The game has
You can crash your ship directly into the ground as much as your heart desires, in survival mode, and nothing will ever happen to it. Won't lose even 1% HP. You and your friends will also clip through a moving ship and fall out if you're not immobilized in a seat.
This game might be something some day, but right now, it's just a planetary scavenging simulator, and a really poor one at that. Planetary flight is completely dysfunctional, manned-vessels are also fundamentally broken and unplayable, and if you don't learn all of this within 2 hours, you'll regret it.

The reason I bought this game some time before was that unlike space engineers it tended to actually pretend to have survival focus from the start - more emphasis on planet visuals, combat, factions etc.
Why I don't play this game now is that they failed to change or even added certain drawbacks during recent patches:
- Graphics optimization. Meeting dusk/dawn in jungle might require some nuts from your pc, much more so than the actual action provided by the jungle could require the player's qualities.
- Atmospheric immersion. Despite the decently drawn planetary environments, most of the things the player builds look like lego toys, even if they look more or less serious, the combat still makes it look like toying with blocks.
- Weapon balancing from bad to worse. Well, there's always an issue of realism vs game balance, BUT having an assault rifle with a firing range of a flamethrower in vacuum is harassment to logic.
- New start system - the character just used to fall with emergency supplies and survival set. Now the character is doomed to find a cabin in the middle of nowhere with just what is needed for the starting base.
- Aliens, despite being okay drawn, still look artificial, which is a result of combination of their stiff model animation, limited ai, and the surrounding areas.
So all in all it is supposed to be better than space engineers by immersion or than 7dtd by crafting in theory, while in reality the immersion factor is only a couple of times you look at the planetary scenery and the crafting advantages are all in a promise to go to space and different planets - while doing all the same there.

Blackguard is a very fun turn-based strategy game. You will come to love most of the characters. The dialogues are simply amazing. Your party members are exactly what you expect your most extreme type of role-playing friends to be during a sesstion of a tabletop game like DnD.
"I AM A MAGICIAN OF LOVE. I WILL SEDUCE EVERYONE!" and then you get into battle because he fails all of his seduction.
Everyone takes it to the extreme. One is hella dumb, funny and racist toward the elves. Another is just always sarcastic and mean most of the time.
That covers most of the story telling. Let's get into the gameplay.
THE
DARN
THING
WILL
TRY TO BREAK YOU.
The hex-based map is great.
The game using the "automated diceroll" system as if you were playing an actual table top is great.
Problem though is that the other side cheats way too often for you to really enjoy the combat.
Somes of them are insanely easy.
And the next one is just demanding you to either get the spell to work on a 50% rate at the start of the turn with the follow up attack from your friends hitting everything on the first turn or you might as well retry the battle.
And to make it worse. Everything, except for some of the weak fodders, are either as strong as you or much stronger than you. It's funny the first few time you see a lizardman sniping your team with a javelin better than your archer can shoot someone with his bow but after about 2 to 3 hits, it stops being funny because they deal much more damage than you do and even has additional effects until you manage to get to a certain point where you can finally learn your cheap spamming moves too just to destroy everything.
And "HARD" mode isn't even hard. It's just frustrating and cheating. Usually, in a strategy game, repeating the same failed strategy oftens lead to the same fail result. However, in Blackguards, repeating the same strategy is what you do until you finally roll enough damage and hit rate to actually carry out that strategy, and that the environment isn't messing with you.
RNG governs everything. Mobs are predictable but overstat as heck that they will deal your critical-like damage on a normal hit so you just have to retry over and over until the 35% hit rate on them actually miss instead of hitting 3 times in a row while your 90-95% are still missing over and over, or dealing minimal damage when it actually hits, leaving the mobs with 1 hp.
Because this game offers no between-combat regen so sometime, delaying a battle to 60 turns + is necessary although you can end it in 7. It wasn't challenging. It was just the game forcing me to repeat the "Whole map kite" for the next 10 minutes just to full heal the whole team. At normal or so, this isn't always necessary. I can try with 75% health and mana on the next map. On hard? You better be full or you might as well restart the whole battle chain.
But that's really the annoying part and it can easily be somewhat remedied by just setting the mode to "Normal" unless you're ready to go through pointless self-torture that makes you want to ragequit because of a single crit or a slip on an overstat mob forcing an instaretry. Other than that, I see nothing wrong with this game. People often makes fun of the voice acting but it's only horrible on the trailer. The in-game voice acting is so much better and really fit the situation when the characters are trying to be mean or sarcasting, which isn't really something you can see on the trailer.
I also recommend getting the big pack. The artbook is simply amazing.

I never really liked the whole "Yes/No" recommentation. A game shouldn't be decided if it is loved or hated solely based on other's experiences but rather on if it is appealing to you. With that said I gave it a Yes since even though it does has it flaws, I personally enjoyed it. Now to the nitty gritty part.
What this game is (if you couldn't tell already) is a turn based DnD style type of game and it is heavily based on DnD mechanics. For those that don't know DnD, Here is a quick breakdown on how combat works: Roll for initiative (i.e. RNGesus happens at the beginning of each battle to determine who goes first), move characters around the map and you can do an action like attack, cast a spell, drink a potion or place a trap. Or you can just wait until your next turn. This process continues until every character has made a move/action. Then it is back to the top and you keep taking turns and making actions until either you or the enemy is dead.
Now, keep in mind that this game is RNGesus based and that even though you have 90% chance to hit that doesn't mean you'll hit..just like DnD.
To keep this short...also my spelling is bad...
Pros: Interesting characters, combat is intuitive and changes per environment (i.e. environment interaction), very challenging scenarios (for those that like to get kicked around).
Cons: Very challenging scenarios (for those that want to get spoon fed victory), Character customization is limited (you can create a rouge/mage or a hunter warrior but you can't create something like a palidin where you hit people in the faces with maces and then cast cure. Reason being is that wearing heavy "Metallic" armor takes away your ability to cast spells and regen mana. This is a con for me because I wanted to roll a palibro). Keep in mind if you do a split class like rouge/mage you will have more skills/abilities however you won't be as strong as a pure rouge or a pure mage.
