A welldone remake of the 1997 cult classic. This remastering in a fully new engine features the same singleplayer experience from back in the day with some great additions. You can now quicksave and -load wherever you are. After initial doubts that this would make the game too easy, that is not the case at all. If anything it makes this already great game much more enjoyable by taking away tediousness due to scarce checkpoints. It still holds its difficulty in executing a perfect sequence of actions to progress in the level. Other new features include a remastered soundtrack, global leaderboards with time challenges, Steam achievements and full controller support (allthough I did encounter a couple parts where the buttom prompts in tutorial messages were still keyboard buttons eventhough I switched the input mode to controller). I had no problem setting up a Xbox One controller for this, allthough rebinding buttons isn't an option unfortunately (maybe through configfiles). One small detail I really like is that even for controller input there is a button dedicated to quicksaving and -loading. More games should have this!
All in all, Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty is a fantastic new version of a great game. If you've never played Abe's Escape, it's still very playable and enjoyable even in 2015 and still sits up there in the Trial&Error genre with others like Prince of Persia or Limbo.

If there is one game that brings back the good old days of gamming this is one that will always comes up my mind. Oddworld: Abe`s oddisee, defnetly the remastered version, so far, is living up to the original with great graphics and a satisfying taste for this classic of the industry.
Im more happy to see that 2015 is becoming the year of rematers and so far very good games like homeworld and Grim Fandango are coming with evrything they`ve got and more and to show that no matter how old a game is, if it is good, it will live long before its time !
Now they just need to make a remaster of Sacrefice and I`ll be able to say that 2015 was good year for games.

The land is calm again as there is a tournament being held. I am a watcher at the border to our enemies territory now, at the Mines of Dunfen. How long will the calm remain? Will I live to see tomorrow?

The graphics are for the most part the same as before. There are a few more parts with extra effects which felt kinda refreshing (and funny). I absolutely adore the graphics since forever, so this was a plus for me.
The soundtrack is as good as in TTM, maybe even better. I don't know how Kan+Laura do it, but you mostly don't even realise the bgm, you just kinda swim in it. It feels natural for it to be there. And ofcourse Laura went all out and gave us a song which I'm starting to like more then Everything's Alright (please don't hurt me ^^)
The story... we again jump through a dying man's life to learn about his wishes. And while it is not that emotional this time (still lost it :) ), the story feels more solid and relatable. I really liked all the main characters and understood them. Not understood them as in "I've heard of Aspergers, oh so they are", but really understood them. So while the story is not as tragic as in TTM, it hit me harder after my 2nd/3rd time watching it. And it got me really thinking the last few days, I guess I have to re-evaluate some parts of my life. In this regard I wanna Kan Gao for this game from my heart, because games (movies) that change the way you think are the most important ones.
This game is definately a must play for every To The Moon fan and for everyone else I would just say, you should play both games (+ the extras).
For me it could replace To The Moon as my most favorite game of all time. I spent hundreds! of hours on YouTube watching TTM stuff and I have no doubt it will be the same for FP. Until Kan Gao will hit me with his next masterpiece.

to play (or at least watch on YT) the prequel to this one: "A Bird Story".
It tells one episode out of Colins earlier life, which gives some nice little background to him and makes you understand him more.

I have not yet heard anyone saying this: This game is relatable. And I'm not talking in metaphor, I'm talking literally relatable. Once upon a time, I too once had similar experience.  Back in Korea when i was 8 years old, I was a lonely little kid who had no friends, and I resort to my imagination to escape from reality and loneliness. One day while i was walking home from school, i stumbled upon a dragonfly with broken wings..  I took this dragonfly home and made him into my friend. I would take him to my make-belief fantasy world and we would be going through adventures together.
One day, this dragonfly died... He was my first and only friend.  Although he no longer existed physically, I turned him into my imaginary friend with the remaining memories i had of him.  I imagined him to be a half boy half dragonfly who was around my age. We would talk to each other causally. My entire elementary to middle school experience was only memories of me playing with my dragonfly friend alone in the corner.  He was there for me when i was being bullied. He was there for me when i was eating alone in an empty classroom. He was there for me when nobody picked me to be in their team when there was a soccor practice.  He was one true friend that comforted me in time of loneliness and depression. He taught me to be strong and be positive about life.
Highschool came. I started making real friends. I spent less and less time with my dragonfly friend.  I start to realize that everything i experienced and learned from my dragonfly friend was from myself.  But i didn't want to let go of him... I learned to be a strong person because of him.  It's because of him that I was able to embrace the reality and make real friends.  But as time goes by, i knew i eventually had to let him go... We promised each other that we will see again one day... Perhaps once i graduate from college and find a job, i will meet him again and tell him all about my life.
However, i soon learned the cruelty of adulthood.  Your imagination isn't as strong as when you were young. I realized that once i let go of him, there was no getting him back.  There are few times i wanted to talk to him again, but my imagination only created a dull empty version of my dragonfly friend.  It was definately not the same...  I wanted to tell him of my current situation; both hardships and happiness i experienced... But I can only confirm that he is gone forever and i can never get him back.
Kan Gao, i don't know if this is the similar experience you had. I dont think i've ever heard of a story so personal that it pierced through my heart and gave me flashback of my dragonfly friend.  When i tell this story to my family or friends (i even wrote stories about this in my english class), nobody understood me.  I thought nobody in the world can understand the strong emotion i had over non-existing friend.  I went nuts and cried so much while playing this game.
SPOILER:

Thank you again Kan Gao. Thank you so much. I realized even though i lost my close friend, I am not alone in this world. You have given me inspiration to move on and not give up at the current situation i am in.  I don't know if my message will get to you... And i really hope it does. I am also very curious whether this is based on your personal story, as it is so scarily close to mine.

If you enjoyed To the Moon, you're pretty much guaranteed to like this game. You take on a new perspective as you spelunk into the memories of Colin, and see the life he's lived. This game is filled with lovable characters, nostalgia, tearjerker moments, all set to a beautiful soundtrack. Fair warning, you'll probably cry(a lot).

Are you ready to cry?
Well, you don't have a choice. In the best way, of course.
Finding Paradise sees Kan Gao re-connect superior storytelling to a point-and-click genre and revitalising it in the same way that To The Moon did. Beautifully attached with poignant comedic moments, emotional peaks and heartbreaking valleys, Finding Paradise will fly a paper plane right through your heart and leave you wanting more, more, and more. Whether you're in love with the hauntingly poetic soundtrack, the words dancing on the screen or the genuine affection for the characters in the game, just like the clouds in the ocean blue sky, you never want it to go away.
Finding Paradise is another wonderful addition to the genre, and one that sticks with you even after you finish it, and that is just scratching the surface for what makes the game undeniably one of the best of the year. A late addition, but no doubt simply worth every asking price.
11/10 I have been waiting for this for years.Highly recommend it if you're a fan of RPG or telltale games
A fiction, a horror, a tragedy, a true happy ending, and above all, a love story that we tell ourselves, our lonely self.

Finding Paradise picks up where To The Moon left off, with Dr. Rosaline and Dr. Watts returning as Sigmund Corp employees to once again, fulfill the wishes of a dying man.
As a huge fan of To The Moon when it came out a long six years ago, and a slightly smaller fan of A Bird Story, I picked up this game once I realised it was out. Kan Gao delivers another memorable and stirring tale, along with the familiar charming visuals and poignant music (Piano and Cello this time!). Laughs, dread, tears, wonder, surprise and even horror do not begin to scratch the tip of the emotional iceberg that is this story-driven experience. That said, while To The Moon was powerful and arguably melodramatic, Finding Paradise finds paradise in moments of thought and reflection, so those looking to relive the tear-jerking journey of the former will find themselves, only slightly, disappointed.
Nonetheless, I give this game
tears.

This game bizarrely does get better the further in you get.  I changed my review to a thumbs up, although my original criticisms still apply so I've left them below.
This could have been a fantasitic game but is mostly just super tedious.  It has moments of brilliance but every step of the way is so padded out that the game just crawls.  Some gripes in no particular order (that more or less all could have been fixed with minor playtesting).
-All minigames drag on for about 3 times as long as they should.  The bullet hell shooter game was fun for a few levels, then went on for a MILLION more levels with no new enemies or weapons.
-90% of chests hold items that are nothing.  Literal "collectible stars" that don't serve any purpose.  A million healing goops that you need to travel all the way to a crafting witch to turn in to potions (but you can only hold one potion so you have way more goops then you will ever need).
-The card game is kind of fun, but there are 71 cards and collecting them all would be a nightmare.  You get some from playing the game against random townspeople, but there is no way to see how strong an opponents deck is until you go into the match and it's pretty difficult to win against a better deck.  Later on you start getting card rewards for completing quests which is pretty terrible if you've already written off the crappy card game...
-Everything takes forever.  At times the puzzles are clever and you feel smart solving them.  This is an impressive accomplishment for an adventure game.  Unfortuntely everything is slow and clunky.  You need to use your party's abilities to solve environmental puzzles, but using these abilities takes time to charge AND time to recover.  So 80% of your time is spent waiting.
-I can't stress enough how much of your time is spent walking from place to place or waiting.  Someone asks for an item and you need to scroll through you inventory to give it to them.   Traveling back and forth through time requires walking to a piller thing at set location inside zones on the world map, going to the piller, watching the stupid wormhole cutscene and appearing in the new time.  You can't even choose the time you want, it just cycles you though eras, so if you are in the past and want to go to the future you have to watch the stupid wormhole scene twice.  This could have been done so much easier if the pillers were accessed directly from the world map with one click (or even better wherever you want from you inventory).
-When giving me the option to name a character in the middle of a cutscene, confirm that I want to name the character.  If you are just clicking through dialogue because you read fast you will just automatically accept the default name every time.  Naming my characters swear words was the one joy I had in this game and I had to keep "Fina" because I missed the naming prompt.

I'm pretty torn on this game, I wish there was a neutral review option. I think as far as stealth games go this is a great game, and despite the many frustrations I had with it I kept coming back to finish because there is fun to be had, (hence the thumbs up) but by the end I was ready to be done.
Where to start...this game requires extreme patience. This means no running through guards, taking the shortest or most direct route to an objective, or getting into every fight you can. In fact I felt the game punished you for doing so, as direct combat is not only not in your favor (ever), but extremely boring and lackluster. When you are confronted by a guard you get into a sort of duel with them, you have to then click to parry at just the right time. After you do it a few times it becomes the worst thing and you will try to avoid combat altogether. In some instances you will simply be shot and killed by a crossbowman and it's over. Despite my best efforts I did find myself dying alot, not just in combat but to bad edge detection. Sometimes I would fall right off a ledge when I wanted to grab it, other times I would pull myself right into a torch and burn to death when I just wanted to hang. Then I would get frustrated and just try and sprint through a level, which would lead to another miserable death by the guards. In some instances the game would bug, and a guard would discover a dead body that wasn't there, only to alert the guards to come look at the invisible corpse and find me hiding nearby, ruining everything.
The levels are absolutely massive, which is a good and bad thing in my opinion. I felt like the game was presenting you with a set of problems and saying "OK figure this out however you want, you have lot of options!" While I certainly appreciate the fact that there are many roads to get to the same destination, it just dragged so bad. I mean this game is way too long for what it is...I think this is seriously my biggest gripe. This is a stealth game with very limited character customization, so you know what you are getting yourself into early on. After the first 2-3 hours in you get it. This does not need to be a 15-20 hour game. The story itself only gets mildly interesting after a major plot twist about halfway through game. So making it longer just made it boring the more I played. Had it been shorter I think the experience would have been more memorable, but there just isn't enough substance here for a 15 hour playthrough, you're sneaking around not grinding to lvl 99 so you can fight Emerald Weapon.
Anyway, once I learned to have some patience the game was much more fun, I don't feel like you have any other choice when you play this game. You have to be patient and accept that you'll die alot, once you do there is fun to be had. The stealth action can be very rewarding at the end of a long mission were you went undetected, didn't use any items, or were able to hide every dead body. All in all I am glad I played through it and got in on a sale, not sure I would have bought it otherwise. Several of the achievements were also fun and fairly easy to get too if you're into that sort of thing.

If you like stealth games then this is a must have.

Tough but rewarding. This is (luckily in my eyes) a typical The Dark Eye game. If you do not know this RPG system: it's Germany's biggest and probably oldest Pen & Paper RPG system that is still maintained. And as many things from Germany it is deep and complex, but needs a certain degree of dedication.
You will not be able to simply start this game, kill some enemies and have fun. You really need to have a look at the rule system and how all the character values influence your fighting, casting and other skills. The same goes for spending your experience points, if you simply raise a stat here and there you will find the game very hard and probably quit. If you decide what role a character will have and raise the necessary stats and skills for this you will have a much easier time and will be able to enjoy the very complex fight options.
One definitive pro from my point of view are the really varied battle maps. Most maps have unique interactive features that you can use in the battle, like alchimistic tables that will poison bystanders when smashed. Or drawbridges that can be raised or lowered. Or cranes with crates that might smash your heroes from the docks - or the enemies if you position yourself smart enough.
Alltogether it is a clear recommendation for me if you like complex strategy games with RPG-like character development. Do not buy if you look for Diabloesque casual RPGs.

This game gets so close that with a few tweaks it really could have been something special. The combat would be great if it wasn't so RNG dependent. Attacks are more limited by being able to actually hit stuff than they are about causing enough damage. Chance to hit of 65% or lower is normal for everything but a basic melee attack even when you've pretty much maxed out your character's relevant stats and weapon skill, and that 65% is actually more like 30% chance to hit because the percentage shown is just your character's accuracy. Your attack can and will still be parried or dodged half that percentage again.
You have to buff your characters with magic before they're worth a damn, but guess what. The magic has a chance of success too. So until you spend a few thousand points levelling up your mages' stats and getting them a certain ability, the highest chance of success with casting spells is ~85%. But I don't know how many times I had a mage miscast 4-5 times in a row even with a (supposedly) 80-90% chance of success.
You lose more battles because of unlucky streaks of whiffed attacks and spells fizzling out than you do from anything else.
In short, it was fun for a while, but became tedious by the end. It's worth picking up for $5 or so, because I really loved the battle set ups (there's very few boring battles because most try to do something unique and no two are the same) and the style of the game, but there's just too much wrong with it to be worth full price.

After having read 70+ visual novels, If My Heart Had Wings is still in my top 3. A lot of that comes down to personal bias and what appeals the most to me. IMHHW is not a story about epic conspiracies, mind-blowing plot twists or time travel. It's a simple, feel-good story about a school's glider club with some bittersweet drama thrown in.
So why do I like it so much? In short, IMHHW has a ton of emotional appeal. Some of that is because of its stunning visuals and amazing soundtrack. I'm a sucker for bright, vibrant colors and this VN delivers them in spades with some truly gorgeous background art. As for the soundtrack...well, take a listen for yourself:
I still get chills listening to that. It's not just about the music and visuals though. The characters are interesting and some of the routes really surprised me with how much they kept me invested. The endings got some tears out of me, not because they were sad, but because they were powerful. And that goes right back to IMHHW's core strength: it will move you.
It's not without its faults though. The translation is shoddy and particularly bad in Ageha's route (which is a shame because it's one of my favorites). What that means is sometimes you will be confused as to what exactly is happening, but fortunately it straightens itself out enough by the latter half of the route. There is a fan retranslation in progress which should fix these issues, so if you're on the fence, it may be worth it to wait for that. My only other minor complaint would be that the sections explaining how gliders work in detail can be a bit boring if you're not into gliders.
Overall I highly recommend IMHHW if you want a VN that draws you in emotionally. If you're looking for "feels", this is where you'll get them.

Stunning visuals, great soundtrack, smooth gameplay. ~8-10 hours of immense, beautiful fun—Without a doubt one of the best experiences I've had gaming for the past couple of years.

Note:  I've tried to write this review as spoiler free as possible.
It's not often that I write a review about a game but Ori and the Blind Forest deserves recognition.  Ori and the Blind Forest is a platform adventure video game designed by Moon Studios, an independent developer, and published by Microsoft Studios.
Moon Studios wastes no time in opening up the story. Reminiscent to the movie "Up", you are introduced to two characters who you are intended to quickly fall in love with as you join them in their personal story of friendship.  When the bond between these two characters is solidified,  that's when disaster strikes and the true journey and story begins.  This tradgedy is the emotional undercurrent as a quest is formed on how to resolve the crisis at hand and perhaps more.
One can not think back on this game without seeing how Moon Studios took its design influence from Studio Ghibli both in emotional tones and artistic design.  There are also a lot of similarities between this game and Child of Light, Trine, and the grandfather of all platformers Super Metroid.  None of these similarities are a bad thing.  It takes the greatest aspects of all of these and rolls them up into one cohesive design that I imagine I'll be gushing about to my friends for a long while.
Art:   10 / 10
Technically masterful when one considers how their use of lighting can almost give the illusion that the 2d landscape starts to shape into 3d, even with the use of it's parallax.  Particle effects are equally stunning and fitting.  Character animations are top notch which conveys the story and message Moon Studios is trying to tell.
As an illustrator and conceptual design artist myself by trade it's easy to look at your work and always think "I could do more and make this better" but alas,  you have to put your art down and just move on.  The fidelity and quality requires no extra work.  It's polished,  refined and displayed beautifully.  Many games you find yourself rushing to the end but I'd be suprised if anyone is capable of rushing without stopping occasionally to smell the flowers here and soak in all it's artistry.
Music:   9 / 10
Orchestrated and robust in it's depth.  You're being given the full package here which is going to hint at very different emotionally driven states.  Anger,  fear,  sadness and joy can all be found within the music,  but also a sense of wonder and tranquility.
I didn't however pick up on any trendy tunes that I'll remember for a lifetime.  That isn't to say that its necessary for a great soundtrack to be rememberable.  It's a beautiful score that'll leave you in a meditative state and that is the bottom line.
Gameplay: 8 / 10
The game has 2 major methods of character development.  You have 9 major skills such as the ability to jump off of walls as most typical platformers do.  However the game always seems to find a way to keep upping the ante.  You'll have to think fast,  pay attention and occasionally puzzle solve using everything at your disposal without heavily rellying on any particular skill and burning out on repition.
Then you have ability points which can be earned by destroying baddies.  This particular aspect of the game I felt came in a bit weak.  You earn points,  you spend them,  you upgrade your abilities.  Sounds great but you can also find skill points hidden through out the game.  The problem with this is that you could just as easily go back to a previous area and farm creatures to get enough points to get the skills you desire anyways which lessens the importance of finding hidden items.
At it's heart Ori and the Blind Forest is about adventure and the majority of it's obstacles and puzzes are based around how one can get from point A to point B.
Plenty of secrets to be found for the adventurous (not all of which are related to ability points thankfully) which is wonderful considering all the fantastic artwork there is to look at.  The game doesn't introduce a whole lot that hasn't been done already but what it does, it does very well.  Many ideas that platformer gamers might recognize as staples will have particular twists to them and I found just about all of these changes to be a joy.
Conclusion 9.6 / 10
Ori and the Blind Forest should be in every serious video gamers libary.  I have a very broad scope and opinion of what I constitute as art seeing how as I'm an artist.  However,  very few, even those with limited understanding of the philisophical question of "what is art?" will walk away from this thinking "I've just witnessed a masterpiece".  What better praise could I possibly give?

First off, I'd say this game is fun solo but has some major drawbacks... Now onto some more detail....
First impressions were not good;
After initial login, stuck at "loading", alt +f4, everything fine on second run.
If you pick a name that exists, you have to redo all the customisations.
After the character is created, you have two characters show up, if you're curious like me and click the top one, bam, stuck on loading again, alt+f4, everything is then fine, only one character shows up.
Once you're in-game it's not too bad;
Tutorial is fine, controls are not too bad honestly - As long as you have some basic expectations of an MMO, you'll not find this difficult to adjust to at all.
I then spent the next few hours continuously playing, leveling, crafting, learning the game, questing - I enjoyed myself a lot, enough so that I took no breaks for nearly 6 hours!
At this point I decided to purchase the game for my wife, bring her along, this was when things started going down hill...
Now I had someone else with me, we started having to play differently, more tactically etc because of level gaps.
We started noticing what seemed like mini-zones where mobs would disappear for a while then randomly reappear.
When another character was with me, I started noticing how other players animations are all wrong, as if while the game is at 60FPS, the character animations are more like 18 - 24 fps, really jarring when getting immersed into an rpg.
There seems to be some significant lag spikes, now I don't know if the team is struggling for server hardware (with a game like this they could likely find GSP's that would actually sponsor their project and provide heavily discounted or free hardware if that was the case) or if their networking code is severely lacking (from the perspective of someone who spent 8 years writing networking code for popular MMO emulators, it's easy to get it wrong - But not too hard once you get the hang of it, good luck if it's this, it'll come), or if there main server game loop is just single threaded so every time something major happens, the whole thing grinds to a halt - Only the developers know the answer to that.
As there is still no way to give neutral reviews, I'll have to ere towards negative - If this is ever on sale at < £8, I'd say buy it, play alone, and have a good few hours worth of solo fun - If you like PvP, this game is likely going to be great for you as you'll barely notice the other issues (Like it being REALLY hard to find flax as a newbie with no knowledge).
Overall I'd say the game is fun, but for 2 years work, I feel that this game will be massively outdated or supersceded by a rival long before it reaches the point it's polished enough to provide a proper immersive rpg feel.
If you're looking for a proper immersive role playing game to play with friends and family - It has YEARS to go at their current pace.

Like its predecessor, Evoland 2 is an ARPG that plays with the idea of letting you switch between different 'dimensions' - that is, graphical and sound styles mimicking those of the 8-bit era, the 16-bit era, and the modern 3d era. Perhaps more importantly, this is not a purely cosmetical effect, but the in-game version of time travel: A tree that blocks your way in the 16-bit era may still be a small sappling you can easily walk over in the 8-bit era. NPCs can be born or die as you move through the ages, and even entire continents sink to the ground or become available for exploration depending on which time your are in.
Gameplay-wise, Evoland 2 primarily sticks to the classical mix of top-down Hack'n'Slash with puzzle elements that became popular with the early The Legend of Zelda games. However, many regions in the game deviate from this formula - in some caves, the game turns into a 2d platformer, but there also are sections emulating anything ranging from beat'em'up sidescrollers, turn-based tactical RPGs, bomberman, and even a Guitar Hero-style rhythm game. Most of these sections are not very long but nonetheless provide a refreshing alternative to cutting bushes and pushing statues.
Evoland 2's writing is a mixed bag. On the one hand, the time-travelling plot opens some interesting questions concerning things such as whether or not destiny can be changed, or who the protagonist actually is. Sadly, these questions are never really explicitly touched upon, and get overshadowed by the game's often cringeworthy attempt of being funny - I do get that the game is supposed to be a bit of a parody of various video game classic, but how does this justify cramming half-arsed jokes and references to other video games and memes into every other sentence? If I wanted "LE EBIN MAYMAY XDDD", I'd play Borderlands, for hell's sake.
Despite of this, Evoland 2's wild mix of genres and art styles still makes it a fairly enjoyable game  that clocks in at approximately between 15-25 hours, depending on how much of a completionist you are.

This game is an amazing homage to old-school games, combining the experiences of various JRPGs, side-scrollers, shoot 'em ups, tactical RPGs, card games, and even rhythm games into a coherant and engaging story.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. I fell in love with the surprisingly fleshed out story and thought the mixing of so many types of games was nostalgic, awesome, and beautifully executed. The first Evoland was breaking new ground, and this installment was what grew from that soil.
All that being said, this game probably isn't for everyone out there. It wants you to explore and figure things out for yourself, and at some points (few and far between) the mechanics can seem clunky. I myself found that charming, but others may find it irritating. It assumes that you've played similar games, so it won't hold your hand by explaining how everything works.
You will often be returning to places that you've already gone. You will have to suffer through game modes you find difficult or unenjoyable. Some puzzles may stump you to the point where the Internet becomes a necessity. But the experience as a whole is worth the 20 (or less, like during the summer sale) dollars. I will never regret paying full price.

Evoland 2 is absolutely worth its money!
When I started playing it, I expected more of the same as the first Evoland was. But while similar, it is very much its very own game. While the first Evoland was as it name says; a game that evolves playstyle as you play it; Evoland 2 is more of a mashup where you have your main gameplay (but different graphics depending on the time you're in) and get to play a wide variety of game styles depending on the situation.
And does it have a variety! Generic hack & slash, Twinbee style bullet hell, Streetfighter, Puzzle Quest bejeweled, Atari classics, Donkey Kong, etc... Of course with such a wide range of styles, there's a high chance you will encounter a part in the game you don't like. For me it was the rooftop race. But that's what you get with these kind of games, and if you can endure the few parts you don't like, the game is a blast to play through!
The game itself is a lot more massive than the first one, and is a full game on its own, console-worthy. It has adventure, quests, a story, etc... The art is solid and each era is represented well. I've heard people complain about the writing, but personally I think it's excellent for this kind of game. The jokes and references and especially the clichés and self-mocking are just what this game needs. A more serious story would have been bad. There are a few parts that might have benefitted from some improvement, but overall the writing just fits this game.
I finished the game 100% with just a little less than 30 hours of gameplay, although part of that is just collecting everything there is to collect, mostly by playing the card game (which is optional.) Without that, I would say I spent about 24 hours on the actual game. So at full price, you get your hour a dollar worth of gameplay. At discount, this game is a steal and a must have.
I liked the first Evoland, but I'm loving Evoland 2. Can't wait to see if this trend keeps up!

Character creation and development was simple and intuitive. I didn't need to spend time trying to figure out how to build my characters by looking up at numerous guides, so it made me focus on my own game.
All in all, this game was what I was looking for. If you love turn-based combat while being able to have some rpg experience without certain tediousness that comes with rpgs, this would be it.

Blackguards is an interesting concept with quite poor execution. The main problem is that it's built around an obscure role playing system that is both punishing and not fun. It's based on the Dark Eye role playing system in Germany. It's a fairly punishing system that gives too much power to the RNG and not enough to the player.
What do I mean by that?
It's just no fun having a 50/50 chance of casting a spell fail 6 or 7 times in a row and that costing you a battle. It's luck, not tactics or skill, that will get you through battles and luck doesn't make for a fun game. The "tactics" are minimal and your choices in leveling a character are severely restricted because if you don't take certain paths with certain classes you simply won't be able to proceed through the battles. This is the core problem with the game. It's like playing chess with an RNG. It simply defeats the purpose.
The game wants you to play it one way. It discourages experimentation and creativity while demanding that you play it the "right" way with the "right" skill and classes or woe to the user. This isn't a strategy game but more of a puzzle and one that's not fun to piece together. Either you read a guide or you will be forced to start over at some point. That's just really poor design.
As for the other aspects of the game, consider me unimpressed. The voice acting is truly horrible and the plotline is both forgettable and so dumb as to be insulting to the player. You can't rotate the camera and often enemies are obscured. The graphics are decent but nothing fantastic. The videos stutter and tend to happen too often.
When it comes right down to it, there's really nothing redeeming about Blackguards beyond the fact that when you finally uninstall it you'll clear up 17GB of hard drive space to use for something better. You'll get better tactics out of King's Bounty and Divinity: Original Sin than this game plus better exploration and more personality. Save your money, buy those and you'll have far more fun than you would with this game.

This is essentially a tug-of-war with swords in which either player must reach the opposite end of a long stage divided into separate sections while trying to prevent the other player from doing the same. Its appeal is similar to a fighting game, being a contest of skill between two people, and though it is mechanically simpler than almost any fighting game, it is complex enough to allow different kinds of players to approach the competition in different ways. For example, a friend of mine likes to rely on his sword skills to kill his opponent, while I enjoy playing simple mind games to trick opponents into giving me openings to bypass them altogether. The level design also promotes diverse and adaptable play, with wide-open sections, bottlenecks, varied altitude, and properties unique to each stage, such as the conveyor belts in the mine stage, the disappearing bridges in the cloud stage, and the tall grass in the wilderness stage.
In short, it's a simple kind of fighting game that's easy to learn while still rewarding skillful play.

Kan Gao has once again crafted a narrative that transcends its own medium and gives its audience a thought-provoking and meaningful experience.
Finding Paradise is heartbreaking, hilarious, but most importantly, beautifully written and once again contains an acoustic soundtrack that effortlessly accompanies significant scenes across the story. Gameplay is fairly minimal, if a step above the amount of interaction present in a visual novel. Nonetheless, the themes conveyed through the dialogue are timeless and there is not a single line in this game unworthy of its space.
I didn’t cry while playing this game (surprisingly), but the interpretations I gathered along the way and the dilemmas the characters were going through definitely resonated with several aspects of my own life. Gao has stated that this was a rather personal project for him but I believe his talent in storytelling has made it personal for everyone. Thank you for sharing this journey with us, for demonstrating the human experience through these lovely characters, and what it means to live a fulfilling life.
Well done, Freebird Games.

Either way, No way could I recommend this (or actually any COD game since MW3) at full price, and honestly, Even at 50% off I felt I paid too much for this. Campaign is great, it really is. Ori and the Blind Forest:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The Forest experience a dashing storm with extensive lightning and pouring rain...  Sitting on the edge of a rock, a rather obese but cute creature was suddenly disturbed by some sort of bright leaf floating by.
Intrigued, the creature (Naru) moves towards the shinning leaf and as she gets closer the leaf transform into this adorable small species called Ori. Naru adopt our little friend and together they enjoy life picking fruit from trees. Life can be peachy at times!
But one night it all falls apart, food is short and Ori is soon alone.
As you play Ori, you have to collect “Spirit of Light” to get ability points, “Life Shard” to restore your health and energy cell which gives you the ability to destroy rocks that block your path, but also to save the game  at anytime (very useful). At every save points, you will also have access to the Ability Tree where you will be able to spend points to acquire new abilities to help Ori.
You will encounter interesting and challenging foe in this game and you will be glad to draw upon your Spirit of Flame weapon on them. Zap...Zap...Zap.
Not only is the artwork stunning but the soundtrack gives you this unique atmosphere of a beautiful, compelling and moving story... and you fall further and further into this game. Really impressive!

If you are making a lowere-level item and you have higher-leveled crafting, you have a higher chance of getting a better item, between +1 and +6.  The higher your level, the higher the typical bonus.

Regardless, it is still very tactical in its current form... if you forget to parry or move around, you will get killed easily.  Block and parry your opponents attacks, manuever around them, and strike when they are stunned. :)
The devs have a long way to go, but... just take a look at the patch notes.  Take note of how frequent patches are.  Take note of exactly WHAT is updated in each patch.  IMO, it looks like they are on a great path, and I'm very happy to see where this game goes!

The game centers around Final Fantasy-like roaming and Zelda like combat, with nods and references to other games thrown in like seasoning on a steak.
Additionally, entire sections of the game shifts the gameplay completly, from the JRPG at its core- into mimicries of other classic games from a wide variety of genres.
I found these (with a few exceptions) fun and exciting since i hadn't tried some particular genres before, allowing me to explore and try them out for the first time.
My biggest gripe with the game lies in the story
The story is similar to Chrono Trigger in that it uses time travel liberally as a plot device. However, this results in a story that seemingly loses control in the late game and ends up suffering from what i found to be a very anti-climactic ending.
The quality of the gameplay and the skill with which the story entranced me earlier left me expecting truck-loads of closure by the end. Instead I was left even more questions about some particularly important characters (including the main character) backstories and motivations.
The game starts hinting, very early- at some pretty drastic twists that I was waiting for to be revealed in the late-game, but this doesn't happen.  The ending expands slightly based on how many details about certain characters you've uncovered, through talking to NPCs etc. but i was still left with a need for closure. This was not helped by the post-credits cutscene which revealed some events that poked holes in many of the theories I had formulated to answer the questions i was left with. I suppose its quite a bit like Souls-games in the way it requires you to heavily theorize from minute details.
I think it's worth playing for the gameplay and the story, regardless of the anti-climax waiting at the end.
If you do dive into it, be aware that you won't get as much closure as you'll want for alot of the games main characters, which I find sad, since I had grown to like them quite a bit.

It is hard to say whether Wasteland Angel is an homage or a blatant rip off of Tank Girl, but between the comic book styled cut scenes, post-apocalyptic setting, and the saucy heroine, the similarities are too striking to ignore.
The “story” mostly involves "Tank Girl" traveling from point A to point B, rescuing townsfolk from slavers at every pit stop in exchange for fuel to continue on her journey. There are about half a dozen towns in total and each one consists of a couple of waves of attackers and a mini-boss, with a final boss at the very end. This tends to get a tad repetitive, but is mostly alleviated by the sheer glory of the vehicular manslaughter, the shortness of the campaign, and bonus missions that switch the camera to the driver seat and set refreshing new objectives to complete. The bonus missions give a whole new perspective to the game and it is perplexing that the camera view cannot be changed during regular levels, which would give the game a whole new dimension. Liberating towns is pretty easy even on the hardest difficulty, with the biggest obstacle to securing 100% of the citizens being their own tendency to get run over or glitch out once the slaver vehicle is destroyed.
While all of these issues detract from the experience, and could have been easily avoided with a bit more effort, Wasteland Angel is still easy to recommend, if for no other reason than to spend a few hours doing donuts in the wasteland and pummeling bandits with hood-mounted machine guns.

The original Oddworld games (and to a lesser extent, Stranger's Wrath) are amongst my all time favourites. Soulful, creative, imaginative experiences that in so many ways were way ahead of the curve. Even now we barely, if ever, see games with quite this degree of imagination, scope and heart. Oddworld meant something and it still means something. The original game still holds up perfectly save for one flaw: the limited resolution of the Playstation, which makes it difficult to go back and enjoy the richness that it once clearly possessed.
Abe's Oddyssey is a marvel in any context but after all these years, with 2D indie releases easily rivalling AAA output, Oddworld is like a beacon of great artistry and game design. So naturally, a technological upgrade is welcome, a means to keep an otherwise ageless game up to date. Enter New'N'Tasty, not simply an HD remaster but a whole re-make built from scratch, with sidescrolling and other advances bringing it quickly up to date. On the whole it largely succeeds in its ambition but there's a little something lost in the translation.
For the good, it's basically the original game with all new 3D graphics and fluid sidescrolling as opposed to the screen-by-screen swiping of the original. Which means certain sections, those demanding speed and reflexes, have been immensely improved and become all the more gracious. The array of colour and environments never fails to impress and the quality of puzzles, interactions and design remains as unique and inventive as it always was. A lot of the magic has really been recaptured and in places, for an old fan like me, is a joy to behold.
But it's not quite there for me. Odd(Hargh) little choices littered throughout the experience, an array of minor changes that on their own seem meaningless but together strip away some of the wonder and effortlessness of the original. For starters, it's a little too saturated. The grim, colossal monument to industry and the mundane that was Rupture Farms is now more of a nightmare factory. It's more cartoonish and the lesser for it. The game as a whole is a little less "real", a phrase delicately applied to a world filled with gun wielding hand-slug monsters. There's a slight loss of grit in the areas of Rupture farms, an excess of colour that deprives it of some authenticity the original offered. The outdoor areas, Monzaic Lines, Scrabania and Paramonia fair far better and are as memorable now as they ever were. But Rupture Farms isn't quite right and surrounding areas, like the Stockyards, are too empty of the understated nature present in the original game.
Some of the animation too lacks the weight the original brought to the table, Abe slipping and sliding, banging against objects and skirting away from gunfire. It's still there, somewhat but not quite as naturally.
All of which sounds like a big downer on what is a pretty excellent game really. But New'N'Tasty whilst perfectly appealing on its own, also give some attention to how effortless Oddworld Inhabitants made the original game look. What seemed so obvious at the time is now quite unexpected. Who knew there was so many tiny nuances to the game? So many seemingly insignificant details that I now see as vital.
For all the love, craft  and success of this remake (and it really is, easily worth the money, honestly) a little something has been lost in the translation. The magic is not gone in New'N'Tasty but it is dimmed somewhat. In spite of being a great game, that can't help but make me a little sad.

Character skill/stat progression seemed like an interesting sandbox you can play with at first, but it just allows you to mess up your stats and totally gimp yourself for fights, making things more difficult. Blackguards has a pretty standard premise, in that it is a save the world fantasy story.  Unfortunately, the dialogue is stilted and often disjointed and the gameplay is dense and perhaps overly complicated.  I can forgive the voice acting, and odd story easily, but it is the game mechanics themselves that perhaps need tweaking.
The dice rolls are punishing and heavily weighted towards failure.  It is laughably common to miss 3 75% chances in a row and taking a risk on anything under a 50% chance is pretty much a guaranteed miss.   It has been said on various forums that there are many mechanics that are affecting the probabilities that don't appear in the shown hit chance.  That sounds to me like a User Interface failure and a pretty important one at that.
Perhaps the most glaring issue of this is the arena fights at the beginning of Chapter 2.  When you have to pull off 6 hits in a row to kill the first enemy and then another 8 hits to kill the second.  Unfortunately you A) will die in 3 hits, B) Will get poisoned if you take a single hit, and C) the NPCs don't have an issue with the weighted hit dice.  Add to this the fact that you can't go back and level due to your captivity, can't buy potions (though the enemy gets 2 or 3) and lose all of your items means that you are pretty much screwed.
All in all I was pretty disappointed.  It was exactly the kind of game I wanted.  It just wasn't.

The good is it can be totally customized to your liking in league set up, you can edit player ratings, make and add players and plenty of options. The game is fast as you can play 5 or 6 years in a 7 to 10 hour time frame. You can create and edit a playbooks, set prices and ticket values.

I did fix this by going into commissioner mode and gave each team 250 mill in cash. Rosters are set at 100 players, no restricted free agency or franchise tags.
Anyway I will keep the game as I have already gone past my 2 hours of play time on Steam. Would I get a refund if I could? Yes. I payed 27 with tax and I think this should be more around the 10 to 12 dollar range. I will play more and see if they update this with some patches. If so I will re-review.

So I managed to beat the whole game, with 98% of the world explored in about 8 hours. Was it worth it? The fact that I almost solidly played this game through in one sitting should be enough of a hint as to how hooked I was on Ori. The art style is fantastic, and I genuinely had to stop at points just to admire how vibrant and gorgeous the world looked.
As for the story, it's remarkably deep and moving, a cast of varied characters over the rather simplistic backdrop of a fairytale world which will tug on your heartstrings and sucker-punch you in the feels at key intervals. It's not the most complex or intelligent storyline ever, by dear God it can make you feel things. If you don't feel moved by the plight of these characters, you might want to get your doctor to check if you still have a heart.
And finally the gameplay. Is it especially original? No. Is it fun? Heck yes. The controls are great, and your little guy Ori feels as nimble and agile as he looks. While at first you might not be able to jump about all that much, unlock a few new abilities here and there and you get to have a ton of fun running around the game's large and diverse world. People have had some problems with certain challenging areas of the game where it doesn't allow you to place checkpoints, but for me it was just challenging enough to keep things interesting. With a bit of perseverance you can get through those sections easily enough.
All in all, I give this game a hearty 10/10. Not many games would get a perfect rating from me, but the fact I'm even bothering to write a multiple-paragraph review here on steam just shows how much I loved playing this game. Here's to hoping we get a sequel!

I thoroughly enjoy Daedalic Entertainment's point-and-click adventure games so when I heard that they would be making a turn-based RPG I was super pumped.  I love the Dark Eye world and the gritty fantasy found therein and I feel that this game does not disappoint.
PROS
1) THE CHARACTERS! I adored the main characters and genuinely felt that each line of dialogue between them was solid gold.  Every one of them had a great personality and contributed to the overall value of this game a great deal.
2) The Dialogue and Story: You can take it or leave it but I what I came across I enjoyed.  While it is true that the story is linear and doing side-missions does nothing but help you grind this was never an issue for me.  I liked the story and the direction it was taken.  You're a bad guy doing bad things for the right reasons and it is not often to come across something that does this trope well.  The game does a great job of putting you into the "antihero" mentality.
3) Combat: This game does not hold your hand.  You WILL redo fights, you WILL get frustrated, and unless you know how to build your stats and abilities you WILL fall behind but as long as you play your hand correctly you will always be able to win the next fight.  Similar to older iterations of D&D (which Die Schwarze Auge/The Dark Eye is the German equivalent of more or less) there are weapon AND damage types to consider.  Knowing what kind of weapons and what kind of damage types to use are crucial against certain enemies.  For example, DON'T USE PIERCING AGAINST THE UNDEAD!  They are completely immune to anything that doesn't impart massive physical trauma to their skeleton like slashing or bashing weapons would.  Some enemies are immune to poison, some to magic, and some to physical damage.  It will be trial and error to figure this out but this is also why you can equip each character with three different weapon load-outs which you can cycle through in combat so as to avoid being harmless to a specific enemy.  Other things to note about combat include the diversity of places you will fight in (it makes you feel like you're actually traveling from place to place), the importance of positioning, the use of environmental effects to your advantage, and bottlenecking.  Combat is the meat and potatoes to this game and after 50+ hours of this game I, for one, can say that it does not get old.
4) Stat Systems and Leveling: DO NOT RAISE BASE STATS! At least not at first.  This game offers a wide variety of upgrade paths with which you can take your party in a multitude of directions.  Wanna be a crazy hefty tank? Upgrade Warcraft, Body Control, Willpower, Strength, Vitality, and the proficiency of two weapons of your choice.  Wanna be everywhere and piercing armor? Upgrade Agility, Body Control, Spear proficiency, Dexterity, and Vitality for that damage you are most certainly going to take.  Wanna mage it up?  Take Bow proficiency, level your spells like crazy (a hefty investment), and make sure you have a tank or two between you and the enemy.  While some might bemoan the lack of class options with there only being three, Warrior, Ranger, and Mage, it isn't that large of an issue.  This is not a game about diplomacy or sneaking around (ignoring two or three AWFUL missions that can be solved with fighting), it's about slugging it out with the enemy.  To play something that doesn't contribute to the fight directly is to take a difficult game and make it impossible.
5) Grittiness: I consider this a plus because I like games that force you to be aware of the number of arrows in your quiver, how absolutely vital healing can be, and how huge a difference is made when you finally buy that new axe that does ONE MORE DAMAGE.  This is a game where all the small things add up over time to take your party from bandit npcs to gods on the battlefield.  Throughout the game you can also learn special attacks which give you advantages in certain situations such as inflicting wounds (Wounds and HP Damage are totally separate things), knocking down enemies, or doing more damage from a distance with ranged weaponry.  The larger and more valuable the effect the more costly the attack will be in terms of accuracy so a very effective trade-off between damage/utility and accuracy is established.
6) The World: Not much to say aside from how much I enjoyed it and all the people you come across.  It is VERY uncommon for you to run across nice individuals so when you do you instantly grow attached to them.  Even then most of the "nice" people you come across are still awful by today's standards due to their desires to brainwash, enslave, or kill off rivals for a plethora of reasons.  Aventuria (the world) isn't a great place and it's heroes reflect that, but maybe, with a great deal of effort, you can change that.
CONS
1) The Probability System: IT LIESSSSSSSSSSSSSSS! Never in a game have I missed five consecutive instances of hitting with a 95% chance of my attack succeeding each time.  It is without a doubt the single most irritating and detracting point to this whole game.  Until you play Blackguards you will not understand how infuriating it can be.  It doesn't just apply to physical attacks, though.  Your spells will fizzle out and do nothing, your arrows can randomly vanish, you will fail body tests where you have a 99% chance of passing and fall down.  This was a HUGE oversight on the part of the developers and if they would just release a patch that made these percentages more accurate I would have nothing against this RPG.
2) POISONS and Enemy Buffs! In the latter half of the campaign in an attempt to balance the gameplay the developers just decided to either give the enemies a flat magic stat buff or give all of their attacks the poison quality which will do continuous damage or give you a stat debuff for the rest of the fight.  Not nearly as irritating as the percentage issue but it does somewhat cheapen the joy you get when your party goes into an encounter that you should faceroll only to discover that the enemy basically leveled up with you.
3) Stat Building: While I did mention this as a plus earlier you can very easily destroy your game by building poorly.  Seeing as how there is no way to undo this it can prove to be game ruining.
Overall, I would give this experience a solid 8/10.  Fun from beginning to end and if you see it on sale for less than 10 you should instantly snatch it up.

Here's a current breakdown of the pros and cons of this game, from the perspective of a gamer who especially enjoys first person, multiplayer, survival-based construction and exploring games.
Pros
- Beautiful environments, especially with 7 update that uses parallax occlusion
- Resource limitation. When building with your faction, you really have to spend your ores carefully.
- Thorough survival system - hunger, cold, heat, open wounds, broken legs, many other interesting status effects
- Incredibly deep ship construction
- System for salvaging wrecks with tools, which is very fun
- Customizable game scenarios
- Level up system's "skill points" too generous, I rarely spend them all. Could be re-thought.
- Decent weapon selection, PVP
- Most importantly, ability to SAVE ALL BASES AND SHIPS AS BLUEPRINTS, so if server wipes you keep all the things you designed!
Cons
- Poor physics, which can break immersion. Ships have maximum speed in space, scale for "orbit" playfields unrealistic
- Weak NPC/trading system, just don't see anything worth buying
- Very difficult to "start" sometimes, especially if you lose your starting gear or if ores are rare.
- Difficult to find a server of active players/engaging PVP that doesn't involve griefing
- Death system can be frustrating, as monsters will take a while to leave "body" when I am retrieving items. It's okay to create a "challenging" consequence for death, but the current system is more frustrating than challenging.

Another minor issue is that the plot can get a little bit messed up if you do certain sections out of the expected order.  In one part of the game, there is a blocked path and a hint that you need the help of someone from a nearby dungeon to open the path.  There is nothing stopping you from going to the dungeon before finding the blocked path, which results in your characters asking for help unblocking the path prior to actually learning about the path.  This does not break the game's plot, but it is a bit of poor forsight.
All in all, this game is a lot better than the original Evoland (which was also a pretty good game).

TLDR -- A lot of good ideas, but iffy execution.
I used to recommend this game, as I really liked it. After I got it, I played through several times, and despite some overly complex -- and not well explained -- aspects, it was a (mostly) fun game. I especially liked the humor, the fact that there wasn't always a clear "good" choice, and that even when there was, it wasn't always mechanically superior -- i.e. better rewards for being "good". It was refreshingly muddy on morality.
But, recently, I'd seen some comments online referencing "crashes" being the reason people stopped playing. So I just played through again -- and it crashed a half dozen times in my playthrough. I still enjoyed going back through this game, but I had the benefit of already understanding the confusing character sheet and knowing how to budget my xp and  money well -- what to buy and when.
I think it's more than likely that most people who ran into the random -- and seemingly non-reproducible -- crashes I did won't get very far, especially with all the other aggravating factors.
If you can get past the crashes, and remember to diversify the party, while focusing each character, you can have a lot of fun with it. But if you want a quick dive in for fun, go elseware.

Recommended, but with a warning: this is a story, not a game.
The first time I played through it, I had four choices in 14 hours, with the first choice coming five hours in. All four choices were trivial at the time and not all choices are always available, yet those choices not only determine the path your story takes, but determine whether you get a real ending at all. The choices I made resulted in a abrupt ending that was a complete letdown. Luckily I had saved the story at each choice point, and I was able to go back and change my last choice and get hours more of story, including a breathtaking romance between two characters
.
While there is potentially a romantic element to this story, it's not really about that, and not every girl in the story is a potential partner. It's a story about young people trying to (re)build their lives and put in hard work to turn a dream into reality. Even with a lack of choices, the story itself still works well, although following any one path alone will leave you with unresolved plot points. With such a long story and not many main characters, the characters are able to reveal many sides and a lot of depth and growth, from the main character (Aoi) to my personal favorite (Amane).
As such a long story, it might work better if it would just play as full episodes and then give you the choice of which to play next, rather than forcing you to click after every line for hours at a time. And I do know that the translation is imperfect: for example, there is a big moment in the story when two characters
start calling each other by their given names instead of their family names, showing that their relationship has changed, but because the translation uses the characters' given names almost all the time before, you won't notice it unless you listen to the voice acting.
Quibbles aside, this story is a rich, moving story with memorable, mostly sympathetic characters, and is well worth watching.

I'll admit: I pretty much never cry at sad movies, video games, whathaveyou. Even with To the Moon, I
sad, but didn't cry.
But this game broke me.
The game is practically everything a good follow-up game should be, and then some. The one thing I liked so much about To the Moon was how small the story was - which sounds weird, but it seemed like the main focus, in that game, was kept to two people just doing their job. Finding Paradise also keeps the focus on the patient and his life, but also starts to address some additional outer plot points encountered in the minisodes and heck, even at the end. It gives you a wonderful story and still leaves you waiting eagerly for the next release.
Also, the banter between everyone was just fantastic. The chemistry between Neil and Eva is impeccable, as are Neil's humourous intentions. And some scary imagery, too!
It seems as though this game does give you enough information that you don't have to play To the Moon first before playing this game. I do, however, recommend doing so, along with the minisodes, if possible. With A Bird Story, yes, this main character is the patient (don't think I'm giving anything away there), though unlike To the Moon and this, doesn't really have a lot of gameplay and no dialogue at all. I actually really did like A Bird Story, but after playing Finding Paradise, I do appreciate it more. It's not absolutely necessary to play A Bird Story to understand what's going on in Finding Paradise, but it might help to set things up in terms of the plot.

One thing I would mention that I didn't like is that I was experiencing a pretty low framerate for a good portion of the game. There's quite a few more instances of control-heavy moments in Finding Paradise that were very hard to control due to this. Switching to the beta "alternative" seems to aid in a smoother, more fluid performance, though.
Man it was hard to put this game down. I almost stayed up the entire night to finish this. Highly recommended.

Welp, I just bought this today and my wrist is proof that I am hooked.
This game is really exciting despite its surface simplicity. Sure, just click left or right. But I had never seen such perfect way to stop you from button-mashing and keep you engaged with all thats happening.
If it wasn't for the carpal tunnel risk, this would be almost like meditating - I could do it for hours on end. :)
:
The gameplay really is amazing. All the skills and weapons give depth to what you do with the very simple controls. There are choices to be made, before and during each level. The fact that the levels are not randomly generated is an excellent thing, as you can plan a strategy and put it to the test.
The extreme simplicity is given quite some variety by the different constraints each level gives: smashing objects, only throwing bombs or daggers, only defending against throws, more or less hit points at the start, timed rounds, boss rounds... This keeps the game always interesting. Add to that the different kinds of enemies and you find yourself wondering what the next level will be like, pondering which path to take in order to get to a particular skill unlock sooner, and chasing after the platinum medals and perfect results.
Another very nice point is how smooth and reactive the game is. Granted, that was to be expected from a 2-button control, but still. Everything feels fluid, and the movements are beautiful - yes, even though it's only stick figures.
The difficulty is given by something equally simple: how fast the enemies come at you. And that means the game can adapt to your skill level instantaneously: it always feels like the perfect amount of challenge. This is some really generous game design, in the best sense: no hand-holding, and no pointless cruelty towards the player.
This game lends itself to some excellent casual play, but it has more than enough room for avid difficulty-queens and leaderboard hunters to find their pleasure too.

I absolutely LOVE this game, and can't wait for the release of Styx (2) Shards of Darkness, I never considered writing a review until now that I have the pre-order for the second game and because of the hype I might as well describe how good the first was.
The world that Styx takes place in is possibly the most interesting I have ever played in regardless of genre, with the second game expanding on the lore of the first, with goblin(s), elves, dwarves, and other very interesting creatures in my opinion this game trumps ALL others of the Stealth Genre (of which I am a big fan) for the sole reason it is a TRUE stealth game.
Other "stealth" games such as Dishonored, or Assassins creed, while still good don't exactly hold up the statement of a stealth game because stealth is more of an option rather than a necessity. You don't
to be stealthy in assassins creed if you can just perform an arial takedown into a restricted area and then proceed to counter and kill all the guards in the area without loosing a speck of health, and you don't
to be stealthy in Dishonored if you have enough ammo to literally go guns blazing, while it is harder to accomplish with enough health "vials" and all the ammo you can find throughout the game, you can toss a grenade to kill two people at once, fire off your pistol 20+ times to get a kill per shot (if you are accurate enough) and set down enough traps around you that anybody who gets even close will either be knocked out or disintegrated. (But this review isn't about other games mistakes, this is about how good Styx is, so I will continue)
Which is why I believe some people don't like this game, because they believe that they are Stealth fans since they've played all the assassins creed games, and then they come here and can't knock down more than 3 levels, much less the side "quests" or achievements. Because Styx isn't any ordinary stealth game it's a
stealth game. Where stealth isn't an option, but rather forced upon the player. If you raise the alarm you can have at least 10 guards tailing your♥♥♥♥♥which will either 1. force you to hightail it out of there, and wait a decent amount of time for everyone to calm down or 2. stand and die (Because there is no way you can stand and fight) and trust me, I have at least 2 screenshots of me hiding away in some obscure room while at least 8 guards are trying to find me. Styx's one weakness happens to be his strength, as Styx himself put it in the final scene: "Small sure, but quick, and mean." Styx
engage more than one opponent at a  time, and even then facing head on one on one can be difficult, requiring to dodge or parry a couple times before you are allowed to strike back, you need to have the perfect timing down pat in order to pull this off. Which can definitely be a struggle at first, however if my own experience is a good reference, I would say many Styx players get this down pretty easily mid-to late game, especially once you get a specific perk which allows you to parry without requiring that perfect exact timing. This is why in other games 8 guards is "nothing much" but in Styx spells out a death sentence. You'd have to be a god at both parrying and dodging in order to accomplish this which is very unlikely because of the variety of guards there are in the game.
Normal ones, (which already by themselves can sometimes be a pain) Archers, who wield crossbows and can one-shot you from a distance (if you have low enough health) Inquisitors, who use freaking magic to immobilize you long enough for them to get one good slash in which can also be enough to get you killed, and finally Armored guards, which you CANNOT kill in hand to hand or even via stealth, you have to kill them using the environment which leads me to my point:
(however don't worry, because the variation is slowly introduced throughout the levels, not all at once from the get-go)
Because of this Styx requires a LOT and I do mean a
of strategy, you don't have brawn, so you're going to have to rely on your noggin from now on. Memorizing endless patterns of guard patrols, map layouts, and potential hazards / creatures among other things. Which can sometimes mean a lot of dying, but that's when the story as well as Styx himself as a character comes in. The lore behind this game is extremely entertaining and interesting (although not much of it is elaborated in THIS game itself shortly after completing this game on my first run I discovered that Styx has appeared in a video game before, Of Orcs and Men styx makes an appearance as a playable character throughout most of the entire game, and where a lot of lore can be discovered in terms of the world that Styx exists). Not only this, but if Styx was to be summed up in a single word I would say sarcastic, and god he can be funny, which can definitely be a nice break from a brief rage quit every now and then.
It's only a matter of time before we finally get to see what's behind the curtain of Styx shards of Darkness before we can see how the developers have expanded upon this universe even further, and boy am I excited.

Wow, what do you get when you combine an entertaining story, colorful characters, and turn based combat with absolutely BROKEN game mechanics?  You get Blackguards!
Blackguards is another in a string of games recently that have such wonderful aspects about them and yet have some fatal flaw that sabotages every good experience you have with it.  That flaw is that the game straight-up cheats.  Now I'd normally be the first person to say "suck it up you sissy, it's meant to be challenging."  But there's a big difference between something that is genuinely challenging, and something that cheats.
-I can't tell you how many times I laughed my butt off watching the number of ways the game abused my characters.  Character killed before anyone can act in a battle.  No problem, reload.  Character recovers from knock down only to be knocked down once more with no apparent cause?  No problem, reload.  The game is full of this kind of stuff.  Prepare to be "loved" in the most brutal way by this game.  There's little else that you can do other than laugh about it...it's baked in.
-Ignore any percentages to succeed on anything you do.  They're meaningless.  You'll realize it's all BS after your 10th time of failing when it says you have a 100% chance of success.  This will be driven home even harder when you see your character who has maxxed out stats in his chosen weapon, the champion of the arena, outfitted in the best gear, and still being unable to hit some highwayman in leather armor.  And if you do, it will be a small percentage of the damage that guy can do to you.  It's depressing, really.
-Forget tactics.  They really have no place here.  You'll find some style that works with your approach to games and work it over and over again (as best as the broken mechanics will let you of course).  The game doesn't give you much reason to try anything else, and you won't want to because you're just trying desperately to win some battle.
It's like the designers were unable to find a way to make the game challenging besides giving the enemies a wholly unfair advantage.  And that's what it feels like...cheap and dirty hits.  That might be ok if it was built into the story and somehow made sense.  But when it's the developers that are doing it, you really don't feel like supporting them again.
Which is a shame, because if they tweaked just that one thing...that one small thing...to play by the rules...it would be pretty enjoyable.  There's a lot of content, some really funny breaking-the-4th-wall comedy, amazing production values in some areas (the world map), and combat with some moderate depth. But alas, it was not meant to be.
Frankly, as much as I want to I can't recommend this game.  I got it super cheap as part of a Humble Bundle, and I still can't recommend it.  I don't know if I'll ever return to the game again, but if the developers fix these problems, I'll certainly update my review.

I have not been so bored with a game in a very long time. Blackguards is a hex turn based rpg type game, with much less of the traditional rpg feel and much more of the board game elements. As a genre, it’s not my cup of tea but I can see why people enjoy the thoughtful strategy of it.
Playing Blackguards felt sort of like playing a chess match over and over again with the outcome being nearly entirely based on luck. Perhaps it boils down to the visuals not being all that visceral, but even things like positioning relative to the enemy seems to have no effect on combat outcomes. In the hour and a halfish I played I did little more than click on enemies and wait to either win or have to reload. It was as if the game was trying to distance itself from me.
Definitely not a recommendation on any of my lists; if I wanted a strategic RPG I’d reinstall Neverwinter Nights, if I wanted a board game I’d find a free online chess game.

Empyrion will naturally get compared to Space Engineers, which is a fair comparison in a lot of settings but really they are two games in a similar genre that focus on different things. We'd all love if there was some combination of both but that hasn't happened yet.
Empyrion delivers on what it's set out to, which is a more engaging PvE experience in a sci-fi/space survival game. The cylindrical planets and weird hemispherical transition aside the game is pretty immersive and multiplayer works a lot better than in Space Engineers.
They've talked about adding NPC crews to your ships, even if they serve no function that idea has me very, very excited. I might even try making a machinima in Empyrion if they're slightly funcitonal :)
I personally enjoy playing both games and Empyrion has improved dramatically in alpha 6 and 7 so I'm confident with its future. If you like survival games this is one that you are unlikely to regret adding to your steam list.
