Before I get into the nittiest of grittys i want to start by saying overall I enjoyed this game and I think most other will too also I did not play Evoland one. My critique of the game may seem extremely contrary to that statement but that really is the bottom line. Yes this game made me sigh heavily often and curse in the languages of dead elder gods from sheer annoyance but it was still fun enough for me to pick it back up every time I got home from work and waste the majority of a Sunday afternoon playing it.
First and foremost Evoland II is a very ambitious project and the developers should be commended for putting it all together. A bit of backstory without giving too much away of the game for those who have yet to see any kind of summary, Evoland II is the story of a hero’s journey in a world ransacked by war and a major catastrophe where the only way to save it is messing with the space time continuum to make things “better”. Difference is that when you travel back or forwards in time in the game your gaming resolution also changes to match. I.e. going back in time lands you into lower resolution pixel graphics a la original pokemon while going forwards in time merits you some sexy 3d curves. They also incorporate elements from a lot of other game genres, and I don’t mean like it has hints of fantasy or rpg, I mean one minute you are slashing your way through a dungeon like the original Legend of Zelda the next you have to execute combos fighting game style like street fighter or experiencing the mania of a top down bullet hell adventure. Evoland II literally brings a lot of stuff to the table and does a lot of things right...but just barely.
Alright real talk time. The story itself (keeping in mind that though I finished I get the impression I needed to complete or collect more things to get the secret or “real” ending) is pretty rote. You could probably guess pretty much everything about it if I told you it involved time travel, an ancient advanced civilization that poofed and only exists in legends, and a mysterious boy with *surprise* super amnesia. The characters also are fairly by the books with really no surprises there except for when they make an anachronistic joke or callout which brings up the humor of the game. The developers obviously first and foremost wanted to make a fun game so the humor is nerdy and generally pretty good. That being said don’t expect to fall in love with any of the characters. The only reason I liked mine where because I gave them silly names like Vajeen and Puddin.
The basic gameplay is where most of my beef lies with Evoland II. It would be both accurate but slightly insulting to the developers to say this is a clone of Legend of Zelda but the basic gameplay pretty much is just that. It is by a large a slash your way to the next objective style of game with lots and lots of puzzles thrown in. The puzzles are mainly solved by using some combination of your sidecharacters special abilities. Each side character has one special ability that can be used to solve puzzles, access parts of the environment, but also can be used in combat. The side characters are summoned by charging up your attack i.e. holding the attack button except if you get hit then it annoyingly resets, also if you attack while its charging it resets, also the cooldown is SUPER slow and does not change at all throughout the game. In combat it seems as if the special attacks are meant to be a hail mary but in reality the fact that you can’t attack while its charging and have to actively running away to avoid damage and the overall weakness when it does hit you’d probably break even if you spent that charging time attacking. The slowness of the cooldown period becomes much more obvious when you have to use their abilities to solve a puzzle. You may have figured out the 8 moves to solve it but it’s going to take you forever to execute them. You're probably wondering since the side characters have special abilities what about the main character what’s his deal? Absolutely nothing is his deal and thats a sad sad problem of this game. You are literally just a kid with a sword that everyone difers to for some reason. You also don’t have a shield or the ability to roll/dodge to maybe spice up the monotony of just horizontally slashing your way through life. Even Link can at least do a whirlwind slash with his sword but in this ambitious game there is no other slash than sideways for you my friend. You will spend the majority of your time running around like a chicken until you can get in close and get in a good slash ad infinitum. While this does add some difficulty it will mostly annoy you especially the lack of shield which would allow a more skilled player to react and avoid the numerous “cheap shot” tactics used by enemies. Your ability to cut down your enemies does also not change with you leveling up in fact not a whole lot changes with you leveling up its rather pointless to be honest. Sure your health goes up and so does your attack and armor but the enemies also scale with you such that there was never a point where I felt it was a benefit to be at “X” level or have this armor or sword vs the other. There really was no good way to grind either in order to test this but my suspicion is that it wouldn’t have mattered. So point being you will stay a boring one trick pony for the entire game with one notable exception that I won’t spoil so if hacking your way through life even with puzzles to spice it up isn’t your bag this game will exhaust you.
Many will praise the versatility of this game and all the different types of games you find within it. I do to actually! It’s very cool how they incorporated different game styles within the context of the story. However, you know how a game of Uno is fun at the start and then towards the end it becomes an annoying loop where no one seems to be winning and you’re tempted to just lose on purpose so you can stop playing? Thats how some of these games within a game feel. Sure they are fun to start but more often than not they manage to overstay their welcome and you want to go back to normal. To be fair there are savepoints fairly frequently so when you die, which will happen often, you usually don’t have to repeat the entire process its just that the endgame of the process is slightly further away than it needed to be.
Alrighty enough ragging on the game, all in all its a pretty fun romp and I enjoyed myself more often than not. Though the game mechanics were slightly grating, the characters and story meh, the humor and overall game design kept me coming back. It can be very tedious at times so don’t go for it if you’re expecting a mile a minute tour de adventure. But if you want a unique title with callbacks to a bunch of classic games and some fairly challenging puzzles, get yo’self some of this!

An interesting and unique RTS game which is somewhat hard to grasp. You have an army of creatures which move around and multiply in a way somewhat resembling the rules of Conway's "Life" game.  You build roads, walls, taverns and other buildings, but all this only controls the army indirectly and in non-obvious ways.
The good:
- intersting basic idea to use game-of-life like principle, I've never seen this anywhere else
The so-so:
- I found the graphics cute and appropriate for the setting, but I can imagine that many players will find them too simplistic.
- sounds are functional but not much more
- the map is really big. Completing a single battle takes ages because the enemies spawn new and new taverns and you need to cover the whole map with your soldiers until you finally win. Or at least that's my impression so far.
The bad:
- the music gets pretty annoying after a while because it's too repetitive. Also, the plain piano track feels very low-budget. I understand it's there to fit the "automata" setting but still I could imagine a much better soundtrack
- everything in the game takes too long. In fact, you could let the game simpy run, go grab a coffee and come a couple minutes later just to see that not much has changed. The basic feel that "you give an order and something happens" is missing here totally. At the same time, a lot of things are happening in the game, all at once, at such fast pace that you'd never be able to fully predict what will happen. This may sound like a contradiction but it's not: you have zillions of small objects moving around but since they can't respond to any commands it all feels like an uncontrollable mechanism which runs mostly on its own according to its arcane rules. You don't have the feeling that you are in control.
- there is no tutorial. Instead, there are several lengthy pages with text and illustrations. The only real advice the game gives you before starting is that you need to build "feedback loops" but how exactly that could work isn't really clear. Even 1 example with 1 picture and an explanation why that works as a feedback loop would be enough, but there is nothing like that. I tried building just a lot of taverns but it's not clear how exactly the microbes move around them. Sometimes I saw microbes strangely disappear even though they weren't too big.
My overall feel of the game is mostly confusion. I wouldn't expect a player of an average intellience to be able to fully understand what's going on here, even if he's patient enough to read thru the instructions. What this game mostly misses is a proper tutorial and maybe a few very small introductory missions which would show how all this exactly works. Despite its interesting core idea, this game seriously lacks accessibility. This is the obvious reason why its multiplayer servers are empty and why it didn't get many reviews (or sales, i guess). I'll still give it more tries and will maybe update my review if I like it more.
I'm really split on whether to recommend it or not, but well, since there is no "don't know" option here, i'll give it a "yes".

There is much I could say about Ori and the Blind Forest. Instead, I'll say this.
I'm a sousick old fart, I reek of world weariness, and I have little faith for anything. I play video games to pass the time because there's really not much else to do now, really, you see? Except time and time again I'm greeted with gormless misrepresentations of humanity borne of xenophobia painting us as some glorious Master Race without flaw, one-dimensional, and almost as fictionally caring as we objectively aren't in reality. In dull, grey, imaginations bereft of imagination and inspiration, creatively bankrupt halls stretch on ahead.
And sometimes you ask yourself whether this is all there is. It's bloody bleak. With all of the wonderment to be taken from the neverending font of novelty that is the mind, all we can achieve is this? That's it? Are we so xenophobic? Do we have such a fetish for the familiar that we cannot accept anything else into us? Are we just, at the end of the day, creatures of hate?
Our entertainment is about combat, death, and Us vs. Them scenarios. And even when it's not, it's about extroverted victories, one-upmanship, manipulation, drama, suffering, schadenfreude, and conspiracy. Because this is what we are. And that is all there is.
Except.
Every now and then there's a little glimmer of hope that this shambling husk, this ravenous, drooling homunculus of a thing that we call humanity may have a soul after all. That it may have passion, and it may be able to set aside its xenophobia, its fears, its fetishistic attachment to verisimilitude in order to be something better. You don't see these glimmers often, but they are there.
Ori is such a glimmer. And for an all too brief moment, it made my heart sing. Then, with the closing credits, it was gone. Yet for a moment, I felt as though I saw something of a better us within it. And that is the highest praise I can give anything.
If only more could be like it.
I think I finally understand now why this game tugged at my heartstrings so. It's Ecco the Dolphin, but relevant to contemporary sensibilities. It's as meaningful now as Ecco was back in the day. And by that I mean the original Ecco on the Mega Drive (or Genesis, if you prefer), and Ecco o the Dreamcast. It's challenging, but at the same time it's beautiful enough to weep over.
I remember that what made Ecco stand out at the time was its tight controls, innovative systems of movement, and the flow of it. Ori has that flow. It's a serene thing that, if you're tuned into it, doesn't really tax you too much. Perhaps it's because of the time I spent playing Ecco in days gone by, but I can sense the purity of fun and exploration in this game every bit as much.
It almost feels as though the '00s never happened. I feel like I've had a glimpse into an alternate Universe where our brains aren't shrinking, where we aren't heading towards an Idiocracy, and where imagination and inspiration are still running rampant in my favourite hobby. That gaming itself hasn't given way to the xenophobia, neediness, and familiarity fetishism of the unwashed masses. It's a bizarre thing. I may never see its likes again.
This is a game I will not -- I cannot -- ever forget. In much the same way that I can never forget Ecco. Just as Ecco was meaningful and relevant to its time in the best possible way, Ori is that, now. It's exactly what I needed. This is what gaming should be.

Where as this game has some neat concepts and some nice ideas, there's just too many problems for this game to be worth it, much less for $10.
The game's physics is a bit too ragdoll like and can really get in the way sometimes. Although there is a reset button for your position, there is not an immediate one for AI and often times you'd find them stuck on each other, you, or other various places such as stuck outside the map that really take away from it.
As far as the combat, it's ok, but not perfect. If too close to an enemy it won't actually shoot them and just go through them. It's hard to tell the terrain in some cases and you'll end up shooting over an enemy. The running over people (who are rather large in scale) isn't perfect and can sometimes be finicky.
The upgrade system is only based on each level. That makes the game actually rather static. Sure, there's a few more special upgrades you can get along the road, your guns upgrades never change and you rely on hoping an enemy drops the right upgrade for that level and even then I noticed it didn't always work. The game gets rather repetative and really doesn't have much variation. Some of the bonus levels were neat to try out the first person aspects, but other than score there's not much incentive to these.
The story was kinda lame with same pretty so-so to annoying/cheesy voice acting. It seemed to jump too far at some points or not really have much a point in others and then ended abrubtly.
Some levels were so simple you could literally sit in one place and kill all the enemies, others seemed to have such annoying terrain to bounce off or get stuck on that the enemies were just a pain to get to.
Overall: The game has some neat aspects and is a simple shoot em up base defense driving around a car, but is "meh" in content/combat, story that kinda sucks (Despite how I like Post-Apocalyptic Themes), and too static/ a drag to get through. Even $5.00 would be a stretch for this game. Unless you really like trying out these types of games, I wouldn't spend much if anything on it.

Wasteland Angel is an arcade shooter and is proud to admit it. You have infinite ammo, you kill a lot of bad guys, and you rack up a lot of points.
However, the setting doesn't seem right for this kind of thing. You'll blow up hundreds, if not thousands of enemy cars and spend tens of thousands of bullets. It just doesn't feel right for a setting where almost everyone is dead and supplies survivors are few. There is technically a story, but you're not really here for that, you're here for the action.
As for the actual gameplay, it is certainly fun to drive about blowing up hundreds of enemies and then splattering their drivers Mad Max style afterwards. However , the gameplay is pretty formuleic. Bandits are attacking a town. You need to stop them from enslaving everyone. Also, every 2 missions, there's a massive supervehicle that can only be defeated with special weapons. Its good the first time, but when you have 6 areas, all of which ask you to do two defense missions and a boss mission, it gets boring pretty fast.
However, there is a very nice highlight to the gameplay. Every fourth level, you drive around on a small patch of wasteland in first person and all you have to do is survive. These levels have the closest thing to a Mad Max type of preformance that you'll find.
However, on the downside, you are driving a car, not walking a person around and the terrain is pretty rough, especially near towns. Which means that you'll easily get caught on the map. This is kind of unforgivable in a game where you have a timed goal (stopping the slavers before they haul towns people away) and are being attacked by about 10 enemies at any given time. Not to mention that the reverse controls are pretty sluggish.
However, despite its glaring flaws, Wasteland Angel is still enjoyable and an acceptable alternative to a Mad Max style game. At least until the officially licensed one hits store shelves.

So, I got me four hours in Wasteland Angel. In that time I've cleared it's story mode and gotten all of its achievements (the first Steam title I've managed to get all achievements on; go me!)
But is it worth your time? Absolutely. There's a decent amount of content here, given you can get the game at a low cost (for example, with a coupon) but at it's normal cost it's not necessarily worth it. So keep that in mind.
The game is basically a twin stick arcade shooter. You drive with WASD, and shoot with your left mouse button and the right mouse button uses special weapons. You drive around, blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, save civilians, and collect power-ups. It's pure mindless fun, with no completed story, or level up systems, or anything of the like. It's plain simplicity, which you need sometimes.
The levels also culminate in big boss battles, with the first two being relatively easy and the last boss (whom you fight twice) being a big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ You also get four difficulties (I played on Medium) and leaderboards if you're the sort who strives to be the best at the game. And you also get bonus levels at the end of the normal levels, which are played from a first person perspective. If you ask me there should be an option to play the whole game like this as it is pretty fun. There's a racing, survival, and frenzy that come up at specific points in the game.
All in all, it's not the greatest game out there but I truly recommend it to anyone who might be interested.

Despite what Steam says, I've played this for nearly 5 hours.
I want to like this game. I really do. It's just not very good. The story is a blatant rip off of Chrono Trigger, but not in a funny or interesting way. There's no satirical commentary on RPG tropes to justify it, it just is. The humour consists entirely of referencing other video games. Every reference makes me cringe. "A guy dressed in green did a thing" is about as creative as the humour gets. It's lazy. Plus "It's dangerous to go alone. Take this" automatically loses points in my eyes. For shame.
The varied gameplay styles just amount to a bunch of half-baked underdeveloped short games. The base gameplay is a mediocre Zelda clone with a charge mechanic. It's nothing special, but it kind of works. Everything else is tedious and drags on way too long and the pacing is all over the place. The last straw for me was going through a long frustrating vertical platforming segment (with ♥♥♥♥ing disappearing Mega Man platforms - those are bad enough in a game with tight controls let alone in this mess) directly to a boring top-down shooting segment that never ends and then right in to a bad Street Fighter clone where you win 4 fights in a row by button mashing. It's all completely unnecessary. I wish they scrapped all of the boring underdeveloped fluff and just polished up the base game more.
The main gimmick, the changing graphical styles, is pointless. It's kind of neat at first but has no relevance to the plot and doesn't affect the gameplay at all.
I can't imagine why people are rating this game so well. I grew up on NES, SNES, and PS1 RPGs. Many positive reviews state that this game brought them back to childhood. I disagree. This game just makes me wish I was playing one of the old games I grew up on instead. Evoland 2 does not respect the time of the player. It is padded out and tedious. The references to old games are heavy handed and unfunny. Give this a pass. If you really want nostalgia, just play a good old game.

I love this game.
A couple years ago I heard about the original Evoland and I gave it a download, and really enjoyed it.  It was a nostalgic walk through some of the best games like Legend of Zelda & Final Fantasy, and it was very fun & educational about the history of games.
Evoland 2 is in a whole other category.  This is a long game, it's deep, it's fun, there are secrets and puzzles, and the time travel aspect is SO COOL and SO elegantly constructed.  One minute, you're playing a donkey-kong style platformer, and the next you are in a tactical turn-based battle.  The story is great, and I really loved how big the map was and how many different styles of games were included.
When I play RPG games, I /never/ play the card/dice mini games... But with Evoland 2, (the "game of cards" resembling a much-simplified version of Magic the Gathering), I was OBSESSED with collecting the cards and playing with random characters throughout the universe.
While I love this game and would absolutely recommend it to everyone, I would say to play the original Evoland first:  This game is really good, but I think the elements in the original of slowly picking up game engine advancements like music / different bit images / etc as treasures along the way was a really great way of showing how games developed over time.  As a sequel, this game definitely surpasses the first, but I think they should still definitely be played in order.

It's got a lot of content but isn't bloated, which is sort of amazing to pull off given its breadth.
I have run into like, one bug and that's it.
It's got a pretty decent plot that Evoland lacked and the jokes are better in my opinion. In fact a lot of the things I felt frustrated about playing Evoland are improved, so if you played that game and felt a bit meh about it, then I would definitely say this is a different one much more fun to play.

The characters, although stereotyped to hell, were absolutely loveable, though they weren't consistently loveable. That's the other thing; the plot was terribly predictable and the story would be thrown into so much filler. From what I could make out, there were three main parts, and the first, which took me 10 hours, was all exposition. However, once the second part introduced the romance options, I immediately attached myself to the girl I chose. Her tropes, personality, mannerisms, and all, were too familiar. The game isn't too crude, actually, quite tame when compared to others. Like with most, the main male protagonist felt like a brutally accurate representation of me. Also, the music, although extremely repetitive(like, seriously, they reused it a ton)was fitting and really nice to listen to whether it was in the background or accompanying a cutscene. I don't regret putting 29 hours into this game. I stuck through it and the payoff was indescribeable.

I feel like it's time for me to write a review for this game, I've played it for over 100 hours after all.
Don't be turned away by the poor animation, dated graphics and mediocre soundtrack, the gameplay more than makes up for it.
First of all, optimization. It's pretty good. Usually when I play these types of games on my meh pc I'm limited by lag, but here you can build massive things without much lag at all.
Speaking of which, building. Being able to build not only bases, but also hovercraft, spaceships and even gigantic carriers is a dream coming true.
The feeling of first taking off in your freshly built ship, fly to the moon and have your ship be destroyed by an enemy base is magical, and thanks to the way the blueprint system works, you can salvage the wreck and build a new one to get away.
The learning curve is a thing though, and it'll take some time before you know how things work properly, but once you do... It's worth it.
Another thing I love is the community. Don't have friends? Make some! There are a lot of friendly and helpful people in the community, and before you know it you and your new buddies will get their asses kicked in PVP.
Empyrion isn't perfect, but it's still a great game.
If you can accept it's issues it has at the moment, you'll have a blast.

I have had at least 5 crashes in the time I've been playing the game, which of course means lost progress if there hasn't been a terribly recent save. On ths plus side, the game does save rather frequently, but I've had enough. Sound also "stagggers" and cuts out momentarily at random/
In addition to the technical issues, this game does not feel like a sequel to the first entry in the series at all. The first was a very, very brief adventure in which you collect upgrades to the very -world- you play in, such as music, 32 bit graphics, etc., and the game concludes not too long after you've obtained all the upgrades to the world, giving a short and fun experience.
This sequel, however, appears to be trying to make a legit action RPG that will last in the teens or twenties of hours (I took a peek at
and confirmed this), and even goes backward from graphical improvements at times. The biggest problem with this is that the story is very old school / simple with a lot of cliches and references to pop culture/other games, meaning it's the same thing as playing a lot of the RPG Maker games out there, except this one will look far worse for much longer because of the deliberately retro graphics.
The reason the first game worked was because the graphical improvements were progress, and the game was so short that the ugly graphics at parts didn't outstay their welcome. Here, the retro graphics set up shop for what appears to be hours on end. Please keep in mind that I like the old Doom better than the new one, so graphics are hardly my normal go-to for enjoyment of a game.
This game isn't awful, but it's deliberately an eyesore and goes on for far too long to have such a hum-drum story. Neither the plot nor the game mechanics have me wanting to continue, despite my enjoyment of the original.
A parody of video games that stands on its own.

In
you play as Aoi Minase, a student that is returning to his hometown of Kazegaura after having left years earlier. Including attending a new school, he also has a job as the dorm mother of a girls-only dormitory. He meets the wheelchair-bound Kotori and his friend from childhood Ageha. Along the way, he learns about the school's Soaring Club, a club dedicated to building a glider. At first they only have one member, the socially inept Amane, but Aoi becomes interested. He learns about Amane's dream of taking the glider and flying it through a rare weather phenomenon known as the "Morning Glory."
As a note for this review, I played the version with the fan restoration patch installed and that is the only version I am familiar with. More on that later.
This game is a visual novel, a type of video game that is entirely story-based. Unlike other visual novels, however, there are surprisingly few choices to make and which route you end up on is determined by those few decisions. There are five main endings to achieve (not counting a truncated "bad" ending), though only two routes are unlocked during the first play.
I think there was another reviewer on Steam that said something along the lines of that the good parts of this game are really good while the bad parts are really bad. I think I would have to echo that sentiment here.
Starting off with the art, I thought it was excellent in
. The background art all around is really pleasing to look at. This is especially true with many of the scenes that take place outdoors as the environment seems to evoke a kind of near-future setting with the focus on renewable energy in the form of windmills. It is also a real treat to look at the detail and colors that are used in the various flying scenes especially with scenes that take place during dawn. Aside from that, the characters are well-drawn, though it does mostly stick to the standard cute anime girls.
The music is another excellent aspect of this game. There is a decent amount of variation that really helps to set the moods of the various scenes. I especially enjoyed the more uplifting pieces. Also related to the audio, the game has voice acting in the original Japanese for all of the characters, with the exception of the player-character, Aoi. I particularly enjoyed the voice work of Aghea's actor, but all around it is an entertaining addition, even if you cannot understand Japanese.
As with any visual novel, the main aspects are the writing and characters. This is where the game really starts entering hit-and-miss territory. To start, the characters are decent enough. There are really no unlikable characters which would have really hurt the game. The characters do mostly adhere to some of the usual anime tropes, but in this case it actually works well. Granted, this means that some of the characters come off as a little flat, though still likable. In terms of development, however, most of them do not change much. Probably the only exceptions are Kotori's story arc and learning some of the background of Amane and her motivations.
Likewise, the story and writing runs the gamut from good to bad. I really enjoyed the first acts of this game as the characters are introduced and Aoi gets involved in the Soaring Club. It may not be a conflict-prone story, but it is an enjoyable, feels-good story about friendship and the ambition of trying to accomplish a goal. As I said, Kotori and Amane get the most development in this game and it made their particular routes the most interesting to play through.
However, the writing is imperfect. While there are not really parts that feel too bad, I did feel like there were areas where it could have used some work. I thought that Asa's route was rather boring as not much of substance occurs and the ending was rather abrupt. Even worse was the twins route which included themes of
which, to me anyway, just felt weird and out of place. Your own opinion may vary. And then there is Ageha's route. Even though it brings up some interesting topics about relationships, unfortunately, even with the restoration patch, the translation here is truly atrocious at some points. Not only are there tons of spelling errors, but sometimes the translation was so bad I was confused as to what was going on in the story. Overall, in other romance-themed visual novels I have played, there is usually an expectation that the quality of the main routes will be roughly equal. Sadly, I found that this is not the case here.
Another issue with the writing, though relatively minor, is the over reliance on some of the usual anime and visual novel tropes. This may annoy some who are not fans of anime. This includes the establishing premise of Aoi getting to live with many cute girls who seem to fawn over him, girls that seem overly eager to have sex once a relationship is established, and Aoi often coming across as the too-gentlemanly nice guy protagonist. Whether or not this is an issue for you is your own opinion.
Of course, no review of
would be complete without addressing the elephant in the room. Should you choose to install the restoration patch, there will be many sex scenes restored. I spent less than $5 on this game during the recent summer sale and I can say that with the number of hours I spent I definitely got my money's worth. EDIT: Note that this review got a very positive reply from the developer. Hopefully some of the issues I have will be addressed soon, at which point this review may switch to positive.
The concept of this game is excellent. They basically took Conway's Game of Life and turned it into a competitive RTS, which is cool... Unfortunately, what jumped out at me right away is that it's lacking any of the metagame to make it really work. When you click "Play", you're just given a few options to setup a custom game. There's no campaign. There's no progression. There's no gradual introduction of concepts. You're just thrown right into the deep end, and the only way to learn the mechanics is to read the help documentation on the main menu.
Further, the UI is rather poor. To select what to build, you click on a tool bar on the left. But I couldn't find a way to dismiss your current "tool", and any click on the toolbar also counts as a click on the ground behind it. If that space happens to be a valid place to build whatever you've got selected, well, you just built it! I ended up with some really badly placed extra taverns early on before I realized I had to be careful about how I clicked on the toolbar.
Finally, in my first game, after playing for about 10 minutes and feeling like I was finally starting to get the hang of it, the game just ... stopped. The music was still playing, the monsters were still doing their look bounce-in-place animation, I could still scroll around, select tools and initiate building, and bring up the menu. But the monsters weren't moving anymore. There was nothing to do but quit my game in progress.
Overall, this feels like an early access game. It's full of good ideas, but it's painfully under-developed.

1. Knowledge of Conway's Game of Life would benefit you greatly. I've noticed a couple people saying they're confused by the mechanics, but it's just a modified version of Conway's Game of Life, turned into an actual game.
2. There are ways to annihilate the computer player easily. If you destroy all your buildings, your cells will propogate into the world quite well. That said, I don't think that's a problem. The idea of the game is to use strategy to defeat the opponent, and that's really fun to do. Letting the game play itself doesn't even benefit you. The value of a victory in this game is that you were able to outplay the opponent, so if you didn't play at all, you gain nothing from a win.
Neither of those are bad things, Just maybe something to keep in mind if you're thinking about buying it.
Overall I like the game, personally I think it's fine as it is, but I'm excited to see where it goes.

- - -
Bear with me, you'll enjoy learning about the system behind the game:
I'm very familiar with cellular automata, and there are tons of different formulas in which the "Game of Life" can be played. Some are made for creating interesting patterns, others can run for hours on end and then fizzle out suddenly, but designing a formula requires balance.
Too many ways to reproduce? The entire screen will be choked out by rabidly deviding cells. Too few and the system will fizzle out with nary an interesting pattern.
This game's problem is with the former. I can literally put one road out of my tavern and overtake 3 AI's on the hardest difficulty, simply because the AI thinks about how to position it's forces, when all I do is let them breed and overtake the enemy with massive numbers.
It's a great game, it's unique, and clever, and frankly I'm impressed with how natural it is in almost a "factory designer" sort of way as you build roads to transport your troops, arm them, and then send them off to the enemy, but like I said, no one is going to need to do that.
How do we fix this? Well we need to take a look at the formula, and I'm sure in time the developers will change it, but as it stands, the game is broken.

if you take a look at my other screenshots you'll see what I mean.
Great idea though guys, keep it up!

Blackguards is a decent turn-based tactical RPG with gameplay mechanics based on The Dark Eye, which is basically the German equivalent to Dungeons and Dragons.  But unlike most games based on D&D, Blackguards (and most TDE games) is based on a relatively low-magic world.  This and some other things makes me think that TDE was perhaps not the best ruleset to base the game's engine on.
THE GOOD
-Challenging difficulty
-Characters are cliche, but well written
-Battlefields are almost always unique for each battle
THE BAD
-Needlessly complex character customization with very linear results
-Extremely frequent loading times
-Occasional chore-like battle
-Story falls flat
Blackguards plays like a more linear King's Bounty, except more linear and with actual party members instead of squadrons of soldiers.  I played Hard Mode on my first playthrough I found it to be very challenging; the game punishes you greatly for building characters incorrectly, doing poorly in certain battles (because you don't get healed for the next at!), and picking the wrong fights at the wrong time.  However, there is a good amount of diversity in game objectives and the battlefields are mostly unique for each battle.
Strategy in this game favors positioning above all else, because the strongest abilities in the game belong to melee and rangers whose primary attack abilities have no cooldowns and insignificant downsides to their use.  Mages are primarily support characters, and their best spells simply involve turning your melee guy into an even stronger skill spammer.  Had they used a different ruleset or made one of their own, they could have improved the strategy element of the battle system.  If you're going to make a turn-based strategy RPG, isn't strategy a lot of what the whole idea is about?
Don't expect the same kind of class diversity that D&D games have.  Despite the complexity of TDE's character customization, there isn't a lot of customization to be done.  Blackguards doesn't take a lot of steps to simplify the rules, but despite all of the little things the player must keep track of, the end result is almost always the same; melee and ranged guys hit hard, mages either cast support spells or suck.
Load times are unnecessarily frequent.  The game features a lot of cities, most of which don't have much unique to offer, yet trying to find quests in them involves watching a loading screen for each one.  It gets ridiculous because some of the cities have more than one section, with each section requiring even more time at the loading screen to move around to.
It was suggested by previews that Blackguards would set the player in the role of being the "bad guy" or at least the guy most people think is the bad guy.  The story even sets itself up with an intriguing mystery of laser guided amnesia, but aside from a couple scenes falls flat after the first chapter.  However, the voice acting is pretty good, and the characters, though cliche and mostly linear, are written quite well. Hell, Naurim is more memorable to me than any of the characters from Dragon Age: Origins.
With all of this negative stuff being said, I had decent fun playing Blackguards.  It's challenging, offers some diversity in scenarios and battlefields, and has decently well written characters.  Definitely try the demo before buying, it contains hours of content.  Buy it on sale.

As of this writing, I am at a point where I believe I am close to completing this game on the hardest difficulty. My experience thus far is that the game is well worth while, and I would recommend it to any fan of tactical RPGs. This review will cover positive aspects of the game, negative aspects of the game (and why they don't matter much), and advice for potential adventurers.
Positive aspects:
First and foremost, the leveling system is vast. You are confronted with tons of options right at the outset, which provides a good degree of clarity about how to plan your path. It is definitely viable to create hard class archetypes, and is likely also viable to create more versatile heroes. There is a solid mix of cheap levelling options that help do what you want your character to do now, and choices that allow you to transition to new skills later.
Second, the tactical combat is varied enough to prevent approaching all battles in the same way. Differences in enemy types  and compositions, apparent environmental attributes, hidden environmental objects, and varied victory conditions  all help to keep things fresh. Depending on these scenarios, I've had success with tactics involving methodical advancement, bait and run, divide and conquer, run and gun, and defensive walling. I imagine that if you built for it, you could plan to finish some battles with ranged attacks before the enemies even reach you.
In addition, it is worth mentioning a few things other than the core gameplay. The story is well-told and evenly-paced, and is compelling enough to justify the  constant fighting. The music is solid (though repetitive). And the world map is easy to navigate.
Negative aspects:
First, the graphical quality for character models is a little poor when seen up close. Characters don't look quite right facially, and when they talk you can even see that they don't have an inside to their mouths. Character portraits look little like their polygonal counterparts. While this can be offputting, it is not so apparent in battle view, and is not a major detriment.
The only other negative point is the tedious exploration. While map exploration is simple, it is a tedious point-and-click affair. Finding a quest sometimes means visiting each town (many of which look and feel the same) on the off-chance that it will have one, and clicking through each of the people to make sure. Because this is quickly accomplished, it is not a huge drawback, but it is a boring aspect of the game.
My advice:
Some helpful pointers for those who do choose to buy this game (my first piece of advice is that you do) are below:
- Start with a notion of what you want each of your characters to do, and focus solely on that at first (melee vs. ranged vs. magic, choice of weapons, choice of spells). Plan to branch your characters out later.
- It is probably best to make your starting character a magic user, even if you don't plan to focus on spells right away. I don't feel particularly disadvantaged by not having done so, but I can see how an additional magic user could be helpful down the road.
- Don't focus on magic for your starting character, even if you make them a magic user. You will get other characters, and you probably don't need more than one pure mage.
- Magic users aren't great early on, but focusing on healing first is a big help to boosting their early-game usefulness without taking away from long-term viability.
- You will want at least one ranged character, and it will be obvious at a few points in the game who can fill that role.
- Stats and skills that accomplish more per turn/action are more valuable than capacity stats like HP and Astral Points.
- Gold matters a ton in the early parts of the game, and not at all after. Your priority spending should be on the best weapons you can find, followed by set armor.
- It is okay to skip a quest you're not ready for. Some builds can't handle some scenarios, and you may need to level up a little more to take it on. This is a likely but infrequent occurrence. As far as I can tell, quests don't disappear just by waiting.
- Don't be afraid to re-roll and start over. It is tempting to try different things, and you may discover early in the game that your build isn't working like you wanted. Your second try will be much improved.
Thank you for reading, I hope it was helpful, and please let others know whether or not you found this review informative.

Codename CURE is a first-person, co-operative, zombie themed game for up to five players. The game was built around the Source engine and heavily borrows gunplay aspects from that of L4D2 and the Half-Life series. With the game being built around the Source engine, the game already looks very dated, appearing to fall somewhere between Half-Life and Half-Life 2 at best, thus the game is not taxing on your PC and looks unfinished.
The game's premise is very straight forward: kill zombies, plant a bomb and escape before the time runs out. If you're playing the newly added "Survival Mode", then you simply have to survive wave after wave of zombies until your eventual demise. As for the plot, there isn't one, really. You play as any number of unnamed soldiers ordered to "cure" an area of infected zombies. For those worried about spoilers: who you are, what happened and who you work for is never answered.
The game is broken up into five classes, with different loadouts, which you may choose from: Pointman (Semi-Auto Shotgun), Support (SMG/Supply Crates), Assault (Assault Rifle), Technician (Pump Shotgun/Turret) and Sniper (Sniper Rifle). Despite having five classes, only the "Support" and "Technician" classes play differently than the rest; the rest being, "run-and-gun" (Yes, even the sniper).
The main game mode consists of five levels with varying layouts that you can pick in any order. Your average level will consist of scattered vehicle props, abandoned and unfurnished buildings and zombies. The levels themselves are bland and uninteresting, making them easily forgettable when you move onto the next stage. That being said, the only redeemable feature is the change in level layout, which is marginal at best (I.E. sometimes you go right instead of going left). The only replayability comes from those wishing to grind out the achievements on higher difficulties, which, too the game's credit, can be rather difficult, though that difficulty is rather artificial; dependent on zombie spawn and level layout.
As far as multiplayer goes, there are dedicated servers, but hosting P2P is also an option. The game is playable for up to five humans with bots filling any empty slots if you desire. The AI is nothing more than a means to avoid damage. They often fail to avoid enemy attacks, use pistols instead of their primary weapon and throw grenades at walls, the ground, and sometimes...a solitary enemy. The AI is hilarious for all the wrong reasons, but playing without these meat shields can be very difficult if you don't have other players helping you. They're a burden, but a necessary one.
The newest patch introduced a "Survival" mode, which pits you against an endless hoard of zombies in ever-increasing waves. For now, survival is rather broken. You start with a pistol and after each wave you're rewarded with a new, random gun. In theory, the gun is weighted against the difficulty of the hoard you're facing, but that's not the case. Instead, you're rarely given anything aside from a variety of pistols, the occasional shotgun and once we earned the MP5.
The bots in survival are even worse, as they never get anything other than basic pistols and have no means to obtain additional ammo once they run out, forcing you to kill them so they respawn with more ammo. It's a clunky system based on a little bit of skill, abusing game mechanics to lessen handicaps and a gun lotto system that either ease the challenge, or spell your quick demise. The name of the game is survival, but you probably won't.

Codename CURE is a multiplayer zombie shooter developed in the sawce engine and is currently (at the time of writing) in Early Access.
The game comprises itself on its 5/6 classes each with different skills and weapons. The Pointman has an automatic shotgun capable of decimating zombies and a couple grenades. The Technician can deploy a sentry. Assault has grenades and an assault rifle with a huge ammo capacity. The sniper has a sniper and incendiary (which means fire) grenades. And finally, support gives support (duh)
Pros -
+ Fast Paced Gameplay
+ Maps occasionally randomize (just doors, it's a nice touch)
+ It has mod support (it is a HL2 mod so it has Hammer)
Cons -
- It's in Early Access (urgh)
- Only 2 gamemodes (objective and survival)
- No class customization (only given a select few weapons with no ability to change or improve)
- Level design is a bit unintuitive (there isn't much detail and the environments are quite blocky)
- Gets repetitive after a while.
The Verdict:
Codename CURE is a well rounded, well balanced shooter which can be picked up and played and can provide quite a bit of fun, although it doesn't last for that long.
So I give it a 7/10

Take a look at
. The text log starts at the very beginning of the scene. Does this make sense to you? It certainly doesn't to me. Is there an invisible man hitting everyone with a cane that I don't know about? , and comparing it with the dialogue only confirms my suspicions. I understand that it's a fan translation and may not be localized perfectly, but it's not even that - it's just completely wrong.

After finishing Batman Arkham City for like 5-6 times, playing the DLC and doing some challenges i feel like it's time to write a review of this already kinda old game.
Let's start with the basic factor all games should be good on: gameplay. First of all i gotta say that Arkham City really improves the formula from the last game (Arkham Asylum). Introducing new enemies, new combos and new character, Arkham City mantains the fun and satisfaction from this combat system. Is the game easy? Well, it depends on how much you get used to the combat system. To be honest i don't mind if a game is easy as long as it's fun and i can say that this game is really fun and entertaining. One thing i'd like to mention about the city is the fact that it feels alive, full of enemies and stories to tell.
Moving on: Story. I don't really want to spoil anything from the main plot so... i'll just say that Arkham City's story is really good and really well developed. If you're a fan of the dark knight the you'll be satisfied with this game's story.
Soundtrack: one of my favorite part of this. Well, this part is really important since being Batman is not as good as it sounds without music, and Rocksteady did i really good job in this aspect. Putting the correct OST (or not putting one) in the correct time is really important when it comes about describing a situation.
Graphics and performance: The game ran kinda well... i mean, i did notice some sttutering from time to time (mostly while gliding) but nothing too significant. Graphics are really good for a 2011 game and for this kinds of game i feel like graphics can improve the general experience. This game did just that, using the correct art and taking advantge of it.
Overall the game is really good and a must have for any Batman fan and general user. It's fun, entertaining, have good ost and story. Some bad parts would be that sometimes sidequest are a little annoying (not all of them, but some), some puzzles are not very intuitive and the stuttering was really bad sometimes.
Recommended price: 5$-10$

Cellular Automata is a fun strategy game about, well, automatons which you will attempt (and miserably fail at first) to control.
Unlike in other strategy games you cannot directly control your units, instead you can influence them through buildings such as roads or catapults, meaning winning is as much about "engineering" as about fighting. The ressource system in this game is that each building costs units, killing said units if they are nearby or otherwise failing to be built which adds more difficulties to building a massive wall for instance.
You can (and will) indeed kill yourself without all the help from anyone.
The principle of the game makes for really fun and interesting gameplay which is quite unique.
There are 5 game modes, war (annihilate the enemy), capture the flag, king of the hill, fort (defend a fort and protect it from enemies) and my personal favourite migration (you have a huge horde comming at you from the bottom and all players have to scramble to flee them while killing each other)
At the moment it does just have singleplayer which despite various gamemodes may for certain people not be worth it.
However if you are a strategy fan you should at the very least follow this game and wait for the multiplayer, which should be great fun.

This is a turn based, hexgrid, dungeon crawler, rpg based on a not unheard of tabletop system.
It plays like a fan created mod to another game, in every way this game screams its lack of polish, it's terrible design and its aweful assets. This game makes NWN 1+2 look cutting edge
*FLAWS*
1) Inconsistant Mechanics; in short, they're half baked. An early mechanic is terrain tiles (water is slippery, bushes are flammable etc) and in theory these could make for some more complex tactical play, but sometimes thats not the case, water may just be a watery looking tile, or it may cause you to fall on your♥♥♥♥♥and be prone for a turn. Enemies never use them either, they just move to attack range throw fire, ice and poison.
2) Incorrect RNG; this is a tabletop system adapted for the PC, so of course its simmulating (with a pretty bad generator I might add) die rolls under the hood. You get told a percentage chance to hit (and can level up enough to see other stats) but the percentage shown is WRONG. That's right, the game actively lies to you because its number generation system isn't implemented right. 100% chance is actualy 90%, 65% is actualy 40%. You will also see the same resualt consistantly for mid range %, every time I fire an arrow at a humanoid enemy with a 65% chance to hit I would miss without fail. same goes for 50% with melee, this makes me think the random generator isn't so random after all.
3) Atrocious Voice acting; Dear gods is it terrible, it's not even laughably bad, the actors are often re-used but its like no-one told them they were doing different characters so everyone they voice sounds identicle. They were also clearly recorded completly seperatly without any lead in or practice because they're all delivered with the same dry detatchment of people with a full frontal lobotomy.
4) Poor story telling; The plot may improve as time goes on, but from what I've experienced so far I can already tell you my version "And so it was that the brave ranger stabbed the annoying sidekicks while they slept and went to live away from the continent full of madmen". Honestly it started out bad enough with the giant wolf having killed (or having been eating) a random damsel, you kill the wolf and then get arrested for her murder. The wolf was right there, you kill it, its body is lying on the ground next to the corpse, yet they arrest you for her murder. The rest of the story was following a bread crumb story into a veriaty of linier dungeons, speaking of which.
5) Dull Dungeon Design; if you're making a dungeon crawler then you need decent dungeons, so far everything has been a straight line with preset encounters, no element of maze, mystery or surprise. You know you will need to enter each point on the dungeon map, you know that each point is going to have an encounter, and you know that you will want to save scum the hell out of it just to preserve your precious resources.
6) Cheap assets; It's ugly. Very Ugly. There is no sense of unifying aesthetic. Everything is the same blocky 3d models with dodgy shadowing, terrain detailing can actualy conflict with mechanics "is that shoreline tile a water tile or a land tile? You won't know till you step on it" the models are barely detailed, only slightly more complex than the 3d models used for CIV V (the ones designed to render quickly at distance and not be looked at too closely). Combine this with a lack luster muZak score and it just doesn't feel good to experience.
7) Poor Performance; for a PC game, its not offering much in the way of performance options. You can set nebulous graphics quality but get no fine choice, you can pick a resolution but theres no windowed mode. In game I've seen multiple graphics glitches caused by lighting effects, flickering textures and even the Hex Grid breaking and flashing at the bottom of the screen.

I think this game has the potential to be something very, very special.
Unfortunately there are a lot of people giving negative reviews for a lot of different reasons; content is unfinished, pve is crap, glitches, hackers, etc., etc. THIS IS AN ALPHA RELEASE! All of this is to be expected! This game isn't finished. Not even close. This is clearly stated on the Steam storefront page.  At this point, purchasing this game basically means you are donating money to the devs to continue and hopefully finish development.
In my opinion, alpha players should focus on where the game is headed and provide constructive feedback to help improve it. But to do so you have to see the overall vision, not just the pixels. If you think the game is total crap, cool. Just be sure to tell the devs why it is crap, and f you’re feeling extra charitable, maybe throw in a suggestion or two as to how they can fix it. As an alpha player, you have one of the rarest and most exciting opportunities as a gamer; you get to help shape the future of a game and truly make it yours.
Hoping the devs read these reviews. If so, here are my two cents.
---The Good---
-Excellent musical score and sound.
-High potential for immersion.
-Very good looking graphics & environment.
-Innovative weather and seasonal system.
-Intuitive controls and default key mappings.
-Outstanding UI. Very logical, minimalist design.
-Skill based combat. Archery is already pretty good as is.
-Outstanding crafting system.
-Hybrid PvP looting system.
---The Bad---
General:
-Bugs, exploits, glitches and optimization issues. You already know about most, if not all of this. Moving on…
Player Movement:
-Walking, running and movement feels slow, unresponsive and cumbersome. Jumping and climbing are awful.
Environmental Interaction:
-Character feels very separate and disconnected from the environment. Character should feel connected to the ground, not floating on top of it. Fences, rocks, bags, etc. seem to have invisible force fields around them. This is very distracting and ultimately hurts immersion.
-Fix tree animations. Trees look like someone is violently shaking them or they are floating in water.
User Interface:
-Separate chat into zones. Otherwise global chat will be an absolute nightmare.
Combat:
-Collision physics and hit reg. This needs A TON of work. Hitting an enemy should feel impactful, satisfying and rewarding. Not random, weak and detached.
-Player animations. I believe you are already addressing this, but it still needs quite a bit of work.
-Responsiveness. Weapon swings and meter charging should be a bit faster and much more responsive. This should help make combat feel much more fluid, organic and immersive.
-Sync graphics, sound and hit reg. If I miss an opponent, I should hear a “whoosh,” not a “cleave” or a “thud.”
-Add visual hit display for melee combat. The point of impact should be visually apparent on the enemy’s body (similar to the system you already have in place with arrows).
Feature Requests:
-Battlegrounds. Lots of them. Capture the flag, king of the hill, etc., etc.
-Medieval siege weapons (trebuchet, etc.) for RvR and PvP battlegrounds.
-Arena (1v1, 2v2, 5v5, etc.).
-Mounts and mounted combat.
-Crank up the gore and animations to reflect medieval brutality. Beheadings anyone?!?!
Final Thoughts:
-Personally, I think the combat system mechanics are the single most important thing to focus on and will ultimately make or break this game. Make Gloria Victis the preeminent medieval MMO it is begging to be! SO MUCH potential here...
THANKS FOR ALL OF YOUR HARD WORK!!!

Wasteland Angel is a Road Warrior/Death Race hybrid themed isometric car battle game. You are Angel, a beautiful but tough woman travelling around the post-apocalytpic United States in search of your friend, Eks, in your armoured car 'Gypsy'. As you travel around, you encounter towns under attack by Wastelanders and you help to defend them.
You are able to pick up weapon upgrades and special weapons to help you do this, and there is a wide variety of each, though the by far most useful is your main weapon, as most of the rest require good placement and the enemy AI is erratic at best. One of the problems with the weapon upgrade system is that eventually your main gun becomes powerful enough you can quite literally pick a spot and just rotate on it like a turret. Thankfully, weapon upgrades do not carry from one stage to the next.
Wasteland Angel, is, however one a game added to the list of games where the minigames are better than the actual game. At the end of each stage is a bonus level, which takes the game from isometric to first person, which I found a lot more fun than the base missions themselves.
The game's physics engine is... well... it's VERY arcady to say the least. Often times collisions cause your car to spin out of control, way beyond what would be reasonable. Fortunately there is a reset button to right yourself fairly quickly, though a lot of time this can mean failing to save and/or running over civilians. Worse yet, often times enemy cars will get 'stuck' offscreen, preventing you from finishing the wave until a car from the next wave hits them to get them unstuck.
Graphically the game is okay. It isn't spectacular, but I have definitely seen a lot worse. The audio is decent, and the voice acting is comically bad but I am left with the impression that this is on purpose. The music gets irritating VERY quickly, but a lot of the time I didn't notice. I had tuned it out because I was focusing on the sometimes very frantic gameplay.
The game is very short. I was able to complete the game and collect all 40 achievements in just under 4 hours. It has the length and the equivalent overall quality to a mobile game, therefore while it is a lot of fun I think $9.99 is asking a little bit too much. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys arcade games, but only if they were able to pick it up on sale for 50% off or better.

Evoland 2 exceeded the high expectations that I had coming into this game.  I was a big fan of the first Evoland, and was expecting a similar gametype (of "unlocking" game features as you play along).  What I got, however, was a fantastic game that didn't rely heavily on a central gimmick.
What I liked:
The Story - The story in EL2 is phenominal.  You aren't held by the hand and force-fed the lore except for crucial game moments.  Without spoiling much, know that there are many plot twists that will keep you guessing and wanting more even up until the final moments of the game.
The Genres - I won't begin to explain the different levels and concepts.  Partially because it would contain spoilers, but also because the shock value of realizing what is going on is too rich to pass up.
The Card Game - I'm a sucker for RPG card games, and this is an optional part of the game.  The card game has a "magic the gathering" feel to it, and I would love to play more of it.
Humor - This game is full of witty humor and outlandish situations. At times, a character will say what we are thinking, and you can't help but laugh at the
What I disliked:
Progression - Since EL2 has an open map, it is easy to spend countless minutes trying to remember where you are supposed to go and what you are supposed to do.  Later in the game, this became easier when a character gave clues as to five main objectives, but there was a few moments I had to google where I was supposed to go next.
Walking -  I would have loved a "run" feature.  Spending time walking around to get to objectives and hunting down key items
Returning Events - I would also like to replay certain side quests.  There aren't any "missable" items, but missable game features.  Perhaps using a NPC to initiate former mini games and game modes would have been great.
I HIGHLY recommend Evoland 2 to any fan of RPGS, Platforming, or gaming in general.  You will not regret this purchase.
10/10

Evoland 2 has been one of the most enjoyable RPG games I have played in some time.  If you played the first game then you get the idea of this game evolving through classic RPG styles.  Yet Evoland 2 goes beyond what the first did.  The larger more in depth story line along with going beyond just RPG game play, but including elements from every classic game style of the early arcade and console generations.  Platforming, side scroll shooter, top base shooter, side scroll beat-up, one on one combat, DDR, tactical and so on.
You are no longer exploring the evolution of the RPG game.  You are experiencing the all encompassing game world.
You follow the story and don't know what will come next.  The game style switches fluidly from one to the other.  No game play style feels out of place.  While there are types of games I am not good at *COUGH DDR*.  Each style provides that bit of challenge but is not impossible even if you hate that style.  Don't like mortal combat game play, well it's a part of the game but you can do it.
There is not enough that can be said about how great this game is.  I don't want to spoil anything.  Just that it is worth FULL PRICE and few games are.

Truly an amazing game with a very real feel of sandbox play. Despite what faction you choose to start out with, maintaining or changing your affiliations via reputation or otherwise is all in how you decide to play a role. I'm not a huge fan of the ship design limitations, especially that adding a small room to the inside of your ship creates a HUGE set of obnoxious and (frankly) off-scale exterior blocks that can seriously ruin your ideal image/design of your creation.
The universe is simply huge and I'd gather it's every bit as big as Elite Dangerous', No Man's Sky's, or Star Citizen's universe. When the ship tells you that it will take 3000+ days to get to a location without accelerating, it means it and it's very obvious from the first time you set to leave a planet's nearby exo-sphere at anything less that Warp 3. I love this game, it's got all the right elements there for PvP and PvE and the amount of grind is also, notably, balanced as well. Combat could use some more polishing, joystick HOTAS integration is still needed, and the ship editor needs some tweaking, but overall the game is pretty awesome and if the playerbase would simply give it a chance, I think we really see a hard hitting competitor in the mix here.

Great fun for designing ships once you figure out how the editor and ship systems work and interact. In sandbox (creative mode) you can just play around and build ships, which works pretty good. Ship building and that is great. I also love how players can multicrew ships, and actually move around them as they fly around, unlike most other games where you have to occupy a slot or station. Thats where this game really shines.
That said: On the servers you have to mine all the resources you need for your ships, which to be honest just feels like a massive grind. There is no real alternative I suppose, unless ship designs were somehow based on ranks or faction.
So you might start by producing a small ship that is simply designed to mine faster so you can build the next ship, until you finally build your big badass exploration ship. This takes days or weeks to do. Now what?
You can go to different systems, but there really isnt anything there for you. There is one kind of AI enemy called Skrill (apart from defence drones/turrets); a dragon like space enemy that attacks you, and it is fun to fight them off, but I really want more variation.
Facing hardcore PVP player ships is really frustrating since you normally are screwed the moment you notice the first missiles hit you. Chances to survive a surprise attack from a decent player is less than slim. It's like being on the recieving end of a wwii german submarine and waking up from the blast of a torpedo. I gave some suggestions about stealth mechanics and early warning systems, but havent seen anything of it.
We spent like a week building a big♥♥♥♥♥exploration ship, and took our crew of four out on a spin to the next system. We went exploring different stuff popping up on the radar and suddenly, out of nowhere, a barrage of missiles and shells started to rain down on us. Another player had stalked us and attacked. Fun, right? Well, turned out it wasnt cause before we even made it to weapon stations the shield was down, and hull started to go critical. We didnt even have time to target or manuever the ship before it went boom, and was lost. A week of grinding gone. Good PVP kill, but it's just a bit too harsh and unfun. I mean even for the hardcore PVP guys playing on empty severs must suck. That server went down not long after, since quite a few crews had the same experience as us. Now all I see is almost empty servers.
Maybe if the game had more players, or if there were AI ships to attack? Lets hope they manage to hold this game together that long and we might return. For now, I can't really recommend for anything other thatn playing around with freinds in creative mode, or with the excellent editor.

The graphics are pretty great, but the rest of the game is mediocre. This is one of those games that's equally bad and good. Sometimes it's fun, sometimes it's boring. The gameplay is whatever. Enemies seem to be blind most of the time, but there is one really interesting mechanic where you can't just walk into items on the floor like a bucket or a mop, since they will fall over, make sounds and alert the guards. It's clever because like an actual stealth mission you have to avoid walking into items.
There's some amount of verticality in almost every level, which is kind of fun. However, combat is downright crap. Once a guard spots you it's like fighting as a stretchy old man who is drunk and blind. If you get spotted it just feels so bad to fight the guards that you mostly just load an old save.
There's a few smart things like blowing out torches with balls of sand (Which for some reason you can't throw at guards and which are also almost never spotted by said guards) but most of the time the game is very bland. I guess it's in need of a makeover, but it's a teeny bit more fun and boring so I recommend it. Still, don't expect this to be your Deus Ex/Dishonored/Metal Gear Solid of stealth.

What Moenovel sell this game as the "All-Aged" version is a little bit different than the original version of the game, which removes the spices of the game which is the R18 contents of this game, and leaves the game with somewhat "crappy" version of what the game is supposed to be. In addition, we would also have to deal with the relatively poor English translation within some parts of the story.
However, this game is a great visual novel at its finest. It has all the things that worth the amount of money we buy for this game, which are the cool soundtracks, the beautiful artwork alongside its entertaining CGs, and also the expressive Voice Actors and Voice Actresses which express the dialogues perfectly.
But above all, the magnificient storyline that the game offers which made me felt quite satisfied even though that this version cuts all of the other "good parts" of the VN, which in other perspective, makes you feel secured in just focusing to the story rather than constantly being alert of emerging into "the scene" and got caught by those misunderstood people.
Overall, it is arguably one of the best Visual Novel that is worth the money, despite the fact that this "all aged" version means that we are buying the rather crappy version of the game

Wasteland Angel is the humble story of a woman and her car trying to make it in America. The Wasteland Angel doesn't have a name, so let's call her Mad Maxine. Her car Gypsy is built like a tank, ready to take on World War
WW3 already happened and everybody lost. The scant remnants of humanity are just trying to survive under the crushing weight of evil. As the vigilante heroine you gotta protect the cities and kill all the bad guys.
This game has been making the rounds on various indie bundle sites. It's likely that you already have it (and you don't even know). My suggestion is to give it a shot and here's why:
First and foremost this is an arcade-styled game. There's a scoring system, multipliers, bonus points, all that good stuff. Your primary objective is the survival of both yourself and 100 civilians. The enemies arrive in various vehicles and they're either targeting you, the civvies, or both. Regularly out-numbered (but never out-gunned) you make short work of everyone as they arrive in waves. Any leftover time in-between waves is best spent recharging in the city for bonus points. Occasionally secondary objectives will pop up. They are of the "do this" or "destroy that" variety.
Aside from the first-person bonus rounds, Wasteland Angel uses an overhead view. It's pretty easy to track the action and indicators will light up if enemies are kidnapping people. Destroyed vehicles tend to drop power-ups. I'd probably be a little worried if everyone happened to have an air strike or a nuke in their car but eh...it's a videogame. Every few stages there's a boss fight. They're pretty standard, though they can only be damaged by power-ups (napalm, mines, etc).
For the most part Wasteland Angel does the job. It's a fun game. Destroying those stupid bad-guys is satisfying, especially when it involves dropping a nuke on 6-7 of them. After you destroy their vehicles you can gun them down. The controls are satisfactory, and with 20+ stages and leaderboards there's no lack of content.
HOWEVER. There is room for improvement. First and foremost, Wasteland Angel runs a bit long for an arcade-styled game. While playing single stages for score is fine, going through the entire campaign is going to take a few hours. Even with the option to save and quit between stages, this isn't quite ideal. I'm thinking instead of one long campaign, just cut it up into three or four. Also in the interest of pacing, each stage would have less but more intense waves.
Another issue is that the controls could be better. Well maybe better isn't the right word. Maybe uh...more technical? Technique? Ehh I'll think of a better word later. Anyway I'm thinking that Gypsy could use some more moves. While getting around the wasteland is fine as is, some tricks would help getting in getting out of screwy situations. It would also give the developers more room to try more ideas. For example, maybe the RB & LB buttons could be used for doing barrel rolls. Yeah I know "Do a barrel roll!" is hilarious & timely but seriously. Give the car a flippy move for dodging dangerous crap like missiles. Or if it looks like you're going to hit a building and crash just WHOOSH look at all the time you're saving. As a bonus, pressing LB & RB together could result in a 180 spin. The controls in this game are responsive as is, but more abilities couldn't hurt.
Updating the controls would also lead to better boss-fights I imagine. The few in Wasteland Angel 1 are lacking. The first couple are indirect fights. By this I mean you're dropping mines or napalm for them to run into, you're not actively fighting them. The current level of maneuverability just isn't enough to take these big guys head-on. Also there's a fight with a super mutant. I guess it's kinda direct in that you actually have to shoot him, but that's only after dropping an EMP to stun him for a couple seconds. Also the tank boss can be annoying, since it prefers to hang back and snipe at you rather than run over all the fresh mines you've laid out for him.
Also this probably counts as more of a nitpick but there have been a couple occasions, where I got stuck on something. There was also a time an enemy seemingly disappeared, but it didn't count as destroyed so I lost out on bonus points. Some of the stages are also a little too cluttered and lack the proper amount of "flow". Maybe for a sequel, they could use a base design for each stage. It doesn't have to be something obvious like a circle, but it has to be easily indentifiable to the player so they're not driving into a seemingly random wall just to rescue some hapless civilians.
Oh and make it so it's easier to run enemies over.
Still, Wasteland Angel isn't too bad a game. It has the right concept, a solid core, it just needs some tweaks and it could turn out to be something really good.
YMMV
PS - Everytime I type "Wasteland Angel" I keep accidentally typing "Wastleand". Yeah I don't know either.

I enjoyed this game (hence the recommendation) but I really must caveat this, because this game is a cruel mistress.
Pros and cons as follows, because how much each point sways you will govern how much you get out of this game.
On the whole I enjoyed it.
Pros:
- Funny dialogue and interesting characters. Naurim might be the greatest character in Western RPG history
- Deep strategy. There are lots of environment effects, ways to optimise and spells to learn.
- Good voice acting. Genuinely good and a nice array of accents. Apart from the main characters female voice
- Dark, gritty artistic direction. Few games capture being and anti-hero so well, with murky non-binary decision making
- Challenge. Good god the challenge.
Cons
-  It's a bit... broken. Little things that seem to have been left incomplete, or lack polish. This includes a few bugs with quests and achievements. A good example is that the combat controls list auto-save, but if you try to use it, the game says you can't.
- Not explaining things. Sometimes you will see environmental effects or objects, but have no idea what they are or do until they kill you. Sometimes it will drop you in a level with a special win condition, but it won't be clear what it is. This is fine once you work it out, but causes a bit of trial-and-error frustration
- The ending is, well, balls. Quite simply. There are apparently multiple endings, but to me the last chapter and ending felt a bit rushed.
