Empyiron Galactic Survival is what Space Engineers should have been.  Even in its current alpha 6.x/7.x release, there are little to no bugs and the game has more features than anything I have ever played in an EA phase game.  The graphics are good enough for the current level of development, nothing is ugly and everything looks decent if not great for the most part.  I haven't found any graphical glitches yet, which once again says quite a bit for an alpha game.
In Empyrion you can start in a multitude of scenarios.  You can start with an escape pod torpedoing to the surface of a planet, you can start on a taken over space station, and a myriad of other scenarios.  You pick the planet you want to start on and what you have at your disposal is dependent on the difficulty setting.  I think I need to make a statement before I go any further.  There is ZERO grind in this game when it comes to getting things you need.  You don't need to farm for 15 hours to get enough to build for 5 minutes.  I can get a base up, hover vehicle, and space vehicle built in under 5 hours and be completely self sufficient so I can focus on building a space station or capital ship that is armed to the teeth.
As far as the survival mode aspect goes, food, oxygen, stamina, and health are your 4 stats you need to keep in good shape.  Stamina for running which regenerates on its own, health can get raised through food, medic bays, health packs, and other medicines.  Oxygen is simple enough, use a oxygen tank or station and recharge whle food speaks for itself.
When building a base, you need fuel tanks, a generator of any size, and a power source to get everything up and running.  Promethium, the games energy crystals are the best source of energy.  That being said, there are hydrogen packs that can be used if you are in a pinch.
Physics such as gravity play an important role in what you are doing.  Each planet has its own gravity which makes vector of approach somewhat important.  Also, if you are building a ship or station in space, make sure you are out of the sphere of unfluence for gravity or your ship/station is going to look like the crashed stuff on the moons and planets before you got there.
Warp drive for other systems and resources you can't accumulate is a necessity which can be put on capital ships and in 7.X small ships as well.  Aesthetics for decoration are plentiful, guns are endless from basic gatling guns to full blown plasma guns and rail guns.  Keeping ammo stocked is important but making sure you are ready to get hit is paramount.  Regular steel is not going to cut it.  I remember when I ate my first rocket in my small attack fighter, luckily I had spare components in my cargo box, I lost an engine and went spiraling to oblivion until I could get the ship pointed in the right direction.
Mining, some people hate it and I don't blame them.  Doing this by hand just sucks but once you get a hover vehicle and strap some drills on them, either mechanical or laser, you can mine an entire node out in 5 minutes and have enough for a long time.  Again, the grind is minimal if not zero.  Additionally, if you host a server, you can speed some of these things up.  Like leveling up which is already quick, you can increase even more, you can turn on ore regeneration, decay rates, etc.
Overall, if you liked Space Engineers but didn't want the botched multiplayer and crap beta implementation then this game is for you.  I really enjoy it and I'm sure you will too if these kinds of games are your thing.  The universe is alive and aliens will attack you.  Drones will seek you out, alien ships will open fire, and dont♥♥♥♥♥♥off the natives.

I felt the game started a little slow, took off and didn't slow down until the anticlimactic ending. I was able to beat the game with over 30 hours which included the DLC. The DLC was integrated into the main campaign, which was nice. I like a game that doesn't overstay it's welcome.
Regarding difficulty, I felt many previous The Dark Eye games were much more difficult and appreciated the fact that I was able to get through this game with minimal issues. It is a strategy game, so if you pick poor weapon and spell combinations,you will hit a brick wall you can't pass. If you are having difficulty with the game, lower the difficulty. Another bonus is the game starts up quick and you can skip the intro and get right to the menu. It is worth mentioning with so many games forcing you to wait through minutes of unskippable logos.

Blackguards would be an overall very good game if it wasn't for a few but very impactfull flaws.
I wont indulge in the pros, you can read on for that, I'll just briefly explain why I abandoned a game that I mostly enjoyed at the beginning of the final chapter.
First it lacks an element that should be at the very core of a game of this genre: character/team customization.
You get a very limited number of characters which is 4, one of them will be swapped with another at a point in the story leaving you with an underpowered character as well. You don't really have a real choice on how to develop them, there is a few things you can decide but since mages are defined by their magic and one of the fighters comes in already half trained the tactical phisionomy of your team is pretty much decided before you start the game. You can customize your main character a bit more but you'll realize that the only role lacking in your team will be an archer which is also the stronger dps in the game...
Second and most important: everytime a loading screens appears cross your fingers because there's a good chance the game is gonna crash. This is most definetly something that can be fixed and it's also something that didn't affect every player,  but given how frequent and long the loading screens generally are it really ruined my experience with this game.
Third: devs brag a lot a about the depth of the story, they also use it as an alibi to justify things like killing fresh characters for no reason and the impossibility to farm. But the truth is there is not much of a story at all, the most of the game is a barely engagefull hunt for clues to unveil the mistery of what happened at the beginning, very linear, not interactive at all, if you're into powerfull story-driven stuff this game will strike you as trivial and stupid at some points.
Also given the price nowadays there's plenty more games of the same genre you might wanna give a shot to on steam that look much more promising.

The question you first need to ask yourself is:
Why should I confront my eyes with a resolution of 320x200 for hours?
The answer is:
- You fly the Grumman F-14B Tomcat
- You feel like being in Top Gun as both Maverick and Goose flying with Icemen on your side.
- You can switch seats between the pilot and the radar intercept officer (RIO)
- Accurately modeled avionics and weapons
- Complex AWG-9 radar (adjustable to make it simpler if needed)
- A big manual written by a F-14 pilot
- Lot's of training missions like (radar training: Identify formations, headons against different fighters etc.)
- 6 campaigns
- Good atmosphere which recent titles struggle to deliver
- And ofcourse: Cold War gone hot
The bad points:
- The graphics are a low resolution texture-mess to be honest.
- The outside view is jerking around planes when panning.
- The AI wingman has some strange flight physics.. jerking around too when in formation (but it's acceptable)
- A bit DOSBOX knowledge is needed to configure the game properly.
- For whatever reason, this sim is not directly sold as the "Gold"-version, but it is with it's two extra campaigns and the videos =>  See damson's video uploads in the community hub (guides).
Final word:
If you don't care about the graphics, you will get rewarded a full sim which isn't far away from titles like ex-"Lock On" Flaming Cliffs 3. This sim expects you to throw some time into it and learn how to operate the F-14B efficiently and keep your situational awareness up, which can be quite hard at the beginning.
Additional stuff:
### DOSBOX
- If you have a 3D Joystick (example Thrustmaster 16000M) you will need to edit the "STEAMFOLDER\common\Fleet Defender\dosbox_windows\dosbox_fleetdefender.conf" file with an editor:
joysticktype=fcs
timed=false
autofire=false
swap34=true
buttonwrap=false
Buttonwrap not experimented with yet. "swap34" means to swap the 3rd axis with the 4th since most games have them setup like 1234 instead of 1243, having the slider for rudder and the Z axis for throttle-inputs.
- While ingame, press STRG/CTRL F12 to cycle up the CPU thus making the game faster and STRG/CTRL F11 to cycle down.
### Important additional information / Errors within the manual and documentation
Not all manuals are without mistakes. This site corrects lots of stuff which the manual explains simply wrong. It's important that you crosscheck what you have read in the manual with this website:

A couple of things you should know. This is abandonware, that means that the company that did this doesn't exist anymore(in fact it doesn't exist since 1999). So that means there is no support and that you can get this for free on most abandonware pages, and run it with DosBox. Yes, the Steam version also runs with DosBox, and also allows you to run it with JukeBox.
Second thing is that if you don't have a US keyboard you are going to have problems with a couple of functions, like the throttle or switching to the RIO seat. There is a fix for this: editing the DosBox config file inside the game folder, line 232, change from "keyboardlayout=auto" "to keyboardlayout=us" and setting your windows keyboard to US, that way you can get it working.
Considering those 2 things mentioned, 7€ is overpriced, I wouldn't pay that much for an abandonware that has problems with non-US keyboards. The good thing is that these games go on sale very often and you can get it for a 75% or 90% disctount, in that case, you should get it. Having it on Steam instead of in a dosfile downloaded from a webpage gives you a guarantee that as long Steam is alive, you will be able to play this without depending on abandonware websites or torrents

I remember when this game was released I was in high school fascinated with airplanes in general and Tomcats in particular. The game was a must for me if only for the single reason that F-14 was the main hero here. But I was not able to adequately appreciate the game back in those days. I took it as just next flight sim out there (I remind you those were the days when you could have had three flight sims for a penny) just with a lovely F-14 models.
When I bought it as a re-release from steam I learned how much I had been missing. Although the game could use better gfx (models aren't very detailed I must admit; the tomcats are "boosted" with pretty detailed textures but opponents' looks just suck), the whole experience of "weapon delivery platform", as the manual says, is unsurpassed. It's not a simple dogfight sim (although it can be played as such in Scramble mode). It's a simulator of a much more complicated concept - an interceptor pair.
Most fun for me in this game comes from working as both pilot and - often overlooked in other games featuring F-14 - RIO (Radar Intercept Officer). The game features a very good simulation of AWG-9 radar and targeting system and puts you in charge of operating it to seek and destroy your targets. Of course, you may set your difficulity level to simple and just fly around and shoot your missiles (or even turn on training mode, reload your missiles in mid air and play a "fighter gunboat" ;->) but you'll miss half of the fun. The better half.
I only wish someone would release similar game nowadays using full potential of conteporary computers.
(Oh, and don't mind my 0,7 hours played - I copied the game out and run it with dosbox on my linux laptop :-D)

One of the most important 90's flight-sims, created by one of the most important 90's flight-sim studios.  F-14:FD is a study sim of said bird, with moderate-to-high complexity, particularly in the AWG-9 radar modelling and carrier landings.  It was one of the benchmark simulations of its day (hard to believe that was 20 years ago as of this writing... where does the time go?) and while the sim's graphics are certainly a smeary, muddy 320x200 mess, the underlying game still holds up well.  There's a campaign mode (blow the filthy Commie Scum out of the North Atlantic), scramble (quick mission builder) mode, and even a full mission builder.
Some caveats:  first, this is a DOS game, running under DOSBox.  I'm not sure if Night Dive Studios made any additional modifcations to the sim other than DOSBox settings, but I know from past experience that FD behaves well under DOSBox so there isn't any problem there.  Still, you'll need to understand and futz with DOSBox settings if you want your joystick throttle to work.  Second: this is a complex simulation, not a kick-the-tires-and-light-the-fires kind of deal.  You will want to read the (hefty) game manual, and you need to understand that you're taking the role of TWO people in the Tomcat -- both the pilot and the RIO.  The workload wasn't everyone's bag of tea even back in the 90's, when simheads were two-fisted men of iron and tobacco spit.
So should you, the reader, buy this game?
YES if you are deeply interested in how the (now-retired) Tomcat worked and fought, and don't mind aged (yet somehow still compelling) graphics.  There will probably never be a better Turkey sim than this one.
NO if ancient textured polygons bother you, or you're not interested in a simulation more complex than War Thunder.  Or are an Eagle pilot, which means you have other problems that nobody can help you with :)

(Note: I have not finished my playthrough of this title at this point and plan to make periodic updates to the review below Also this review will contain spoilers below the intro paragraph so be forewarned)
"If My Heart Had Wings" Being my first foray into the visual novel genre has not made the greatest impression of the genre as a whole. As far as being a novel goes the english script is poorly written: littered with grammatical, structure, and occaisional spelling errors.  The motivations behind each of the charcters goes from questionable at best, to non-existant. The music in the game suffers from being stereotypical Moe style background music, simply included as an obligation rather than an effort to make something that could draw the reader into the work as a whole. On the bright side of things the art style was pleasing and it is apparent that the developer put more stock into the visual part of this work rather than the novel part.
The text of the game has to have gotten lost in translation somewhere. not a single one of the lines of dialogue that I have read so far in the game feels natural. Instead of opting for a more conversational tone when characters are speaking the readers eyes are graced with lines such as "Hey, why is she here!? You said we were going out to do shopping for the dormitory!". Lines of that quality and worse are littered throughout the work, it just does not sound natural. the next issue with the text is the novel's apparent need to explain every little title and annotation added that someone would not find in most western cultures, even in anime they keep such explanations restricted to little footnotes so as to not draw the audience's attention away from the more important dialogue. however the developers just had to add these explanations into the main text boxes alongside the dialogue of the characters rather than allocate a small portion of the screen away from the meat of the text. Honestly as the audience trying to invest oneself into this are you really all that curious as to why a character is referred to as "Chan" rather than "San"?
The cast of characters is the other issue i take with the game. Most of them, including the protagonist Aoi feel unfinished and bland rather than fully fleshed out characters. Maybe the game is a really slow burn but so far no one, with the exception of Kotori (although I have a feeling I know how her story ends) is very interesting. Also the developer seems to be trying to paint Aoi as some sort of white knight/ paragon type character, but he comes off as really controlling and selfish the incident that comes to mind is when he
could it be Itsuka who in the cover ?

Overall a pretty fun game to play. Worth the full price if you're really into stealth games but if you just somewhat like stealth games I'd wait for a steam sale.
Pros:
-Good graphics and color palette.
-The game really does create a beautiful game environment that goes through various changes throughout.
-Brilliant level design.
-I haven't played a stealth game that really gives you this many options for completing objectives.
-The levels truly have multiple ways to complete them which really zeroes on in your preferred play style.
-Fun stealth mechanics.
-Whether it's throwing sand at a torch to put it out, dropping a chandelier on an enemies head, or popping invisibility to get around tough to beat enemies there are many many ways to sneak around.
-Plot
-Overall I thought the story was decent. There was mystery behind who you are/were was interesting. It just was told in a very interesting way.
-Length
-I was able to get a solid 16 hours out of the game on the first play through. Replaying missions with your unlocked abilities is pretty fun but I don't feel like it's too necessary.
-A.I.
-Unlike other reviewers I found them to get pretty decent. You'll find that enemies guarding upstairs typically wont check a noise downstairs from them and vice versa. However, if they spot you from downstairs they'll come get you.
Cons:
-Inconsistent Storytelling.
-Sometimes it's an ingame cutscene other times it's just a picture slideshow with voiceovers. It made me not care about the plot.
-Overall the story was decent but it ended up a jumbled up mess towards the end. This is disappointing as the first half of the game did a great job with plot anticipation.
-Combat mechanics.
-This was absolute crap. Stealth game or not, if you can scale walls for 16 hours then it's apparent you're strong, agile, and formiddable.
-Once an enemy honed in on you it goes to a locked fixed camera on that one enemy all while others are slashing at you. If you plan on getting into combat, be aware of your surroundings first.
-Escaping is extremely annoying and challenging as every swordsman in the game seems to be an expert knife thrower.
If anyone had problems with anything but the combat then it's possible they didn't play all the cards in their deck. This game really offers an amazing variety of ways to complete missions and levels. Putting out torches, using bodies at attention getters, and using your chosen abilities in the most clever ways made this game a pretty fun experience.
I score it 7/10.

While the idea of combining Left 4 Dead, Team Fortress, and Counterstrike is a fairly sound (and dare I say conservative) plan, the execution needs a lot of polish. Lacking the fine presentation and boundary-pushing which distinguish all of those, CURE feels very flat and derivative.
The issue of the maps being mediocre (the consistent but strange scaling made me feel like we were three feet tall!) has been covered in many other reviews. However, I would like to note that one map in particular, CityBlock, had extremely low framerate when I looked forward, but not in other directions. This is probably due primarily to a lack of culling (which in Source Engine is implemented (well, poorly, or not at all) within each map). This sort of thing is often worsened by a fancy shader on something near the end of the map with a heavy performance cost (which, without culling, will always be drawn when you look in its direction even if it's in the basement at the end of the map).
That being said, with enough polish, this could be a gem. :)

Starship Titanic is very hard to judge by today's standards. It probably even was in the late 90s. Many of its quirks and features were rather bold at the time and may strike modern gamers as eccentric - point and click mechanics combined with a chat interface, a first-person-ish perspective based on still images, really whacky puzzles... You'll find yourself right in the middle of all that glorious weirdness before you even have the faintest idea of what you're even supposed to do. Frustrating? Yupp. But you'll have to live with that if you want to enjoy Starship Titanic.
That said, there is indeed a lot to enjoy. The witty writing and quirky voice acting are arguably the game's strongest points. That very British humour still stands the test of time. There is actually a muddled sort of logic to the puzzles, funny and frustrating at the same time, and they deliver a great sense of accomplishment every time you figure something out.
Quirky, charming and bold, Starship Titanic definitely is a remarkable part of Douglas Adams' legacy, but you do need a soft spot for classic adventure games and general weirdness to enjoy it. This game may be a classic, but it isn't quite timeless. If the old-timey stuff is your thing, then what are you waiting for, you probably don't want to miss out on this. If not though, you may find it difficult to appreciate this game for what it is.
The puzzles are extremely random and just way too difficult and illogical. I have no idea how I could ever have played this without a walkthrough...

(Although this account has around 5 hours logged playing Starship Titanic, I played a good portion of the game through another account via family sharing. My actual time spent playing is closer to 8 or 9 hours total.)
Starship Titanic is an extremely silly game. If you are a Douglas Adams fan, or a Monty Python fan, and especially if you enjoyed the Hitchhiker's Guide text-based adventure game, you should certainly consider picking this up. If you're not a fan of that sort of humor, you probably won't enjoy Starship Titanic very much.
It really says something about a game when, nearly 20 years after its release, it still manages to do something that seems impressively creative by modern gaming standards. I won't spoil it, but there is a puzzle towards the end of the game that does something that actually made me say 'oh, wow' out loud. That being said, most of the other puzzles in the game range from 'decent' to 'practically unsolvable'.
If you're familiar with the text-based Hitchhiker's Guide Adventure Game (also written by Douglas Adams), you probably know that many of the puzzles in that game (particularly the infamous Babel Fish) are nearly impossible without a walkthrough. In a good environmental puzzle, the player should be able to logically determine the sequence of actions that must be taken to complete the puzzle. The Hitchhiker's Adventure Game is so completely illogical that one almost wonders how anyone ever managed to solve it at all.
Unfortunately, Starship Titanic makes the same mistakes. A walkthrough is essentially necessary to complete the game. (Later reprints of the game even included a walkthrough that was originally published on GameFAQs; it is very useful, and can be found easily on Google. This review originally contained a direct link to the walkthrough, but Steam didn't seem to like that.)
Despite all that, Starship Titanic has a lot to enjoy. The graphics are very nice for 1998, and the designs of the ship and robots are lovely to look at, despite the game's age. I particularly like the DeskBot, who folds out from a bell. The robots all have very distinct personalities, and are very fun to talk to. The voice acting is hilarious, even featuring appearances from Terry Jones and John Cleese. The story is what makes the game worth playing, and it is very, very funny.
The game creates an excellent atmosphere that feels very similar to the Hitchhiker's books. The ship is enjoyable to explore, especially after upgrading above SGT class. I almost found myself wanting to stay longer after completing the game.
Overall, the story, characters, and atmosphere are what make this game memorable and worth playing. If you can overlook the poor puzzle design, and appreciate Adams' humor style, this is definitely a game to check out. Even if you're not familiar with Douglas Adams' other work, consider checking this out if you like good old adventure games and fun stories.
Note that you will need a pair of anaglyph (red/blue) 3D glasses to complete the game. The physical releases of the game originally came with glasses, but that sort of thing is difficult to distribute digitally.

Starship Titanic is a callback to an earlier time in video games.  I picked this up on a whim when it was first released.  I still have the CD's, but I was still perfectly willing to buy a new copy on Steam just so I can play it again on modern OS's without having to fiddle through a thousand toggles and settings.
I'm going to start off with the bad.  This game was put out when full motion video was a reasonably new invention, and consequently has some features that may annoy modern gamers.  The most obvious are the repetitive scene transitions.  Anywhere you go, you will be treated to a little video showing you wandering the that direction, admiring the sights, floating down canals, riding the lifts, etc.  There is an obvious degree of "look what CD Roms can do!" peppered all over the place, and it is in desparate need of an HD update.  Some of the puzzles are a touch unforgiving, and it is not always clear where you should be going... so you get to see these scenes over and over and over.  And over.  Once more.
Otherwise, this is a stellar game.  The scenery is quite nice.  The design of the Starship and its android crew are all very creative.  The premise and story are fun, and you get a real sense of accomplishment when you figure out the solutions to some of the nastier puzzles.  The dialog is about what you would expect from Douglas Adams (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy), hilarious and vastly entertaining.
In short, this is not an action filled game.  It's a slow wander around a derelict luxury starship, repairing things as you go and uncovering clues to what happened to the ship while you try desperately to upgrade to a 1st class room.  It won't appeal to those who can't go a dozen steps without shooting something in the face, to those who are easily frustrated by logic problems, or to those who refuse to accept that the most useful thing in the Universe is your towel.  To everyone else, get a copy.  You'll have fun. :)

As a result of this, you die several times without even knowing what hit you (and this is a capital sin for a shmup).
I would really like to recommend this one, because it gets a lot of the things right. Just don't bother and go play better shmups like Super Galaxy Squadron, Jamestown, Crimzon Clover and a ton of others available on Steam.

Cons

If you're a 30-something guy like me, and your childhood consisted of playing games from the golden age of the NES, SNES, and a whole host of other platforms, this game will put a smile on your face. There are countless subtle references (and many straight-up emulations) of a wide variety of games, and to spoil any of their appearances here would be a shame.
If you strip all of the nostalgic elements away, and judge the game for its story and gameplay alone, it's still an absolute masterpiece.
The only gripes I have about the game are the lack of character customization (there is virtually none) and the time-travel plot driver, which is almost point-for-point lifted from Chrono Trigger. And to be fair, those are hardly criticisms at all, as not every game needs to involve 20 minutes on a character creation screen. And Chrono Trigger was incredible, so you really can't blame them for retelling that particular classic tale, with a few new twists.
I find it incredibly hard for a game to capture my attention these days, but this one offered up just the right mix of everything to keep me from tabbing out and browsing Reddit after a few minutes.
Solid 9/10. Well worth the asking price.

Allow me to start by saying I have fond memories of the original Evoland. It had charm, and though it was short, it didn't have any real padding to speak of. Disappointingly, I can't say the same for its sequel.
In the two hours I have played so far, I have seen so many mind-numbingly cliche sequences that if I didn't know any better, I'd say this game was just a paint-by-numbers exercise in game development. I've already gone through the boring tutorial, the forced stealth section, the generic coliseum, and I decided it wasn't worth continuing when I hit the sewer level filled with insta-death pits and bats. That's not even mentioning the plot so transparent that at least 2 of the major "twists" are already in plain sight, or the unimaginative characters.
I'm sure that there are people who will argue that it's satire, or a loving parody or somesuch. Thing is though, simply implementing a well-known setpiece doesn't make something satire. Satire requires you to implement it, point out its prevalence, and then give an alternative, or twist it somehow so it's not the same as every other time you've seen it. I would have greatly appreciated it if, for example, midway through the stealth section your companion just knocked out a guard blocking the way forward, letting you bypass the circuitous route through the patrols. Instead the concept is played completely straight, right down to the cardboard box.
I want to love this game. I really do. I might even keep struggling through its numerous flaws in the hope of finding something good underneath. But if you want a skilled satire of RPGs, I suggest you look elsewhere unless you have a strong desire to waste a few hours on tedium before anything fun shows up.

First impressions a couple hours into the game - it's generally OK and if you (like me) grew up on SNES games and Game Gear this game will throw you back and make you feel like an 8 years old again. I'll try to keep updating the review as I progress through the game.
For the moment here's what I think:
Pros
- Nice and colorful
- Lots of (quite obvious TBH) references to other games
- Witty item descriptions
- Really nice animations and more generally sprites
Cons
- Dialogues seem to have been written for a *very* young audience (but then the game is full of references to Metal Gear Solid, Super Mario, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and many other games which makes you think that the game is actually targeting people around their 20s and older). I wasn't expecting amazing scripts but nonetheless, sometimes the dialogues are just.... meh.
- Mechanics are a bit clunky for the moment (in the 2D top-down view it feels like you should be able to swing your sword diagonally rather than just up/down/left/right), don't know if they'll get better as the game gets more "modern"
- Similarly, save points. Seriously - you have a chance of making an retro-style game with modern mechanics. Save points are horrid, just let us save from the pause menu.
- Main character does not say a word and always replies with "..." but it can interact sometimes with yes/no choices. I feel he likes of personality and you can't really make it up yourself because of the standard "..." answer. The game doesn't let you imagine what he's saying, it *tells* you what he's saying, and he's saying that he's just a big duck.

I can't praise this game enough. Do note that I try to prevent spoiling as much as I can as I write this and this is all my opinion.
A little background, I played part 1 (Evoland) and enjoyed it, though it was more of a time killer than a real game, which in my opinion isnt bad, but could be better. The sequel changes this and is a worthwhile game!
Evoland 1 was lots of fun, where the game evolved as you played through the game, music became more detailed, colours popped up, 2D became 3D, 8-bit became 32-bit music, I loved every little part of the game. But the only issue I had with it was that it was incredibly short.
The sequel doesn't grab the same "evolving gameplay" that Evoland 1 had, however it does so differently which really suits the game. You see lots of different game genres that most of us have enjoyed through the years, from the 90's to the 00's games. All boss fights are different with new kinds of strategies necessary (literally, because the game mechanics keep changing from Double Dragons to Megaman to top-down shooters).
This everchanging gameplay allows for loads of enjoyment and sometimes even surprise because some titles were enjoyed in the past, but sadly the names were forgotten. This game brings them all back and allows you to re-live your most cherished moments in gaming history with just a single game.
The little card game also allows for an enjoyable time waster (in a good way, because I enjoyed it). The mechanics of the card game as really easy to grasp, pretty similar to Yu-Gi-Oh or Hearthstone in a way, but then you get to enjoy the thrill of collecting all cards and a good aspect as well is that if you win from a certain person, he will give you the card you are supposed to win. Nothing random, although winning once from a single person is enough, because the wins afterwards are just for funs and gigs.
The only issue I have with this one is that the replayability (finishing the game more than once) leaves some things to be desired once you have cleared it 100%. (But I will most likely still play this game again some time soon in the future.)
So in summary,
You cannot really complain about the graphics of this game because it just looks awesome, playful and changes all the time by swapping from past to future.
Gameplay is very enjoyable, there are some hard bits if you aren't used to the way those games are meant to be played, but they are easy to understand and require some practice.
There is the possibility of leveling, giving you more health, it helps but it doesnt allow you to become overpowered, which is good in my opinion because it keeps the challenge present, while also giving you an edge of not taking the effort of leveling at all.
The music was enjoyable, from nostalgia to pleasant, in my opinion nothing weird.
If you like to have a good time playing a game, enjoy a few laughs, collect cards (without having to spend ages for getting all of them), don't mind the nostalgia trip this game will take you through, I'd say get it!
You may want for it to become cheaper, because in my opinion 20 euro's may be a just a tad too high, because the replayability of this game isn't very high. So anywhere from 10 to 15 euro's and its a good buy (in my opinion! <-- important, because opinions differ).
Hope it helps those who aren't sure of investing in this game.

First let me state that I played this game as a new stealth fan coming from deus ex: human revolution and dishonored so I will be comparing the game to those. I played hitman games later but they do not really match with the gameplay of the former.
1. The visuals. Are honestly not impressive. The game looks clunky at best but since the game levels are well designed and the graphics are stylized  it doesn't show after the first level and the game draws you in.
2. The gameplay. Is by far the best part of the game and, in my opinion, overshadows the gameplay of dishonored and deus ex in regards of stealth. One notable exeption is that unlike those, Styx has no way to properly fight through situations after being spotted, the combat is terrible and there are some enemies that will kill you even without the minigame. However, the level design of Styx is far superior to it's competitors, in that you can finish the levels in about five different ways WITHOUT any upgrades, whereas in deus ex, any shortcut requires a different upgrade, and in dishonored, the routes you can take without upgrades are usually one or two, at most. Styx also earns points by being genuenly fun as a power fantasy, in that stalking and killing people is very fun and challenging and rewarding unlike deus ex wich, at least for me, made all the weapons and even the takedowns seem to have no weight or impact, and without messing itself up with morality like dishonored did. Instead, Styx balances out the level design with risk and reward, where the heavily guarded routes are the most obvious one and also the most expedient, but if you take the time to look around (Ususally up) you will find less expedient ways with more verticallity.  Another great thing about Styx is that the upgrades, while fun and cathartic, are not necessary, you can play the whole game without any of them if you take the right routes and not feel like you missed anything too important unlike Dishonored and Deus ex. Finally, as mentioned above, the pace is what you choose to make of the gameplay. It took me twenty hours for a full story completion with almost all the upgrades on my second playthrough, trying new things with traps and exploring new routes, and about nine hours for my first playthrough, missing about half the upgrades. Also one final thing, as always with modern stealth games the qicksave key is your true best friend.
3. The story. It's allright, not aweful and confusing like the latter part of dishonored, not great and intersting like Deus ex. It does the job of keeping you interested in the universe and draws you in well enough, but not the meat and bones of the game, and certanly not what you'll remember after beating it.

Just finished this game 5 minutes ago and boy it is HARD! Maybe not Dark Souls hard but you'll see the "You died" screen more than enough during the playthrough. And by hard I of course mean really challenging. So here is a short review about all the things I like and hated about this.
The game is challenging, so it is natural to talk about gameplay first. It's a stealh game, in the purest sense. The game wonät end if you're seen, but run like hell and hide because the combat is, well, difficult. I wouldn't call it unfair. In Styx, the combat is merely parrying a strike two or three before you can actually kill your enemy (some can't be parried), and the challenge is in the timing of the parry, the window for it is small so you have to precise. One enemy you can propably kill, but two or more and it's game over, you, will, die. So run, don't be seen, hide, sacrifice clones! Control's are good and respond well (played with Xbox 1 controller) and overall gameplay and mechanics, I liked them, only the combat is something I loathe, and there were few times you had to fight just to progress the story.. Also, didn't like they way the game reused tha same maps, just chanching the direction from A -> B to B -> A....
Music was alright, nothing special there and the graphics are good, nothing groundbreaking, but I absolutely loved the drawn artstyle of the cutscenes between missions. That's all I have to say about those so then, the story. At first I thought "ok the story is this and blaablaablaa nothing interesting..."  THEN, at about midway of the game, won't tell at which part, there is a huge plot twist that breathed new life to the story making it much, MUCH more interesting! And at the very end, after anticlimatic fight that almost ruined the feeling for me, the last cutscene gave me the "WOW" factor, did not see that coming.
All in all, if you enjoy challenge and stealh games, give this a try!

For example, if I were to drop from the same rafters onto the same carpet next to the same stationary guard repeatedly over different game re-loads, one of the following things would happen:
1. Nothing, allowing me the stealth kill.
2. I will immediately be detected, and enter combat.
3. The guard will be alerted (but not alarmed) with just enough time for me to kill him loudly.
Those are pretty much the only three things that can happen in this situation, and you have zero control over which one it will be, even if youve been 100% stealthy.
Personally, I get more fulfilment out of rolling a dice and guessing what it will land on.

This game is a trap! Avoid! (I'll explain in more detail) Keep in mind I'm something of a veteran. I've played this all the way through.
Early on in Interstellar Rift, you will find yourself in a ship editor where you build custom internals end externals in a fashion you may have never seen elsewhere. If you're like me, the autonomy to design your craft to this extent will hook you, HARD. You will see things you can't reach yet, lofty heavy gear like nuclear reactors, Cargo teleporters, and a gigantic machine known as the Strip Miner. IT'S A TRAP. RUN WHILE YOU STILL CAN.
The gameplay, in all conceivable fundamental ways, unfortunately, is awful. Extremely awful. You will likely build your ship and be almost immediately destroyed by something totally unfair before you could hope to really figure out anything. OK. That sucked. Let's try again... wait a minute... the resources or money you spent on the ship is 100% GONE. No safety net, no buffer to speak of, and to make matters worse, you started off the game with LESS than two ships' worth of resources (unless you ALREADY know how to design a very cost-effective starter ship, and I gaurantee that if you're new, you didn't). And rest assured, you will be chided by arrogant bastrds telling you how stupid you are and that your failure is your own fault and that this game is super easy and various other ridiculous mean♥♥♥♥♥♥like that. Meanwhile, from a novice's perspective you are now condemned to possibly hours of the most boring♥♥♥♥♥♥in the world to mine your way back up to the point you started from. And mining on a starter station is SUPER BORING. Don't worry though. That mining is basically the entire game. it will NEVER get less boring. Even "hunting" skrill aliens isn't any more fun, and that's literally the ONLY other thing you can do in this game.
The game is unbeleivably punishing.... for no particular reason at all. It is very, very easy to lose your ship and therefore lose enormous chunks of everything you've worked for. Even as an advanced player. It never gets any better. In fact, it gets worse. Your ship will definitely become more expensive even if you're keeping a reserve, so your inevitable losses will become more devastating as well. Worse, some (SOME lol) of the ways you can get ♥♥♥♥ed exist by design. It's intentional.
I could ramble on forever. Im going to try to simplify this a bit -

At first, I thought Ori and the Blind Forest was just going to be a beautiful game with basic gameplay. Not only does it play really well, but it also blew me away with its graphics, music and its touching story even though I knew what the game looked like before I played it. But it's only when you start playing (with a controller or keyboard/mouse, both work well) that you get it. Just watching the game is not enough ; you have to play it to fully understand what the game really wants you to feel.
It's not an easy game, but it's not so hard that it makes you wanna punch your screen or anything. I've read some complaints about the game having too much "die & retry" in it. I disagree, as there are only 2, maybe 3 scenes in the game that can be considered that. The game always stays fair though, and it's just hard enough to make you feel like you're never really safe, even though you already picked every single health bonus you can get.
And those bonus can be really fun to look for. As a metroid-vania, you'll have to come back to some parts of the world using shortcuts you just created with your new powers. There's no teleportation here, everything is connected, yet it never feels like a pain to go back anywhere. Maybe it's thanks to the amazing graphics and music, but travelling back to a place you've already been to is always a pleasure. But it won't just be running, as enemies are always present in the game and will respawn.
Combat is pretty simple and easy ; press a button and a homing attack will deal damage to an enemy. You still have to dodge though, as Ori is very fragile, especially early in the game when getting killed in one or two hits is not rare. It gets easier though as you gain points by killing enemies and finding sometimes well hidden orbs to make your little guy stronger or to show things on the map. You can create a save point yourself, and you should since the default save points are rare. It has a cooldown and requires energy though, but those can be reduced if you spend your points in the right place.
And saving is really important, since you'll die a lot. Not necessarily because of enemies, but because of the platforming element of the game. Don't get me wrong; the game controls perfectly and some moves are just amazing both to look at and to do. Some jumps are not easy, even though it never gets as crazy as, let's say, Super Meat Boy, but none of them feels unfair. Sometimes you'll get to a place and wonder how you're supposed to make a jump that seems impossible to do, but in the end you just do it naturally. I won't spoil the moves you get later in the game, but I'll just say that I've never liked the "Y" button on my controller that much before.
In short, this game is a masterpiece. If I had to find something wrong with the game, I'd say the game is a bit short (I read 10+ hours, I finished the game in less than 7 hours, taking my time and exploring a lot). For 20 eurodollars (I'd say the same for 40 though), this is a game I highly encourage you to buy. And buy the soundtrack too, even though it isn't the same without the rest of the game, it's still amazing.

This game somehow reminds me of the mid-90s sci-fi flick Tank Girl, but maybe the similarity begins and ends with the post-apocalyptic setting, the cartoonish art style and the main characters, both girls whose favourite activity seems to be shooting mutants. You take on the role of Angel, who drives around in her car and saves the inhabitants of post-world war III settlements from mutant attacks. So much for the backstory.
Gameplay wise, Wasteland Angel is a no-nonsense top-down shooter. You're looking at a desert landscape from an isomotric perspective, drive around with a car whilst shooting at other cars that likewise shoot at you. That's pretty much all there is. Your main armament consists of two fixed guns, additional weapons can be aquired by driving over power-ups. Each level has three stages and, after you defeat the stages final boss in the third, a short bonus stage that leaves the top-down view and switches to a first-person perspective. The game never breaks from this pattern.
Your car can be controlled with the keyboard or a controller, both work equally well and what you prefer is just a matter of personal preference.
I chose to write a negative review but that doesn't mean there's no fun to be had. There certainly is. There's nothing wrong with the simplistic approach to vehicular combat, driving around in a car blasting everything in sight. The game plays smoothly, the controls are responsive and intuitive, there's nothing bad to say about the sound effects, music and voice-overs and the visuals, while definitely not on par with bigger budget titles, are pretty much what can be expected from an indie game, at least they won't give you eye cancer.
The main problem with Wasteland Angel is that its initial appeal wears thin all too fast. It's incredibly repetitive. Every level offers the exact same scenario, level structure, you're fighting the same enemies again and again, even the environment looks exactly the same in every level.
The game is very short and not particularly challenging. You can easily play through the whole game in one session. While most players probably consider this a downside, achievement hunters might appreciate the fourty easily obtainable unlocks.

Full disclosure: I received this product free from a generous Steam user whom I am thankful toward. That user has no ties to the developer which I am aware of, nor do I. I was not asked to review the product. It simply sates my OCD to do so.
I'm one of those heretics who was bored by Minecraft, ARK, and The Forest, Different people enjoy different things, and for some, crafting/survival games are largely focused on the survival. For me, the crafting is what I love the focus to be on. I need a purpose aside from aesthetics to craft the stuff, the stuff has to interest me, and once crafted, I need to enjoy what I crafted. The aforementioned games don't appeal to me for that reason, while Subnautica totally does. It was the first crafting/survival game I liked (Terraria was decent at times, too). However, all the rest I either played or watched on YouTube turned me off on the genre. I had given up on it.
Empyrion has many weapons to craft, Unlike many of these games, you get guns, and the game doesn't make you wait until 20-30 hours in to get them and have a decent ammo supply. Heck, you start with a pistol. There's only one melee weapon: the chainsaw, and it's intended for cutting down trees, really. The shooting mechanics are okay, though hardly on par with any "legit" first person shooter. It works well enough, though, and shooting a pack of space raptors to death with well-placed headshots whilst running backwards is pretty fun each time, despite its simplicity in mechanics.
You can craft several basic versions of pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, a pulse rifle, a minigun, and quite a few more. The guns worked quite nicely, and were pretty fun to wield. I will reiterate that this is not a technical gunplay marvel, but I had a nice time here.
POI's, or "points of interest," are locations you can visit, typically filled with enemies and goodies, some of which are impossible to build and can only be found in these or bought at traders, such as night vision goggles (so good), armor mods that give you defense against extreme cold, etc. If you take out the "core" of the base, you can even break down the entire base for scrap to use in building whatever you like! These bases seem to always have multiple turrets which can kill you very, very easily, even on the lowest of difficulties, so you might wait until you have an SV...more on those later.
This game is not masochistic torture porn like a lot of crafting/survival games. Or at least, it doesn't have to be. There's a difficulty slider you can fiddle around with when opening the game, letting you make enemies more powerful or weaker, giving yourself fancy goodies when you start or beginning with next to nothing (I actually did that one.), etc. There is quite a lot of customization and it allows people with different interests to have an experience closer to what will make them happy, as opposed to a uniform experience that will please some and alienate others. It gives you a level of freedom that is refreshing for the genre, though I do realize a few of these sorts of games have that feature. So for those who want to have a hellish time, you can do that...heck, you could even start yourself on a planet with no oxygen and terrible starting supplies if you want to really fight to live.
On the topic of difficulty and player preference, yes, you do drop everything you're carrying when you die. That tends to really annoy me a lot in games. I love making progress, and losing all my stuff I had on me is aggravating. The good news is that your items are marked on your HUD, they stick around in a little box where you died for about 25 minutes or so, you can respawn within maybe 100 yards or so of where you died by choice, and as long as you didn't go on a total suicide mission the first time, it should be easy enough to get your stuff back. I played well over 100 hours, and there's only one time I couldn't get my stuff back...and that was because I didn't know how to use the jump jets (jetpack) to move around in space...heh, more on space later.
I hate grind in games; despise it. That said, sometimes you can find a grind that mesmerizes you and sweeps you off your feet. Perhaps not everyone can experience that, but for me, it was the mining in this game. A friend and I would mine, and while drilling ore, we kept wanting to stop, but we just couldn't. We were watching the rock walls reshape and the ore pieces fall in chunks on the ground, and kept digging and digging. We actually hollowed out a massive ore deposit (just the two of us) with the starting drills, which took us about 3 hours. It went on a little longer than we would have liked, but we couldn't help ourselves. If mopping blood in Viscera Clean-Up Detail mesmerizes you or gives you a satisfying feeling, this might too, because it felt similar in terms of the level of satisfaction for me.
Later on, you can build an "HV," which is short for Hover Vessel. Essentially, it's a hovercraft, and they move quite quickly, serving as a nice means of speedy transport, and more importantly, slap some level 1 drills on the front in a smart layout, and you'll be tearing through the rocks and ore, automatically collecting it in a box/device on your HV in huge quantities. Zip back over to your base you've built, which is quick and easy, since you can move so fast in your HV, and store your goodies in boxes you can build and label with some nice storage space inside.
Small Vessels, or "SV"s, are essentially space ships. You can build them, though you will need some parts, fuel, and oxygen to leave the planet. You can spend dozens of hours on a planet with plenty to do, and then when you build a ship, you design it yourself. It's actualy not difficult at all. While you could import a design easily, I preferred to make my own. As utilitarian as I am in these, there was this amazing since of pride and delight that I had from successfully constructing a tiny, laughably-designed SV, getting it to take off, making modifications, and finally leaving orbit! It was a total thrill and I was wide-eyed and giddy. I will never forget how good it felt getting into space, and just sitting there with my engines off, floating. Then I look, and there's the moon that's always been in the sky. Well, I fly right toward that sucker!
I brought plenty of oxygen, and I stocked an adorable little mini-fridge with snacks for my trip. I found new ores that couldn't be mined on the starting planet, so I happily mine those, and rare equipment now becomes easier to make, improving what I could craft greatly. There were more points of interest there, too, which was fun, and a bunch of blue crystals. Now I'm master of the planet,
the moon. Mind you, this is dozens of hours of content for me between the planet and moon. Finally, I decide I'll go to another planet, so I design a Capital Vessel "CV." It's a warp-capable ship bigger than a house, and you can lay it out how you like! It was daunting, but I did it and loved the simple but useful end product. You can even make a landing bay and park your HVs and SVs inside it to transport to other planets!
Finally, I warp to another world...and I'm basically done. I can go to other planets and moons, but there's nothing left to do except get more stuff. There is no new tech for me to build, and without honest story objectives, I'm essentially "done" in my playthrough. It feels a bit disappointing and empty at that point, but I'm a hard♥♥♥♥♥with games, and will whole-heartedly say that I had a fantastic time with what there is to do in Empyrion. I'd play through it again from scratch sometime, I imagine. The usefulness and feeling of progress makes the game for me, and if you liked that about Subnautica, Empyrion might just be for you.

This is an unbelievably fun game, especially for only being in its alpha stages. Unlike most MMORPGs where you just get epic loot from killing a monster or big boss, here you have to work long and hard to expand your knowledge of weaponsmithing, engineering, metallurgy, etc in order to get what you desire. And the game executes this in a way that doesn't feel like an unending grindfest, especially when you're constantly wanting to help out your nation conquer territories belonging to your rivals.
Coming into the game, I didn't care much about what nation I was in, and just picked the one most appealing to me, as neither seemed to provide anything unique for joining either one. I quickly found out that the unique factor was in the players themselves. Both nations each seem to have a certain mindset and war strategy that their playuers possess. And while this cannot be said for EVERY player in each nation, it is an apparent majority. And as I said, I originally did not care about the nations. Very quickly however, I felt pride for the nation I was in, which is something most games never seem to get quite right, even when they are far more worked out and thurough.
I entered this game with the mindset that I'd have to entertain myself for more than two hours, or get a refund. I easily surpassed that two hour mark, and plan to dump more than fifty times the amount of time I have in the game at this moment.
Not to mention, this game is in ALPHA.
Rarely do I write reviews for games on Steam, much less ones that have more than 30 or so words, but with a game this surprisingly fun that isn't even finished yet, it more than deserved a few paragraphs of praise.

Blackguards is a flawed game. But one that I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with so far.
Let's go over the problems first.
1. Difficulty. Particularly early on, the difficulty of each encounter can be horribly inconsistent. There's a reason why there is a "try again" button during fights - you're going to use it. Quite a lot. A lot of the more difficult fights have some kind of trick to them that might a try or two to figure out, and a lot of the time said fights require an element of luck too. One or two bad rolls or a few fizzled spells and it's time to try again. Anyone familiar with D&D probably knows that it's hard to create a balanced party with only three characters, which is all you start off with in this game: A mage, a fighter, and your main character who you can build as you wish. After a few hours you pick up a ranger too, who happens to be pretty good with traps, but until I acquired her, any map with hidden traps was a real pain to deal with. There was one fight where I had to memorise the location of the traps through multiple attempts before I could succeed. Additionally, sometimes quests force you through multiple fights with no escapes, and no warning beforehand, which can catch you off-guard if unprepared. In summary: Save often, and be prepared to try again.
2. The interface. The combat system is excellent, but the controls are a little clunky. There's some oddity to the character models which can make it hard to target enemies at times, and the camera is rather awkward at times too. It can get quite frustrating, but it's not so bad that I find myself making accidental moves or anything like that.
3. Information. The game can be very unclear about things. If you're not familiar with the RPG system the game is based on, trying to figure out how it all works is awkward, and the game basically only tells you things once. Being able to mouse over raw stats to see how they affect things would be nice. I have a parry rating of 7 on a character, what sort of parry chance does that actually equate to? How are these stats modifying dice rolls? You can get a rough idea of how things work over time, but I'd like to be able to see exactly what's going on. Contrast with, say, the original neverwinter nights, where if you wanted you could see every single roll being made.
So those are the negatives.
And the positives? Well, the combat system is fantastic, the RPG system, while incredibly deep and unclear, is also very flexible, you have a lot of freedom to let your characters grow in any way you want them to. The quests are enjoyable, the story is simple but engaging, the characters have some actual personality to them.
If you're willing to get over the initial hurdles of an incredibly complex system and some very frustrating battles, there is a deep and enjoyable game with a wealth of content available for you. The world itself is pretty unique, it does a good job of avoiding a lot of fantasy tropes and creating something a little more engaging, and there's something rather refreshing about having a party that aren't a bunch of do-gooders.
You're blackguards. My party consists of a wrongfully imprisoned warrior, a dwarf arsonist obsessed with dragons, a pompous upper-class noble from the south, and an elf who got high on drugs and owes everyone money. You're not evil, but you're certainly not good either. You're labelled scum by the people around you and hunted across a kingdom, adding to your list of crimes on the way.
I've completed chapter 1 and am partway through chapter 2. I'm eager to see how the game develops from here. If you can handle some difficulty and frustration at the start, this game is well worth it.

A chest that says: “this chest could be opened if the developers had time to code it”. A statue whose inscription says: “lorem ipsum dolor sit amet”. The most prominent issue I have with Evoland 2 is its inability to take itself seriously. It lingers in a weird limbo of humor and seriousness without fully committing to either. It’s littered with dank memes and clichéd, self-referential jokes which downplay the game's attempts at evoking emotions.
Dungeons, upgrades, levels, collectibles, dialogue options and NPCs are all ingredients to a decent RPG adventure but they’re not enough for an excellent one. The progress in Evoland 2 isn’t easily perceptible because the story is a convoluted mess. It sort of keeps moving and throwing twists, most of which overstay their welcome.
I also begun to hope that the NPCs would alter their lines the second time I spoke to them because I found myself repeatedly doing that by accident. The occasional meaningless yes/no choice adds nothing to the script, and there were some cases of continuation errors where my characters were talking about an obstacle they hadn’t yet seen in the game. Then there was the quite literal manic pixie dream girl calling me and my party member a bunch of pessimists, continuing to spout a mass of motivational quotes, which made me skip dialogue until my wrist hurt.
Music isn’t bad, it’s mediocre. The Haunted Forest area has an uptempo rock tune with a church organ giving it a Castlevania vibe and making it sound like a comedic boss battle. Compared to the music in Zelda, for example, Evoland 2 sounds like a Disneyland ride. Zelda’s Lost Woods tune is more ambiguous in its harmonization. It creates a contemplative ambiance, despite being upbeat.
The 3D environment simply fails to appeal. The saturated colors and the low-poly props look like they don’t belong on PC. The isometric world doesn’t encourage exploration because you can’t view a single vista in perspective.
Minigames in Evoland 2 are fine, but their framing isn’t. There’s a library with eight small puzzles. In Professor Layton the puzzles pace the gameplay through interesting locales. You’re compelled to investigate and just happen to come by tiny puzzles here and there. In Evoland, I ran from NPC to NPC and solved all eight puzzles in a row for "study credits".
I could say that the main problem is that Evoland 2 is a jack-of-blah-blah and master of blah. While that is true, one of the biggest problems is that it doesn’t induce nostalgia. It falls into the trap of covertly name dropping specific games, without the pleasure of mastery that the referenced games provide.
I play Ocarina of Time annually and I know others who do this. Why? Because I get something out of it every single time. Sometimes I think about Link as the Hero with a Thousand Faces and sometimes of Ganon as the face of good that has been corrupted. But every time I find pleasure in the mastery. It’s subtle, it’s elegant, it’s titillating. Evoland 2 is none of those.

From 2D top-down perspective to 3D navigation, from turn-based battle mechanics to real-time fighting and puzzle solving, from card games to shoot 'em up, this game excels in variety.
In addition, unlike the first game, Evoland 2 has a solid plot which in my opinion was very nice and enjoyable (no spoilers here).
For completionist this game is pretty much ideal as it offers many not-so-easy-to-find collectibles (non of which are missable, hurray!)
And finally, one does not simply write a review of this game without mentioning THE SOUNDTRACK. The music is so, so good! I find myself sitting and listening to the soundtrack of this game over and over again (including now as I'm writing this review).
So, what are you waiting for? JUST BUY THIS GAME AS SOON AS POSSIBLE! You won't regret it!

If you like to experience the history of games, then you have to play Evoland 2.
It takes you to the time of the gameboy and the green graphics, and from there on you can go trough time.
The fun about his game is that it has a good story that will get you busy for hours, while you explore tons of different game genres en easter eggs from well known games.
You will meet new people and old ones who will be somewhat familiar.
I will recommend this game to anyone who enjoys different genres and the different graphics and play styles through time.

Raiden IV is one of the best old school shmups out there. This is a great port with extended modes, various stages, and the option for multiple players along with a fantastic selection of weapons. There is room for bullet hell fans, casuals, top scorers, et cetera. The graphics while a bit dated more than get the job done. I added in some FXAA from Nvidia CP as I couldn't find anything else that worked. The resolution is basically what you got in the arcade, and they have a couple themes you can use to round out your screen.
As far as shmups go this one is actually quite a looker overall. While older, the gun effects and the stages are very well thought out and increasingly more exhilerating the farther you get into each stage and more you unlock the full potential of each weapon and sub weapon. Absolutely no complaints on the weapons here. This is Raiden at its best and your arsenal is fluid, exciting, and most of the tools are totally different in control from one to another. You can play this shmup pretty much anyway you want. You also get a choice of three ships, one being a fairy lol. Got to have a little of that Gundemonium vibe or something. Classic chip tunes keep the energy flowing and your mind on the action.
For difficulty you should not be disappointed. There is the classic arcade mode, practice, easier modes, and they also added some hardcore levels of difficulty for those troopers looking to show off their insane skills. Everything here is well done and it looks like they actually cared about this port. I really cannot see any real shmup fan being disappointed with this one. It's one of the best out there and the port is excellent.

After spending about 6 hours playing Interstellar rift I have seen some of the good and bad sides. My experience though in this game is limited to the ship editor which is what I will do a short review about. I will compare Interstellar rift with Space engineers because these games share many elements.
For the recent years i have been playing quite a lot of SE and the building style differs quite a lot. Like many others have said, building interior in Interstellar rift is like doing interior decorating in Sims, which is very nice because you can drop several objects into a tile, where as in SE you can't. This helps out with scaling and makes the design less bulky(interior wise) compared to SE. One major drawback though, to the Interstellar rift ship editor is that I have found no support for mirroring blocks when building both interior and exterior.  This makes it very time consuming making symmetrical ships. This is something that has existed in SE from early on, and i can't stress this more, this is something that must be implemented to attract bigger player base. Building should be easy and fun.
One great thing about the editor is that there are two modes when building your ship, interior mode and exterior mode. This is something that I have lacked in other games. This makes it more simple to get a good grip of scale for interior building but also to freely work on the exterior when the interior is finished.  I have trouble with the current camera controls though. They are very inconvenient when building the exterior of the ship. I would rather see the free fly mode like you have in Space engineers. It would make it easier to move around the ship/station when placing blocks for exterior.
I would also like to see a convenient way to explore my ship(interior) from a first person perspective while building my ship. At this time I have to create a new game, then scramble some resources, build the ship, bring resources to the ship to power it, hopefully i will have a generator in the same room as the teleporter, then put hydrogen into the generator and only then i will be able to leave the room with the teleporter. This is very time consuming for someone who wants to get a quick glance of the interior of the ship.
I do understand that the game is in early access and that more building blocks will probably be added in the future. Maybe one could add scalable cockpits so your cockpit is not limited to one or two squares. It will make it easier to build symmetrical ships/bigger ships.
To summarize my thoughts about the game's ship editor. I like it very much although it has some shortcomings. It makes ship interior building much easier than in other games. Exterior building on the other hand is need of some love. Like I mentioned before, when building larger ships it will be hard to place proper bridge/cockpit when the only two cockpits available are one or two squares wide. I also like the different displays you find around terminals and equipment. It makes the game more immersive.
I will keep exploring the game and hopefully some of the shortcomings will be fixed in the future. Keep up the good work!

After a bit of a wait, Astro Port and Nyu Media deliver another fine shmup to their extensive libraries, and I can definitely say that this baby was well worth buying her on day 1.
+full controller support
+the gameplay is fun and the warp mechanic is damn cool, but takes strategy so it's thankfully kept from being OP (think Satazius meets Witchbot Meg-lilo, but her warping ability can also be used offensively). You can also receive upgrade points which you can use to power up aspects of your Zan Fighter. I always love the ability to do that, since it makes you feel stronger as the game goes on
+the music is distinct from other Astro port titles, having a more otherworldy instrumental. For example, you won't the hard rock kind of vibe that Satazius loves, but rather think more Steel Strider mixed with Wolflame.
+the levels are long and throw many challenges at you, alot of which are unsurviveable without the Warp Strike: a good use of the ability and I'm glad it wasn't just a gimmick you use once or twice.
+the game is generous with achievements, so if you're a hunter of those, it'll give you quite a few (though expect alot more in the beginning. The game is none too shy from sharing them with you. I got like 10 in 10 minutes). Not that I'm complaining.
+save system just like in Steel strider, so you don't lose you progress (and considering how easy it is to die on higher difficulties, this will be a boon for anyone)
+I'm also a sucker for nice pixel art, a step above what you normally see on Steam Greenlight. Rest assured, the only devs who can deliver better sprite work would be industry veterans like the devs behind Metal Slug. I can say this for pretty much all of their titles.
+can change the resolution at your whim
+various difficulty modes for replayability, and don't expect the game to give you mercy. As the Warp Strike is a handy tool, the game will ask you to make the most of it. My worry going into this was that it would be overpowered, and it does help dispose of larger enemies, but make no mistake: you will be using every ounce of the warp bar, praying that it recharges in time before you're cut in two by giant bloody axes.
+overall a light experience that's more than worth the 6 dollars they ask
There's only one downside; some of the achievements are slightly bugged, like the ones involving upgrading your weapons to max level. Some are also broken. It's a pity, as this seems to be a constant issue with Steam releases of Astro Port titles. And sadly, I don't think Astro port knows how to fix all of them. But really, it's almost a miniscule complaint and doesn't impact the game in the long run, even if you're a stickler for achievements. The game is likely one of their finest to date, and it shows in the polish. You can't go wrong with a simple, yet addicting, title. Expect me to be addicted to this for the rest of the year, as I'm gonna be score-hunting. This and the new Zelda are making this year out to be the best yet, although I am gonna have no time to spare between playing them.  It's a problem i don't mind having.

As the previous reviewer stated, the puzzles are procedurally generated, so you are virtually guaranteed a new puzzle every time. I also agree that a current puzzle reset option would be nice if you fubar it.
