I really wanted this game to be fun.  Only 6 hours in doesn't make me an expert by any means, but 6 hours of frustration and boredom is enough for me.
The towm screens are all static,  with certain activities highlighted.  You can shop which doesn't take long as everything costs allot of coins and what the player gets on drops is insignificant.  Weapons drop and they are all inappropriate for the "basic" games preset skills.  For example, your warrior is proficient in single handed axes and the only bladed weapons that drop, initially, are swords.  So, in order to even hope to survive any of the battles you have to pump AP ( which are earned by combat and quests) into a weapon that you have found, rather than saving them for other talents.  Armor is virtually non existant as drops so you have no defense really.
There is virtually no game here other than scrounging for gear and combat.  Your path is pretty much preset with no real exploration and each location is either a static town or a combat grid.
The other really stupid mechanic is your starting companions.   You get a dwarf warrior that is pretty good and a mage that is as useful as a box of combs for a bald man.  Now if you choose a mage as your class, the party has great ranged dps ability and very weak melee.  If you chosse a warrior its the reverse and you are in even worse shape as the preset companion mage is useless.  When looking at the mages's stats, you wil see he has the best "ranged weapon" skills of the three.  He also has the most Astral Points ( mana ) of the three.  Yet when equipped with a ranged weapon like a bow he misses every time.  His casting skills are not bad but the only really good spell is an AoE fire attack that does little or no damage and uses up all his mana in 3 turns.  Oh, your mana regens at the alarming rate of 1 to 2 points every 5 turns.  You are long dead by then as a mage can't wear armor, has little or no melee skills and now cant use magic.
Casting is a thrill, the effects are nice especially the failures which occur more than 50% of the time and the melee companion will miss 80% of the time on the only attack that does decent damage and the attack that has a high chance of hitting does insigificant damage.
Now I know that any starting party is releatively weak and there is an expected number of failures in any combat until the combat system is learned.  However, the punishment vs reward system in this game crucifies a new party.
The typical battle has the odds at 3 or 4 enemies to 1, so you have 3 party members that miss and fizzle spells most of the time with no armor and medocre weapons against 6 or more enemies that miss maybe 1 in 10 times.  Your mana is used up pretty quick and the regen might let you cast one 10 pt heal just before the 3 enemies around you hit for 10 pts of damage each.
There was one battle in a cave of sorts, the 30 odd enemies were seperated from the party by twisting tunnels, but you can see them, so you know what is up a ahead.  After killing the 1st batch of enemies, about 10, I got to sit there mindlessly pressing the space bar until our mana regenerated enough to heal.  Yes heal pots, well they are  very dear, almost never drop and best saved for combat.   After healing the party I sat there pressing space bar for another 40 turns to regen enough mana to move forward and take on the next batch of enemies.  Needless to say that aside from the very deep skill system this game is visually boring and the combat is more so.
Quite a few words come to mind for this game:  Dark, Dismal, Uninspirering, Frustrating, Boring.  It seems that the publisher is punishing the player for being stupid enough to actually give them money for the priviledge of being bored!
Blackguards is the sort of game that if you had a choice of getting a root canal or playing the game, you'd rush to your dentist with a smile on your face rather than load this game up!
I may get back into it, but there is no desire to spend many hours in this mess as there are other more rewarding games out there.

Blackguards is great. Based on The Dark Eye setting and tabletop roleplaying game rules this game really captures those rules and lets them shine in a way previous real-time titles have not. The turn based nature of the combat system in the game really lets you see the benifit of the various different builds of characters where in a realtime combat game such as Drakensang based off of the same rule set does not.
The plot is engaging, lengthy, and at times really does feel like a transcript of a tabletop campaign, which is great for someone who maybe used to tabletop and just doesnt have the time to, or doesnt get the opportunity to as often as they would like.
All things said, I paid full price for the game, and don't think I spent even a penny more than the game was worth.
as someone who finished the game, this is not a good rpg. lacks pretty much everything that makes an rpg work, and i do regret my decision to acquire it.

Though it has some severe spikes in difficulty and has a system that, like Drakensang, is very hard to get a handle on quickly...it's remarkably good if you want oldschool turnbased combat. Long story, sharp dialog and some very cleverly planned-out combat scenarios. Can't go wrong if you have the skills for a real CRPG.

Highly recommended for fans of turn-based fantasy and role-playing games in general.
Pros: The adventure system is a welcome relief from wandering around huge towns of useless NPCs. It's similar to point-and-click adventures of old. Let's you get to the story and/or combat quickly.
Cool level-up system. Characters really start to feel powerful at later levels.
Attractive graphics and runs smoothly.
Neat battle set-ups. Battles have traps, special objectives, secrets, and ambushes. There are a good number of straight up fights, but the set piece battles really spice things up.
Interesting (but not completely original) story with an compelling (but really not original) cast. It keeps you interested enough to follow along rather than just clicking through the dialogs, and the cut-scenes are simple but well done.
Cons: I strongly recommend starting on "Easy" difficultly. This really feels like it should be the default and is best for first-time players. The mechanics of the game are a little obscure, and having one play-through under your belt is best. Easy offers a good challenge without being frustrating, and gives you freedom to explore the game.
Again, obscure mechanics and no way to respec makes the game progression rather unforgiving.
Sparse loot. Don't get me wrong, I think it is a nice chance of pace to have magic items actually be rare and not drop 11 times each battle, but it feels like the game is really stingy with the rewards. It does make the few items you get feel more special but, unfortunately, they're not even that much better than the standard ones you can buy.
The characters you get aren't very customizable in their roles. But they do what they do well.
Low replayability. You could replay the game on a harder difficulty, but why? It's a long game and nothing is really randomized. It's not really much of a con though since the game is so long with lots of optional quests.

It's been one hell of a ride. A vast improvement over the previous installment. The basic premise remains the same: this is the ultimate chimera of a game, mixing all the genres and volumes you can possibly think of, within the grand frame of a JRPG. However, while the predecessor was more focused on simulating the gradual improvement of gaming and graphics technology over time, this one is no longer merely just a homage to the technological development of the video game field. Evoland 2 is a proper game in and of itself - perhaps even two or three games in one.
I'd finished Evoland 1 in about 8 hours, and I jumped into this one expecting much of the same, but I ended up spending over 40 hours getting up to 100% completion. (Though, considering how much of a perfectionist I am, you will most likely take a far shorter time in finishing the game.) The game's got good volume, and it stays fresh all the way through, thanks to all the different genres the developers managed to implement and squeeze into one game.
I have but a single con I can mention about this game, and it's that the plot leaves something to be desired (after all, that's what tends to happen when you have heavy time travel involved in a story), but it is my firm belief that it's the journey that matters most, not the destination; and the journey has been nothing short of spectacular indeed.
Need I still say more? You should definitely play this game.

If Evoland was a love letter to console gaming, Evoland II is the Mona Lisa of tributes to the best of portable gaming.  A story taking the best of Chrono Trigger, The Legend of Zelda, and Lufia, is merely the tip of the iceburg.  Including full sections dedicated to other games including Super Mario Bros, The Legend of Zelda, Double Dragon, Fire Emblem, Professor Layton, Raiden, Gradius, Street Fighter, Mega Man, Metal Gear Solid, Bomberman, Chrono Trigger, Guitar Hero, and Secret of Mana among others, Evoland II shows the best of these games' genres without holding onto worn out mechanics.  Sprinkled with 4th wall jokes and pop culture references, each new moment in the game brings fun and nostalgia with small allusions to great games, such as waking out as Chrono, or the chain walls from Super Mario World.
With an absolutely great ending, Evoland II is a most player for all gamers, even those who didn't like the original. About ~40hrs to full achievements.

The many stations throughout the many different systems you can go through creates plenty to do in a sort of Elite: Dangerous-esque fashion, such as shooting up enemy ships or aliens, hauling cargo, or defending other places.
-You can customize or create your own ships, down to block level, which is
nice for people like me who like to have their own spacecraft rather than prefabs. The editing isn't live such as in games  as Space engineers, but rather uses a separate 'editor mode' in which you can place the blocks, sort of akin to how The Sims does it.
, which is a little buggy sometimes but really nice to have compared to games like Space engineers which will use up a full 1x1x1 space despite being tiny. This game does not have that limitation.
-Few (physics/gameplay) bugs thanks to the game being rather simple in concept, especially compared to games like Space engineers.
Now the bad. Keep in mind this is an
game, so take it with a grain of salt and good hopes on the future;
-There are a bunch of bugs due to unforeseen consequences of gameplay mechanics. For example, Aliens can attack stations, but also those part of hauling missions, and it'll
the mission, costing the amount of money that you'd normally gain from completing the mission. This has happened so often that I couldn't make any progress, due to being left with millions worth debt for 'stealing' 75,000 worth resources.
-The amount of variety in the random generated missions isn't super big, and after a few hours will start to feel a little grindy.
-There is a rather steep learning curve initially as the tutorial only explains the basics, not details such as that yellow missions on the mission board are in other systems (and therefore often not worth it unless you have your own rift generator).
-It's hard to find enough to do on public servers where everyone takes all the missions in the current system so that despite of full mission boards there's nothing viable to do for new players.
-The ship editor, although decent, feels a little clumsy, especially when trying to add different levels to your ship. It would be nice to have a better undo function with more history, and it's easy to ♥♥♥♥ up and delete the wrong object, or add a 1x1x1 room where you don't want it, destroying the armor on the outside, removing all the objects, etc., and it's always nice to have more variety in blocks, although there's a lot to choose from already.
-It would be nice to have a more clear indication of when the next update is coming out, because the current schedule seems to be pretty much 'whenever it's ready', so I have no idea how long I have to wait to see if any of the above issues have been fixed :P
All in all I do think this game has a lot of potential, at least for myself to be one of those games where I can sink thousands of hours into idly doing things and upgrading my ship and building stuff, but it's perhaps a liiiittle early to get full on attached to it, because there's a few issues such as mentioned above that can really get in the way.
I recommend this on the condition that the developers continue updating this game, which they at least seem to be doing so far :)

As a general rule of thumb, I try to avoid early access games because they've burned me too many times.  Every once in awhile I see one that is niche enough and in line with my interests of the moment enough that I feel compelled to take a chance.
Empyrion is one such chance and I could not be happier I took it.  At the risk of sounding like a broken record with other reviews this is the kind of game I had hoped No Man's Sky would at least attempt to be (and seems to be gradually creeping toward more than a year after launch) but Empyrion is just flat out more enjoyable.  Being able to design pretty much anything that can be flown or driven from scratch and to then leave the atmosphere of whatever planet you elected to crash land on for the first time is one of the absolute most rewarding experiences I've had in a game in years.
By comparison, the experience in No Man's Sky lacked any sort of feeling of triumph, probably because it takes maybe 15 minutes to repair your ship and there's no real pomp and circumstance to leaving a planet.  Granted this is just my experience, obviously others will and should feel differently but I've loved every minute of entering space in Empyrion.  From tearing apart alien bases to strafing an enemy capital ship's gun emplacements with my small, self-made space plane to seeing a new solar system for the first time with the capital ship I built, the entire offering of the game feels good.  Does it occassionally feel like a grind? Yes, it's a survival game.  That's more or less par for the course.  Are the shooting mechanics about as rudimentary as they can be? Yup, 20+ year old FPS's have tighter shooting mechanics.  Does this make it a bad game? Absolutely not.
Empyrion in its current early access state is a game of firsts.  First time to build a vehicle, first time in space, first time in a dogfight, first time destroying a base, first time finding that rare mineral you need to make the best weapons, first time having a space raptor treat your corpse like sloppy joe day in the school cafeteria.  I would have to imagine the PvP elements of the game could be exceptionally fun though I've done nothing more than play PvE with some friends to this point.
All said and done, Empyrion is a good game with an excellent feel to it that has all the potential to be a great game so long as the developers continue with the road map they set out for it earlier in development.  If you're looking for a space game that let's you genuinely feel like an explorer in space without the random yet monotonous sights and experiences of No Man's Sky or the bug-filled right-angled learning curve of Space Engineers, give Empyrion a try.  It deserves it.

There is enough to do in Empyrion that a casual singleplayer survival game lasts longer than a major release cycle (several months).  When the next release comes, there are usually enough new features and content to justify starting over from a new escape pod on a fresh planet with a new random seed.  At some point a release cycle (maybe the beta) will last long enough that I actually have time to visit all the planets, see all the stuff, build all the things, and go on all the adventures.
The developers at Eleon are some busy little bees.
There is complexity in the details of harvesting, crafting, tactics, logistics, and so on but the learning curve is approachable thanks to the tutorial content and in-game help.  The planets are designed in a sequence of escalating difficulty levels.  On top of those baselines custom difficulty parameters (a dozen or more, subject to change) are available to create exactly the gameplay experience you want.
The biggest downside (currently) is the planets are a bit small and there are artificial seams (barriers to movement or detection) at certain longitudes and latitudes.  At some point there will be a major rework of the planet code to remove these, and hopefully (probably) it will also make the planetary playfields larger and more complex as well.  The current planets have only a few inter-related biomes, but each is unique among all the planets and richly detailed.  There are numerous stock planets.  Also, tools for player-created planets and scenario content have been under development for the past few release cycles.
Expect the assets and rendering to gradually improve over time.  They get a little better with each release.  When I first started playing Empyrion, the planet Akua didn't even have any trees but there was still enough gameplay to keep it interesting.  Now the jungle is so thick I can't see very far through the undergrowth and I get jumpy when I hear the critters moving around.
I haven't played every single sandbox/survival game on Steam but I have sampled enough of them to suggest that this one is probably the best of breed.  Give it a try.  What's a $20 bill worth these days?
10/10 would start from a fresh escape pod again.

It makes me sad to say that this game OOZES potential, but takes advantage of absolutely none of it and often squanders it. The few good things are:
- the graphics/visuals are nice
- a few bits of the writing are decent
- movement is fun (for a while) with a few different paths through a level
- all the lore established outside of what takes place in the game is interesting
These points are swift brought down the more you progress into the game though. My biggest complaints and the most abhorrent issues I have with the game are mainly the A.I., some mechanics, "level design, and the plot,".
First on the list is the A.I. This is short as all the A.I. in the game are either omnipotent (sometimes even skipping alert levels), or dumb as rocks. There is zero consistency in the game with how the guards react even between save states. I could be killed by Jesus guard who heard me through 5 walls and crossbowed me from 100 yards away in the dark, reload, and the same guard would be licking the wall for 45 minutes.
Mechanically the game functions, but having been released in 2014 when something like assasin's creed came out in 2007 makes me wonder if they were trying to distance themselves from it. I get that you're a smaller goblin and a hostile city but that doesn't excuse the fact that you can't even swing your weapon until you've been spotted and are locked into a 1v1 duel. I assume they wanted to make combat a last resort but FFS this was not the way to do it. In these duels your camera is locked in place at your back and you can only circle strafe the enemy and parry their attacks until they go "off balance" and then you can murder them. This is a complete joke since the camera angle can often lead you into running into a corner, some boxes, or a hoard to the side you didn't see. And since you can only 1v1 and the other 6 guards can still fight you while this is happening you either have to get lucky that they go stupid, have bad dagger aim or they wiff.
Also for added "fun" there are about 5 nigh unkillable enemy types in the game. Heavy knights that can only be killed by dropping chandeliers on them, "blind" insects that have "acute hearing" (they just know where you are at all times and rush you) can only be killed by throwing knife (which a limited), orks (no idea if you can kill them), ghost skulls that trail you and explode (requiring a roll dodge), and elves (see insects). A hand full of these also one shot you no matter your HP and, aside from the elves who show up in the last 10 mins of the game, ALL NPCS ARE HOSTILE TO YOU AND FRIENDLY TO EACH OTHER. That's right, the chained up ork will ONLY one shot you as you lead a pack of humans by him. The hyper aggro insects only target you after running by 5 guards. Even the elves are only hostile to humans in the cut scenes since all the humans are dead by the time you reach the elves.
Laughably with the horrid combat they actually make you go through a "final boss fight" which might as well be an open room. Better hope you didn't waste all your consumables on the way to it.
Next is "level design". There are about 7~ levels in the game. These levels are fairly nice with secrets and multiple paths throughout. They were fun to play through the first time... the second... not so much. You might be asking what I mean by "the second". You see, in this game you go through levels in this order; 1,2,3,4,5,5,4,3,2,1,6,6,6.5. For WHATEVER REASONS they thought it would be a good idea to have you go through five levels and then literally go backwards through all five again to the first with the ONLY difference being more and harder enemies. I just can't forgive that.
Finally let's talk about the plot. This is where spoilers might happen so if you're still interested in the game skip this. The 'plot' is a nearly non existent patch work of quarter fleshed out ideas with so many holes it should have been packaged as swiss cheese. You're Styx, a character who apparently originated from "Of Orcs and Men" (not that it matters in the slightest). You're in a human city searching for the heart of a magic tree (you don't know why). There was an elf/human war for the tree and there is a tense truce so they can share the tree. The tree produces "amber" which is like a drug essentially for humans, but the elves use it to connect their minds with one another and are born from it (?). You plod through five levels of the game setting your "plan" in motion (stealing a key here, finding a map there, etc.). In level five you are going to free a guy (you don't know) from prison. This guy turns out to be you! He says this was his plan all along, you're a clone, and he stabs you and leaves. You didn't die and decide you want to take revenge. I bought this game having read a lot of the reviews. I was expecting it to be primarily centered around hex-grid combat. I knew this and dived in - I love games like HoMM and Kings Bounty. Other reviews have mentioned that the game is essentially battle to battle, with a few static village screens thrown in to try and create a background. Even so, I was expecting so much more. Everything in the game seems to have been implemented with the minimum amount of thought. There are relatively few upgradable skills and I found it fairly easy to just divide skill groups between party members and max them out fairly early in the game. Other reviewers have mentioned difficulty spikes in certain battles and this is occassionally true - some of the early battles are harder than the 'legendary' arena battles you have to overcome later on.
Actually, one of the main sticking points for me was the distinct lack of equipment - or at least variety of equipment. If the game is going to be based entirely around battles, surely you should feel like winning is going to bring some great bounty, but in the end all you get is a pair of boots and 5 coins, or whatever. There aren't even any item conditions to mix things up (rusty swards, superior buckler, etc). The amount of XP you get after a battle seems to bear very little resemblence to its difficulty either. All of this leaves the game without any reason for you to be excited or want to carry on into the next battle (apart from the inherent addictiveness of turn-based RPG combat). You feel like maybe you should be progressing the story, but I also found the story boring for the most part, apart from a few of the cut-scene events. I recently bought the Baldurs Gate 2:EE and played for a few hours, the contrast in characterisation is ludicrous - straight away I was enjoying the quips and comments from party members - while the characters in Blackguards just aren't really memorable, I found myself interested at the beginning, but raply lost interest, either through poor writing or due to the incredibly slow pace of storytelling.
Overall, I felt there weren't really any redeeming features for Blackguards - sure its graphically competent (although by no means pretty), sure the combat and strategy is acceptable (but by no means exciting or ground breaking in any way), sure the character concepts are interesting, but they just don't go anywhere. It's all a bit of a muddle really.

Scripted mis-chances and rather insane mis-chances are just the start. (I had a 5% chance to hit a troll 7 hexes big...really? Or tried to cast a spell and had it fail 3 times with a 90% and then another 85% all in a row...which is about a 1 in a million chance I believe)  As well I at least disliked both the dialog and the leveling system which rather then letting you pick what you want if you do not go up in certain skills you will make the game impossible since there are no methods of leveling up other then the pre-set battles.  I tired with 4 different setup and every time(sometimes sooner then others) ran into a just stupidly setup battle where I would have selected a much different skill set then I had.
I did end up not playing this game much but unless it takes off(always a possibility) it seems that you are just meandering through life without much direction other then random people giving you quests that I mean go to X and have a battle...no real interesting battles other then some I get to run through enemies with everyone killing me in a time limit or press a button causing some other random thing to happen that I feel was just put there to make the battle go on longer rather then for flavor.
I am sure there are plenty of people who like this game but I just don't see why I would play this when there are so many better games out there even in this genre then this.

Pretty good SRPG, decent graphics,gameplay and leveling mechanics in terms of many choices to level up in and really create characters you want for your tactics.
Some of the fights, or rather mechanics in the games are kind of broken. You can miss like 10-15 times on a row, even with maxed skills and thus lose fights on it, and other times you might hit and crit on bosses constantly and wipe them extremly fast... A quick examples are bosses that has 40% dodge on any attacks you do. Now imagien that they also poison you, and spawning mobs that are basically impossible to kill. Now, you can lose this fight, like I did 10+ times because you keep missing everytime. And yes, then another time, you might hit basically every swing and boss is down before you know it. Thats not balanced, its just random and in a SRPG based on tactics luck should never play a big part into it. I can understand some luck mechanics for the rpg-elements, but 40% miss on a boss that hit hard back? and he is a tank? Come on...
I would give this game maybe a 7.5 or 8.0 of 10. When this game is at its best its actually really good, but when its at its worst its horrible. Probably need better beta test for the sequal in terms of balancing out battles, be more open about what to level up in, lots of trial and errors if you dont know what your supposed to level up or not. Also, the story and sidequest need to be better... basically as it is now, side-quest are kind of neccessary to finish for that vital AP which you level up in. So its not even a choice to do them or not.
I finished the game in 40 hours on normal difficulty, so this is a pretty lenghty game I guess 35 to 45+ hours.
Would I buy the sequal? Probably, yes, especially when its on some kind of a cheap discount, because I love srpg's and wanna support them (Final Fantasy Tactics need a sequal...) - but if the sequal for Blackguards, which is in development at this moment, get good reviews from the critics, I would probably buy it at launch.
As I said this game could be great, it isnt however atm in this state in terms of balancing and storywise.

Myself and my hubby purchased Interstellar Rift the other day from the Steam sale. Here's my take on the game so far. Take my comments with a pinch, I'm well versed playing EA/Alpha games, but also I'm only 25 ish hours in.

I see a great opportunity for RP play within this game, if only my character could punch!
I play as an engineer. My Hubby pilots the boat, (my driving usually gets us killed so I'll leave that to him and I'll take care of the ship).
I have found Interstellar Rift to be quite persistent with drawing me in to play it. The Ship Editor is fantastic,
(Tel'Tek Stargate style I plan to upload on the workshop after testing in game), had a really lovely evening designing and tweaking that ship, but then all of a sudden I realised I had missed dinner, forgotten about the real world and it's 4am and I have to go to work in 3 hours....

As it's in development I'm not going to say much here, having a good time playing an unfinished/Alpha/EA game is simply something people strongly differ on, it's like Marmite, you either love it or you hate it. Or in the way of EA games, you either deal with the bugs/issues or you don't. All I can say is if you see/experience a bug or issue, report it. Split Polygon have a forum for bug reports, and also the Dev's seem to be very responsive to bug reports, at least acknowledging them even if they cannot address them instantly.
This game is not particularly (in it's current state) beginner friendly. Server setup is a bit finicky. Navigation is tricky and there's a lot to learn about the game, especially all the systems and resources, but this is something time will cure, a steep learning curve is something I prefer, but the introductions given are adequate enough to get you started and not spoil it all in the process.
Navigational improvements.
Being able to punch someone (something I missed straight away, not being able to punch my friends or Hubby for no good reason).
Being able to take my character's helmet off... Would bring in more immersion and also would provide the danger for possible issues if something went wrong with the ship.
Would I recommend this game? To a person who was OK with playing an EA/Alpha game, yes. To those who are not, just wait and follow this game's progress, keep an eye on it, I'm sure it's going to go far (crosses-fingers for luck).

There is enough to do in Empyrion that a casual singleplayer survival game lasts longer than a major release cycle (several months).  When the next release comes, there are usually enough new features and content to justify starting over from a new escape pod on a fresh planet with a new random seed.  At some point a release cycle (maybe the beta) will last long enough that I actually have time to visit all the planets, see all the stuff, build all the things, and go on all the adventures.
The developers at Eleon are some busy little bees.
There is complexity in the details of harvesting, crafting, tactics, logistics, and so on but the learning curve is approachable thanks to the tutorial content and in-game help.  The planets are designed in a sequence of escalating difficulty levels.  On top of those baselines custom difficulty parameters (a dozen or more, subject to change) are available to create exactly the gameplay experience you want.
The biggest downside (currently) is the planets are a bit small and there are artificial seams (barriers to movement or detection) at certain longitudes and latitudes.  At some point there will be a major rework of the planet code to remove these, and hopefully (probably) it will also make the planetary playfields larger and more complex as well.  The current planets have only a few inter-related biomes, but each is unique among all the planets and richly detailed.  There are numerous stock planets.  Also, tools for player-created planets and scenario content have been under development for the past few release cycles.
Expect the assets and rendering to gradually improve over time.  They get a little better with each release.  When I first started playing Empyrion, the planet Akua didn't even have any trees but there was still enough gameplay to keep it interesting.  Now the jungle is so thick I can't see very far through the undergrowth and I get jumpy when I hear the critters moving around.
I haven't played every single sandbox/survival game on Steam but I have sampled enough of them to suggest that this one is probably the best of breed.  Give it a try.  What's a $20 bill worth these days?
10/10 would start from a fresh escape pod again.

Pretty solid early access. I don't condone early access as a development model either as it turns into a scam 95% of the time. In this case you get a decent blockbuilder/space survival game with decent mechanics that has seen major improvment since I got the game. (version 4.xx)
The developers are reasonably responsive to the community- which is an excellent thing. For that reason I'll start with the negative things first.
1. Flight mechanics are a real let down. I know how difficult it is to make realistic but fun mechanics for flight, however its extremely arcadely right now. For example each class of aircraft has a top speed that all builds within that class have automatically. From my experience rate of turn seems to be dependent on contruction style (which is great) but the mechanic is funky and hard to predict. I would suggest revising the blueprint system by adding a ship builder module wherein the player can design their own aircraft, modify existing ones, upload to steam workshop ect. If implemented correctly this could enable some more physically streamlined and aesthetic vehicles. The other way the system could be improved is by making blueprints rare items worth exploring/killing for, which leads to my next point.
2. Survival is underwhelming both due to mechanics and immersion. Getting started can be a bit rough but once you have a base the survial mechanics become really grindy and don't really serve a purpose. As for immersion there is just a general lack of diversity. There are usually ~5 types of critters of varying difficulty, ~5 plants and ~5 types of enemies per planet, but maybe 10 models in total for each category. The same plants will show up on multiple planets and the same is true for the bases and other models scattered across the planet. The 'seed' function does a cool job mixing things up, but at the same time parts of every planet will be marked out of bounds. For all of these reasons the first couple hours of gameplay are usually the most challenging and entertaining.
3. Combat mechanics are kinda awful. Models of just about every enemy are worse than models I saw 10 years ago. I hope they are placeholders. The AI is straightline attack with 100% accuracy. The enemies don't scale with your level or equipment so once certain weapons are obtained there isn't really any challenge. Drones are a perfect example of this. They are 10x larger than your character in game but fire handheld small arms. With anything better than the starting pistol 90% of drones won't present any threat. The 'special' enemies are also pretty lame with very little creativity applied (giant blob, spiders, bigger mech ect). My suggestion is to focus on animation and AI.
4. The plot/character development system also really needs expansion in depth and purpose.   If you want a capital ship you will need to grind via mining- or flying around collecting ore from auto miners. Either way its busy work.
5. The game is not well optimized at the time of writing this review. Better than some like PUBG, but there is a lot of improvment that should be done.
THE GOOD:
1. The latest update massively improves the graphics without any major hit to performance. The game engine is also rock solid for a game in alpha, I haven't had a crash yet.
2. For $30 you will get your moneys worth of entertainment. Survival is good enough, crafting/building works well, space exploration is there.
3. Multiple game modes and starting locations with a good amount of diversity. Co-op as well. The sandbox elements all work together well.

I'm in a love-hate relationship with this game. This review is mostly considering single player experience.
I bought Empyrion a way back when there was only few things to offer even then it had the feel of large planets and endless possibilities. Nowadays Empyrion offers about 10 or so star systems with different kind of planets, a lots of crafting and building, few places of interest, blueprints, lively workshop community and lots of more. So there's plenty of stuff to love.
Designing, crafting and building different kind of ships are just plain fun. I've spent hours to mine iron to get enough minerals for my plans. With the little experience, you start seeing good and bad designs in vessels. When you start a new ship, you get plenty of nice ideas that you want to see in action. Building capital ship gives an nice perspective, because you think that this time my ship is going to be huge, it will be relatively small. On the other hand it is so nice to get a compact model to work for you, without being total chaos. With texture & color tool you can make your signature touches to your creation.
After all it is so great to take your brand new toy to a test drive trough space. Get some rare minerals so that you can improve your ships even more.
so what's missing?
I remember the excitement when my capital vessel took off from the home planet and punctured the clouds for the first time. I saw a endless space with endless adventures ahead. At that point I was already bored to my home planet. At first I got to the moon. I thought everything would be different when I get to the surface, gravity, feel of being in a thin ice, different consistency of the stone.. well, everything on the moon was pretty much like back in the home except that moon didn't have any breathable air. (And it was little bit colder.)  Same thing happened when I got to the other planets of the other systems. I think my biggest disappointment was to realize that all the flora and fauna similar in every planet, no matter how far you go you always get aloe vera and corn.
This same thing happens with micro scale too. Every biome in every planet has always same kind of plants. so planets itself don't invite you to explore anything exept POIs. And POIs on the other hand are pretty much the same in every planet. Some planets have different levels of difficulty, but character-wise they are images of the easier ones.
Other thing that makes me hate this game is overall clumsiness in textures, creature design, plants and so on. The sounds are little bit weird too. Like, drilling sound, for example. Drill sounds like it has few loose parts, it needs to be oiled real bad. Sound gets very irritating after 15 minutes. It's kind of okay for the tier 1 drill because you get that one for free. And it encourage you to get better equipment faster, but in tier 2 I really expect to get a drill with nice smooth sound, nope, it is the same sound. Also the sound of the automatic turrets are so loud that you hop in air every time they start shooting some random beast somewhere. Controls happen to have similar issues. The game has a good signal system, which provides a possibility to control you vessel better, and in a creative way. In order to use those buttons you need to open menu and use your mouse for that. Would be nice to use hot keys so that in fights you could open weapons hatches, change colors in your cockpit, do things that is actually possible to do, but without proper controls pointless. Motorcycles and hover vessels glides like hell and sometimes you cannot stop them. As I described the sounds of drills earlier, I think it's okay to have bad controls if you plan your ship that way. But it really needs an alternative.
Fortunately, developers in this game are being active. And they tend to improve things that matter the most. For example newest version of the game (7.0.0 experimental) gives a opportunity to make planets by hand (a big improvement to seed-based system). Mineral system took a big leap forward too. The beginning of the game needs nowadays more survival skills. Textures and graphics have improved a lot within a year.
I have high hopes that some day I will see variation in flora and fauna in different planets. I also hope that some day small low-end vessel feels different to fly than huge planetoid-size flying mega bases. Maybe in near future swamps have their own characteristics, like little frogs and flies and deserts burns hot. I dream that the game itself encourages me to build a well thought base where I could hang out and feel being safe from the rest of the cruel world. Maybe one day I find more motivation to do something else than build a ship after ship, have an adventure, have a npc-driven quest in a local settlement. Have a reaction from the natives when I arrive to a local shop for the first time. I want to get into a trouble when a loot someones private home, use her shower and eat her food.
Before that I just keep building my ships isolated from the rest of the world (and be rather happy of doing so).

Empyrion is a very solid space exploration and building game.  Right away I will say that this game is still early access, most definitely, but I will also start by saying get it anyways.  If not to enjoy it now then to help the developer of this awesome game.  It is similar to space engineers but is much more survival and interaction centric.  You have to gather food, farm, get water, mine, build, research, and defend yourself.  This game has a decent variety of weapons to protect yourself with as well as armors, but sadly a small variety of enemies to employ them against at the moment.  The content on the first planet rarely gets boring as every object has a reason to exist and you always feel like you are progressing.
The next step is getting vehicles setup and this is great either way you choose.  If you want to build cool go right ahead, and you can make really cool designs that aren't as limited as other space games like it.  If you are like me and you enjoy the exploration and usage more than the building then good news for you too, because if you have the resources you can have the game make the ship for you as long as you have a blueprint.  Vehicles make the game change pretty quickly as you are able to take an offensive stance and you become able to sap the world of all the resources you need.
After awhile you make it to space and currently this is where the early access shows the most sadly.  The ships, warping, the star map, and versatility of designs are great.  Ships can be decorative in this game which is a nice touch, but when you go into space the controls immediately become a problem.  Massive ships can glide around like pondskaters.  Hopefully that is fixed, but the next problem shows in the planets which are.. empty in general.  Still interesting because they are each fairly diverse with different atmospheres, minerals, gravity, and so forth so it isn't terrible, but still it isn't where it will need to be for official release, though you can help that happen.  I greatly suggest this to everyone that is looking for a space game or survival game to give it a try as it is only $20 which is less than many games of its type

Before buying Anomaly 2 you have to ask yourself one question.  Do you like escort missions?  If you do then you should probably consider this game.  It's all about the escort missions.  Really.  That's the whole point of the game.  If you are like me... and most people I hear from, and find escort missions to be tedious and frustrating, then you should probably steer clear.
Don't get me wrong, there is nothing wrong with the game.  It seems to be well done.  Decent art and acting.  No detectable glitches.  But tower defense in reverse... is really hard to make work.  Here you have from 1 to 5 rather fragile units protect with decoys, repairs, stuns and something called A.I.M.  (Which I assume is an air strike.  I haven't seen it in action.)  You can tell the trucks which way to turn at the next intersection... But that's it.  You have no more control than that.  No stopping or turning around.  No shooting at the enemy from outside of their range.  The trucks are going full throttle into the next area no matter what.  Why are the escourtees always twits?
Its a tower defence game where you are fighting the towers.  So a sort of reverse tower defence.  Cool concept, didn't really like how it was executed.

At first Huygens Principle seems like another Hotline Miami knockoff but it's actually quite different. The whole game is built around "you become who you killed" feature. It adds more chaos and fun to the game. There are 13 chapters, each with its own soundtrack. Each level has its own theme like present, future, past and even hell. In some chapters you have an ability to slowdown time and one chapter is like top-down version of Super Hot. Sadly there's no story it to except names of the chapters, which give you not much to go on.
Pros:
- Adrenaline gameplay
- Different abilities
- Many levels
- Exciting soundtrack
Cons:
- Though levels are different in theme, structure is always similar
- If you ragequit, you have to complete chapter from the beginning
- Levels in hell might hurt your eyes
If you like Hotline Miami, then you should definitely play this. Don't let the graphics and Dagestan Techonology's logo fool you. The game is a true hidden gem.

Wasteland Angel is a nice little top down vehicular combat game.  The feel of the game (not the gameplay) reminds me a bit of Death Rally, though not as polished.  The car handles a bit strangely at first but I got used to it pretty quickly.  The game revolves around defending wasteland settlements from mutant slavers, who come in waves and try to steal your citizens.  Every couple levels you will fight a boss, followed by a bonus level.  For some reason the bonus levels use a first person camera and I wish it was an option to switch between the two modes.
Gameplay-wise, the game is quite simple.  Waves of enemies come at you, and you must destroy them before they destroy you or steal your citizens.  Only certain vehicles can steal citizens so you have to keep an eye out for them.  You can recover citizens by destroying the vehicles before they can get away, but then the citizens are vulnerable to being run over and gunfire, and will often be accidentally killed by you just by destroying the vehicle.
Overall it's some quick fun.  It doesn't take long to complete so I wouldn't say it's worth $10 but when it's on sale, it's not a bad deal.

My Review for "Right In the Childhood: Oddworld Edition". AKA, *Whistle* *Whistle* *Fart* "Ok."
The Good:
-Somehow manages to be better than the original.
-Welcomes newcomers with a health system and slightly dumber Sligs while giving the old players some love with "Hard Mode" and achievements.
-Old gamespeak works even better with new dialogue, it sure beats "Hello.", "Hello.", "Follow Me.", "Ok."
-An "ALL 'O YA!" button! Man, it was a pain only calling one Mudokon at a time.
-QUIK SAVE!
-Still fun chanting and controlling Sligs...then killing them.
-The game scrolls instead of cutting into "Scenes" see: Slideshow.
-Graphics look "Next Gen", whatever that means.
-A little bit of PC love with rebindable keys and graphics options!
The Meh:
-Co-op mode is kinda silly...."Oh i died, here buddy, take my keyboard....oh you died, here, give it back." Yeah...
-Some muddy textures here and there.
-Some iffy animations.
-No Exoddus love...yet.
Overall:
Oddworld was that old gem that brought a great story, fantastic characters, incredible art, and unique game mechanics to the platformers back in the day that STILL hasn't been done like it to this day. Now with New 'N Tasty, newcomers can enjoy that old game but in a completely new(and tasty) way. If you have never played the original, no need, just play this, trust me, it'll save you some money in keyboard replacements. Now Lorne, get crackin' on that New 'N Tasty for Exoddus!

Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty has been in development for quite some time now, and all I can say is it was well worth the wait. The game is absolutley gorgeous and rebuilt from the ground up, I can absolutley say that it is worth the £14.99 asking price, you get more out of it than some AAA titles that cost £50+. Not only are the graphics beautiful, but the game is also suprisingly easy to run at 1080p (i can run it at 50Fps medium settings) considering it is built in a 3D environment.
The gameplay does not at all let you down, with a few control tweaks which are easily accessible in the settings menu, you can create quick and easy controls for fast action platforming. The gameplay is very fluid and exciting, you might think it is another silly kid's game that can be abandoned in a dark corner of Steam, but no, it is one of the most thrilling and exciting experiances you will have as a gamer. The story, gameplay, graphics, sounds and animations are some of the best I have ever seen in a platformer. You won't be disappointed.
Finally, as a player of the original game, Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee (also available on Steam), I can say for definate that this game is a 100% improvement on it's original. If you want to experiance Abe's story, this is the way to do it.
Story - 10/10
Game design - 8/10
Graphics - 9/10
Sound - 5/10
Gameplay - 7/10
Replayability - 3/10 (Mainly for achievments only)
Overall - 9.5/10
What are you waiting for!? Buy it now, it's awesome, fun and original, Just Add Water did a fantastic job, show 'em you are grateful and get your hands on a copy.

This game has a lot going for it. There is a lot to customize. There are some interesting story elements, but it is just isn't fun to play. I love SRPGs. It's my favorite genre. This game isn't a great example of them, however. The characters are flat. The battles are uninteresting. The voice acting at times is horrendous.
My most major issue, however, is the rate at which hits are calculated. You can have a 95% chance to hit, and only hit 60% of the time. It's very frustrating.
If you wish to buy this game, you're not making a terrible choice. This game isn't terrible by any stretch of the imagination. I just don't recommend that people play it. It doesn't hold your attention long enough to get into anything interesting.

I thought it would be fun. It kind of is, but it's incredibly frustrating. Poor detection on clicking enemies and random luck screws you over worse than it does in XCOM. It's really inconsistant in its mechanics. You'd think it would be simple, that highest initiative goes first. But it doesn't. It seems like it only improves chances of going earlier in the turn order. Because I'll restart a level and a different character gets the first move. You'd think this would make things interesting but it just makes it incredibly difficult to learn from your mistakes when it constantly changes. Wounds just break immersion so much it's baffling that they put them in. Your characters get "wounds" that carry over from one fight to the next, which cripples them somewhat and you have to see a healer constantly if you didn't invest heavily in some kind of "do-it-yourself" wound healing. Really kills the immersion for me at least to leave a dungeon, go get healed and come back after every room. Some maps are just really unreasonable and you have to try over and over again to even almost win. I mean, it speaks volumes when the first option in the esc menu is "Try Again". I mean, I'm trying to be fair. The game is fun and the concept is great. Overall it's an okay game but if it weren't for the overwhelming swarm of tiny annoyances, it would have been amazing. All in all, it's far from a waste of money, but I honestly wish I had bought something else.

Nice Medieval open world crafting PVP focused game. with a somewhat heavy learning curve at the beginning.
1. create a character
2. join server.
3. Follow basic tutorial (and get lost, not knowing what to do next).
4. Start farming up resources and kill low lvl NPC's to build up your character.
5. explore the map a bit and get better gear from other town npc's or craft them your self.
6. find some ppl in game to join up with or play with some friends. (you will have a hard time alone)
7. Start your adventure: kill other faction players, take over towns and strongholds to get more control over the map, search for high lvl bosses and survive the medieval open world as you build up your character more and get even better gear.
Game has alot to offer for still being EA, and has alot of potential with what the dev's will do in the near future.
Definaly worth to check out while its still on sale now on steam!

HEAD'S UP: I cannot speak to the game's actual core gameplay, as I haven't tried it, nor do I really intend to as odd as it sounds. I am STRICTLY REVIEWING THE SHIP EDITOR here. If that's what you wanna read about, please, carry forward.
I'm an interesting case. I bought Interstellar Rift specifically for ship design. I'm an engineer at heart and I love building things. Spaceships? Pretty high up on the list of "awesome things to create" I think. I've tried many games to get my fix. Kerbal Space Program scratched the rocketry itch, but didn't offer me the nitty-gritty of internals. Building rooms, placing systems, connecting a power grid...
I tried Space Engineers, but I'm a rather impatient man. As good as Space Engineers is, the building aspect didn't give me the freedom I wanted, as even in Creative you have to do everything in first person and it gets a bit fiddly.
Starship Corporation has a ton of promise, but confines me to set fuselages. It'll be great fun as a corporate management game going forward, but it's not what I'm after in terms of absolute design freedom.
Kinetic Void is okay as far as externals, but the internals are a matter of "click on a section, select systems that are in there somewhere" which isn't the complexity I'm after. (Plus it kind of... stopped updating.)
So as I'm starting up my first tabletop campaign of Uncharted Worlds with a friend (highly recommend it if you're a tabletop roleplayer by chance), I decided I wanted to give this search another go, and I noticed this $15 Early Access game I'd kept putting off trying. It was time. Enter Interstellar Rift.
It. Is. MAGNIFICENT. It takes the basic premise of constructing ships in Space Engineers and simplifies the mechanics to drag-and-click, with tons of systems placed in a matter not unlike placing furniture in The Sims. It requires that life support, power, all that good stuff be accounted for.
While it's maybe not perfectly complex (IE, you don't have to manually build ventillation shafts to connect your fans to your life support), it does an excellent job of balancing availability with depth. I can build a little maneuverable heavy fighter akin to Elite: Dangerous' Cobra, a bulky freighter the likes of which I couldn't even access in Elite: Dangerous, all the way up to a huge capital ship the likes of which would make xenos the galaxy over tremble... All by clicking and dragging. And the best part? I can walk around my ship, and should I so desire, even take it out and do stuff with it (then again, that's getting into core gameplay, which again is NOT WHAT I'M REVIEWING, I haven't touched it.)
This perfect marriage of simplicity and freedom, having an easy to use placement system while still providing mechanical depth and potentially grand scale... This is EXACTLY what I've been searching for, for the better part of five years. For the ship editor alone, it was worth my $15, no question.
DISCLAIMER: If you want more than just a ship editor, please don't assume it'll be worth YOUR $15. Best to look to other reviews first. If your unique tastes match up with mine, however, and a game that lets you build the internals and externals of your ship with minimal fiddling... Don't overlook this. Seriously, don't.

I hope the devs actually get a chance to read this review...
Anyway, i'll start with the game itself. The idea is very good, similar in many ways to Elite Dangerous, but making it much more immersive, less Superglue-on-my♥♥♥♥♥ Stuck-to-my-Seat issues, and just an overall better experience. I really enjoy the game and foresee a very good game near its final release.
The Visuals; Bravo! I don't think i've seen a voxel based game where everything looks so smooth. Even space engineers looks blocky, but IR has a very smooth, almost fabricated look. No matter how your ship comes out, it all looks like it was a prebuilt ship. And i appreciate that.
Ship Building; needs a lot of work. Things need more in-depth information when building, the exterior block building needs a much better organization method, and we really need some automated turrets... not everyone can run a crew, and its not fun trying to make a super large, super heavy ship fight against small little skrill swarming you.
Now my critical issue right now though, is that i dont feel any progression... You start the game with next to nothing, you kill yourself for hours to get materials to get a really nice, big, powerful ship. Then you design another, even better ship! And... now you gotta repeat the process, identically, just as slow. See, when i go from a small little 3 room freighter, to a massive carrier-sized ship with 4-8 refineries and 4-8 extractors, i expect to feel like i actually got somewhere in the game, like all that work paid off... cuz right now, it doesnt. We can only do so much as a single person, or even a crew. Cool, i might have 2 million of iron, steel, copper, silicon, carbon and whatever else you use to make ships, but why should i make a bigger ship when i cant even manage a few extractors and refineries? This game seriously needs more benefits for people who get further in. Automation would be a huge step forward. Automation enough where i can have 20 extractors and refinieries and have it all neatly fill up my cargo space. Of course, for that you would need the automation chips, but at least have a teleport or conveyor system that doesnt need a chip... so we can just run to an extractor, let it mine, run to the refinery and let all the ores just teleport to it! That way, if you only have extractor or only refinery chips, you can still get some of the automation done.
End conclusion: Get this game, but for the time being, dont expect a lot of satisfaction. Making your first non-creative ship, maybe even your second, will be nice (ignoring the insane grind), but after that it just gets old, fast.

Styx: Master of Shadows takes place in the world Of Orcs and Men. The action taking place after Styx parts ways with Arkail and sees about his daily life activities befiting a rogue.
You play as Styx, a nimble goblin with many strange talents backed up by a winding and strange past. He is sarcastic, vulgar, greedy and sometimes a good guy.
The actions starts in The Tower of Akenash, a massive tower built for mages and elves, where Styx wakes up unconcious in a dungeon and suffers a memory loss. Throughout the story Styx has moments where he remembers bits and pieces of his past and the reason why he is there.
As gameplay Styx allows you to infiltrate an area by assasinating your way through enemies or taking full advantage of a goblin's abilities and remain undetected.
Unlike other stealth or infiltration games where you play as a human, Styx is a goblin, meaning he is able to hide is unexpected areas such as drain pipes, under the tables, baskets and effortlessly pass though small or cramped areas offering you new paths to explore and achieve your objective faster.
Styx is able to use his trusty dagger to make quick work of his enemies, But he is also able to use throwing daggers, acid bottles, poison food or water and make sand balls to create shadows for him to sneak through places undetected or create a distraction.
Styx's supernatural abilities are his Amber powers. He has grown addicted to amber that leaves a visible "amber scar" on his body (and throughout the story he will complain about head aches) but in return, Styx can see though walls or turn invisible. Lastly Styx is able to create clones of himself and take direct control of them. The clones have lesser abilities and aren't as nimble as Styx, but they can distract enemies or reach areas Styx is otherwise unable to. Upgrading the clones will enable them to take out targets or even ambush enemies if they hide in a trunk, chest or pot.
Overall Styx is a unique experience with a unique character that you will grow fond of (if you don't mind his mature humour). The combat won't be to many people's liking but they forget that Styx is a goblin; he is small and isn't phisically strong enough to send enemies flying across the room like Arkail was.

Great pixel art, fantastic music (though it kind of bothers me that the diagetic music doesn't actually match what the characters describe it as; just because it's all in one octave doesn't make it a scale), feels, laughs, token gameplay, lots of hints to a larger mystery,

Anomaly 2 is a reverse tower defense game and it's pretty dang hard. I like the power ups and the way you have to strategize and balance avoiding and engaging enemies in order to gain power ups. The presentation is simple but well done. Voice acting is well done. The story's aight... It's sentient robots try to eliminate the remnants of humanity terminator type stuff.
My one complaint is the hectic feeling of trying to stay alive. I had this complaint with the game Bad Hotel. Tower defense games need to have balance. These types of games almost always have power ups and upgrades and give the player a good sense of progression (a feeling that a lot of games use to keep us coming back for more). The trick is to give us that sense of progression without making the game feel easy. You can never feel overpowered. In Anomaly 2... you won't. In fact you often feel underpowered (good for a sense of apocalyptic desperation I guess...). I always felt like I was scrambling to heal my units. It's more of a battle to keep them alive than a battle to conquer. It's like you're the wimpy kid and you're trying to patch up your wounds in time to get ready for the next beating. Games should'nt feel like that.
In conclusion, Anomaly 2 is an okay title but I think it would have been better if your units had shields or a slow health regeneration. I would take more risks as a player if I knew that my units would stand a chance without me having to repair them after every single attack.
6/10

For many small games I've never heard of, I put the game to a simple test: is the game still fun after one hour? Honestly, many games fail this test. But this one does not. The core mechanics of this game, of supporting your line of mechs, controlling their route, and turning them into the correct form, is enough control over the battle to be very engaging but, unlike highly convoluted space strategy games or other RTS games, not enough to be truly overwhelming. Your main unit has distinctive and strategic abilities, but positioning is very important. Do you create a hallucination to draw away enemy fire, or keep spamming the heal button every two steps? Can you afford the time it takes to run off the main path, putting you further away from healing, to put up the hallucination?

If you have this game in your library, it is definitely worth the installation. I would even consider putting it in the "top 10 steam games you never heard of", especially if you like RTS.

OK, Sad, Very SAD update.
Version 17 has ruined the mining experience completely and means I put the game on the shelf to play no longer.  This is one of those sad moments when developers do the wrong thing for the wrong reason, and then can't ever backtrack for fear of losing face, and so the game is ruined.
So here it is, instead of what you will see in all the earlier Youtube demos, a nice mining tool drilling into the ground, in a few seconds, at a reasonable depth, you locate the desired ore which is obvious from its coloration in the ground.  Now it's clear where to continue to drill for it and things proceed straightforward.
On to the clusterf&ck that is version 17.  Now, you will drill 'til Hell and never see colorful patches of ore.  Instead, you need a critical tool a "scanner" which, wait for it, will show you some blue outlines below you that represent "blobs" of ore.  You'll also find the ore is much, much deeper down, IF you manage to locate it.  Without the "scanner", you might as well close your eyes and drill in random directions hoping to to find some ore.  With, or without a scanner, you'll also have to risk drilling SO DEEP that if you do it straight down without paying attention, you could trap yourself and be unable to get out without having spare drilling fuel, fuel you didn't need prior to this foolish update.
Since drilling is so critical in the game, this new design is a complete game changer and completely ruins this critical aspect of the game.
To sum up the changes:
1. Ore no longer is something colorful you drill to a reasonable deptht to acquire and without undue searching at the drill site.  Instead, you need twice as much drill power, search frustratingly long to even find the small "blobs" of ore.  Now instead of easily drilling down to colorful ore in an orderly process, you now have to drill towards a "blule outline" on the ground and will then even have a very hard time even finding it when you get near it.

I cannot say enough good things about this game.  I tremendously enjoy the freedom and options it offers.  It has TREMENDOUS replay value in that I endlessly enjoy starting from ground zero on a random planet location without even enough resources to build a base, and racing before sunset of the first day to gather enough randomly scattered resources  to start a base or at least a motorcycle to travel further.  Then sneak into an abandoned site and gather enough materials to advance (better mining tool or weapons) after escaping on the motorcycle as the drones try and kill you to get back to your base before your oxygen runs out.  I've literally been on my last breaths when getting back several times.  No, it's not perfect and has flaws; the enemy AI can be lacking and you can avoid all the nastiness of base attacks altogether by building your base underground (I prefer right where I mine my Iron) since you just won't risk any damage at all from the enemy.  But the flexibility of building your base and vehicles the way you want (or grab some pre-designs to skip that if you want) and then having enough planets with different resources to travel to keeps it interesting with the NPCs there.  Weapons are nice and varied and scoring a special enhanced weapon from an enemy base is a nice bonus.  I think it's a steal at 20 bucks and hopefully we are headed to a future where the universe expands like Elite Dangerous and the richness of NPC and enemy experience continues to enhance the game.  Running 3.4Ghz 4 cores and 750GTX video and it runs smooth w only a bit of slowdown in a massive enemy base at times.  Great game that I rotate for replay value with Ark and 7 Days to Die since all have replay value in random locations...
I like that games like this make you think and solve seemingly real scenarios that pop up.  Example is back climbing the learning curve, I left my ship somewhere where it got attacked and ended up to where I didn't even have resources to build a tool to mine resources when I died attacking a base and had no chance to get back in and survive to grab my dropped items, so seemingly dead end, right?  Well I still had a lone tool to dissasemble items and was able to get just the right parts from dissembling bits of my fragmented ship remains to be able to build a mining tool and claw my way back to survival...  Good fun and definitely a recommended game!

Empyrion  has everything you could ever want in a survival game.
Empyrion has everything you could ever want from Devs who care.
This is by far my favorite survival game, the crafting is fantastic (just throw a bunch of stuff in a constructor and craft from that inventory rather than your own!)  and the building mechanics are great too.  Being able to build your own ships from scratch without giving them that minecraft look gives this game one of the best building mechanics out there.  Combat mechanics have been greatly improved too.
I only have a couple issues that I only bring up because I havent heard anything about it from the list of planned updates, but anyone reading this should know that the Devs are VERY ACTIVE!!!
My first issue is repairing a ship.  There needs to be a save state attached to specific structures that repair bays can fix when blocks get destroyed.  building a massive capital ship is an amazing feature but good luck replacing every destroyed block after a big fight.
When building it doesnt matter how small an object is that you place it takes up the space of the largest block you can place.  Decorations and Cargo boxes can not just be placed in a room that you make, the room has to be made with the items already in mind.
You can get to level 25 on your first planet easily, and usually mine every kind of resource in asteroid fields nearby from the very start, which kind of lessens the excitment of exploration when going to other planets.  There should be more rare resources than there are now that create higher level equipment and structures that can ONLY be found on certain kinds of planets.
But don't let that discourage you from buying this game.  It's fantastic and I highly recommend it, it feels like this game was made from a place of passion and care.  It constantly has updates and I'm very much looking forward to Alpha 7.

Wasteland Angel is a fun, if shallow action game in the mold of micro-machines, set in a post-apocalyptic future. If you're looking for a quick desctraction from a AAA title, then you could do a lot worse than this game.
Arm your car with weapons, power-ups and amror. Point in the direction of the enemy vehicles and shoot away. Getting power-ups is addictive, as is using the special weapons to destroy the enemy cars. Gameplay is repetitive. Missions are mainly defending town population from slavers. There are a few that are variations: such as first-person drive-by levels and the kill or be killed boss levels. Six camapign stages provides 4-6 hours of play in story-mode, but you can play to beat the leaderboards on a per level basis afterwards.
Overall the game is one of those easy to overlook, but if you take a chance in a sale it will give you a good few hours of destructive fun. One of those to keep on your hard-drive for a quick blast now and again.

Currently, this is a very open ended simulator, with the primary focus on building your own ships. You can design anything you want from building a basic shuttle to copying your favorite sci-fi series ship. (Or build a 1:1 scale death star if your really ambitious.)
Even if you don't like to build, you can just grab ships from the workshop and fly. Outside the building aspects however, the content is fairly sparce. There are aliens (and other players if your inclined) to fight against, but the quests are fairly generic and the lack of story and NPC characters may drive off some folks.
Gaining the resources to build your creations is, thankfully, rather simple. You just fly to an asteroid field and start up your extractors, then refine the ore (sometimes several times). It's no harder then just moving around crates that are given to you. Alternatively, you can earn money in the missions and just buy the resources from a trading station.
If you like to design your ships all the way down to utility grids and aestetics, this is a good buy currently.
If your not a fan of building and rather dive into an exciting and vibrant game world, your better off waiting.

I've been on Steam for nearly five years now and Gloria Victis is the first game to motivate me to write a review. PvP is a truely rewarding experience, it is easy to grasp but if you manage to master it you will make a name for yourself amongst your allies and your foes. There is a partial loot system which is perfect I believe. The risk of losing something you put time and effort into crafting causes you to choose your fights carefully, but not so much so that you never see PvP.
If you really want to get the most out of Gloria Victis join a guild and get to know them, learn how they fight, and discuss strategies. Top tier gear and weapons will not save you from an equally numbered enemy with a well thought out/executed strategy. Another rewarding feeling in GV is being part of a guild that has made itself well known even across servers.
Crafting in this game is amazing. See something you'd like to have? First of all you have to find the recipe. Then travel throughout the world gathering the resources you will need to craft all of its components. Bring your materials back to a castle your nation owns, and take those materials through numerous processes at various workstations. What you just made could be a standard piece of equipment, but with a little luck it could be Pristine. Every piece of armor and weapon in the game ranges from base stats to +6. Your chance to create a +6 item depends on your reputation, the crafting station you are using, the level of your profession, and the amount of territory your nation owns. This motivates even the crafters to come out and PvP.
The developers are constantly making improvements and fixing bugs found by the players,and has made a lot of progress since I began playing. Gloria Victis shows potential I have never seen in another game, which is why after 5 years on steam I have to decided to write my first review. Try it out, join a guild, and make a name for yourself.
