ATTENTION: Had an issue with Rivatuner/D3DOverider being turned on which caused the game not to be able to switch to fullscreen or change resolutions without freezing. Just a heads up if anyone is experiencing the same issue.
Other than that the game runs great. Has plenty of options. It does have a scarce graphics menu, but the game still looks fantastic for what it is. There's even keyboard AND controller prompts, something a bigger company like Koei Tecmo can't seem to grasp.
The game keeps things fresh by giving players different ships (and a fairy) that utilize power ups and bomb attacks in different ways while also changing ship maneuverability. I'm fan of the flagship...ship of the game personally. I find it easier to maneuver and the weapons feel great to me. The overkill system is neat and a great way for players to try and wrack up points by bring more death to those that are already dead. Although, I find my greed into trying to rack up scores by doing this gets myself killed in the process.
The difficulty of the game is unrelenting. I find it difficult even on normal settings. I can't bring myself to go any lower than that, but seeing as how I'll probably never get to the end of the game if I don't do it, I'll probably just have to swallow my pride. The game isn't very bullet helly to me. It has more to do with enemy shots moving fast as lightning and sometimes being hard see due to them blending in with the backgrounds sometimes. It might just be because I'm finally getting up in age and my eyesight just isn't as good as it used to be.
The soundtrack for the Raiden games have never really wowed me, but their pretty good and always go along with the feel of each stage. I'm more of a fan of their sound effects for their weapons than anything else and this game doesn't disappoint. I just love hearing that laser baby.
The game also has a gallery that allows you to view and play around with some of the models in the game. You unlock them through game progression and gives gamers another level of replayability. While the models look pretty rough up close, it still a nice little bonus to just mess around with.
Overall all, H2 Interactive did a fine job with their port of this game. If you're a fan of the genre in general this is one game that should be in your library. It definitely won't disappoint your if you're looking for something to fill that shoot'em up void in your heart.

First off, let me say that I'm a fan of the original Evoland. It was a simple game that had a unique gameplay thing that I've always wanted to see: graphical progression from 8 bit all the way to high definition polygons of the modern era. I think the original pulled it off with a simple charm to it. Having said that, it was also short and a little too heavy on the meta humor, not that I think that it's bad or anything. The second Evoland from my experience so far does indeed take this premise and give it more life. They play with the concept more and you're given alot to work with, and it's not just there for jokes and references, although they'll still give you plenty of those. Gameplay is tight and the characters are funny but functional. When it comes to the kind of gameplay you'll experience, I would compare Evo 2 to a platter of appetizers and finger foods. You get a little taste of various genres and playstyles, and there's just enough to give you a taste of each. a little caramel turn based strategy, some autoscrolling shmups covered in garlic butter, a creme freche platforming that switches from 2 D to 3 D constantly, that kind of thing. If each was expanded upon greatly and given a little more polish, I think they would be solid as standalone games. evo doesn't do that to the extent that I described though. What you get is good, but it's limited. It leaves you wanting more at least, so I give it that.
Unfortunately, there's a large batch of downsides to this game, on a technical level. There's a rather unpleasant sound freezing that occurs once in a while, which is like when a sound effect is interrupted and you hear a very loud screeching noise. I've also encountered difficulties with windowed mode and resolution changes. Although you can press alt+enter to bring up this mode, there's not much you can do to change the resolution, and I'd appreciate it if you could at least do this from the menu. The worst among these problems is a very bad screen freezing bug, which prevents you from playing the game period. It's fixed with a restart, and with the checkpoint system in place, you won't lose hours of progress thankfully. Still, it's a noticeable problem that really makes the game tough to recommend, but since I still want to finish it in spite of these problems, I can say that the positives outweigh the negatives. It has much room for improvement though. Let's hope the devs one day get to that.
I give it two thumbs slightly pointing upward, as most of my complaints are from hardware issues, possibly on my end, possibly from the game, but I had little issue with the gameplay itself.

If you were ever looking for video game nostalgia, then play Evoland 2, or as I call it, Video Game Throwback: The Game.

If you're looking for a tl:dr, I do recommend Evoland 2 despite it's faults. The gameplay is extremely varied, it has a unique mechanic regarding time travel that alters the graphics of the game, and there are also lots of references and jokes to other games in the genre making for some funny moments in a somewhat forgettable story. The story itself isn't bad, but it's nothing special. As long as you don't take it too seriously and ignore some of the paradoxes they've most likely created, you should find the story somewhat enjoyable.
Seriously, this game has the most varied gameplay I've ever seen. A good amount of the game is spent in the Zelda style top down view but there are sections where it goes completely 2D and turns into a platformer, a section where the game goes Final Fantasy style completely turn based, a Street Fighter style boss fight, a bullet hell segment, and even a village where you fight people in a modified version of Bejeweled! Every time I get to a new section, it feels like I'm playing a different game. This game does a lot to make sure it's not repetitive.
As much as there is to experience in this game, gameplay varied to this degree does have it's drawbacks. When you have so many different genres melding into one game, you're going to lose people at one point. Some sections you'll have a blast with and will be disappointed when they're over, while other sections will bore you and you'll be glad when that segment ends. Personally, I enjoyed the Bejeweled section but I was having a hard time getting through the Final Fantasy part since it felt like all I was doing was the same commands over and over again for every battle. Another unfortunate problem is that since the game has so many different mechanics regarding all the genre shifts, they aren't as fine tuned as their respective games. This was especially true during the Street Fighter segment. The controls were pretty clunky and when I pressed pause, it would show my moves list but not only did it disappear if you go to another tab but it also didn't list the move that uses your special meter.
Since Evoland 2 borrows a lot from other games, it only makes sense to have a little fun with it. I had a good laugh when one of the ladies in town said I should be wary of a boy wearing green clothing who goes into people's houses and smashes their pots. As for the main story, there's not much to say really. The game starts off with a main character with amnesia cliche but after meeting the girl who took care of you while you were out cold, you quickly start your adventures through time. The characters all have funny dialogue and do have character progression. It is a time travel story though so expect some paradoxes and the usual confusion that comes with quantum physics. With the amount of jokes it makes towards other games and even at itself, I don't believe the story is too serious. As long as you don't expect it to be the next Mass Effect or something with it's storytelling, you'll most likely enjoy what the story has to offer. Now the interesting thing about time travel in this game is that when you go back in time, the graphics do much of the same. It starts out looking like a Gameboy Advance game but when you go to the past, it looks like somewhere between NES and SNES. Going into the future makes the game go entirely 3D which could definitely pass as a late Gamecube/PS2 era game. With a mechanic like this, it makes exploring the world in two different time periods interesting in more ways than one.
Evoland 2 is a pretty decent game. I finished the game in 15 hours with a 67% completion rate so for you completionists out there, you can easily get another 5-10 hours out of this game. While the first Evoland was more of a brief parody of the adventure game genre, this game was more focused on standing out on it's own. They've taken a bunch of different gameplay styles and mashed them into one game. With all the references to other games, this game feels like a retrospective of not only what the adventure genre has branched off to, but also to what gaming has evolved into in general. We may have started out with simple games like Pac-Man and Super Mario but now we've got side scrolling beat em' ups like Final Fight, strategy RPG's like Fire Emblem, shoot em' up games like Star Fox, and so much more. I feel like that's where this game shines the most. It does have it's problems but in the end, it was nice to experience a taste of all the different genres the gaming industry has created.

First off: I haven't played a platformer as good as this one in a long time.
While the mechanics aren't exactly the most you can get out of the genre everything else is pretty much spot on.
The soundtrack is amazing, the very ghibliesque and mellow visuals can switch from a calm stroll over a meadow to full on action chase scenes and the overall presentation is stellar, which becomes evident from the second you start up the game and browse through the snappy menu.
The intro starts off very strong and builds the premise quickly and lets you easily empathize with your main character. Although it's a very simple and basic storyline it'll hit you right in the feels from the very first minute again shining especially in the visual department.
The gameplay itself is basic metroidvania with a big interconnected map with lots of places to explore and resources to gather (that enhance your character either through the skill tree, health or mana upgrades). Enemy variety is alright, though not great either. They fit well into the world, even if they are rather generic and don't vary too much from level to level, but the interaction with your abilities that you'll unlock later (separate from your skill tree that enhances them further) adds another degree of gameplay on top of what you're getting used to, so it's unlikely that you'll get bored easily.
I'm only roughly 3 hours in, but so far the (mini?-)bosses are a bit underwhelming. Games like Outland made them feel a lot more epic while in this game they seem to be very generic, small enemies that have more health than the regular ones and only slightly differ from the non-boss enemies.
But yeah, that's pretty much all my criticism right now. Despite the little flaws the developers behind this made a huge effort to craft a very well put together videogame that is absolutely worth it's 20$/20€ price tag, so my verdict is:

The Amber Throne is an excellent little game that pushes the envelope for what can be done with RPGMaker. It takes the classic JRPG formula and either tweaks or polishes features so they stand out from the crowd. The hand drawn backgrounds and sprites and impressive music add a great amount to the game. The game's combat, while not straying far from the elemental rock, paper, scissors that tends to be common in JRPGs, mixes it up with enemies stances, and with it their weaknesses and resistances, changing throughout combat. Content is reasonably lengthy, at about 14 hours from start to finish. The game's few detractors were a number of typo's, syntax errors, and minor bugs that did not detract from my experience. Overall, if you're a fan of the genre, give The Amber Throne a look and you likely won't be disappointed.

The story starts as so: The Amber God had a prophetic vision that there would be a rebellion that would claim his life. He perceived that, if the throne fell into the wrong hands, the destruction and carnage that would fall upon the land would be catastrophic and unparalleled. He raised his kingdom high into the sky and protected it by encasing it inside of an impenetrable cloud. The events unfolded as he knew they would and he was killed by the rebellion. Prior to raising his kingdom into the sky, he hid his sleeping daughter away with the hopes that she would someday awaken and destroy the throne once and for all. The reason why the throne had to be destroyed is because the Amber Throne grants any wish that can be imagined to the person that sits upon it. There have been several Amber Gods. However, this particular Amber God wanted to stop the cycle. Will his daughter Arra be able to fulfill her father’s dying wish?

I hadn't played a CoD game seriously since CoD4, so I was super excited for this entry and wanted to get back into the franchise a bit, BUT the multiplay here sucks♥♥♥♥♥♥
They split up the PC multiplayer market. People who bought the game on the microsoft store ARE NOT ON THE SAME SERVERS as people who buy it here on steam (they do not play together). That means the population was cut in half before the game was even released. Not only that, but the game did not sell well, and there are only like 5000 or fewer players on at any given time. I have sat in the queue waiting for a game for over 10 minutes.
Even when you find a game, they use peer-to-peer connections, and I personally felt like every single game was laggy. All that is sad... because once you get your bearings the mode is pretty good... but holy ♥♥♥♥ the conditions must be perfect in order to enjoy the mode. Played and solved the title on the XBox 360 some time ago and decided to get it for the PC while it was on special late 2016 around the holiday season to finish up on aspects overlooked during the console run. Definitely better in numerous ways contrasting the console version and improves upon what Asylum established. The storyline develops on Asylum and branches considerably with DLC for Catwoman and Robin as well as providing the Game Plus mode offering serious re-playability and affordably with the GoTY Edition. Batman afficianados already know this, but any newbs to the franchise or the generally curious will definitely have a good bit of fun with the open map/world aspect, challenges, side missions and a fairly engrossing plot.
.
Anyone unfamiliar with Batman, the series or simply just looking into an action/adventure title to cool their heels with a bit of entertainment on the side are best suited entering the series at this point. If interest peaks one may opt to go back and obtain Asylum for background story and introduction to when and where the plot picked up. Both Asylum and City installments play closely to one another for a comprehensive treatment and inway into the Batman universe with very professional level direction and voice acting. Once again, newer players will more than likely enjoy Arkham City with the various open world offerings while purists & fans will also enjoy Asylum.
BAC (Batman Arkham City) GoTY Edition is worth $20, but a must have when on special for open-world, action/adventure fans without question. Combat is more involved than spamming a button as some reviews state -there are precision attacks as well as timing constraints in addition to powering up attacks and chaining combos. There are skills and equipment upgrades reliant upon experience leveling (RPG style) and challenges that, upon completion, provide upgrades otherwise unavailable (Augmented Reality Training scenarios; etc.) allowing the player to progress their presence in the City formiddably. In addition to the generally advanced hand-to-hand, stealth combat is real as well as evasion using cover and concealment allowing you the choice of engagement or avoidance. BAC suits completionist players and speed runners ammicably where one can pick and choose as much or as little lateral to the main plot without penalizing either form of play.
I've played Asylum and City both, solved both and enjoy both immensely as well as recommend both; Asylum is more story-driven-linear while City is open-world advancing upon Asylum mechanics greatly evolving the series. You can't go wrong with either, but BAC is more wide open. Game has weathered 5 years (as of this review) well and I still play the game when I'm not distracted by other titles -10/10 and definitely understand the Meta Critic Score.

You can also choose your starting equipment, this is pretty neat, if it weren't for the fact that you lose all of your equipment after your first combat.
Speaking of combat, every action you do has a high chance of failing, from casting a spell to setting a trap to swinging a club. The chance to hit or be succesful is made harder by your enemies' defenses. Wait, that's not all, the damage range of your weapons goes from 1-6, 5-10, or 4-12 for example, this damage is further reduced by your enemies' damage reduction %, and flat damage reduction. This means that on top of the abnormally high miss chance(plus dodge and parry chances!), actually dealing damage is stupendously hard. Now imagine most enemies have around the same health as you, 30ish. So what do you do? You wail on the enemies until they fall down, hoping you even hit them. This makes combat feel sluggish, your actions meaningless, and generally make you waste time.
The story? You get to choose which lines are said first.. sometimes. It also appears you get some dialogue options at times. None of these worked, and didn't work the few times I did try them. Perhaps they work later in the game when you have a higher Charisma? Thing is, I maxed my charisma, it wouldn't go higher, so why have those options there at the start anyway? To waste my time? Make me feel like I have a choice? No, this is another kick to the nuts this game gives.

If you're looking for a tl:dr, I do recommend Evoland 2 despite it's faults. The gameplay is extremely varied, it has a unique mechanic regarding time travel that alters the graphics of the game, and there are also lots of references and jokes to other games in the genre making for some funny moments in a somewhat forgettable story. The story itself isn't bad, but it's nothing special. As long as you don't take it too seriously and ignore some of the paradoxes they've most likely created, you should find the story somewhat enjoyable.
Seriously, this game has the most varied gameplay I've ever seen. A good amount of the game is spent in the Zelda style top down view but there are sections where it goes completely 2D and turns into a platformer, a section where the game goes Final Fantasy style completely turn based, a Street Fighter style boss fight, a bullet hell segment, and even a village where you fight people in a modified version of Bejeweled! Every time I get to a new section, it feels like I'm playing a different game. This game does a lot to make sure it's not repetitive.
As much as there is to experience in this game, gameplay varied to this degree does have it's drawbacks. When you have so many different genres melding into one game, you're going to lose people at one point. Some sections you'll have a blast with and will be disappointed when they're over, while other sections will bore you and you'll be glad when that segment ends. Personally, I enjoyed the Bejeweled section but I was having a hard time getting through the Final Fantasy part since it felt like all I was doing was the same commands over and over again for every battle. Another unfortunate problem is that since the game has so many different mechanics regarding all the genre shifts, they aren't as fine tuned as their respective games. This was especially true during the Street Fighter segment. The controls were pretty clunky and when I pressed pause, it would show my moves list but not only did it disappear if you go to another tab but it also didn't list the move that uses your special meter.
Since Evoland 2 borrows a lot from other games, it only makes sense to have a little fun with it. I had a good laugh when one of the ladies in town said I should be wary of a boy wearing green clothing who goes into people's houses and smashes their pots. As for the main story, there's not much to say really. The game starts off with a main character with amnesia cliche but after meeting the girl who took care of you while you were out cold, you quickly start your adventures through time. The characters all have funny dialogue and do have character progression. It is a time travel story though so expect some paradoxes and the usual confusion that comes with quantum physics. With the amount of jokes it makes towards other games and even at itself, I don't believe the story is too serious. As long as you don't expect it to be the next Mass Effect or something with it's storytelling, you'll most likely enjoy what the story has to offer. Now the interesting thing about time travel in this game is that when you go back in time, the graphics do much of the same. It starts out looking like a Gameboy Advance game but when you go to the past, it looks like somewhere between NES and SNES. Going into the future makes the game go entirely 3D which could definitely pass as a late Gamecube/PS2 era game. With a mechanic like this, it makes exploring the world in two different time periods interesting in more ways than one.
Evoland 2 is a pretty decent game. I finished the game in 15 hours with a 67% completion rate so for you completionists out there, you can easily get another 5-10 hours out of this game. While the first Evoland was more of a brief parody of the adventure game genre, this game was more focused on standing out on it's own. They've taken a bunch of different gameplay styles and mashed them into one game. With all the references to other games, this game feels like a retrospective of not only what the adventure genre has branched off to, but also to what gaming has evolved into in general. We may have started out with simple games like Pac-Man and Super Mario but now we've got side scrolling beat em' ups like Final Fight, strategy RPG's like Fire Emblem, shoot em' up games like Star Fox, and so much more. I feel like that's where this game shines the most. It does have it's problems but in the end, it was nice to experience a taste of all the different genres the gaming industry has created.

Like Evoland 1 the graphics change throughout the game.  But this time there's time travel.  Depending where you are in time will depend on what the environment looks like. Units can morph about, giving more depth in the strategy used to blow up the towers. For example, a unit has 2 attack modes now and can be given the ability to switch between either mode at any time. Each mode has their own respective advantages and disadvantages and can be combined with the original Anomaly strategy of unit swapping, and throwing in special abilities such as smoke, repair or decoy.
The soundtrack is in my opinion, way better than the original. But then again, Anomaly had a great soundtrack to begin with.
The graphics are great, both the friendly and enemy unit designs looks really good, the weather effects and the explosions look awesome. The soundtrack doesn’t really stand out, but the sound effects really heighten the intensity of the carnage even further.

IF you haven't had enough of Anomaly, there's always Anomaly Korea, the original Warzone Earth and even the mobile campaign on Steam to purchase!

Full Review:
I didn’t really have any expectations for this game. I had never played a game in the series and I had only gotten this one when it was in a bundle. I was thoroughly impressed. The concept is simple; it’s a tower defense game from the other perspective. You are not the towers, you are the assaulting force. Unlike most tower defense games, however, you are not a seemingly endless wave but rather an elite group of vehicles.
Each map has you select your vehicles before moving out. You are given a set amount of money that you can spend on new vehicles, different vehicles, or upgrading your existing vehicles. You then map out your course through the level and get to shooting. You can also morph your vehicles to be better suited for the fight ahead. As you defeat enemies you pick up powerups that you can use to help your vehicles out in a difficult fight. Should you want to change up your team mid level you can do so. The gameplay seems balanced and rather unique.
To not give too much away, the story is essentially that aliens have taken over and you are a part of a resistance movement. The story seemed pretty alright to me but wasn’t a real focus. This game really shines in gameplay.
Perhaps the only negative I can think of for this game is that there isn’t a ton of depth here. There are only about 5 or so enemy types and not a whole lot of vehicle types. Everything that is there seems pretty great so perhaps the developers didn’t want to overcomplicate the game and risk hurting what was working.
Overall, this is a great twist on the tower defense genre and definitely worth a look.

I can wholeheartedly recommend this for anyone with even a passing interest in JRPG-style games. Steam is loaded with RPG Maker games that rush to compare themselves to Final Fantasy VI and Chrono Trigger at every given opportunity, but The Amber Throne is the exception both in being confident enough to sell itself on its own merits and, ironically, in being brilliant enough to actually deserve mention alongside the classics.
Story:
The Amber Throne is the story of an entire world, and as a result the focus is less on the characters that what you'd typically expect from a JRPG-like. The 5 playable characters are all well-written and interesting, but they exist to strength the story of Arra and the planet itself rather than to be traditional leads.
The story is fond of only telling you what you need to know at any given moment, and it's absolutely loaded with symbolism that only makes sense in context of events you learn about later. It takes effort to fully understand and appreciate at times, but having finished it I can safely say it's among the best RPG stories I've ever played.
Gameplay:
Never the focus of a JRPG, but it's actually pretty good. AT's battle system is an agility-determined turn-based system that sets itself apart by having loads of skills and absolutely no requirements to use them. Initially, this seems like a questionable decision, since you'll only have a handful of abilities and little reason not to just spam the same ones in every fight. Thankfully, it gets much more interesting later on when you have more characters and full ability loadouts for each of them. It's further enhanced by the introduction of enemies that change states both on their own and as a result of the attacks you use. State changes have an accompanying shift in battle sprite and, especially by late game, can force you to adopt a completely different strategy while they're active.
Skills are unlocked by the player. You get 50JP to spend per character with each level up, and since most skills cost 100JP, you effectively get a new skill every two levels. Most characters have 5-6 classes of skills that unlock partially linearly, and there's generally a huge variety between and within character skillsets. Better yet, the game subverts the trope about powerful skills with no actual use. Although some enemies may be more resistant to attacks than others, all skills are usable on every enemy in the game. Even the final boss is vulnerable to your status effects and traps.
Beyond skills, characters are highly customizble through gear and craftable purchasable upgrades. Stat boosts on armor and accessories can be pretty dramatic, so it's possible to significantly alter a character's function in battle with the right gear. The one complaint I have with regard to the combat is that there's no XP leak. I never used the game's final two characters because they were already horribly underleveled by the time I got to them, and there wasn't an easy way of catching them up.
Area progression is almost entirely linear, but individual levels usually have a decent amount to explore, and there are optional dungeons scattered throughout the game. There's apparently even an entire uber-boss quest that I missed entirely. Someone who really went all out on exploration and side content could probably get another 3-4 hours out of the game. There's no real reason to play a second time, but I felt I got more than my money's worth from my ~10 hours.
Sound:
Phenomenal. Every track fits its environment perfectly, and there are a frankly incredible number of them considering the game's price and length. Save for a glitch that occasionally results in area music continuing to play during a battle, I really don't have any to criticize here.
Graphics:
Equally phenomenal. They combine with the sound to create one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played. The screenshots really don't do it justice - there are some incredibly creative and well-realized locales and creatures in this game. Even the good RPG Maker games I've played have always had that "look" that betrayed the engine's identiy, but AT looks truly unique. The art and soundtrack were both done by one person each, amazingly.
All that being said, I do have one complaint about the graphics: RPG Maker has limitations on the number of frams in character animations, which unfortunately means character motion on the overworld looks a bit silly. Not a big deal, but it stands out when everything else is perfect.
Conclusion:
I haven't been this surprised by a game's quality for years. It's one of the best RPGs on Steam - or any other platform - and thoroughly deserving of your attention. Hopefully we'll see much more from this developer.

Honestly, such a great concept for a game. If a team managed by Blizzard had ran this, it'd be the best game of the 21st century. I was an early adopter of this game, and its come in leaps and bounds since then.
Yes, its Early Access, and yes there are bugs and lots of systems that need polish and refinement, but unlike all the other cookie cutter MMO's out there, we have something here that is more hardcore and realistic for players who are looking for that.
It hits the spot well with its art style, PVP action and the limited safe zones, PvP is really fun, especially when you go raiding in a group. Crafting is quite in-depth, and it is certainly not a 'do it all yourself' crafting system. You will be reliant on other players for materials, you will be reliant on a guild to progress rapidly in this game, and enjoy it for what it is. But isn't the reason why we play MMO's to be social and interact with other players anyway?
I'm also impressed that they have an Oceania server (Australia/New Zealand). My ping is 49ms on average, which is imperative for a game like this. They have a decent amount of servers, well distributed, which I cannot say for a lot of other MMO's out there.
The potential for this game is huge, and I strongly urge you to support this game, if not for what you get out of it now, but for what you will get out of it in the future.

text: Hands down the best stealth game to come out in about 10 years. It's criminally underrated and worth your time if you're a fan of classic stealth games like thief (The originals, NOT the modern abomination).

Some maps or quests are quite tough and you'll need to use all you can to deal with the sheer brutality of special enemies. That's very refreshing from the usual strategy game curve (mildly difficult beginning to mid-game then disappointingly easy as your characters get IMBA).
The interface is neat and even rather classy.
All in all, quite a nice game if you're into the system.

Fantastic game set in Germany's most popular fantasy world
I am really baffled by some of the luckwarm reviews that this title was getting. I found it to be a fantastic, visceral turn based strategy RPG set in a refreshingly dark fantasy world.
Perhaps the initial bad press was due to the fact that it wasn't X-Com: The current turn based darling.
Indeed, there is no permadeath and the story is relatively linear. However; about 40% of gametime is dedicated to non essential side quests.
I especially liked the art design on the game; the battlefields, warriors and beasts seemed stylized as living toys; I could almost imagine this game being played on that chessboard in the Millenium Falcon.  Expect to see dozens upon dozens of battle maps and a variety of winning conditions.

Have you ever played Dungeons and Dragons with a Dungeon Master that absolutely hates you? Do you like campaigns in which dialogue options are almost meaningless and the plot is confusing? Well if you haven't, Blackguards can fill that void for you.
The plot isn't bad. It captured my attention fairly early and has some nice twists in it. The main focus of this game, however, is the combat system. I love the combat in this game. Blackguards uses a version of tabletop rules to fuel its combat. There are even simulated dice rolls for damage and hit chance. Unfortunately, (or fortunately depending) pretty much every dialogue option leads to some sort of cliche combat. Very rarely is there a non-combat solution to anything.
The character creation is pretty cool also. There are two modes; basic and advanced. The creation is very open and is manipulated by AP (adventure points (I think)). Using these points (earned from combat and completion of quests), you can add talents, special abilities, spells, and basic attributes to your character, none being restricted to your character (except spells in some cases).
Unfortunately, this game does have some downsides. Some of the encounters are downright frustrating and (at least for me), very difficult. A number of times I've had to walk away from the game or take a break. These particular encounters seem to me generated specifically to be hard and not at all story oriented. I won't go into much detail about them so I don't spoil the "fun" for you. On the plus side however, there is no penalty for losing as the game forces you to keep trying unless you load a previous save before the encounter.
The graphics are actually quite nice and are better than I expected. The layout for combat is excellent, using hex-tiles and a partially destructible environment. The cities however seem more like pretty backdrops for my character sheets and are fairly dull.
I would recommend this game if you are an avid tabletop gamer looking for your D&D fix, or someone who appreciates tabletop games.

Full Review:
Blackguards is a turn-based fantasy RPG from German outfit Daedalic which is solely based on the Dark Eye roleplaying system. It provides a welcome return to the true turn based RPG combat genre which forces you to greatly consider every action you make, whether that be skill points, combat skills and many more. It provides a good level of difficulty, without going too over-board whilst allowing you a ‘life-line’, a bone for when things get tough – i.e. the all-important and crucial save feature between battles. The overall storyline, writing, voice-acting is good whilst providing enough depth to avoid it being a drag.
Combat is where Blackguards best feature occurs and is perfect for players who enjoy the battles on hex tiles to that of the stories behind them. The use of objects on battle-maps combined with an easy to understand combat interface and a variety of character abilities/skills allows the player to get in and get on with gameplay.
Difficultly in digesting a variety of character abilities, skill points and equipment load-outs, specifically the equipment system, as that proved most challenging and somewhat confusing due to the amount of resistances available. However, once you’ve taken the time to understand how they all interlink, this section opens up to provide the player with a great variety of levelling up elements.
Can appear to be somewhat repetitive if players aren’t enveloped in the storyline. Far too many loading screens which stops the flow of the story and battles far too often.
A very stylish and graphically intense RPG, scoring high on the styles category, specifically in the gorgeous looking towns/outposts, where players are faced with beautifully designed shops and scenery which differs throughout the storyline.
A mediocre score for value with its current (09/03/14) price tag of £26.99.
Blackguards provides players with the opportunity to play for hours on end, experiencing a whole array of new content/utilising new tactics, however players are forced to read every snippet of information/guide to fully understand its complicated character system and some battles can appear to be rather repetitive.

Just finished the game.  After getting to the last battle and finding it frustrating not to have Aurelia, I went back through chapters 4-5 changing strategies.
The good:
-If you really miss Temple of Elemental Evil, this game will be nice for you
-Not a lot of min/maxing of gear (some of the best gear is available early in the game, and most of the stuff you'll find in the game will not be an upgrade)
-Each of the companions have really well-drawn out personalities (the dwarf, for example, will complain when you heal him that he "doesn't need it"; the playboy mage will flirt with NPC's you meet).
The bad:
-There are not a lot of varieties of bad guys in the game.  You'll find yourself saying "didn't I just fight this battle?" a bit too frequently
- For people that like seeing gear progression, you will not get it here.
- The ending was quite a bit of a let-down.
- During combat, there is no way to speed up the monsters' turns; and you will sometimes literally be waiting a minute between turns while a slug slugs its way across the screen.
Will you like it?
-If you liked Temple of Elemental Evil because it was super "true to the rules"--Yes
-If you liked Baldur's gate because your Party AI would let you not have to micromanage--No

To the Moon had a story that was truely made you care about the main character but also the spouse of that main character that we find has shaped his life in so many ways. The affects of this character on the main characters fate is what makes us so sad when the main character (not really a spoiler) dies. This is not the case for the second game. The main character in this story is potraid as a dreamer. It makes the character pretty uninteresting for the first 1/3 to 1/2 of the game. Not only that but the implications of a girl that he liked in his childhood that we think is the cause of his modern day sorrow caused me to even look at him like he was selfish, just a bit. Of course in the "twist" this is turned on its head. but in a way that is so bizare and wierd that it is kind of hard to even relate to the main character.
That being said the humour, the music, the soft moments are all there. In the end it makes for a good story, but not one that creates feeling of sadness. What kind of saddness am I talking about? If you ever loved a story so much that when it concluded you cried, that is the sadness I am talking about. But I did not experience that here. I was very pleased and content.  But, I did not yearn for more.
One last thing, the music. The music is beautiful but takes TOOO much inspiration from the previous game. This is a new story, but I heared too many old themes from the previous game. Adding a little quitar here or some Cello there is not gonna do it! Sadly I could barely tell what the theme of the main character was. The theme for To the Moon was so clear that everytime you heared it you could guess what scene you were in. That wasn't the case here :(
But enough of my rant! buy the game! as soon as a discount comes ;)

- I bought this game on a whim after seeing it in the Steam Store for the first time. I watched the promotional videos and was immediately interested in it.
- I love this game, therefore this review
. I am not some professional games journalist who makes a living off of reviewing games and tries to provide an objective and totally unbiased point of view on the subject material. If you were expecting such a review from the average Steam user, then your standards might be a bit high. No offense, high standards aren't really a
. My intention with this review is to convince others who might be interested in the game to take the leap and drop $20 on it. That's all.
- At the time of this review, I only had about two hours of playtime invested. Overall the game isn't terribly complex, and the gameplay is what you'd expect from the average Metroidvania title (with more focus on platforming than combat). It's polished, the art is beautiful, and the story is engaging while not getting in the way of playing the game. After two hours, I felt that I could wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who might show interest in it.
If I had to briefly describe the game, I would say it's a very artistically-driven 2D platformer with common elements from both the Metroid and Castlevania series. But that merely scratches the surface.
I won't go in to excruciating detail regarding the gameplay. It's a branching world with areas you can't access without certain abilities. You progress naturally until you unlock a new ability, then more options open up and you can progressively explore more freely. Naturally, the world is littered with hidden goodies like health and energy powerups (like energy tanks and missiles from Metroid). Platforming does become rather challenging, and the fact that the movement is very responsive and feels polished makes platforming a blast despite the difficulty. However, a certain ability you are given right from the start can detract from the challenge by essentially removing the consequences of dying.
Combat is pretty simplistic (you basically just spam the attack button and it auto-locks to the nearest target), but it is clearly not the focal point of the gameplay. The majority of the abilities you unlock cater towards more efficient and complex platforming maneuvers. There is a simple experience system which rewards you with skill points that allow you to unlock an assortment of abilities that are split off in to three different skill trees. These abilities are either unique passives, or augment the main abilities that you acquire through progression in the game.
As far as visuals go, this game is in my humble opinion at the very apex of gorgeous. The art style is surreal and brimming with color and personality. I'm not exaggerating when I say you could take a screenshot anywhere in the game and it would make for a great picture. There are certain areas in the game where you just have to stop and marvel at how downright beautiful the art is. Not many games these days are capable of that (the last one that comes to mind is probably
). People might say that gameplay is all that matters, but this game is a prime example of why that's simply
anymore. I believe that in regards to modern games, visuals will always play an important role in making the game what it is. Games are a from of art now, not just pure entertainment. Anyone who plays this game and says otherwise is
insane.
The musical score is just as good as the visuals. There's heavy use of woodwind instruments and a touch of harmonic female vocals that really set the mood. There are overaching themes throughout the score that gives the whole soundtrack real cohesion. The best part is that the music doesn't overplay itself during cutscenes to create a sappy, melodramatic mood. During general gameplay, the music is calmer and more relaxed. In turn, it helps to keep the player feeling the same even during the tougher platforming areas.
The story, while somewhat simple in nature, does a great job of presenting the game's gorgeous world and giving you a solid sense of pace. It's not a really big RPG story with tons of lore or anything, but you can still
be enveloped by its provocative and charming nature. The game can even be surprisingly emotional and deep when you least expect it. Think of the art as a painting and the story as a frame. The frame may be simplistic, but it just goes great with the painting.
Moon Studios have made a strong debut with this game, and I can't wait to see what else they have in store for us in the future. If you have the money to spare, I highly recommend you pick this up; or wait until the next big sales event and maybe you will find it for cheap. Either way, it's worth every penny.

The Amber Throne is an absolutely lovely game with roots in a bygone era of RPG gaming. At times slightly obtuse, it rewards patience and exploration thoroughly. Something like a simple background object can be an interactable bit of lore with a minor experience reward attached. Rich, seemingly hand-painted art and a dynamic, ambient soundtrack completely destroy expectations of what RPGMaker is capable of.
On the mechanical side, while stats are assigned automatically at level up, the player has a nice variety of choices in regards to which skills to buy with JP, a currency earned upon gaining a level. Nearly all of these skills have an effect on enemies; one might break an armored enemy's defenses and turn him into an "Unarmored Enemy" or a particularly fast enemy into a "Wounded Enemy". This gives battles a more involved feel which is refreshing for a turn based RPG.
While I normally ignore RPGMaker games as a whole, I can say this is worth full price. The game's creator has been highly active in addressing the very few issues the game has and patching them. If you are a fan of the JRPG genre at all, the overall experience of The Amber Throne is for you.

Interstellar Rift is a sci-fi ship building MP semi-survival/sandbox game MMO-ish.
IMHO it has a lot of potential, from what I've seen so far. Compared to a many other sci-fi builder games, Interstellar Rift's lack of automation promotes well the need for a co-op crew. When your ship gets larger, you'll need at least 1 or 2 other people to help you pilot, fight, repair, gather resources, and manage your ship's energy more efficiently. Your point of view in the game is very immersive where there are no "game menus" but ingame interactive menus on ingame screens and holo-displays where you make your choices.
At this time, It is still an alpha game and I do forgive the bugs and lack of optimization of an alpha game (crashes and laggy gameplay, at times). I'm just hoping that the devs will be able to flesh this game out nicely, especially since they are not planning on any kind of planetfall at this time. With that being said, I am giving this game a thumbs up on the hopes that they will make it a great game, dispite it's current state of stability and content.

So i bought this game on a whim, Despite the warnings of trolls in servers, despite the buggyness i heard of, despite the fact that numerous friends have told me its not worth the money, i gave it a shot.
My experience:
Upon launching the game, i found a huge irritance being you can't change your graphical, controls, or gameplay mechanics through ingame menu's. But that's just personal preference so ill let that slide. (You have to go back to main menu to change them, thankfully the game loads fast so changing isn't that hard, just more clicks involved).
Now, The tutorial was pretty informative and covers the core features but needs more emphasis on things like Rift Generator Fuel, This one in particular can ruin your tutorial or even just gameplay. There's 3 types of Fuel for Rift Generators, Rift's are "Wormholes" to other places. Rift's require a special fuel which iv yet to discover in the natural world, but that may be my own fault due to the fact i can't fight alien's or drones yet, Which is a milestone of sorts as you need to acquire things like Silicon, Steel and lots of iron to produce a ship that can even defend against them such as shields and engines and power.
But that aside, Once you can correctly identify what fuels you need, Proper icons for it to boot, Your exploration just became far easier!
Now, Onto gameplay. Initially most people don't, especially myself don't notice the mining facilities in most stations. This is where you go to build your first starter ship or if you die, a replacement ship. Typically these only have your core elements, That being Iron ore, Copper Ore, Carbon, And Water. These items make the following:
Iron Ore = Iron
Copper Ore = Copper
Carbon + Iron = Steel
Water = Hydrogen(Ship Fuel) / Oxygen(Life Support)
These few items your gonna need lots of, Depending on your structures you intend to build. For example, my medium sized ship required me to have 22k steel, 80k iron, 12k copper, 2k silicon, and 1.5k carbon to create. That had Two Extractors(Mines asteroids), Two Refineries(Refines ore/water into other stuff), Lots of cargo space, Crew quarters(Not required but more aesthetically pleasing), Conference Room(Not required), Lunch Room(Not required), Engine Room(Housed Generators, Power storage, And fuel storage). I also created an Armory which housed lockers and hacking equipment(Which i havent dived into yet). And lastly a Cockpit with a Ship Editor(Lets you make ships, edit and salvage ships), A Holotable which is your map of sorts, Helps you chart your way around. A Engineering station which let me modify rooms such as life support, locking, know the power status, etc. Very useful station, A teleporter, And last but not least, the Cockpit.
Now the Cockpit requires its own paragraph as its a bit of a mess initially, None of its controls are really explained, specially in the tutorial. So here are some useful tips covered by the tutorial and just by trial and error:
WASD = Movement
R = Up
F = Down
H = Weapons On/Off
J = Warp drive  (This is on EVERY ship, regardless of structures installed etc, just aslong as theres a cockpit)
Q/E =Rotate
X = Stop/Halt Ship.
Z = Third Person
Tab = Switch between mouse control flight and click and drag mouse flight(Explained in tutorial)
Right click = Free look/Move camera. This HELPS GREATLY when trying to view the information panel on the left/right of your screen in flight. You can interact with it aswell if you wish.
I could go on, But since im reaching the limit, I gotta say the ship editor is REALLY tricky to use and sensitive and kinda broken at times, after 12 hours of play i finally mastered how to use it without deleting/altering something in the background.
TLDR; / Down to it, Would i recommend this? Yes, Provided more of the bugs get patched and the tutorial gets a bit more work. Bugs being: Lighting bugging out and showing shadows for props no longer in game world, Removing floors when just deleting a chair etc.

I gave it a few hours, then I gave up. The game is just too unpolished at this time. I think this is what separates the commercial games from the enthusiats ones: The game doesn't "just  run", it also addresses all those little kinks and annoying bits.
I started with the tutorial. There being a tutorial was a plus, and the tutorial isn't half bad. But there are a few instances where you can take a wrong turn and then the turial will just be stuck at that point. You have to restart, and do it all over. After the second such hickup I decided to just skip the tutorial and start a game.
Joining a server was the first disappointment. The game kept crashing with a runtime.exe error. Supposedly, the area around the starter station was liittered with starter ships from other player's tests and failures, and the game apparently doesn't have a cleanup routine.
So next I picked the "official test server #1" and I could at least spawn in the station and buy my first ship. Unfortunately that's when the griefers struck. When I teleported onto my ship some stranger jumped onto the teleporter pas along with me and hitched the ride. Over on my ship he attacked and killed me with that secondary function of the repair tool. When I logged back in I saw that he was demolishing everything. I'll shelf this game (at least I got it during a sale for a discount), maybe in a year or so when the game is less prone to crashes and when the guys developping this game have added some mechanics that prevent jerks from ruining  other people's game within the first few minutes.

Hello again to those who may have read my other review, and merely hello to others. This game, Nidhogg, is a great game of competition and an overall epic struggle between two elite knights with incredible acrobatic capabilities. Of course, like any great game of our time, it comes with a much deeper, more human struggle. This isn't a game posing to be something it's not, it only strikes out at the most vulnerable parts of the human soul. Vulnerable isn't to say that it hurts you where you're not protected, but rather that it forces even the most aloof people to come back to their roots and their true emotions. So, in order to explain all of the talking that I have been doing, it starts something like this: there are two brothers, each of which have their own abilities and sets of particular skills, even from birth. As the lore is read into more and more (although there will be some amount of spoilage here, the lore is very difficult to come about, and there is much more to be found), their lives were forever altered when there was a siege on the hold where they had been. Once they were separated, they were raised amongst different backgrounds and with various trainings. Although they had been separated, due to their inate skills as warriors, their trainings became more and more complex and individual, but still, entirely similar. Once the player joins the story, they are briefed with the very basics of what I have just told you, and then thrown into a bitter-sweet reunion of the two brothers. Neither had ever met the other, but they had both been entirely aware of the other's presence. They work together to tackle the same threat that had attacked the same hold that they were both raised in and spent the beginning of their lives in. Nidhogg, the name of the supernatural villain, is an absolutely corrupted tyrant with incredible powers, so with only each other and the swords that they had, the singleplayer story begins. Although, as I'm sure some of you have noticed, there is also a multiplayer aspect to this title. In this alternate timeline/parallel universe, the two brothers have turned against one another and must fight to win the respect of the Nidhogg. There has not been much lore discovered on my end about this gameplay, and almost all of what I have gleaned from it, I have shared with you. So, to finish, the magic of this game cannot be experienced without shrouding yourself in it's beautiful set of graphics, diverse and incredible plotline, and the character development. After writing and playing this game, I'd give Nidhogg a nearly perfect 9/10, only missing the point due to the fact that it may be seen as gory for those new to the first person shooter (FPS) genre that htis game falls into.

Finding Paradise is a bit of a mixed bag for me.
Throughout the story, I was able to get emotionally invested in Colin's life. I like how Colin's wish is handled and how unorthodox his last request is. I enjoyed seeing how the smaller seeming moments added up in his life, as well as the little regrets of things that he may have wished could have gone better. It made his story more resonant and relatable. I honestly wish a greater emphasis was placed on this, even though there was already a great emphasis on it in the game.
It does seem misleading to say that this is a standalone game. While you technically would be able to play the game and understand the story without playing either To the Moon, the Minisodes, or A Bird Story, there are references to them or plot points that they brought up that are so blatant and difficult to ignore that this game might run the risk of being confusing to completely new players. That being said, I absolutely enjoyed the references to A Bird Story, even though that game did not do much for me on its own. It was a sweet and heartfelt touch for this game.
The pop-culture references were my least favorite part of To the Moon, and it seems as though there were more added in Finding Paradise. When the playstyle shifted in these moments, it felt so jarring that it sucked me out of the experience. However, the mechanics themselves were not bad in and of themselves. They just felt disracting to me as a part of this particular game.
The ending is where I have the most problems. The spoiler in this section is fairly detailed about important reveals toward the end of the game, so I advise that you don't read it if you are already planning to play Finding Paradise.
I'm sure some people could either suspend disbelief at these parts or just not think as much about them in general, but it was a problem for me and my enjoyment of many of the ending portions of this game. It also sucked a lot of the emotion out of the end of Colin's story that I feel could have otherwise left me in tears.
The soundtrack is amazing, as it was with the other games before it. It was beautifully composed, and it is a pleasure to hear throughout this game. I will buy the soundtrack in a heatrbeat once they have that option here.
The game itself can run slowly at times, though I don't remember any significant moments of lag that hurt the overall experience of the game.
In spite of it's flaws, I do not regret having played this game. I played through it from start to finish with only an occasional restroom break getting in the way of one long continuous play. I look forward to to seeing whatever new game Kan Gao comes up with next for this series.
I don't think this is a great game, and your mileage may vary with some plot points and pop-culture references, but I am glad I played it and reccomend it to others. Though they mention that you don't have to play any previous games before playing this one, playing To the Moon and the Minisodes (and maybe A Bird Story, if you're so inclined) beforehand would be a good idea to understand the full picture.

I played and enjoyed Evoland, so I was expecting not much more from Evoland 2 than what the first game had to offer. I was extremely pleased to find that Evoland 2 takes concepts from the first game and refines them, and adds one of the better stories I've seen in any game for a long time. I beat the game with 95% completion in about 24 hours of play time.
The game is an action/adventure/RPG game along the lines of Zelda (except you gain levels and HP), but throughout the game are homages to a surprisinly wide variety of genres, such as Bomberman, Street Fighter, Bejeweled, vertical scrolling arcade shooters, Chrono Trigger styled turn-based RPGs, DDR/Beatmania, Metal Gear Solid, Fire Emblem, Mega Man, side-scrolling shooters, platformers like Mario Bros, and even cameos of Pong, Snake, Space Invaders, and Pac Man. There are some challenging but clever puzzles throughout the game.
The music is good, with a few great/memorable tracks, but you will hear the same tunes repeated and re-used throughout the game. Not a problem at all for me since I enjoyed them, but I could see that being a low point for others.
The plot is definitely a strong point in the game. While it is fairly predictable for the most part, there are a few twists to keep it interesting. Overall, I found myself really enjoying and wanting to proceed with the game just to find out what would happen next, something that an RPG hasn't done for me in forever.
This game easily ranks as one of the best jRPGs I've played. It's at least as good as any classic SNES title.

I have just finished this game and the journey was incredible.
Gameplay
Evoland Two is a tribute to classic video games, especially games like Final Fantasy and the lagend of Zelda. Most of the game has gameplay similar to that of the pre-N64 legend of Zelda games with RPG elements. However the game is also packed with MANY other sections based on classic games. There is a dugeon that plays like bomberman, an endless runner portion, a match free game, a turn based RPG, a tactical RPG,  a scrolling shoot-em-up portion, a beat-em-up portion and more. What surprised me about these parts of the game is that they are not just thrown in for a quick laugh. Each of these sections are filled with depeth and interesting elements, that make them almost like short bursts of full classic games rather than just minigames. The problem with all these elements is that they are all required so if you are bad at a certain game style or just do not like it you still have to play through it. Also on the subject of gameplay this also pays tribute to its sources difficulty, which can be difficult for the modern gamer. Finally it is incredibly hard to play through this game with a keyboard, though not impossible as I was able to do it, but if you have a controller use it.
Graphics and Sound
Again this game's graphics and sound pay tribute to the classic games it is based on. Music is excellent but onfortunatly some of it is repeated far too much, especially the music during a boss battle. This game actually has three graphics styles that change as you travel through the past present and future of the game world. In the past the graphics are simple pixeled 2D graphics, in the present they are much more detailed richer 2D graphics and in the future they are full 3D graphics. The graphics are well done, and again pay tribute to the games of yor, (although the 3D portion only has about the graphics level of a PS2 game)
However what really won me over was the games story. Again it centers on time travel and using that ability to change the future. It is really interesting to see the kingdom and NPCs evolve with time, and  with your actions. The game is chock full of refrences to classic games movies, television, and even real world history. It has a script that is funny, yet also surprisingly deep, as the charecters sort out the ideas of revenge, loyalty, free will, and wether they have the right to change the furtue. This adds a great deal of deeper meaning, but it can be heavy handed at times. However the game usually quickly gets back to the action  and humor. The world has a rich backstory and many charecters beyond those in your party are have very real feeling personalities. The main problem I had with the story is that it is very linear and you cannot change the past outside of the main story. I would have loved to have explore different ways to change the future but that may have required more rescources than Indie studio Shiro games could possibly take on. However the ending is indredibly deep and a little upsetting. While it was powerful, it was would have been more satisfying to have a different ending.
Conclusion
This is one of my favorite RPG's I have ever played. It is full of variety and the story will stick with me for a long time. I recomend this to any fan of RPG's, the classic Legend of Zelda games, or someone who fondly looks back on a golden age of gaming.

Evoland 2 was the surprise break-out hit of the holiday season, for me. the first Evoland was just a pretty well-implemented gag you could play through, a one-note nostalgia joke about the development of game engines.
This sequel, however, instead has a well-crafted (if somewhat simplistic and over-acted) plot about time travel, fate, race relations, personal development, and the lessons of history.  This is coupled with a time-travel mechanic represnted by 8-bit, 16-bit, and modern 3D graphics respectively, that isn't just a gimmick or a joke about game development, but a solidly integrated gameplay mechanic, with challenging but not frustrating puzzles, and loads of mini-games and constantly varying game modes that take you through a retrospective of genre development in gaming, and keep the game feeling fresh and fun throughout.

The graphics and sound are pretty good, as they were in the original game. Can't complain there.
This game does have enhanced multiplayer support, so I suppose if that's what you're after you could get this game. But I haven't tried it so can't comment on it.
All in all, don't buy this game just because you liked the original. I don't really think it adds much to the experience.

Edit: Ok, now that I have beaten the time, I'm going to go into more depth of my review without spoiling any big parts of the story.
Gameplay:  As I said before the gameplay is nearly flawless and pretty much everything works the way it's made for. Some of the puzzles can be quite confusing at first but with a little thinking you can solve them. The game starts out easy, but as you progress and get more power ups and upgrades, the game gets alot harder. I mean A LOT harder. One example would be out climbing the flooding ginso tree they showed at gamescon. Sure it looked easy when they showed it, but when I tried it myself, I was kind of surprised at how tough it was, and it took me about 15 tries before I got it right. I'm not going to say whats going to happen to future escape sequences so I don't spoil you guys, but just a heads up, they get HARDER as you go. But when you finally beat them, it's very fulfilling. Timing is also a key factor in solving puzzles. One more recommendation, use PLENTY of soul links whenever you can. It gets very frustrating when you get far in a part of the game, only to die and go back like 20 minutes of game-play simply because you for got to make a check point. The health system in my opinion is kind of useless, as later on in the game enemy attacks and stage hazards are pretty much a instant death.
Sound and music: The sound affects and music are what make up a third of the game. Just like the story and the visuals make up the other two thirds.  Everything you do has a very unique sound to it such as branches and twigs sound like wood breaking and rocks sound like crumbling an so forth. Even down to when Ori emerges from the water, just the cute sound of him gasping for breath is amazing. Some of my favorite sounds would be the wind. Just the sound of the wind blowing through the leaves is outstanding. The music is very fitting for the situation. Slow and peaceful music in the bright open areas of the forest, while you get more suspenseful and intimidating music in a place that's more dark and secluded. You also get fast paced music for sequences that are more fast paced and each one is different so it feels like you just are truly in a different place, not just in terms of look, but in feel. The music is just great and I even bought the soundtrack to prove it.
Visuals and graphics: This was the big eye catcher for most people, I'm no exception. The look of the game is very vibrant and clean. Even if it's a 2-D plat-former, the games background has some 3-d elements to it such as trees in the background, and rocks and water more close to the screen. Everywhere you go you will see something new and will never once see the same thing twice.
( unless you're back tracking to a place you've already been.)  I really have nothing else to say about the graphics other then that it's great and goes along great with the music and sound.
Verdict:  Ori and the blind forest is a Great action game that I recomennd to anyone. While I'm am a little disappointed that the game wasn't as long as the developers said it would be at around 10 hours, ( me about 5 ) it's still a great game regardless and at $20, you cant really complain, and the game does get frustrating at times but it always feels good when you get past whatever was giving you trouble.
9/10

Once you finish the game in a save slot, that's it, done, it won't let you play that save file anymore, meaning you have to start a new game from scratch from a new save file or delete the one you just completed. How to make you cry in the first 5 minutes: the game.
I can honestly say after hours of gameplay that this is probably one of the most enjoyable games I've played in quite a long time.
The presentation and graphics make it (in my opinion) one of the most beautiful "2D" games ever! The main character, Ori is just so cute too!
As far as the gameplay is concerned, I think it is similar in style to the Metroid series, which is perhaps one of my most favorite series of games. Basically you start out with not much, then get new powers which allow you to do more things and explore new areas of the map. You progress through four (I think) major areas before the game ends. You can also earn Ability points which allow you to activate special upgrades such as more powerful firepower and say, breathing underwater, as a couple examples. Sometimes the game can be quite frustrating because sometimes timing everything perfectly and such (for quite a length of time at some parts) can be fairly difficult...but in all honesty a game should be challenging, and it's good that Ori is to a larger degree than many games nowadays.
As far as the story, for the most part it's told while you're playing (I think there's only a few cutscenes total) and the prologue segment had me in tears after the first five minutes (which is hard to do, actually). I don't want to spoil any of the story or anything (if it matters to anyone) so all I will say is it's probably not /the best/ or anything, but I have found it quite enjoyable thus far.
I totally recommend it to anyone who likes oldschoolish platformers and/or want a game that is just in general very enjoyable and lovely to experience. Definitely a $20 well spent, in my opinion (for me, anyway). =w=

Controls are pretty straightforward:
Attack to the left using: ←, S, B, or left mouse button
Attack to the right using:  →, D, N, or right mouse button
When an enemy (which is everyone) enters your range of attack on the left or right of you, you press the corresponding button to attack.
You can also use a controller if you wish.
Note:  That if you wish to use keyboard or mouse and you have a controller connected to your PC, it will detect the controller and switch over to that for menu navigation (which you need to use the controller to switch back to K/M if you want), but the actual gameplay can still be mouse or keyboard even with the controller connected.
Most enemies are one-hit kills (though, there are a LOT of them), some require a couple hits while other enemies are closing in, and then there are bosses who get an uninterrupted fight with you until one of you win.  Also, some enemies will bring weapons to the fight, so kill them and use the weapon against the rest.
There is a rating system for how you fight, so spamming keys and/or getting hit will count against you.
There are plenty of levels for each skill/difficulty tier, so if you plan on getting the highest rating for each level, the game will last you quite a while.
OFDP's resource requirements are rather low and so is the time to complete most stages, so it can be installed on almost any PC and you can always slip in a game while you wait.
On a related note:  If you practice kung-fu/Wushu, you'll probably recognize a lot of the forms.

This one will be breif.
It has the potential to be fantastic.  It's actually pretty much there, and a damned fine achievement for an indy developer to accomplish.
In short, its like Space Engineers meets Star War Galaxies meets Eve Online.
Mining is ridiculously easy.  You set the machine to grab the 'roid you want, and let it do its work while you get other things done.  You don't have to build the ship block by block, you just make a blueprint in the editor, or simply pick one up in the Steam Workshop.  When you have the resources, "build it" and its there.
If it IS your thing, spend hours making multicrew ships of grandious scales, with all types of artistic flourishes, or a hyper efficient box of death.
Oh, and the ships CAN be multicrew.  In fact, the larger and more funcional it is, the more likely it's going to HAVE to be multicrew to get the most combat efficiency out of it.
Or have your big boy boat and use everything in it at your leisure.
Oh!  And your mates and you can walk around the ship while it is moving!  No flying out the back while at warp.  Pilot can drive the bus while you get work done back in the workshops.  It's flippin fantastic!
There are Factions to join.  NPCs to do missions for.  Reptuations to gain or lose.
So, I like it.  Obligatory Cons at the moment:
Player dedicated servers - This is sort of a double edge sword.  Player deds can be a bit problematic, and it could take time to find one you like.
Small-ISH Playerbase -  It'd be nice to have a huge playerbase, with people bumping into eachother all the time, but the server can lag a bit when someone first logs on, and I'm not too sure how player run dedicated servers would handle the large loads.  In my experience, not the best.  But this game will trully SHINE if that can get sorted out.
...bah... and I said it was going to be breif.  Can't ever do it.
It's on Sale for under $11.  I'd call it pretty much a no brainer.  At $15, still a for sure thing if you're interest is piqued.  If it's $20 at the moment of reading this... I was not going to buy this game originally, but after reading some more about the game and its developer team I took the plunge.
Normally I dont want to invest with EA titles after my past experiences. Yet this one was on sale and seeing as a lot of the comments that the majority of players were posting it encouraged me to try my luck. I did. And after my bit of play time so far, I am 110% behind this team and support their vision.
I Find the game mechanics to be clean, logically sound, and with a solid depth of play geared towards an immersive and fun system. The Graphics are really good, where many others who are working on similar Indy EA titles have put graphics as an after thought. The difficulty or learning curve is not bad. If you have ever taken a trip on EVE or SWG, or even S.E.'s then you will do just fine. Again it is an EA Indy title, so there is still things to be completed. However the game so far in its current state is a full multiplayer space sim sandbox experience which, if you have enough people can provided a long enjoyable experience. The solo game is very calm and allows for crafting or explorer types to enjoy all of the game with out the added hassles of PVP.
I say if you have the extra money to give this game a try especially if you enjoy other titles which offer survival, construction and crafting and space exploration and combat.

So it's yet another early access open world spaceship building sandbox game like Space Engineers or Empyrion: Galactic Survival.
I played this for about 8 hours after buying it, and it looks like it may be my favorite so far. What makes it different and better than the similar games is the open world feel of the game - you can run automatically generated missions and do commodity trading. Other similar games just have you mine, refine, and craft. Of course this game also has mining, refining and crafting, and it feels really neat.
Traveling around a star system feels great. The distances are vast, but you have a fast warp drive. This gives traveling around the star system an excellent feel, similar to games like EVE online, Elite Dangerous, Star Citizen, etc.
Ship design also works differently from other games of this type. Rather than building spaceships block by block, you define rooms and place equipment in them. This gives ships a much better, less uniform look and allows for quicker designing. You can also place blocks or slopes on the exterior of your ship in order to define its overall shape.
I haven't tried ship combat yet.
As for what I don't like, well... Some of the controls are bad.
(update: I've figured out that escape does this).
The cockpit itself needs work, there are buttons to turn off HUD navigation icons but I can't tell what's on and what's off, except by pressing it and seeing if it adds or removes icons.
There are also all sorts of interface glitches. I've been stuck in cockpit mode (mouse doesn't move the camera/turn my character) after leaving the cockpit. It should return me to FPS controls after doing that, but doesn't always for mysterious reasons.
Sometimes I get something like "please select destination" on my HUD while flying my ship
(update: I think this has to do clicking the mouse to steer the ship being interpreted as a double click to target something).
The ship editor has all kinds of quirks. It's too easy to accidentally place or delete rooms, and there doesn't seem to be any undo/redo. I've accidentally placed rooms while clicking to get the save/load design menu, it's just bad. Early access and whatnot, there's definite room for improvement here.
Both of these issues have been fixed.
Again this is an early access game, so these problems will hopefully be fixed eventually. I don't find them dealbreakers though, the game is overall good and unique enough that I enjoy playing it more than the competition, at least for now.

I don't do reviews, but...
Five people are offering a game with a concept and immersion I have not seen anywhere else. For a five person team I cannot believe what they have made. Things as simple as the door unlock and open animation are out of control - the mechanical detail is amazing. They wrote their own game engine for this one.
Yes it is early access, it has issues from time to time, but if you want to build a ship from scratch, crew it with friends, have them run down and grab an aim-able gun turret, shoot some aliens, and run around the ship while underway to work with various systems and machinery, all while exploring endless star systems, it is worth checking out.
Of course there is room for more content, but this small group is quite responsive and has accomplished some feats other larger companies still strive to achieve. For $15 (current Steam) it's cheaper than a few beers at the pub and will provide a lot more entertainment. Updates are fast and frequent, dev interaction quite swift and personal for the size of this team. If you like the 1st person Build genre and detailed machinery, this one is worth checking out.
