So I see this game has been out for 1 1/2 years, but has small workshop presence and no player base. I see it is well- rated, so I think "maybe hidden gem." Then I play tutorial, and I see exactly why the game is not more popular. It's clunky, ship editing is horrible, and tutorial is easy to break with vague directions.
The tutorial is not well programmed. There's a lot of eye candy and some nice animations (for games of this type), but directions are horrible, and you are left to run around trying to figure out where something is. Do something wrong? You get to restart. There's no back-story, and no explaination as to how bugs got to your generators. My favorites are the directions given both to and in. "Go to the <>." It doesn't matter that there's a buncho of [ ], O. and <> out there. You have to find the right one with a warp drive that sounds and feels like a '63 volkswagon shifting gears. There should be a hotkey to exit the cockpit, but instead, you have to figure out where the button is with (again) vague directions like "leave the cockpit." My favorite came In the mining station, when I was directed to refine ore "there's a refinery right over there." Wherever the hell "over there" was. I eventually found it NOWHERE NEAR the mining device. Transferring between devices is awkward and slow, but once you know where to look, the device feedback is useful and logically located. It does not get any faster. There's a lot of running around between different machines, even on the most optimized ships, and that gets annoying.
I wondered why there were so few ship models on the workshop, compared to a game like Starmade or Empyrion. The answer is simple: take what many people consider to be the most enjoyable aspect of the game, and then put it into an editor that is the most sorry example of junk I have ever seen in my life. Is it powerful? Yes... maybe... I think so... possibly... if you can figure it out. Again, no useful directions, so 90% of players will NEVER make a ship to post on the workshop. Rotation of shapes? No clue. Can you just stand inside your ship and place things where they need to go? Nope. Then you have the overlay layers, brought to you by people who think an easy key series to remember for jump is "ctrl+u+up arrow+w." Honestly, it makes Empyrion's ship building method look good, AND THAT ONE I thought needed work. NONE of them are even as good as Minecraft in this respect.
I can see that the game has a lot of potential, but if it cannot be made more available to the players, that will never translate to anything. The player base is rabidly loyal, but tiny. That will never change unless the various game interfaces are made more intuitive and easier to apply.
Personally, I'm going to play around with it for a bit more, since it was relatively cheap; but it will never be a replacement for the other games I have, and it's likely to remain sitting in unused obscurity forever. It's not a bad game, and it has some features I wish the other games I play had; it's just very badly implemented.
I hate to say this, but don't buy it.

This game is an open world MMO heavily based on farming, PVP, castle sieges, and tournaments. It is a good game for people who have friends that like MMOs and like making big war parties. THIS IS NOT A LONEWOLF GAME.
+Good leveling system, very complex
+Fun gameplay when in parties
+farming based (you must grind to be the best)
+Fun tournaments where you fight the opposing faction for loads of EXP
+Freedom to play as you please
+no defined roles (tank,dps,etc)
+Loads of gear to choose from
+challenging Giant fights (up to 900+ damage per hit)
+balanced stats ( skilled and geared low levels can compete with high level skilled and geard people)
+Good party and guild system
+somewhat balanced farming (still implementing balancing issues)
+ability to come up with complex tactics and formations to win battles!
+a skyrim third person feel (also first person but is a bit lacking)
+Good graphics for the Engine it's on
+A variety of weapons
+passive abilities that keep the realism aspect but also are well defined in helping you achieve your build
+ability to upgrade captured Keeps and Castles
+small castle defense mechanisms (dropping logs, burning oil, etc.)
+bushes to ambush the enemy!
+good targeting for arrow drop rate (you can hit people from pretty far away and aiming above them at a 45+ degree angle.
+Unique passives for specified weapons (maces do bludgening dmg while axes do slashing, spears do penetration and bleed)
+armors have passive stats that give you slashing, stabbing, and bludgening resistance
+economy in the sense that people sale items for in game currency
+Devs that listen and play their game!
+Arena area to have fights with both your team mates and your enemies
+ability to revive downed firendlys
+traitor system (if a midlander hits a midlander that person becomes a traitor and can be killed by midlanders or town guards)
+reputation system ( you gain loot, experince, crafting, etc, bonuses the more reputation you have. You get reputation by capturing keeps, winning tourneys, and killing enemies)
+the looting system is Noob friendly. It is impossible for someone to take even half the items in your inventory assuming you have a bag full. It is a point system and time system. You have 30 seconds to loot every second you lose a loot point starting from 30 loot points. Every item depending on the type of item (chest peice, helmet, weapon, materials, etc.) will have a point value. Once your timer hits 0 or your points run out you can no longer loot.
now for the negatives
-server lag is common but is bearable
-extreme freezing for a second or two when loading towns, keeps, and castles
-exploits, rare, but there
-tade system is currently bugged but still possible if done right
-some items cannot be crafted
-some items are not in game
-some bosses seem to not drop items (they could just be that rare)
-you will hate this game if you play alone
-server restarts once or twice a day to help with lag
-No Asian servers as of now
-botters that auto farm stuff
-occasional door bugs where doors will not open or close after a keep/castle is taken
-some items will not craft yet still take the materials
-larger guilds tend to control servers
-must exit game and re-open to get into a new server
-some people have taken advantage of exploits and are richer than you will ever be (wipe will fix this whenever it happens)
-occasional unknown bugs
-annoying weather effects (opinion)
Conclusion:
This game is excellent for those who don't mind a bit of lag and understand that it is a Multiplayer ALPHA MMO. It is a very fun game when you have people in a Teamspeak call and actually have plans.

DEC 17, 2017: Fresh update, and finally some good news. Today I spent 11 hours on this game with a friend hosting. Not a single crash. No stuttering, though the occasional black flicker. Some odd lag here or there, but that should be expected during any hosted p2p session.
So, what have my 11 hours of steady Empyrion taught me?
One- make my friend host. We tried this before, but didn't help with crashing. This time the game just ran better overall for both of us. May be from recent patches.
Two, the grind is strong with this one, even on fast leveling. Granted we've been going around kicking down POI's, but just getting the stuff up for a basic HV, though large and powerful, has taken us... well. 11 hours. Now, in the past I spent an amount of time on a guild server and had a blast. I also have spent time on a creative world building a couple vessels. One of these, the SH-1 Saiph, named for a star of the Orion constalation, is what we are working towards. It's available on the workshop, if you like.
Three- No story to speak of. Plenty of adventure. I believe there are story senarios though. And you can get them through the workshop if memory serves- an aspect I have yet to explore. Personally- I think it likely does not need a story. Minecraft didn't. Terraria didn't. Starbound pulled it off, but its a beast, and I had hundreds of hours of fun before then.
Four- This game can give me panic attacks. Real ones. Not something I have ever experienced before, and don't really enjoy. Today we delved into the abandoned mine on Akua. I have familiar and very bad experience with this particular dungeon- its where I was having many crashing issues previously. I know this dungeon quite well. Wellllll. Not so much it turns out. Along with fixing the crashing, the dev's overhauled it. Complete with a significant number of genuinely nasty surprises. And the slime drip? Seriously? *shudder*
Five- NOT FOR CHILDREN. You will encounter things in this game that the noises alone are nighmare fuel, much less the foes themselves- some of which are literally called Nightmares.
Overall? Much better. I can finally flip that thumb. We're still on the first planet. But not for much longer. I have a general feel for the game now, enough to say I kinda know what to expect from it in the future. But, always, always bear in mind- This is early access. Everything is subject to change. So far? Things are very much so looking up for this very promising early access game.

So...I spent almost 500 hours playing Empyrion, perhaps it is time for a review. I am a fan of this game regardless of what I am about to write, but I can't help myself but to be fair in my review. I know, it will be a long one.  Brace yourselves!
First off, don't let yourselves be too impressed by players saying it's the best game, that it is what No Man's Sky should be, etc. This game is not the best game, it is in alpha stage and it shows. I also played a considerable amount of time in NMS and for the most part both game has absolutely nothing to do with each other. People should rather compare Empyrion to Space engineers, but they prefer to use NMS as a reference. Ok, I can do that too :P
Also don't be fooled by players who spent only a few hours in Empyrion and declare this game is bad or unplayable. Empyrion won't hold your hand and take you through the game. Empyrion is a sandbox game and you have to make your own story, your own game, and understand the fact that it is in alpha.  So, yes, it comes with bugs and other annoying things that, hopefully, will be fixed. If you can play long enough to get your first 'small vessel', things will get very interesting from that moment. Most people won’t get there after the first 5 hours of playtime, so they leave the game.  Too bad, they will miss an interesting game.
That said, the review.
The devs:
they are great, they listen to the community and keep updating the game every week.  nothing else to say here. great job guys!
Game performances:
Before I proceed any further, I should specify I have a brand-new rig on which I can play a triple A game at max resolution while my son plays another game on the oculus rift and neither of us have lag. I also have a very good internet connection.
Still, Empyrion will lag sometimes even if I tried all sort of different configurations and keep my computer up to date. Empyrion behaves ok most of the times as long as I play in single player, almost no lag. But it is a different story in coop or whenever I host a server. Then I decided to host my server on Nitrado with the voodoo 2 scenario. Same thing. The friend I play with in coop doesn’t have a rig as good as mine and he lags a lot more sometimes.  I guess the devs will keep optimizing the game and eventually this won't be a problem anymore.
just to clarify things here, here is a quick example of lag we are experiencing (single or coop): we are aboard a capital ship and we enter a planet's atmosphere. The game freeze and controls become erratic. when we are finally near the planet's surface, everything takes some much time to appear (trees, water, etc.)  I got used to that and my gameplay changed accordingly, but I know this is not normal. there are other performances issue but that one is the worse, which isn't that bad all things considered.
Graphics:
Graphics are pretty good for an alpha game. There are glitches here and there but nothing bad or what I consider being a deal breaker. Some Textures need rework,etc.  But overall the game is very playable and in my case, it didn't crash too often. Of course, the game doesn't have this final, polished look of a triple A game, but it will get there, eventually.
Planets:
If there is one aspect of the game we can really compare Empyrion versus NMS, it is the planets biomes. So... some players pretend Empyrion is way better than NMS.  Ok, lets talk about that for a moment. For now, planets in Empyrion s**k big time compared to NMS. they just do. Let’s call a cat a cat.  In Empyrion, planets are much smaller, also in much smaller numbers and most of them feel empty. On the plus side, pretty much every POI in Empyrion have aliens you can kill. In NMS, all you have to play with are stupid flying drones and space pirates. (space combat is much better in NMS).
To fully realize how empty planets are, all you have to do is go on any moon you want (or on any planet that is not like Akua) and see how empty the scenery is. Ore nodes and alien POI is all you will find. But if you stick to Akua-like planets, things are much better and nice looking. Of course, there are mods and scripts you can find online to change that, but they don't come with the game by default when you buy it, so do not take that in account when it comes to a review.
Story:
If you play this game in single player mode, do not expect a story driven game. There is no story in Empyrion. No narrative, no voice acting.  At best, you have a few missions to do like killing creatures at night, preparing food, etc. This can entertain you for an hour at most if you decide to dedicate time doing missions. Maybe they will add something in the future, just not there yet in the game development.
Crafting:
I think this is where Empyrion shines the most. In my opinion, the devs found the sweet spot when it comes to crafting. Not only Empyrion has a wide variety of things you can craft and design but you don’t have to craft everything you need to build stuff. Here's an example: you don’t have to craft all sort of blocks.  just craft, let's say, a steel block and then the game lets you decide what is the shape you want to use. And things get even better! Texturing and coloring your blocks is 'free'. You don't have to recharge your guns. This makes the bases and ships designing a lot more fun and less tedious.
Vehicles:
Empyrion need to provide players with more ways to explore planets.  Don't get me wrong here.  The Empyrion community is Fantastic and all you have to do is go in the Steam workshop to find amazing blueprints to fly, hover, warp or go wherever you want to be. But when it comes to land exploration, the motorcycle gets old very quickly and you cannot dock it inside a ship and take it with you in your star trek adventures on a far, far away planet. The game lacks other means to move around and I hope the devs will arrange that. (Quick side note, the vehicles in NMS work flawlessly well. The Nomad will give you an amazing ride).
Food:
My Capital ships can travel at warp speed between planets. I can conquer and control any planetary base I want. I can subjugate aliens, kill them, spare them, do whatever i want with them and yet...I can die from starvation and I have to farm and process food. At first it is fun, but eventually it gets very, very annoying to deal with food. Dealing with food isn't fun because it adds no value to the game as you progress.  You must farm food the same way when you start the game as when you are conquering planets with your almighty-mega-uber Star Destroyer.  To my opinion, players should be able to automate the process at some point. Maybe in a future update, who knows. But for now, not fun at all in the long run.
Combat;
In pvp, things are fine because you fight other players, but in pve it is a much different story. The aliens in Empyrion aren't evolving to match your level so the combat system becomes unbalanced very quickly (in your favor) and need a lot of rework. The alien you fight at level 1 is the same at max level.  So, at some point, you become so powerful with your spaceships that aliens cannot offer you any form of resistance.
Verdict:
At this point in the game development, I think Empyrion is incomplete and is a niche game. If you like to build ships, space bases and have fun with friends, then you will you will have a lot of fun playing this game.  But eventually it simply gets boring as Empyrion still lacks this little something to keep you hooked to the game once you passed a certain threshold. All you do then is collect ore to build more stuff.  Rinse and repeat a few times and then you go play another game.
On the other hand, the game is only 21$ and I often saw it going down to 10$.  At this price, you cannot be wrong to buy Empyrion, even at full price.

The meat of this game is developing your characters and engaging in challenging tactical combat. I played on hard difficulty and it was no joke. You know you have a winner when your first time through a fight feels like a hopeless battle you can’t possibly win, but coming back for another try (or 5) you start to see a path and sure enough you snatch victory from the claws of your enemies. I found myself saying a lot of “No no no!! and Yes yes yes!!” and that is a good sign indeed.
A decent system for equipment and hard choices to make for what kind of characters to develop and when make for pretty reasonable strategic choices between fights. I never quite felt like re-starting to make different choices but I switched focus and direction a few times as I learned what worked and what didn’t. Better yet, different fights call for very different approaches and play to the strengths and weaknesses of your character. There is no one right answer or best build, just a lot of different good choices you need to learn how to utilize. The only mistake you can make is not learning the mechanics and failing to do any specialization at all.
On the other hand, while the voice acting is fine and the writing is decent, I was never all that compelled by either the characters or the story. It was never daft or cliche or bad in any way, but rarely all that awesome or intriguing. There are minor choices to be made here and there but rarely do they feel all that impactful and while the order you do quests is often open, there is rarely a feeling it matters all that much either.
The game is worth the money, especially if you love tactical combat and like a stiff challenge. If you are looking for a story driven RPG or something with a feeling of grand adventure, this might not be your game.

When I look at this game in my library I have to wonder why I even bought it. I bought this game over 3 years ago and I cannot for the life of me recollect why I had the feeling this game was good or what attracted me to it. The developer is completely unknown, the screenshots look fine, the trailer is a tad bombastic and shows off the main mechanic of the game fairly well but it's still a very standard puzzle game. But boy am I happy that I did buy this game because this is easily
Constant C is a puzzle game but with 2 extremely compelling and well-rounded mechanics: gravity switching and time dilation. Gravity switching is a fairly obvious one but the time switching mechanic is easily one of the most impressive puzzle mechanics I've seen. There world has frozen in time and only a small radius around the character has time flowing at normal speed. This means any object within that radius would move as normal but the moment it leaves the radius it instantly freezes in place. Unlike some puzzle games where the main mechanic is used sparingly because the level designer couldn't come up with puzzles good enough to use it well, this game is almost ENTIRELY around these mechanics with a couple of small and (again) REALLY well rounded twists to the time dilation mechanic.
The level of polish on display here is INSANE. Since the time dilation is a fairly confusing mechanic, great pains were taken to make it extremely obvious and easy to know which objects are currently being affected and how they would move if you were to bring them into your field. The level design is amazing with a slow ramp up to some REALLY challenging puzzles later on that will rack your brains which also require a fair degree of platforming precision. The music is quite good and muted for the most part making for a good background while you conjure up solutions to these conundrums. HOWEVER
While I like those mechanics, the game suffers from poor pacing and uninspiring level design. The difficulty curve could be more consistent, and some things could be explained a bit more, but my biggest gripe pacing wise was the time cube thrown in at the last section. It's essentially a second you which only moves through gravity, and it's another mechanic I really enjoy, but it comes in too late to be used very much.
The game boasts 100+ levels, but here's a rough breakdown of them:
~20% I'd call easy enough to be filler levels
~40% are
filler levels which are trivial just to pass, but also have collectibles
~25% solid, enjoyable puzzles
~15% unclear, at times frustrating levels
The story didn't catch my attention and I didn't even pay attention to it.
I want to reccoment this game because I enjoy its foundation, but its bland level design and meh execution makes me hesitate to suggest it. At the very least, just know what you're getting into and it'll be fine. 75/100

Evoland 2 was the surprise break-out hit of the holiday season, for me. the first Evoland was just a pretty well-implemented gag you could play through, a one-note nostalgia joke about the development of game engines.
This sequel, however, instead has a well-crafted (if somewhat simplistic and over-acted) plot about time travel, fate, race relations, personal development, and the lessons of history.  This is coupled with a time-travel mechanic represnted by 8-bit, 16-bit, and modern 3D graphics respectively, that isn't just a gimmick or a joke about game development, but a solidly integrated gameplay mechanic, with challenging but not frustrating puzzles, and loads of mini-games and constantly varying game modes that take you through a retrospective of genre development in gaming, and keep the game feeling fresh and fun throughout.

First things first, As I write this, Steam says I have only played 16 minutes. Well Steam is wrong. I have completed the entire game story-wise.
. On to the review!
Intro
====
The original Evoland was surprisingly good. Its main focus was on the gameplay and the concept of 'evolving' the game with sound effects, music, graphics and gameplay but the storyline was very simple. Evoland 2 took its predecessor and improved on pretty much everything!
Improvements
===========
-Shifting through time (changing graphics) is used lots later in the game and the shift is done very well.
-There are so many different locations and most contain their own unique gameplay or genre.
There's the main gameplay of the Legend of Zelda, 2D platformers, Street Fighter, 1942, Fire
Emblem and so many others!
-Each gameplay genre also has its own boss and if you are good at it/enjoy it, they won't last
for too long so that you get bored
-The game has a very deep storyline and will give you more hours of playtime than the first.
-Leveling up is relevant now! Your stats from leveling up carry through *most of* the different gameplay types.
-The card game is better if you want to waste time playing it. You find people to battle scattered across the map in
different times and you unlock more cards from beating other people.
Conclusion
========
Evoland 2 is a great game that improves on everything from the first Evoland. There are many different gameplay genres, the time travel is improved greatly and if you play through it all the way, it will provide you with much more playtime than the first. It doesn't provide me with many - if any major negative comments at all. Fantastic game!
Evoland 2: A Slight Case of Space Time Continuum Disorder - Highly Recommended
Note: Be prepared though because if you are bad at a genre that shows up or just don't like it, you have to complete it so if you find it too difficult, the only thing to do is practice, practice, practice. (Or find a loophole)

THIS REVIEW IS FOR PEOPLE WHO HAVE PLAYED EVOLAND 1
Evoland 2 is not Evoland 1.
IMO though, it's better. Lets go over the major points:
Gameplay:
-This is one of the only things relatable to Evoland 1. Only difference is it has A LOT more variety. There are more genres introduced than you would think could fit in a game.
-The different elements of gameplay are a lot better introduced and more seamlessly fit into the game than Evoland 1.
-They completely removed the chest mechanic of finding new gameplay types to make it seem like the gameplay changing IS the story (which I will talk about later). Instead they will just surprise you
-As with the other game, if any section of the game is too hard or boring for you, you can tone down the difficult to greatly speed up the game.
Story:
-Evoland 2 is a much more story driven game than Evoland 1. If you don't like dialogue in games or don't like story, Evoland 2 might not be for you.
-The story fits the theme of Evoland 1 (progressing though gameplay and graphics) directly into the world without breaking the 4th wall.  The changing of graphics is given a reason and is a cannon part of the world (I won't spoil any more than that)
Music:
-Great soundtrack, although only a slight improvement from Evoland 1
Graphics:
-Compared to Evoland 1, they are "worse" at the parts their supposed to be bad, and better at the parts where they are supposed to be good.
Overall:
-Evoland 2 is more of a game complete with plot, whereas Evoland 1 was more of an ongoing gimmick.

Evoland 2 manages to walk the tightrope between retro callbacks and story advancement, and does a good job of it.  There's a bit of everything to do here, and without spoiling too much, you transition between so many genres of games, specifically classics from that genre that provide a feeling of nostalgia with a touch of modern gaming thrown in that feels exciting, but more importantly, fresh.  One hour you might be doing a 2D platformer, the next youre playing a Bejeweled type game, and the next moment, a 3D dungeon in a JRPG.  Played it once, couldnt put it down, and I was anticipating what genre would come next.  Also the music was great throughout.
But to be fair, this game is not perfect.  Great game, but not perfect.  The camera sometimes was a headache as it would obstruct the views of many things in the 3D worlds, especially in the very last dungeon of the game.  The story is clever and well done, but sometimes the many callbacks and challenges work to its detriment by derailing momentum in the story and notably the characters.  Also, I thought a dash button couldve been nice, but that it a very minor issue.
But as I said, this is without a doubt a good game, and I definitely recommend getting it.

Anomaly 2 is a tower defense game in reverse style, where you take a
squad through a group of enemy towers to destroy them.  They provide a well
implemented leader-board, which gives a chance to see how one compares with
other players.  The story as well as the voice acting pulls you into the
game, which is nice.
One nice feature to this game is being able to pick from multiple
routes in the levels, so you don't feel as though you are trapped.  The
level of detail in available pathways gives you the option to build the
way you want to-whether it be challenging yourself to a difficult route, or
trying to find the way of least resistance.
Each unit you chose is affected differently by the enemy towers.
Your units can morph into different units with different assets, which
provides more options.  There is a large variance in the difficulty levels,
where you feel like you have to fight through the levels, and be aware of
what you are facing; trying to rush through a level can result in massive
loss of troops, and possibly death.  Overall, the combat is balanced, and
requires strategy in order to succeed, not just brute force.
The game is balanced and smooth, I never felt as though my time were
wasted, it runs smoothly, and the story is done well.  The only fault I can
find is a lack of content with not enough missions.  I have no problem
recommending this game to those who enjoy replaying missions to get  better
scores.

Honestly, for me, this game is a bit of a mixed bag. There are alot of pro's and cons to this game that make it hard to decide if its a truly good game, or kind of broken.
All the emphasis for this game is on sneaking around, and not getting caught.
Whilst maybe a tad generic or cliche'd, the game story is pretty well written overall, and features an interesting twist around the games mid-point.
The game features several skill trees reminscent of RPG's that help spice up the game and help your progression. Their included in the game in a well done manner that feels satisfying and well crafted.
At the start of the game your given a few standard abilities, as well as a set of magical abilities fueled by Amber. As you progress through the game, these can be upgraded using the aforementioned skill trees, which can help enhance the gameplay quite a bit.
The levels in this game are pretty large, and can take awhile to progress though, especially if your after a perfect stealthy playthrough like I was, or if you like exploring. There are alot of hidden pathways and so on to be found, which can keep things interesting, and add some replay value.
Whilst a bit less of a concern for me, if your the kind of gamer that loves good graphics, ya may be disappointed.
Whilst maybe somewhat forgiveable to an extent since the enviroments in this game can be pretty expansive, the second half of the game features you doing the exact same levels as before, but in reverse, which feels somewhat lazy if Im honest.
The game features a number of these, and you can't help but wonder how they got to appear in the game. For example, gaurds can get stuck in infinite loops of telling each other to "stay alert" if you put them on alert somehow, and if you unlock the skill to do aerial assassinations quietly, you'll often still hear your victims make screams and yells as you kill them.
Honestly, the game itself is pretty good, and I think I would still recommend it to anyone who wants a hardcore stealth game. Really in my book, the game is just kind of unpolished, but its got a good structure in place, and I reckon had it had a few more months in development that could have made all the difference. Even with its lack of polish however, its a good game, and Im very keen to play the sequel.
The graphics are meh, and its kinda buggy, but its a good game otherwise, with good stealth mechanics well mixed with RPG and fantasy elements.

Let me just say off the bat, I'm a huge fan of turn-based rpg's/strategy rpg's. I'm a long-time player of the Heroes of Might and Magic games as well as the King's Bounty games. Now, I'm not saying that these games are the same, they aren't, but they should at least have prepared me for Blackguards. I felt at home in the first few fights, and had a great time leveling and progressing. But, and this is a big but (tee hee), things soon fell apart, and I could not be more disappointed. Here is the list:
1) Difficulty Spikes - Elitist players can go on and on about how 'you aren't playing the game right', but this game is fundamentally flawed; with *five pages* of things to use your AP points (think leveling points) on, it becomes *incredibly* easy to spec your character incorrectly, thereby completely and utterly breaking your game, forcing you to start over. Not to mention the fact that the first handful of fights are pretty easy, then suddenly the game shoots up in difficulty. A game like this should have the ability to respec your characters, or to at *least* give you more of a guide on what you should be spending your points on; it's WAY too easy to make a mistake if you're not familiar with the system the game is based on.
2) The Fighting - The basics of the battle system seem quite good; all of the things are there to make them an enjoyable experience, however... The sheer amount of missing, dodging, and obviously AI-weighted dice rolls makes this game ridiculous. People can say what they will about "99% chance to hit still isn't 100%", but there are clear patterns of AI-rubber banding/favoritism, making the game *incredibly* frustrating, and fights lasting WAY longer than they should.
3) Spellcasting - Never have I played a game where spells fail so. bloody. often. What is the point of playing a mage? Their spells fizzle so incredibly often, and they take so much damage that you're pretty much forced to use bows or crossbows to keep them alive, and, as another reviewer mentioned, the only point in having them around is to heal/buff/debuff. Incredibly disappointing.
4) Poor Battle Structuring - I probably should have put this onto the fighting or difficulty section, but I felt it merited it's own section. There are times where you're in a tough battle, but you manage to scrape by by the skin of your teeth, and you're elated. Bask in your rewards! All those AP and Go...wait what? There's ANOTHER battle IMMEDIATELY after? And you don't get a chance to heal? What? You're out of Mana??? Guess that means you're going to have to start the first battle all over again! What's that? There's no potions left? Etc, etc etc. There *needs* to be a way of either warning you of multiple fights in a row(some places like the Gladiator Arena does), or at *least* give you the chance to heal between battles. I'm currently at said gladiator arena and have basically given up on the game and wish I hadn't spent my time and money on it.
This game could have been SO much better; the story is interesting enough to keep you going, and the visuals are quite nice, (and DWARVES!) but the poor battle structure, difficulty spikes, flawed dice rolling (Seriously, a weak 'normal' monster dodged me literally 11 times in a row from all four characters..?), and unfortunate leveling flow choices make this a "do not buy unless changes are made". If things are tweaked, this could be a fairly good game, but at it's current state it's nothing more than a frustrating game of blindfolded tennis, (Whiff, whiff, whiff, whiff) and I regret spending money on it.

I really enjoyed Blackguards. For the same reason I enjoyed other old school CRPGs. It had enough of a story to keep it interesting, the combat was challenging and very tactical, and the character/skill/spell system was deep and interesting. If you like old school CRPGs, I highly recommend this game.
What does old school CRPG mean?
Graphics - while good for a CRPG are nowhere near cutting edge. If you must play something to justify your $1000 dual video card setup, this game is not it..
Sound - voice overs a generally very high quality and clearly done by professionals
Combat - this and the skill system are the meat of any CRPG. Combat is very tactical which makes it fun for me. Anything on the field of combat can be pushed over, destroyed, lit on fire, etc. So for example you can lure your opponents to stand in bushes and cast a fireball on them and not only will they take the initial damage they will take per round damage when the bushes catch fire. Lots and lots of tactical depth and different options make combat fun and at times quite challenging.
Character/Skill/Spell System - the other key part of any CRPG. I like The Dark Age system and this game uses that system to create a very deep and interesting set of skills, spells, and attributes to choose from to build your main character and your party of NPCs.
Party-based - Old school CRPGs are almost always party-based and this game checks that box with 5 NPCs that join (and in most cases stay) with your group throughout the game. You'll play most of the game with you PC and 3 NPCs.
LInear - all good old school CRPGs are linear so they can control the level of opponent you face and unfold the story in a particular way. Books and movies and are linear too and that's what makes them good. I like old school CRPGs to be linear and tell a story and create custome encounters (rather than random ones). Don't get me wrong, I like games like Skyrim, but I generally prefer old school linear CRPGs as the rule and open games like Skyrim as the exception.
Story - good enough to keep it interesting.....
If you like old school CRPGs don't miss this one.

Every now and then I come across games like Constant C, games I really like but yet my puzzle solving skills do not allow me to progress any further in game. So what do I do? I go on Youtube and watch a walkthrough or a let's play from where I stopped playing until the end, and that's what I did with Constant C.
It got to the point that the amount of time and dedication I needed to put into this in order to succeed in various levels were just too much for me, I don't mind playing games that are hard by nature, but when it involves timing certain actions with precision, I just can't do it. Call me weak, whatever -.-
In Constant C you play as an emergency robot that was made in the event of a failed scientific experiment. The game is a great platformer with a very unique mechanic, around your character there's this "bubble" and inside that bubble time happens. Well, this actually sounds weird but the plot of Constant C is that a science investigation on a space station unleashed some kind of anomaly that stopped time and it is by using this bubble device that you can actually make anything in the game. You might see a box in mid air a few meters away but once it gets inside your bubble it will react to gravity. Besides this you also have to manipulate gravity in order to get through the levels. The levels are filled with deadly traps and crates that you must use in order to survive those traps. Most of the levels takes some time to get used and figure out what you exactly need to do in order to succeed, and this was what frustrated me the most, I was just taking too long to figure out the later levels. You can select which level you want to play in a room, which you might call it a "hub", and that's where the AI that is your friend and that is helping you is located. In various levels you'll find "data tubes" which will serve to unlock later levels and pieces of video that tell you a bit of what happened in the space station when all the scientists were alive.
Eitherway, Constant C has a very unique atmosphere to it but the art style reminds me of Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe so if you've played that you know what to expect. The descriptions and preview video for this game are misleading. Yes, you play a mighty space robot with superluminal powers of gravity manipulation and time-distortion, fit to solve platform puzzle mazes and collect trophies. However, under your matte-black stealthed paintwork, your body is biomechanical blancmange. Your ninja-coating is actually a sweet sugary crust coloured with squid ink. You will want to run away from many environmental elements. You will be afraid, and you will die. A lot. So much so, you will even get achievements for dying the most.
The levels are fairly well-designed puzzles involving physics which is quite "oily". Moving about feels like gliding on an oil-slicked surface; rarely will you be able to get objects to move the exact same way twice. You mainly interact with environments by moving near things to cause them to move, and by adjusting gravity in three directions. Causing objects (and you) to fall about. Haphazardly chaotic at first, then merely dangerously with more skill. This will cause you to die a lot, because touching almost anything which moves within your time-distortion field causes it to summarily destroy you with great violence. Sometimes falls no more than twice the length of your character's height cause you to explode. Anything falling on you causes you to explode. Touching anything which looks remotely harmful causes you to explode.
Thankfully there are no lives in this game, and restarting the level is a matter of waiting out the inevitable explosion animation (which is mercifully short). It is likely the restart button will be pressed early and often in anticipation of subsequent attempts. You will also lock yourself into various puzzles from which your only way out is suicide in order to restart. To give a basic impression of the game would be to say players spend most of their time quietly contemplating static puzzles, before dying over and over trying to solve them within the confines of the physics engine. Eventually, the frustration at things never quite falling the way you want them to will make you quit for awhile, unless you're being paid by the level, or suffer from obsessive-compulsive disorder.
At the time of writing, the "kickass soundtrack" hasn't kicked in yet. Don't be fooled by the upbeat tune in the preview video, I've not heard anything like it after hours of play. So far the music has been very soothing, minimalist, or so atmospheric as to be barely present. The writing comprising the plot is an interesting dichotomy, because there are many child-like elements interspersed with mature ideas. In my view the exchanges and monologues don't last quite long enough to be satisfying, and unfortunately there is no voice acting. Perhaps because the dialog is not the game's strongest point.
There has been a little foreshadowing of the only other active character in the main storyline. It gives away very little as to why characters do whatever they are doing, and without playing more even I won't know what nefarious deeds have wrought the situation onboard the superluminal project space station... only time-travel will tell (see what I did there?). However, I'm not sure I have the patience to  complete Constant C levels at a rate which would keep me interested in the story. My seven-year-old would become frustrated with this game in about ten minutes before going back to playing Minecraft-esque games where the feeling of achievement can be much stronger. This game is like a cross-pollination of: "Super Meat Boy", "Splosion Man", and "Braid", so if you're buying for children, perhaps try those before playing Constant C or frustration and engagement failure await you.

"We are the Ultramarines, the Sons of Guilliman. Whilst we draw breath, we stand. Whilst we stand, we fight. Whilst we fight, we prevail. Nothing shall stay our wrath."
What has not been said about one of the greatest games almost made? We know the kind of polish that Relic aims for when creating a game. While this game falls short of what we’ve come to expect from Relic, it has so much of what makes a great game wired into it. The story is par for the course for Warhammer 40K storytelling. It’s difficult to assess if it’s possible to appreciate the world and story presented if one is not already a fan and follower of the Warhammer 40K universe. The single player campaign is weighed down by a disappointing boss fight and unpolished combat animations. Combat requires very deliberate effort. While this is fun, the restricted variation in combat almost leads to repetition.
Is there a multiplayer game more underrated and underappreciated than this one? This game’s PvP multiplayer easily captures a level of gameplay that can only be claimed by the greatest. If you did not play this game at its peak, you missed one of the greatest periods in multiplayer gaming history. Sounds like hyperbole? What defines a the quality of multiplayer gaming better than the memories you have of the instances where teamwork and pure skill allowed you a chance at survival or victory? What’s a better measure of your multiplayer experience than those memories etched into your mind? This is what Relic’s effort produced. Multiplayer modes include deathmatch and capture ground. While three hard classes are available, all are customisable. Classes afforded you the opportunity to choose a tradeoff between firepower and mobility. You’re able to effectively build your character to fit your playstyle. This is what multiplayer rests on; the ability to exercise your skills against the skills of your enemies. The seamless addition of melee combat adds a richness to multiplayer that demands concentration and quick reflexes. Team based game modes were designed in such a way that teamwork is truly invaluable. Tactics range from travelling in packs to eliminate stragglers in team deathmatch, to coordinating ranged and close quarters combat in capturing points in seize ground.

Awesome. The gameplay, visual design, and sound are superb. This is some of the most fun I have had in a multiplayer game for quite some time (cooperative Exterminatus mode is my favorite so far). If you never heard of Warhammer 40,000, you should play this game. If you like Warhammer 40,000, you would be stupid to miss this epic-laden masterpiece.

So (almost) 100 hours further, I have spend enough hours to make a review about this game. And yes, I still like it.
I will not give you a full historical report about the game, how Gloria Victis developed through the years etc, but more a look how I experienced the game in his current state. Keep in mind, the game is still in Alpha which brings pros and cons with it. *Thanks to 'Peon' and his first impression video I bought this game on steam.
First things first, time to make a character. The character customisation is in my opinion a bit scarce. Right now, players can chose out of 2 factions, couple of hair styles, tattoos and you can change your character a bit. Do not expect a indept-character customisation.  Conclusion: I created a Midlander.
When I first joined a server, it showed me a 'okey' tutorial. Just a common tutorial without any specialtys, supported by a starterpack, which provide you a bow, shield, sword and other stuff. (Still, I recommend a more specific tutorial eventhough the game is not hard to understand.)
So far, so good. The graphics looks good, no lagg, a decent ping and weapons to start with. After my glorious start I went outside and explore the world. Luckely I found a helpful guild who showed me the world, while grinding mobs and crafting stuff. PVPing in a guild or a party is awesome, unless you lose ofcourse.
The tournaments are also a good feature of the mod. PvPing others while you can not lose any stuff and gaining a lot of experience.
Even the upgrading system is decent, while you get a decent amount of experience and do not forget the money which you will get.
I forgot one big thing in the game, Crafting. Yeah, the game has a indept-crafting system. From gaining/looting recipes to leveling up your specific 'skill'. For example, Weaponforging, Armoursmithing etc. Right now, the active members of my guild have all their own specific skill/role. You provide each other with recipes and materials to get the desired weapon/armour.
Everything which is stated above, is positive. Guess what, every game has pros and cons and like CV, this game also has cons. Starting with the fact that it is in ALPHA. Do not expect a perfect 4-hour game run, without encountering numerous buggs and glitches. Yeah, sometimes your arms disappear or mysteriously lose stuff while logging in on servers.
The combat is 'okey', but really needs a optimisation. It really feels buggie from time to time.
Crafting system is good, but you have to grind a lot to reach your desired level.
Overall, I personally have more pros then cons. The community is very helpfull, but as far as I know, can also be a pain in the ***. But yeah, there are always people who **** up the game. I would say, when you buy the game and join a server, join a guild. The game is way more fun when grouping up with a guild. It is also more rewarding when you find the right guild, which are capable of making good weapons and armour.
With the right party you can literally do everything, from bossing till massive pvping. I recommend this game to people who likes this style of game and do not mind  the combination of PVEing and PVPing. Also, grinding is part of the game, but you will enjoy it when you fully understand the game. My advise is simple, find a guild or group and explore the world!

This game is based on a tabletop RPG called "The Dark Eye" which will likely be new to even most pencil and dice junkies out there.  It's a turn-based, hex-based, combat-oriented game that presents some of the most wickedly challenging combat scenarios I have had to face in a turn-based game.  The developers have made excellent use of the environment, using traps, environmental effects, hindering terrain, and interactive objects integral to most combats.  This, combined with a wide array of special abilities available through warrior training or spell effects, makes combat very dynamic and challenging.  It can also be very frustrating.  On the plus side, when you lose a tough battle, there is an option to replay the battle from the beginning of the battle, as well as from your last save, so you need not redo extensive amounts of replay to "get to the good stuff."
There are four character generation options for this game, three basic with pre-builds of a melee warrior, a hunter archer, and a mage, and fourth option to custom build a character from scratch.  I have tried all four, but recommend trying building a character from scratch only after having tackled at least the first chapter of the game to get an idea of what the game is like.  I wanted to build an archer-mage, and found that it was easier (and you got better abilities) by starting as a straight mage and then investing experience points in archery talents and proficiencies to make up the difference.
The NPCs in the game are fun and all dialogue is voiced.  The dwarven NPC (your first ally) has some really good lines.  The story is VERY linear, literally a "go here and do this" with arrows pointing your next route, which is nice in some ways and very frustrating in others.
You get advancement points for every fight and story event, and you get a lot of them.  They accumulate quickly, but you need a ton to advance a stat or skill.  Stats, talents, weapon talents, and spells all rank from 1 to 18, with varying costs from 6 to over 480 to advance to the next level.   Experience comes in multiples of 25, depending on encounter difficulty, with more coming in the later stages of the game. Still, your Special Abilities are what makes your character be able to do extraordinary things like being able to regenerate Astral Points (mana) or Knockdown an opponent in combat.  These are relatively cheap to buy, at around 300 Advancement Points, but Special Abilities often have stat and weapon talent prerequisites that in turn cost advancement points to purchase, which all adds up to more advancement points....  I could not imagine playing "The Dark Eye" without a computer to aid me, especially as your Attack Value, Parry Value, Dodge Value, and Ranged Attack Value are all based on three stats added together and divided by five.  And that every roll in the game is a test against three ability scores.  All of this is handled by the computer and done very nicely in a battlelog that summarizes it in a percentage chance for you.  It can be a bit confusing when your 100% chance to hit misses, because evidently the computer rounds to the nearest %(?) but that's a quibble.
In all this is an exceptionally fun game.  I keep telling myself I am tired of getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me by the game and will quit THIS TIME for sure, but in minutes I am back to beat the fight that got me.  It's so linear you can hear the train whistle when you play.  You will have your butt kicked routinely.  But if you like challenging turn-based combat and designing your own characters, you will likely love this game.

I didn't think I'd recommend any of the games in the Anomaly series but this one stood out among the rest. I only played the single-player campaign so that's what this review is based on. With that said, the story of the game definitely has a much broader feel compared to the previous ones as it takes place across three continents as humanity struggles against the machines for survival and a better tomorrow. It also has two endings which are determined by your decision in the final mission.
The gameplay, units and towers are pretty much the same as the previous games with one difference: each unit can transform which repurposes it for a completely different function, so the amount of different units is essentially expanded to 10, each of the five purchasable units can be switched to its counterpart by simply double-clicking it at will on the battlefield. Still, the game is fairly simple and has four difficulty modes that can be chosen before the beginning of each mission.
Again, I recommend this one over the others and perhaps the only reason to play the others is for what little storyline they have leading up to this one but it can still stand by itself because the opening cinematic can get the player up to speed on how Earth was thrown into a perpetual Winter. So I suppose it's safe to ignore the others and only play this one!

Pros:
*Interesting system mechanics, with a LOT of depth to advancement.
Cons:
*Tutorial and Tips are useless.  I had been playing for over 2 hours (8+ combat missions) before I got a couple of the tips on how to do basic things.
*Horrible camera system.  Unable to rotate the camera, forcing you to revert to top down view in many areas just to be able to see the hex map behind objects/allies/enemies.
*No resource regeneration out of combat.  You can camp to restore Health and Astral points, which isn't bad, but when you hit one of the first major fight areas, you are prevented from camping.  You are forced to use town healers to restore HP out of combat, even if you have 2 mages with healing in your party.  No Astral Point (mana) regeneration outside of combat, even with talents that grant passive Astral Regen per turn, forcing you to use your very expensive Astral Potions to be able to actually use a mage character.
*Treating injuries with bandages has a chance to fail (very high chance) outside of combat, and almost useless to try in combat (6% chance of success at first rank).
*You are forced to buy belts to be able to carry many items into combat with you, but you are encumbered in combat by ALL the equipment in your bags, even you quest items and camping resources.
*Almost no income, with horribly high priced item.  At one point, you are given a large amount of money and told to go to the armorer to get equiped to help defend a town.  The armorer has 1 type of armor, 2 sets of it, and you are given enough to buy 1 piece of equipment.  Not a set, 1 piece.  You have to choose between upgrading a single piece of heavy armor, or to buy Astral and Health potions.
*Horrible UI.  Almost no explanations as to what means what, or as to how anything is calculated.  When comparing armor pieces, it does not compare piece to piece, only how it will change your whole, and armor/encumbrance always shows a penalty, even if it is an upgrade.
*Horrible combat encounter design.  In many of the fights, all of the mobs will sit back throwing poisoned javelines at you, each of which hits your heavily armored character for 15-30% of his total HP, and also poisons him.  Was forced to use the fighter as a tank, both of my mages as pure healers, while slowly grinding down the mobs hp with my archer (arrows cost a lot, and have weight.  I overmaxed my encumbrance just from provisions, which you need to camp, and arrows alone).
*Buff, healing and utility spells have default fail chance, which until you pick of a very very expensive talent, are almost impossible to cast (22% fail chance to heal an ally, 68% chance to fail to dispel a poison with a spell that only dispels poisons, 48% chance to fail to cast a "wall" spell, etc).  Combined with no innate astral regen, very low astral point pool and high astral point cost to cast makes playing a mage character feel like your being penalized for playing the game.
It's a pretty crappy game. The visuals are okay, but the gameplay is lacking and underwhelming. Overall, there are better RPG's to play.

Definitely a thumbs down. Let me explain.  We have a playerbase of three that playes together at all times. Three different PC configurations from two different states. There is two game breaking problems that occur on all three platforms. First and foremost runetime error during combat. Last night we had ship damage around 1/4% of total hull and I kid you not all three of us were dissconnecting every 30~ seconds or so. Only during damage does this happen. So basically when your ship is on the line and you are taking fire you spend most of your time trying to reconnect, not good, not good at all.
Our second problem is absolutly game breaking. In the span of time we played we built three ships. Every ship an upgrade from the last. Our last ship took an entire day to collect, design and build. That's all three of us on one ship project. All three ships simply disappeared. Not destroyed, not lost, not misplaced, simply vanished. I decided to get on this morning to play. We had to make some modifications on the design. Simple modifications, took two or three minutes. Completed the adjustments and BAM ship is gone. This happened to all three of our vessels during simple modifications. Remember thats three people in two different states on three different builds all with the same results.  Thats a ship build that took all day and hours of collecions in the cargo bay, all gone. This is absolutly game breaking. This was my text this morning to my friends.....  "went to modify, Ships gone again.We are done with this game." Yes, that frustrating.
Yes I know, Early Access. Seems to be the excuse of 2016. We will return again sometime down the road to retry gameplay but as it stands it is offically shelved. Want to support the developers? One last thing.. 5-6 servers one "busy" with 6-10 players. I assume we are not the only ones to shelve it.

Interstellar Rift is a fun early access sandbox space sim.  The game does crash infrequently, but constant auto-saves have prevented me from ever suffering any significant loss.  The game's early access state is managed very well by the developer through regular small updates and communication with the community.  While it is currently focused on multiplayer, I've enjoyed all my time so far just playing alone and surviving in the universe.  This is good news for the casual player since a public server hosting a game of this kind would certainly be prone to griefing.  It is challenging usually only when you want it to be and if you prefer to stay away from danger and just do your own thing you are typically able to do so.  When I have decided to take on challenges or explore a known hostile site, I was surprised to find a semi-roguelike experience which typically turns me off to a game.  In Interstellar Rift, however, your survival depends greatly on how prepared you are regarding how your ship is designed and if you discover you weren't well prepared, it won't take you long to get back on your feet.  The first-person oriented interface of EVERYTHING in the world really makes the game quite immersive although tweaks will be needed here and there to reduce some of the aggrevations associated with such control.  The flight controls are aggrevating, but manageable; I hope to see an overhaul of this aspect of the game and a move toward a more typical flight simulation experience, but only in that area.  I did not encounter the difficulties many players reported regarding the complexities of the ship-builder.  It is certainly not a shake and bake style process, but decreasing the capabilities it offers would take away from the highly personalizeable point of it all.  It's alot of fun just to spend hours designing a ship (or less... it's surely up to you how complex you make it!), spend some time mining the resources, and push-button build it.  Later on as your needs change, your ship can be freely modified in the ship-builder at a cost only of the resources associated with the changes you make--no real penalty or waiting period.
Highly reccommended and excited to see where this game goes in the future.  As a note to the developer, however, the high focus on multi-crew-member gameplay is a HUGE hinderance to this game.  A sandbox game such as Interstellar Rift will appeal to a very large population of casual players who still want to be able to hold their own when playing alone.  As it is now, they will find it difficult if not impossible and lose interest eventually.  I hope I do not reach that point myself, but I see it heading in that direction even with as much fun as I have had so far.

You don't remember your name nor who you are, you also seem unable to speak: yet as you set out to discover your identity accompanied by the girl whose father you have been rescued by you'll soon find yourself the hero in a story where time itself can be manipulated.
Evoland 2 uses this plot to explain the back and forth between different graphics and game systems and will provide you with a lengthy story backed up by a simple action rpg gameplay often interpunctuated by puzzles and short sections played as a shoot em up, fighting game, beat em up etc: the final result is an enjoyable game despite a few difficulty spikes.
-good graphics and art style for each era
-nice soundtrack goes from standard action rpg music to retro chiptune depending on game era
-a decent, serviceable story with a good ending
-the combat, while simple for the most part (just a basic and charged attack), works well and provides a fair challenge
-you'll be playing through quite a bit of different genres (2d platforming, puzzles, shoot em up, beat em up, a guitar hero section, turn based strategy etc etc): the variety really helps with keeping the game fresh
-the whole game doesn't take itself too seriously and there's lots of humorous moments to be found
-tons of reference to old games, movies, cartoons etc will make your inner child happy
-the game map is quite large and changes depending on era, this means you'll see alot of different areas that, paired with collectibles, provide alot of things to keep you busy
-quite long at 20 to 25 hours
-the mix of different gameplay systems is a boon on variety but can leave you a bit stumped if you don't enjoy and/ or are not good at one of them: these sections are part of the story and you can't skip them
-a few difficulty spikes too many even on its easiest difficulty setting: certain bosses or sections can get quite aggravating
-some puzzles can be somewhat hard to figure out and are a bit dull to begin with
-certain game modes lack polish when compared to others
-the game can lack direction at times leaving you wondering where exactly you're supposed to go next
Evoland 2 has alot to offer both in its story and gameplay if you won't get bored by the simple combat and can keep up with its demands in terms of reflexes and platforming skills: the way Shiro Games has tied its design choices to the narrative helps the game justify the game modes it throws your way while also keeping the story interesting.
While I'm not terribly good at most of them them I personally enjoyed the various sections I had to play through and was happy to see clear homages to the games of my childhood both in their controls, graphics, music and even dialogues.
That said having this many genres crammed into one game means some sections will feel a bit "meh" sometimes...it'd be some slightly awkward controls, a convoluted puzzle, excessive length or just a somewhat punishing difficulty but there's no denying that at times things can be less enjoyable than they'd be. Still I have to admit that the easier difficulty level'd be good enough for any player afraid to be excessively frustrated and most people'd be able to complete the game without wanting to throw their keyboard/ controller out of the window if they stick with it.
If you find its action rpg roots, mix of gameplay and tons of homages interesting then Evoland 2 is an easy recommendation and will easily give you several hours of good, old-school fun.

CoD: I.W. is a good & fun game that is the most successful title of 2017 because it does a few things, & does them well. The action is tight & fairly thoroughly scripted. Dave Stohl, lead developer at Infinity Ward of this temporary project, must be very very proud of the work of the team on the game! The online play is well-structured. The singleplayer campaign gets you into that frame of mind & gets your blood pumping. This version of CoD has a sci-fi take on things that I enjoy, as I'm a fan of the Metro 2033 franchise & Doom franchise, also sci-fi in nature. Batman, too, but I guess that's not really sci-fi but more of a "hero fantasy" thing, I suppose. Without a shred of doubt I can say that Jacob Minkoff, lead developer of the CoD: IW temp work project, is very impressed with himself as far as how successful the game has been.
Locations: The main character hangs out on a spaceship in a room with a bed & a computer between missions. He chooses his expensive spacesuit & semiautomatic weapon there. Then he is brought to places on different planets & completes temporary projects where there is a specific goal: to take a hostage out or to kill an enemy or perhaps regain control of a base. A national & international news corrospondent is included as a member of the group.
Novelties: There is a thing that is new to this series that is very well done. The jet flying is AMAZING. You play several levels where you take control of a fighter jet, sort of like a TIE-fighter, and engage in firefights in outer space!!  If you have read a lot of military sci-fi books as a kid, CoD: IW is like a dream come to life. It's fantastically well done. I have read the whole "Ender's Game" series of books, and the "Dune" series, and that seems like something straight out of that lexicon. What I encountered of the flying was in the singleplayer portion of the campaign, & was not a multiplayer option, I'm sad to report.
If you play a ton of FPS video games, you have a fairly specific vision of what constitutes good multiplayer, & CoD is IT! Years ago, the Unreal Tournament franchise sort of fit into that "AAA Big-Budget Blockbuster" slot, especially UT2004, & that was pretty fun if basically mindless free-for-all combat. That's OK, I get the idea that plenty of folks like that. The Battlefield & CS franchises I see as "not-quite-as-polished as CoD but still pretty good," & there is space for that in the market, for sure. VR games, I don't think so, no offense to the no doubt die-hard VR fans out there in the wilderness. Just too "gadget-y" at this point in time
Negatives: The double-jumping is irritating & gives the gameplay more of a comic-book feel rather than a mostly-realistic FPS experience that you can believe in. Basically there ends up being a lot of people jumping around super high in the sky, which just seems improbable. I understand that it is a fake video game world, so you have a suspension of disbelief & you are taking their rules at face value & just rolling with it. Still hard to believe in flying soldiers with no jet packs in sight. That kind of takes me out of the action a bit & makes me go,
In Crysis 2, which is fairly similar in terms of style & look & feel & so forth, there wasn't any of the "sky-jumping," even though there was some pretty weird weapons & some pretty wild costumes & definitely there were conflicts that were going on.
Final Take: 8/10 stars, the sci-fi style is something new, & the action is still good otherwise. They play it safe as far as variety of gameplay modes goes but that is ok enough I suppose. The zero-gravity warfare is something new and you feel sort of like an army astronaut. Visiting a relative in New York City at the moment, the big Apple!
[edit] on a sad note, I've since deleted CoD: IW & have moved on to spending my spare time playing the video game RAGE, purchased in the summer 2017 STEAM sale

You start out on the planet surface- In the gentle sun, sweltering heat or cold that creeps into your suit. Or your occasional radiated fog.
You eke out a living, eat all the wrong plants and overestimate your aim. You hunt and get hunted by those drones roaming the ore nodes; fleeing on a cheap folded emergency motorbike.
You huddle into a self-dug pit into the ground to avoid the critters of the night... While that huge patrol ship lumbers above with it's plasma cannons scanning for puny humans. You construct your first long -range rifle, and draw a breath of relief. Finally you may be able to strike back- With your limited supply of bullets. You bust in and out of abandoned (or not really abandoned) structures and settlements and loot everything you find and are able to carry. On the way to the place's core you try out some levers because, what could go wrong? And there is a Star Gate inspired teleporter on that plain. Where will it go? (Hint: Into deep space, and it's frickin' cold. Improve your suit.)
You settle down. Build your shack; care for an oxigenated interior since all your collected plants really like it. And you put an anti-drone cannon on top of it all.
- Because that's what you will need when the attack waves begin. While moving out of the cover, you start shooting drones, giving 'em a payback for all those times you had to 'spawn close' to reclaim your backpack. And you loot their remains for parts.
Then you cobble together something of an vehicle. Maybe it's a hover one that will shelter you from the poision spitting spider you really start to hate. Or it's a small bomber, ready to attack one of the alien outposts and nimble enough to dodge their shots, and to flee before the reinforcements arrive...
Whatever you build (or spawn by an in-game factory of community and self-build designs), some day your small vehicle waits for you in your backyard on the meadow, glistening in the sun. All the while the moon gets up.
... Or maybe just fly there?
There are drones in space, too. And even bigger ships, which launch more drones. And a station that punches holes into little nosy player ships, like a cookie cutter.
- Half of the side thrusters are gone, a spare fuel tank has popped and took the turning control with it. But you have included a constructor, tucked away a little more safely behind your cockpit in the middle of your ship, and recycle and replace thrusters to keep yourself going...
You collect and build and fight yourself up... - To a capital vessel rivalling the size of the planetary patrol; ready to take it down. A ship, a nomad base, that is filled with the bombers and strike craft and hover drilling vessels of your (or the best people's) design. To explore the planets and their bases, bombarding them from above and inside.
--
That struggle to get to the literal peak of a world and to fly to the stars was the selling point for me. Naked space suit drop from stratosphere to regain it all, one more time? Check.  That's 'Space survial' for me.
If that get's boring, try one of the included scenarios to test your skills, or download from the workshop a sea of space regions and systems, with player designed fortresses and planets.
And then there's multiplayer. But I haven't touched that yet.
--
Side note:
Players comment and complain about stuff on the official forums, give feedback, vote in a poll, and then... suddenly, out of nowhere, it gets changed, improved.
Have seen this again and again. More places to explore. And spotlights for capital vessels, too. Mobs can shoot while nearly turned away from the player and always hit- stop that! The planting pot debate. Quick groups for ship systems. More block shapes, plz! Added sensor logic...and on and on. - Beautiful. :)
The devs churn out updates on an at least two-weekly basis. If your'e not getting them, enable the experimental branch, but be aware of bugs that need to be sqashed for the public release.
This constant flow of improvements has kept me from giving this game a rest.
--
It's Alpha. So it has it's bugs, rough edges, placeholders, strange polar walls and a green veil warning you about the map seams. ('We'll change that later'- And I believe them, they will)
This is not triple A smooth shiny space trucker. It can't be, with just such a small team of developers and no massive Kickstarter around.
And I don't care, as long as the gameplay (and player feedback) is supreme ruler. This has been much beyond to what other games have offered me so far.
And franky, I always wanted to build my _own_ 'Cobra MK III', or build my own star colony for flight citizens of the X-universe. No 'spreadsheets in space', either. -All hands on deck, and man the turrets.
--- TL;dnr ---
I like gameplay and atmosphere; space, shooters, exploration, building; and struggling to grow and make the best out of a tight situation. Graphics are nice for me but kind of secondary -as long as the sunset is beautiful. I've sunk endless times in Minecraft and it's mods, but this seems to have far surpassed it.
Can't really say that I was disappointed by this purchase, like, at all. ;)

The game was fun at times, challenging at times, boring and tedious at times, a real mix.   While it is an RPG, and you can buy/sell equipment, you can't buy or sell armour or weapons (except for bracers) which felt incomplete.  You can buy/sell rings and charms but rarely do you bother or need to as the loot you pick up often ends up being far better.
There are places in the game where you can take advantage of the nature of enemies respawning, in particular enemies that give loot drops that include potions that increase your strength or other attributes by one point permanently, simply by staying in the area and continuing to kill the same enemies as they respawn over and over, then hoarding up a nice supply of stat point potions and bumping your character up significantly.  Likewise, there are places where enemies drop a lot of loot, and once you've fully completed the potion guy's 3 quests and unlocked all of the potions he makes, you can just go raid high-money-loot enemies for a while, return to the potion guy and buy stat point potions and bump your character up significantly again.  It doesn't even take that long to do, but gives a significant advantage that somewhat debalances the game.
The game crashes very often, and you lose everything that has happened since the last progress auto-save which can be frustrating.  There are other bugs in the game where large blocky areas go completely black and you generally have to exit the area to a save point then restart the game to continue.
Throughout the first 90% of the game, casting spells is extremely tedious especially while in battle, having to hit a number key or click an icon, then click on either yourself or an enemy, then click 3-6 more times in a pattern to make the spell cast, I found that annoying so I didn't use spells very much at all in the early game.  In fact, I didn't even understand how to use them until I did it by accident then tinkered and figured out the awkward spell casting mechanic.
Overall the game had long stretches where it was fun, but it also had long stretches where it was rather tedious, or where you had to figure out some extremely complex jumping manoeuver that was not immediately obvious either in order to proceed at all, or to collect some special beneficial item.
If someone really likes Metroid/Castlevania platformer semi-RPG type games then they might like this if they can handle it crashing every few hours and messed up graphics on occasion requiring a restart.  Otherwise I wouldn't recommend it as the story was kind of weak.
Final rating:  5/10

If you like PULSAR: Lost Colony, you're going to LOVE this; The idea is the same, a coop / pvp multiplayer game where you work together on a ship as crew, or on several ships in a fleet and perform missions / fight other players.
What makes this game, in my oppinion, better than PULSAR, is that you can design your own ship. Design a small freighter for quick but light transport of goods, a larger mining ship for those minerals that are just waiting to be mined in the asteroids, or take a more 'diplomatic' stance and design a fighter, or gunship.
It's been about a year since I bought the game, tried it, and waited for it to mature a bit more, as I tend to do with most EA games. Over that timespan a lot has changed; There are now more solar systems, and a means to travel between them, the forementioned missions have been added, ranging from transporting goods, to shooting down the local wildlife (aliens 'swimming' in space and feeding off of asteroids), to hacking into stations and retrieve lost contraband or information (Yes, you can now hack other ships / stations).
I am not much of a multiplayer gamer. Sure, I've had over a year as officer in the TSN fleet for Artemis Bridge Simulator (as Michael Seer), and spent a lot of time in Guns of Icarus and the forementioned PULSAR, but on the whole, those are exceptions. This game was presented to me as single player, and although it is designed with multiplayer in mind, I'm glad that the game doesn't require it of you.
There are some problems people should be aware of though; The game is EA, meaning it isn't finished and it shows. There are awesome effects when your ship is damaged, from doors that refuse to open the first click, consoles flickering and engines stuttering. It adds a dramatic flair to a dangerous situation, excellent...except it starts doing this if you have just 0.01% damage... Other problems I've experienced include graphical glitches when flying at warp speed, your ship not being stored when storing it at a space station (ship disappears but isn't stored at the station, everything lost), your ship drifting off when you board a station to handle some business, only to find you cannot return because it is out of range...
This last one is particularly annoying, especially since there are stations that don't sell ships, or provide a means to contrstuct your own, or don't provide the means to collect to resources to do either. I've found myself stranded because of this several times, and it's the same as when you try to store your ship; You lose the ship with no hope of ever getting anywhere (would probably not be such a big problem in multiplayer though).
The missions are lacking as well; Play for a few hours and, not unlike my experience in PULSAR, they become repetetive, boring and a waste of time.
All in all, at this point in time I really love the game, but I can't recommend it. At the moment it is a ship editor and testing environment, as expansive as it may be; It's not yet a game. But they are getting there, and they are working hard on it too. But at this time, if you buy the game, you buy the game, not the potential it has, because we all know how quickly an EA game can just drop dead, sometimes for no apparent reason.
So if you can afford the risk, it is well worth it, but for a game, it is far from complete.
