Anomaly 2 see's you take up the role of a commander, who's squad are wrapped in a struggle against an infestation of machine towers who's only goal is to destroy all which enters their firing range.
Anomaly proved you could make a great game by switching the roles of Tower Defence, forcing you to be in command of the troops rather than the towers and making strategic choices of what your squad is composed of, how and when to assist that squad during battle and the route you shall take to your objectives. Anomaly 2 goes a step further by giving your squad the ability to transform on the fly, expanding your options at any given time and also throws in a few more enemy towers.
The gameplay can be quite frantic as you manage your abilities in the heat of battle and scoop up additional abilities from destroyed towers, you can also pause the action to assign a new route for your troops or change the order your squad is currently in at anytime.
On a normal play through, I quickly found a squad set up that worked and while the transformations are useful at times (switching a front arc fire cannon to 360 degree missile fire for instance), I could largely switch to the preferred role and leave them be.
Anomaly 2 doesn't really do anything the original didn't already do. In fact, I preferred the original over this game (both the story and gameplay balance). Anomaly 2 feels more like an expansion than a sequel in many ways and as such, I wouldn't recommend the game unless you've got and enjoyed the original Anomaly: Warzone Earth and fancy more of the same - but I'd stress the original Anomaly is indeed recommended!

I enjoyed this game thoroughly. Evoland 2 switches between multiple genres of gameplay that are sure to entertain every kind of RPG fan.

Evoland 2 makes Evoland 1 look like a technical test.  Evoland 2 is a great game; the best rpg I played in 2015.
GAMEPLAY:
Evoland 2 has a variety-show sort of gameplay.  The "core" combat system in the game is a Secret of Mana-esque combat system where you can summon one of three allies to defeeat enemies or open up new paths in the environment [breaking boulders, clearing vines, freezing water, etc.].
However, the game likes to mix things up from time to time by introducing a new combat system for a boss or gameplay segment.  It helps keep the game fresh throughout the 20 hour playthrough.  You'll have segments of gameplay that use the mechanics of Bomberman, Tekken, Shoot'em'up's, and many more.  Personally, I loved the card game a little more than I should have, given how simple it is.
Combat and quirky game mechanics aren't all this game has.  There is a lot of platforming in this game that mix simple platforming mechanics with the game's core combat system.  It also has some very interesting puzzles.  The puzzles are often Legend of Zelda-style block manipulation and activation of switches from afar.  However, once you unlock the ability to manipulate time, the puzzles can be immensely fun and surprisingly difficult.  Even progressing in the plot can be a "thinking with time travel" style puzzle to figure out what you need to do in what timeline to make progress  in the story.
STORY:
As mentioned above, this game is about time travel.  The game's story should instantly draw comparisons to Chrono Trigger.  However, the game seems to take a very different stance on time travel than Trigger.  If Trigger is about using time travel to fix everything and build a beautiful future, Evoland 2 is surprisingly sober about the topic.  This game is more an exploration of fate, destiny, and inevitability.  Even though you can travel through time, everything that happens was destined to happen and Evoland 2 successfully tackles the question, "if we could alter time, should we?"
The story of the game was excellent and it was the most memorable game story I have experienced in a long time.
OVERALL:
This is an amazing game for people interested in time travel, sci-fi, and it successfully blends elements of many genres.  10/10 would play Evoland 3.

Stealth is my favourite genre and this is possibly the best stealth game I've ever played. At least, for me, the most enjoyable.
+There is no fat on it, everything in this game is designed to keep the player engaged fully. Cutscenes are also skippable but I recommend you watch them. In fact playing the game a second time (or even a third as I did) will make you understand the layers to the story you missed the first time.

+it has one of the most interesting worlds and settings I've ever come across and a fantastically voiced character.
+Story is very good.
+ The level design is impeccable, I've not seen AAA game studios come even close to making levels like this. This developer is a master of their craft and has created absolutely incredible, large, beautiful, multiple route maps that have not only new ways to play the game each time and explore but to also listen in to conversations guards have that you may have missed.

In summary its a true stealth game, for people who deeply love stealth. Its my favourite genre and I enjoy planning and challanging ways of overcoming things undetected. You can assassinate people and use a variety of items to help you.  If you get caught the combat is intentionally difficult to dissuade you from getting caught, so other reviews complaining about it clearly don't understand the game's premise and its pure stealth routes.
Other than that it has a great story, especially if you played "Of Orcs and Men" it will have added value.
The characters are fantastically written and have great personality which makes them likeable.
The environments are gigantic and have so many routes and hidden passages throughout that they are a marvel to play through.
A great game and definitely one I'd recommend for those that love the sneak.

One simple reason to buy this game: Ship construction and design
If you're into the idea of creating your own spacecraft, this is the game for you. Forget the game, it's a bit empty right now, jump straight into the ship editor. It has it's foibles; placing ceiling tiles is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ for instance, but you have more choice & freedom to place systems in the interior and larger selection of blocks for the hull compared to Starmade.
Interstellar Rift is a little more expensive than Starmade, the other ship builder of note in this genre, and the two games have their own pro's & cons. Both have merit, so if you can afford them, get both and decide for yourself which is the one for you.
There are several emerging issues for ship building games like IR & Starmade however.
The first is placing one block at a time to build structures: The bigger the structure, the more laborious & exhausting it becomes. A drag and fill approach would benefit hugely. Same approach for selecting areas for copying or templating.
The menus show blocks by submenus, so finding the block shape you want is a chore. Far better would be full palette list of available blocks - think of how Too Many Items displays blocks in Minecraft and you get the idea.
Good ship editor, but a bit clunky.
Large selection of blocks to build truly unique ships
Early acces, so expect bugs & general weirdness at times.

NO, THIS IS NOT ANOTHER SPACE ENGINEERS CLONE!
(even using ship exteriors that look like voxels)
At first, I was skeptical. Then, I gave it a try... and I don't regret I did it. The game is still in alpha, but it is awesome and full of potential. For the ones who remember, this game resembles "Battlecruiser Millenium", where you had to manage a ship, fly it, engage in combats, etc. The difference: at that game, everything was too complicated and too full of numbers; here at Interstellar Rift, things are way easier and - best of all - first person.
You build your ship (in an editor, not in real time) and run it. The game lets you build your ship from scratch or edit a pre-existing model, and the building scheme is NOT voxel-based, just look like it. It seems a bit boring at first glance, but when you notice you are building a custom ship which you will be piloting, you become involved in a quest for the excellent ship for your needs.
After that, you gather ingame resources by operating machines (a miner - called extractor - and a refinery to smelt the ores) in your starting space station to build your ship. The amount varies according to the mass (the size) of your ship, with each component included in ship's design adding to the total. In case you are not prepared for this, you can simply purchase an initial ship with your initial U-nits (ingame currency) and begin piloting immediately.
Depending on the size of your ship, the game becomes better played with a crew. Player Community seems to be a bit shy at the moment, since we can't easily find a crew, but as I said, you can fly your ship alone. In fact, it seems the game is still growing and that everyone wants his own ship, so that's why we still need some time to let things settle down.
The game is enjoyable in its current state. The staff is present in forums and due to game updates we can see they are working hard to make a great game, fixing bugs and including content. Despite of the ships "blocky appearence", the graphics are very good (in fact, only ships are blocky, ship interiors are very detailed). The price is great for an early development title. Recommended.

The story is simple but not bad, it progresses through dialogues as there is no actual exploration. But the whole point is developing your party and fighting cleverly designed fights. They require you to use terrain, positioning, traps and other tricks to survive. If by RPG you understand a game where you just click on an opponent - this game is not for you. Actually I would rather recommend this game to a strategy fan not an RPG one.

Evoland 2 makes Evoland 1 look like a technical test.  Evoland 2 is a great game; the best rpg I played in 2015.
GAMEPLAY:
Evoland 2 has a variety-show sort of gameplay.  The "core" combat system in the game is a Secret of Mana-esque combat system where you can summon one of three allies to defeeat enemies or open up new paths in the environment [breaking boulders, clearing vines, freezing water, etc.].
However, the game likes to mix things up from time to time by introducing a new combat system for a boss or gameplay segment.  It helps keep the game fresh throughout the 20 hour playthrough.  You'll have segments of gameplay that use the mechanics of Bomberman, Tekken, Shoot'em'up's, and many more.  Personally, I loved the card game a little more than I should have, given how simple it is.
Combat and quirky game mechanics aren't all this game has.  There is a lot of platforming in this game that mix simple platforming mechanics with the game's core combat system.  It also has some very interesting puzzles.  The puzzles are often Legend of Zelda-style block manipulation and activation of switches from afar.  However, once you unlock the ability to manipulate time, the puzzles can be immensely fun and surprisingly difficult.  Even progressing in the plot can be a "thinking with time travel" style puzzle to figure out what you need to do in what timeline to make progress  in the story.
STORY:
As mentioned above, this game is about time travel.  The game's story should instantly draw comparisons to Chrono Trigger.  However, the game seems to take a very different stance on time travel than Trigger.  If Trigger is about using time travel to fix everything and build a beautiful future, Evoland 2 is surprisingly sober about the topic.  This game is more an exploration of fate, destiny, and inevitability.  Even though you can travel through time, everything that happens was destined to happen and Evoland 2 successfully tackles the question, "if we could alter time, should we?"
The story of the game was excellent and it was the most memorable game story I have experienced in a long time.
OVERALL:
This is an amazing game for people interested in time travel, sci-fi, and it successfully blends elements of many genres.  10/10 would play Evoland 3.

If you enjoyed the first Evoland game, you might be in for a slight dissapointment. But, before you go on and rant on how it's not exact. Read on. The reason for this 'dissapointment' is because Evoland 2 steps away from the linear straight-forward evolution of video game progression. Instead, Evoland 2 gives you all that the first Evoland had, improves, rewrites, and adds to it in a fantastic blend of multiple gameplay, graphics, and also a satisfying story that will keep you on your toes.
There is multiple genres of gameplay, including 2D platforming, Mortal Combat-esque battle, Tactical Turn-based, and also many, many others.
In Evoland 2, you start within the 'present', which is a sprite-based full-body graphical style. Evoland 2 main story-line involves Time-Travel. Going to the past will have graphics revert to more 'ancient' looking apperance, but still retain a modern fludity that will leave you breathless. As you go toward the future, it will transition to an 3D graphical apperance.
With Time-Travel comes the different gameplay methods as mentioned above. Though they will make their apperances as you progress through the story-line.
One of Evoland 2's main features is its companions. These memorable friends of your character each have their unique personality and abilities. Their abilities are neccessary for both story progression and completionist objectives. I personally found my first green-haired girl companion, whom I named 'Sinai' to be my character's best friend. I truly cared for her comments, personal story, and the way she acted.
There are a few segments I did find a bit irritating, sometimes overchallenging. In a few instances I had to tone down the difficulty from classic (Normal) to, uh, this game's version of 'easy'. If only just to get past and continue the story which I eagerly awaited to see it's next part.
The true Final Boss was not totally unexpected, and also seemed to come a little out of nowhere. It was one of the few kinks in the story that lacked some development. I wished they had fleshed out the Final Boss's story a bit more for me to actually care about the character instead of viewing her like somebody I just had to beat to finish the game.
Also, there are references everywhere... I spotted three clearly Dragon Ball Z references. And a whole lot more. But it's not a bad thing, it adds a certain flavor that fits well with Evoland 2, given its prequel.
My personal rating for this game is a solid 9/10. It's fantastic, keeps you interested, is fun to play, but does have a few annoyances and story-related holes. But don't let that deter you, Evoland 2 will keep you wanting to play, and if you love collecting things, you'll expand the 18-20 hour story to an addition 22-26, possibly more.

If I can't have precise control over my character in a stealth game I have no fun. Styx feels like a game I should be able to control, or at least innately understand, but instead I find myself stuck and dying over and over to the stupidest nonsense.
There is a heavy emphasis on verticality and scaling objects if you want to avoid enemies, but the level of vertical control is worse then even most non-stealth puzzle platformers. For example, precisely raising and lowering myself on the edges of platforms without falling while remaining unseen is absurdly difficult to the extent that I keep falling to my death.
Enemy behavior is at times completely different from what I've come to expect from other stealth games. I've completely given up on sneaking up on enemies when they have their back against or near a pillar as they will always see me.
Light level and the amount of sound I'm making are either nearly impossible to guess or the AI has simply been glitching out and seeing me when it shouldn't or ignoring me when it should see me.
All of the above might not have been a problem if the combat were a solid fall-back or if you were at least able to run easily from combat. However, current combat is based on countering enemy attacks. The countering window is presented to you via a zoomed-in view that obscures everything else and therefore makes running away much harder.
Overall, not fun.

I was really happy to find this game on steam because I do feel that with exception of the Thief series there are very few fantasy stealth oriented games, something I think really needs doing more (sure allot of RPG's will have a stealth option but I often find them dull or easy to exploit).
In Styx stealth really is your best option because open combat is deliberately fiddly, with you locked in a slow, clumsy fight with a single enemy requiring precision button presses while likely being cut down by everyone else who heard you. Thankfully stealth in this game works pretty well with plenty of alternate routes that take advantage of the verticality of the setting, allowing for a nice mix of slow methodical sneaking and swift acrobatics, and complemented by a nice array of spells and tools that can make for some great moments where you can slip out of normally hopeless situations.

This contains content that may be considered spoilers.
TL;DR
While not as profound as To the Moon, Finding Paradise provides a valuable experience that not only forwards the plot, but is nearly as enjoyable as the first.  9/10
-------------------
I'll try not to spoil the plot-twists details, but I will review other mechanics and details that could ruin some of the fun.
Before playing this game, it is very essential that you play both of the SigCorp Holiday Minisodes (included with To the Moon), and while playing A Bird Story definitely adds to the story, it's not essential.  In addition to being part of the overarching plot, the minisodes provide both important background on how some things came to be as well as some character introductions.
The game's premise is very similar: a call to a dying patient.  This patient, Colin, has an unconventional wish to
.  Eva and Neil navigate through Colin's memories in a mechanically similar way to To the Moon, but
.  Neil has some secrets that are discovered, and he struggles to keep them under control.
Finding Paradise is significantly less depressing than To the Moon.  The heavy-hitting emotions arrive near the end, where everything is coming together and Colin is in his final moments, but the story isn't as tragic as Johnny's.  I do not see this in any way as a bad thing- it's a different game, different person, and not every life has to be tragic.  The comedy in this game is arguably better, as I found myself laughing pretty hard in some sequences.  With great art and music old, new, and remixed, the atmosphere in this game easily matches that of To the Moon.
Mechanically, this game is very similar to To the Moon.  You can either play in a small window or fullscreen.  The launch menu is identical, just with different music and art.  The controls are nearly the same, with some sequences requiring keyboard control.  In any interaction, always try to exhaust the dialogue; just because they stopped talking does not mean they don't have more to say.  I believe it is better to play with a mouse, because you will be able to find interactable components that you wouldn't find with keyboard controls.
Try not to expect the same thing as To the Moon.  If you play this game expecting to feel emotionally ruined at the end, you may be disappointed.  In fact, this game is much more optomistic.  Johnny died with a life made happy, which was bittersweet because in reality, he was a very tragic man.  Colin, on the other hand was already content, he just wanted to have no regrets.
Another excellent title by Freebird Games.  Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys story drive games.

When I first heard of Anomaly Warzone Earth I knew I'll love it.
I played the GOG version twice and the Steam version 3 times.
I played Mobile Campaign & Korea when the games got on HIB site and once more after I got the Steam keys.
Seeing Anomaly 2 trailer got me all hyped out and decided the game is a must have for me.
Unfortunately the game suffers from the same issue all indie series that took the step from single player to multiplayer/co-op (Torchlight,Orcs Must Die,Trine,Sanctum).
The game looks great, the level design is awesome and the new units are interesting, however, it lacks the feeling of the first game. This is hard to explain since I assume it depends from one gamer to another but if I were to put it as simple as I can I'd say Anomaly 2 doesn't feel as "nice & cozy" as the previous games in the series.
While Anomaly Warzone Earth has small, very indie-like designed(read this as unique and with a personal touch) and somehow symmetric levels that make you think you can play the game over and over again and try new strategies without getting bored (and in my case that's exactly what happened with Anomaly WZE - and the ones mentioned above), Anomaly 2 feels like a non-indie game and looses that "nice & cozy" feeling.
The levels, while beautifully designed, are big and lack symmetry, yet not very repayable in single player mode (but excellent in multilayer or co-op). However, if you're not a MP/Co-Op person, you might consider this a dumb down.
Overall, the game is great and if you're a series fan you should play it but if you can't get over the first games in the series and if you don't intend to play MP/Co-Op, the game will feel big yet short and unsatisfactory.

Interstellar Rift is a little gem that has been sitting in my steam library for quite some time. It's one of those games that you pop back to every now and then just to see how it's coming along. Every so often there's a good update that gets me back into it for a while, which is exactly how I got started with Space Engineers.
At the moment Interstellar Rift appears to be in an awkward phase. Some people want to buy it but haven't because they're waiting to see what happens, and others have it but don't play online because nobody else is playing it online right now (!). There's no denying that it's a good game - the basics are all there, what I think a lot of people are waiting for is a big feature or update to come out that really offers something new and interesting to play with. It doesn't take long to get through the content that's offered already, which itself is worth the low price tag. So like many of you, I too have been VERY skeptical of alpha games here on Steam. Also this style of combat helps large scale PvP battles to run more smoothly and be more entertaining (which is the direction i believe this game is moving towards). So far in the game there are 4 factions (2 unavailable right now) and each faction has a main city and all across the world map are bases for you to take over and dominate. -Graphics: Simply amazing. That's really all i can say.. the graphics are just awesome. I'm running a gtx 770 4gb and im able to do high settings and maintain 75 fps without my gpu getting too hot. this game is still a bit unoptimized, however it is by far the best optimized alpha I have ever seen.
-Audio: Sound is fine, the only thing that irritates me is the sound that wearing heavy armor makes, but other than that I haven't come across any sound bugs or anything like that. The music is awesome so far with I think 6 songs which were composed by some famous composer that I'm too lazy to look up but has also composed music for many other famous games.
Yes my review is long, but I really want more people to play and support this game.. I miss games like these where they are just simple games in medieval times. Gunpoint is a fun little action-puzzle-stealth game, where you're a private eye implicated in a crime you didn't commit while trying to find and bring justice to the one who did it.
Your primary tools?  A pair of gloves that let you climb any surface and even stick to ceilings, some motion-assist augment pants that let you leap vast distances, and a device known as the Crosslink, which lets you remotely on-the-fly rewire the functionality of objects in the game world.  Need to open the door and disable an alarm that will trigger if a camera sees you?  Wire the camera to the door instead of the alarm, then walk into its field of view - the camera spotting you will open the door instead of sounding the alarm.  You can even gain the ability to rewire a guard's firearm to a light fixture, so that when they attempt to shoot you, the gun just clicks and the lights go off.
Discovering various ways to complete your objectives with the tools and mobility you have available is the draw of the game.  Each stage represents a unique series of infiltration challenges, ranging from various sorts of guards to various interactable objects that respond either to your Crosslink or your physical actions.  You need to quickly learn how each behaves and how to use them to your benefit to make your way through the stages, complete your objectives, and escape.
Gunpoint's 2D pixel graphics are simple, but functional, well-animated, and stylish, doing a fine capturing the sort of detective noir ambience of the game.  Its soundtrack is a mix of light techno and smooth jazz, and while the number of tracks is a bit limited, it's seldom unfitting or obtrusive.  The interface is minimalistic, and most interface elements hide themselves when not needed.  This is a game very much focused on its gameplay, and does its level best to stay out of the way of its gameplay as much as possible while still looking fine.
All in all, you could do a lot worse than Gunpoint if you want a game to stretch the critical-thinking and problem-solving parts of your brain on.  While the game's rather unfortunately short, it's got Steam Workshop support, and user-created levels are plentiful - though as always with user-created content, quality varies.

This is the longest VN I've ever read. I'm sure plenty of people can get through it faster than I did, but even so, it's quite time-consuming if you want to go through all routes/endings. I played the For-All-Ages version, because I don't give enough sh*ts to patch a game just to see some ecchi stuff. Besides, after playing this, I think ecchi stuff would seem extremely out of place given the overall wholesomeness of the story.
:
It's a slice-of-life story about a group of high schoolers partaking in what is known as The Soaring Club. The Soaring Club was founded by Isuka and Amane (one of the romance options) in order to pursue the dream of flying through what is known as Morning Glory with a glider. Morning Glory is a rare weather phenomenon in which an extremely large, tunnel-shaped cloud appears horizontally across the horizon (Google this for an image). Long after Isuka's disappearance, other students want to join The Soaring Club, beginning with Aoi (the MC). Kotori (an anti-social, disabled girl Aoi meets at the beginning of the story), Ageha (Aoi's childhood friend), Amane (Soaring Club founder), Asa (the friendly twin), and Yoru (the aloof twin) are the potential romance options.
:
- Translation: Apparently, this VN is well-known for having a terrible translation. It isn't nearly as bad as people make it out to be, but yes, it could definitely use some work. Occasionally, you'll run into some dialogue that doesn't make any sense at all or that'll make sense after you've switched some words around.
- Typos: There was an atrocious amount of typos even when the translation was fine.
- Gender stereotypes & gender roles: At one point, Aoi mentions that he doesn't see his female friends as girls because they act so masculine, but what he's referring to is the fact that they all like technology and science. This is the kind of crap that discourages women from being interested in STEM curriculum/fields. There are also other examples of gender-based nonsense scattered throughout the VN.
- Problematic MC: Besides the gender-based nonsense, the MC is also slightly problematic in other ways. Mainly, I hated how he patronizes all of the female characters in some way or another. One example being that he thinks they're all cute even when they're angry. Compared to other MCs, Aoi isn't so awful that it completely ruins the VN, but it's still worth mentioning that he's got issues.
- Lack of racial diversity: Everyone's pale as f*ck. No dark-skinned people at all. I know the story takes place in Japan, but whatever. There are darker-skinned Japanese people, and plenty of foreigners residing there.
- Too much slice-of-life: This is a slice-of-life/romance genre VN, but that doesn't mean there needs to be a copious amount of filler scenes. I do not care about what they're having for dinner. I do not care about Aoi's duties to the dorm. I do not care about them going out shopping. Too much of that kind of stuff can (and did) make the reader/player bored.
:
- Glider/flying info: This was actually a fairly educational VN. I learned a decent amount about gliders and the Morning Glory. Even if you're not interested in romance that much, this VN might still be worth reading to those who find gliders/planes interesting.
- Character development: Because the VN is so long, there's a great deal of character development. You really get to know each of the characters well, even when you're not pursuing them as a romance option.
- Romances: I really enjoyed the romance aspects, overall. There were plenty of times I had butterflies-in-the-stomach sensations.
- Artwork: The character art, backgrounds, and cutscenes were excellent. No complaints whatsoever about the art.
I recommend this VN for what it is worth. While there are more cons than pros, it's still a really enjoyable VN.

Batman: Arkham City is one of those games that rightly garnered much attention with the end of 2011 Game of the Year lists. Maybe it didn't get as much attention from PC gamers, but it should. If you want to have the definitive Arkham City experience, I'd say PC is the way to go.

With its atmospheric setting, thrilling movement, immensely satisfying combat, and tremendous assortment of secrets to discover, side quests to complete, and other attractions, Arkham City is a fantastic adventure game. It's winter in Gotham City, but the streets of the part of town now known as Arkham seem particularly cold. Snow falls on the criminals who roam this place, making the asphalt shimmer with reflections of the neon signs advertising shuttered shops that once upon a time bustled with business. Gotham faced a prison crisis in the wake of the events of Arkham Asylum, and certain unscrupulous characters took advantage of the situation by acquiring the run-down neighborhood of North Gotham, walling it off from the rest of the city, and tossing the criminals in there to fend for themselves. It's an inhumane and immoral operation; food and warmth are scarce, and some inmates are people whose only crime was voicing a negative opinion of Arkham City and those who run it.
But their misfortune is your gain. The area of several city blocks that makes up the superprison isn't especially vast as open worlds go, but what it lacks in scale, it more than makes up for in atmospheric detail. Arkham City is home to an old courthouse, a former police headquarters, a musty museum, a disused subway terminal, and other fascinating places. These structures, with their faded portraits, old billboards, and plentiful other features, convey a sense of history. The exceptional art design draws on 1930s art deco and makes Gotham seem like a once elegant and shining city that has fallen into darkness. It's clearly a work of imagination, but as you explore it, its richness pulls you in, and it becomes a world you can't help but believe in. That allure is particularly strong on the PC, where atmospheric details like snowflakes visibly landing on Batman's cape make this wintry, downtrodden environment even more convincing.
Batman has no choice but to explore the alleyways and underground tunnels of North Gotham. Within the prison's walls, Joker is dying, and the villain's schemes force the Dark Knight to help him find a cure. That quest brings Batman into contact with the Penguin, Mr. Freeze, and numerous other members of Batman's rogues' gallery. Each character is represented terrifically, with plenty of nods to their histories as established in the comics, and part of the fun of progressing through the story lies in seeing what character might make an appearance next. The excellent Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill reprise their roles as Batman and the Joker, heading up an ensemble of voice actors who never miss a beat. Also returning from Arkham Asylum is that game's accessible and satisfying combat system. At its core, it's quite simple: one button performs your attacks, while another counters enemy attacks. The combat rewards good timing, and when you get into the rhythm of battle, chaining your attacks together and turning your enemies' attacks against them, it's deeply absorbing. It's also as graceful as it is brutal, making it a joy to behold. The varied attack animations make most tussles look as if they might work as choreographed fight sequences in a movie. In response to your inputs, Batman might simultaneously counter two attackers with a single impressive move, or take advantage of a convenient surface and slam a thug's head against it. As you progress, you encounter enemies equipped with things that make taking them down more complicated. Guards with stun batons can be attacked only from behind; enemies with shields require the use of an aerial attack; and foes with body armor can be injured only with a rapid-fire punch attack called the beat down. It's especially satisfying to defeat large, diverse groups of enemies against whom you must use a variety of techniques. Zoomed-in camera angles that give you a close look at moves that finish off a battle add impact to your attacks and make your triumphs all the more rewarding. Keyboard and mouse controls are as responsive as gamepad inputs, so you can choose whichever method you're more comfortable with.
Batman's assortment of gadgets plays a bigger role in combat than it did before. In Arkham Asylum, you could throw batarangs and keep your combo going; here, you can quickly fire off many of your wonderful toys in the heat of battle. A blast from your remote electric charge device can make an enemy involuntarily swing his hammer at surrounding thugs, and a quick placement and detonation of explosive gel can knock nearby foes off their feet. The variety of "quickfire" gadget options and other special moves that Batman has at his disposal can actually be overwhelming, and you may occasionally find yourself pressing the button combination for one gadget when you want to use another. But the game does an excellent job of easing you into the finer points of the combat system, displaying button prompts when you have a good opportunity to use a particular technique. And if you don't quite grasp a move the first time, you can go into your upgrade menu and re-enable its tutorial for a refresher. The addition of quickfire gadgets gives you a number of new options, and skilled players can benefit a great deal from the smart use of these techniques, but you never need to rely on these abilities. If you prefer to keep things simple, you can certainly get by relying primarily on your fists. Of course, thugs with shields, blades, and body armor are one thing; enemies with guns are something else entirely. Batman is tough, but far from invulnerable, and when faced with such firepower, it's time for him to rely on stealth. As in Arkham Asylum, you sometimes find yourself needing to take out rooms of gun-wielding enemies, and all of Batman's techniques from that game are still every bit as fun to use. Sneak up on an enemy from behind and you can take him down silently. By hanging from a gargoyle, you can ensnare an unsuspecting enemy below with an inverted takedown. Your detective vision gives you an edge, letting you see the positions of enemies patrolling the room through walls and floors. And Batman has a few new tricks up his sleeve. When spotted, you can toss a smoke pellet, aiding your escape and possibly leading confused enemies to accidentally attack each other. And you eventually acquire a new gadget that's great fun in these situations: the disruptor, which lets you can remotely disable a thug's gun. It's especially satisfying to do so, then jump down in front of him and watch as he attempts to shoot you, and then knock his lights out. The disruptor's use is limited, so you can't overdo it, but it's a great new addition to Batman's arsenal. The excellent sound design adds tension to these stealthy standoffs, with bad guys becoming increasingly frightened as you pick off their buddies one by one.
But more than anything else, it's your adventures and explorations in the city of Arkham itself that make this game extraordinary. The game's boss fights look dangerous and spectacular, but they're disappointingly easy, and on occasion, context-sensitive actions may thwart your efforts. You might intend to evade an enemy attack, for instance, but instead your button press makes Batman slowly disable some device as bullets are shredding your health. But these criticisms are nitpicks in a game that does so much so well. From the speedy exhilaration of soaring high above the streets to the atmospheric thrill of discovering long-forgotten secrets in the tunnels below Gotham, this is an unforgettable adventure that will keep you coming back to the cape and cowl long after you've seen the credits roll.

Blackguards is a turn-based strategy game with deep RPG elements based on the popular German pen and paper RPG The Dark Eye. You assume the role of your own custom character who is accused of killing the princess in the opening cinematic. Your only choice is to run away, assemble a cast of shady characters such as the suave mage Zurbaran, the feisty dwarf Naurim and the tribal warrior Takate. The storytelling and the characters are solid, but they really don’t stand out in any significant way, for the most part it really feels like a poor man’s BioWare story.
What makes Blackguards truly shine are its great combat system and wonderful game world. The combat system is hex based and may at first remind you of fantasy turn-based strategy games such as Heroes of Might and Magic or King’s Bounty. In reality, it’s more like a combination of Disciples III and Neverwinter Nights, a heavy mixture of classic turn-based strategy and role-playing philosophy. The fantastic thing about the combat system is that every single battlefield is completely unique. Not only are they all different from a visual standpoint, but they are all set up differently as well. Sometimes you’re surrounded, sometimes you have multiple goals, sometimes you have to defend something. You can also use the environment to your advantage. Cut the rope to make the heavy wooden chandelier fall on your foes or burn down the walkway spiderwebs causing deadly poisonous spiders fall to their doom.
Another big thing different from usual turn-based strategy games is that you’re not building an army, you have a party of up to five characters. As you progress through the game, you acquire adventure points which you can use to upgrade your characters in a wide variety of attributes, abilities, spells, talents and weapon talents. It’s a really robust system that allows for truly deep customization and experimentation. The only negative thing is that the game assumes that you’re familiar with The Dark Eye ruleset when in reality you will need some time to really figure it out.
The other problem stemming from the use of The Dark Eye ruleset is that almost any attack can be a hit or miss. Because the game is really tough and the opening battles are rather grueling, it can be really frustrating missing a 95% attack. There are ways to upgrade your characters to offset this, but again, this will take some time to figure out as the game doesn’t really explain much of anything. This can cause some really ugly bouts of frustration and anger, but it’s not a deal breaker.
The vast majority of the gameplay is in the battles. Apart from that, you’ll be using a lovely 2D map to travel from location to location. Towns are represented with a single screen depicting various points of interest such as shops, healers, blacksmiths and quests. The graphics are absolutely beautiful, the wonderful art style is sort of a mixture between fantasy, medieval Spain and 16th century Caribbean which is actually seldom seen in games. The accompanying soundtrack reflects that as well and fits the game very well. However, the animations aren’t that great and the voice work, while mostly solid, can be a bit cringe-worthy at times.
Blackguards is a hardcore game for hardcore gamers and it is completely unapologetic about it. So be prepared for some truly grueling stuff and a steep learning curve. The great thing is, it’s absolutely worth playing thanks to the great combat system, deep RPG elements and a wonderful game world.
8 OUT OF 10 (GREAT)

For Blackguards, the whole is less than the sum of its parts.
I wanted to wait until I beat the game to review it. I felt obligated to do this. If you’re like me you bought in to all the good reviews this game had on Steam. A mature, turn-based rpg, starring anti-heroes? How could it be bad?
Well, for starters, the “Key Features” that Blackguards lauds itself on are deeply flawed. Character choice and combat tactics are undermined by balancing issues - certain abilities and spells are clearly better than others to the point where your characters will be at a severe disadvantage if specced the wrong way and beating some of the harder fights will be near impossible if you don’t have one or two specific spells.
Additionally, the game suffers from sudden spikes in difficulty that leave the game almost unplayable. Battles go from challenging and needing strategy to just plain unfair and needing luck to win out.
Outside of combat, Blackguards doesn’t fair much better. The story is piecemeal and uneven - with the whole second chapter being nothing but a combat-only reenactment of “Gladiator” that only seems to be put in place to fill time. The rest of the main quest is further hampered by a multitude of random side quests that hold no weight in the game world and only serve to distract you from your objective. Narrative elements and choices are frequently brought up only to never be talked about again. And finally, when the story actually manages to come together, it’s a rushed case of too little too late - leaving you with an ending that is worse than Mass Effect 3. Because despite what the game says, you don’t decide the course of the story at key points - nothing you do matters.
Characters are also largely underdeveloped and remain that way. Although, the voice acting, for the most part, is passable aside from one annoying companion. However, the male protagonist is the clear winner between the two gender choices (think the opposite of Mass Effect).
When the game asks, “What happens when the only hope of a threatened world lies not with heroes in shining armor, but in the hands of a band of misfits and criminals?”. It turns out the exact same thing that would happen if it were heroes in shining armor - because for a game starring “criminals”, you spend most of your time helping people and doing the right thing.
Blackguards has so much potential. It’s just like that really cool looking kid that has tattoos and fashionable clothes but when they open their mouth you realize that looking cool doesn’t mean you have substance. And as much as I wanted to like Blackguards, I can only recommend it to someone if it were deeply on sale.

Sigh...I enjoyed the first Evoland as a fun, quirky trip through RPG history without to much substance.  Evoland 2 tries to have a more grandiose story and more varied gameplay, but...it's so frustrating, clunky, and...unfun.  Where do I start...the music is repetitive and painful.  Turn it down early and often.  The graphics are charming and we go through a number of different palattes but overall it feels very thrown together.  The story and script try very hard to be funny, but they're...just not.  Not really.  And the game modes...Evoland 2 tried to throw as many game modes into a blender as possible to appeal to everyone.  If you've seen the trailer, it probably looks cool, right?  The rpg modes, the fighting game modes, the shooter modes...except that no one thought to ask if these SHOULD be thrown together.  These modes are all very clunky and clumsily executed, go on for way too long, and are frankly, tiresome and frustrating.
The game, on the whole, is glitchy and buggy in many small ways, from controls locking up after passing doors, to the poor hit boxes, to the overall inexperience and clumsiness we feel in some of the newer modes, fighting game especially.  In some cases, there is a distinct lack of clever level design, such as the frustrating megaman style jumping sections on disappearing and reappearing blocks when we shift to side view.
This game feels like it was trying to copy Chrono Trigger in story and be a grand ride through game genres in execution, but it fails to do either.  The story falls flat for me and the game modes, while varied, are poorly executed at best, especially the 3d segments.
Give this game a pass.

I wanted to like this game. I really did, I ultimately just can't play it in it's current state. From the footage it looks basic but potentially fun but there are a slew of issues that honestly shouldn't even exist thanks to years of game design to borrow from.
1.) Enemies can shoot you before they are drawn on screen. The length of rooms/halls in the environments can exceed the draw distance of the engine. I had many moments where I was being shot at without knowing where the enemy was until moving forward a little bit and them popping into existense.
2.) Poor contrast for enemy models. The little green mutant monsters blend into the environment half the time on the first level and you have them biting your ankels before you know what happened. This wouldn't be that big of an issue except...
3.) Turn speed! There is no adjustment for turn speed and you can't turn fast enough to deal with the sheer amount of enemies in some of the rooms. You either have to inch forward and then try to lure some towards you (good like, the enemy pathing is also very poor) or you run and gun and hope that you can turn to each enemy before you are killed.
4.) Sometimes you can't shoot. I am not quite sure but it seems like the game gets confused when too many inputs were activated. So when you are trying to navigate and turn and shoot at the same time, it sometimes prevents your character from shooting.
5.) Less a gameplay complaint and more a rendering complaint but there were many times were weird graphical glitches occured, chunks of the level would pop in and out with a weird white or other color chunk taking their place. It was very frustrating.
I hope they will take the time to at least address the controls issues, because then this game would be playable, not necessarily fun, but playable.

Interstellar Rift, with a little more time and content, could be an incredible space sandbox game. It has already shown an interest in developing features that would create a brilliant roleplaying environment where players can struggle, co-operate, and take on the vast galaxy before them. For those of you who are like me, and enjoy roleplay, you must be able to see the potential this game being excellent for roleplay. But, like any good roleplaying game, it requires variety: and right now there is not much of it - but i have a lot of faith in these developers. They have shown that they are determined to implement all of the key features, and they have also taken an interest in what the players have to suggest! I feel that in the future there will be a large amount of content sufficient for creating exciting roleplaying servers.
The one thing that is not lacking in variety are space ships. Not only are there space stations to explore when you first pop into a server, there are space ships! But these spaceships are not made by the game (some of them are), they are made by you the player! The spaceship designer is incredibly detailed and easy to use. A long standing server could have unique ships flying all over the galaxy - each with a different purpose! You decide what your ship's purpose is, and if you get tired of designing ships, go ahead and make a space station: heck, you could even make something like the death star!
Overall this game has great potential, and i cannot wait to see what they bring out next. I just hope that they realize that there is more to a co-op space game then just blowing up ships and stealing from one another.
The universe, or just "'Verse" if you're a Firefly fan, is...i don't know! I have not ever had enough fuel to explore to the edge of the map: and that is only if there is one. All it says in on the Steam page is "A vast open universe".
This universe, untouched by the player, is filled with a few stations (each belonging to different companies with different purposes), and a lot of asteroid fields. In the future they want to include "Stellar phenomena, derelict stations and more". For now though i feel that asteroid fields and stations are sufficient because you can easily populate the world with ships and stations of your own design!
Asteroid fields are not just floating conglomerates of rock: they are where you gather you mine your resources - and the process that the developers have in game is entertaining! To mine you first need a mining unit. These are placeable in the ship editor, or you can find them already on mining stations. From here you scroll through a screen showing all of the asteroids within a certain distance of the mining unit, and the resources they have inside of them. When you find one you like, you click on it, and then press "mine" (or whatever the button is!). You will see it brought inside of a square glass room where it is stripped apart by machines, and placed onto a platform next to you. It's freakin' cool to watch!
The list of current raw resources are as follows:
- Iron
- Copper
- Silicon
- Water/Ice
- Zinc
- Nitrogen
- Carbon
From here you can refine these resources into fuel, different types of metal, weapons/ammunition, and oxygen (the biggie). The process for refinement is also pretty cool to watch!
That about covers it for The 'Verse in my opinion, but if you have any questions, i'm sure someone would be more then happy to answer you!
I've noticed that not too many games get the management of spaceships right - but i feel that Interstellar Rift does, and the road it is taking to further develop the management process, is absolutely fantastic!
There is a long list of items and machinery that you can place inside a ship to make it both luxurious, and "alive". By alive i of course mean that it moves, provides power, doesn't slowly devoid you of oxygen...
You can really make spaceships as big as you want - but will you be able to move them? You really need to think about that. It may be a huge moving space station (essentially), but it will be nothing more then a station if you don't have the power necessary to move it. You need to be smart about how you build your ships. You need to make sure that it has the purpose you want it to have, the rooms/sections required, and also be workeable for your crew.
A basic ship design requires the following: engines, batteries, shields (optional), a life support system, places to access the systems of your ship other then the cockpit, data cores, cargo space, a teleporter and a cockpit. But if you're anything like me, and you want to make a cool environment where people can roleplay, you will optionally include: bathrooms, med-bays, cafeterias/clubs/lounges, indoor forests, libraries, bedrooms, kitchens, work rooms, gun stations, ammunition rooms, observatories ect.
(I've missed a few things here like sensors, beacons, ect.)
Remember though, you will need to think logically about how you design your ship and everything it includes.
Combat right now is pretty simplistic. Once you are able to smash through a ship's/station's shields it's just about hitting it until you deplete it's armor. There are also only two types of weapons. Gun turrets, and mounted turrets (fired from the cockpit).
Right now there is also no player-to-player combat: only ship-to-ship. What i mean by that is you can't board someone's ship and shoot them with a gun. Right now, if someone manages to get into your ship, you cannot stop them from stealing everything you have.
There are fun NPCs to kill though! In some Asteroid fields there are sentinels that will automatically engage your ship until you are out of range of the asteroid field, or if your ship is destroyed.
Though the combat is pretty simplistic (at the moment), it is rather enjoyable. Depending on what section of the ship the bullets are hitting, you may know very well that you are being attacked, or you may just continue to enjoy your relaxation time on the toilets. You'll need to do a bit of running around (if it is just you), or you will have to make sure your engineers are keeping the power levels up, and that your gunners are doing what they need to be doing (saving your♥♥♥♥♥♥).
Interactions with players is pretty decent right now. I stated in my overview that they have shown interest in roleplaying in game, and that is almost exclusively shown through the dialogue options. They have in place a global chat, a ship chat, and a whisper chat. They also have an emoting system in place! The only thing they really need now is a proximity chat!
My review is obviously limited to what i have actually done in game - and i am sure that I've missed out on some components of the game that are more important to other people. Simply understand that there is more to the game then what i have stated in my review!
I greatly enjoy this game, and i cannot wait for the developers to take development further and show us what they can do. I hope that they give the roleplaying aspects love - because this game would be absolutely amazing for it!
It's still lacking in a lot of places, and not all of the components have a purpose yet, but the developers have assured us that they will soon.
Not too good with ratings, but for what i enjoy in the game, i give this an 8/10!

This game, no matter how awesome, is lacking a few features. Nothing deal breaking, but some I've got some tips for SplitPolygon (which I'll refer to as 'SP'):
More Workshop Support:
The game has workshop support already, but you know what I mean; Mods. Modding is something that IR needs, badly. Almost all the other features I'm going to present could be added by the community ourselves. I understand why SP won't release a Modding API, as IR is in Early Access, but KSH, the devs of Space Engineers took the risk, and it payed off MASSIVLY. Mods my from time to time lose compatiblity for the latest version of IR, but just do what SE did, have the mods semi-server-side, have the server owner add the mods to his/her server, and the server will cashe the list of those mods and semi-download them for each player. It would probably work beautifully.
Escape pods and shuttles:
Escape pods; the first version of an escape pod block (or maybe a first tier) could be just the pre-weapon update turret, before it had the gun pods. Implementing a docking system would be needed, and then make these act like small ships. These could also serve as one-person shuttle crafts, and in the editor, it would probably be in two parts: 'tier 1 shuttle craft port', and 'tier 1 escape pod', or something along those lines.
Docking:
As I stated in the previous section, a docking system would be a great addition, as it would help make hangers to coordinate with the rest of your fleet; no more need to stop the entire fleet when one member has to log-off just so he knows where the rest of the fleet is. Just dock up, and your ship is with the rest of the fleet when you log back on. This could also make in-ship combat more plausible, as the best way to get resources is to board the ship, not destroy it. The current way to combat this boarding system is simple, yet impossible to counteract; turn off the teleporter. If docking became a thing, you could attach docking ports, and force the other door open. Docking could also help with trade, as servers with a lot of ships does bad things to TPs, such as failure to teleport, super delayed teleport, and game crashes. Docking could fix this by, instead of unloading and reloading nearby ships, it just semi-locks to ship meshes together, like the SE connector block, and thus making the transition between two ship seemless while still making a forced disconnection possible (as in ripping the two docking ports apart while the doors aren't sealed depressurizing both ships, and sucking out players killing them instantly, making a glitch-EVA impossible. I say that because I know SP wants IR to be interior focused, not exterior).
The smaller option:
What I mean by that is the ability to make smaller ships. Take the A-Wing replica, for example: It's absolutly massive, being nowhere near its actual size. I'm talking ships having the interior be the cockpit, and nothing else. This would also mean hangers. The kind where it depressurizes, the doors open, the ship comes in, the doors close, the hanger repressurizes, and the pilot of the ship get out and goes and gets some coffee out of the Mr. Coffee while more ships are being tracked by Mr. Radar, waiting for landing clearance. The addition of smaller blocks for 'cockpit interior' ships would allow actual fighters, not the 'fighters' that are in reality larger than Homeworld corvettes.
Voice Communications:
Voice Communications, or VOIP, would be an essential feature to implement into IR. It would make fleet operations possible, and player-based trade easier. It could help player-based diplomacy easier, by, for a small-scale example, allowing you to quickly utter a life-prolonging 'wait, don't shoot!' right before a soldier/hitman/disgruntled player pops you in the head with a pulse pistol.
FTL:
A system of 'Faster Than Light', or FTL, travel, would be a vital addition to IR, as, as of now, you can only go 1000 m/s (which is acually quite easy to achieve, just go solar!) However, even at 1000 m/s, it took me over five minutes to get to the Sentinel Security Systems Trade hub from the Hurles Co. Starting Station. A Hyperdrive, Wormhole Drive, or Warp Drive system would cut down a 1263.9Km trip from two hours in an average ship to two seconds. Of course, you would need the XYZ Coordinants to jump, otherwise you would be 'blind jumping'. Wait... That actually sounds like a good idea, not remembering the coords of your base, and having to manule-override the FTL controls to make a blind jump, not knowing where you'll end up. Of course, I used inspiration from Sliders (anyone remember that old♥♥♥♥♥TV show?) for that bit.
In-Ship Combat:
I know this is already planned, but I have a few recommendations/suggestions for some handheld (and some not) weapons and tools, having to 3D print the guns and explosives or buy them from an S3 (S3 would be the best canitate to buy these from) kiosk, and the hacking/robots from a logicorp (as logicorp is the more techy megacorp) kiosk. Explosives and charges would also be needed (for instance to, as I refered to in 'Docking' 'forcing open the other door' to breach 'Access Denied' doors, docking port doors. These weapons would obviously be in the 'Item' inventory bar, as SP probably wouldn't add a second toolbar just for cartriges (although it saves a lot of 'pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ moments). Another suggestion for in-ship combat weapons/tools would be RCCVs (Remote Controlled Combat Vehicles) that wouldn't have any weapons that a player wouldn't, but would instead carry a player weapon/tool (you would need to add a 'robot assembly station' or something similar to assemble 3D printed parts and deploy them). Styx is hardcore stealth at its finest. It will not hold your hand (save for the tutorial) and is brutal on higher difficulties. The game also has some issues with platforming that you need to get a hang of in order to enjoy the game to the fullest. If you overcome them, you'll be rewarded with a game that features excellent level design, rewarding stealth mechanics and a story that's pretty good as well.
While other stealth games lets you choose which path you can take, lethal or non-lethal, Styx is all about not being seen. Most enemies are way bigger than you and ten times as powerful. While you can encounter them in one-on-one combat, you'll need to do some parry timing and even then that's not a sure fire out of the situation. Additional mobs may come in, and soon half the level might be after you. Considering these levels are ENOURMOUS, that's quite a buttload of enemies you don't want after your tail.
As stated earlier the game features masterfully designed levels. There are never only one way to do things, and each level have optional imposed challenges for you to complete. Like get all tokens, beat it in a set time, set off no alarms and don't be seen. If you're up for a machocistic challenge, try getting all of the challenges in one go.
There is something to be said about re-usage of levels though, something that isn't very apparent until you hit around the half way mark. You'll be entering where you exited on a previous mission, play some levels in reverse, with some sections closed off, while others are made available or adjointly jumping from one previous level to another. Styx do suffer from having most of these levels in dark, undergroundic areas, making for some very closed off sections that somewhat plays against the game's otherwise great sense of verticality.
In between levels you're back at your hide-out where skillpoints can be distributed. You cannot change them outside this place, so choose carefully. It also serves as a gallery of what challenges you've completed so far, and a jarring reminder of those you forgot or didn't do.
The game also manages to tell a tale that does a tail flip around half way through, something I definitely didn't see coming. It offers up a fresh story that, however trite and true at times, you want to see finished to the end. I ended up coming from it surprised and looking back and from where the game begins and to the climactic ending that leaves many questions unanswered. I'm guessing we'll be seeing more as to what happens next in the sequel; Styx: Shards of Darkness.
The PC version of Styx: Master of Shadows seems a bit better than the PS4 version, as the platforming seem more forgiving (or has gotten patched better). Also, save and load times are way, waaay better and you can quickload/quicksave much easier than on the console. Neither versions are bug free though, so expect to not make some jumps for some random reason, enemies glitching through walls, AI stuck in dialogue trees and more. For the most part they're not game breaking, albeit amusing at times.
Bottom line is that this is a must-play for stealth fans. It is butt hard, but for the most part rewards players who do their homework, offering a very solid and entertaining story to boot. Now's also a good time to brush up on your sneaky skills, as the next game has now hit the shelves which promises to continue where this game left off.

Is it good? Definitely.
Is it better than "To The Moon"? It depends.
If you're looking for a good shedding of tears, "To The Moon" provides the much necessary chopping of onions type of story to have a good cry. "Finding Paradise" does not share that sentiment.
In "Finding Paradise", you will find more scenes that will make you laugh, with the witty banter between the two player characters, the numerous video game and movie references (Even "The Godfather" makes an appearance), and the insanely fun scenarios and mini-games our heroes find themselves in along the journey.
While it is good fun, it doesn't tell a story with the same impact as "To The Moon" did. The plot is fairly disjointed in places, and pacing got really rushed in the last two hours.
Still, it is a story worth playing, especially for the price. Credits to Kan Gao and the Freebird team for yet another great game, and here's hoping for more from them in the near future.

Anomaly 2 is the sequel to the innovative 2011 Anomaly: Warzone Earth. It’s a reverse tower defense game or tower offense in which you protect the attackers and destroy the towers. The premise of the game is simple – alien machines have invaded and Earth is in ruins. You are the only hope to reach the titular anomaly and destroy them. Regrettably, Anomaly 2 has more story exposition than its predecessor which wouldn’t be a bad thing if it wasn’t very poorly written and voice acted. You have all sorts of terrible cliches including hillbilly marines, an elderly German scientist and a younger female doctor all with equally horrible accents. At least you can skip all the cutscenes.
Anomaly 2 is all about the gameplay and that’s where it shines. The player takes over the role of the Commander unit which is tasked to protect and guide the military unit convoy. You can choose your route on the fly and you can buy, sell and upgrade units at any time. The novelty in Anomaly 2 that provides a pretty big twist is that you can morph any of your units to suit the challenges of the current battlefield. For example, the armored vehicle with a long range gatling gun morphs into a robot with devastating short range flamethrowers. The morph mechanic does a great job at keeping you on your toes as different situations require different tactics.
Your convoy can only consist of up to six vehicles and you only have five unit types (ten if you count the morph ability). The enemy towers are more varied than that. Apart from the low level towers, there are also big boss towers which deal great amounts of damage, predator towers which only appear as you’re already passing through, hacker towers that form a disruption field in which your units will attack your Commander unit and so on. As the Commander, you have four different abilities – repair units, launch a decoy, target a selected enemy and disable enemy tower. All of these enemy towers and the morph and Commander abilities come together to create a a very dynamic and at times extremely intense experience.
The campaign goes on for 14 missions across a slightly disappointing variety of environments. The first half of the game takes you across a frozen United States mid-west and New York City whereas the other half you’ll be fighting through the jungles of South America and Rio de Janeiro. Even though each mission is different enough, it all kind of boils down to snow levels and jungle levels. It also feels too short, the game only starts to really get going and then pretty soon after that it’s over.
The graphics are great, both the friendly and enemy unit designs looks really good, the weather effects and the explosions look awesome. The soundtrack doesn’t really stand out, but the sound effects really heighten the intensity of the carnage even further.
Anomaly 2 successfully manages to carve out its own place in a rather saturated genre thanks to its new ideas and interesting tactical gameplay mechanics.

I first heard of this game way back in 2011 and was pretty excited for it, despite it being an indie game. (I pretty much never get excited for Indie games)
Anomaly follows up the story of Anomaly Warzone Earth. Earth's been invaded by aliens, you're going to lead a bunch of vehicles to blow up towers. If one has ever played custom maps of Tower Defence in Warcraft 3 or what me not, you'll find it pretty similar.
Except this time, you're on the attacking side.
Units can morph about, giving more depth in the strategy used to blow up the towers. For example, a unit has 2 attack modes now and can be given the ability to switch between either mode at any time. Each mode has their own respective advantages and disadvantages and can be combined with the original Anomaly strategy of unit swapping, and throwing in special abilities such as smoke, repair or decoy.
The soundtrack is in my opinion, way better than the original. But then again, Anomaly had a great soundtrack to begin with.
For its low indie game price, I'd recommend that strategy / tower defence lovers go for the game. It's fun, addictive and equally hair pulling at the same time in various situations.
IF you haven't had enough of Anomaly, there's always Anomaly Korea, the original Warzone Earth and even the mobile campaign on Steam to purchase!

Blackguards
Blackguards eschews the traditional “you are the hero!” trappings of most games and instead places you into the shoes of escaped convicts. Granted you are still on a quest to save your world, but you do go about it in a slightly different manner. Does the game differentiate itself enough from similar competitors, or should it have remained in solitary confinement? Suppose you’ll have to read on to find out eh?
Let’s be honest, if you have enough interest in the game to have happened upon this review then you’ve probably seen a couple of videos. From there we can assume you know what kind of art style is at play here. It’s dark, it’s got a lot of browns and grays, and it’s a high-fantasy setting. Dwarves, mages, swords and archers are all present. This is all to be expected, so we won’t cover the art beyond that. It’s pretty generic but it does the job. So we’ll go ahead and move on to cover something you’re more interested in instead.
The gameplay! This is what you were looking for, right? It’s alright. You don’t have to be ashamed that you skipped directly to this section. I won’t hold it against you. I’ll still tell you all about the game and help you decide if it’s worth the price or not. Let’s begin shall we? Blackguards is an isometric turn-based strategy game with all the expected trappings that come along with it. You begin by creating a character via a fairly detailed skill/attribute tree using a preset number of character points. You may begin as either a warrior or a mage, with the mage class costing you extra points to unlock. Points may be spent on spells, skills, attributes and upgrades for all of those. Further character points are earned by completing quests and missions throughout the game.
As you play, you collect various companions who can be fully customized in the same fashion, giving a great deal of customization options and variations to be had. Each character, including your own, is fully voice acted and animated. Though it is hit or miss, none of it is particularly bad. It certainly doesn’t detract anything from the game even if it doesn’t always add to it either. The gameplay itself boils down to what you might expect; characters act in turns based on their initiative values, which are affected by what armor you have equipped. Heavier armor lowers initiative, light armor lowers it less. It’s fairly straightforward. Combat is equally typical of the genre. During a turn you may move and attack, or move a little further and not attack. It has a bit of depth, but not so much that it needs any more detail listed here.

Where Blackguards separates itself from the pack is with its tone. You aren’t a band of heroes out to save the world. You are a band of outlaws, cutthroats and brigands who just happen to be on the path that might end with the world being saved. As a result a lot of your quests have to do with helping a party member engage in some…bedroom fun times, we’ll call it, with a local baroness. Also robbery, murder, chaos and overall mayhem. It’s a nice change of pace from the usual save this person or that thing and be all heroic that usually come in games like this.
Overall, Blackguards is a fun game. It has some downsides, being low-budget, but nothing that detracts in any meaningful way from the quality of the game. It’s worth the price of admission if you’re looking for a turn-based rpg to sink some time into. Give it a shot if it looks interesting and you like the genre. I don’t think you’ll regret it too much.

This game is basically tug-of-war mixed with a 2d fighting game. There are 1-hit kills, and whoever killed most recently controls which direction the screen moves. When one player makes it all the way to the end of the screen, they win. As they progress, the opponent respawns in front of them. The tide of battle changes constantly, but with identical characters and symmetrical levels, it is purely fair. There are only two buttons, but they allow a multitude of moves. With two buttons, you can attack at 3 heights, roll, throw a projectile, and do a divekick, with very simple inputs to do all of these. The game is accessible to players of all skill levels, and after only a handful of rounds, almost anyone can compete. Rounds last only a couple minutes, which lends the game a high energy level. Great fun at parties, and has a long lifespan.
If you see this with a huge discount it might be worth the buy as it is quite fun to play with friends, but as it is there is not enough content to justify the price.

Gunpoint is an 8-bit puzzle game, with you taking the role of a wise-cracking freelance spy Richard Conway, complete with trench coat, gadgets, and wide-brimmed hat. Indeed, Conway’s attire is indicative of the atmosphere the game provides- a dark, humorous noir setting paints the environment you play through. In Gunpoint, you break into high-security facilities for one reason or another, but your methods are always the same: You use the Crosslink, a special device that allows you to re-wire circuits remotely. Using this simple mechanic, you navigate past guards (and maybe give them a bop in the head… or many) and alarm systems, re-wiring elevators, switches, lights, and anything else with an electric current.
The gameplay in Gunpoint is simple, but that doesn’t make it unfun. The game is a puzzle, but the open-ended feel of the Crosslink makes the simplicity of it satisfying and enjoyable to use, despite being at its core a mechanic that would normally grow quite old. The addition of some various gadgets integral to any good spy’s kit, including spring shoes, boobytraps and yes, a gun- allows for additional complexity to levels.
The story in Gunpoint has a few turns, but follows a formula popularized by the noir genre. It’s not especially creative or thought-provoking, but it moves the game along well. The story plays itself out with Conway taking on contracts from various clients, with the player deciding exactly how pleasant Conway is when he takes these jobs on via text message. The player’s choices here for the most part doesn’t impact gameplay sadly, but it’s still good for a quick chuckle.
The characters of Gunpoint are, despite being very minor for the most part, enjoyable to listen to. Fritz Gessler and Conway stand out as both the most “important” and also the most amusing, with Gessler’s sailor mouth and Conway’s potential smarminess providing life to the characters.
Gunpoint doesn’t offer terribly much in the way of replay-ability. Story-driven puzzle games do tend to have that problem, but the compact design of Gunpoint extends to it’s story- it’s relatively short, and enjoyable enough that playing it through a second time is still fun and short enough it doesn’t get tedious.
As mentioned, Gunpoint styles itself after the noir genre, and that shows in its visuals. The pixelated style of the game is neither a plus nor a negative- it doesn’t lend terribly much, but it doesn’t detract from the gameplay either.
The level design can simply be described as “appropriately compact”. They are small, but breathable and allow the player to interact with them from most angles. The inside areas don’t feel cramped, and don’t emphasize a singular “coming together” moment; instead, the levels are designed to give the players freedom while they work towards that solution. When puzzles leave you standing at a door and indicate exactly what the puzzle is but don’t show how to solve it, the player can easily become frustrated. Gunpoint’s levels, however, are designed to allow you to piece things together, resulting in a greater “depth” to these small levels.
The 2D platforming aspect works perfectly with the Crosslink ability, and the levels are built to allow the player to make full use of all their abilities.
Again, the noir theme shines in Gunpoint’s sound design. Despite being relatively simplistic, the music of Gunpoint is pleasant to listen to and fits the game perfectly.
Overall, Gunpoint is a fun puzzle game inside a 2D platformer, wrapped up in a noir setting. It’s enjoyable and crammed with content in its short playtime. My biggest critique would be that it almost feels too short- just when the puzzles start getting truly complex it’s already over. However, what we do get is a lot of fun. I highly recommend picking Gunpoint up!

Konosora is a moderately long, lighthearted VN about friendship and flying (hence the title). As an engineer with great fascination towards aeronautics and commercial aircraft, I gravitate to this VN very much in the way that I, myself, wish to fly a glider. So I'm biased regarding that aspect.
The story is interesting overall, though mostly paced excrutiatingly slow. The common route is filled heavily with plot conveniences and character interactions with little to no relevance to the plot, but they can be fun nonetheless. The flying sequences are, however, amazing, however biased I may be. That's mostly thanks to the nice, subtle music as well as amazing art that got my mouth agape several times. I can't stress that enough, from character sprites to all the CGs and the clouds in particular, they're outstanding. In short, the VN is easy on both the eyes and the ears.
> KOTORI's route is obligatory, it has the most cohesive story and is the most consistently paced of all routes (next to Yoru's). Kotori is arguably the most dynamic and (personally) interesting character in the VN. I enjoyed her route a great deal and it wrapped up quite nicely towards the end.
> AMANE's route is arguably the most canon to the plot, and is just as good--if not better--than Kotori's, in the way that it has more stakes involved and is most plot-oriented, though it's still pretty slow.
> AGEHA's route I found to be the least interesting, and is incohesive to a fault (possibly due to the translations). It takes really long to pick up. In the end, Ageha didn't evolve by much and her motives are still quite vague to me.
> ASA's and YORU's routes are surprisingly entertaining. They turn out to be quite interesting characters and Yoru's route especially, feels consistently paced albeit just as slow as Asa's. Asa's route was pretty anticlimactic and Yoru's route was nonstatisfactory, but they're still fun in the way that these routes are probably the least serious of all the others.
To wrap it up; I like flying, so I got easily immersed by the game. Kotori's route has best characterisation, Amane's route has best plot (no pun intended). My waifu is Amane. Music is nice, art is amazing. The VN generally moves slow but has a couple of nice climaxes (no pun intended 2).
