Styx is hardcore stealth at its finest. It will not hold your hand (save for the tutorial) and is brutal on higher difficulties. The game also has some issues with platforming that you need to get a hang of in order to enjoy the game to the fullest. If you overcome them, you'll be rewarded with a game that features excellent level design, rewarding stealth mechanics and a story that's pretty good as well.
While other stealth games lets you choose which path you can take, lethal or non-lethal, Styx is all about not being seen. Most enemies are way bigger than you and ten times as powerful. While you can encounter them in one-on-one combat, you'll need to do some parry timing and even then that's not a sure fire out of the situation. Additional mobs may come in, and soon half the level might be after you. Considering these levels are ENOURMOUS, that's quite a buttload of enemies you don't want after your tail.
As stated earlier the game features masterfully designed levels. There are never only one way to do things, and each level have optional imposed challenges for you to complete. Like get all tokens, beat it in a set time, set off no alarms and don't be seen. If you're up for a machocistic challenge, try getting all of the challenges in one go.
There is something to be said about re-usage of levels though, something that isn't very apparent until you hit around the half way mark. You'll be entering where you exited on a previous mission, play some levels in reverse, with some sections closed off, while others are made available or adjointly jumping from one previous level to another. Styx do suffer from having most of these levels in dark, undergroundic areas, making for some very closed off sections that somewhat plays against the game's otherwise great sense of verticality.
In between levels you're back at your hide-out where skillpoints can be distributed. You cannot change them outside this place, so choose carefully. It also serves as a gallery of what challenges you've completed so far, and a jarring reminder of those you forgot or didn't do.
The game also manages to tell a tale that does a tail flip around half way through, something I definitely didn't see coming. It offers up a fresh story that, however trite and true at times, you want to see finished to the end. I ended up coming from it surprised and looking back and from where the game begins and to the climactic ending that leaves many questions unanswered. I'm guessing we'll be seeing more as to what happens next in the sequel; Styx: Shards of Darkness.
The PC version of Styx: Master of Shadows seems a bit better than the PS4 version, as the platforming seem more forgiving (or has gotten patched better). Also, save and load times are way, waaay better and you can quickload/quicksave much easier than on the console. Neither versions are bug free though, so expect to not make some jumps for some random reason, enemies glitching through walls, AI stuck in dialogue trees and more. For the most part they're not game breaking, albeit amusing at times.
Bottom line is that this is a must-play for stealth fans. It is butt hard, but for the most part rewards players who do their homework, offering a very solid and entertaining story to boot. Now's also a good time to brush up on your sneaky skills, as the next game has now hit the shelves which promises to continue where this game left off.

I remember back in my younger years when video games were harder. Or maybe it's just because I've gotten better at them that I remember them being way more difficult than todays games. Either way, Styx: Master of Shadows is a hard game. Now I could say quite a few bad things about this game. The graphics in-game are somewhat poor (in cutscenes they're great). The models of moving things in the game are constantly clipping inside themselves. The lack of variety in voice acting is extremely noticeable. They certainly make the game less immersive.
But in terms of gameplay, Styx is an incredible game. It's a stealth game that is VERY heavily focused on you not being seen; if two or more guards catch you sneaking about, you're screwed. But the controls are so smooth and work so well with the environment that, with some clever thinking, you might never be seen by anyone. The levels are extremely well-designed as well. They have a great amount of verticality to them, and there are hundreds of routes you can take through any level. There are collectibles you can find around the map that give you bonuses, as well as secondary objectives that can be completed on the way.
Styx also has a fairly customizable skill tree, where you can put points into being sneaky, becoming a killing machine, or having invisible clones. One thing I don't like about the game is how it gives you lots of options for how you can kill people, which are all great fun to pull off, and yet the game gives you extra rewards for not killing anyone in the level.
Overall, Styx is definitely worth buying, especially if you catch it on sale. The customizability of Styx himself and the varied level designs mean you'll be able to spend a great deal of time on this game and not get bored.

After delving deeper into the Multiplayer part, I have to say, it is really good. As you can imagine, Multiplayer pits 2 opponents against each other. One controls the Convoy (attacker) and one controls the Towers (Defender). The Convoy and its abilities mostly stay the same as singleplayer, but it's the Towers where it gets interesting. To balance out the odds, the developers added a few "twists" for the Towers.
The objective of the attacker is to destroy the defender's core structure - the Generator. Games are based on point-system. Whoever reaches the designated amount of point first is the winner, or you can win by leading the oponent by X amount of points. The attacker gains points for destroying towers and some will provide more points than the others. The defender gains points for damaging the attacker's convoy.
The Tower player will be provided with 7 available towers from the Singleplayer with the addition of the Harvesters. The Harvester is only available in Multiplayer and it harvests Abilities, Points and Carusaurum. You can have multiple Harvesters, but only one can harvest at a time.
Towers' Abilities: Regen, Berserk, Taunt and Kamikaze. Additionally, similar to the Convoy's ability to morph their units, the Towers can emit Energy Waves when you double-click on them. Each tower comes with a unique type of Energy Wave that can turn the tides of the battle.
Multiplayer also introduces Tech Upgrades. With each upgrade, the effect of the later one will get stronger, so planning is vital along with play styles. Amount of upgrades varies depending on the map's size.
So, what do you get out of the Multiplayer section of Anomaly 2? A whole lot, I have to say, that is if you have someone to play with. The flow of the battle always changes, there's no clear winner as the points can rack up rapidly if done right. The Tech Upgrades give both players a wide array of play styles, from Endurance, Ambush to Full-on War. All of which will create very exciting battles against friends, or foes.
Keep in mind though, there are no hot keys for the Towers, so clicking a lot is expected.

I reserve words for certain games. Words which define the game itself and help encapsulate what I'm trying to get across. This game merits one such word, and that word is :
"Chewy"
Here's the deal. Blackguards is a strategy game which has been dipped, liberally, in the world of The Dark Eye, think Dungeons and Dragons germanic cousin and you'll be in the right area. It's got a wonderful, thick, rich backstory, with a lot of history, gods, cults, personalities, politics and intrigue. This is a world that over the course of several games (Check out Drakensang when you get the chance if you find yourself a fan of Blackguards, it's worth the time invested) has become every bit as nuanced and subtle as the more accessible DnD counterpart. The operative word though is accessible.
The Dark Eye is to Pen and Paper roleplay what Dark Souls is to videogames. A stern, rock faced, cold hearted, unyielding dominatrix who seems impenetrable and who demands your complete and total servitude, and at the slightest folly will beat you bloody and raw and tell you to start over again. You will, multiple times, due to a flaw in your build that down the line results in your character ending up stunted and a fight proving a little beyond your reach or poor choices when you level your character.
But each time, you will learn, through the beatings and the whippings, much like Dark Souls, you will learn, and you will improve. Eventually once you get past the gatekeeper and once you've survived the rite of passage that is the near vertical learning curve of the games mechanics, you'll find a world that richly rewards, and deserves every minute you spend within it.
The graphics finally have shaken off a lot of the shoddiness and rough edges that have pervaded a lot of the TDE games, Blackguards is slick, smooth, and carries a glossy sheen with it, it's not QUITE melt your eyes gorgeous, but it's certainly pleasing to look at, and the spell effects certainly carry with them a definite sense of satisfaction as they connect and fly about the battlefield. So too has the voice acting and musical score improved, as presentation goes, Blackguards has matured TDE into a strong, and at last truly sellable product.
But it's not for novices. Noooooooo sir. This is not a new player friendly game. So far to date no actual "Roleplaying game" set in the TDE universe has managed to be even -remotely- new player friendly, this is not about to buck that trend, not when your character sheet runs to five seperate tabbed pages with more numbers to make sense of than the US Federal Budget. Not when the wheel that surrounds your character can offer dozens of possible options as to what action you might wish to take during a turn. Not when a conversation option can turn a story down a route that results in a fight you may not have been prepared for. This game does not go lenient on people who are not careful, not methodical, or not thoughtful.
The main story arc I'm going to leave spoiler free and focus on the mechanical side, the game follows a two-beat system, the world map, being a parchment map overworld that you zip around and visit static settlements to partake in various pleasantly rendered towns and villages, which offer side quests, conversation dialogs, healing and merchants. Then there's the meat of the game, a mix of single encounter and multi-encounter dungeons.
These take place on hex based maps which are closer to things like Kings Bounty : The Legend, however in this case, we're dealing with -single units-, and in this case the strategic rendering is done with TDE levels of detail. Characters are solid, so you can't shoot or cast spells through them, ditto for static objects and moveable objects. This means positioning becomes a factor, you can't just layer your melee in front of your casters, you need to play smart and ensure people are in the right place. Equipment too has significant impacts overall on the fight, with bows having minimum and maximum ranges before major penalties are applied. Spells have granular levels of "to hit" based on the casters skill... you get the idea. We're talking pen and paper levels of detail, rendered lovingly in the game.
Once you set up hotbars for your most frequently used abilities, fights run pretty smooth and fast, and the strategy element is as the word I used to begin with implies - "Chewy" - you'll be constantly thinking and rethinking your moves, and the AI puts up a respectable fight even at default difficulty. Environmental hazards too present a real and significant problem, and throw in an extra layer, thankfully there's no time constraint, so feel free to get a coffee as you ponder each move.
Do I recommend it? Yes. With the caveat. This is not a game that will appeal to everyone. It's a niche game. I celebrate it's existence. It's a strategy game for strategy gamers. If hexes, math, and stats excite you, get stuck in.

A beautifully cohesive, dubstep-driven bullet hell that often feels more like a futuristic rave than the arcadey shoot-em-up it is.
Positives:
-Amazing soundtrack
-Clever level design
-Addictively difficult and satisfying gameplay
-Meaningful replayability
Negatives:
-No hardcore mode
-Limited sound and video settings
-No color blind-assist
-A few glitches within the BETA build
Dubstep driven bullet hell. My ears are still ringing. Originally for Android, iOS, and Windows Phone and now available on PC, Beat da Beat is Russian developer Nekki’s aptly deemed “bullet hell rhythm game.” Highly addictive, tough as nails, and rife with hard-hitting tunes, clever enemies, and mesmerizing visuals, it doesn’t take long for this scrolling shoot-em-up to wholly entrance you. Just don’t hit mute.
You start off flying the Helix M-2, a “standard civil ship” armed with a meat-and-potatoes, rapid-fire cannon and a bullet-time special, and quickly delve into the process of acquiring new ships. Gold collected during Story mode can be used to upgrade your ship’s health, weapons, and bomb capacity or to purchase new ships. Each of the ten unlockable ships feature unique weapons and specials, inviting players to try on a multitude of playstyles. For example, Ghost Needle, my preferred ship, features a force field for dire situations and fires homing lasers that allow you focus less on aim and more on evasion.
Gameplay is fast and fluid and features four difficulty modes - Casual, Normal, Hard, and Badass. Heightened difficulties increase the number of enemies, projectiles, and the density of bullet patterns as well as the value of gold coins. As ships, upgrades, and cash carry across difficulty settings, the upgrade and unlock process, which sometimes feels essential to progress, can be expedited if you’re up for a challenge.
Gameplay shines in Badass mode where you take on the full spectrum of tightly-knit bullet sprays; and trust me, few things feel better than weaving your way through a screen ablaze with bombs, bullets, and lasers. Casual and Normal serve as decent entry level modes but can feel quite boring after playing on Hard or Badass and drudging when you realize you need to complete every difficulty setting in order to unlock the final five ships. While Badass mode seemed sufficiently challenging to me, I did feel like the game was missing a fifth, hardcore, one-hit-death difficulty. An even denser ultimate bullet hell may not have worked well on the game's previous mobile platforms but could have been a feasible addition to the PC version, given the precision capable with a mouse.
Every level features a memorable track and unique enemy encounters. Even after just a few runs, I began to associate bullet patterns with their corresponding musical segments: Enemies might stack up during the build to a chorus, peppering the field in step with sub bass pulse, until suddenly, “BAM,” the song drops into a headbanging half-time chorus as all the lights on-screen seem to supernova. It’s amazing to watch and even better to play. I particularly adored Level 3 which features line-stepping ships and a wild laser show kicking in to the heavy drop chorus of JBroadway’s “Lucid Dream.” It’s jaw-dropping.
Bosses feature their own “evil” musical themes and clever attack patterns. Boss “Evil Twins Boom and Bam,” for example, splits into two ships to launch criss-cross bullet patterns simultaneously from above and below but then unites directly in front of players to launch a devastating barrage. Boss attack patterns take some time to memorize but are especially fun to overcome without relying on specials or bombs. The BETA build submitted for review did have an annoying albeit occasional glitch during boss levels wherein my ship would cease fire and the boss would return to full health from the brink of death. Hopefully developers resolve the issue for the launch version.
The brilliantly executed interplay between music, content, and visuals is what truly makes Beat da Beat stand out among other bullet hells. While the concept of rhythm-based bullet hell has been visited before in games like Beat Chaser and Bullet Audyssey, I don’t think it’s ever been done so well. The dubstep cohesively sells the futuristic, star-fighter setting and space-punk ship designs just as the rave-worthy bullet hells beautifully embody the dubstep. Furthermore, small details like the loading screen that reads “use headphones for maximum awesome” and the purposefully broken volume adjustment in game settings - the cosmetic volume slider actually looks like someone shot it with a ray gun - speak volumes about the developer’s admiration for its composers, and rightly so. The game couldn’t have done it without its soundtrack.
Despite its mobile ancestry, the port holds up relatively well, outside of a few missing, user-friendly options and, in fact, plays much better on PC, thanks to the mouse and larger display. Gameplay runs smoothly and feels responsive with even the busiest screens maintaining a steady, high frame-rate. Laser effects, bullets, and dense patterns aren’t demanding but are consistently pretty and, more importantly, always distinguishable from backgrounds. While the game sounds great with and without headphones, presets for Dolby Digital 5.1, headphones, or built-in speakers would’ve been much appreciated, as the soundtrack is absolutely worth listening to in an optimal setting. Disappointingly, there currently aren’t any video options to make gameplay suitable to colorblind users or those susceptible to seizures. Options to limit screen flashes or dial back vivid colors as well as various colorblind assists would help the game become much more inclusive.
There isn’t much left to say about Beat da Beat other than “it’s fantastic.” It’s artful, clever, worth dozens of hours of play, and thus far one of my favorite games of 2016. Even if you aren’t a fan of bullet hells or dubstep, you’ll still find something to love.

Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game, even if it does use the Steam additions for games effectively. I got this game for free from voting on Greenlight, but it was 5 months wasted of waiting to see how this turned out. To be honest, I would preferably give this a "decent" option if the Steam Reviews had those, because it wasn't as awful as others I've played, like

The visuals were nice at first, but they got more boring and had the same old cartoony look most platformers I've seen have. Nothing too eye popping for me, but it isn't eye meltingly horrible as other games. Not much to say on the visuals other than it seems to have the same old, cartoony, bland look to it.
The gameplay was actually enjoyable at first, but it really doesn't bring much to the table here. It was solid, the puzzles actually require thinking, and the level maker was pretty fun to use. However, the earlier levels have some kind of huge difficulty spike in them. Yes, I just said they actually require thinking, but it's better if they actualy make them a bit more simple at first, and then have the difficulty go up and up. The difficulty spikes were not fit for a game like this to me, unfortunately. Also, I can't stand hitting Enter every single time I want to restart a level. Why not just use the LMB? It makes life a lot easier, because using Enter just seems like a weird way to do things. In it's defense though,
Not much to say, other than the annoying abuse of Enter and the fact nothing was really added to RRR.
The story, well, there isn't really much of one. You save robots for a vague reason. It's straightforward for the most part, but maybe they could've explained the robots' story some more? Pretty vague, but at least it isn't nonexistent.
The audio is probably the best thing to the game, shockingly. I began playing my games with headphones recently to add on to my experiences, and I realized RRR has a pretty impressive main menu song, and the songs that play in the levels sound great, too. I highly praise this game's music. The sound effects also sound nice, but at times, they sound way too loud.
The replayability is hard to determine at the moment (look at my hours) but it does have a level editor, and you can also get levels made by the community in the game's workshop, so that's a good (and rare) thing in a game like this. The high scores seem meaningless, but I was never much for high scores anyway.
A major pro to this game is that it implements the Steam additions effectively. It's one of the main reasons this game gets the "meh" and not the "bad" score. Also, the dev seems to be very generous because they're doing it with other games, too. They're also dedicated to the game, even when it isn't in Early Access. Kudos to them for being dedicated.
In the end, RRR does NOT suck, even with it's plenty of flaws. However, it falls short of being a good, fun, cute game and has too many flaws, and rely heavily on some pretty major things I've only seen few games do. In the end, you could get the game, but you won't have as much of an experience as other puzzle games out there.

The game looks cheerful, with vibrant, colorful graphics. It makes good use of Steam features such as  Steam Cloud, achievements, leaderboards and Trading Cards. It supports Big Picture and has full controller support. I use a XBox 360 controller, works like a charm. It also has an ingame level editor, were you can create and share your own levels. I got the game for free but I don't have any problems recommending it for the price. It's quite cheap for what you're getting imo.

This game gives you a lot of freedom to do what you want, such as, turn lights off, break glasses, knocking police officers, shoot police officers, and so on. This game is set in a future where guns are banned and you get to have futuristic technology. You are equiped with a bullfrog hypertrousers that allow you to jump at great heights and distances, gloves and boots that allow him to scale buildings and hang from ceilings, a trenchcoat that protects him from long falls and he's also an excellent hacker. Early in the game he also gains the ability to crosslink, which allows you to rewire the electronics of buildings in a city. He's very overpowered.
The missions in this game usually involve a client who requests you to infiltrating a building and steal something or hack a computer for information. You will soon find out that the story is full of plot twists but I won't spoil any of that. The game starts off linear but you will have to make some choices that will have an impact later on. The author also seems to have had some fun with the answers you can give.
Although you have all those powers you are instantly killed with one shot and even though you can knock police officers or crash window glass you will lose points if you do so. The freedom you have should be used so that you are never found out. Odly enough you are can get caught on camera and open doors without anyone noticing but these little unrealistic things don't really spoil the fun. You will have to rely on the crosslink hacking ability to never get caugth. In this regard the game works like a puzzle. In many levels you have to be creative. Of course you can always just knock everyone out cold and not bother with the point system.
The only major flaw I found in this game is that the menu graphics are not very polished. The best way I'd put it is that it looks like a window from an retro operating system. It's easy to use but doesn't look very good. Worse than that is that the font used for the missions is hard to read. Perhaps it would have been a much better choice to do something like a visual novel. Thankfully, unlike the menu, the game itself as decent graphics.
If you like stealth games that give you a lot of freedom this is a game for you.

Interstellar Rift has some amazing potential.
It's art style and concept alone were enough to make me want to play it. Seriously, it's damn beautiful. Aside from it's visual appeal, the gameplay and mechanics are very solid too.They are complex enough to feel challenging and like I am actually building a spaceship, but not so overy complex that it's a pain to build anything.

There are many things that still need to be added, like light speed and warp speed, because trying to cross a galaxy takes a little while at sub light speed. As I have said before, the building looks and feels amazing, the best I've seen in any space game. one of those small games that way more people should know about
gameplay?
the mechanics work perfectly. nothing feels out of place or tacked on; everything has it's place. few (if any) other games have people reacting to having a gun pointed at them the way they do here - not shooting unless you're too far away and slowly backing away if you get closer, but then shooting if you get too close. the jumping is fun, the various upgrades make different approaches to the same level incredible, and the level customization (plus the workshop) gives the game a ton of replayability.
graphics?
i'm generally a sucker for pixel art so it's no surprise that this game hits all the right buttons for me, but the artstyle here in particular just feels right. i blame it on the cyberpunk-y setting.
story?
charming, to say the least. the story has it's neat little twists, isn't entirely boring and certainly has it's fair share of humor - the ending in particular, but let's not spoil anything here. the dialogue options are clever, and i loved the tongue-in-cheek humor ("real data").
all-around it's a great game with a lot of replayability for a low price. no reason not to get it, especially if it's in a sale aswell.

Batman: Arkham City is a game where you play as Batman, taking down enemies and flying through arkham city, swiftly destroying packs of random thugs, completing side quests. Let's start off with what people always talk about,
The Combat and Flying/Gliding as Batman.
The combat is rhythmic and combo based. It's fun, flashy and addictive. I wouldn't really say that it makes you feel like batman, because as videogamedunkey pointed out in his review: "I don't really remember Batman being a f**king ballerina". I don't either, although that doesn't stop it from being an enjoyable experience.
The flying is infinitely more fluid once you complete the AR missions and unclock a certain ability that I've decided not to....spoil.... I guess. Trust me, it's awesome.
The story is something to be desired, however it's solid enough, as this isn't really what the game is supposed to be focused on. In conclusion, if you're looking for a game based on a superhero, I'd have to say you can't really go wrong here. If you're looking for and action/adventure game, you can't really go wrong here. It's a good game that you should definetly try at one point in your gaming life.

I didn't really like Batman: Arkham Asylum that much (assuming that you've read my Arkham Asylum review). While not a bad game, it had many flaws in my opinion, which most people seem to ignore. Combat felt unfinished as Batman failed to do actions that I wanted him to do (For example is counter attacks). Open world seemed pretty pointless, because there wasn't much to do.
Now that I've played Batman: Arkham City, it's clear that Rocksteady Studios improved many aspects. The world is much more open and you can move from area to area much easier, since you have upgrades to your tools (don't remember the names) and can dive down to get yourself back upwards. This already makes the game much better and actually gives you the feeling that you're Batman. Open world still isn't that impressive, but atleast it's more open and there are a few side-activities, which can keep you interested for a while.
I finally love the Arkham combat unlike in Batman: Arkham Asylum. In Batman: Arkham City, Batman seems to do less mistakes when trying to beat up criminals. He actually can counter every attack if not doing anything else and usually goes for target you want. Though sometimes in tight spaces he does weird actions but this is rare.
Not only you have more gadgets for movement and opening up paths, you can also use them against enemies. Also, all gadgets (except multiple batarangs) from Batman: Arkham Asylum are here with available upgrades. Explosives gels can be used against enemies even in combat. All the options makes the combat feel much less repetitive.
I do think that
The writing is pretty good. There are many villains with their motives. I think all the characters are very well written and their voice acting is superb. I still would've liked if there were more encounters with Joker. There are little things that I don't like such:
It's also weird why criminals are afraid of Batman sometimes, but othertimes not. One thing is for sure that Batman doesn't kill, so if he takes out thugs, they only get knocked out. I swear that some of them have experienced Batman multiple times, so......they should know what will happen. Though provoking Batman also seems very idiotic thing to do.
GOTY Edition adds some nice skins that are mainly cosmetics, some challenge maps (also three new characters to play in those maps), a few story sections with Catwoman and Harley Quinn's Revenge DLC campaign. The base game and all of the DLC's for 19,99€. Considering that Arkham City is a pretty good game and the amount of extras, it's an amazing value.
I give 8/10 for Arkham City. It's a major improvement over previous installment and I actually understand why this game is popular unlike Arkham Asylum. Fluid movement, the amount of gadgets, improved combat, better story and great characters makes this game probably one of the best Batman games.
I should mention that I haven't played next installments yet, so I cannot say if it's the best one yet. Though I will play them in a near future.

Billed as a response to the cover-oriented combat system of Gears of War, Space Marine ironically does cover-based combat better than GoW did. The game rewards you for getting up close and personal, but it's also always better to start an attack by flanking the enemy. Gears of War let you hide under any cover and do fairly well. Space Marine forces you to move about, from one cover to the next, in order to succeed.
The team-based versus is good, but the multiplayer really shines in the 4-player wave-based co-op mode. Dudes with jetpacks and chainsaws, dudes with heavy missile launchers, all working together to kill a few hundred Ork. Hectic? It feels like Armageddon.
Best for fans of the 40k universe, but this is the game I wanted Gears of War to be: Tactical Badassery. Recommended.

I really wanted to like this game.  I am a big fan of D&D and have played more RPGs than I can count.  I am also a huge fan on XCOM and that style of strategy so this looked like a match made in game heaven.
Alas it was not to be though.  Here is the good the bad and the ugly.
Good:
- Graphics are wonderful.
- Voice acting is top-notch.
- There "appears" to be a lot of character customizations.
Bad:
- Storyline beats you up in the second chapter and you lose your "investment" arbitrarily.  Sad really.
- There really is a lack of "strategy" as you are at the whim of roll of the dice.  Not XCOM calibre, not even close.
- $39.99?  I got is pre-release cheap.  Save your money it isn't worth that much.
Ugly:
- XCOM style strategy doesn't play as such.  Random roll really makes this a flawed game.  You can employ the exact same strategy move for move and breeze through a level, and other times get decimated.
- There is no place to "grind" it out to build up your characters if you are so willing to do so.  Early in the game you will find yourself redoing levels because you got a bad roll and you haven't enough Ducats (money) to do what you need.
- Some levels (first one) become closed the moment you go to another map.  There is no turning back until later.  A big map, but very linear and very unforgiving.
You have to REALLY love D&D style play to get into this game.  It will take a while to get used to, and even longer to become skilled at this game.  It feels more like work and less like fun.
I would not buy this game again.

If you've ever played the first Anomaly game, you pretty much know what to expect here. Anomaly 2 brings nothing new to the table, but what it does, it does well. For those of you that never played the first one; Anomaly is a reversed tower defense game. Meaning you create a path for your tanks and decide the order in which they drive to their destination. And, of course, you upgrade them as you see fit. You won't be building any towers. Your goal is to destroy the towers.
The player has direct control over a commander. This commander will throw decoys, tell your convoy to aim at a specific target, repair them or disable them by using an EMP. These items are limited, although killed enemies will frequently drop these as well. You have to use them strategically in order to survive, because the difficulty increases with every level you play.
The game has 12 missions. Each one should take approximately 30 minutes to complete. So in the end you'll probably end up with 7 hours of playtime, which is more than enough for a game this size.
The game uses a top-down perspective to keep things manageable from a strategic aspect. Anomaly 2 uses lots of colors for its enemy designs and environments, and it shows. The levels are either snowy or tropical and they both look brilliant in motion.
I will gladly recommend both Anomaly games to those who like a little twist in their tower defense games.

Batman: Arkham City is a game where you play as Batman, taking down enemies and flying through arkham city, swiftly destroying packs of random thugs, completing side quests. Let's start off with what people always talk about,
The Combat and Flying/Gliding as Batman.
The combat is rhythmic and combo based. It's fun, flashy and addictive. I wouldn't really say that it makes you feel like batman, because as videogamedunkey pointed out in his review: "I don't really remember Batman being a f**king ballerina". I don't either, although that doesn't stop it from being an enjoyable experience.
The flying is infinitely more fluid once you complete the AR missions and unclock a certain ability that I've decided not to....spoil.... I guess. Trust me, it's awesome.
The story is something to be desired, however it's solid enough, as this isn't really what the game is supposed to be focused on. In conclusion, if you're looking for a game based on a superhero, I'd have to say you can't really go wrong here. If you're looking for and action/adventure game, you can't really go wrong here. It's a good game that you should definetly try at one point in your gaming life.

Now that I've played Batman: Arkham City, it's clear that Rocksteady Studios improved many aspects. The world is much more open and you can move from area to area much easier, since you have upgrades to your tools (don't remember the names) and can dive down to get yourself back upwards. This already makes the game much better and actually gives you the feeling that you're Batman. Open world still isn't that impressive, but atleast it's more open and there are a few side-activities, which can keep you interested for a while.
I finally love the Arkham combat unlike in Batman: Arkham Asylum. In Batman: Arkham City, Batman seems to do less mistakes when trying to beat up criminals. He actually can counter every attack if not doing anything else and usually goes for target you want. Though sometimes in tight spaces he does weird actions but this is rare.
Not only you have more gadgets for movement and opening up paths, you can also use them against enemies. Also, all gadgets (except multiple batarangs) from Batman: Arkham Asylum are here with available upgrades. Explosives gels can be used against enemies even in combat. All the options makes the combat feel much less repetitive.

2048AD - the year in which humanity was faced with bio-terrorism. The desire to reach the next stage of evolution, which ran contrary to the facts of nature, formed the study of illegal modification to human cells. Because of this, a special unit was formed by mercenaries who opposed human experimentation. One of the major terrorist groups created a secret base in the jungle and started the project "Confluence", combining plant cells with human cells. The group of scientists that worked on this experimental process also raised an army of soulless bio-soldiers to guard the project. But during the final experiment, "Confluence" went out of control and began taking over its surroundings. You, as one of the best mercenaries, will have to stop the project in the only way possible: break into its epicenter and blast it to smithereens!
The game takes its roots from classic first-person shooters, a series of games such as Wolfenstein 3D, Spear Of Destiny, Operation Bodycount, Blake Stone and many others. The color palette is taken from Operation Bodycount, while the game uses a unique graphical style, approximately similar to Wolfenstein 3D. In Merger 3D, you'll need to pass through long levels, breaking through many crowds of enemies.
FEATURES:
15 levels
many crowd of angry enemies, each led by an unusual boss
classic old school gameplay
a large arsenal of powerful weapons with unique characteristics
musical arrangements by Jimmy

How to Not Make a Retro Shooter: The Video Game.
aka
How to Not Combine Wolfenstein 3D and First Two Doom Games: The Video Game.
Merger 3D is a retro FPS that appears to be trying to combine Wolfenstein 3D-style engine with fast gameplay in style of Doom 1 and 2. The result is not as good as someone would expect upon reading something along the lines of "Wolf3D x Doom".
The problems start on the very first level. The first type of an enemy you meet are these strange creatures that are so fast, you need to have very good reflexes in order to kill them before they reach you and start biting off your health. The second type are these gun-using ♥♥♥♥♥ that I would accuse of using hacks if they were characters in a multiplayer game, because they appear to be able to shoot at the player from around the corners and through not-yet-completely-open doors.
To make this even worse, these human enemies can be very difficult to notice because of the game's color scheme. For some reason, starting at level two, this game's dev decided to use a color scheme that makes the enemies blend in with the walls and thus difficult to notice. Contrast this to Wolfenstein 3D enemies, which can be spotted relatively easily. And to top all of this, these enemies barely even make any pause between their attacks, meaning they can drain your health VERY fast before you manage to shoot back.
Still reading this review instead of already deciding not to buy this game? *sigh* Very well.
Now would be a good thing to mention this game's difficulty. Where should I start? I mean, besides the stuff I already mentioned? Maybe with the fact that you're running a risk of running out of ammo AT THE FIRST ♥♥♥♥ING LEVEL OF THE GAME? To quote AVGN, what were they thinking? And, not only does the game potentially not give you enough ammo, but it's also gets somewhat stingy with giving you health kits, starting AT LEVEL TWO, at least in comparison to how many enemies it throws at you and how much health they can drain from you in a split second.
There's also something weird with the ammo system. It seems the player can't pick up ammo for any specific gun unless they're ACTUALLY HOLDING THAT GUN AT THAT EXACT MOMENT. I would ask how the hell did they manage to do THAT, but I already have an idea and it involves being the same kind of a beginner at programming as I am. Believe me, I'm talking from personal experience. I know how I would do it and, even though I'm a noob, I still think I'm experienced enough to realize that this solution of mine is probably ♥♥♥♥ing terrible, and I feel it would result in the same situation I described at the beginning of this passage.
This ammo system is somewhere between how it SHOULD be and Slaughtering Grounds. Yes, I know. Something IS wrong if I have to mention Slaughtering ♥♥♥♥ing Grounds.
And to add salt to injury, this game, which features labyrinthine levels, has no minimap. Yeah. No minimap. I myself am speechless. After Doom 1 and 2 introduced the minimap into FPSes that feature non-linear level design and made it the standard in such FPSes, these people come to the conclusion that not including one in this game is a good idea. Dear God, even Super 3D Noah's Ark (!!!!!), a game that actually uses the Wolf3D engine, had a minimap, at least in its Steam version.
At the end, I cannot think of any redeeming factors.
So, can I or can I not recommend this? Gee, what do YOU think?

Alright, so to begin, I decided to give this one a try because of the aviation theme, and myself being a pilot. I haven't really "read" too many visual novels, so I'm not exactly an authority on what a visual novel should be, but I liked this one. First and foremost, it is mostly a drama with comedy mixed in, but the overall theme could be summed up as "letting go of a painful past to experience something better." All of the characters that show up in the first chapter have something from their past that they need to overcome to move forward, and character developement is driven by the plot of them working together to try something most of them had previously not thought of doing: building and flying their own glider. Apparently there are six total endings, five of which appear to be romantic stories involving one of the disproportionate number of girls in the soaring club. I realize based on the core story cutscenes that the main story is a romance with Kotori, a girl who has been confined to a wheelchair after an accident, but I felt the most natural story was with Ageha, the childhood friend who recognizes the main character right off the bat after he returned to his home town. So, that's the only one I've completed so far. I saw in another review that before being translated by MoeNovel and put on Steam, this VN was originally in the "eroge" genre. If you don't know what that means, I'll save you some time, it basically means pornographic. I'm glad they edited that out for the steam release, I think it would have detracted a lot from the more innocent story that I read. Not to say there isn't anything suggestive, and you can call me a prude all you want, but I think that if there was more explicit material it would not have fit my pallete as well. Also, I liked the OST, if you've heard music inspired by flight as much as I have, a lot of the instrumental themes will bring up feelings of nostalgia. I feel that I've heard it before, but I honestly haven't, if that makes any sense. Now, for some complaints... Ok, just one, I think I only made three or four choices in a story that lasted nearly twenty hours. I would have greatly appreciated it if I'd had more say in what the main character does, and there were many times that the character wrestles with a decision, but the audience isn't asked. Ok, I get it, too many decisions in something this long, and you're writing and animating and paying voice actors for a lot of different scenes. I understand that, but there were just too many decisions made that I felt would have been more fun to put into the audiences hands, instead of just asking which girl the audience wants the character to spend an event with a few times, and then deciding which overall story to tell. Overall, though, as nerdy as this story telling medium seems to be considered, I like it. It reminds me of the Goosbumps: Choose Your Own Story books I read as a kid, but these tend to be directed at a more mature audience, and there's so much more stimulation from the visuals, the music, and the voice acting, which mostly for my English-only speaking self mostly just clarifies the tone in which something was said. Anyways, if I had to give this a rating on a scale of 1-10, I'd put it in the 8.5/10 ballpark. My complaint, despite in my mind actually being a semi-serious issue for me, is well outweighed by everything that went right, from theme, to characters, to art, the soundtrack, to the story told. Well, safe flying ya'll.

Great game, lots of fun.  Well worth the money if you are into tactical, turn-based combat.
The characters and voice acting are top notch.  The dialogue witty.
Character advancement is done by earning adventure points that you apply to the skills and stats you wish to improve. There's no set levels. The more skilled or powerful you are at something, the more adventure points it costs to improve that skill or stat further.  It makes it impossible to make a character that is unbeatable at everything, so you really need to put some thought into party roles and utilizing each character's strengths and weaknesses.
Most of the battlefields have static and dynamic features that can add an advantage to your party or spell their doom. This keeps combat interesting.
One thing I found fun, but some might find frustrating is that you don't get to choose where your characters start on the battlefield.  For the most part, your characters are started in such a logical position that you don't even question it, but every now and then a battle is added with your characters scattered all over the place. Sometimes it makes sense within the story line, sometimes not.
The enemy AI does fairly well as an opponent. While it doesn't always use the battlefield features to full advantage, it does it often enough to keep you on your toes.
Overall, two thumbs up !
One thing to note - if you are the kind of player that has to have tons of sparkly, magical loot, this game is not for you.
If you are the kind of player that needs to have five sets of armor, fifteen weapons, and a house with fifty chests to store all those weapons and armor in, this game is not for you.  Gear upgrades are mundane and modest, and you'll have the same armor and weapons with you for large portions of the game.  Encumbrance penalties dissuade you from carrying much more than the armor on your back and the weapons on your person.
The game is more about tactics and skills than it is about loot.

Anomaly 2 is a really good sequel, and fans of the original should be pleased with what they find here. The core gameplay of guiding your units around maze-like streets, while using abilities to help defeat enemy towers, remains intact. There are new units, each of which can morph between two different forms at will. For example, the artillery unit can either fire straight ahead at long range, or 360 degrees at medium range. This adds more depth and makes it easier to adjust tactics mid-mission, to take advantage of the new enemy towers' weaknesses. The presentation of graphics, music, voice acting and story is all very good. The campaign took me around 6.5 hours, and although I'm disappointed there's no singleplayer skirmish mode, there is multiplayer to add replayability. The controls work great with mouse and I didn't notice any bugs. I think this developer deserves to be rewarded for their efforts with a full price purchase.

Update 2: the only way to get a soundtrack for this game is to buy Anomaly 'bundle'. There's no way to obtain it otherwise by purchasing separately. Despite numerous attempts to contact them, they conveniently ignored it. Do not support this developer.

Disclaimer: I played this game much longer than the hours Steam shows, but it was on PS3.
The second installment of the Arkham game series, taking place in an entire section of Gotham turned into an open-air prison. Lots of Batmanning included.
+It should go without saying being this series' greatest strength, but this game, possibly even more than its predecessor, perfectly captures the sensation of "being the Batman". Atmosphere, gameplay, tools and even the HUD ditching its sketch style for a new hi-tech feel: it all serves to get the player in character, which works splendidly.
+The map and exploration is a massive step forward from Asylum, being much larger, with a great deal of outdoor space and content and effectively being a free roaming experience, while still maintaining its trademark enclosed spaces. The graphics also got a good upgrade and every square inch of the scenery overflows with detail. Character models, especially those for the basic enemies, are also superior and more varied.
+The plot is quite fantastic: unlike the previous game, where it was more of an excuse to be the Bat and kick some butts, here it's actually very interesting, very well made and sure to be loved by fans of the character.
+There is much more to do than simply following the main plot, however: apart from the challenge maps and riddler collectibles being back with a vengeance, there's now a copious amount of sidequests to follow and complete, each starring an awesomely portrayed villain from Batman's vast roster of opponents.
+Everything you hear in this game, be it sound effects, the awesome soundtrack or the equally awesome voice acting, is top notch.
+Megatons of nerdy material, descriptions and obscure references, as always.
+The game is substantially longer than the previous installment, clocking at anywhere between 12 and 20+ hours minus the annoying collectibles hunt, depending on how many secondary missions you want to complete.
+The combat and stealth mechanics, while fundamentally the same, received lots of little tweaks, additions and reworks that make them better, more varied and even more fun that before. There are more types of enemies, more gadgets with different, more practical uses, more special moves and the animations are also improved. Stealth is significantly harder and less abusable than before...
-...but, while the AI goons are sensible enough to group up and watch each other's backs while their numbers dwindle, some patience can still make these sections a relative breeze.
-More enemies on screen and more variants of them is nice, but sometimes it leads to a mess that's a bit hard to read. Nothing serious, however.
-The GOTY content is redundant, being some new challenge maps and a very, very short campaign that takes place after the main game and is a completely separate entity stats- and exploration-wise.
-The boss fights have improved. One of them is actually brilliant, and would be considered awesome even in a game where bosses aren't bland. Still, the other boss fights present are far from being the icing on the cake.
-Some performance issues with DX11 have been acknowledged long ago.
The Arkham series in general is made of good games created by fans of the character for fans of the character. While Asylum was a hit, with Arkham City Rocksteady Studios managed to create the perfect "bigger and better" sequel, the best Batman game ever made as of today and a great game in its own right. That's no small feat. Unless you can't stand action games or Batman specifically, this is a game you should own.

If you have a remote fancy for the world of Warhammer40k you will absolutely love this game.
Nothing has ever captured the feel of raw power that is a space marine.
Yet as strong as they are and as god like as they seem to regular humans, they are only small things in the lands of 40k.
A space marine is only as good as his skill in battle, this theme comes across consistently in the game as you wade through countless enemies but can still be brought down by the lowest of the low if you are not careful.
Solid game mechanics assist in the "always forward never back" feel of a space marine unit.
There are no health packs, there is health and shield regeneration akin to the halo series, however its simply not fast enough in the ruthless 40k universe, instead a marines best option is to rely on his faith in the emperors protection and gain health from slaying his enemies .
Learn the execution mechanic well and you will be a god, try to hide and cower behind cover waiting for regen and you will be crushed and given the death only a coward deserves.
Its very sad that there are no dedicated servers because the multiplayer is outstanding with its flavour, balance, fantastic unlocks and amazing customisation all held back by filthy console net code, while it has improved since launch via patches the main multiplayer remains unplayable for most due to the lack of even a basic region lock for game finding.
Not is all lost however, Exterminatus mode is outstanding.
A lot like the hoard/wave/invasion modes from older games it is more at home here than in any other game, hoards of enemies out for the blood of the universe and its only you and your three friends to stand in their way, the addition of random challenges during the play bring a new risk reward element to an already established game mode.
The single player campaign is nice and lengthy and is full of meaty content and progression.
Unlike many games these days were the main story can be completed in a hour or two and the rest is just filler missions/side quests to keep you busy.
The campaign here is like reading a book with imagination mode set to extreme.
This game will entertain any dark-scifi fan and warhammer fans new and old

Styx is a hardcore stealth game. I see many people complain about the combat. This game is about stealth, there is virtually no combat. The combat in this game is when an enemy sees you, then comes up to you so he has to get close enough to initiate some sort of lock on your character in this timing game. You have to parry the enemies sword to eventually kill him and get away. Which afterwards you can hopefully hide back in the shadows. The game doesn't focus on combat, it focuses on stealth.
The story is interesting, nothing that will blow you away. Some Amber stuff and a big tall castle you climb around in. Plus Styx's voice actor I believe is cheesy But honestly fits the character and the game. But where this game excels at is gameplay. Most if not all the levels are basicly big sandboxes. How you do objection A is up to you, as well as getting from point A to B. You'll end up wanting to find all the collectables in the levels simply because it's fun climbing roofs and walls, waiting for that perfect moment to make a kill or grab an object and then slide back into the shadows.
Graphics aren't bad either, there were so moments where I was "hey that looks cool". Especially at the outdoor levels in the day time. But this isn't a tripple A game so don't expect triple A graphics.
And for the $30 price tag, I'm not sure. If you're a big fan of stealth you'll get your moneys worth. But still I would wait for a sale, the game is usually about $7 when it's on sale. I say it's a steal for that price.

“Styx Master of Shadows is one of the best titles the infiltration genre has to offer.”
9/10 – HardcoreGamer - One of the most murderously innacurate things I've ever heard. You give a 9/10 to games that are phenominal masterpieces that are near perfect. Not Styx, in which it is unmistakably not that. Not even close.
“In a lot of ways Styx is a hardcore stealth fan’s ideal game.”
7,2/10 – MMORPG - Again, egregious and fallacious. Some games that fit that desc. would be MGSV, Dishonored, and Hitman Absolution, just to name a very select few.
Dialogue/Story:
Almost 3 hours was enough for me. Everything in the game is way too contrived, namely the combat, extremely linear levels, and dialogue. As for the dialogue, it is riddled with strong language that feels more awkward and out of place than any game I have ever played. Quite literaly every single time I hear him say f-ck, sh-t, or whatever else, no matter what the context is, it makes me cringe and it just sounds so wildly misguided that it is unbelievable how badly delivered/misplaced/unneeded every single curse word is. I'm all for cursing in games, whatever, but here every time it is cringe-worthy. The story is nothing worth worrying or caring about either.
Graphics/Combat/Level Design/Stealth:
The graphics are nothing special but are the least of this game's worries. In fact, the actual game looks nothing like the store screenshots whatsoever. They look beautiful. The actual game is a far cry from looking anything even remotely like them. Combat is generic, level design is bereft of anything more than even mildly interesting, and contrary to professional reviews, user reviews, and its "very positive" review status, the main selling point of the game, its stealth, is just very sub-par and forgettable. Stealth here is nothing innovative even by the wildest imagination, nor does it even earn the right to be mentioned in the same company as other mastercraft games that make great use of the stealth aspect, such as Dishonored, Hitman Absolution, MGSV, Splinter Cell Conviction and Blacklist, and even Thief 2014, just to name a very few. Hell, even Watch Dogs has ten times better stealth than this game, and you can even use a ton of gadgets and stuff to make the stealth and gameplay more fun. Nothing whatsoever like that exists in this game.
Linearity/Controls:
Levels are extremely linear also. Some appear to give you choice, but ultimately it is just very very linear. That can sometimes be okay if the game is pretty good, like earlier MGS games, but definitely not here. The game's controls and combat are fine and will service you well enough to do what you need to do without hassle, however much so that everything just feels pretty generic.
User review status:
There are many obvious reasons, which I won't get into here, that the steam user review system is horribly abused, and this game's user review score is a bright shining example of that abuse. Definitely a strong example of the steam user reviews for a game being savagely innacurate. I imagine the people who like this have never really played any truly fantastic stealth games such as those I mentioned earlier, maybe because they can't afford them who knows, or they are just so starved for more stealth games and are such over the top hardcore stealth fans that they actually enjoy this. Or maybe just have a high tolerance for mediocrity in video games.
SCORE/PRICING:
The metacritic score of 71/100 is much closer to being accurate. I suppose I would give it a borderline 5/10. $30 for this game is a hilarious price. But who knows. Hopefully they made a good profit at that price so if they make a Styx 2 it can be much better than this which plays like a bottom sales bin budget title. I got this on sale for I think $10 and had I known how boring and generic and linear this was with the most misguided, worst, forced cursing dialogues I've ever seen in a game, or maybe even in a movie for that matter, I would've saved that money for something much, much better. Which coincidentally can easily be found in a matter of seconds. If you have to see what it's all about, don't pay more than $5 tops.
You know what on second thought don't make a Styx 2 because even if it is better than this game that's not saying much.

Having spotted this on the Steam New Releases it quickly caught my eye, as I'm a poor sucker for retro/old school shooter games (as I was literally raised with games like Wolfenstein 3D and DOOM II,) and having $2 in my Steam wallet, I grabbed it to give it a shot...
Well this game has some problems.
The first minor problem, the weapon graphics are WAY more detailed than everything else. While the game has the same graphical levels as Wolfenstein 3D and Operation Bodycount, the weapons look like they came from a Duke Nukem 3D mod. They just simply don't fit with the game.
The second minor problem,
and how AI can hit you from pretty much around corners. You will just see your health start dropping, and look around to try and find who's hurting you, only to see an enemy on the other end of the room, just barely poking out from around the corner shooting you. I've only made it to the 4th level, and this is the common situation it seems.
The third minor problem, the levels are big and are easily confusing to navigate. The FIRST level is all brown and green, with tons of trees and vines. There is no map feature in this game, so you will end up getting turned around and end up wandering trying to figure out where the hell you are supposed to go.
But...
*This is fixed with the "No Mouse" version, but as that is not included in the main game, and you have to OPT into it, therefore it's still present.*
The BIGGEST problem with this game that makes this a Not Recommend, needs to be explained.
You are FORCED to use mouse to look around and shoot. Why is this bad? Well when you try to look around with the mouse, you get a very nauseating screen tear that really hurts the eyes and very hard to focus on what your looking at. Now here is where it gets better... YOU CAN ONLY SHOOT WITH THE LEFT MOUSE BUTTON!! There is no keyboard button for shoot, and you can't change controls either, cause there is no options menu. You can use the WASD to move, and arrow keys to look around (which does NOT have the screen tearing effect), but then you can't shoot. So you are forced to use the mouse, which has a slow and painful turn speed, when it works. Combine that with the tearing effect make this game 100% unplayable. I was only able to make it to level 4 before I had to stop.

Blackguards is an  average game at its best . Follows genetic fantasy tropes . Character creation is bare bones , you cannot modify starting stats .  Game offers large world map , but due to its linear nature you will be just staring at places you can't go . Story progresses by clicking on hubs where you will either enter a city screen or combat . Side quests are very limited .
Appearance customization is limited to picking  out of five pre-made characters per gender.  There is significant shortage of light and leather armor variety . 85-90% of all armors in a game are metal which means you spell caster wont be able to use it . Game has nice sandbox system where you are allowed pick whichever skills/perks you like . Perks require xp and trainer .  It can be difficult to find trainer to teach you perk . For example you might unknowingly leave act 1 and lose access to mage trainer for rest of act 2 .
Combat is dull . Most of it involves using same spell/melee attack and hoping you will get lucky.
Graphics and are style are uninspiring .  There is no camera angle rotation and overall camera controls are poor . This can lead to some frustration such as inability to target or see enemy hiding in a corner .
You can interact with some environment and there are some environmental hazards like methane gas in swamps. You characters and enemies can slip on wet floor . Some maps with lots of water spills turn into some kind of comedy involving every character falling to the ground at start of their turn .
Voice acting is decent . And dwarf you get in beginning of the game is awesome .
In terms of bugs and glitches game was polished in its early stages . I've only encountered one minor bug that was quickly fixed .

As has been stated in other reviews & from
, the game is based off a tabletop role-playing game from Germany. This is my first foray into this system in any case.  The story is OK, but not much more then that.  You don't gain levels per se, but you gain adventure points (AP) when either defeating foes or completing a quest.  You use these points to raise just about everything pertaining to your character, be it statistics, your skills, your resitances, & for magic users how effective spells are & the astral points needed to cast them.  The higher the "level" of the STATS, skills etc, the more AP they cost.  Unfortunately, I've not come into any battle where my group has had a "windfall" of AP, so far  I've either gotten 30, 60 or around 120 AP depending on the battle (
).   I've gotten a bit more AP when completing quests though. In fairness here I'm playing it on the easiest difficulty, maybe battles give you more AP on the harder ones, though I doubt it.
The hightlights of the game are the battle system, I've yet to encounter any "cut & paste" battle area.  The upgrade system for your characters is fairly subtle, but noticable for the most part.  In short, you don't feel like you're spending AP to upgrade your character & they don't feel like they're more powerful.   The spells are diverse & effective. Mapwise there is a fairly large area to cover in both the in battle maps & world map.
The weaknesses of the game, thus far are:
No areas to really grind for AP,
.  You can't actually make things, not armor or weapons, at least not at the point in the game that I'm at.  There's no height or lowlands difference in battles; in short I've not had so much as 1 battle where either I or the enemy started at the top of a hill.  I've also yet to have been involved in a battle where I've gotten a huge amount of AP. I'm roughly at the halfway mark, going by what the creators wrote on the main page, but I've yet to see so much as one magical item, whether defensive or offensive item.  I don't know the tabletop RPG this is based off of so perhaps the world lacks magical items or if they're simply more subtle in nature when compared to games like Final Fantasy Tactics.   The spellcasters also need work, I find them more useful as party "buffers", and from what I've read on the forums I'm in the nearly overwhelming majority.
This game needs some minor tweaks to really grab you & keep you in it's grip; but so far any issues I have with it, in the scheme of things, are relatively minor & not game breaking.

Its not a bad game and I do appreciate a developer bringing turn based fantasy RPG's back to the market. However, it just feels like it fell short of its potential. Not to knit pick but starting with the lack of facial customizations. I know its not a big deal but in my opinion, it starts the game off on the wrong foot and goes on from there.
there is really no exploration, its extremely linear and predictable as far as the encounters go. The rules of turn based combat are also not the greatest and are very vanilla. No attack from behind bonuses that I could see so you can retreat and not worry about taking a blade to the back if you were standing in a hex next to an enemy.
My biggest frustration was in upgrading my gear. Theres RNG involved for what you can loot from battles, so dont count on picking up that axe that this guy just done done whacking at you with for the past 10 minutes.  It just vaporizes apparently leaving you with your trusty ol' starter torch.
Weapons and armor cost a lot of money and while you may be able to gear your guy up with a basic sword after the first half dozen encounters, that will be it for quite a while until you can afford more. Meanwhile, wave after wave of baddies wielding swords, shields, axes, armor, bows and arrows will make sure you pull your hair out before you can afford to gear your party adequately enough to fight them.

This is a cautious recommendation. Gunpoint is fun, but it's somewhat pricey for what the game offers.
Gunpoint is a stealth puzzle game. Each level is a small sandbox for you to figure out how to complete the level. One of the game's core mechanics is rewiring buildings, allowing you to do things like open a locked door with a light switch. The issue I have is the lack of a challenge. As with many stealth games, the game suffers from being able to take out guards fairly easily with not much of a consequence. I also found the AI very exploitable. I even knocked a guard through a door once on accident.
Gunpoint's gameplay also never really evolves much. You'll meet only three enemy types, and the sandbox really isn't that big or deep. There are only a handful of things to interact with, making your approach fairly obvious most of the time. The game could have used more enemies, obstacles, and fun things to interact with. What you're left with is a fun, brief, but by no means amazing 3 hours.
The best part of Gunpoint is actually the choose your own adventure style story. The choices do matter a bit, and the game cleverly lets you talk yourself into a corner at times. Even if there is no real punishment for it, it does encourage the player to pay attention to what they're reading. You might even get another playthrough or two out of the game if you want to see everything the game offers.
Overall, I found the game fun and charming, but it failed to really go the extra mile and be something truly special. At a 3 hour game length, I find it hard to recommend at $10, but you're certainly not going to have a bad time.

Great game!
This is my 3-part review of the game. 1. The RPG system, 2. The actual roleplay, 3. The feel of the game. It is worth mentioning that I am a RPG guy with long experience in both Pen and Paper RPG (mostly PF, but also Vampire), and a lot of CRPG. So, naturally, this has an impact on how I liked or disliked the game.
1. The roleplaying system The Black Eye is really nice and has a lot of depth and will be candy if you, like me, havent tried it before. I cannot accout for the differences between the pen and paper 4th edition (witch the game mechanic is derived from) and the system Blackguards has implemented. But as far as I am concerned its really nice. Different attributes combinate to give different base statistics - and control how well you fight / use talents / casts spells. There are no levels for characters, insted you gain Adventure Points from combats and finished quests that you either continually spend or save up to spend on more expensive upgrades. It really is a fun system and has similarity with the way Vampire the masquerade works. The turn based tactics is nothing but pure enjoyment!
2. The actual roleplaying is somewhat linear. If you like that then no problem. If you want more choice, then it has shortcomings. Things are pretty much set up and you cannot deviate too much from the path. The choices you are given doesnt even have that much impact. For instance one side quest presents you with two identical twins, the one is evil and the other is good - but who is who. In the end, if you chose to root out the good guy OR the bad guy there is no impact on the game other than your own conciousness. (...and honestly, who cares abouth truth when it comes to a book worth 50 ducats?!)
3. The acutal feel of the game is, at least to me, awsome. The characters you pick up are rather strange, a paranoid dwarf, a sleezy magician and later on a drug addict elf to name some. But this is what strangley keeps it interesting - actually highly enjoyable. Bugger off with the lawful good paladin that does good at every turn. Here its like "plant unlawful poison at a highly esteemed noble to get him arrested" or "Get a new slavegirl / trophy for the master of the city".
To sum up, I really enjoy the game - (not finished yet as this is written) and I see a replay possibility with choosing differet abilities. If you enjoy RPGs and in particular the combat part - this is a game for you.

The game is Interstellar Rift, and the game is quite literally as cool as its name.  In its present state there is little more to do than design and pilot your ships (or stations) and do resource harvesting, but even that is really impressive when you factor in how immersive this game is.  Absolutely everything, even the menu access, is done through consoles both on your person and at the various equipment.  Want to adjust the engines?  Forget quick keys, sit in the pilot seat and look at the console to your left.  Want to convert raw materials?  Load them into the refinery and use the console to produce your resources.
If I had to pick a gripe with this game it would be the (current) lack of a tutorial.  That said, there is a lot of content yet to be added to the game so adding a tutorial at this phase wouldn’t really be practical.  After all, you can’t make a tutorial on combat when there currently is none.  It only took me about 15 minutes to figure things out on my own, so for the moment I’m not actually considering the lack of a tutorial a “bad thing”.  Just make sure when you beam to your newly crafted ship you bring along some oxygen for air and hydrogen for fuel (both refined from water) or you're totally screwed.  Also, check out the information kiosk because it'll help you too.
I’ve heard that multiplayer can be buggy, but I have yet to do any multiplayer so I can’t say for sure.  I know there have been a lot of patches, and will continue to be a lot of patches, so patience is a virtue in this case.
All in all I’m extremely impressed with the state of Interstellar Rift.  Taking into account all of the things promised for the future (NPC’s, Combat, Exploration, Vast Universe, Economy, etc.) recommending this game is a no-brainer.  And hey, if you’re a little nervous about getting involved with a game that’s early access, there’s always the ability to place it on your “Wish List” so you can keep an eye on it.

Although lacking in a real goal currently, Interstellar Rift is a very enjoyable ship building game.
At first building a ship is confusing: you have to work out power distribution, life support/air flow, fuel. The interior design is very well done even at this early access stage, allowing great customisation and huge ships. The interior design allows for various colour schemes, furniture, necessary systems, different rooms, multiple floors and more. It would be nice to see more furniture options, more walls, lights etc.
The exterior design is not nearly as in-depth as the interior however. The exterior has one colour, and looks very blocky, even when smoothing by using various block types to create a nice flowing exterior design. It would be nice to see varying aesthetic designs for colours or insignias on the exterior.
Currently, there is not much to do outside of building ships and testing them. There are no tutorials ingame, and the tutorials online seem to miss out some vital aspects, such as power distribution. I'd recommend the game if you're willing to go into it ready for trial and error.
There is a LOT of potential, and this game can only get better and better.

One of the most immersive glimpse of the dark ages I've ever played.  For an alpha state this game is solid gold!  I forsee Gloria Victis becoming one of the great MMO's, and cannot wait to see where the Dev's take it from here.

Overall a fantastic experience that has kept me fully immersed for the last 115 hours of gameplay.
What Gloria Victis does really well...
1.  Loot - After over a hundred hours of gameplay it is still exciting to open the loot after every kill.  Equipment drops are very well balanced for the level of mobs.  Mobs also have a chance to drop crafting recipes and there is an active market of people seeking out some of the rarer recipes.   Each mob type has a different loot table and each loot table has sought after drops.
2.  XP Farming - There are a wide variety of mobs and mob locations to farm from.   There are a lot of options for solo mobs as well as mobs that require groups.
3.  Variety of ways to level and improve your character - Mob XP, Crafting XP and upgrading cities all give character XP.  There is enough variety that when it starts feeling grindy there are different ways to play the game and they all help improve your character.
4.  Death - PVE death has no negative consequences.  PVP death allows the victor to loot only a few items based on a maximum point system.  Higher value items such as worn equipment have a higher point value.  It is enough of a loss that you always try to keep anything you do not want to lose in your bank but nothing you lose will cause you to lose hours of time to replace.
5.  Inventory space - Space is limited at level 1 but it is not difficult to expand your storage through purchasing or crafting larger bags.  It is reasonable to have over 300 item slots between your inventory and your bank by level 30.

Batman: Arkham City is an excellent sequel to an already excellent game. It's one of my favorite games, if not my absolute favorite.
Like the previous game, the gameplay is really satisfying. The freeflow combat still controls amazingly well and the combat animations makes every fight amazing to look at. New combat moves and new enemy types were added to give combat even more depth and the boss fights are way more varied this time. The overall gameworld is quite a bit bigger then the one in Arkham Asylum and navigating it is a real pleasure. You can grapple unto just about any structure and use your cape to glide along the buildings. This also blends together well with the stealth elements of the game. Looking down from the rooftops unto a bunch of unsuspecting thugs before taking them down really gives you that Batman feeling.
The story is decent, serving mostly as a catalyst for the gameplay, but it has some really powerfull, Batman-lore significant moments. A ton of Batman characters make their appearance and Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill once again shine as Batman and the Joker. Compared to Arkham Asylum the pacing of the game doesn't feel as tight, but for an openworld game it still feels paced pretty well.
The visual and sound design are also on point and really capture the right Batman tone.
The gameworld, although much larger than Arkham Asylum is still really detailed and filled to the brim with Batman eastereggs, Riddler puzzles, challenges, sidemissions and more. So there is a lot to explore. And once you've done all of that there are still a ton of challenge maps to hone your skills and a new game+.
These days Batman: Arkham City GOTY is regularly on sale for $5.-  , but for this quality and amount of content even at full retail price it's an absolute steal!
