NOTE: Evoland 2 is actually very different than the first Evoland. The progressive graphic and gameplay improvement is not in this game, and it focus A LOT more on the story than the humor. Don't get me wrong, there is definitely humor and satire, but less so than in the first Evoland. Now, on to the real review.
Evoland 2 is a fantastic game. Absolutely fantastic. Evoland 2 is mainly an RPG that plays very similar to The Legend of Zelda (like A Link Between Worlds or The Minish Cap, not like Ocarina of Time or Skyward Sword). You may know Evoland as a game that tried to make fun of the other types of gameplay and gaming itself. Evoland 2 doesn't "make fun" of others games, but it mimics them. For example, you'll be running around in LoZ style gameplay, then you enter an area, and all of a sudden it plays like Final Fantasy, or it may play like Fire Emblem in another area. Just note that the main gameplay is LoZ RPG style, but you'll be forced to play very differently in some areas. Note that when it does change gameplay, the difficulty isn't all that hard (except the Street Fighter spinoff...ugh...).
The different gameplay can vary from a side-scrolling brawler to a match 3 kind of thing, or from a tactical RPG to a rhythm game. The different gameplay is actually what seems to keep the game interesting. Honestly, if it stayed like LoZ, it would've gotten terribly boring after awhile.
The story is a much bigger focus this time around. The first Evoland didn't really focus a whole lot on the story, and this game makes up for it. If you don't like convoluted storylines, then sorry. But both the gameplay and the story work really well, and if you're the kind of guy that skips the story, it's still a fun game, you'll just be confused. Also, see my playtime? That's 1 regular playthrough. Not a 100% run, not a speed-run. I ended up with 67% completion, if you need a scale of reference.
Anyway, do I recommend this game? Absolutely. Yes. This game isn't just an RPG, it's a lot more. If you're not sure what kind of genre you want to get into, and you like RPGs, then get this game. There's a lot of diversity, and it's a lot of fun. Even if I mentioned a certain genre that you don't like, get it anyway. You might like it.

That feeling you get when you create your first full adder and suddenly realize what has been hand-waved and glossed over when they first taught you arithmatic in kendergarten: There is a logic more fundamental than 1 + 1.
Full disclosure: I'm a computer programmer. I can write in assembly. I shift bits for work every day. I simplify randomly generated quadratic equations to pass the time like others might solve a crossword puzzle. Finding and following simple logic steps is enjoyable for me. And this game is all about that.
This is currently one of my favorite games. I think if you're the type who likes to play with redstone in minecraft, or likes to create elaborate traps in dwarf fortress, this game is for you. If you're like me and like to play with electronics on a breadboard for fun, but don't always have time or space to work on a learning project, then this game is for you.
Levels are simple enough to knock one out at work while I'm on break, so far.
I've had no problems with the interface and the program has run well for me.
I can see myself putting a lot more time into this.

The author is going to annoy you with stupidity like this excerpt: "We could surely build a new truth table and try to face the problem of subtraction by elementary means, but we leave that as an exercise to you and as a catastrophe for your sandbox. Equipped with the wisdom of elderly, we can cease the fact that A - B = A + (-B) for our own good." There is only a very small amount of actual useful information there, left almost passive-aggressively unexplained to the reader. If an actual person spoke like that to me, I'd want to give him a wedgie.
You'll also have to find settings and disable the clunky retro minimal techno soundtrack because its about as irritating as the writing.
All that said, there is one redeeming quality to this app. You will learn something, which is the whole point.

When I played To The Moon all those years ago, I teared up. The story, the simple yet beautiful retro graphics, THE MUSIC. I knew that it was a very special game that could not be duplicated. I didn't think that FreeBird themselves could make anything of that calibre again. Even to this day, It's a personal favourite.
A Bird Story proved me utterly, utterly wrong. Using the same graphics and amazing music, It made an amazing and thought-provoking story with no words. And I too, had NO WORDS when playing it.
And now this, the gem in the crown. Where do I start?
The graphics? They're just the same as always, they look retro, yet add themselves very well to the game. They are simplistic, but they take the best of To The Moon and A Bird Story and consolidate them into something that is visually stunning without trying hard. The visual effects look amazing, and they really mold well with the retro aesthetic. I honestly don't know how they could be made better.
The Music?
It is, once again, outstanding. Kan uses the same classical theme that worked so amazingly with the two previous games, but it is somehow better this time around. It conveys the same emotion without appearing out of place. Anyone that has played To The Moon or A Bird Story will notice that some of the tracks are remixes from those games, giving the game a nice, familiar feel in some of the segments. I can't wait for the OST to be released.
But how could I forget, the story!
What am I meant to say? It's made by Freebird, so it is good of it's own admission. I think that this is one of the only 'Indie' games of this year to succeed in creating a story that is both captivating and worthy of tears.
The game might only be around 5 hours long, but in those 5 hours there is so much amazing story that it ends up being better than RPGs that are twice, or even 4 times as long. The story is a masterpiece, laced with just the right amount of humour (Which I really was looking forward to), emotion and thought-provokingness. It manages to stay within the world that the previous games had created, making little references to them and building on what has already been established. But it avoids the 'Electric Boogaloo' trap, making sure that it doesn't hang in the dogma of the previous games, but is equal or surpasses them. And believe me, this is one story that you really, REALLY don't want to not see. I cried unbelievably hard, I laughed my head off, and left the game feeling better and stronger than before I pressed play.
Go in blind without any expectations, and this game will not disappoint.
Just as with the earlier games, my only complaint is that you can only really 'Play' a Freebird game once before the initial amazingness is lost. It's one of those RPGs that are so good, you can't really replay with the same effect, but personally I think that's quite beautiful in a way.
If Sigmund really do exist, I hope they can just erase my memory of playing the game so I'm able to play it over and over again as if it was new. But, don't be sad that the game is finished, be happy because you were there to experience it. When the credits are rolling, you'll have found Paradise.
So, I can say without a doubt that Finding Paradise is my game of the year for 2017, or possibly for longer than that. Have a merry christmas Freebird, and we'll see what you have in store in the coming years!

So far the game is pretty fun, although a little light on content.  You build ships, stations, and mine.  Right now the world is huge, but lightly populated (around 100km).  The only limit to building is your imagination and patience.  There is a learning curve for most things and balancing, weight, power, engergy use, etc. can be a challenge in itself.  Sure you can make a beautiful looking ship, but it may never go over 10m/s or worse, not even move.  Also damage is a thing, however its in a very early state and can only happen by bad flying with and without shields.
On the downside though, there are several bugs that do harm the total experience, crashing, and even save deleting ones (although somewhat rare).
There are plans to add a lot more to this game and I will add to the review as they do.  There will be trading, world (universe) will have more in it, combat, NPCs, etc.
Should you get this game??  Well that depends, do you like to build stuff?  If so then you will probably enjoy this game.  If you are looking for more (like combat, trading, exploring) then I would say wait.

Wow.  I bought Styx on sale ages ago but only booted it up for the first time a few days ago.  I'm glad I did.  I love stealth games, and Dishonored is one of my favorite games of all time.  Styx is clearly and deeply inspired by Dishonored, and it does its predecessor great honor.
The controls are some of the best I've felt, the AI is brutally unforgiving, the textures and animations are top notch, and the voice acting is a masterpiece.  It is also /huge/ -- it goes on for so long it almost becomes exhausting in its length.  If you enjoy stealth games, you owe it to yourself to give Styx a try.
Now, that said, the game is not perfect.  It is riddled with annoying bugs that crack the veneer and reveal that it is not the AAA title it appears to be.  But most of these are forgivable, and are only worth mentioning because the game is otherwise so excellent.
The one that has been dogging me through my entire playthrough is that for some reason, when you restore a saved game, you become momentarily hyper-visible, and enemies that did not see you originally will aggro.  Styx has no quicksave function (attention developer: please add one in the sequel due out this year), so the player often finds himself saving the slow way in dangerous circumstances to make sure their progress is preserved.  Dangerous situations often become deadly for no reason upon restore.
This sort of AI instability is fairly common, with enemies sometimes bugging out and going catatonic or walking in circles or catching sight of you through a wall, but it is not so common as to be gamebreaking, and if the occasional error is the price to pay for such genreally excellent AI I will pay it.  Styx is a mean game.  If you try to fall back on your bad habits from Metal Gear Solid or Splinter Cell, Styx will punish you over and over again until you learn.
My one serious complaint with the game is the ability unlocking system.  The abilities in the game range from the absolutely mandatory to the completely irrelevant, and you don't start with any of them.  You can't unlock any abilities until you've finished the first mission, which consists of three zones each of which would be a level in and of itself in any other game.
This process repeats itself for every mission, each of which is three or four massive zones long.  Although there are eight missions (the game is enormous), the length of each mission makes it feel like you never have an opportunity to experiment with abilities.  You can return to the hideout, where you purchase abilities, at any time, but doing so resets your mission progress.
On the one hand, it is nice that the game does not lock you into your ability choices -- you can unlearn them and learn new ones at the hideout -- but on the other the game does not give you a surplus of ability points.  You only get what you need and only if you complete all primary and secondary goals in a mission.
Ultimately the ability system is a complete failure -- a lot of the abilities the player should have access to from the beginning, like drop kills and cover kills; others are just irrelevant or actually non-functional, like powers that silence falls and loud kills but don't actually make them quiet enough to not be heard.  Fortunately, as with most stealth games, the real challenge is in not using these abilities and making your way without them.
If I sound critical it is because I have that luxury due to the quality of Styx as an overall experience.  Again, if you enjoy stealth gameplay, this is a must buy.  Pick it up.  Not even the standard-issue terrible final boss encounter can ruin it.

This complements how overpowered you are as a Space Marine, as the ridiculousness of the encounters still requires you to play smart and use your ammo wisely but feel as glorious as the fluff any fan has read about a handful of Space Marines taking on impossible odds and surviving.
Perhaps the only truly disappointing thing is that there will not be a continuation of this story, as it follows the established universe well and utilises the terminology correctly to make even the most cynical fan relax and enjoy the games story. The Warhammer 40k universe sorely needs games like Warhammer 40k: Space Marine, in a time when there are so few strong Warhammer 40k titles available.

I decided to rewrite this review from Scratch, as the edits were getting confusing to weed through.
Interstellar Rift is a Space Ship Simulator played from a largely 1st Person perspective in what is intended to be a online enviroment (although you can play it solo without internet). If you've played Pulsar it's similiar to that except that instead of entirely co-op gameplay this universe has a PvPvE dynamic. Your ship can be attacked at any time if it's not stored (including when your offline) and other players may hack or otherwise disable your ship through gameplay mechanics.
This is a game where teamwork is very much encouraged; Anything you can do solo in this game you can do much better with 2 or 3 people working on the same ship for different tasks. Unfortunately as it is Early Access the game's online populace is quite sparse and can vary quite a bit depending on server and time of day.
Let me say this: Solo play CAN do everything in this game, but it may not be the most efficent - and in a universe where other players can and will band together to destroy your ship or ruin your day, you are forced (in an online enviroment) to either be very cautious or learn alot of lessons the hard way - with the destruction of one of your ships.
In Interstellar Rift, you can own any amount of space ships, and even assemble fleet's and crew's from Real Players (not NPCs).
The best thing about Interstellar Rift is that it tends to be a very rewarding experience when you finish a task - but this also means that the task in question will not often come without due sacrifice and diligence.
In Interstellar Rift there are materials that you will be required to collect and manage for the construction, operation, and battle of your ships. Ammo is literally on a ship-based loading mechanism, that a crew member must manually feed ammo when you run out. Ammo is far from the only operational resource however, for any ship that you want to survive on for any length of time will need Oxygen pumped through it's life support systems, and although you could choose to design an entirely Solar Powered Ship it is much cheaper and more effective to build a ship that requires fuel to run it's electrical grid (fuel is hydrogen in most cases).
Rifts in Interstellar Rift are wormholes between star systems, and they are both artifically generatable and naturally occuring (although rarely). Inner-System Flight is handled mostly by Warp Drive Mechanics, and Ship "Operations" like - say Combat, or Mining, or teleporting are done in a state of "Sublight" Movement (or stillness as the case may be). There are some unique caveats to Warp Drive that make it difficult to manage maximum warp but entirely possible if you know how to do it.
Planets in IsR are not "landable" so don't be upset when you can't set foot on dry land. That Said, there are plenty of places in space where you can use your feet to get around.
The Tutorial - This is one of the things that's under massive construction - if you need step-by-step instructions - the game isn't ready for you - yet. If your good at winging it and figuring things out on your own no matter the consequences then welcome aboard. This WILL change in due time but for now the game is a learning experience both to new and old alike. The Devs have promised to refine the somewhat Vague existing tutorials to explain more detailed concepts however there is a rudementry tutorial already in place. In all honesty the tutorial is very very basic in the current form but it is being discussed actively in the forums and is a known topic for improvements.
Early Access - Yes Interstellar Rift is Early Access, but before you go shoving it off just because of that, allow me to inform you it is not "fresh" Early Access - infact in the last year alone it has made great strides with patches biweekly and rarely delayed. Each "Major" Patch brings with it new content. experiences and mechanics, but there are often several "Hotfix" patches to each Major Patch to fix immediately known issues.
The Developers are engaging and open to criticism be it good or bad. They may be a small team - but who isn't in modern gaming industries? They take such pride in their work they often pop on the Official Server to play a bit of their own game on their off hours; what kind of dev does that anymore? My Point is these people are dedicated to making their game the best thing since Hotsauce.
If you don't like Bugs then granted this is by that definition an Early Access Title in full, but these bugs are often not gamebreaking nor are they particularly inexcusable. (most bugs can be fixed with a simple relog at most).
A Recent set of patches just introduced FPS-style weaponry into the Main Branch; and if I do say so myself it is rather well done. You can't be "Ganked" on starter stations, but once you leave into the big bad galaxy your vunerable anywhere else. Of course to FPS you most of the time they need to hack your access first (unless your on an away mission on a 3rd party non-starter station).
In addition to FPS "Player-VS-Player" Combat - you may also elect to repair or destroy individual devices on ships that you board (and randomly for ships that you attack with ship-based weapons); Repairs are currently handled in 3 ways: "Buy" Repairs from a station with a store-o-tron (all starter stations have these - and several nonstarter stations may have them as well), Use Repair Drones you launch out your disposer along with iron to repair the ship from outside, or the handheld repair gun which can only repair interior objects (naturally) and does not really help with hull damage.
Missiles are live on the experimental branch and are looking to be formally installed in the game within the week or so. Missiles are NOT ultimate weapons, they can be shot down in flight and while they pack quite the punch they tend to be slow and have difficulty seeking at extremely close range.
One thing that you might not expect is that this game actually has two types of drones: One for Repair and one for Attacking Ships; The Repair Drones Require Iron but the "turret" drones just require to be deployed by a disposer; Turret Drones can be accessed remotely where they can then be commanded to attack specific targets and/or attack all non-fleet members who wander into range of their weapons (~2-3km)
One thing is certain - if you would dare to adventure - then Interstellar Rift has a place you can find a unique blend of Comradere and Peril - mostly due to the influence of other living breathing people.
Although anyone can Captain a ship in IsR - only a Skllled leader with a dedicated crew by his side can overcome any challenge the void may throw your way.
This is a game where patience, peril, and fun are the key cornerstones of the gameplay.
As for those who read my prior edit about my ships getting deleted - I've gotten over it; I played on that server for over a year without losing my character - and even when I thought my ships were destroyed in bugs they always came back; Unfortunately a mandatory server reset claimed all my progress (but it also equalized the playing field).

I've clocked about 34 hours with this game at the time of my writing this and have gotten through a fair portion of Chapter 3, so I think it's fairly safe to say that I've formed a solid enough opinion. Simply put, Blackguards turned out to be a rare gem and has already, surprisingly, found its way to my personal list of all time favorites. A few minor glitches aside, it's a lovely blend of dark fantasy storytelling, challenging tactical combat, and flexible charachter development that so far hasn't failed to delight. And it looks quite attractive to boot, with a fantastic UI and lovingly crafted imagery.
The cast of lovable rogues that comprise your party is well acted and well written. The story as a whole, at least so far, is engaging without being overbearing, maintaining a light touch while never failing to be consistently interesting. It ain't Shakespeare, but it never aspires to be. Instead, it accomplishes exactly what the early hours of the game promise: it is  a damned enjoyable caper of a kind that perhaps we need more of in the world, a slice of true, unabashed, adventure escapism that somehow evokes the simpler, formative days of a young nerd's nerddom. The subject matter is often dark, but it always feels like an exciting journey above all else. And sometimes that's more than enough to make something worth one's time.
While I am sure it's not for everyone, players who enjoy tactical combat, roleplaying games, and being entertained can find plenty to love here.

This is a difficult review to write because I feel rather conflicted about the game at the moment. Ultimately it comes down to the question, "Do I recommend Finding Paradise?"
...................Yes. Very reluctantly, yes.
First and foremost, Finding Paradise is every bit a sequel to To The Moon. While the game stands on its own, it is a continuing story and you will be doing yourself a disservice by jumping into the series anywhere but the beginning.
The game is very much like its predecessor in formula and presentation. Having played the first one recently, it feels like I've barely even left and have started up on the next chapter. If you want more of the same, that is exactly what you can expect.
........with one exception, unfortunately. Unlike the first game, the core subject matter of this one is, in a word, silly. It is very difficult to relate to the plight of the central character, and while it is presented with every bit as much sentimentality and poignancy as the first game, the lack of relatability and gravity makes it fall emotionally flat. It almost feels as if the author wanted a huge plot twist more than he wanted a relatable story, and that's just what we're left with.
The writing still has quite a lot of wit, charm and touches of humor, and combined with the excellent soundtrack, made this an overall enjoyable experience.
I do very much look forward to the continuation of this series.
